FOREWORD
Mary Christina Wood1
We have thrown the planet we inhabit violently out of balance. Humanity’s
disregard for nature’s laws glares through razed forests, vanished species,
acidified oceans, polluted rivers, and cascading climate catastrophes. The
annihilatory trajectory of industrial civilization over the last seventy years
threatens to trigger Earth’s sixth mass extinction—the kind that has not
occurred since the death of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago. Should the
assaults persist even for a few more years, future humanity and other species
for untold generations will face a hellish struggle to survive while pummeled
by floods, hurricanes, heat waves, fires, disease, crop losses, food shortages,
drought, and sea level rise. In The Bridge at the Edge of the World, Gus
Speth puts it simply: “[W]e’re headed toward a ruined planet.”2 And time is
not on our side to reverse course. With greenhouse gases flooding the
planet’s atmosphere, we face an urgency in which to act before crossing
climate tripwires poised to send the planet into a state of runaway heating.
So, here we are. We are the granules of sand falling through a minute glass
between two worlds — our past world in which nature supported life in
infinite ways, and a potential hellish world ahead filled with global chaos and
devastation leading to humanity’s own self-destruction. One may reasonably
ask: Where is environmental law in this apocalyptic picture?
Environmental law helped deliver this ecological emergency to our planet’s
doorstep.
The Failure of Environmental Law
In the United States, statutes passed five decades ago were supposed to

reverse the arc of destruction that was obvious even then. The U.S. Congress
passed the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act,
the Toxic Substances Control Act, and a multitude of other laws to prohibit
environmental harm. This legal model was considered so promising that
countries throughout the world emulated it in their legal systems. A
burgeoning set of bureaucracies gained authority and funding to carry out the
laws. Yet, as agencies became captured by politically powerful interests, the
system as a whole degenerated into a monumental failure. The dysfunction
now operates on a dangerous, systemic, global level.
Statutes characteristically vest agencies with breathtaking authority and
discretion to issue permits allowing the very harms that the laws were
designed to prevent. If the agencies were intent on protecting ecosystems and
the public in carrying out the laws, they would use their authority to prevent
damage. But instead, with few exceptions, agencies operate in alliance with
politically powerful corporations and profiteers, using the permit system to
legalize massive destruction in the form of oil and gas drilling, coal mining,
toxic water pollution, forest clearcutting, habitat eradication, and other
injuries too numerous to inventory. Today, rather than organizing an
emergency response to an existential climate threat, environmental agencies
push the destruction even more, bringing the world to the edge of the climate
precipice. Elizabeth Kolbert says, “It may seem impossible to imagine that a
technologically advanced society could choose, in essence, to destroy itself,
but that is what we are now in the process of doing.”3 Environmental law
now serves as the cane on which humanity leans as it walks the plank toward
its own destruction.
The Judicial Role in Climate Emergency
In the United States, the President holds power never contemplated by the
Founders — the power to push America, other countries, and a vast part of
the natural creation over the climate cliff. In this time of extreme climate
danger — when the Secretary-General of the United Nations implores nations
to slash carbon emissions 45% by 2030 to avert runaway planetary heating4
that would leave Earth largely uninhabitable5—President Trump uses his
agencies’ statutory authority under environmental laws to promote massive
domestic fossil fuel development, consumption, and exportation. The United

States has expanded oil and gas production four times faster than any other
nation and now leads the world in both.6 Environmental law is affirmatively
legalizing these actions.
In 2009, President Obama’s science advisor warned that the climate situation
was like being “in a car with bad brakes driving towards a cliff in the fog.”7
President Trump, showing frenzied intent, now floors the accelerator with the
world’s children, future generations, and other species on Earth trapped in the
back seat. The 16-year old climate revolutionary Greta Thunberg implores,
“Pull the emergency brake.”8
Courts have authority to do just that through their powers of injunctive and
declaratory relief. As the third constitutional branch of government, the core
duty of the judiciary is to protect fundamental rights. In the landmark case,
Juliana v. United States,9 21 American youth ask the courts to step into the
climate emergency before it is too late to save their prospects of future
survival and well-being. Challenging the entire system of federal fossil fuel
policy as violating their Constitutional rights to life, liberty and property
under the Due Process Clause and the venerable Public Trust Principle,10 the
young plaintiffs seek a court-supervised federal plan to shrink the nation’s
carbon footprint at a rate necessary to stave off disastrous levels of climate
change. The youth won a landmark victory in the District Court of Oregon in
2016 when Judge Ann Aiken ruled that plaintiffs had a constitutional right to
a “climate system capable of sustaining human life.”11 But an ensuing
appellate opinion bears the marks of environmental law’s Dark Ages.
On review, two judges of a three-judge Ninth Circuit panel acknowledged
that the U.S. government’s fossil fuel policies present a threat capable of
destroying the nation, but said that courts can do nothing about it.12 Quoting
the song, “Eve of Destruction,” Judge Andrew Hurwitz (writing for himself
and Judge Mary Murguia) decided that the courts have no role in stopping the
government from hastening an “environmental apocalypse” — one capable of
burying cities, unleashing life-threatening disasters, and jeopardizing crucial
food and water sources. Judges Hurwitz and Murguia did not refute that the
young plaintiffs hold constitutional rights to a stable climate system. They
observed that atmospheric carbon levels have “skyrocketed to levels not seen
for almost three million years,” and emphasized the crisis is “approaching the

‘point of no return.’ ” They recognized that the growth of U.S. fossil fuel
development “shows no signs of abating” in spite of government’s
longstanding knowledge that carbon dioxide emissions can cause
“catastrophic climate change.” Yet, in face of these surreal prospects, Judges
Hurwitz and Murguia “reluctantly” concluded that courts have no role in
putting brakes on the federal government’s fossil fuel scheme. They said that
climate policy is a matter for the legislative and executive branches—the
same branches that created this climate cataclysm. The young plaintiffs have
appealed to the full Ninth Circuit asking for en banc review by the full panel
of 11 judges.
When a fundamental right has no remedy, there is no justice. The majority’s
Juliana opinion embraces a judicial approach that Professor Douglas Kysar
and James Weaver call judicial “nihilism”—rejecting their extensive power,
the courts “cower before catastrophe.”13 This judicial timorousness has been
the pattern over the past few decades as judges have repeatedly analyzed
ecological harms through the narrow lens of statutory claims and have
reflexively deferred to the agencies on the grounds that they alone hold the
expertise necessary to carry out the public interest. As obeisance to the
political branches grew, the courts, which had sometimes courageously acted
in areas of civil rights, abdicated their constitutional role as the guardian of
fundamental rights with respect to the environment despite acknowledging
clear and present danger of a climate apocalypse.
Still brave voices stir in the judicial branch. In a scholarly and poignant
dissent to the majority’s Juliana opinion, Judge Josephine Staton countered:
“It is as if an asteroid were barreling toward Earth and the government
decided to shut down our only defenses. [T]he government bluntly insists that
it has the absolute and unreviewable power to destroy the Nation. My
colleagues throw up their hands, concluding that this case presents nothing fit
for the Judiciary.” Delving deeply into the purpose and structure of the U.S.
Constitution, she found an embedded “perpetuity principle” obliging courts
to prevent the other branches from bringing the nation to its demise. In face
of “an existential crisis to the country’s perpetuity,” Judge Staton’s opinion
forcefully challenges judges in the United States and elsewhere to choose a
side of history: “When the seas envelop our coastal cities, fires and droughts
haunt our interiors, and storms ravage everything between, those remaining

will ask: Why did so many do so little?”
The Paradigm Shift
Law mediates the struggle between power unjustly wielded and moral truth.
It is a system that defines reasonable outcomes. The searing reality of our
moment will cause judges around the world to redefine their roles. As they
do, one thing is clear: legal reform cannot tinker around the edges of the
failed regime of statutory environmental law and practice. That regime lacks
ideas truly calibrated to the magnitude of the problem and the roaring pace of
change. At this late date, tweaking the law becomes a fool’s errand by
throwing out a rescue rope that is too short. Even if there were time to
accomplish massive regulatory reform, the system as a whole is
dysfunctional. The entire paradigm of ecological responsibility must change,
and the power of governance must recalibrate before environmental tyranny
takes permanent hold. Courts remain singularly positioned, through their
constitutionally vested authority, to rein in government actors and redirect
them to protect fundamental rights.
A new legal paradigm must be articulated, examined, rigorously critiqued,
and proposed. Then, positioned at the edges of the old destructive regime, it
must impart the inspiration needed to animate key moments of
transformation, drawing law into the epochal task of restoring vital ecology.
Earth Law: Emerging Ecocentric Law—A Guide for Practitioners (Earth
Law) pulls together the most promising jurisprudential and legal approaches
world-wide aimed at harmonizing human existence with the natural world. It
is a must-read for judges, lawyers, and students who not only want to
understand, but also respond meaningfully to the central challenge of their
fleeting moment in history. As is often said, we are the first generation to
understand the impending cataclysmic consequences of our mode of
development, and we are the last generation that will be able to do anything
about it. Lawyers, through their advocacy, skill, and position in society, hold
unparalleled potential to build new governance structures and operating rules.
New ideas remain paramount to this epic endeavor. We need, as Gus Speth
says, a “fresh conceptualization and a new way of thinking.…”14 Ecological
paradigms will present a vision of co-responsibility and reciprocity among
nations, societies, corporations, and nature, and robust and practical legal

footholds by which citizens can hold government officials and members of
society accountable. New values will power a global assertion of rights and
duties in defense of humanity, fellow species, and all future generations of
life on Earth.
This book gathers, distills, and analyzes pioneering approaches in law — for
the Earth and for our time. It is an assemblage of approaches, not a system.
Earth Law takes the reader around the world, from the Colombia Supreme
Court which recognized bio-cultural constitutional rights of Atrato Basin
communities in their battle against toxic mining; to India’s Supreme Court
which announced a right of glaciers to exist; to the Federal District Court of
Oregon (presiding over Juliana v. United States) where Judge Ann Aiken
declared for the first time in U.S. history an American environmental
constitutional right to a “climate system capable of sustaining human life;”
and to the Washington Court of Appeals in the United States where a panel of
judges found that Ken Ward has a constitutional right to assert the “necessity
defense” to justify his peaceful climate civil disobedience when he illegally
entered a Kinder Morgan pipeline facility and shut down tar sands oil
entering the United States. Compiling a multitude of other cases as well as
recent statutes, Earth Law anchors these innovative approaches in the shared
human experience and transcendental ecological reality of our times. This is a
textbook about ideas and what is possible; it cannot help but inspire and
guide present and future practitioners.
If there is hope that law will respond to the environmental crisis, it is a hope
lodged in a diversity of ideas, realizing that one singular solution does not
hold all of the answers. All over the world, judges, legislators, lawyers, and
citizens are pioneering new concepts and tools adapted to vastly different
bioregions, cultures, and societies. The widely varying approaches presented
in this book share four unifying themes that provide common ground for a
truly global legal revolution.
Nature’s Supreme Laws
All of the approaches recognize the need for recalibrating industrialized laws
to the laws of nature. Indigenous leaders have taught since time immemorial
that Nature’s own laws rank supreme over human laws. Oren Lyons puts it
this way: “The thing you have to understand about nature and natural law is,

there’s no mercy…There’s only law.…”15 In one fundamental respect, the
most basic task of environmental law is to bring society into compliance with
these laws of nature. But industrialized environmental law legalizes the
rampant violation of these supreme laws not only at the level of individual
species and ecosystems, but also at the level of atmospheric function, ocean
health, and biodiversity — a truly planetary level. As Thomas Berry wrote,
Only a self-destructive arrogance would enable a society to assume the rights
to devastate what nature could bring into being but which no power in heaven
or on Earth, not even nature herself, could remedy once destruction had taken
place.…
…We need legal structures and political establishments that will know that
our way into the future is not through relentless industrial development but
through the living forces that brought us into being and are the only forces
that can sustain us in the coming centuries.16
Fundamental Rights
Earth law, as it continues to develop, will redefine and reorient environmental
law as a realm of fundamental rights. These include human rights, civil
rights, rights of dignity, biocultural rights of communities, rights to assert the
necessity defense in climate civil disobedience cases, rights of nature (such as
those increasingly accorded to rivers and wildlife), animal and non-human
rights, and rights of present and future generations under the public trust
principle to force government protection of the crucial resources supporting
all life on Earth. Underlying all of these approaches is a basic reframing of
environmental law to pull it out of the narrow confinements of current
statutory provisions and connect it to a deeper and more legally forceful set
of rights engrained (implicitly or explicitly) in constitutional frameworks.
This necessarily involves reformulation of legal assumptions that drive the
law—above all those concerning property concepts. An entire body of
Western law has developed around the assumption that nature belongs to
humans and they are entitled to exploit, subjugate, and destroy its gifts and
vitality. As Thomas Berry wrote, “This mechanistic world controlled by
humans, for human advantage, saw the surrounding world as a vast assembly
of natural resources put there for human use, not as manifestation of the

sacred and sublime to be experienced in the wonder of its mountains and
oceans, in the beauty of its meadows and birds and woodland creatures, in its
healing of the loneliness of the human soul and the ills of the human body.”17
Earth Law brings to the forefront leading cases, such as the Colombia
Supreme Court’s Atrato River decision, which recognizes and invokes, after
centuries of suppression, indigenous conceptions and instructions regarding
nature. Earth Law also reports on “ecocide,” which reverses the notion that
nature is here for human use, even to the point of destruction, by
criminalizing the eradication of nature.
Recalibrating Governance
Earth Law illuminates ways of recalibrating governance. Judicial authority is
needed to break the power held by fortune and corruption, exercised with the
support of legislative and executive branches through statutory laws
permitting the devastation of air, oceans, forests, fisheries, wildlife, rivers,
aquifers, lands, and countless human communities — or by statutory
omission and permissive nonenforcement of laws that would prevent such
devastation. The Netherlands Supreme Court is leading the way by ordering
its government to reduce CO2 emissions by 25% as compared with 1990
levels by the end of 2020.18 In Pakistan, the High Court of Lahore created a
climate commission. In Colombia, the court created a system of guardianship,
supported by advisory commissions and expert panels, to protect the Atrato
River.
When courts fail to create meaningful remedies to protect fundament rights,
their passivity implicates them by omission in violations of rights they could
prevent. As Douglas Kysar and Jim Weaver emphasize, “inaction can inflict a
symmetric violence.”19 Judges must not allow the other branches of
government to manipulate their constitutional and statutory powers to
become environmental despots and bring the world to the “eve of
destruction”…and beyond. Further, the public and conscientious legislators
and administrators must not allow this. Earth Law provides examples of
where constructive action is being taken and proposes ideas and principles in
furtherance of ecocentric environmental governance.
Inspiring Transformation

Earth Law positions the law in the broader context of society, philosophy,
and history, which it must do to provide any true reform. Law is a powerful
organizing force in human society for better or worse. As Oliver Wendell
Holmes famously wrote: “The law is the witness and external deposit of our
moral life. Its history is the history of the moral development of the race.”20
When the law feels untrue to our deepest sense of justice, it stings our
collective soul and presses us towards reform.
As sentinels of the legal system, lawyers, judges, and lawmakers must take
care to not quash the righteous sense of the citizens, but instead continually
inspire and empower them to pursue justice. If these sentinels fail to attend to
that spark of justice, they imperil democracy by dispensing despair,
defeatism, and disempowerment—the breeding grounds of oppression and
tyranny. The judicial system in the United States teeters precariously close to
that point, such as in the Juliana Ninth Circuit majority’s opinion in which
two judges found there was no conceivable judicial remedy in face of an
apocalyptic future directly propelled by the young plaintiffs’ own
government. As the dissenting Judge Staton wrote, “Where is the hope in
today’s decision? Plaintiffs’ claims are based on science, specifically, an
impending point of no return. If plaintiffs’ fears, backed by the government’s
own studies prove true, history will not judge us kindly.” By presenting cases
in which courageous judges worldwide are developing jurisprudence to steer
the world to safety and justice, Earth Law kindles the democratic impulse
needed to bring new paradigms to fruition.
Earth Law throughout its pages invites practitioners and students as future
practitioners to co-create this field using the resources it offers. It calls out to
those resolute judges, lawyers, lawmakers, students, and citizens across the
planet who refuse to relinquish their collective moment in time. This book
will guide us all—as Earth’s citizens—inclaiming this moment to stop the
onslaught on Mother Earth and work with her to preserve a habitable planet
for present and future generations of all species.
Earth Law comes to the world not a moment too soon.

INTRODUCTION
The Emergence of Ecocentric Law
and Ideas for the Future
of Environmental Law
Earth law is the body of law for protecting, restoring, and stabilizing the
functional interdependency of Earth’s life and life-support systems at the
local, bioregional, national, and global levels. Earth law may be expressed in
constitutional, statutory, common law, and customary law, as well as in
treaties and other agreements both public and private.
The year 2020, the date of the first publication of this coursebook, is the 50th
anniversary of the modern environmental movement. On April 22, 1970, 20
million people participated in the first Earth Day, and in that same year the
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency came into being and the U.S. Clean
Air Act was enacted. There followed myriad environmental laws and
environmental protection agencies in countries around the world, as well as
international environmental agreements. These developments were meant to
halt the decline of the global environment. Yet, in 2008, James Gustave
(“Gus”) Speth, cofounder of the National Resources Defense Council and a
leading advocate for the international environmental movement, sadly
concluded:
The environmental movement has grown in strength and sophistication, but
the environment has continued to deteriorate.…How serious is the threat…?
[A]ll we have to do to destroy the planet’s climate and biota and leave a
ruined world to our children and grandchildren is to keep doing exactly what
we are doing today.…But, of course, human activities are not holding at
current levels—they are accelerating, dramatically.”1
The situation has only grown worse since he penned these words.

This is a book for students and practicing lawyers who seek to preserve a
habitable planet and question whether current environmental law is enough
for the task. It is for students and lawyers who want to move beyond “exactly
what we are doing today.” They know nature and human environmental
rights need to have seats at the table of law—in courts, legislatures, and
administrative bodies.
Earth law is the emerging field of ecocentric environmental law that puts
nature front and center. As described in this book, there are recently
developed laws that do this and there will be more such laws because nature
is putting herself front and center through climate change, dying coral reefs,
sea level rise, stronger storms, forest fires, plastic and other pollution, water
shortages, extinction of species, and many other ways. Humans are
increasingly realizing nature counts, her bounty is not inexhaustible, and
humans have duties to protect and restore her and develop sustainable,
mutually enhancing relations with her.
It takes imagination and spirit to be an Earth lawyer. Can you imagine a
world where a gorilla can sue a zoo? Where whales can sue for lack of krill?
Where children can claim the right to a habitable planet? Where rivers are
given legal personhood? Where all ecosystems have legal guardians? Where
constitutions recognize and protect the rights of nature? Where governments
maintain the resource base of society as a fundamental obligation? Where
humans have legal obligations to maintain the health of soil? Where there are
ecological courts? Where care for the health of the Earth community is a
primary objective of law?
EARTH LAW WILL BE DEVELOPED IN
PRACTICE
The subtitle of this book is “a guide for practitioners.” As much as an
educational foundation, this book is intended to serve as a guide for lawyers
who, through their practices, will develop Earth law. Representing the Earth’s
interests doesn’t fit the legal system as we know it. This book intends to give
students some basic understanding of issues they will face in trying to pound
a round peg into a square hole. Part of Earth law concerns pedagogy. Earth

lawyers will not only be advocates; they will be teachers. This is not unusual
in the practice of law. Educating judges, juries, legislators, and administrative
decision-makers is a critical aspect of client representation. The educational
burden is greater for Earth lawyers because there is little precedent for
representing the interests of nature in the ways that will be needed in the next
50 years.
The material presented in this book is intended to enable lawyers to practice
Earth law with realism and creativity. Many issues raised by the study of
Earth law will not have readily apparent answers. Judges, lawmakers,
policymakers, and others will find themselves engaged in a balancing of
interests that may seem impossible. There are innumerable factors,
interconnections, interrelations, and dynamics, many of which are unknown,
that will challenge the generally accepted linear mode of legal thinking.
While Earth lawyers must be constructive and work with their clients to
obtain results within the law, at times they may find it beneficial to advocate
legal positions for which there is no precedent when this yields opportunities
to ask more questions and critique more deeply the issues at hand. An entire
chapter of this book is devoted to conceptual frameworks to consider in the
practice of Earth law. It alerts Earth lawyers to issues they may face and
provides guidance for dealing with them.
Earth law is a developing body of both substantive and procedural law
reflecting new understandings of the Earth systems’ interdependencies and
dynamics. In the past 50 years, environmental law has addressed the negative
consequences of industrial development, including the destruction of nature
and natural systems, generation of toxic waste, and adverse human health
effects. While addressing the side effects, a primary objective of
environmental law, akin to occupational safety law, has been to promote
conventional industrial and commercial development by making it safer for
humans. Earth law seeks to make human endeavor safe for nature as well as
humans and for future generations of all species.
Since the inception of modern environmental law, new understandings have
been gained that require a reevaluation of legal and social norms, including
the following:
The extent of human impact on Earth is orders of magnitude greater than

anticipated;
The scope and scale of issues considered to be environmental issues
have vastly increased;
Knowledge of ecology, biology, geology, evolutionary dynamics, and
Earth systems is broader and deeper;
Perspectives on the nature–culture divide have changed with greater
awareness of how the human species is both a part of and the
exceptional agent in relation to nonhuman nature;
Understanding of sentience and consciousness in nonhuman animals has
grown;2
Scientific awareness of ecological limits, tipping points, and the
potential for irreversible decline and catastrophic state shifts in Earth’s
functioning has increased;
Climate change has emerged as a primary environmental concern; and
Issues of North–South relations and global inequities have come to the
fore.
The Anthropocene Working Group of the International Commission of
Stratigraphy has voted favorably on the question of whether the term
“Anthropocene” should be treated as a formal chronostratigraphic unit (a
strata of rock established to serve as the material reference for other
sediment).3
People have come to understand that nature is not merely something humans
live with or live from. Nature is something humans live within, and the
human species is but one of many interrelated and interdependent
components, all of which serve a purpose in the balance of biological life. A
global movement has arisen to address sustainability and care for the Earth. It
challenges the existing globalized system of economic development on which
people depend for water, food, clothing, shelter, energy, transportation, and
jobs.4 Current environmental law and practice have been unable to halt the
degradation of Earth’s life-support systems. Bringing Earth law into being
will require transformational changes in the law and social norms, and its
application will reflect and reinforce the increasingly urgent quests for human
sustainability and a healthy Earth community.
EARTH LAW TAKES AN ECOCENTRIC

APPROACH TO ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
Practicing Earth law will involve working with new ideas and ways of
thinking that are not currently recognized in the legal system. This book will
consider various proposals for making environmental law ecocentric. For
example, Earth law may expand the legal community by giving nature
juridical personhood and standing as a basis for adjudicating nature’s rights
and human obligations. Practicing Earth law will also require a strong
application of the precautionary principle.5 More broadly, Earth law
necessitates reexamining entire areas of the law, such as property law, which
currently treats all that is nonhuman as human property. It may be as
challenging to change this perspective as it was for abolitionists to change
laws treating slaves as property. Representing nature in courts, administrative
proceedings, legislative hearings, and other lawmaking processes will present
novel opportunities and obstacles. A nearly blank slate exists for determining
when and how nature should be represented, who should represent nature,
and how nature’s competing interests should be weighed. The roles of
science, social dynamics, tradition, human psychology, and ethics will
present strategic and tactical issues for Earth lawyers to consider.
Rights of nature, while only one approach to Earth law, is presently
prominent in the field. New legal rights may be legislatively created when
those seeking the rights challenge a social norm as, for example, with the
legislation of civil rights in the United States in the 1960s. New legal rights
may also be recognized by judicial declaration when it is perceived to be
necessary to better reflect the intent of laws as applied to changing
circumstances. Rights of nature will be examined in this context and will be
compared and contrasted with human rights. The examination of rights will
include basic questions about what a legal right is, the balancing of legally
recognized rights, the origin and evolution of property rights, and a critical
review of the achievements and setbacks from rights of nature litigation.
The legal corollary of rights—duties and responsibilities—will also be
examined. Despite humans’ dependency on the Earth’s ability to support
them, the law does not provide a structure to limit human behavior in a
manner that conforms to planetary boundaries.6 Where there is a right to
human life, there is a responsibility to act in a way that will support it. Earth

lawyers will define and enforce laws that establish human responsibilities for
the Earth community.
Earth law will develop within the current global economy. Along with the
promotion of ecological well-being, Earth law will encourage and enforce
limits on economic growth. Laws developed to sustain a habitable planet will
consider factors such as population growth, resource use, the allocation of
greenhouse gas sources and sinks, and aggregate limits on production and
consumption. In this context, the concept of equity will be considered both in
a fundamental sense, ensuring sufficiency for the poor, and in a relative
sense, providing for fair distribution of wealth and income among all people.
Applying Earth law will involve new systems of governance at all levels.
Effective enforcement of Earth law will depend on a widely held sense of
responsibility for the welfare of the planet and future generations, and the
acceptance of an obligation of care by all members of society. Since many of
the issues of Earth law cross national boundaries or apply to areas of Earth
such as oceans that are beyond national control, there will be a need for new
global institutions and conventions, and these new formations will need
support from nation-states and, within those states, from the executive,
legislative, and judicial branches.
Practicing Earth law involves working with new ideas and ways of thinking
that are not currently recognized in the legal system. This will involve a new
philosophical base, or jurisprudence, for law. Earth jurisprudence posits that
the welfare of humans, as members of the Earth community, is dependent on
the welfare of Earth as a whole and that the viability of human society
depends on its ability to regulate its members and its systems in a way that is
consistent with the physical, chemical, and biological functioning of Earth.7
In addition, Earth lawyers will need to understand Earth systems and
reciprocity. Reciprocity is inherent in the way Earth works. It occurs at many
scales, ranging from interactions among individual organisms to the Earth
system’s stabilizing feedback mechanisms among land, ocean, biosphere, and
atmosphere.
The ultimate goal of Earth law is to provide the laws and legal structures
needed for humans to live within planetary boundaries, prospectively care for
ecosystems, restore damaged ecosystems, and justly share the burdens of

mitigating and adapting to climate change and other environmental stresses.
Success will be measured, inter alia, by the effectiveness of strategies to
expand the protected legal community to include nonhuman nature and future
generations.
OVERVIEW OF THIS COURSEBOOK
This coursebook has been developed by the efforts of the Earth Law Center.
To produce the first coursebook on this subject, many academics, practicing
lawyers, law students, and others participated in researching, writing, editing,
cite-checking, and reviewing scores of ecocentric legal materials. Many of
the contributors are leaders in the field of Earth law and their contributions
reflect lessons learned through practice.
This coursebook has introductory material followed by five major sections:
Section I on “The Emergence of Earth Law,” Section II on “Addressing
Threshold Challenges,” Section III on “Litigation Strategies,” Section IV on
“Transforming the Law,” and Section V, “A Global Survey of Earth Law
Developments.” Each of these is summarized below. The coursebook ends
with an Afterword.
Section I: The Emergence of Earth Law
Earth law is more a response to a common set of environmental challenges
than it is a common body of law. Each response involves developing a legal
theory that goes beyond conventional environmental law. Chapter 1 gives a
brief history of conventional environmental law and a general critique of why
it is unable to respond to the current environmental challenges. Chapter 2
gives a history of the emergence of the diverse approaches to Earth law. As
well as being a response to a common set of environmental challenges, the
different approaches to Earth law are tied together by a relatively common set
of ideas. Chapter 3 deals with “The Conceptual Frameworks of Earth Law.”
These concepts are not only important to the history of Earth law but also to
its future development.
Section II: Addressing Threshold Challenges

In anthropocentric environmental law, human needs are given priority.
Ecocentric environmental law also gives a high priority to human needs but
considers thinking that human needs and the needs of nature can be separated
is a fallacy. Ecocentric law is holistic and organic. Thinking of nature only as
being composed of parts (including the human parts) is, for ecocentric law,
like considering whether the heart or the brain is the most important organ in
the human organism. Each aspect of the body and the interdependencies and
dynamics of the body need to be considered. In terms of health, each has
“standing,” or a recognized position or status. The threshold challenges for
Earth law involve how the various aspects and dynamics of nature gain
standing or are taken into account in the human legal system. The first issue
deals with the idea that nature belongs to the owner of the property that the
nature occupies. This is addressed in Chapter 4. Another issue concerns the
way the concept of legal standing operates to prevent nature from being
represented in law in its own right. This is addressed in Chapter 5. The final
threshold challenge is who speaks for, or who represents, nature in the legal
system and who ensures or guards its rights. This is addressed in Chapter 6.
Section III: Litigation Strategies
Litigation is an important tool for extending the reach of the law, and this is
what Earth law is about: extending the reach of the law to grant protections to
nature. In Section III, various legal strategies for extending the law to protect
nature are given: Chapter 7—“The Public Trust Doctrine”; “Chapter 8—“The
Rights of Future Generations”; Chapter 9—“The Rights of Nature in the
United States”; Chapter 10—“Co-Violations: Human Rights and the Rights
of Nature”; Chapter 11—“Nonhuman Rights”; Chapter 12—“Ecocide”; and
Chapter 13—“The Climate Necessity Defense.”
Section IV: Transforming the Law
The reach of law may also be extended by changing the laws themselves, the
procedures for litigating disputes, and the ethics and modes of legal practice.
An idea advanced in this book is that the current practice in Western law of
adversarial representation of a client’s interest is narrowly defined by the
legal system as well as by the adversaries and is often principally defined (in
economic terms). Treating anything that is not “against the law” as

acceptable, such as pollution allowed by government permit, is unsuitable for
Earth law. Transforming the law for Earth law purposes means inculcating in
the legal system, and also in the larger society, richer senses of the commons,
of rights, and of duties. Earth law begins with the propositions that we are all
in this together and we share a global commons, so we must work together in
mutually beneficial ways for the sake of present and future generations.
Section IV covers transforming the law from three vantage points: Chapter 14
—“Through the Eyes of a Bear: Integrating Ethics into Wildlife Law”;
Chapter 15—“The United Nations Sustainable Development Initiatives”; and
Chapter 16—“Ecocentric Environmental Governance.”
Section V: A Global Survey of Earth Law Developments
Chapters 17 through 25 cover developments in Earth law in different
jurisdictions around the world. The exception is Chapter 25 on “Indigenous
Legalities,” which deals with groups of people in various nations who have
continuous traditions and lifeways that predate the time of the West’s
colonial expansion. Indigenous laws and belief systems that have existed for
millennia are a major source of guidance for Earth law. Many believe that
turning to Indigenous wisdom is one of the most important sources for
developing Earth law.
AFTERWORD: THE FUTURE OF EARTH LAW
Earth law, or ecocentric environmental law, is a new field. What exists now is
just a beginning. Earth law is coming into being and will always be coming
into being because it needs to be as dynamic and responsive as nature herself.
Students and practitioners who study this coursebook will create and enforce
Earth law through their practices.
Let’s get started.
