CHAPTER 2
The Origins of Earth Law1
I. INTRODUCTION
This chapter continues the history of environmental law given in Chapter 1
by discussing the origins of Earth law. Before beginning, it might be helpful
to restate the working definition of Earth law given in the introduction to this
book:
Earth law is the emerging body of law for protecting, restoring, and
stabilizing the functional interdependency of Earth’s life and life-support
systems at the local, bioregional, national, and global levels. Earth law may
be expressed in constitutional, statutory, common law, and customary law, as
well as in treaties and other agreements both public and private.
It is also useful to restate that Earth law is both a departure from
environmental law and a new context for its extension. Earth law is a
departure from environmental law in that it covers matters simply not
covered in environmental law. Earth law’s philosophical presuppositions and
approach are so different that it can be thought of as a new body of law. Earth
law is a new context for the extension of environmental law in that many
functions of environmental law—such as conserving wild areas, penalizing
polluters, containing or restoring damaged ecosystems, and granting permits
for projects and activities—will continue, yet, in the Earth law context, the
way these functions will be carried out will change. As the transformation
occurs, Earth law and environmental law will not proceed along parallel
paths. Rather, transformed environmental law will become a part of Earth
law, though perhaps maintaining its identity as a subset of functions within
the larger category of Earth law.
Building on the foregoing, there are two things to understand about the

origins of Earth law: (1) the new context that is common to Earth law and
transformed environmental law; and (2) the departure from environmental
law, which consists of transitioning to Earth law approaches that diverge
from contemporary environmental law.
This chapter begins with the new context by discussing the movement from a
legal system based on separation between the human species and the rest of
the world to one based on interdependence, entanglement, and mutuality.
Then the chapter discusses the emerging approaches to Earth law covered in
this book, namely: (a) the public trust doctrine and atmospheric trust
litigation, (b) the rights of future generations, (c) the rights of nature, (d) co-
violations: human environmental rights and the rights of nature, (e)
nonhuman rights, (g) ecocide, (f) Indigenous legalities, (g) ecocentric
environmental governance, and (h) other approaches global and local.
II. THE NEW CONTEXT: FROM AN
ORIENTATION OF SEPARATION TO AN
ORIENTATION OF CONNECTION2
A. Why Environmental Law Falls Short
Although regulation of human relationships with their environments is an
enduring feature of history, “environmental law” is a definable set of laws
that came into being in the latter half of the twentieth century to remediate
urgent problems around the globe involving localized pollution of air, water,
and land. By the beginning of the twenty-first century, there was a broad
awareness that environmental threats went far beyond localized pollution, and
that they extended to the ways that human activities negatively affect the
biosphere as a whole through climate change, desertification, deforestation,
ocean acidification, habitat fragmentation, species extinctions, and many
other ways. Environmental policymakers at the national level failed to
respond to the systemic changes that were occurring and instead focused on
still more localized responses while taking care not to disadvantage business
activity in the increasingly competitive globalized economy. There was
environmental policymaking at the international level, as well, but it also

failed to respond to these systemic changes.3 What stands out from this
experience is that while environmental law has expanded, the large-scale
environmental problems facing the planet have grown worse.
The inability of environmental law to solve the problems is not because these
problems are unsolvable or intractable. Environmental law has failed because
it relies on a flawed orientation. Most environmental law wrongly, and
strangely, presumes that separation is the key to effective environmentalism.
Environmental law will succeed, and environmental problems will be solved,
only when this separation-based orientation is replaced with one based on
connection, entanglement, and mutuality—in other words, an orientation of
interdependence. The movement to the orientation of interdependence is at
the heart of Earth law.
B. The Orientation of Separation
Both the harm that humans have done to the environment and the efforts to
remedy or control those harms have been grounded in the presumption that
humans are separate from nature. This illusion of separation developed over a
long period of time. It began around 11,000 years ago at the end of the last
ice age and the beginning of the Holocene epoch. The climate became
favorable for agriculture involving crops and domesticated animals, and
agriculture-based societies emerged in various parts of the world. This has
been called the beginning of civilization—the first culture in civilization was
agriculture, and agriculture continued to be at the base of all societies until
the Industrial Revolution began about 250 years ago.
In agriculture-based societies, food became more abundant and reliable.
There were even food surpluses, meaning that not everyone needed to be
involved in food production. People could now live in villages, and later
larger communities, and divide labor. Writing began around 3,000 BCE.
While there were oral histories before this time, the beginning of writing has
been considered the beginning of history, because written records could be
kept. This was also the time classical civilizations began in the Middle East,
Egypt, the Indus Valley, and later, China and Latin America. Each of these
developments took humans further from the wild nature by which they had
been surrounded as hunter-gatherers. The human drama focused on the

relationship with nature. Increasingly, the drama shifted to relations with
other humans and building civilization and even empires. Nature could not be
taken for granted—there were droughts and floods and volcanic eruptions
and plagues—but the steadfast endurance of nature with all of its vicissitudes
began to be taken for granted by many.
In a period beginning around 800 BCE and ending around 300 BCE, the
Hebrew prophets, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Gautama Buddha, the Hindu
mystics, Confucius, Mencius, and Lao Tzu gave birth to the wisdom
traditions that undergirded the classical civilizations.4 The Jewish and
Christian religious traditions that followed this period included the idea of a
deity that entered into human history, bestowed special favor on humans, and
granted them dominion over nature. Only humans were made in the image of
God. This was another step in the separation of humans and nature.
Separation of a different kind and degree occurred in modernity beginning in
the sixteenth century. The science of Francis Bacon (1561–1626), Galileo
Galilei (1564–1642), and Isaac Newton (1643–1727) came to understand
nature as mechanisms. The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650)
separated the minds/souls of humans—which are unique to humans—from
their bodies and all of the rest of nature, which could be understood as
mechanisms.
The latter part of the eighteenth century brought the Industrial Revolution,
modern economics, democracy, and a burst of human freedoms and rights.
Modern science and the technologies of the Industrial Revolution gave
humans almost god-like powers. Over time, nature became a resource for
industrial development. Industrial development became the secular religion
and the prime obligation of Western nations.
Economics supplied the discourse of development with a focus on individual
initiative and accumulation of goods and capital. It explained that in the
economic marketplace, individuals make choices to maximize their own
personal welfare,5 not for the good of society or nature.6 When humans
engaged in resource-use decisions, they ignored social and environmental
values if the social consequences did not promote individual utility.7 This
behavior was not only seen as characteristic, but as normatively good, and

something to be harnessed for economic growth and efficient allocation of
goods and services.
Democracy and human rights also focused on individual initiative. Individual
choice, regardless of morality, was to determine the direction of society. It
was assumed that the good—largely defined as economic progress and an
increase in human welfare—would be the result of free expression of ideas
and preferences. Nature was to be the servant of humans, and now it was
increasingly under apparent human mastery and control. Nature in this sense
became a collection of objects to be used.
The post-World War II world produced yet another stage of separation, an
explosion in economic growth and technology, along with the globalization
of the economy and a Westernized materialistic culture. This period is called
the “Great Acceleration.”8 Since 1945:
The number of motor vehicles (cars, trucks, buses) worldwide increased
from 40 million to more than 1.3 billion;9
The human population more than tripled and currently stands at about
7.7 billion. The number of people living in cities increased from 700
million to more than 4 billion (more than 54 percent of the total);10
Plastic production increased from 2.3 million tons in 1950 to 448
million tons in 2015. Half the plastic ever produced has been produced
in the last 15 years and production is still increasing;11
Synthetic nitrogen production (mostly for fertilizer) rose from 4 million
tons annually to 85 million tons;12 and
75 percent of human-loading of the atmosphere with greenhouse gases
occurred—half in the last 30 years.13 Atmospheric CO2 concentrations
went from around 310 parts per million (ppm) to around 410 at the
beginning of 2020.14
Connections with nature for most of the world’s people has become more and
more tenuous.
C. The Orientation of Separation’s Effect on Environmental
Law

The orientation of separation led to numerous errors in perception and
thinking that carried over into environmental law. There was, for example,
the mythology of human exceptionalism—the belief that humans were
separate from nature and superior to it, and that nature existed for the benefit
of humans. There were also the mythologies of boundless resources15 and of
inexhaustible sinks.16 Until recently, people thought there could be localized
shortages of resources and sinks and localized pollution, but that on the large
scale of Earth as a whole, there were unlimited resources and sinks and
human pollution could only have minor effects. During the Industrial
Revolution and especially during the Great Acceleration, humans reached out
to tap Earth’s bounty on ever-larger scales.
There was also the mythology that Earth, which was understood as an
inorganic physical and material reality, provided the sustenance for life. This
is true to an extent, but complex life is dependent on other life, and not just
for food. The interactions of living organisms create the conditions for the
existence of complex life of which humans are a part. James Lovelock and
Lynn Margulis pioneered the idea that Earth’s inorganic and organic
components have evolved together as, and are, a single living system. This
theory, first called the Gaia theory and now called Earth systems science,
suggests that this living system has automatically controlled global
temperature, atmospheric content, ocean salinity, and other factors that
maintain its own habitability. In a phrase, “life maintains conditions suitable
for its own survival.” In this respect, the living system of Earth can be
thought of analogous to the workings of any individual organism that
regulates body temperature, blood salinity, etc. So, for instance, even though
the luminosity of the sun—the Earth’s heat source—has increased by about
30 percent since life began almost four billion years ago, the living system
has reacted as a whole to maintain temperatures at levels suitable for life.17
There are many other examples of how Earth as a living system adjusts itself
to maintain a dynamic homeostasis—i.e., to self-regulate. One example is
that life has maintained oxygen levels in the atmosphere at around 20 percent
for millennia.
A twist on the foregoing myth is that this living system, with the exception of

the human part of it, works autonomously to sustain itself. Therefore,
changes in the human part of it alone will restore the planetary conditions
conducive to complex life, including humans. This conclusion is not
warranted. The planetary system is interdependent and entangled. To restore
Earth means not only changing human activity, but also restoring all the
many plants, animals, and their life support systems that have operated
mutually to create the conditions in which human civilization has flourished.
These errors in thinking and perception carried over into environmental
policy and enforcement by separating what we humans now know—through
science—from what we do. This has led to environmental law based on an
orientation of separation that has not succeeded. Earth law has arisen from
the need to place environmental law on a new foundation—the orientation of
connection.
1. Separating what we know through science from what we do
The Industrial Revolution and its culmination in the Great Acceleration are a
triumph of science and technology. Science and technology, however, should
be distinguished. Science yields knowledge and theories of a wide scope, and
technology draws on parts of scientific knowledge that can be turned into
useful products, many of which give humans the ability to control large
aspects of the natural conditions in which they live. Environmental law has
taken a largely technological approach to the control of the environment.
Science from the sixteenth century to the late eighteenth century was
reductionistic and mechanistic. While such science continues today and gives
rise to new technology, a different, more connected and dynamic science
arose beginning in the late nineteenth century. This science encompasses
fields such as evolution, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, relativity,
quantum mechanics, physical cosmology, systems theory, chaos, complexity,
genetic coding, ecology, non-equilibrium dynamics, digital technology,
information science, and Earth systems science. Through science, we have
come to better know the beauty and elegance of the natural world, even of the
universe beyond Earth, and we have a deeper understanding of what it takes
for humans to live sustainably in the world.

Science has been restricted in the role it could play in policymaking.18
Science assesses how human alteration of nature affects human health and
welfare, then turns the data over to lawmakers who determine how that
information should be incorporated into a legal standard that is binding on
humans.19 Science is then used in calculating whether these standards have
been met and what the consequences of not meeting standards might be.20
There is much more that science can do. Science—through such fields as
biology, ecology, and Earth systems science—can inform a dynamic, holistic
approach to protecting the biosphere as applied through our legal and
economic systems. Environmental law typically supports pollutive activities
where the economic benefits outweigh the perceived ecological costs through
a traditional cost-benefit analysis (CBA). A dam project producing $20
million in annual revenue might receive a permit if that financial benefit is
perceived to outweigh the degradation of a river ecosystem. By contrast, a
science-based approach to policymaking favors activities that promote
ecological systems (of which humans are a part), and disfavors those that do
not. The same dam project might not receive a permit due to its negative
impact to functioning river systems and the ecosystems and species that rely
upon that system.
In the United States, in 2020 (the time of this writing), there has been
growing resistance to the use of science in environmental policy. Science that
provides economic benefit is readily accepted, but when science identifies
costs from such things as climate change, biodiversity loss, and exposure to
toxic substances it is not.21 Notably, scientists working through the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have determined that if
the present trajectory of CO2 emissions continues, the global mean surface
temperature will rise by 3.7 °C by the end of this century over the mean
average temperature for 1986–2005.22 The IPCC has specified targets that
must be met to avoid this result, yet there are no environmental policies in
place at the national level in the United States to meet these targets. Thus,
localized issues of pollution are addressed in environmental policy while the
greatest threat to the global environment is not.
2. Separating our communal and ecological selves from what we do

Humans know the world in part through science. In the West, the world
known by science, i.e., nature, is thought of as “out there”—it is something
waiting to be “discovered.” Even when science studies human bodies, it
studies them as objects. This idea of the world being composed of separate
parts extends throughout Western thought beyond science into economics,
politics, and the humanities, and into Western law as well. In the modern
period, the idea of a shared commons given by a creator God.…
was replaced by a humanist emphasis on the individual and human reason,
which resulted in a mechanistic legal vision.…
[There was] a transformation from commons-based folk legal institutions into
legally formalized, concentrated private property and eventually into capital.
Private ownership—individual dominion over land—became the most
important legal concept, dividing the whole into individualistic components.
The mechanism governing the relationship between these parts was found in
what became the sovereign state.23
Thus, the concept of the “rule of law” arose. Owners’ rights were to be
protected by “due process of law.” The law became proficient at protecting
individual rights but not collective rights. Customary law based on local
practices and customs gave way to “professionalized, common, and
potentially scientific” law.24 This orientation is reflected in the work of
Francis Bacon, the father of the scientific method, who was also Lord
Chancellor in England and contributed to rules of evidence and other changes
in civil procedure to make law more scientific.
These changes were a marked improvement, but they also had the effect of
furthering the separation of law from life. As discussed further in Chapter 25,
“Indigenous Legalities,” natural law for Indigenous people meant laws
derived from observation of the natural world. These laws are based on how
Earth maintains herself and help humans understand their role in the world.
These laws also pertain to relationships, describing how all beings are
connected to each other and must be respected for their roles.
Western law in the modern period developed from natural law in a different
sense. Western natural law was understood as a body of unchanging moral
principles existing independently of human understanding and positive law,

yet discernible to humans through reason. Modernity was understood in the
West as scientific, as Enlightenment, as the Age of Reason, and, thus, law
was reformed accordingly. As top-down legal order developed, the idea of a
single legal order within a jurisdiction took hold, and power became
centralized in the sovereign. Mechanical jurisprudence took hold—law was
to be applied with little interpretation.25
Gradually, Western jurisprudence moved away from its moorings in Western
natural law (with a notable exception in the area of human rights) to legal
positivism, which means the legal justification for a law is simply its
adoption in written form by the state. The law is what it says, and there is not
necessarily a connection between law and morality (or, in terms of Earth law,
ecology). Rather, the law is determined through a process of political
preferences and power relationships.
Western society’s embrace of this mechanistic approach to law is due in large
part to its service to the needs of capitalism, which transformed nature and
the commons to human property for the production of profit. The following
essential protections thus arose in Western law: (i) ownership as the right to
enjoy and dispose of property; (ii) contractual agreements to legally bind
parties as law; (iii) transfer of ownership regulated by consent of the parties;
(iv) the fault concept in tort law, which shields entrepreneurs from liability
for harm caused without fault; and (v) juridical personhood for legal entities,
which among other things shields investors from loss by making the entities
liable rather than the investors.26 The need for a mechanical, rule-based legal
system led to a highly complex system of law interpreted by private and
public legal professionals and inaccessible to others.
Thus, “just as taste, scent, color, and beauty [were] banned from scientific
inquiry [in modernity], so too were customs, ethics, values, justice, morals,
manners, and sentiments—everything that gives life to the law.”27
No doubt, this absence of life is one reason that aboriginal sensitivities are
being recovered in Western thought and, in particular, in Earth law. Contrast
the mechanistic, individualistic, ownership-based vision of community in
modernity with this account of the aboriginal vision in Australia:

So why didn’t aboriginal people parcel up their land? The answer has been
well rehearsed. It is that they saw, they see, the world very differently. In
Aboriginal cosmology this isn’t a volume or a surface with features, or a
space to be occupied by people. Instead it is a process of creation and re-
creation. The world, including people, but also what Europeans would think
of as topographical features, plants, animals, ritual sites, and ancestral beings,
are all necessary participants in a process of continuing creation. And if this
doesn’t happen then the world starts to hollow itself out. It stops existing.28
D. Environmental Law Based on the Orientation of Separation
Has Not Succeeded
Those who brought into being environmental law presumed, in accord with
the understandings of their time (one not so long in the past), that with the
use of utilitarian science, environmental laws could be fashioned that would
alter human behavior and environmental conditions to benefit near-term
human interests. Within this legal framework, humans could both continue to
exploit nature and “protect” the environment. They believed that
environmental law would give humans both the legal and natural power to
transform their natural surroundings within some limits to suit themselves.29
These environmental laws enacted to “protect the environment” have, in
reality, created a perverse dependence. People, believing in the efficacy of the
laws, have relied on them to address the problems. Corporations, so long as
they obeyed the laws, were thought to be compliant with “environmental
protection.” Science described the risks, policymakers wrote the laws based
on these assessments, and governments applied a top-down command-and-
control approach to modify human behavior. People did not rely on
themselves to take needed action; they relied on the law to protect them.
Environmental law based on the orientation of separation has not succeeded.
E. The New Context: The Orientation of Connection
For environmental law to succeed, it needs to operate out of the orientation of
connection, which is more fully stated as the orientation of connection,
entanglement, and mutuality. Doing so gives rise to Earth law, which, as

stated above, includes new bodies of law not presently covered by
environmental law, and a reformed environmental law, the functioning of
which is transformed by this new context. Some of these bodies of law are
discussed in the subsequent section and then explored in detail throughout
this book.
III. EMERGING APPROACHES TO EARTH
LAW
Earth law is an emerging body of law. The editors of this coursebook have
pulled together accounts of various approaches that offer promise in
developing Earth law further. While each of the approaches differs, they all
arise from the following understandings:
Earth is precious, for all intents and purposes, and it is the only home for
the humans and other living beings that inhabit it;
Earth is composed of interdependently functioning systems and living
and nonliving beings—it has an organic unity and cannot survive in
parts;
Earth as a living planet exists contingently, and it is subject to
irreversible damage in its life-sustaining capacities;
Earth is in a human-caused ecological crisis resulting in unnecessary
suffering by both humans and nonhuman beings;
Conventional Western law, including environmental law, is contributing
to this crisis and is in need of reform; and
Reform of law must be based on an ecocentric approach.
The approaches to Earth law presented in this book are not all new. For
example, the public trust doctrine goes back at least to ancient Roman law.
Indigenous legalities go back further. What is new is that the approaches are
prominent in their expression of ecocentric law and each has been shaped or
newly shaped by the awarenesses listed above.
For purposes of discussing the origins of these approaches, they are grouped
as follows:
(a) Public trust doctrine (including atmospheric trust litigation);

(b) Rights-based approaches, which can be subdivided as follows:
 i. Rights of nature;
ii. Rights of future generations;
iii. Human environmental rights and the rights of nature (co-violations);
iv. Animal rights (nonhuman rights approach);
(c) Ecocide;
(d) Indigenous legalities;
(e) International Earth law developments; and (f) Other approaches, both
global and local.
A. Public Trust Doctrine
The public trust doctrine has antecedents in law dating back to the Roman
Institutes of Justinian and the Magna Carta.30 The public trust means “that
the public owns in common certain property interests in natural resources and
land within the territory, and that the government is the people’s designated
trustee with the obligation to protect such property on behalf of the
citizens.”31 Traditionally, the doctrine applied to the protection of large
watercourses and their banks for navigation, fishing, drinking water, and
other uses by the public. According to Joseph Sax, there are three types of
restrictions imposed on the government by this doctrine: “[F]irst, the property
subject to the trust must not only be used for a public purpose, but it must be
held available for use by the general public; second, the property may not be
sold, even for a fair cash equivalent; and third, the property must be
maintained for particular types of uses.”32 The lodestar public trust case in
the United States is Illinois Central Railroad. v. Illinois, 146 U.S. 387, 455
(1892), which is discussed in detail in Chapter 7, “Public Trust Doctrine.”
The use of the public trust doctrine in litigation has been contentious as it pits
claims of private owners against claims of the general public for protection of
natural resources for various public interests, including economic,

recreational, and aesthetic interests. Joseph Sax’s 1970 article on The Public
Trust Doctrine in Natural Resources Law: Effective Judicial Intervention,33
and the work of other scholars, spurred the use of the public trust doctrine by
environmental advocates and policymakers.34 It has been successfully used in
courts in support of various environmental interests, such as to protect
recreational use of coastal beaches, bar the filling of privately owned
wetlands, extinguish a legislative grant of tidelands in the San Francisco Bay,
protect Lake Tahoe, and protect flowing waters and water rights.35
In the twenty-first century, a radical extension of the public trust doctrine has
been pioneered by Mary Christina Wood in her 2009 two-part law review
article, Advancing the Sovereign Trust of Government to Safeguard the
Environment for Present and Future Generations: Ecological Realism and
the Need for a Paradigm Shift,36 and in her 2014 book, Nature’s Trust:
Environmental Law for a New Ecological Age.37 Wood’s argument went far
beyond prior ones. It was not that the public trust doctrine could augment
environmental law, it was that environmental law was failing, notably on
climate change, but on other aspects of environmental degradation as well.
The failure of environmental law fell on the legislative and executive
branches of government, and Wood saw that under the public trust doctrine
courts could use their authority to impose fiduciary obligations on
governments to protect and restore the environment.
Her work on the public trust doctrine became widely-known when young
persons in Oregon filed a lawsuit alleging that the U.S. government had, with
knowledge of its effects, enabled fossil fuel production and thereby increased
climate change, which deprived plaintiffs of their constitutional rights to life,
liberty, and property and violated the government’s obligations under the
federal public trust doctrine.38 This litigation became the most well-known of
many “atmospheric trust” or “climate” lawsuits. As of December 20, 2019,
there had been a reported 1,442 atmospheric trust lawsuits worldwide. In the
most far-reaching decision related to this litigation, the Supreme Court of the
Netherlands ordered the Dutch government to reduce greenhouse gas
emissions by 25 percent from 1990 levels by 2020. The State of the
Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation (Urgenda), is examined in Chapter 23.
This book covers the public trust doctrine and atmospheric trust litigation in

Chapter 7.
B. Rights-Based Approaches
Numerous rights-based movements—for nature, specific animals, and future
generations of humans—also play a central role in the development of Earth
law. Previous rights-based movements for humans can serve as a blueprint
for how these may develop.
1. Inspiration from previous rights-based movements
In the aftermath of the horrors of World War II, international humanitarian
law39 and international human rights law40 emerged in the Western legal
system as part of a concerted effort to ensure future generations would be
protected from such atrocities. A number of international human rights
instruments came into being in this post-war period, including the modern
Geneva Conventions, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (or ICCPR). Though
humanitarian law and human rights law has had a mix of success and failure
since the late 1940s,41 the expansion of these rights has made the lives of
millions of people safer and more dignified.
Looking specifically to the United States, other rights-based movements
demonstrate how the legal system has evolved to correct injustice and expand
rights. Less than 200 years ago, “the United States Supreme Court could
straight-facedly tell us in Dred Scott that [African Americans] had been
denied the rights of citizenship ‘as a subordinate and inferior class of beings’.
…”42 In the United States, women,43 Jews, and Chinese people likewise were
denied the full legal status and voting rights that for decades had been given
to white men.44
The work of a rights activist seems extreme in the beginning as is illustrated
by this account of the effort to abolish slavery:
Abolitionists in the United States were called radical and extreme, they saw
their businesses burned, their printing presses destroyed, and were subject to
mob violence. Over a century later, seeking to have the rights driven into the

U.S. Constitution by the Abolitionists finally and fully implemented and
enforced, members of the Civil Rights Movement similarly saw their houses
burn, their property destroyed, and faced violence from those seeking to
preserve the status quo which systematically subordinated blacks in America.
…
[W]e find those who took to the written word, perhaps instead of the spoken,
have often been essential to the origins of a movement. Those who write bear
witness to the immorality and illegitimacy of the current state of affairs, and
are often calling for change. People like the prolific American Abolitionist
William Lloyd Garrison, who in the early days of that movement began
writing his newspaper, the Liberator, which he published for over thirty years
advocating for the urgent end of slavery while blasphemously calling the U.S.
Constitution—which codified slavery—a “covenant with death, an agreement
with hell.” Incidentally, Garrison, who not only wrote widely but also
publicly spoke about the need for abolition, would burn the constitution at
rallies, which to those in attendance provided perhaps the clearest indication
of how tightly the problem of slavery was woven into the American
framework, and thus how deeply the work of the Abolitionists needed to
go.45
When rights activists succeed, denial of the rights for which they worked
seems unthinkable. People in the rights of nature movement acknowledge the
debt they owe to slavery abolitionists, suffragettes, and civil rights activists
for expanding rights to different peoples throughout history. These efforts
established the foundations that have inspired and informed many of the
social movements now advocating for the rights of nature.
As Christopher D. Stone, a pioneer in the rights of nature movement, wrote:
“[u]ntil the rightless thing receives its rights, we cannot see it as anything but
a thing for the use of ‘us’—those who are holding rights at the time.”46
Rights-based law is ever-changing and, based on historical precedent, moving
toward expansion.
2. Rights of nature
One of the scholarly underpinnings of the modern Earth law movement in the

United States came in a U.S. Supreme Court case. In Sierra Club v. Morton,
405 U.S. 727 (1972), discussed in detail in Chapter 5, “Standing,” the Court
considered standing requirements for the Sierra Club to bring suit for
violation of environmental regulations related to the development of a ski
resort in the Sequoia National forest. The issue arose because the Sierra Club
did not suffer personal injury from the development. While the Court ruled
against the plaintiffs due to lack of standing, Justice William O. Douglas
wrote a dissent47 that foreshadowed the rights of nature movement. He
asserted that nature itself should be treated as the central legal party in a case
involving environmental law violations.
Justice Douglas’s recognition of nature as a rights holder has received
significant support from the legal community.48 From Stone, whose law
review article, Should Trees Have Standing?: Toward Legal Rights for
Natural Objects, inspired Justice Douglas,49 to Cormac Cullinan, author of
the influential book Wild Law: A Manifesto for Earth Justice,50 to David
Boyd, author of The Rights of Nature: A Legal Revolution That Could Save
the World,51 legal minds have been advocating for and cultivating this field
for decades. Sierra Club v. Morton and a growing body of subsequent
scholarship have elucidated the legal workability of the rights of nature and
its critical role in forestalling the ecological crisis.52
Chapter 9 of this book covers the rights of nature in the United States.
3. The rights of future generations and human environmental rights (co-
violations)
At least 155 national governments have recognized that humans possess a
right to a healthy environment.53 Recently, the Inter-American Court of
Human Rights also “recognized a fundamental right to a healthy
environment.”54 In researching this precedent, David R. Boyd, now the
Special Rapporteur on human rights and the environment for the United
Nations, argues that the human right to a healthy environment has led to
environmental laws as well as court decisions supporting stronger
environmental protections.55 Moreover, as indicated in the 2015 and 2016
Earth Law Center co-violations reports (see Chapter 10, “Human Rights and

the Rights of Nature”), violations of human rights are also oftentimes
violations of nature’s rights.
A related rights-based movement has focused on the rights of future
generations since the existential threat of climate change mandates a
consideration of the rights of those not yet born.56 Advocates argue that
today’s population owes a legal obligation to future generations who should
therefore be granted standing in court.57
The human right to a healthy environment, the rights of future generations,
and the rights of the Amazon rainforest were all recognized and supported in
a seminal 2018 decision by the Supreme Court of Colombia, which found:
[I]t can be preached that the fundamental rights of life, health, minimum
subsistence, freedom, and human dignity are substantially linked and
determined by the environment and the ecosystem. Without a healthy
environment, subjects of law, and sentient beings in general, will not be able
to survive, much less protect those rights, for our children or for future
generations. Neither can the existence of the family, society, or the State
itself be guaranteed.58
Chapter 8 of this book covers the rights of future generations and Chapter 10
covers human environmental rights and the rights of nature (co-violations).
4. Nonhuman rights approach
There is a growing movement to recognize the rights of nonhuman animals in
law. An Argentinian court recently held that Cecilia, a chimpanzee long
caged in a zoo, had juridical rights and should be released into a Brazilian
sanctuary.59 Likewise, in 2018 in India, the High Court of Uttarakhand held
that horse cruelty was illegal because “[e]very species has an inherent right to
live and are required to be protected by law.”60 The “Nonhuman Rights
Project” has likewise pushed U.S. courts to recognize these rights.61 The push
for rights for animals differs from traditional animal welfare efforts as
illustrated by the following objectives of the Nonhuman Rights Project:
1. To change the common law status of great apes, elephants, dolphins, and

whales from mere “things,” which lack the capacity to possess any legal
right, to “legal persons,” who possess such fundamental rights as bodily
liberty and bodily integrity.
2. To draw on the common law and evolving standards of morality,
scientific discovery, and human experience to consider other qualities
that may be sufficient for recognition of nonhuman animals’ legal
personhood and fundamental rights.
3. To develop local, national, and global issue-oriented grassroots and
legislative campaigns to promote recognition of nonhuman animals as
beings worthy of moral and legal consideration and with their own
inherent interests in freedom from captivity, participation in a
community of other members of their species, and the protection of their
natural habitats.
4. To build a broad-based coalition of organizations and individuals to
secure legally recognized fundamental rights for nonhuman animals.
5. To foster understanding of the social, historical, political, and legal
justice of our [nonhuman rights] arguments and the scientific discovery
of other species’ cognitive and emotional complexity that informs
them.62
Chapter 9 of this book covers nonhuman rights.
C. Ecocide
Ecocide refers to the destruction of ecosystems and the species they support
on a massive level. Like atmospheric trust litigation, ecocide is a theory used
by Earth lawyers to address the environmental crisis in a way that matches its
scale. A significant difference from other approaches presented in this book
is that ecocide is a criminal law approach.
The term ecocide was first used to describe the massive harm caused by the
spraying of Agent Orange by the U.S. Army in the Vietnam War. The
chemical was used to defoliate forests so that guerillas could not live or hide
in them. In “Operation Ranch Hand,” 20 million gallons of Agent Orange and
other chemicals were sprayed over an area the size of the state of
Massachusetts.63 This chemical warfare against nature was not prohibited by
international conventions as it would have if it had been against humans.

Subsequent to that war, in 2002, the Rome Statute of the International
Criminal Court came into being. Without using the term ecocide, the statute
makes it an international crime to intentionally launch an attack with the
knowledge that the attack will cause “widespread, long-term and severe
damage to the natural environment” that is clearly excessive in regard to the
military situation.64 This provision was drafted so narrowly that it might not
have applied to the use of Agent Orange by the United States in Vietnam and
it has no applicability to ecocide in peacetime. Polly Higgins devoted her life
to making ecocide a peacetime crime under the Rome Statute. She and others
believed that an international crime was needed to deter, for example,
widespread deforestation such as that which has occurred in the Amazon.65
Chapter 12 of this book covers ecocide.
D. Indigenous Legalities
Indigenous peoples have coexisted in harmony with the land for millennia.
Their laws, customs, and way of life are based upon respect and care for
nature. While Indigenous peoples comprise less than five percent of the
world’s population, they manage or have tenure over 25 percent of land, with
such land accounting for 80 percent of global biodiversity.66
As the natural world suffers, so too have Indigenous peoples. Environmental
degradation and climate disruption disproportionately impact the human
rights of Indigenous peoples,67 who often live in those ecosystems most
impacted by environmental declines. There is also an onslaught of violence
perpetrated against Indigenous defenders of the environment,68 including the
murder of Indigenous Goldman Environmental Prize winners Isidro
Baldenegro López from Mexico (2005 winner for protecting ancient forests)
and Berta Cáceres in Honduras (2015 winner for opposing a dam).69 To
protect Indigenous rights is to protect the environment and vice versa.
International law has begun to develop the foundations of Indigenous rights
recognition and enforcement. There have been numerous international
instruments recognizing Indigenous rights in recent decades—the Indigenous
and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (“ILO-convention 169”) and the UN
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) amongst them.

There have also been landmark court victories both in national and
international venues by Indigenous peoples seeking to enforce their rights
and correct injustices,70 although their struggle for rights continues. Many
believe that addressing Indigenous rights as they relate to the environment is
necessary to help solve the global ecological crisis.
Indigenous people enter Earth law not only in respect to protecting their
rights, but also for their insights into human-Earth relations. Since the ways
that Indigenous peoples govern themselves are different than in conventional
Western law, in this book we use the term “Indigenous legalities.”
Several chapters in this book concern Earth law and Indigenous people:
Chapter 18 (Colombia); Chapter 19 (Brazil/Mexico); Chapter 22 (New
Zealand); Chapter 24 (Africa); and Chapter 25 (“Indigenous Legalities”).
E. International Earth Law Developments
Since the 1970s, international law has attempted to introduce a series of
stronger environmental protections, and there are dozens of international laws
that aim to protect the environment.71 There are also numerous non-binding
international legal instruments, from the 1972 Stockholm Declaration to the
2016 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.
However, just as domestic environmental law is criticized for not
successfully reducing environmental harm, so too are traditional international
laws frequently condemned for lacking the capacity and force to rein in
human consumption, production, pollution, and devastation of the living
world.
Civil society declarations and agreements are leading the way in highlighting
an Earth-centered approach to international law. In 2002, nearly a decade of
work by thousands of people in civil society resulted in the Earth Charter,
which recognizes that “all beings are interdependent and every form of life
has value regardless of its worth to human beings.”72 In 2010, thousands of
civil society leaders meeting in Cochabamba, Bolivia, wrote the Universal
Declaration for the Rights of Mother Earth.73 It is used as a guide by many
rights of nature and Earth jurisprudence advocates around the world. This

book surveys emerging international principles of ecocentric law, including
the Global Pact for the Environment.
The United Nations Harmony with Nature initiative has recognized the
importance of Earth jurisprudence and aims to weave its concepts and
approaches into the work and consciousness of the United Nations. The 2019
United Nations Harmony with Nature report describes the growing support of
Earth-centered laws and policies worldwide as follows:
20. Federal, state and local governments around the world are increasingly
adopting laws that recognize the rights of Nature and the natural world to
exist and flourish. In many cases, these new laws are the product of
collaboration between non-governmental organizations, civil society
associations, legislators and legislative bodies, working together to draft,
adopt and implement laws recognizing Nature as a subject of rights and/or a
legal “person”, protected by law.
21. Likewise, non-governmental organizations and civil society associations
have successfully expanded their efforts to obtain judicial recognition of
Nature’s rights and of rulings that protect the natural world. Additionally,
countries with Nature’s rights already incorporated into their laws are
implementing those rights through judicial decisions protecting Nature.
22. Customary and Indigenous laws continue to serve as models for the
expansion of Western positive law toward respecting Nature and Nature’s
rights. An increasing number of Indigenous groups have taken formal action
to incorporate into their governing laws what they have long understood as
the basic truth of life: humans are part of the natural world and must live in
harmony with Nature.74
Chapter 15 of this book covers United Nations Sustainability Initiatives.
F. Other Approaches Global and Local
In addition to the foregoing approaches, chapters in this book cover a way of
considering the ethical issues in wildlife through the eyes of a bear (Chapter
14), ecocentric environmental governance (Chapter 16), amendments to the
Constitution of Ecuador recognizing the rights of nature (Chapter 17), and

developments in Earth law in Colombia (Chapter 18), Brazil and Mexico
(Chapter 19), India (Chapter 20), Israel (Chapter 21), and New Zealand
(Chapter 22). These chapters present a number of other approaches, both
global and local.
IV. CONCLUSION
This chapter describes how Earth law is both a departure from modern
environmental law as well as a new context for its extension. It also explores
how Western legal systems became separated from humans’ role within
nature, and how this separation is resulting in global environmental declines.
Finally, the chapter surveys Earth law topics that are covered in this book to
provide the reader with a taste of how current legal movements are working
to create a more ecocentric legal system.
Chapter 3, “Conceptual Frameworks of Earth Law,” describes in more detail
the legal and philosophical theories upon which Earth law is based. It also
explores the work of Thomas Berry, whose principles of Earth jurisprudence
have inspired many of the authors of this book. As Thomas Berry famously
said, “The universe is composed of subjects to be communed with, not
primarily of objects to be used.”
Consider whether society can once again realize this truth through the
evolution of our legal system toward Earth law.
STUDY QUESTIONS
1) One critique of Western laws is that they treat nature as a machine that
humans can tinker with and control. What analogy might you give for the
treatment of nature under Earth law?
2) Rights of nature laws are seen as Western-style positivist laws that may
not be suitable in some jurisdictions. Can you think of any legal system
where a rights-based approach might not be appropriate?
3) In his dissenting opinion in Sierra Club v. Morton, Justice Douglas
expressed his opinion that the Mineral King Valley in Sequoia National Park

should have legal rights. How would you respond to this poetic commentary
published in the American Bar Association Journal in 1973 by John Naff?
If Justice Douglas has his way—
O come not that dreadful day—
We’ll be sued by lakes and hills
Seeking a redress of ills
Great mountain peaks of name prestigious
Will suddenly become litigious
Our brooks will babble in the courts,
Seeking damages for torts
How can I rest beneath a tree
If it may soon be suing me?
Or enjoy the playful porpoise
While it’s seeking habeas corpus?
Every beast within his paws
Will clutch an order to show cause
The Courts besieged on every hand,
Will Crowd with suits by chunks of land.
Ah! But vengeance will be sweet
Since this must be a two-way street.
I’ll promptly sue my neighbor’s tree
For shedding all its leaves on me.
4) Of the various Earth law approaches surveyed in this chapter, which do
you think are most promising? Why?
5) As an ever-emerging body, Earth law is still in its relative infancy. Do you
think any approaches to Earth law will be mainstream, if not universally
adopted? If so, do you think this will take closer to 10 years or 100 years? If
not, why do you think they will not become mainstream?

CHAPTER 3
Conceptual Frameworks of Earth
Law1
I. INTRODUCTION
The subtitle of this book is “A Guide for Practitioners.” The intent of the
editors is to offer law students the best tools that have been developed for
practicing Earth law with the goal of having students further develop the field
through their various practices. There are opportunities to practice Earth law
as litigators; judges; advisors of governments, businesses, nonprofit
organizations, and individuals; lobbyists and members of bar committees;
and scholars teaching and interpreting laws, analyzing legal systems, and
working for reforms of both. Further, Earth law concerns legal ethics and
how lawyers set up, conduct, and are remunerated for their practices. Given
the difficulty of constraining and regulating conduct through positive law
alone, Earth law also concerns customs and norms, the symbols and rituals of
law, and what has been called customary law, unwritten laws governing
behavior.
Earth law focuses on the role of law in the survival, health, and well-being of
humans and the larger community of life and life systems in the context of
the Anthropocene (discussed below). Its purpose is to provide the legal
framework needed for humans to: (1) live within planetary boundaries, (2)
prospectively care for ecosystems, (3) preserve biodiversity, (4) restore
damaged ecosystems and loss of biodiversity, (5) protect human
environmental rights, and (6) justly share the burdens of mitigating and
adapting to climate change and other environmental stresses. A distinctive

feature of Earth law is that nature is taken into consideration in its own right
and the benefits, protections, and remedies afforded by law are extended to
nature in its own right. In a sense, nature becomes a third party in every legal
process. Earth law also gives new attention to human environmental rights
and justice.
This chapter explores the distinctive characteristics of Earth law approaches
and delves into questions and assumptions underlying them. It begins by
examining the role of humans in nature as we enter the Anthropocene epoch,
which is notable for its fundamental degradation of Earth’s life systems. It
then turns to foundational questions regarding the goals of our legal system to
determine its alignment with the aim of restoring ecological balance. It also
delves into the various definitions of optimal and equitable outcomes of
ecological legal approaches and then explores the role of law in society.
Finally, it examines the role of ethics, the social contract, and myriad goals of
justice and peace. The inquiry into Earth law involves the convergence of all
these aspects, with the ultimate aim of restoring and protecting this planet’s
life.
There are ten sections in this chapter:
 (1) Understanding the Anthropocene Epoch

Systems Science and the Gaia Theory

 (6) Rights, Responsibilities, and Reciprocity

Commons
