II. UNDERSTANDING THE ANTHROPOCENE
EPOCH
Earth law is the resumption in a new historical context of what Eric Freyfogle
called “our oldest task,” that of “living on land without degrading it.”2 That
new context is the Anthropocene epoch, which was beginning, but not clearly
evident, when modern environmental law came into being in the 1960s and
70s. It has not been taken into account as environmental law has developed
and been practiced since that time.
The term Anthropocene epoch was coined by Paul Crutzen and Eugene
Stoermer in an article published in 2000,3 where they proposed a name for a
new geological epoch to succeed the Holocene epoch. The Holocene is the
roughly 10,000-year period that began after the last ice age. All human
civilization has developed during the Holocene Epoch. Crutzen and Stoermer
identified large-scale changes humans have made on Earth and to the
atmosphere and argued, considering these still-growing impacts, the role of
humans should be recognized by naming the current epoch the
Anthropocene.4
In May 2019, the Anthropocene Working Group (AWG) of the International
Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) voted to recognize the new epoch as
beginning around 1950 and said it intended to submit a formal proposal for
recognition of the epoch to the ICS in 2021. The AWG identified the
Anthropocene epoch (often referred to simply as the Anthropocene) by
phenomena related to it, as follows:
An order-of-magnitude increase in erosion and sediment transport associated
with urbanization and agriculture; marked and abrupt anthropogenic
perturbations of the cycles of elements such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus,

and various metals together with new chemical compounds; environmental
changes generated by these perturbations, including global warming, sea-
level rise, ocean acidification and spreading oceanic “dead zones”; rapid
changes in the biosphere both on land and in the sea, as a result of habitat
loss, predation, explosion of domestic animal populations and species
invasions; and the proliferation and global dispersion of many new
“minerals” and “rocks” including concrete, fly ash and plastics, and the
myriad “technofossils” produced from these and other materials.5
To make the case for the designation of the Anthropocene as a geological
epoch (in geology, an epoch is a period of thousands of years), the AWG
stated: “Many of these changes will persist for millennia or longer, and are
altering the trajectory of the Earth System, some with permanent effect. They
are being reflected in a distinctive body of geological strata now
accumulating, with potential to be preserved into the far future.”6
Clive Hamilton, in Defiant Earth, made one of the strongest statements on
the foreboding aspects of the Anthropocene when he wrote: “The idea of the
Anthropocene was conceived by Earth System scientists to capture the very
recent rupture in Earth history arising from the impact of human activity on
the Earth System as a whole.”7 His analysis of the implications of the
Anthropocene for humans serves as a background for discussing the special
elements of Earth law.
Hamilton called for a new anthropocentrism.8 The old anthropocentrism saw
human mastery of Earth as a moral right, whereas the new anthropocentrism
sees human mastery as a fact that puts humans in a place of responsibility and
peril not heretofore imagined:
We may have acquired it foolishly, but we now have a responsibility for the
Earth as a whole and pretending otherwise is itself irresponsible. So the
question is not whether human beings stand at the center of the world, but
what kind of human being stands at the center of the world and what is the
nature of that world.…
Contrary to the comforting expectations that in the Anthropocene we can
have “the kind of nature we wish to have,” as we enter the new epoch, we

will meet an Earth that is further and further from the Earth we might want.
And against the belief that “the world we will inhabit is the one we have
made,” the world we will have to live with is the Earth we have turned
against us.9
Regarding nature, Hamilton wrote that the cosmology of the Anthropocene
must be based on a concept of agency that extends beyond humans to the
freedom woven into nature itself. In this view, nature is a “dynamic, self-
organizing system, characterized by emergent properties.” Emergent
properties “cannot be found in any individual element [of the Earth system]
and evade all cause-and-effect explanations.…The future always evades full
predictability and inevitably holds surprises.”10 Earth is not simply a passive
victim of human neglect and abuse; it has more than equal reactive power.
Earth is not just a benign mother; it has a dangerous quality that we must
respect.
The new anthropocentrism acknowledges that humans are agents more
powerful than ever, yet it also confirms our ultimate inseparability from the
forces of the natural world we inhabit. “The new anthropocentric self does
not float free like the modern subject, but is always woven into nature, a knot
in the fabric of nature.”11
Though so enmeshed, we humans are, according to Hamilton, the exceptional
agents in relation to nature, and we differ from the other agents in that we act
with volition. In the Anthropocene, “Our inescapable responsibility for the
Earth defines us as moral beings, [even more than] our own welfare, our
virtues, and our duties to one another.” Hamilton observes that a
characteristic of humans is that we are world-making creatures. We imagine
and then create buildings, companies, states, cities, and so on. “For
humankind, how to create worlds while remaining within nature’s limits is
the supreme challenge.”12
The promise that Hamilton offers to humans in the Anthropocene is that we,
in a unique way, manifest the spontaneous creativity of nature. Our “creative
powers embody the possibility that they be used to enhance the life-enriching
potential of the Earth as well as to improve the human condition. Nature
therefore contains within it the possibility of mutually harmonious human-

Earth enhancement.”13
III. EARTH LAW, PHILOSOPHY, AND
JURISPRUDENCE
Jurisprudence concerns the philosophy of law.14 Contemporary approaches to
jurisprudence include: (1) natural law: law exists independently of positive
law and is accessible to reason (since the eighteenth century this has largely
been tied to the natural rights of humans); (2) analytic jurisprudence (or
clarificatory jurisprudence) with two sub-categories: (a) legal positivism: law
comes from basic social facts and there is no necessary connection to
morality, and (b) legal realism: the real-world practice of law is what law is,
and this practice can be studied using the methods of natural science; (3)
critical legal studies: related to legal realism, but the focus is on power
relations and oppression in the legal system; and (4) normative jurisprudence
(or evaluative jurisprudence): What is the purpose of law? How can it be
improved?
In terms of the above, Earth law is related to normative jurisprudence, critical
legal studies, and natural law. The philosophical issues in Earth law,
however, go beyond those covered in contemporary jurisprudence. Hamilton
raises two such issues: “What kind of human being stands at the center of the
world?” and “What is the nature of the world?” In philosophy, these are
questions of philosophical anthropology and philosophical cosmology. The
modern world (meaning the world since 1500) has given philosophical
answers to these questions that are so embedded in our consciousness and
institutions that we are barely aware of them. These answers are now called
into question by the Anthropocene.
Because Earth law challenges some fundamental assumptions, it is instructive
to reflect on the capacity of humans to shift dramatically their world views
and their systems of organizing society. Judith Koons provides a brief
historical account of how our current understandings of humans and nature
developed. Following Koons’s analysis, there are three key periods: (1) the
Enlightenment period, (2) the Industrial Revolution, and (3) the twentieth-
century rise of the modern corporation and of environmental law.15 For the

purposes of this chapter, we will add a fourth period, one that is coming into
being, which is (4) the ecological period. While there is no consensus that the
fourth period will be considered to be the ecological period, Anthropocene is
the name advanced here because the changing and deteriorating conditions of
nature as it affects human civilization is the paramount concern of this
emerging period. Ecological has a normative connotation, but here it is used
to indicate the centrality of human-Earth relations in this period whether the
outcome is benign for humans and other beings or not. While many have
argued that the alarm about the conditions of nature that gave rise to the
designation of the Anthropocene is overblown, the conviction that this is not
the case is a touchstone for Earth law. As noted above, Earth law concerns
prospectively caring for ecosystems. This is not only because caring for
ecosystems is a morally good thing to do, but also because the Anthropocene
requires ameliorative action based on foresight—action must be taken to
address ecological problems before they become too great to handle.
Contemporary environmental law has a bias toward taking remedial action
after problems arise rather than acting prospectively to avoid problems.
In the first period, as described by Koons, leaders of the Enlightenment
privileged human reason and rejected traditional religious dogma and values.
Humans were separated from nature. Nature was studied as a machine to be
controlled and exploited for human use. In this period, Western discovery and
colonialism arose. Certain people were objectified, conquered, killed,
enslaved, and made, together with their lands, subservient to European
interests (or in the case of settler colonialism,16 the interests of the settlers).
Concepts of liberty, progress, human rights, property, and social contract
arose during this period.
In the second period, the period of the Industrial Revolution, the legal system
shifted to support industrial development, and humans and nature were
subordinated to industrial growth. Power shifted from agrarians to merchants
and industrial barons. Economic utility became a paramount value, and a
cost-benefit analysis was applied to weigh damage to person and property
against the gains obtained.
In the third period, corporations and capital markets became the drivers of
economic growth, economic activity was globalized, and corporations gained

extensive political influence. The chief task of corporations was to maximize
returns for the benefit of shareholders and management. The legal system
continued to privilege economic growth, and the environmental laws that
arose to make this growth safer were made explicitly or implicitly subject to
cost-benefit analysis. While many corporate leaders objected to
environmental regulation and liability, these environmental laws spurred
innovation (supported, in some cases, by limited liability protections) and
accompanied a period of economic growth unmatched in history—the period
of the Great Acceleration in the second half of the twentieth century
extending to the present.17
The fourth period, the ecological period, will be greatly affected by the
Anthropocene. According to the Ecological Footprint Network, humankind
currently has an ecological footprint that is 170 percent as large as the
carrying capacity of Earth.18 According to another measure, that of the nine
planetary boundaries identified by Will Steffen and others,19 humans have
exceeded the boundaries for (1) flows of nitrogen and phosphorous, (2) land-
system change, (3) genetic diversity, and (4) climate change, and are nearing
the boundary on (5) ocean acidification. There are two other sectors in which
the authors were unable to specify boundaries, those being (6) chemical
pollution and the release of novel entities and (7) atmospheric aerosol
loading. The two remaining categories, (8) ozone depletion and (9)
freshwater use, were assessed as safe.
Many scientists write that humans are causing the sixth mass extinction in the
history of this planet.20 Further, among many other evidences of ecological
degradation, the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
has stated that Earth has warmed by 1.0°C from pre-industrial times (pre–
1750),21 and, according to the United Nations Environmental Program, we
are on a path to 3.2°C of warming,22 a climate very different from the one to
which both human civilization and many other species have adapted. All
these situations are the result of human impact on Earth over the last 250
years and especially the last 50. Because of the unsustainability of our present
situation and the reactive power of Earth, nature will force itself upon human
societies, and thus upon their legal systems, as the most fundamental concern.
Nature will be perceived in three ways—as a destructive force to which
humans must respond, as degraded life systems in need of restoration, and as

a resilient source of physical and spiritual sustenance.
The most common response to the demands of the Anthropocene is that
people must move from conventional economic development to sustainable
development. Sustainable development means economic development with
greater attention to environmental concerns and social issues. To date, for the
most part, sustainable development has been based on a weak notion of
sustainability, one that places economic growth first, people (or society)
second, and the environment third. Based on a strong notion of sustainability,
the order is reversed with the environment first, society second, and
economics third.
Earth law takes the strong sustainability approach based on the premise that
the health of Earth is a precondition to the health of society and economics.
To improve health, the economy should be subservient to social well-being
and cultural values rather than society and culture being subservient to the
economy. It is a fundamental choice and it changes everything. In the second
and third historical periods discussed above, the focus of law has been on
defining human-economy relations. In the fourth period, the focus of law will
be on defining human-Earth relations and this will have implications for all
fields of law and all aspects of human societies.
Now let us look more closely at the questions Hamilton asked concerning
philosophical anthropology (“What kind of human being stands at the center
of the world?”) and philosophical cosmology (“What is the nature of that
world?”). According to the New World Encyclopedia, “[p]hilosophical
anthropology is the philosophical discipline that inquires into the essence of
human nature and the human condition. In making this inquiry, it
[philosophical anthropology] seeks to unify or critique philosophically the
diverse scientific methods and humanistic approaches to answering the
question of human nature.”23 Concerning philosophical cosmology, Rémi
Brague explained it this way: “As humans construct their understanding of
the physical aspects of nature, they also construct their understanding of what
it means to exist in this physical reality. Thus, from the standpoint of
philosophical cosmology, the ‘world’ is more than a description of physical
reality, it is a reflection on the nature of the world and what it means for
humans to be in the world.”24

Many philosophical assumptions undergird the present practice of law. As
Earth law comes into being, those assumptions will be rethought. For
example, in contemporary law, nature is converted into real property owned
by humans and this property is fixed in space and time. Plate tectonics, wind,
erosion, sea-level rise, floods, and more, however, have taught us that
property is not fixed in space or time. In contemporary law, property is
thought of primarily as land, and what happens on the owner’s land is
inconsequential to the planet so long as the owner’s immediate neighbor is
not harmed. We have learned, however, that Earth is an integral, living
system. It is not just Earth’s material structure that keeps the planet habitable
but also the activities of living beings, which, for example, keep the level of
oxygen in the atmosphere at about 20 percent. In contemporary law, humans,
for the most part, are regarded as the only subjects that matter, and,
otherwise, nature is composed of objects to be used. We have learned,
however, that while humans have a unique kind of intelligence, other animals
too have intelligence and, even where intelligence is not present in any
meaningful sense, sentience goes far down the life scale. Every living being,
human and nonhuman, has a unique role to play in the community of life.25
Technological and scientific developments present yet another set of issues
that may greatly define the emerging fourth period. These issues concern
potential modifications of humans and intelligent robots. Scientists have
developed and are developing the ability to change our species through
genetic modification, biomechatronics,26 and brain-computer interfaces.
Scientists are also developing artificial intelligence to extend human
capacities and to replace humans in various decision-making and control
functions. Some scientists are also working on robots that would have
intelligence and physical capacities superior to humans. Robots may never be
developed to be human, i.e. having the ability to experience—the way
humans do—empathy, emotions, meaning, purpose, judgment, and wisdom.
Nevertheless, robots have been and will continue to be developed to replace
humans in many situations. All these changes will have ecological
consequences as well as human consequences. Bill McKibben, in his 2019
book Falter: Has the Human Game Begun to Play Itself Out?, gives two
imperatives for the future: (1) to keep the human game going, and (2) to keep
it human.27 Earth law is committed to both.

Thus, questions of “what kind of human being stands at the center of the
world?” and “what is the nature of the world?” come very much to the fore in
Earth law and answers given to these questions will shape Earth law. If the
reasonable/economic/individual human is the standard for the responsible
person in the third historical period above, who is the responsible person in
the fourth period, the ecological period? In the ecological period, would all
those interacting with nature—farmers, developers, governmental agencies,
and laborers—be responsible not just for human safety but also for ecological
safety? Would we continue to think of landowners as being responsible only
for their individual plot of land because it is theirs and not for the
surrounding ecosystems and bioregions? Would we continue to think of the
world as a series of transactions between individual humans or human entities
affecting only parties to the transactions rather than a world that is a dynamic,
evolving, organic system of interrelations in which every transaction affects
all? Would we replace history with geostory (the geobiological evolutionary
story of Earth of which human history is only one aspect)? Would lawyers,
legislators, administrators, and judges need to become ecologists?
IV. WHAT IS NATURE? THE NATURE-
CULTURE DIVIDE
Earth law understands nature as one integrated, organic, evolutionary whole,
which includes humans.28 Yet, in many situations, Earth law distinguishes
the human world from nature because the overall concern of Earth law is
human-Earth or human-nature relations.
So, what is nature when it is distinguished from the human world? Nature
may be thought of as all of the physical world, including all living beings
other than humans, all minerals (all inorganic matter) other than human
artifacts, and all forces and processes other than human-initiated forces and
processes. Granted, this distinction is artificial because human activities
affect nature’s activities and vice versa.
While it is necessary in many cases to distinguish nature and humans in Earth
law, it is also important to understand the arguments against nature-culture
dualism (culture meaning the human world), also called the nature-culture

If Earth law is to preserve, protect, and restore nature, what nature is the
object of its care? Is there good nature that needs to be protected and
preserved and bad nature that needs to be restored? The answer is that Earth
law does involve decisions about what is healthy nature or desirable nature,
and nature of this type—good nature—is the object of its care. This section
discusses aspects of making such determinations.
Two different notions of good nature have historically guided environmental
law. One is the preservationist approach espoused by John Muir (1838–
1914), founder of the Sierra Club. The other is the wise use or the
conservationist approach espoused by Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946), first
chief of the U.S. Forest Service in 1905. The early issues addressed by Muir
and Pinchot largely concerned the use of public lands in the United States.
Muir wanted to preserve wilderness. Pinchot also wanted to avoid widespread
exploitation, but for different reasons. Pinchot felt the land should be
managed for optimal use based on the greatest good for the greatest number
of people. To Pinchot, optimal use included wilderness value, but also
grazing, mining, forestry, hunting, waterpower, and other uses.
The preservationist movement continues and seeks to preserve areas in their
natural state, thereby protecting land, water, and natural forces and processes
from human interference and pollution. For preservationists, good nature
means nature in an undisturbed state or restored to a prior natural state. The
wise-use movement continues also and favors private property rights, less
environmental regulation, increased human access to public lands, and
opposition to government intervention. Wise use is associated with maximum
sustainable yield, which holds that renewable natural resources may be
exploited so long as the exploitation does not result in long-term depletion.
For conservationists, good nature means nature that provides the most human
benefits.
Traditionally what constitutes good nature concerns nature in situ, or in other
words, what is good nature in a particular locale? In the Anthropocene, the
traditional question remains, but the question must also be asked and
answered on larger scales. Questions arise concerning what kind of nature
and how much nature is needed on a global and a bioregional basis, among
other needs,

To provide carbon sinks for anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions?
To preserve biodiversity?
To protect coastal lands from flooding?
To sustain fish stocks and other marine life?
To regulate climate?
For disease control?
For waste treatment and filtration?
For biochemical and genetic resources?
For essential raw materials?
For cultural services, including recreational, cognitive, aesthetic, and
spiritual services?
To sustain ocean currents and other flows?
For human agriculture, living spaces, and other uses?
Good nature in the Anthropocene presumably would mean the type and
amount of nonhuman nature needed to perform the above ecosystem
services.30 This guideline, while a good one, is, however, difficult to apply
when determining which local areas should serve these bioregional and
global needs.
Until the twentieth century, nature was thought of in largely local terms; for
example, weather was thought to be the result of local variations. Donella
Meadows’s modeling of Earth’s resources, Lovelock’s Gaia theory, the view
of Earth from the moon, the results of Antarctic ice-core drilling, and many
other scientific developments ultimately led to understanding Earth as a
system. Hamilton wrote:
The new Earth System thinking…is the integrative meta-science of the whole
planet understood as a unified, complex, evolving system beyond the sum of
its parts. It is a transdisciplinary and holistic approach assimilating earth
sciences and life sciences, as well as the “industrial metabolism” of
humankind, all within a systems way of thinking with special focus on the
non-linear dynamics of a system. It represents a markedly novel way of
thinking about the Earth that supersedes ecological thinking.31
This holistic understanding of Earth as a system does not, however, in itself
offer a way of understanding what good nature is, especially at the level of

particular localities. The science is descriptive, not prescriptive. Science with
some degree of certainty can model Earth’s processes and resources and how
they will change given certain inputs, but alone it cannot decide what an
optimal state for Earth is and how this could be maintained. For example, an
advocate may soundly argue that based on science a local woodland is an
ecosystem and should be protected with the implication that this term
ecosystem is decisively normative. Another advocate could soundly argue
that suburban lawns are also ecosystems as are vast fields of corn, pastures,
feedlots, and even confined animal feeding operations and should be
protected. Which of these are good nature and based on what criteria?
Science is necessary for decision-making in the Anthropocene even though it
may be contested or misused.
While the science of the Anthropocene emphasizes the importance of
weighing the value of nature on global and bioregional levels, legal
controversies are generally locally situated. One’s perspective on good nature
in resolving the controversy may be determined by where one lives and one’s
social position and culture. Property owners may agree that good nature, in
terms of their bioregion, would include wildlife corridors yet dispute that a
corridor should be on their property. A country may agree that CO2 emissions
are harmful yet claim the right to develop and that this right should not be
carbon-constrained. A company may agree that deforestation is harmful yet
claim the right to clear forests for palm oil plantations.
Further, in the Anthropocene, human rights to freedom of action may run
counter to social constraints imposed to maintain good nature. Some people
will see environmentalism as a threat to freedom…even as ecofascism.32
These views, however unreasonable as they may seem, will challenge the
Earth law movement. Surely Bruno Latour was right when he said that
decisions regarding good nature would arise out of a political process, not as
the result of some transcendent, commonly agreed-upon truth…not even
science, which will be contested.33 Earth law will arise out of this same
political process—the work of practitioners of Earth law will be an important
part of it.
There is one principle of Earth system science advanced by James Lovelock
and Lynn Margulis in their Gaia theory which may serve as a very useful

guideline for resolving the global-local/situated tensions in agreeing on what
is good nature for purposes of Earth law. As Latour explains, the Gaia theory
—the idea that Earth is self-regulating in a manner akin to an organism—has
been misunderstood as meaning that there is some transcendent global
organizing mechanism performing the self-regulation in the way that human
bodies are self-regulating, when, in truth, the self-regulation of Earth occurs
as a result of multiple intercommunicating actors engaging in reciprocal co-
evolution.34 What is needed now, Latour says, is “the relocalization of the
Globe, [a] move from the Globe to the quasi-feedback loops that tirelessly
design it in a way that is broader and denser each time.”35
What Latour means is that while we have come to understand Earth as a
global system, in reality, the system is composed of countless self-organizing
subsystems interacting and co-evolving with each other. Nature over billions
of years somehow arrived at this system of self-organizing subsystems that
have been able to maintain a measure of stability in the face of internal and
external challenges. In other words, these systems have been able to maintain
a dynamic equilibrium or dynamic homeostasis…what is popularly known as
the balance of nature.36 Human civilization, as presently constituted,
however, has interrupted these homeostatic processes. A goal of Earth law as
well as other like disciplines is to restore this balance by reshaping human
culture and social structures such that they mimic nature’s self-organizing
local systems in ways that are coherent with those systems. People who fear
that environmentalism imposes oppressive, top-down restraints should find
some relief in Latour’s proposition that the key to sustaining good nature is
ecologically responsive localism, though it is necessary to remember that in
nature the homeostatic processes take place simultaneously at both macro
(more global) and micro (more local) scales within larger systems and
subsystems that are co-evolving with each other. Thus, if humans are to
mimic nature’s processes, Earth law will need to enable responsive globalism
and regionalism as well as responsive localism.
VI. ANTHROPOCENTRISM, BIOCENTRISM,
ECOCENTRISM, OR COSMOCENTRISM?
Anthropocentrism puts humans at the center of the world and considers

humans to be superior to and separate from nature.37 Consequently, since
humans are the measure of all things, as the Greek philosopher Protagoras
stated,38 the value of everything other than humans is measured by human
values, desires, and utility. Many authors locate the roots of anthropocentrism
within the Judeo-Christian tradition as reinforced by Cartesian dualism and
other modern Western philosophy.39 The secular successes of humans since
the industrial revolution, the globalization of economics, the emergence of a
Westernized universal global culture, and the resulting disruption of
traditional cultures have spread or augmented anthropocentrism globally.
While extreme anthropocentrism entails a profoundly utilitarian,
materialistic, and deterministic view of nature, another version of
anthropocentrism exists that does not see itself in contradiction with an
environmental approach. The former version supports an approach in which
nature is seen as unlimited resources and unlimited sinks to be exploited at
will in order to further unending economic growth; the latter acknowledges
that the well-being of humans is both connected to and dependent on the
well-being of the environment. In the latter, human needs are still central, but
they are articulated around principles of human health, well-being, and
sustainability.
A biocentric approach, in contrast, recognizes the inherent value of all living
organisms, irrespective of their utility for humans.40 Although not operating
from an explicitly biocentric perspective himself, Christopher Stone’s
argument, in which trees were to be considered worthy of standing,
introduced a biocentric perspective into legal discourse.41 An ecocentric
approach, as understood by deep ecologists,42 goes further, and values the
natural world independently of (or potentially even contrary to) any value it
may hold for human desires. The meaning of ecocentrism in the context of
law and legal systems will develop as lawyers and policymakers continue to
identify and confront the limitations of anthropocentrism.
The philosophical axis around which Earth law initiatives are articulated
covers a spectrum, from an instrumentalist view of the environment as a store
of goods that is necessary for human sustenance, sustainability, and even
survival, to the idea of the environment as inherently worthy of recognition,
respect, and protection irrespective of—and potentially in opposition to—

human interests.
A proposed shift from an anthropocentric to a biocentric or ecocentric
perspective raises several normative questions. Is it ever possible to transcend
anthropocentrism in legal theory and/or in legal practice? At a deeper level, is
it ever possible, as Aldo Leopold suggested, for humans to “think like a
mountain?”43 Some authors suggest that if the human mind is the term of
reference for both observation and theory alike,44 then it is impossible to
transcend and move beyond an inevitably anthropic (i.e., human) perspective.
To paraphrase Leopold’s invitation, it may be possible to think like a
mountain, but it will never be possible to think as a mountain. Thus, the
attempt to transcend anthropocentrism does not permit an escape from
inevitable anthropic perspectives but rather challenges the “centrism,” the
idea that human interests ought to take priority in ethical decisions
concerning the environment.
Law is anthropocentric in another sense in that the object of law is the
regulation of human activities, not nonhuman activities or processes; for
example, a fictional act to regulate the operation of gravity would be comedic
at best. It may be helpful, then, to distinguish clearly between
anthropocentricism inasmuch as it concerns human attitudes, orientations,
perspectives, and philosophies, which can be theoretically transcended and
moved toward biocentrism and ecocentrism, and anthropocentrism inasmuch
as it concerns developing norms for human conduct and regulation thereof,
which is inherently human-centered. Thus, while it may never be possible to
think as a mountain, Earth law requires humans to rethink the mountain itself
and human relationships to it.
Like biocentrism and ecocentrism, cosmocentrism might be thought of as
another extension of awareness beyond anthropocentrism for science now
embeds Earth in the evolutionary journey and dynamics of the universe, and
space law is an emerging field of study. Cosmocentrism is included here,
however, primarily to represent a more ancient way of understanding Earth as
a cosmic phenomenon. Many Indigenous people have based their
understanding of their place in the world on cosmogonic and cosmological
myths. The theory of ontological politics recognizes that differences in
ontological understandings—meaning understandings of the nature of reality

and of relationality—among different peoples have political and, thus, legal
consequences. The Spanish word cosmovisión—the manner of seeing the
world—is often used with reference to how people in pre-Columbian
societies of Mesoamerica viewed the world and, also, with reference to how
their descendants carry those cosmovisions today. Contemporary law, on the
other hand, assumes an analytical, scientifically oriented Western worldview.
Symbols and rituals in legal institutions from courtrooms to legislative and
administrative buildings and lawyers’ offices are generally devoid of a
cosmic vision.
Earth law is concerned with re-understanding and re-framing human roles
and relations in the universe (cosmos), Earth (ecology), and the community
of life (biology). With the qualification given above that human law cannot
avoid being anthropic, Earth law strives to move from anthropocentrism to
bio-, eco-, and cosmocentrism.
The subtitle of this book is “emerging ecocentric law,” and in various
chapters of this book, authors write of ecocentric in contrast to
anthropocentric approaches to law. The way in which ecocentric is used does
not correspond to any formal meaning given to the term by others. It is not
used to mean the opposite of anthropocentrism. Ecocentric means that
humans are a part of and dependent on a larger community of life called
Earth, and law must operate to ensure the health and safety of the total
community of life, even for the sake of the human part of it.45 Earth law
codifies the responsibility of legal subjects to behave in this manner.
VII. RIGHTS, RESPONSIBILITIES, AND
RECIPROCITY
The concept of nature’s rights or the rights of nature is prominent in the
practice of Earth law.46 Thomas Berry, an influential person in the
development of Earth law, in his Ten Principles for the Revision of
Jurisprudence, gave this description of the rights of nature:
1. Rights originate where existence originates. That which determines
existence determines rights.

2. Since it has no further context of existence in the phenomenal order, the
universe is self-referent in its being and self-normative in its activities. It
is also the primary referent in the being and the activities of all
derivative modes of being.
3. The universe is composed of subjects to be communed with, not
primarily of objects to be used. As a subject, each component of the
universe is capable of having rights.
4. The natural world on the planet Earth gets its rights from the same
source that humans get their rights: from the universe that brought them
into being.
5. Every component of the Earth community, both living and nonliving,
has three rights: the right to be, the right to habitat or a place to be, and
the right to fulfill its role in the ever-renewing processes of the Earth
community.
6. All rights in nonliving form are role-specific; rights in living form are
species-specific and limited. Rivers have river rights. Birds have bird
rights. Insects have insect rights. Humans have human rights. Difference
in rights is qualitative, not quantitative. The rights of an insect would be
of no value to a tree or a fish.
7. Human rights do not cancel out the rights of other modes of being to
exist in their natural state. Human property rights are not absolute.
Property rights are simply a special relationship between a particular
human “owner” and a particular piece of “property”; so that both might
fulfill their roles in the great community of existence.
8. Since species exist only in the form of individuals, rights refer to
individuals, not simply in a general way to species.
9. These rights as presented here are based on the intrinsic relations that
the various components of Earth have to each other. The planet Earth is
a single community bound together with interdependent relationships.
No living being nourishes itself. Each component of the Earth
community is immediately or mediately dependent on every other
member of the community for the nourishment and assistance it needs
for its own survival. This mutual nourishment, which includes the
predator-prey relationship, is integral with the role that each component
of the Earth has within the comprehensive community of existence.
10. In a special manner, humans have not only a need for but also a right of
access to the natural world to provide for the physical needs of humans

and the wonder needed by human intelligence, the beauty needed by
human imagination, and the intimacy needed by human emotions for
personal fulfillment.47
The above is a well-known statement of the rights of nature, but it is not
definitive. There are other ways that the rights of nature have been expressed.
Some governments have amended their constitutions to include the rights of
nature. For example, in 2008, the Republic of Ecuador adopted a Constitution
with far-reaching provisions regarding the rights of nature. In Title II,
Chapter 7, the Ecuadorian Constitution states:
Chapter 7th: Rights for Nature
Art. 71. Nature or Pachamama, where life is reproduced and exists, has the
right to exist, persist, maintain and regenerate its vital cycles, structure,
functions and its processes in evolution.
Every person, people, community or nationality, will be able to demand the
recognitions of rights for nature before the public organisms. The application
and interpretation of these rights will follow the related principles established
in the Constitution.
The State will motivate natural and juridical persons as well as collectives to
protect nature; it will promote respect towards all the elements that form an
ecosystem.
Art. 72. Nature has the right to restoration. This integral restoration is
independent of the obligation on natural and juridical persons or the State to
indemnify the people and the collectives that depend on the natural systems.
In the cases of severe or permanent environmental impact, including the ones
caused by the exploitation of non-renewable natural resources, the State will
establish the most efficient mechanisms for the restoration, and will adopt the
adequate measures to eliminate or mitigate the harmful environmental
consequences.
Art. 73. The State will apply precaution and restriction measures in all the
activities that can lead to the extinction of species, the destruction of the

ecosystems or the permanent alteration of the natural cycles.
The introduction of organisms and organic and inorganic material that can
alter in a definitive way the national genetic patrimony is prohibited.
Art. 74. The persons, people, communities and nationalities will have the
right to benefit from the environment and from natural wealth that will allow
well-being.
The environmental services cannot be appropriated; its production, provision,
use and exploitation, will be regulated by the State.48
Other rights of nature provisions have been proposed or adopted by nations
and subdivisions of government within nations.49 Further, the rights of nature
have appeared in United Nations Documents and Conferences.50 On April 22,
2010, approximately 40,000 people at the World People’s Conference on
Climate Change and the Rights of Mother Earth adopted the “Universal
Declaration of the Rights of Mother Earth.”51
The rights of nature approach, while popular, has had little success in
practice. Obstacles include procedural issues concerning standing for nature
in court cases52 and who has the right to represent nature,53 but there are also
very basic issues in defining the rights of every aspect of nature. Berry says
every species has its own rights appropriate to its role in nature. Given that
there are millions of species, the task of spelling out these rights is daunting.
Berry also says that each species and each individual in each species has a
right to be. Most human activity involves violating the right to be of some
individuals of some species. A blank prohibition on the killing of humans,
with limited exceptions, is enforceable, but obviously a blanket prohibition
on the killing of any members of all species is not. Another problem is
defining relative rights. Humans have rights, but these rights are always
relative to the rights of other people. Defining the relative rights of each
aspect of nature in relation to the rights of each other aspect is doubly
daunting.54
Given the difficulties of the rights of nature approach, some Earth law
practitioners prefer a human-responsibilities approach. Conventional

environmental law is generally based on human responsibilities. Humans are
responsible for acting in such a way that they do not harm other people by
damaging their environments in ways prohibited by law. Major agreements
among nations regarding climate change, biodiversity, and other matters are
also based on responsibilities of the parties
Rights versus Responsibilities cannot, however, always be seen as opposing
approaches because rights and responsibilities are often interrelated. Rights,
once recognized, impose responsibilities on others with respect to those
rights. And, in many situations, responsibilities imposed are grants of rights
to others. If, for example, a parent has responsibility to provide support to
their child, then the child has the right to be supported by their parent. Which
of the two approaches is emphasized, however, makes a difference. If a
person, under the obligations approach, had an obligation to protect native
species on their land by removing invasive species, then, if there were a
recognized list of invasive species and a neighbor were to spot an invasive
species on that land, the neighbor could sue for enforcement of the obligation
against the offending landowner. If, on the other hand, under the rights of
nature approach, a native species had the right to live without undue
incursion by invasive species, and a person were to spot an invasive species
on their neighbor’s land, then the person would have to bring suit on behalf
of the native species. The court would have to hear the claim that the invasive
species was harming the native species and, if upheld, fashion a remedy to
protect the native species. Then, perhaps, a guardian would need to be
appointed to ensure continued protection of the native species.
Lawyers are familiar with rights and responsibilities, but not so much with
reciprocity, which is a third way of defining relations between humans and
nature that is familiar to many Indigenous people. Reciprocity is a norm
under which one responds to a positive action by carrying out another
positive action. Many Indigenous people have seen Earth as bestowing many
benefits that require a response in kind. The duty of the reciprocal act is
grounded in gratitude, which is more appealing than responsibility grounded
in duty, even though, looked at another way, the reciprocal act is a duty.
Reciprocity has been interpreted in other ways too, such as tit-for-tat, an eye-
for-an-eye, and reciprocal concessions. In these interpretations, the element
of gratitude is missing. Reciprocity grounded in gratitude may be a fruitful

concept in the development of Earth law. It is not to date, however, a
recognized concept in Western legal systems.
VIII. PROPERTY RIGHTS, INDIVIDUAL
RIGHTS, COMMUNAL RIGHTS, AND THE
COMMONS
The challenge to traditional conceptions of property law, as advanced by
many Earth law advocates, is more profound than simply suggesting the
introduction of a number of limits to existing rights of owners of property.
Nicole Graham suggests that natural landscapes do not merely exist as a
background upon which human activities are cast, but rather are shaped, even
created, by the dominant legal paradigm, which, through the subtle operation
of property regimes, imposes a set of parameters that define the spectrum of
environments allowed to exist.55
Though legal property regimes clearly affect land, they also de-physicalize
nature and create a paradigm of placelessness.56 If nature is but an object of
someone’s property rights, and if property rights, such as the right to control
the use of the land, are conceptually disconnected from the life community
related to the land (the nature, above, on, in, and passing through the land),
then most forms of ecological destruction become legally invisible within this
network of de-physicalized property relations. The emergence of nature as a
subject of legal rights separate from the rights of property owners has
occurred, in large part, against these dominant, de-physicalized property
regimes.
Similar observations might be made of the macro effects of taxation policies,
corporation law, health law, or environmental law itself. Laws create
lawscapes. The dominant means of resisting either the negative aggregate
effects of legal regimes or tortious or other unlawful offenses is through
asserting individual human or human-entity rights. A member of an
Indigenous community in Colombia may make claims, for example, on their
own behalf for personal injury where a mining operation contaminates
drinking water or for trespass if a company clearing forest for a palm oil
plantation has violated property laws or creates a nuisance on adjacent

property, but the community as a whole may have no rights (known in this
collective form as communal rights) to control its destiny by having the right
to determine what takes place in the area affecting the community. The
Community Environmental Legal Defense Fund (CELDF) in the United
States has helped cities and towns draft home-rule statutes declaring the
rights of the community to a healthy environment and renewable energy,
among other things, are superior to corporate rights in the home-rule area.57
A related issue concerns the role of the commons in Earth law. Traditionally,
the commons concerned the “control of access to and extraction of resources
seen as limited but essential for the survival of local communities.”58 In
environmental law, concerns arose about the misuse of resources in the
public domain with open access.59 A particular issue concerned externalities
such as pollution discharged into the air or waterways. A more recent and
increasingly important understanding of the commons acknowledges the
interests of multiple stakeholders in environmental goods and services, which
leads to a demand for regulation or control of the areas of common interests,
which may be global or bioregional. The new conception of the commons
concerns, among other things,
Sinks for pollution (including carbon sequestration);
Biodiversity (ecosystems, species, genes, and existence values);
Watershed protection (flood control and freshwater supply);
Disaster mitigation (landslides and avalanches);
Soils (soil erosion, pollution, and water runoff);
Climate (reduction of greenhouse gases);
Clean air (reduction of pollution);
Forests (sequestration of carbon and oxygen and cloud production);
Oceans (avoidance of dead zones, acidification, fish stocks, and water
currents);
Ice (albedo effect, and water source); and
Aesthetics and recreation (preservation of beauty, access, and protection
of nature).
Protection of this new understanding of the commons will in most cases
infringe on individual or entity property rights and, when considered on a
global basis, will also infringe on national sovereign rights. For example, in

the summer of 2019, countries in Europe appealed to the president of Brazil
to reduce the burning of forests in the Amazon on the basis that those forests
supplied 20 percent of the world’s oxygen. President Macron of France,
implying that the Amazon was part of the global commons, tweeted “Our
house is burning.…It’s an international crisis.”60 Further protection of the
new conception of the commons raises concerns about who has the duty to
protect the commons, how this duty will be exercised, and who will bear the
costs of protection and the burden of infringement of pre-existing rights. If
nature’s rights are thrown into the mix, many additional issues arise.
IX. REPRESENTING NATURE: DYADIC
THINKING, SYSTEMS THINKING,
CUSTOMARY LAW, AND CULTURE
The last three sections of this chapter consider problems that the current legal
system presents for Earth law. The rule of law is a great accomplishment of
civilization that has deep roots. The reason so many terms in law are given in
Latin, such as habeas corpus, is because the concepts first appeared in
ancient Roman law. Many have come to think of our systems of laws,
whether they are common-law systems or civil-law systems, as the law. Yet,
if law is understood to include a more general notion of how societies
regulate human behavior in accordance with normative standards, then there
are other past and present means of doing so, including religion, culture,
customary law, and non-Western legal systems. In our time, we would also
need to add science in that scientific findings have important effects on public
policy and the behavior of people whether or not those findings result in
written laws.
In modern societies, the state has a monopoly on the legitimate use of
physical force within a given territory. A key characteristic of law,
conventionally understood, is that the law may be enforced by the coercive
powers of the state. Related characteristics are that people who obey the law
will not be subject to coercive state action, and they may rely on coercive
state action to protect them against unlawful violations of their recognized
legal rights, including their recognized environmental rights.

This way of thinking about the law places a premium on what the written law
or a legally enforceable agreement says and forces either-or (dyadic) choices
as to whether a law has been followed or not, or whether a party to an
agreement has complied with an agreement or not.61 This dyadic approach
has merit and goes a long way in structuring human relationships. It has
limitations, however, when applied to Earth law and may be one of the
reasons why the rights of nature approach has had little success in practice.
Dyadic thinking is based on subject-object relationships and contributes to
the othering of nature. In addition, nature is a dynamic system of co-evolving
systems and does not yield to either-or logic.
Arthur Tansley first used the term ecosystem in 1935. A system has many
interacting parts and positive and negative feedback loops. Early system
models emphasized structure, adaptation, and dynamic equilibrium or steady
states—in other words, they emphasized how given structures became
stabilized and could remain in a steady state indefinitely. This was important
in the application of cybernetic models and specialized systems theory to the
maintenance of complex machinery, but insufficient for biology. Even so, the
complex-machinery understanding is prevalent in how people, including
many scientists and lawyers, think about nature. Application of this type of
systems model leads to a belief that nature, like a machine, can be broken
down into parts, rules can be developed for the operations of the parts, and
relative rights can be assigned to the parts.
Later systems models have moved beyond equilibrium or steady-state models
to non-equilibrium or dynamic models that better reflect nature.62 Nature is
neither a static order, nor is it composed of closed systems. It is highly
dynamic with dissipative systems that exchange matter and energy with
neighboring systems and with larger systems of which they are subsystems
and, in each case, co-evolve with them. Evolution takes place simultaneously
at both macro and micro scales. The result of this openness is the emergence
of novel properties, relations, and systems.63 Human systems that enter into
nature’s dynamic system of systems, which are co-evolving with each other,
especially in the Anthropocene, contribute greatly to the emergence of novel
properties, relations, and systems in nature.
Rather than dealing with issues of what a person can or cannot do as

described by static written laws and dyadic decision-making, the bases of
Earth law include the principle of relationality and the human duties of care
and reciprocity. Legal questions based on this philosophy can more
effectively address what it means to be responsible within a given situation.
Given the complexity and dynamism of nature, one’s sense of what would be
responsible in a given situation could not be determined solely by going
through a checklist of either-or choices and would need to arise in part from
an intuitive sense of what is right after considering the circumstances or
context in which the situation occurs.
The problem of unsolved problems in artificial intelligence is context.
Computers using if-then logic may be programmed to achieve certain
objectives and may even learn in achieving those objectives, but they are not
able, and may never be able, to understand context in exchanging information
with humans and, by extension, with and about natural systems. When law is
understood as a series of dyadic decisions, it runs into the same problems that
AI based on binary computer logic encounters, which is to say law loses
context. For Earth law to lose context would mean concentrating on the
particular, which is separate from the surrounding environment and culture.64
Indigenous ways of dealing with violations of communal norms avoided
dyadic, either-or decision-making and there is much to be learned from them.
Decisions were made by a council and began with invocation, symbol,
ceremony, and context. Questions concerned what the group’s obligations
were to preserve the community, including the larger community of life.
Decision-making was collaborative, not adversarial, and was attentive to the
varying contexts and changing circumstances in which decisions needed to be
made. A taboo was understood as breaking the norms needed to sustain the
community. When someone violated these norms, the primary concern was
not punishment of the offender but rather how to bring the offender back into
the community of mutual obligations. To be an outcast—to be cast out of the
community—was the ultimate penalty. To be expelled from the community is
also a form of punishment described in the Old and New Testament. The
community and each member of the community depended on and was
supported by the mutual performance of obligations.
Today we live in a complex world filled with interactions and transactions.

Most humans will not live in Indigenous or fundamentalist religious
communities with a single culture in a limited geographical area. Still,
Indigenous practices provide a compelling vision for Earth law. While it is
not clear how a legal system based on relationality, care, duty, reciprocity,
and context would operate in the emerging field of Earth law, these terms are
evocative and will inform the discussions in the final two sections of this
chapter.
X. THE ROLE OF LAW AND LEGAL ETHICS
Law is a system of rules that is enforced by a state or other society to
maintain public order and promote public welfare by:
Regulating behavior (enforcing obligations);
Settling disputes;
Redressing injury and grievance;
Punishing illicit (forbidden) conduct;
Protecting against harm, including violation of rights;
Preserving assets; and
Enabling social transactions and decision-making.
Earth law adds to this list, ensuring that Earth remains a viable habitat for
humans, other species, and future generations, with the understanding that
this involves prospectively caring for ecosystems, preserving biodiversity,
restoring damaged ecosystems and loss of biodiversity, and justly sharing the
burdens of mitigating and adapting to climate change and other
environmental stresses.
Developments that have already taken place in Earth law, as discussed in this
book, raise questions about whether Earth law can operate within the
strictures of conventional Western law. For example, plaintiffs in
atmospheric trust litigation cases argue for expansion of the doctrine of the
public trust to include protection of the atmosphere from greenhouse gas
(GHG) emissions. The most important of these cases in the United States is
Juliana v. United States. In this case, the plaintiffs, a group of young people,
alleged that agencies of the U.S. government had—with knowledge that the
life, liberty, and happiness of the plaintiffs would be endangered—permitted,

encouraged, and otherwise enabled fossil fuel production and the use and
escalation of atmospheric CO2 emissions to the detriment of the plaintiffs in
violation of their constitutional rights to due process under the Fifth
Amendment and to equal protection under the 14th Amendment, and, further,
that the defendants had violated the public trust doctrine secured by the Ninth
and Tenth Amendments to the Constitution.
The public trust doctrine goes back to the Code of Justinian in ancient Rome.
It is a limitation on the power of the sovereign and an imposition of a duty on
the sovereign. The fundamental idea is that the sovereign must protect—that
is, hold in trust—the resource base on which present and future generations
depend. It is a duty that cannot be abdicated, and petition may be made to
courts to hold the sovereign accountable.
With respect to this doctrine, there are at least two areas where the Juliana
case breaks new ground. First, one interpretation of the public trust doctrine
in the United States is that it only applies to states, not to the federal
government itself. There are existing legal theories and precedents for
arguing that there is a federal public trust doctrine as well, so this area is not
as novel as the next. Second, the public trust doctrine has never been invoked
to require such a sweeping set of remedies as those proposed in Juliana,
namely that the defendants be enjoined from further violation of the
Constitution and the public trust, and that defendants “prepare and implement
an enforceable national remedial plan to phase out fossil fuel emissions and
draw down excess atmospheric CO2 so as to stabilize the climate system and
protect the vital resources on which plaintiffs now and in the future will
depend.”65
This case raises questions about whether the plaintiffs’ claims are justiciable
on the ground that they involve political issues that should be resolved by the
legislative and executive branches of government rather than the judicial
branch and, also, whether the plaintiffs lack standing on the basis of lack of
redressability—lack of redressability means a court is not able to fashion a
remedy for the injuries claimed. To overcome these defenses requires
sufficient evidence to support the argument that the situation presented is
extraordinary and the courts are the last resort for the plaintiffs. There must
be persuasive evidence that the other political branches have proven to be

incapable of dealing with climate destabilization. It is not enough to prove
that the government facilitated the use of fossil fuels, which has led to the
destabilization. Their prayer for relief through the issuance of an injunction,
which must always be justified on the basis of the need for this extraordinary
remedy, argues that the extraordinary injunction they seek is justified by the
exceptionally extraordinary need to address climate change.66
Another example of where Earth law has broken with conventional Western
law is in constitutional amendments and statutes in Bolivia, Ecuador, and
other jurisdictions that grant rights to nature and, in some cases, give any
citizen the ability to enforce the rights.
A final example, though many others could be given, concerns co-
governance between states and indigenous people. Under the 1840 Treaty of
Waitangi, signed by representatives of the British Crown and Māori chiefs,
New Zealand became part of the British Empire. For over 700 years, Māori
lived in harmony with and depended on the Whanganui River. It was their
awa tupua, river of sacred power. Although the Treaty guaranteed the Māori
the paramount authority they had exercised for time immemorial over their
lands, habitations, and all that they treasured, it was dishonored from its
inception. In 1975 the Treaty of Waitangi Act established the Waitangi
Tribunal to hear claims of the Crown’s violations to address those concerns.
In 2017, Parliament passed legislation declaring that Te Awa Tupua—the
river and all its physical and metaphysical elements—is an indivisible, living
whole, and henceforth possesses “all the rights, powers, duties, and
liabilities” of a legal person. The law appoints two guardians to serve as its
voice in legal proceedings.
Earth law has come into being out of the conviction that humans are facing
an existential crisis because they are living in a way that violates the great
law—the laws of nature—and that human laws must conform to the great law
with due recognition of the extraordinary measures that need to be taken at
this time. It further recognizes the inability of conventional Western law to
address the present and threatened harms, much of which will be irreversible.
Within this context, a dimension of time is frighteningly relevant. Given the
proximity and imminence of tipping points and feedback loops of nature,
Earth Law practitioners must ask how the law can best be invoked—deficient

as it may be—to prevent actions that would irrevocably unravel life-
sustaining systems.
XI. THE NEW SOCIAL CONTRACT: CULTURE,
DEMOCRACY, JUSTICE, EQUITY, AND PEACE
A body of law in response to the novel environmental conditions of the
Anthropocene is not optional, but the form that this body of law will take is.
Law can continue to take nature against the grain, seeking mastery and
control of it, or law may be based on working with nature under a new social
contract. The latter is Earth law.
Enlightenment thinking, the Industrial Revolution, technology, markets,
capitalism, liberalism, and representative democracy have led to great
historical achievements. Because they have brought about unprecedented
economic growth and material wealth, they are now sustained by the
narratives that endless growth is possible, and that technology can overcome
any limits nature imposes. Bruce Jennings speaks for many when he observes
that we now have a social contract—the old social contract—in which
“ordinary citizens, the demos, have given elites political control in exchange
for the promise and performance of economic growth and material
affluence.”67 This contract is now fraying because a greater and greater
concentration of wealth is occurring while many find their living and working
conditions stagnating or declining. At the same time, the old social contract is
being reinforced because people at both the bottom and the top of the scale
express a desperation to keep the old social contract in place by entrusting
leadership to those who will roll back environmental and health regulations in
hopes of spurring further industrial growth and trickle-down benefits.
As discussed in Section III of this Chapter, many believe this is no longer
tenable. We are crossing thresholds we dare not cross. The old social contract
can no longer ensure the health, safety, and welfare of people because of
natural limits that technology cannot transcend. As Lester Brown wrote, these
limits are not susceptible to political negotiation.68 Climate change is either
real or it is not. The outcome will not change because a political party does
not believe in climate change. The situation presents a novel political

problem, however, because those who push for a new social contract cannot
prove with certainty what will happen as a result of global warming in the
future or that technology will be unable to solve or avoid the problems that
might arise. The pattern in the past has been to wait for disaster to happen,
then deal with it. Response to climate change, however, requires acting in
uncertainty and incurring present sacrifice to avoid disasters that will happen
later if action is not taken now.
Already, there are natural interventions that require immediate responses:
fires, extreme heatwaves, droughts, water shortages, flooding of small islands
and low-lying coastlines, and much more. These are more than warnings of
what will happen; they are present disasters. Jennings observes that the
narrative that we can continuously adapt nature to human will and activity is
an illusion born of hubris: “Earlier natural limits were overcome not because
they were truly superseded, but most often because science and technology
found ways to tap into natural pathways and potentialities so that the
resilience of natural systems could handle the burden human extraction and
excretion [i.e., waste disposal,] were placing on them.”69 He then asks the
supreme question of our time: “Have we reached at last a kind of
thermodynamic and ecosystemic bedrock?…Can we reengineer the global
atmosphere, or is geophysical fluid dynamics at last saying to us: ‘Enough is
enough, change your way of living or reap the whirlwind!’?”70
There will be laws in response to changes in nature that come out of the old
social contract and there will be laws in response that come out of a new
ecological social contract. Earth law, as presented in this coursebook, comes
out of the latter. This could be seen as a kind of capitulation, a settling for
less. Clearly the authors of this book reject that characterization. We see it as
an optimal choice, one that is a recognition of what we have learned about
Earth from our science, an acceptance of reality, an embrace of Earth
community, and a doorway to freedom, within the limits of nature, to cultural
and social revitalization and to the flourishing of life on Earth.71
The shift from one social contract to the next will not take place all at once.
The changes will be contested and will accelerate over an extended period of
time. The changes do not just involve law, but law and lawyers are necessary
to bring about the needed changes. Lawyers bring a particular set of skills to

the transition. Ultimately the result will be decided, not in theory, but as the
subtitle of this book suggests, in practice.
The Anthropocene will test the ability of democracies to make long-range
plans to deal with future threats. Further, as discussed above, Earth law must
ultimately be based on a new ecological social contract and a new political
alignment. The impulses individually and at the level of international
relations to domination, control, material consumption, the accumulation of
wealth, and military power are real, but, if we are to have a habitable planet
and a viable human future, they must give way to collaboration and shared
responsibility for the care of our planet. The crisis to which Earth law is a
response is one of peril and possibility—the ending of the old and the
discontinuous transition to a new era of greater justice, equity, and peace. All
disciplines will be affected. Law will be an essential part of the transition.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) The second paragraph of this chapter describes the purposes of Earth law.
Earth law is “the legal framework needed so that humans
a. live within planetary boundaries,
b. prospectively care for ecosystems
c. preserve biodiversity,
d. restore damaged ecosystems and loss of biodiversity, and
e. justly share the burdens of mitigating and adapting to climate change and
other environmental stresses.”
How would you define Earth law? Would you distinguish it from
environmental law, and, if so, how?
(2) Proponents of the designation Anthropocene epoch argue that we have
moved into a new geo-biological period in Earth’s history. While people
commonly speak of an ecological crisis, this may be misleading because a
crisis is usually thought of as a short-term situation but, if we have entered

the Anthropocene epoch, we have entered a new ecological condition that
will be of long duration. Would you distinguish the ecological conditions that
brought into being environmental law in the 1960s from the conditions that
are bringing Earth law into being in the 2020s? If so, how?
(3) In contemporary Western studies of jurisprudence, the focus has been on
justice and procedural issues and not on the philosophical foundations of law.
In what ways, if any, do you think the Anthropocene epoch and Earth law
challenge the existing philosophical foundations of Western law?
(4) There are many components, living and nonliving, of nature (which
includes humans). If nature has rights, how would a court decide among
conflicting rights? For example, consider a situation in which an Indigenous
community in Alaska has hunted whales for centuries. The community
particularly prizes hunting a certain species of whales that has dwindled to
the point where it is now endangered. If you were the judge in a lawsuit
challenging the community’s hunting of the whales, what considerations
would guide you in determining whether the rights of the Indigenous people
to hunt or the rights of the whales should prevail?
(5) Assuming that nature has rights, name some of those rights and describe
how those rights might be protected in the legal system? Assuming that
humans have obligations to or responsibilities for nature, name some of those
responsibilities and how those responsibilities might be enforced in the legal
system?
(6) Earth law is sometimes called ecocentric law. How would law change if it
were ecocentric rather than anthropocentric? Western law emphasizes
individual and human-entity rights and freedoms. Ecologists emphasize
protection of nature against harms by humans. These harms are currently
regarded as both economic and legal externalities and, as such, are not taken
into account. Further, ecologists call attention to global, regional, and local
effects in assessing these harms. If ecology were the basis of law, how would
legal thinking be changed? Suppose a developer has applied for a permit to
build 500 homes in an old-growth forest. The development is opposed by a
nonprofit environmental group. Give traditional arguments for the developer
and the nonprofit group. If the tribunal were governed by Earth law, how
would your arguments change?

(7) Many environmental disputes are decided not on the merits but on the
basis of who has the money to engage in prolonged litigation. Great attention
in these disputes is given to whether damaging behavior is prohibited by the
letter of the law, whether proper procedure has been followed, whether a
court has jurisdiction, and whether the law provides for a remedy. Given the
complexity of nature, is it possible to protect nature based on the rule of (the
letter of the) law? Should there be special ecological courts for deciding these
disputes? How could the legal system be modified to have the latitude to deal
with the complexity of nature and of human-nature relations so that more
attention is given to the harm caused and restorative justice rather than to
positive law and procedure while still protecting the rights of defendants?
(8) If you were to draw up a new ecological social contract, what elements
would you include in that contract?
