inherit a land capable of sustaining life?
IV. THE PUBLIC TRUST DOCTRINE: FROM
CONCEPT TO A LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE

DUTY TO PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT
FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS
As discussed in the preceding chapter, the public trust doctrine is built on the
principle that the power of governing is a trust committed by the people to
the government, no part of which can be granted away. Not even statutes can
supersede a government’s public trust obligations to protect the
environment.41 With respect to future generations, a sovereign’s public trust
obligations prevent it from “depriving a future legislature of the natural
resources necessary to provide for the well-being and survival of its
citizens.”42
The public trust doctrine has a prominent role in the development of Earth
law within our legal system because it requires sovereign governments to
protect the land, water, wildlife, and other parts of nature for the benefit of
the public. In this context, this section looks more closely at what an attorney
asserting the right of future generations to a habitable Earth could argue
under the public trust doctrine. Specifically, such an attorney could assert that
(1) the government is a trustee, (2) future generations are beneficiaries, (3)
the environment or nature as broadly defined is the subject (or the “res”), and
(4) the government has a fiduciary duty to sustain certain ecological
processes.
A. Trustees: All Levels of Government
The United States is a democracy that can be described as a dual sovereignty.
That is, the Constitution gives the state governments all powers that are not
assigned exclusively to the federal government.43 Since the doctrine of public
trust is built on the principle that the power of governing is a trust committed
by the people to the government, it is logical that in the United States, both
the state and federal governments serve the role as trustee consistent with
each government’s respective authority. To put it simply, they are co-trustees
of the environment. With that introduction, let us look at the rights of future
generations at the state and then the federal level.
1. Domestic state governments as trustee of the environment for future

generations
As explored in Chapter 7, the public trust doctrine is most familiar in the
context of states. The next chapter, “The Rights of Nature Movement in the
U.S.,” examines state constitutions in the context of developing law to
explicitly recognize fundamental rights of nature. By way of example, the
Pennsylvania Constitution provides as follows:
The people have a right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the
natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment.
Pennsylvania’s public natural resources are the common property of all the
people, including generations yet to come. As trustee of these resources, the
Commonwealth shall conserve and maintain them for the benefit of all the
people.”44
The Hawai’i’ Constitution likewise provides:
For the benefit of present and future generations, the State and its political
subdivisions shall conserve and protect Hawaii’s natural beauty and all
natural resources, including land, water, air, minerals and energy sources, and
shall promote the development and utilization of these resources in a manner
consistent with their conservation and in furtherance of the self-sufficiency of
the State. All public natural resources are held in trust by the State for the
benefit of the people.45
While these written sources of law establish strong precedent for the
development of rights of future generations, it is important to remember that
a state’s obligations under the public trust doctrine are inherent and thus not
reliant on codification by the legislature.46
2. The Federal government as trustee of the environment for future
generations
As discussed above, there is ample support for public trust claims as they
pertain to state governments. However, the public trust doctrine has not been
widely applied at the federal level.47 While the state government’s public
trust obligations are more explicitly stated, the federal government’s public

trust obligations, including to future generations, are increasingly important
due to the global scope of ecological threats. For example, the Juliana case
seeks public trust accountability for future generations to be borne by the
federal government since climate change is best addressed through sweeping
federal action. NEPA is another example where the federal government was
envisioned as serving a trustee role on behalf of future generations.
3. Indigenous tribes as trustees of the environment for future generations
Tribal sovereignty in the United States is the concept of the inherent authority
of Indigenous tribes to govern themselves within the borders of the United
States. Professor Wood explains that “[a]s the original governments across
the land, tribes possess inherent sovereignty pre-existing the federal
government or any state.”48 In the development of Earth law, tribes may take
their rightful place as co-trustees with federal or state governments of shared
ecological assets.
The role of trustee for the Earth and future generations is inherent in
Indigenous customary law. Recall the Bemidji Statement:49
The health and well-being of our grandchildren are worth more than all the
wealth that can be taken from these lands. By returning to the collective
empowerment and decision making that is part of our history, we are able to
envision a future that will restore and protect the inheritance of this, and
future generations.
Therefore, we will designate Guardians for the Seventh Generation.
Chapter 25, “Indigenous Legalities,” and Chapter 6, “Guardianship
Arrangements in Rights of Nature Provisions,” discuss this concept in greater
detail.
B. Beneficiaries: Current and Future Generations
Looking to the future through a connected time continuum is at the center of
the public trust doctrine. As the Supreme Court explained in Newton v.
Mahoning Cnty. Comm’rs, 100 U.S. 548, 559 (1879) “[e]very succeeding

legislature possesses the same jurisdiction and power with respect to [the
public trust] as its predecessors.” A government’s public trust obligations
prevent it from “depriving a future legislature of the natural resources
necessary to provide for the well-being and survival of its citizens.”50
In establishing the United States Constitution, the Founding Fathers were
explicit about forming a government structure that secured “the Blessings of
Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity.”51 The word posterity means
descendants and future generations. Recall Professor Wood’s point that
including posterity in the Preamble to the Constitution “underscores an
inalienable duty ingrained in government itself as part of its constituted
purpose: to govern for the endurance of the nation, and thus for the benefit of
future generations as well as present ones.”
Judge Staton’s dissent in the 2020 Ninth Circuit Juliana case observes that
the harm from climate change is unique in “not just its magnitude, but its
irreversibility” and that the “devastation might look and feel somewhat
different if future generations could simply pick up the pieces and restore the
Nation.” Judge Staton also observed that the “perpetuity of the Republic” is a
fundamental underpinning of the U.S. Constitution’s structure that serves as
the “guardian of all other rights.” Simply stated, without the organized
society known as the United States, “all the liberties protected by the [United
States] Constitution” are “meaningless.” In emphasizing this point, the
dissent recalled President George Washington’s 1783 Circular Letter of
Farewell to the Army in which Washington recognized, “the destiny of
unborn millions” rested on the fate of the nation itself.52
Other nations’ courts have recognized the principle. In Reliance Natural Res.,
Ltd. v. Reliance Indus., Ltd., the Supreme Court of India explained:
[t]he concept of people as a nation does not include just the living; it includes
those who are unborn and waiting to be instantiated. Conservation of
resources, especially scarce ones, is both a matter of efficient use to alleviate
the suffering of the living and also of ensuring that such use does not lead to
diminishment of the prospects of their use by future generations.”53
Similarly, as discussed below, the Philippines Supreme Court has made clear

that “The right to a balanced and healthful ecology…concerns nothing less
than self-preservation and self-perpetuation.”54
C. The Subject of the Trust—the “Res” or “Corpus”
Public trust doctrine case law has expanded “the trust” far beyond navigable
waters. Beginning with the proposition that “the essential feature of the
public trust [is] the right of the people to have the waters protected for their
use,” the Supreme Court of Hawaii, in In re Water Use Permit Applications,
9 P.3d 409, 458 (Haw. 2000), went a step further and held “the state water
resources trust…demands adequate provision for traditional and customary
Hawaiian rights, wildlife, maintenance of ecological balance and scenic
beauty, and the preservation and enhancement of the waters for various uses
in the public interest.” The “body” of the trust (corpus is Latin for “body”)
has traditionally been described as the property protected by the trust. Also
known as the trust res, through the judicial development of the public trust
doctrine, the corpus has been recognized to include legal rights.
Some cases have cast the subject of the trust in terms of the current and future
condition of the environment as an ecological whole. In Robinson Twp.,
Washington Cty. v. Commonwealth, 83 A.3d 901, 955 (Pa. 2013), the court
found that “the concept of public natural resources includes not only state-
owned lands, waterways, and mineral reserves, but also the resources that
implicate the public interest, such as ambient air, surface and groundwater,
wild flora, and fauna (including fish) that are outside the scope of purely
private property.” Similarly, in Just v. Marionette County, 56 Wis. 2d 7, 16-
17 (1972), the court explained the development of the breadth of the public
trust doctrine in relation to advancements in scientific understandings of
complex and interrelated ecosystems:
The state of Wisconsin under the trust doctrine has a duty to eradicate the
present pollution and to prevent further pollution in its navigable waters…
What makes this case different from most condemnation or police power
zoning cases is the interrelationship of the wetlands, the swamps and the
natural environment of shorelands to the purity of the water and to such
natural resources as navigation, fishing, and scenic beauty. Swamps and
wetlands were once considered wasteland, undesirable, and not picturesque.

But as the people became more sophisticated, an appreciation was acquired
that swamps and wetlands serve a vital role in nature, are part of the balance
of nature and are essential to the purity of the water in our lakes and streams.
Swamps and wetlands are a necessary part of the ecological creation and
now, even to the uninitiated, possess their own beauty in nature.”55
Professor Wood’s Nature’s Trust paradigm supports a similarly broad
application of the public trust doctrine. She argues for a holistic conception of
the res, or subject of the trust, that “[encompasses] all natural assets and
ecology.”56 This approach, she argues, “brings the public trust doctrine in
alignment with Nature’s own laws and resurrects the original doctrine with
the range necessary to carry out its purpose not only for this generation, but
also for those to come.”57
D. The Fiduciary Duty: To Sustain the Welfare of Current and
Future Generations
Once the government is established as a trustee, present and future people as
the beneficiaries, and balanced and healthy systems as the subject of the trust,
the last component to determine is the fiduciary duty. Courts have considered
what fiduciary duty entails in many contexts: attorney-client disputes,
financial advisor-customer disputes, insurer-policyholder disputes, and
disputes in trusts and estates law.58 While the description of the duties vary,
in all contexts the duties owed to the beneficiaries are both procedural and
substantive. Over thirty years ago, advocating for the concept of a planetary
trust, Professor Edith Brown Weiss put forth her vision of the government’s
duty that was based in part on the 1980 World Conservation Strategy:59
The basic purpose of the [the Planetary Trust] is to sustain the welfare of
future generations. This purpose can be broken down into three sub-purposes:
to sustain the life-support systems of the planet; to sustain the ecological
processes and environmental conditions necessary for the survival of the
human species; and to sustain a healthy and decent environment.60
In Nature’s Trust, written 20 years later with the environment substantially
more degraded, Professor Mary Wood posits a more demanding duty than
identified by Weiss. She delineates six substantive fiduciary duties of a

public trust trustee:
1) to protect the environment;
2) to conserve the “natural inheritance of future generations”;
3) to maximize the “societal value of natural resources”;
4) to restore the environment where it is degraded;
5) to “recover natural resource damages from third parties that injured the
environment”; and
6) to refrain from privatizing the trust except in limited circumstances.61
Wood concludes with an inspiring vision of a nature’s trust concept:
If citizen beneficiaries and courts hold public officials accountable to these
obligations, environmental management will aim toward replenishment,
rather than depletion, of the natural commonwealth—and the people’s
interests, rather than corporate interests, will rank supreme in ecological
decision making. Viewed in aggregate, these obligations present a necessary
paradigm shift in environmental law.62
Establishing a fiduciary duty to protect the Earth we live on today for
sustainable life by future generations is an extraordinarily difficult legal
objective, despite its conceptual existence since the time of the Roman
Empire and in Indigenous customary law before then. As the law responds to
the increasingly dire need for a legal solution that may protect the future of
nations and their posterity, the development of the public trust doctrine into a
nature’s trust or planetary trust can play a meaningful role.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) In their articulation of the public trust, are the state supreme court
decisions In re Water Use Permit Applications; Robinson Twp., Washington
Cty. v. Commonwealth; Marks v. Whitney; and Just v. Marionette County
cited above consistent with the International Union for Conservation of

Nature Species Survival Commission’s statement? What is at the core of
these judicial opinions and the IUCN plea? How do they relate to protecting
the rights of future generations?
(2) How do the statements made in these cases tie into Professor Brown’s
Planetary Trust and Professor Wood’s Nature’s Trust reviewed above? And
how might this all tie into the fiduciary duty owed to future generations?
(3) How might a planetary trust be different in application if instead of the six
substantive fiduciary duties delineated by Wood, there was only one: to
conserve the natural inheritance of future generations? How might the
“inheritance” be defined in practice?
V. CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS FOR FUTURE
GENERATIONS
At the national level, Bolivia, Norway, and South Africa constitutionally
recognize the rights of future generations to a healthy environment. The
Constitution of Bolivia states: “Every person has the following fundamental
rights…to enjoy a healthy environment, ecologically balanced and adequate
for his wellbeing, safeguarding the rights of future generations.” The
Constitution of the Kingdom of Norway states: “Every person has a right to
an environment that is conducive to health and to a natural environment
whose productivity and diversity are maintained. Natural resources should be
managed on the basis of comprehensive long-term considerations whereby
this right will be safeguarded for future generations as well.” The Republic of
South Africa’s Bill of Rights, found in Chapter 2 of its Constitution, provides
that “Everyone has the right—to have the environment protected, for the
benefit of present and future generations.…”
While the development of Earth law based on national constitutional
recognition of rights of future generations may be more well-grounded than
other approaches, it seems unlikely that the U.S. Congress will soon pass
such an amendment. Nevertheless, there is ample opportunity to develop the
rights of future generations in the state context.

A. U.S. State-Level Constitutional Rights for Future
Generations
As discussed above, some state constitutions provide for protection of the
environment for the current and future generations. Pennsylvania’s Supreme
Court interpreted its Commonwealth’s constitutional guarantee in
Pennsylvania Environmental Defense Foundation v. Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, 161 A.3d 911 (Penn. 2017). The Court found that the state has
a constitutional obligation to manage state parks and forests, including the oil
and gas they contain, as a trustee, with present and future generations as the
named beneficiaries of the trust. As part of the reasoning for its decision, the
Court described the history and purpose of Section 27 as follows:
That Pennsylvania deliberately chose a course different from virtually all of
its sister states speaks to the Commonwealth’s experience of having the
benefit of vast natural resources whose virtually unrestrained exploitation,
while initially a boon to investors, industry, and citizens, led to destructive
and lasting consequences not only for the environment but also for the
citizens’ quality of life. Later generations paid and continue to pay a tribute to
early uncontrolled and unsustainable development financially, in health and
quality of life consequences, and with the relegation to history books of
valuable natural and esthetic aspects of our environmental inheritance. The
drafters and the citizens of the Commonwealth who ratified the
Environmental Rights Amendment, aware of this history, articulated the
people’s rights and the government’s duties to the people in broad and
flexible terms that would permit not only reactive but also anticipatory
protection of the environment for the benefit of current and future
generations.63
During the case, a question arose as to whether Section 27 is self-executing,
meaning whether the judiciary can enforce the provision without the aid of a
legislative enactment. An amicus curiae in the case, the Republican caucus,
argued that the rights enumerated in Section 27 are not self-executing and
therefore needed implementing legislation to become effective for the benefit
of current and future generations. However, the Court disagreed:
There can be no question that the Amendment itself declares and creates a

public trust of public natural resources for the benefit of all the people
(including future generations as yet unborn) and that the Commonwealth is
made the trustee of said resources, commanded to conserve and maintain
them. No implementing legislation is needed to enunciate these broad
purposes and establish these relationships; the [A]mendment does so by its
own ipse dixit.64
This case set a precedent for applying the public trust doctrine to protect the
rights of future generations at the state level in the United States. Federally,
recognizing the rights of future generations has been more of a challenge.
B. U.S. Federal-Level Constitutional Rights for Future
Generations
Unlike some other countries, the U.S. Constitution does not articulate a
fundamental right for future generations to a habitable Earth. Nor has the
Supreme Court yet found such a right arising from the Constitution.
However, scholars65 and litigators66 alike have argued that the Fifth
Amendment’s Due Process Clause and Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal
Protection Clause require the federal government to uphold the right to a
healthy environment, including a stable climate system, for both present and
future generations.
“Future generations,” as represented by guardian James Hansen, asserted
their constitutional right to a stable climate in Juliana v. United States.
However, the U.S. district court dismissed the case for lack of standing
before ruling on whether future generations were capable of holding this
right.67 As long as lawyers continue litigating on behalf of future generations,
opportunities to develop Earth law expand.
C. Minors Oposa: A Landmark Decision in the Philippines
As the constitutional embodiment of rights of future generations continues to
progress, more courts will also examine the concept. The most deeply
developed common law recognizing the rights of future generations is the
Philippines Supreme Court’s decision in Minors Oposa v. Sec. of the Dept of
Env. & Natural Resource. This opinion provides an expansive and

comprehensive interpretation of the rights of future generations to a healthy
environment in the absence of any constitutional authority. In this case, the
Philippine Supreme Court was presented with the question of whether the
Philippine Constitution confers a right to a “balanced and healthful ecology”
for not just the current generation of its people, but also future generations.
The 2018 Companion to Global Judicial Handbook on Environmental
Constitutionalism: Selected Cases and Materials, Selected Edited Judicial
Opinions from Around the Globe provides a comprehensive edited version of
Minors Oposa, which is excerpted below.
Juan Antonio, Anna Rosario and Jose Alfonso Oposa & Others v. The
Honorable Fulgencio S. Factoran, Jr.
(Supreme Court of the Philippines, 1993)
The court recognized the principle of intergenerational justice and granted
standing to petitioners, who represented their generation and generations of
unborn Filipinos in a petition opposing timber license agreements.
This petition bears upon the right of Filipinos to a balanced and healthful
ecology which the petitioners dramatically associate with the twin concepts
of “inter-generational responsibility” and “inter-generational justice.”
Specifically, it touches on the issue of whether the said petitioners have a
cause of action to “prevent the misappropriation or impairment” of Philippine
rainforests and “arrest the unabated hemorrhage of the country’s vital life
support systems and continued rape of Mother Earth.”
The principal petitioners [include] all minors duly represented and joined by
their respective parents, [and the minors] further asseverate that they
“represent their generation as well as generations yet unborn.” Consequently,
it is prayed for that judgment be rendered:
…ordering defendant, his agents, representatives and other persons acting in
his behalf to—
(1) Cancel all existing timber license agreements in the country;
(2) Cease and desist from receiving, accepting, processing, renewing or

approving new timber license agreements. and granting the plaintiffs “…such
other reliefs just and equitable under the premises.”
The complaint starts off with the general averments that the Philippine
archipelago of 7,100 islands has a land area of thirty million (30,000,000)
hectares and is endowed with rich, lush and verdant rainforests in which
varied, rare and unique species of flora and fauna may be found; these
rainforests contain a genetic, biological and chemical pool which is
irreplaceable; they are also the habitat of Indigenous Philippine cultures
which have existed, endured and flourished since time immemorial; scientific
evidence reveals that in order to maintain a balanced and healthful ecology,
the country’s land area should be utilized on the basis of a ratio of fifty-four
per cent (54%) for forest cover and forty-six per cent (46%) for agricultural,
residential, industrial, commercial and other uses; the distortion and
disturbance of this balance as a consequence of deforestation have resulted in
a host of environmental tragedies, such as (a) 15 water shortages resulting
from drying up of the water table, otherwise known as the “aquifer,” as well
as of rivers, brooks and streams, (b) salinization of the water table as a result
of the intrusion therein of salt water, incontrovertible examples of which may
be found in the island of Cebu and the Municipality of Bacoor, Cavite, (c)
massive erosion and the consequential loss of soil fertility and agricultural
productivity, with the volume of soil eroded estimated at one billion
(1,000,000,000) cubic meters per annum—approximately the size of the
entire island of Catanduanes, (d) the endangering and extinction of the
country’s unique, rare and varied flora and fauna, (e) the disturbance and
dislocation of cultural communities, including the disappearance of the
Filipino’s Indigenous cultures, (f) the siltation of rivers and seabeds and
consequential destruction of corals and other aquatic life leading to a critical
reduction in marine resource productivity, (g) recurrent spells of drought as is
presently experienced by the entire country, (h) increasing velocity of
typhoon winds which result from the absence of windbreakers, (i) the
floodings of lowlands and agricultural plains arising from the absence of the
absorbent mechanism of forests, (j) the siltation and shortening of the
lifespan of multi-billion peso dams constructed and operated for the purpose
of supplying water for domestic uses, irrigation and the generation of electric
power, and (k) the reduction of the earth’s capacity to process carbon dioxide
gases which has led to perplexing and catastrophic climatic changes such as

the phenomenon of global warming, otherwise known as the “greenhouse
effect.”
As their cause of action, they specifically allege that:
CAUSE OF ACTION
7. Plaintiffs replead by reference the foregoing allegations.
8. Twenty-five (25) years ago, the Philippines had some sixteen (16) million
hectares of rainforests constituting roughly 53% of the country’s land mass.
9. Satellite images taken in 1987 reveal that there remained no more than 1.2
million hectares of said rainforests or four per cent (4.0%) of the country’s
land area.
10. More recent surveys reveal that a mere 850,000 hectares of virgin old
growth rainforests are left, barely 2.8% of the entire land mass of the
Philippine archipelago and about 3.0 million hectares of immature and
uneconomical secondary growth forests.
11. Public records reveal that the defendants’ predecessors have granted
timber license agreements (“TLA’s”) to various corporations to cut the
aggregate area of 3.89 million hectares for commercial logging purposes.…
12. At the present rate of deforestation, i.e. about 200,000 hectares per annum
or 25 hectares per hour—nighttime, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays
included—the Philippines will be bereft of forest resources after the end of
this ensuing decade, if not earlier.
13. The adverse effects, disastrous consequences, serious injury and
irreparable damage of this continued trend of deforestation to the plaintiff
minors’ generation and to generations yet unborn are evident and
incontrovertible. As a matter of fact, the environmental damages enumerated
in paragraph 6 hereof are already being felt, experienced and suffered by the
generation of plaintiff adults.
14. The continued allowance by defendant of TLA holders to cut and deforest

the remaining forest stands will work great damage and irreparable injury to
plaintiffs—especially plaintiff minors and their successors—who may never
see, use, benefit from and enjoy this rare and unique natural resource
treasure. This act of defendant constitutes a misappropriation and/or
impairment of the natural resource property he holds in trust for the benefit of
plaintiff minors and succeeding generations.
15. Plaintiffs have a clear and constitutional right to a balanced and healthful
ecology and are entitled to protection by the State in its capacity as parens
patriae.
16. Plaintiff[s] have exhausted all administrative remedies with the
defendant’s office. On March 2, 1990, plaintiffs served upon defendant a
final demand to cancel all logging permits in the country.…
17. Defendant, however, fails and refuses to cancel the existing TLA’s to the
continuing serious damage and extreme prejudice of plaintiffs.
18. The continued failure and refusal by defendant to cancel the TLA’s is an
act violative of the rights of plaintiffs, especially plaintiff minors who may be
left with a country that is desertified (sic), bare, barren and devoid of the
wonderful flora, fauna and Indigenous cultures which the Philippines had
been abundantly blessed with.
20. Furthermore, defendant’s continued refusal to cancel the aforementioned
TLA’s is contradictory to the Constitutional policy of the State to—a. effect
“a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth” and
“make full and efficient use of natural resources (sic).” (Section 1, Article XII
of the Constitution); b. “protect the nation’s marine wealth.” (Section 2, ibid);
c. “conserve and promote the nation’s cultural heritage and resources (sic)”
(Section 14, Article XIV, id.); d. “protect and advance the right of the people
to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony
of nature.” (Section 16, Article II, id.)
21. Finally, defendant’s act is contrary to the highest law of humankind—the

22. There is no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy in law other than the

On 22 June 1990, the original defendant, Secretary Factoran, Jr., filed a
Motion to Dismiss the complaint based on two (2) grounds, namely: (1) the
plaintiffs have no cause of action against him and (2) the issue raised by the
plaintiffs is a political question which properly pertains to the legislative or
executive branches of Government.
Petitioners contend that the complaint clearly and unmistakably states a cause
of action as it contains sufficient allegations concerning their right to a sound
environment based on Articles 19, 20 and 21 of the Civil Code (Human
Relations), Section 4 of Executive Order (E.O.) No. 192 creating the DENR,
Section 3 of Presidential Decree (P.D.) No. 1151 (Philippine Environmental
Policy), Section 16, Article II of the 1987 Constitution recognizing the right
of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology, the concept of generational
genocide in Criminal Law and the concept of man’s inalienable right to self-
preservation and self-perpetuation embodied in natural law. Petitioners
likewise rely on the respondent’s correlative obligation per Section 4 of E.O.
No. 192, to safeguard the people’s right to a healthful environment.
This case, however, has a special and novel element. Petitioners minors assert
that they represent their generation as well as generations yet unborn. We
find no difficulty in ruling that they can, for themselves, for others of their
generation and for the succeeding generations, file a class suit. Their
personality to sue in behalf of the succeeding generations can only be based
on the concept of intergenerational responsibility insofar as the right to a
balanced and healthful ecology is concerned. Such a right, as hereinafter
expounded, considers the “rhythm and harmony of nature.” Nature means the
created world in its entirety.
Such rhythm and harmony indispensably include, inter alia, the judicious
disposition, utilization, management, renewal and conservation of the
country’s forest, mineral, land, waters, fisheries, wildlife, off-shore areas and
other natural resources to the end that their exploration, development and
utilization be equitably accessible to the present as well as future generations.
Needless to say, every generation has a responsibility to the next to preserve

that rhythm and harmony for the full enjoyment of a balanced and healthful
ecology. Put a little differently, the minors’ assertion of their right to a sound
environment constitutes, at the same time, the performance of their obligation
to ensure the protection of that right for the generations to come.
The locus standi of the petitioners having thus been addressed, We shall now
proceed to the merits of the petition.
After a careful perusal of the complaint in question and a meticulous
consideration and evaluation of the issues raised and arguments adduced by
the parties, we do not hesitate to find for the petitioners and rule against the
respondent Judge’s challenged order for having been issued with grave abuse
of discretion amounting to lack of jurisdiction.…
We do not agree with the trial court’s conclusions that the plaintiffs failed to
allege with sufficient definiteness a specific legal right involved or a specific
legal wrong committed, and that the complaint is replete with vague
assumptions and conclusions based on unverified data. A reading of the
complaint itself belies these conclusions. The complaint focuses on one
specific fundamental legal right—the right to a balanced and healthful
ecology which, for the first time in our nation’s constitutional history, is
solemnly incorporated in the fundamental law. Section 16, Article II of the
1987 Constitution explicitly provides:
Sec. 16. The State shall protect and advance the right of the people to a
balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of
nature.
This right unites with the right to health which is provided for in the
preceding section of the same article:
Sec. 15. The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people
and instill health consciousness among them.
While the right to a balanced and healthful ecology is to be found under the
Declaration of Principles and State Policies and not under the Bill of Rights,
it does not follow that it is less important than any of the civil and political
rights enumerated in the latter. Such a right belongs to a different category of

rights altogether for it concerns nothing less than self-preservation and self-
perpetuation—aptly and fittingly stressed by the petitioners—the
advancement of which may even be said to predate all governments and
constitutions. As a matter of fact, these basic rights need not even be written
in the Constitution for they are assumed to exist from the inception of
humankind. If they are now explicitly mentioned in the fundamental charter,
it is because of the well-founded fear of its framers that unless the rights to a
balanced and healthful ecology and to health are mandated as state policies
by the Constitution itself, thereby highlighting their continuing importance
and imposing upon the state a solemn obligation to preserve the first and
protect and advance the second, the day would not be too far when all else
would be lost not only for the present generation, but also for those to come
—generations which stand to inherit nothing but parched earth incapable of
sustaining life.
The right to a balanced and healthful ecology carries with it the correlative
duty to refrain from impairing the environment.…The said right implies,
among many other things, the judicious management and conservation of the
country’s forests. Without such forests, the ecological or environmental
balance would be irreversibly disrupted.
STUDY QUESTIONS
What might be the most promising ways to test U.S. state-level constitutional
rights for future generations? To gain recognition of federal-level
constitutional rights for future generations? To develop rights of future
generations through common law in the United States?
VI. STANDING FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS
CLAIMS IN THE UNITED STATES
As explained in Chapter 5, standing is a constitutional doctrine that
determines whether an aggrieved person is allowed to bring a claim (i.e.,
“stand”) before the court. Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 delineates only the
substantive limits of “[t]he Judicial Power” of the federal court system as the
adjudication of “Cases” and “Controversies” concerning “the Laws of the

United States, and Treaties.” From this basic limitation, the Supreme Court
has developed the requisite elements of standing over time through its case
law. By way of review, standing has three elements:
1. Injury: The plaintiffs’ alleged injury in fact must consist of an invasion
of a legally protected interest, which is (a) concrete and particularized,
and (b) “actual or imminent, not ‘conjectural’ or ‘hypothetical.’”
According to the Supreme Court, the element of “injury in fact” is a
“hard floor of Article III jurisdiction that cannot be removed by
statute.”68
2. Causation: The plaintiff must allege a causal connection between the
injury and the conduct complained of—the injury has to be fairly
traceable to the challenged action of the defendant, and not the result of
the independent action of some third party not before the court.69
3. Redressability: It must be “likely,” as opposed to merely “speculative,”
that the injury will be “redressed by a favorable decision.”70
The requirement of standing “tends to assure that the legal questions
presented to the court will be resolved, not in the rarified atmosphere of a
debating society, but in a concrete factual context conducive to a realistic
appreciation of the consequences of judicial action.”71 This section explores
the challenges and potential that an Earth law practitioner representing future
generations faces with respect to each of these elements.
A. Injury in Fact
The injury to a future generation plaintiff is the damage and destruction of the
Earth’s life-sustaining biosphere. As we explored earlier, that injury might
rest on claims that the government body(ies) breached their fiduciary duties
to protect natural resources under the public trust doctrine. The injury might
likewise be asserted as a violation of constitutional rights. Either way, it is
imperative for an attorney to plead a cognizable injury in fact to future
generations for purposes of Article III standing. Challenges to meeting this
first element of the standing test include establishing the environmental harm
or imminent threat to an ecosystem as an “injury in fact” and proving the
injury within the plaintiff’s lifetime.

Attorneys for future generation plaintiffs can learn from the difficulties that
members of the present generation have had establishing an injury in fact in
the context of Article III standing. For example, establishing that an injury is
sufficiently “imminent” to constitute an injury in the Article III context
requires a plaintiff to establish that it will occur within their lifetime. In Lujan
v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992), the Court ruled that the
plaintiffs had not shown how extinction of endangered animals would
produce any imminent injury to the plaintiff since they did not have any
definite, concrete plans to return to the countries and native habitats of the
animals.72 In 2004, the Eighth Circuit in Shain v. Veneman, 376 F.3d 815,
818 (8th Cir. 2004) found that the plaintiff lacked standing to challenge the
building of a sewage-treatment plant on a 100-year flood plain because the
possibility of a 100-year flood was not an “imminent harm.” In so holding,
the court stated: “If the possibility of a 100-year flood is remote in the
abstract, the possibility the flood will occur while [the plaintiffs] own or
occupy the land becomes a matter of sheer speculation. Indeed, one wonders
whether any of the parties (or the court) in this case will be alive the next
time a 100-year flood occurs upon the land.”
The Supreme Court has consistently recognized that threatened rather than
actual injury can satisfy Article III standing requirements.73 In Friends of the
Earth v. Laidlaw, the Supreme Court held that the threat of injury in fact is
sufficient to confer standing and that citizen affidavits attesting to reduced
use of a waterway out of reasonable fear and concern of pollution.74 Relying
on Laidlaw, in Ecological Rights Foundation v. Pac. Lumber, 230 F.3d 1141,
1148 (9th Cir. 2000), the court of appeals wrote that that “the ‘injury in fact’
requirement in environmental cases is not…reducible to inflexible, judicially
mandated time or distance guidelines, as Laidlaw makes clear.”75 Finally, in
Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Gaston Copper Recycling Corp., 204 F.3d 149,
160 (4th Cir. 2000), the court found that a threatened injury arising from
water pollution was enough to establish injury in fact. “[A plaintiff] need not
wait until his lake becomes barren and sterile or assumes an unpleasant color
and smell before he can invoke the protections of the Clean Water Act.”76
However, while severe damage to ecosystems—from neighborhood wetlands
to vast national forests—will occur within the lifetimes of future generations,
will the courts be able to say a harm is “actual and imminent” when the

lifetime of the plaintiff has not even begun? Turning back to Juliana,
although Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit did not address this issue
directly, it did agree with the plaintiffs that “…the federal government has
long promoted fossil fuel use despite knowing that it can cause catastrophic
climate change…”. It also found that the injury requirement was met for “at
least some plaintiffs,” such as one who was forced to leave her home due to
water scarcity. However, the court did not specifically address the injury to
future generations.
In practice, tying the harms of future generations to those harms faced by
current generations seems to be a viable solution. In Mass. v. EPA, the
Supreme Court considered affidavits alleging future harm to the state of
Massachusetts through the year 2100 from climate change, which of course
would implicate future generations. “The severity of that injury will only
increase over the course of the next century: If sea levels continue to rise as
predicted, one Massachusetts official believes that a significant fraction of
coastal property will be ‘either permanently lost through inundation or
temporarily lost through periodic storm surge and flooding events.’”77 The
Court then tied this future harm to current harm, finding that “at least
according to petitioners’ uncontested affidavits—the rise in sea levels
associated with global warming has already harmed and will continue to
harm Massachusetts. The risk of catastrophic harm, though remote, is
nevertheless real.”78 In this case, arguing that environmental harms impact
both present and future generations seemed to work in practice.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) The Eighth Circuit’s Shain v. Veneman decision demonstrates what might
be described as “gatekeeping” of scientific evidence by the judiciary. In
Shain v. Veneman, how could that court know, particularly in light of climate
change, when the area would or would not flood?
(2) In Lujan, on what basis does the Court conclude that species extinction
and damage to ecosystems (in itself) has no perceptible effect on human
plaintiffs? Does the opinion reflect an understanding or appreciation of
ecology? Why or why not? How might a court have considered these cases
applying the precautionary principle?

(3) In the United States, an individual state possesses quasi-sovereign
interests and, as such, can bring suits by acting as parens patriae (Latin for
“parent of the nation in law”) on behalf of its citizens. This legal doctrine
may permit a state’s attorney general to present a cognizable claim to protect
future generations. Do you think a state government can adequately represent
the interests of future generations? If not, who should have that
responsibility?
B. Causation: Injury Fairly Traceable to Challenged Conduct
The second element of the standing test examines the connection between the
alleged misconduct and the injury. The chain of causation for a future
generation plaintiff rests on the core allegation that the government, by
failing to protect the Earth’s biosphere, has breached its fiduciary duty to
protect the subject of the trust pursuant to the public trust doctrine. In so
doing, the government has also violated the fundamental rights of current and
future generations to a habitable Earth (at least and perhaps only within its
national borders). In addition to presenting evidence of harmful conduct that
ties injury to current and future generations together, meeting the causation
element of the standing test may require closely tracing the present conditions
complained of into the future.
Establishing that the injury to future generations is “fairly traceable to the
challenged conduct,” is the intergenerational connection discussed under the
“injury in fact” element applied in the causation context. Antonio Oposa, the
attorney who brought suit on behalf of himself, his children (Minors Oposa),
and others, including “unnamed children of the future,” provided the
Philippines Supreme Court with Brown Weiss’s Intergenerational Equity
article as “proof” that the legal concept of intergenerational equity was real.79
Whether as a direct result of reading the article or not, the court’s holding
expresses the concept:
the right to a balanced and healthful ecology belongs to a different category
of rights altogether for it concerns nothing less than self-preservation and
self-perpetuation…Without “a balanced and healthful ecology,” future
generations “stand to inherit nothing but parched earth incapable of
sustaining life;” moreover, “the right to a balanced and healthful ecology

carries with it the correlative duty to refrain from impairing the
environment.80
In the context of tracing the challenged conduct to future generations’
injuries, the degree of difficulty will increase the farther into the future the
future generations’ claims extend. One way to establish how future harm may
be connected to present-day wrongs is to rely on what science can reasonably
estimate. In Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.,81 the Supreme
Court established what is now known as the “Daubert standard” for courts to
use in assessing the reliability of scientific evidence. The key factors include:
1) Whether the expert’s technique or theory can be or has been tested—that
is, whether the expert’s theory can be challenged in some objective sense, or
whether it is instead simply a subjective, conclusory approach that cannot
reasonably be assessed for reliability; 2) whether the technique or theory has
been subject to peer review and publication; the known or potential rate of
error of the technique or theory when applied; 3) the existence and
maintenance of standards and controls; and 4) whether the technique or
theory has been generally accepted in the scientific community.82
In the context of recognizing the causal connections between present actions
and the effects on future generations, current science on the impacts of
present actions on the future might allow courts to consider the interests of
the future generations claimant within the next hundred years. The United
Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which draws on
expert opinions from around the world, has made detailed estimates and
projections concerning climate change through the year 2100.83 In finding
“the risk of catastrophic harm, though remote, is nevertheless real,” the
Supreme Court in Mass. v. EPA relied on the work of the IPCC in
recognizing the harm, demonstrated through climate modeling, facing the
petitioner over the next 100 years.84
C. Redressability—Will Judicial Relief Requested Relieve the
Harm
The third element of the standing test is redressability. Under this element, an
attorney representing future generations must establish the connection
between the alleged injury and the requested judicial relief. To establish

Article III redressability, the plaintiffs must show that the relief they seek is
both (1) substantially likely to redress their injuries; and (2) within the court’s
power to award. Redress need not be guaranteed, but it must be more than
“merely speculative.”85
In addition, the redressability element can be met by showing that the
requested remedy would slow or reduce the alleged injury. As explained in
Mass. v. EPA, “while it may be true that regulating motor-vehicle emissions
will not by itself reverse global warming, it by no means follows that we lack
jurisdiction to decide whether EPA has a duty to take steps to slow or reduce
it.”86
The recent Ninth Circuit decision in Juliana held that the plaintiffs did not
meet this second prong of “establishing that the specific relief they seek is
within the power of an Article III court.” The court reasoned:
There is much to recommend the adoption of a comprehensive scheme to
decrease fossil fuel emissions and combat climate change, both as a policy
matter in general and a matter of national survival in particular. But it is
beyond the power of an Article III court to order, design, supervise, or
implement the plaintiffs’ requested remedial plan. As the opinions of their
experts make plain, any effective plan would necessarily require a host of
complex policy decisions entrusted, for better or worse, to the wisdom and
discretion of the executive and legislative branches.”
As explained in this section, Article III standing requirements and the
jurisprudential considerations that have been developed through the arc of
application of this constitutional law present challenges to Earth law
practitioners who represent future generations claimants. They may be
difficult to overcome; however, encouragement directly from the Supreme
Court lies in Chief Justice Marshall’s statement in Marbury v. Madison, 5
U.S. 137 (1803): “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial
department to say what the law is.” Dismissing a case based on the standing
doctrine is a means for a court to avoid saying what the law is. If the time
comes that the Supreme Court determines that it is up to the judiciary to
exercise its constitutional power to protect the nation, and its people, present
and future, from further destruction of Earth’s sustaining power, it will

discern that the rights of future generations lies in the Founding Fathers’
original intent, or will through other means of judicial construction recognize
the existence of these rights.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Consider the additional issue that would have been presented if the youth
and future generation plaintiffs in Juliana were joined by a state. Recall the
majority opinion’s distinguishing Juliana from the Mass v. EPA decision:
That case, however, involved a procedural right that the State of
Massachusetts was allowed to assert “without meeting all the normal
standards for redressability;” in that context, the Court found redressability
because “there [was] some possibility that the requested relief [would]
prompt the injury-causing party to reconsider the decision that allegedly
harmed the litigant.” [Citation omitted.] The plaintiffs here do not assert a
procedural right, but rather a substantive due process claim.”87
(2) Decisions based on the technical legal criteria for standing can be viewed
as form over substance. In the context of claims by future generations, what
judicial objectives are served by adherence to formality? What arguments
might persuade a court that the benefit of considering a future generations
claim on the merits requires an exception to the adherence to legal
formalities?
VII. CONCLUSION
Future generations face an existential threat—the damage and destruction of
the Earth’s life-sustaining systems. As explored in this chapter, a legally
cognizable injury can rest on claims that governments have breached their
fiduciary duties to the governed as is established by the public trust doctrine;
the injury might concurrently be asserted as a violation of fundamental rights
to life, liberty, or the pursuit of happiness under the due process clauses.
Many judges will agree with the proposition that both sovereigns and private
actors should act to preserve our planet for the health and well-being of future

generations. Yet, it will difficult to find judges who will impose duties on
sovereigns and private actors based on the rights of, or a duty of care owed
to, future generations. Federal courts in the United States continue to defer to
the political branches of government and continue to interpret the Article III
standing elements as a barrier to plaintiffs seeking to protect the environment
for present and future generations. Compounding this problem is the federal
judiciary’s hesitancy to interpret its constitutional embedded power to
balance that of the legislative and executive branches.
Advancing the application of the public trust doctrine to protect future
generations will require lawyers to convince judges to embrace the wisdom
reflected in Indigenous customary law and culture and what modern science
has established through ecology and other disciplines—all life on Earth is
interconnected with the Earth systems that created life. As observed in the
CLI Paper on Intergeneration Justice: “The planet earth does not suffer and
submit beyond a point. Thereafter, it rejects species that do not comply with
its rules, which supervene all legal systems. The earth is the ultimate court of
appeals.”88
