CHAPTER 9
The Rights of Nature Movement in
the United States1
I. INTRODUCTION
Traditional legal practice models do not prepare lawyers to practice law in a
way that changes the law. One way that Earth law is being developed is by
practitioners who work within social movements seeking systemic change,
namely, changing ecosystems and other parts of the natural world from
property to beings with rights.
The development of rights for nature in the United States is starting at the
grassroots: in townships, cities large and small, and counties. It is now
building toward state-level lawmaking, even while opposed by powerful
corporate special interests. This chapter examines strategy, tactics, and skills
that have been utilized to develop rights of nature law in the United States
through movement lawyering. It considers how rights of nature in the United
States may follow the course of the development of the rights of corporations,
which once were as rightless as nature is today, and how corporations
exercise the rights they now have to thwart efforts to grant rights to nature. It
will also examine rights of nature expressed in the laws of Native American
nations.
II. HOW DID WE GET HERE?
Like its European antecedents, U.S. law reflects the concept of human
exceptionalism and dominion over nature. The U.S. legal system is based on

federal supremacy and the protection of individual property. The capitalistic
economy developed based on the belief that there will always be enough
“natural resources” to support “economic growth.”2 These foundational
principles reflect the rootstock of the United States’ legal system, which
values nature as a tradeable commodity based on its economic worth.3 In
stark contrast, Earth law does not treat nature merely as property, rather it
recognizes value in nature itself.
A. The Colonial Legacy
How did we get here? Beginning in the late-fifteenth century, European
explorers claimed sovereignty and ownership over the “New World”—
already inhabited by millions of Indigenous Americans—based on the
assumption that the Earth was human property to be acquired through
conquest or bargained for and exploited for economic gain and national pride.
Under the Doctrine of Discovery,4 the land was theirs for the taking. They
killed and displaced Indigenous people. Needing labor, they kidnapped,
enslaved, and killed Africans. The legal system that Europeans brought to the
“New World” protected their right to claim its land as their own and validated
genocide, slavery, and plunder of the environment.
The U.S. Constitution enshrined strong protections for commerce and
property rights. The Contract and Commerce Clauses protect private
agreements and the flow of commerce. The Bill of Rights, which was
fashioned to protect individual freedom against governmental tyranny,
particularly safeguards private property. These bedrock legal principles all
foster economic growth through private endeavor. With these protections in
place, a vast expanse of resource-rich lands to the West, and a history built on
conquest and colonialism as a legal right (and, through the eyes of the church,
a moral right), the United States grew with little protection for nature.
Environmental laws enacted in the last 50 years have made environmental
protection a national policy but left many gaps in coverage and enforcement
(see Foreword and Chapter 1—“History of Environmental Law”).5
B. The Indigenous and Ecological Heritage
What one might consider the origins of Earth law depends on where one

looks. Indigenous communities have practiced Earth law in the United States
for centuries. Indigenous governance is at odds with the Western laws that
settlers brought which uphold human rights to property without adequate
concern for the rights of other members of the Earth community and our
responsibilities to them.6 The ancient wisdom of Indigenous people is an
important part of Earth law.
For this reason, the development of Earth law in the United States does not
have a simple linear history but rather continues to evolve through the
melding of ancient wisdom with reawakened and newly found consciousness.
The organization Honor the Earth describes how rights of nature brings these
together:
Since Indigenous communities constantly negotiate from a place of reduced
efficacy, it is essential to identify methods of engagement that do not
compromise Indigenous thought patterns while also providing better land
protection. A movement that may allow this engagement is the advancement
of the Rights of Nature.7
Ecologist Aldo Leopold in the 1940s was among the first non-natives to call
for the rights of nature. His statement on this also shows how ancient insights
and newly found consciousness come together:
There is as yet no ethic dealing with man’s relation to land and to the animals
and plants which grow upon it. Land, like Odysseus’ slave-girls, is still
property. The land-relation is still strictly economic, entailing privileges but
not obligations.…
All ethics so far evolved rest upon a single premise: that the individual is a
member of a community of interdependent parts.…
The land ethic simply enlarges the boundaries of the community to include
soils, waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the land.8
There are many twentieth century authors, philosophers, and cultural
historians who have led the way in re-thinking the human relationship with
the natural world as reflected in our current legal system. Today, a growing
body of lawyers and others—including many contributors to this book—carry

forward their thinking by calling for systems change that would harmonize
the legal system with the needs of nature.
This being said, because the United States adopted the framework of an
English (settler) legal system, we have to address legal developments within
that paradigm, as it is this paradigm that currently prevails.
III. MOVEMENT LAWYERING
A. Background on Movement Lawyering
Movement lawyering is a theory of legal practice in which lawyers work
within (rather than for) social movements fighting for systemic change.
A traditional legal education teaches us to reify and enforce statutes, rules,
and above all, case law. While these are important skills for practicing
lawyers, ultimately, these laws are only some of the rules that govern human
behavior. Cultural and social rules, “norms,” govern human behavior as well.
An underexplored but critical area of legal education is the origin of our legal
structures and how those structures change based on these norms. Certainly,
the law influences culture and society. But more often, the law is dragging
behind social progress, with judicial opinions ultimately legitimizing a new
norm that society has already accepted. Felicity Jones, playing Ruth Bader
Ginsberg in the film On the Basis of Sex (2019), which tells the story of
Ginsberg’s early cases against gender discrimination, embodied this reality
when she says to the court, “We’re not asking you to change the country;
that’s already happened without any court’s permission.”
Purvi Shah, a leading theorist and practitioner of movement lawyering, and
Chuck Elsesser, co-founder of the Community Justice Project, have critiqued
the different legal models typically used to drive social justice. They describe
the civil legal-aid model, which considers the lack of lawyers as the major
problem with the legal system; the test-case or impact litigation model, which
pursues systemic social change through carefully targeted class action
litigation; and the social-rescue model, which believes that poverty is the
result of the failure of social and other support services, including legal
services.9 Shah and Elsesser write the following criticism:

The first two of these models believe in the underlying justness of the legal
system—if you can simply have a lawyer to enforce the law, or have the right
case argued to the right judge justice will result. The third model assumes
that poor people…are simply “broken people” who need comprehensive
services to be “fixed.” Not one of these models takes into account the long-
standing systems of class and racial discrimination and oppression, which
have resulted in systemic powerlessness of whole communities. Many of the
classic conflicts between organizers and traditional legal services lawyers can
be attributed to this disconnect between their differing theories of social
change. Traditionally, lawyers and organizers have vastly different analyses
on why our world is the way it is.10
Shah and Elsesser then introduce their own model of community lawyering:
We use legal advocacy to build the power of communities to challenge and
eradicate these systems of inequality. In this model, rather than saviors or
gatekeepers, lawyers are tacticians in the struggle for change. We call it
community lawyering.…
By using legal advocacy to support organizing, community education, and
leadership development, community lawyering allows lawyers to have a
much larger impact than any one lawsuit.…
[W]e also believe that community lawyers must be engaged in a regular
practice of self-scrutiny and self-reflection. If lawyers want to practice law in
a respectful, responsible and accountable manner, we believe you have to be
constantly evaluating your work to determine if it perpetuates racism, sexism,
homophobia, classism and elitism. To that end, we believe that community
lawyers should be engaged in a process of political study and growth
collectively with organizers. Poor communities of color face multiple and
intersecting injustices and good lawyering requires a deep understanding of
race, class, and power. 11
While Shah and Elsesser focus on economic and social justice, these
frameworks also apply to environmental and ecological justice and the rights
of nature.

B. Rights of Nature Movement Lawyering
Today, many organizations and networks participate in the movement in the
United States to develop Earth law. Some of these organizations use
strategies that can be described as movement lawyering. Not unexpectedly—
in a legal system rooted in corporate rights, state and federal preemption, and,
ultimately, human dominion over nature—this approach has faced strong
pushback. But along the way, a blossoming grassroots movement has
emerged, equipped with many lessons of how rights of nature can take hold
in the United States.
Some of the organizations involved in the legal development of rights of
nature in the United States include Earth Law Center, the Community
Environmental Legal Defense Fund, Indigenous Environmental Network,
Honor the Earth, Movement Rights, the Global Alliance for the Rights of
Nature, Center for Earth Jurisprudence, Center for Environmental Ethics and
Law, the Ecological Law and Governance Association, Boulder Rights of
Nature, International Rivers, and the National Lawyers Guild’s
Environmental Justice Committee and National Lawyers Guild’s
International Committee’s Environmental Human Rights Committee. These
organizations are pursuing diverse strategies to catalyze the shift toward a
legal system that incorporates Earth law. Many different approaches are
being taken, each with strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities.
C. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11
Practitioners of movement lawyering in the U.S. rights of nature field may
find themselves representing ecosystems in courts based upon relatively
untested or unprecedented legal theories. Because representing ecosystems in
court requires arguing for a good faith change in the law, Federal Rule of
Civil Procedure 11 (“FRCP 11”) and the Rules of Professional Conduct must
be understood. Typically, lawyers make arguments in court based on the law
at the time. However, the FRCP and state corollaries allow litigants to make
“claims, defenses, and other legal contentions [that] are warranted…by a
nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or
for establishing new law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2). The 1993 Notes of
Advisory Committee on Rules state:

Arguments for extensions, modifications, or reversals of existing law or for
creation of new law do not violate subdivision (b)(2) provided they are
“nonfrivolous.” This establishes an objective standard, intended to eliminate
any “empty-head pure-heart” justification for patently frivolous arguments.
However, the extent to which a litigant has researched the issues and found
some support for its theories even in minority opinions, in law review
articles, or through consultation with other attorneys should certainly be
taken into account in determining whether paragraph (2) has been violated.
Although arguments for a change of law are not required to be specifically so
identified, a contention that is so identified should be viewed with greater
tolerance under the rule.
American Bar Association Model Rule of Professional Conduct 3.1
“Meritorious Claims & Contentions” similarly recognizes the value of good
faith arguments for changes in the law. It reads, in part: “[a] lawyer shall not
bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue therein, unless
there is a basis in law and fact for doing so that is not frivolous, which
includes a good faith argument for an extension, modification or reversal of
existing law.”
Because lawyers advocating for rights of nature are seeking to extend,
modify, or reverse existing law, adversaries may rely on the threat of Rule 11
sanctions both to gain leverage and, if they are successful on the merits, to
punish proponents of rights of nature. As explored below in Section VI,
Federal Lawsuit for the Rights of the Colorado River Ecosystem, lawyers
arguing for rights of nature face this risk.
IV. CASE STUDIES IN LOCAL LAWMAKING
Thus far, movement lawyering for the rights of nature in the United States
has taken form largely through ordinances and resolutions at the local level—
in townships, counties, and cities large and small. Advocates have also
attempted to integrate rights of nature into state law.
Because of the federalized structure of the U.S. legal system, proponents of
Earth law has the strongest legal authority if recognized through national
constitutional-amendments and enforceable international agreements.

However, in the face of inadequate federal action to protect the Earth, and
based on the beliefs that the residents of local communities have a right to a
healthy local environment and that nature has inherent rights, local
governments have used legal theories that draw from local authority to
develop Earth law in the United States. This local lawmaking follows a
tradition of local grassroots movements based on a strong democratic ideal:
the idea that a community should get to decide to make stronger laws to
protect its land, water, and air, and its inhabitants’ rights to live in a healthy
ecosystem.
In addition, tribal nations have written and begun to enforce laws recognizing
the rights of nature.
This section examines strategy, tactics, and skills that have been used in
movement lawyering for the rights of nature in the United States.
A. Introduction to Local Rights-Based Lawmaking
Beginning in the early twenty-first century, the rights of nature movement
took root at the local level, spearheaded largely by community groups, local
governments, and supportive legal organizations like the Community
Environmental Legal Defense Fund (CELDF).12 Their approach has focused
on passing laws recognizing human rights and ecosystem rights as superior to
corporate interests. These laws address the injustice of corporations (a form
of organized property) possessing enforceable rights while basic rights for
ecosystems do not even exist.13
This strategy was based on the premise that conventional environmental law
does not recognize a community’s authority to say no to a federal or state
permitted project. This meant that while administrative successes might stall
a project (such as by denying a permit because of failure to follow NEPA or
state corollaries), a business entity intent on a development project would
eventually return with a completed permit application.
This approach reframed the problem from being one of pollution to one of
corporate control over the community’s ability to decide whether it can
protect its own air, water, and soil. In other words, it’s a democracy problem,

not a pollution problem. In effect, this strategy attempts to move
environmental law from a regulatory law framework of permits and
administrative procedures, to a constitutional law framework of decision-
making authority and rights. Thus, the problem was not merely corporate
power, but the structure of law (legal principles such as the dormant
commerce clause, Dillon’s Rule, ceiling preemption, and corporate
constitutional rights) that enables and authorizes that corporate power and
prevents the people from having any say in their own communities’ ability to
expand their human rights and ecological rights.14
As a result, some of these local laws expressly limited corporate
constitutional rights and asserted that the local law is not preempted by less
protective state or federal laws. This strategy has sometimes resulted in
aggressive pushback by corporate opponents. In some cases, opponents
convinced courts to invalidate the local laws to maintain the paradigm in
which corporate rights take precedence over the rights of communities and
ecosystems. These cases provide the opportunity to consider whether the
benefits of challenging the root problems outweighs the burdens of targeting
corporate rights. The key argument for taking the more aggressive approach
is that while there may be setbacks in the short run, it lays the foundation for
future success. Historically successful rights movements have faced setbacks
in the beginning when they challenged root problems.
B. Grant Township, Pennsylvania
This section begins with a case study of a local Community Bill of Rights
Ordinance passed by Grant Township in 2014, which included recognition of
the rights of nature—including the rights of Little Mahoning Creek. As you
read this section, consider some of the practical questions faced by lawyers
representing an ecosystem, including: Who should be named as the party?
How is that party represented, or, put another way, who speaks for the
ecosystem? If the ecosystem has been damaged, how are the damages
proved? What risks are presented making novel arguments and pressing those
arguments if they have been rejected? The community of Grant Township
adopted a community rights ordinance that included a recognition of rights of
nature. Pennsylvania General Energy Company contested the validity of the
ordinance and these practical questions were explored in the ensuing

litigation.
1. Representing the Little Mahoning Watershed as an ecosystem
In 2014 and again in 2017, the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental
Protection approved an application by Pennsylvania General Energy
Company (PGE) and issued a permit for PGE to inject runoff from its
fracking operations in a 7,000 foot-deep, abandoned well in Grant Township
(the Yanity Well). The well is near Little Mahoning Creek. Residents of the
tiny township, with a population of about 700, were concerned with the risks
the project posed to their drinking water, their health, the creek, and its
watershed. Grant Township adopted a community rights ordinance that
included recognition of the rights of nature.
As to nature, the law provides: “Natural communities and ecosystems within
Grant Township, including but not limited to, rivers, streams, and aquifers,
possess the right to exist, flourish, and naturally evolve.” After listing these
rights, the ordinance also attempts to diminish federal, state, and corporate
power when it conflicts with the protections for ecosystems and residents in
Grant Township: “any state or federal authorization, through permit or
otherwise, which would allow violation of the ordinance is invalid within
Grant Township” and that “corporations violating or seeking to violate the
ordinance, shall not be deemed legal ‘persons.’”15
PGE filed a federal lawsuit to overturn the Grant Township Ordinance.16
PGE claimed relief under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983 (the federal Civil Rights
Law) because the ordinance deprived it of its constitutionally protected
rights. It also claimed the Grant Township Ordinance was preempted by state
law. Grant Township filed a counterclaim, alleging that PGE’s lawsuit
violated the township’s people’s rights to local community self-government
as secured by the American Declaration of Independence, the Pennsylvania
Constitution, the federal constitutional framework, and the Community Bill
of Rights Ordinance itself.17
A nonprofit organization of township residents, the East Run Hellbenders
Society (named after the hellbender salamander, which is native to the area),
and the ecosystem in the township, the Little Mahoning Watershed, moved to

intervene as real parties in interest.18 PGE vehemently opposed the motion
and argued:
Watershed (the “Watershed”), allegedly, and the East Run Hellbenders
Society, Inc. (the “Hellbenders”) (collectively, the “Intervenors”) seek to
intervene in the above-captioned matter.…Incredibly, the Motion to Intervene
seeks, apparently for the first time in American jurisprudence, for a condition
of nature, in this case the Watershed, to intervene in a lawsuit.
The Watershed does not meet the definition of a “person” under the Federal
Rules of Civil Procedure, and lacks the most fundamental capacities
necessary to be a participant in the judicial process. The Watershed is neither
an appropriate candidate for party status in a court of law, nor feasibly
represented. The Watershed obviously cannot consent to this intervention,
cannot be a party to a lawsuit and cannot be provided the ethical protections
represented parties are afforded by the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional
Conduct.…
A watershed lacks consciousness, intelligence, cognition, communicability,
or agency. A watershed can neither recall nor forget; neither articulate nor
remain silent; neither agree nor dispute. The Watershed cannot decide to
intervene, cannot accept representation or engage with counsel as a client,
and cannot appear in court or testify. It cannot knowingly participate in the
adversarial system of justice.19
The Little Mahoning Watershed replied to this specific argument:
Adequate client representation is no joking matter, yet the irony here must be
pointed out. PGE’s lawyers represent a legal fiction, which is itself incapable
of doing the things PGE’s lawyers require an ecosystem to be able to do:
A [business entity] lacks consciousness, intelligence, cognition,
communicability, or agency. A [business entity] can neither recall nor forget;
neither articulate nor remain silent; neither agree nor dispute. The [business
entity] cannot decide to intervene, cannot accept representation or engage
with counsel as a client, and cannot appear in court or testify. It cannot
knowingly participate in the adversarial system of justice.

Pennsylvania General Energy Company, L.L.C., a limited liability company,
cannot do any of those things (its members, managers, and lawyers do them).
Yet, we pretend that it is PGE acting. PGE’s lawyers’ argument is that our
system of justice allows lawyers to accommodate legal fictions, but not
accommodate the living ecosystems upon which we all depend and within
which we are a part, even when those ecosystems are recognized by law to
have rights. If that is indeed true, then it is the greatest legal fiction of all.20
The District Court did not rule on whether the Little Mahoning Watershed
was a proper party, and instead denied the intervention motion by holding
that the Watershed’s interests would be adequately represented by an existing
party, the township. On appeal, the Third Circuit affirmed on the same
grounds, and only addressed the ecosystem as a party separately in a footnote
expressing doubt as to its capacity to sue or be sued as prescribed in FRCP
17(b).
We do not see, however, how a watershed could be considered a proper party
under Rule 17. Under that Rule, in order to be a party to a lawsuit, the
purported litigant must have the capacity to sue or be sued. On this point, the
rule speaks only in terms of individuals, corporations and others permitted by
state law to sue or be sued. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 17(b). The plain language of
Rule 17 does not permit an ecosystem such as the Little Mahoning Watershed
to sue anyone or be sued by anyone, and for that reason alone we have
misgivings with the Watershed being listed as a party in this litigation.21
Little Mahoning Watershed filed a motion for rehearing, arguing that FRCP
17(b) defers the question of who has capacity to the “law of the state” which
requires finding that the Little Mahoning Watershed has capacity under the
applicable law, namely, the Grant Township ordinance. In this motion, the
proposed intervenors argued:
The panel Opinion misreads Rule 17(b) to reach this conclusion. Rule 17(b)
provides that “capacity to sue or be sued…for all other parties [not
individuals or corporations, is determined] by the law of the state where the
court is located.” Courts apply local law, in addition to state law, when
considering capacity under “the law of the state where the court is located.”
[Citation omitted.]

Here, there is a law on point that provides ecosystems, such as the Little
Mahoning Watershed, with the capacity to sue. The Ordinance provides
“[a]ny action brought by either a resident of Grant Township or by the
Township to enforce or defend the rights of ecosystems or natural
communities secured by this Ordinance shall bring that action in the name of
the ecosystem or natural community.…” App. at 38 (Ordinance §4(c)). This
is the relevant law for determining whether the Little Mahoning Watershed
has capacity under Rule 17(b), and it clearly confers capacity on an
ecosystem to defend its rights by appearing in court with the help of “either a
resident of Grant Township or…the Township.”
The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure do not bar the ecosystem’s participation
in this suit.22
The Third Circuit denied the motion for rehearing.
The underlying litigation over Grant Township’s Ordinance lasted over three
years. While the Ordinance’s rights of nature provision was not at issue, the
court invalidated other portions of the Ordinance, namely the prohibition
against the disposal of fracking waste, and ultimately agreed with PGE that
the Ordinance violated some of its constitutional rights. The court’s decision
illustrates the challenges communities face when confronting corporate rights
head on and in asking the courts to uphold laws that give more power to
communities and ecosystems than corporations.
But, Grant Township’s story does not end there. Shortly after the court
invalidated portions of the Ordinance, the people of Grant Township enacted
a Home Rule Charter by popular vote. The Charter contains the same
provisions as the Ordinance. This time, the Pennsylvania Department of
Environmental Protection sued the township alleging that state law
preempted the Charter’s prohibition against the disposal of fracking waste.
The Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania rejected the township’s argument
that the Charter was a valid exercise of the people’s right to local self-
government, but recognized that the township may be able to show at trial
that the state laws at issue—the Oil and Gas Act and Solid Waste
Management Act—and DEP’s enforcement of these statutes, violate the
Environmental Rights Amendment in Article 1, section 27 of Pennsylvania’s
Constitution and that they are therefore powerless to preempt the Township’s

Charter. A few weeks after the court’s ruling, the DEP rescinded PGE’s
permit for the injection of fracking waste. In doing so, DEP recognized that
the injection of oil and gas waste fluid into the well would violate the Home
Rule Charter. It remains to be seen whether PGE will file its own lawsuit to
challenge the Charter. In the meantime, the township has remained fracking
waste free.
Communities and their lawyers should consider the risks versus rewards of
laws that directly confront corporate rights, preemption, or both and the
resources required to sustain what may become protracted litigation.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Courts have considered the characteristics of being a legal person to
include: (1) the ability to contract, (2) the ability to own property, (3) the
ability to sue, and (4) the ability to be sued. What arguments might be made
for and against holding nature legally accountable? How might a monetary
judgment against an ecosystem be enforced? Where legal persons, humans,
corporations, governmental bodies are members of an ecosystem, could they
be held liable under rules of joint and several liability? Should ecosystems, if
recognized as legal persons, be able to contract? To own property? How do
they participate in a lawsuit if they cannot contract (e.g., agree to a
settlement)? Should “legal person” be the concept that we try to fit
ecosystems into, or do we need a new concept in the law to accommodate
ecosystems?
(2) How does an ecosystem speak in court? For the Little Mahoning
Watershed, the human residents of the ecosystem—members of the East Run
Hellbenders Society—volunteered to speak for the ecosystem’s interests.
What other options are there for getting ecosystems heard in court?
For instance, in Seneca Resources Corporation v. Highland Township (W.D.
Pa., No. 1:16-CV-289) and Capri v. Jenkins (Lincoln Cty., No. 17CV23360,
filed June 6, 2017), human members of the ecosystem, independent of the
intervening community groups, represented the best interests of the Crystal
Springs Ecosystem and Siletz River Ecosystem, respectively. In such a case,
the Ecosystem’s rights and interests are advanced by persons focused solely

on the Ecosystem’s unique interests.
(3) If you were representing the Little Mahoning Watershed, would you have
appealed the denial of its motion to intervene? Why or why not? Does your
answer consider the interests of the Little Mahoning Watershed, as well as
the movement as a whole? If those are in conflict, what legal advice would
you provide? How can the client make the decision?
(4) In 2010, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, became the first large city to adopt a
local ordinance recognizing the rights of nature by adopting Pittsburgh’s
Community Protection from Natural Gas Extraction Ordinance. Section
618.01 of the ordinance “bans commercial extraction of Marcellus Shale
natural gas within the City of Pittsburgh.…” Section 618.023 explicitly
recognizes rights of nature. Pittsburgh’s law also purports to deprive
corporate violators of existing legal rights conferred by federal or state law.
Today, there are no gas wells within the Pittsburgh city limits. However,
there are about 10,000 gas wells within the state, and large clusters of the
wells lie in the city’s suburbs, some within 4 miles of the city boundary. Why
do you think this law has not been challenged? Do you think it will ever be
enforced? If you could amend the law, how would you do so?
C. Lake Erie Bill of Rights, Toledo, Ohio
While many local governments passed laws recognizing rights for
ecosystems in the years between 2006 and 2019, this grassroots movement
gained global attention when the people of Toledo, Ohio, voted to adopt a
Lake Erie Bill of Rights (LEBOR) into their city charter.23
LEBOR recognizes the rights of the Lake Erie Ecosystem in proclaiming that,
“Lake Erie, and the Lake Erie watershed, possess the right to exist, flourish
and naturally evolve.”24 It also recognizes that the people of Toledo have the
right to a clean and healthy environment, including a clean and healthy Lake
Erie. LEBOR prohibits any corporation or government from violating these
rights. LEBOR states that the city or any city resident has standing to sue in
state court to enforce these rights and prohibition. LEBOR also provides that
Lake Erie itself may enforce its rights, as a named plaintiff and real party in
interest, through a suit brought by the city or any resident of the city. A

corporation or government that violates LEBOR’s rights or prohibition
provisions is subject to criminal fines and strict liability for all harms
resulting from its violations, including damages for the cost of restoring Lake
Erie.
The impetus for LEBOR, in 2014, was a harmful algae bloom caused by
fertilizer pollution carried by runoff into Lake Erie. Toledo residents went
three days without drinking water because the city’s water intake in the lake
was polluted.
The day after LEBOR passed, Drewes Farms Partnership, supported by
industrial agricultural interest groups, sued the City of Toledo to attempt to
overturn the law.25 The complaint sought a declaratory judgment and
injunction, arguing violations of the First, Fifth, and Fourteenth Amendments
as well as preemption. The complaint included a plea for a civil rights
attorneys’ fee award—as a corporation seeking to defend its constitutional
rights in a claimed Section 1983 action.26
Lake Erie Ecosystem (with rights recognized under the new charter
amendment) and Toledoans for Safe Water (the community group that
petitioned for the ballot measure) attempted to intervene under FRCP 24. The
district court denied intervention on the grounds that Lake Erie Ecosystem
did not have capacity to sue or be sued under FRCP 17, and that Toledoans
for Safe Water did not have a substantial legal interest in defending the
charter amendment, one of the FRCP 24(a) elements, because Toledoans
interest was shared by the people of Toledo as a whole.27 Meanwhile, the
State of Ohio intervened in the trial court action against the City of Toledo.
Meanwhile, corporate interests took action against LEBOR in the state
legislature. After the charter amendment passed, the Ohio Chamber of
Commerce submitted a late addition to a budget bill to the state legislature,
which promptly adopted it.28 This legislation, now codified at O.R.C.
§2305.011, provided:
Sec. 2305.011. (A) As used in this section:
1. “Nature” means the phenomena of the physical world collectively,
including plants, animals, the landscape, other features and products of

the Earth, the natural environment or wilderness, and generally areas
that are not human or human creations, have not been substantially
altered by humans, or that persist despite human intervention.
2. “Ecosystem” means a complex community of living organisms in
conjunction with their physical environments, all interacting and linked
together as a system through nutrient cycles and energy flows in a
particular unit of space.
b. Nature or any ecosystem does not have standing to participate in or
bring an action in any court of common pleas.
c.     i. No person, on behalf of or representing nature or an ecosystem,
shall bring an action in any court of common pleas.
 ii. No person shall bring an action in any court of common pleas against
a person who is acting on behalf of or representing nature or an
ecosystem.
iii. No person, on behalf of or representing nature or an ecosystem, shall
intervene in any manner, such as by filing a counterclaim, cross-claim,
or third-party complaint, in any action brought in any court of common
pleas.
d. Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent the state or any
of its agencies from enforcing the laws pertaining to environmental
pollution, conservation, wild animals, or other natural communities or
ecosystems.
As the Ohio Chamber of Commerce lobbyist implied, this new state law was
in direct response to concerns that policymaking like the Lake Erie Bill of
Rights would spread, and that state preemption would be an effective tool to
stop it.
Undeterred, three Toledo residents filed suit against the State of Ohio for
violations of the Lake Erie Bill of Rights.29 The trial court dismissed their
action on the State’s motion to dismiss. As they prepared an appeal, the
federal district court decided Drewes Farms Partnership v. City of Toledo, on
February 27, 2020, a year after the people had voted to enact LEBOR.

The federal district court ruled that “LEBOR is unconstitutionally vague and
exceeds the power of municipal government in Ohio.” The court explained:
LEBOR’s environmental rights are even less clear than the provisions struck
down in [Coates v. City of Cincinnati, 402 U.S. 611 (1971), Belle Maer
Harbor v. Charter Twp. of Harrison, 170 F.3d 553 (6th Cir. 1999), and
Springfield Armory, Inc. v. City of Columbus, 29 F.3d 250 (6th Cir. 1994)].
What conduct infringes the right of Lake Erie and its watershed to “exist,
flourish, and naturally evolve”? How would a prosecutor, judge, or jury
decide? LEBOR offers no guidance. Similar uncertainty shrouds the right of
Toledoans to a “clean and healthy environment.” The line between clean and
unclean, and between healthy and unhealthy, depends on who you ask.
Because of this vagueness, Drewes Farms reasonably fears that spreading
even small amounts of fertilizer violates LEBOR. Countless other activities
might run afoul of LEBOR’s amorphous environmental rights: catching fish,
dredging a riverbed, removing invasive species, driving a gas-fueled vehicle,
pulling up weeds, planting corn, irrigating a field—and the list goes on.
LEBOR’s authors failed to make hard choices regarding the appropriate
balance between environmental protection and economic activity. Instead,
they employed language that sounds powerful but has no practical meaning.
Under even the most forgiving standard, the environmental rights identified
in LEBOR are void for vagueness.30
In the state court lawsuit, the three Toledo residents filed their appeal
anyway.31 The Lake Erie Bill of Rights in Toledo, Ohio, put the concept of
ecosystem rights into the mainstream. Once one can conceptualize a thing
having rights, it is very difficult to go back.
D. Santa Monica, California
In 2013, Earth Law Center, Global Exchange, and other organizations and
partners worked together to advocate for the first-ever West Coast rights of
nature ordinance—the Sustainability Rights Ordinance in Santa Monica,
California. This section explores its roots and discusses how its approach to
rights of nature differs from the prior case studies.
In 2011, the City of Santa Monica Task Force on the Environment

recommended that the city support and join the world-wide effort to address
the mounting environmental crisis by recognizing the rights of people, natural
communities and ecosystems to exist, regenerate and flourish in a sustainable
environment.
The city council responded to the task force recommendation by unanimously
adopting a resolution “Declaring the City’s Commitment to Sustainable
Rights.”32 Legislative findings supporting the resolution document the
inadequacy of current environmental laws and the need for a paradigm shift
to recognizing nature’s rights. Further, the findings recognize the rights of the
Santa Monicans to a clean and sustainable environment and expressly support
“local recognition of the fundamental rights of natural communities and
ecosystems to exist, thrive and evolve”33 by “modifying local law and policy
as needed to better protect and sustain, for current and future generations, the
natural environment upon which we all depend.”34 In addition to adopting the
resolution, the council directed city staff to prepare a Sustainability Rights
Ordinance.
The staff report concluded by proposing to highlight the city’s commitment
to sustainability rights for both humans and the natural world by creating a
new article of the municipal code to collect and/or reference all of the city’s
existing environmental laws, which were scattered throughout the
voluminous code, as well as environmental laws adopted in the future—the
goal being to create a cohesive body of municipal environmental governance,
readily accessible and available as a model for other cities.
The ordinance was adopted unanimously by the city council. Its legislative
findings declare:
Santa Monica’s welfare is inextricably bound to the welfare of the natural
environment; the expanding environmental crisis demonstrates the necessity
of examining societal and legal assumptions about humans’ relationship to
the environment; and the rights of humans and natural communities and
ecosystems must both be legally recognized.35
The substantive provisions of the ordinance recognize the “fundamental and
inalienable rights of natural communities and ecosystems to exist and

flourish”36 and the rights of Santa Monica residents to clean marine waters,
clean indoor and outdoor air, a sustainable food system, a sustainable climate,
a flourishing biodiverse environment, waste systems that do not degrade the
environment, and a sustainable energy future based on renewable energy. The
ordinance requires a biennial report to the community and a public hearing on
the state of the local environment, the realization of the rights secured by the
ordinance, and the effectuation of provisions of the Sustainable City Plan. In
March 2020, the city released its 2019 Sustainability Rights Report which
includes its progress on various sustainability metrics that give effect to rights
of nature.37
Santa Monica’s resolution and ordinance do not purport to diminish corporate
rights secured by state or federal law or to protect city laws against federal or
state preemption claims. Instead, the ordinance provides that its several
purposes include “to the full extent legally possible, subordinating the short
term, private, financial interests of corporations and others to the common,
long-term interest of achieving environmental and economic sustainability.”
Additionally, the ordinance provides that “corporate entities, and their
directors and managers, do not enjoy special privileges or powers under the
law that subordinate the community’s rights to their private interests.”38
Following its passage, the Sustainability Rights Ordinance was incorporated
into the city’s Sustainable City Plan as a guiding principle for administration
of the plan. Additionally, the City Council created a new municipal code
article devoted to environmental sustainability, with the Sustainability Rights
Ordinance as its foundational introduction. Consistent with its decision to use
the concept of nature’s rights as a foundational principle for future
environmental work, the next environmental ordinance adopted by the city
(prohibiting private water wells), referenced the Sustainability Rights
Ordinance as a policy basis for the new enactment. Santa Monica’s ordinance
recognizing nature’s rights has enhanced the city and its inhabitants through
its incorporation in existing environmental laws, policies and programs, as a
guiding legal, philosophical and ethical principle that reinforces ecocentric
awareness.
Consider how the different local rights of nature models differ. For example,
compare the Santa Monica Sustainability Rights Ordinance to the Lake Erie

Bill of Rights. One major difference is that Santa Monica’s model does not
limit corporate rights or fight permitted projects that cause pollution. For this
reason, some rights of nature advocates felt the ordinance did not go far
enough. But other advocates support this model because it can strengthen
environmental protections and works to transform community consciousness
without risking lawsuits for preemption or corporate rights violations.
Another distinction is that the Sustainability Rights Ordinance applies to the
jurisdiction of Santa Monica, whereas LEBOR sought to protect an entire
watershed. It is important for Earth lawyers to understand the distinctions,
and to think about new approaches, too.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) In promoting recognition of nature’s rights, what are the advantages and
disadvantages of local laws and resolutions, that proclaim aspirations, rather
than establish prohibitions? How can such laws be effectuated? What factors
might propel or impede the way resolutions and policy statements may lead
to changed conditions on the ground?
(2) Governments often pass resolutions on topics of public concern: making a
statement without creating law. A resolution is a useful tool for building
awareness about the issue. The downside is that it does not create any
enforceable law. A resolution might also expressly state that it will be
followed by an ordinance. However, that provision itself is also
unenforceable, and unless it is followed by strategic community organizing,
resolutions often merely provide elected officials with an opportunity to
placate public pressure with words rather than deeds. What might lawyers do
to promote the development of enforceable laws based on resolutions?
(3) In 2019, the town of Crestone, Colorado adopted a resolution recognizing
that “the Town of Crestone does officially recognize that nature, natural
ecosystems, communities, and all species possess intrinsic and inalienable
rights which must be effectuated to protect life on Earth.” While nonbinding,
in what ways might you promote rights of nature in Crestone to ensure it is
part of the community consciousness?
(4) The federal district court in Drewes Farms Partnership invalidated

LEBOR for vagueness grounds. If those same provisions were part of the
Ohio Constitution, how might that have impacted the consideration by the
court? The people of Toledo adopted LEBOR as part of their City Charter;
what are the arguments for and against interpreting the city charter provisions
like constitutional text?
(5) What lessons can movement lawyers take from the Drewes Farms
Partnership decision for: (a) legal strategy and (b) organizing strategy?
(6) How and why might the Earth law advocacy in Toledo, Ohio, and in
Santa Monica, California, help or hurt the Earth law movement? In what
other ways might movement lawyering contribute to the body of Earth law
and the reformation of the legal system?
(7) What would your strategic and tactical advice be on how to advance the
development of rights of nature if your client were: (a) the City of Santa
Monica, (b) a community group in Santa Monica, (c) the City of Toledo, (d) a
community group in Toledo? What legal advice would you give to an
opponent of rights of nature in these communities?
V. DEVELOPING ECOCENTRIC LAW IN
STATE CONSTITUTIONS
About fifty years ago, people in many states enacted Environmental Rights
Amendments into their state constitutions. These amendments guaranteed
humans’ rights to a healthy environment. By way of example, the
Constitution of Pennsylvania, Art. I, §27, states:
The people have a right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the
natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment.
Pennsylvania’s public natural resources are the common property of all the
people, including generations yet to come. As trustee of these resources, the
Commonwealth shall conserve and maintain them for the benefit of all the
people.
While these provisions are important advances in human environmental
rights, they do not extend the community of rights-bearing entities beyond

people. In contrast, the recognition of nature’s rights seeks, in the words of
Aldo Leopold, to “enlarge[] the boundaries of the community to include soils,
waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the land.” Human environmental
rights and nature’s rights are compatible advances in environmental and
ecological justice. The mechanisms for their interaction and mutual
reinforcement is an important consideration for the continuing development
of Earth law. The proliferation of local lawmaking may stimulate additional
state-level lawmaking to advance Earth law. Below are brief case studies of
several of those campaigns.
A. Vermont
In 2012, Vermont was the first U.S. state where a group, the Vermont Rights
of Nature Campaign, sought to establish an amendment to the Vermont
constitution that would grant legal rights to Nature. A constitutional
amendment has yet to take hold, but, so far, two Vermont municipalities have
adopted resolutions urging the state legislature to amend the Vermont
constitution to include rights of nature. The resolutions call for an
amendment that would “recognize in the law the natural, inherent and
inalienable rights of forests, natural areas, waterways, and fish and wildlife
populations of Vermont to exist, thrive and evolve.”
B. Colorado
Since 2014, Colorado organizers have pushed for a Colorado Community
Rights Amendment to the Colorado constitution. The proposed amendment
adds “Section 32. Right of Local Community Self-Government” to the
Colorado constitution.39 The proposed amendment includes in that right “the
power of the people, and the power of their governments, to enact local laws
that protect health, safety, and welfare by recognizing or establishing rights
of natural persons, their local communities, and nature; and by securing those
rights using prohibitions and other means deemed necessary by the
community, including measures to establish, define, alter, or eliminate
competing rights, powers, privileges, immunities, or duties of corporations
and other business entities operating, or seeking to operate, in the
community.” The intent of the amendment to expand, and not restrict, rights
is expressed in part 3(b) which says: “Such local laws do not weaken

protections for natural persons, their local communities, or nature provided
by state, federal, or international law.”
C. New Hampshire
In 2018, community organizers persuaded legislators to bring forward a
resolution for a state constitutional amendment to recognize the right of local
community self-government to establish, inter alia, rights of nature. A
resolution was introduced, which if passed would put the proposed
amendment on the general ballot.40 The proposed amendment incorporates
language from Article 10 of the New Hampshire Bill of Rights, enacted in
1784, which states:
[Art.] 10. [Right of Revolution.] Government being instituted for the
common benefit, protection, and security, of the whole community, and not
for the private interest or emolument of any one man, family, or class of men;
therefore, whenever the ends of government are perverted, and public liberty
manifestly endangered, and all other means of redress are ineffectual, the
people may, and of right ought to reform the old, or establish a new
government. The doctrine of nonresistance against arbitrary power, and
oppression, is absurd, slavish, and destructive of the good and happiness of
mankind.41
The proposed resolution provided that: “the people of New Hampshire have
an inherent and inalienable right of local, community self-government in each
county, municipality, city, and town to enact local laws that protect health,
safety, and welfare by recognizing or establishing rights of natural persons,
their local communities, and nature.” The proposed resolution also would
have conferred on local communities the right to “establish, define, alter, or
eliminate competing rights, powers, privileges, immunities, or duties of
corporations and other business entities operating, or seeking to operate, in
the community.” The House of Representatives voted and deemed the
proposed resolution “Inexpedient to Legislate.”42
D. Oregon
Organizers in Oregon have advanced a similar state constitutional

amendment by initiative.43 Like with local lawmaking, the procedural
mechanisms for lawmaking vary by jurisdiction. For example, both Colorado
and Oregon have direct constitutional amendment by the people, while New
Hampshire requires that proposed amendments originate in the state
legislature.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Many of these state constitutional amendments advance ecocentric law in
connection with expanded local lawmaking power. What are the advantages
and disadvantages to making that connection?
(2) How would you draft a state constitutional amendment to recognize earth
rights? What would your amendment’s strengths and weaknesses be?
VI. FEDERAL LAWSUIT FOR THE RIGHTS OF
THE COLORADO RIVER ECOSYSTEM
In 2017, the nonprofit organization Deep Green Resistance filed a complaint
in federal district court in Colorado, naming the Colorado River Ecosystem
as plaintiff and the state and governor as defendants.44 The relief sought
includes a declaratory judgment that, among other things, the Colorado River
Ecosystem possesses rights to: exist, flourish, regenerate, be restored and
naturally evolve; protections of the Due Process and Equal Protection
Clauses; and First Amendment protections, including the right to petition the
government.
Unlike the Little Mahoning Watershed’s attempt to intervene under the
authority of an ordinance, the Colorado River Ecosystem filed suit based on
the ecosystem’s fundamental and inherent rights. It was the first lawsuit in
the United States filed by an ecosystem without another plaintiff.45
The amended complaint asserted:
[I]t is within the Court’s authority to recognize that Plaintiff Colorado River
Ecosystem enjoys rights, including those belonging to ‘persons.’…

Recognizing the Colorado River Ecosystem as a “person” is indeed no stretch
at all. It is dictated by the logic that ecosystems are living, and that human
life is inextricably intertwined with, and dependent upon, ecosystems.
Honoring this symbiotic relationship is much more profound than the idea
that corporations are made up of people and that they, therefore, enjoy many
of the same rights.46
The relief requested focused on obtaining a declaratory judgment from the
court that:
a. The Colorado River Ecosystem is a “person” capable of possessing rights;
b. The Colorado River Ecosystem possesses the rights to exist, flourish,
regenerate, be restored, and naturally evolve;
c. That [Deep Green Resistance] members, Owen Lammers, Living Rivers
Executive Director, and John Weisheit, the Colorado Riverkeeper, may serve
as guardians, or “next friends,” for the Colorado River Ecosystem;
d. That Plaintiff Colorado River Ecosystem is protected by the Due Process
and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Petition
Clause of the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution; and
e. That certain activities permitted by, or carried out by Defendant, may
violate the rights of the natural communities creating the Colorado River, and
that the Plaintiff may proceed to file for injunctive relief to enjoin Defendant
from taking action related to those activities, or to force Defendant to take
certain actions, as violations of the rights of Plaintiff Colorado River
Ecosystem.
114. Plaintiff Colorado River Ecosystem further seeks to enjoin Defendant
from continuing to violate its inherent rights to exist, flourish, regenerate, be
restored, and to naturally evolve and its rights under the First and Fourteenth
Amendments by failing to recognize its legal status as a “person.”47
The State of Colorado, represented by the Office of the Attorney General,
filed motions to dismiss, challenging the complaint on various constitutional
and other grounds including, but not limited to, federal immunity, lack of

standing, and lack of jurisdiction under a federal statute. Colorado also
asserted that the complaint and amended complaint failed to present a
justiciable legal issue and instead made a policy argument, which was more
appropriate for legislative determination.
The attorney general then wrote a letter to plaintiffs’ counsel, notifying him
that she would seek sanctions based on the pursuit of frivolous claims unless
the suit was withdrawn. Plaintiff’s counsel agreed to dismissal and filed an
“Unopposed Motion to Dismiss Amended Complaint with Prejudice,”48
which stated:
The Complaint represented a good faith attempt to introduce the Rights of
Nature doctrine to our jurisprudence. The rights of nature—specifically, the
legal standing of natural entities—was first recognized by the Honorable
William O. Douglas in his dissent in Sierra Club v. Morton and is being
increasingly utilized as a legal doctrine by countries around the world.
The undersigned continues to believe that the doctrine provides American
courts with a pragmatic and workable tool for addressing environmental
degradation and the current issues facing the Colorado River.
That said the expansion of rights is a difficult and legally complex matter.
When engaged in an effort of first impression, the undersigned has a
heightened ethical duty to continuously ensure that conditions are appropriate
for our judicial institution to best consider the merits of a new canon.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Would you have brought this case on behalf of the Colorado River
Ecosystem? If not, why not? If so, how would you have responded to the
state attorney general’s Rule 11 notice letter?
(2) Aggressive legal tactics, such as seeking sanctions against lawyers using
new or emerging legal theories in defense of ecosystems and communities,

(3) What are the advantages and disadvantages to ecosystems appearing in

(4) The premise of the Colorado River Ecosystem case illustrates how the

(5) Given that the law of standing currently allows humans with a special

(6) In some countries, courts have recognized the rights of nature even

VII. TRIBAL GOVERNMENTS AND NATIVE
HAWAIIANS—THE SPIRITUAL DIMENSION
OF SACRED PLACES
A. Native American Nations’ Recognition of Nature’s Rights

In 2003, the Navajo Nation tribal council amended its code to emphasize the
rights of all creation. Title 1 of the code states “all creation, from Mother
Earth and Father Sky to the animals, those who live in the water, those who
fly, and plant life have their own laws, and rights and freedom to exist.”
In 2017, the Ponca Nation in Oklahoma recognized the rights of Nature in the
context of a law prohibiting fracking. Tribal representative, Casey Camp-
Horinek, said, “We are proud to be moving into the future by honoring our
original instructions to respect all life on our Mother Earth.”
In 2018, the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, whose homelands are in
Minnesota, adopted a law recognizing the rights of wild rice, which the
Ojibwe call Manoomin.50 Manoomin is central to Ojibwe culture. According
to the resolutions adopting the law, these rights were recognized because “‘it
has become necessary to provide a legal basis to protect wild rice and fresh
water resources as part of our primary treaty foods for future generations.’”51
The law begins: “Manoomin, or wild rice, within all the Chippewa ceded
territories, possesses inherent rights to exist, flourish, regenerate, and evolve,
as well as inherent rights to restoration, recovery, and preservation.” The law
was based in part on the decision by the Supreme Court in Minnesota v. Mille
Lacs Band of Chippewa Indians, 526 U.S. 172 (1999). The Court considered
whether the descendants of several bands of Chippewa that entered a treaty
with the United States in 1837 retained the usufructuary rights recognized by
the treaty. The State of Minnesota claimed that the Indigenous people lost
these rights through an executive order in 1850, an 1855 treaty, and the
admission of Minnesota into the Union in 1858. The Court held: “After an
examination of the historical record, we conclude that the Chippewa retain
the usufructuary rights guaranteed to them under the 1837 Treaty.”52
In 2019, the Yurok Tribe of the Pacific Northwest adopted a “Resolution
Establishing the Rights of the Klamath River,” making it the first river in the
United States to have its rights recognized by governmental action. The
resolution describes the relationship between Weroy (the Klamath River) and
the Yurok people: “since time immemorial Yurok culture, ceremonies,
religion, fisheries, subsistence, economics, residence, and all other lifeways
are intertwined with the health of the River, its ecosystem and the multiple
species reliant on a thriving Klamath River ecosystem.”53 It also declares that

the Yurok people have sovereign rights to conserve and protect their territory,
including the river, its ecosystem and species, and to sustainably harvest
plants, salmon and other fish, animals, and other life-giving foods and
medicines. The declaration notes that its provisions comport with
international legal norms set forth in the United Nations Declaration of the
Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Noting their sacred responsibilities to the river and its ecosystem and the
present threats to the environment, the enactment recognizes “the Rights of
the Klamath River to exist, flourish, and naturally evolve; to have a clean and
healthy environment free from pollutants; to have a stable climate free from
human-caused climate change impacts; and to be free from contamination by
genetically engineered organisms.” Finally, the council declared that the
resolution serves as notice to all entities threatening the river that the threats
have necessitated the provision of a legal basis to protect the river and that
the council will adopt an ordinance to achieve that purpose.
B. Native Hawaiians Petition on behalf of Mo‘oinanea
An Earth law approach also reflects a responsibility to care for sacred places.
In 2019, Native Hawaiians, and those standing with them in solidarity,
gathered at the base of Mauna Kea on the Big Island of Hawai‘i to not only
protest the installation of a gigantic telescope atop their sacred mountain, but
also to speak against the desecration of sacred places, the displacement of
Indigenous peoples, and the present imbalance between humans and the rest
of nature.
Eight years prior, in litigation over the permit to build the telescope, Native
Hawaiians brought the sacred into the hearing room by filing a petition on
behalf of Mo‘oinanea. That petition identified Mo‘oinanea as a “nature spirit
and guardian of Lake Waiau [who] presently resides on the summit of Mauna
a Wakea” and requested that she be allowed to participate in the legal
proceedings pertaining to the permit decision.
The final decision by the State of Hawai‘i’s Board of Land and Natural
Resources (“BLNR”) describes the request:

On February 23, 2011, Mr. Flores also filed a petition for contested case on
behalf of “Mo‘oinanea et al.” That petition identified Mo‘oinanea as a
“nature spirit and guardian of Lake Waiau [who] presently resides on the
summit of Mauna a Wakea.” The petition stated that Mo‘oinanea “has never
been previously consulted regarding this and other projects on this sacred
mountain,” and “wishes her expressed concerns to be disclosed.” It stated that
Mo‘oinanea’s “insight” is needed “to avoid obstructing the piko/portal on the
summit of Mauna a Wakea that connects with Ke Akua (The Creator) and
‘Aumakua (Ancestors),” which “is a major portal for the life forces that flow
into this island.” The petition recites that Mo‘oinanea “has a substantial
interest in this matter, resides on the summit of Mauna a Wakea, and can
demonstrate that she and others will be directly and immediately affected by
the requested action”; it further asserts that “her interest in the proceeding is
clearly distinguishable from that of the general public.” Exhibit A-318.54
The BLNR denied the request, refusing to allow Mo‘oinanea to participate
because she was not a “person” as defined in the law and therefore lacked
standing.55
The BLNR provided a very literal analysis in support of its decision to
preclude Mo‘oinanea’s participation:
A plain English reading can be applied to the definition of “person” under the
Hawai‘i Administrative Procedures Act. See County of Hawai‘i v. Civil Serv.
Comm’n, 77 Haw. 396, 400, 885 P.2d 1137, 1141 (1994).
Webster’s Dictionary defines a “person” as a “human being, individual.”
Webster’s Dictionary 877 (9th ed. 1983).
Black’s Law Dictionary defines a person as follows: “In general usage, a
human being (i.e., natural person)…”. Black’s Law Dictionary 1028 (5th ed.
1979).
A plain English reading shows that Mo‘oinanea, identified in the petition
submitted on its behalf as a “nature spirit and guardian of Lake Waiau who
resides on the summit of Mauna a Wakea,” does not qualify as a “person”
under the Hawai‘i Administrative Rules.

Under Haw. Admin. R. §13-1-10, Petitioners Flores and Case do not have
authority to appear on behalf of Mo‘oinanea. Under Section 13-1-10, a
person can only appear on his or her own behalf, or represented by counsel.
For these reasons, Mo‘oinanea lacked standing to be a party to the contested
case proceeding in this matter.56
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Allowing Mo‘oinanea to formally participate in the BLNR proceedings

Would it help to amend the definition of “person” to include nature spirits,
along with natural communities and ecosystems? What needs to be done to

(2) Assuming the rights of nature continue to develop in the United States,

representation from Native Americans and Native Hawaiians be important
within these guardianship bodies?
(3) As you read in Chapter 23, the Māori tribe of Whanganui and the Crown

was a manifestation of the longstanding relationship between the Whanganui

(4) After reading about the petition that named Mo‘oinanea in Hawai‘i, do

Or can the two approaches be harmonized?
VIII. NATURE’S RIGHTS AND POPULATION
ECOLOGY
Ecological sciences look at systems at different scales. Population ecology
focuses on an individual species, the number of organisms in that species,
and how that population is changing over time and why. For example, a
population ecologist may study American Crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos)
behavior and how that behavior affects the population of crows in an area.
Community ecology looks at a group of species in an area. For example, a
community ecologist may study how crows interact with other birds and their
habitats. Systems ecology focuses on all the biotic and abiotic parts of the
natural world: the whole ecosystem. For example, a systems ecologist may
study how crows change their habitat through altering the behavior of other
birds and thus their seed distribution patterns.
Most of the laws examined above have focused on Earth rights at an
ecosystem scale, protecting Lake Erie, for example. The White Earth Band of
Ojibwe’s recognition of wild rice, or Manoomin, supra at 254-255, explores
recognizing the rights of specific nonhuman entities. Historian Roderick
Frazier Nash, in The Rights of Nature: A History of Environmental Ethics
(1989), examines the development of environmental ethics beginning with
early animal welfare laws that focused more on treatment of individual
organisms, and moving toward the land ethic, or ecosystem recognition, of
Aldo Leopold, supra at 233. In extant U.S. law, the Endangered Species Act
is a form of population scale protection, but it is limited in that it only comes
into effect after a species is listed as threatened or endangered, as if we
recognize a species’ value only when we are about to lose it. But even with
the Endangered Species Act, many species continue to go extinct.57
Something is not working.
In Washington state, a group called Legal Rights of the Salish Sea has
embarked on a campaign to recognize the rights of the Southern Resident
Orcas.58 The Southern Resident Orcas, an apex predator in the Salish Sea, are

on the brink of extinction. The group is circulating a Declaration of the
Rights of the Southern Residents that recognizes not only the rights of the
Southern Residents, but also the rights of the ecosystems, including the Salish
Sea, Fraser River Watershed, Columbia River Basin, and Snake River
Watershed, upon which salmon, the Southern Residents’ food, depend for
their survival. In this way, the Southern Resident Orcas show the connection
between multiple ecosystems. The campaign’s goal is to educate and build
support for a rights-based approach, leading to legal changes at the local,
state, national, and international level.59
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Consider how plant and animal species-specific laws advance the Earth
law movement as a whole. In EVENING THOUGHTS: REFLECTING ON EARTH AS
SACRED COMMUNITY, Appendix 2 (“Ten Principles for Jurisprudence
Revision”), Thomas Berry said that we can talk about species’ specific rights
while recognizing that specific species are part of, and have a role in, the
entire Earth community. Berry described one of the three rights by virtue of
belonging to the Earth community as the right to fulfill a particular role in the
ever-renewing processes of the Earth community. What are the advantages
and disadvantages to focusing on a particular species rather than an entire
ecosystem?
(2) Chapter 11 covers “Nonhuman Rights” with a focus on the quest of the
Nonhuman Rights Project to seek habeas corpus relief for captive animals in
the State of New York based on principles of state common law. How does
this legal strategy compare to the one taken for rights of Manoomin and
Southern Resident Orcas?
IX. CONCLUSION
Looking to the future of the rights of nature movement in the United States,
consider the following excerpt from Christopher Stone’s Should Trees Have
Standing:
The fact is, that each time there is a movement to confer rights onto some

new “entity,” the proposal is bound to sound odd or frightening or laughable.
…[T]here will be resistance to giving the thing “rights” until it can be seen
and valued for itself; yet, it is hard to see it and value it for itself until we can
bring ourselves to give it “rights”—which is almost inevitably going to sound
inconceivable to a large group of people.
The reason for this little discourse on the unthinkable, the reader must know
by now, if only from the title of the paper. I am quite seriously proposing that
we give legal rights to forests, oceans, rivers and other so-called “natural
objects” in the environment—indeed, to the natural environment as a
whole.60
Movement lawyers advocating rights of nature laws have thought the
unthinkable and will not go back. Representing ecosystems and advancing
rights of nature in the United States requires taking a long view. Seeking
fundamental systemic change requires transforming the legal system’s
relationship with the earth. Nature is not property. Legal history demonstrates
that when only certain parties have standing to litigate about ecosystem’s
rights, those parties become susceptible to succumbing to regulatory capture
and to compromising those rights with economic impacts or to bartering one
ecosystem for another. Developing rights of nature within local, state and
federal legislative processes is no less susceptible to compromise. Rights of
nature advocates will face difficult decisions in preserving and strengthening
the paradigm shifting elements of this work.
As lawyers work to advance the rights of nature in the United States, the
issues below may frame the context:
Will ecosystems become another kind of legal “person”? If so, how
might they fit within the present division between “natural persons” and
“artificial persons”? Is it necessary to create a new category of legal
being for rivers, forests, species, and whole ecosystems?
How will ecosystems and the human communities that are part of them
interact legally?
Could recognizing ecosystem rights invoke constitutional takings? Will
it require amendment of the U.S. Constitution to prevent this, as was
done with the Fourteenth Amendment? (Section 4 states: “But neither
the United States nor any state shall assume or pay any…claim for the

loss or emancipation of any slave; but all such debts, obligations and
claims shall be held illegal and void.”)
How might rights of nature, Indigenous rights, human rights, including
the right to a healthy environment, and other rights-based frameworks
support and conflict with one another?
Considering these questions, and more, will facilitate the work of lawyers and
others to create a legal system that honors and respects the earth on which we
all depend.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Giving rights to a particular ecosystem makes sense from an ecological
perspective. But political boundaries (e.g., a state border) often do not closely
follow nature’s own boundaries (e.g., a watershed). How might this be
tackled in developing rights of nature laws?
(2) Boulder Rights of Nature is a grassroots organization based in Boulder
County, Colorado, that works to advance rights of nature. One of its current
projects is establishing legal rights for the Boulder Creek Watershed. What
strategies and tactics could be developed to achieve this, considering the
previous study question and other challenges faced by rights of nature
advocates? What stakeholders should be involved? If there were a legal
guardianship body developed on behalf of the watershed, who would be
invited to be a part of the body? What new ideas might become part of the
rights of nature movement in the United States?
(3) Recalling the guardianship models examined in Chapter 6: Legal
Guardianship and Representation, consider the potential conflicts. For
example, the interests of a river that is part of the ecosystem may be in
maintaining a higher flow rate than farmers, also part of the ecosystem, who
want to use the water for irrigation. The interests of some aquatic life may
thrive under a reduced flow, others only if the flow is higher. How might the
guardian work to represent the rights and interests of ecosystems? Is that the
right approach as guardianship implies that the ecosystem is incapacitated?
(4) How do you see rights of nature playing out in the United States in the

next 10 years? 50 years? 100 years?

CHAPTER 10
Human Rights and Rights of
Nature: 
A Symbiotic Relationship1
I. LAND AND ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENDERS
In 2016, Berta Cáceres, the internationally recognized Honduran community
and environmental activist and recipient of the 2015 Goldman Environmental
Prize,2 was murdered in her home in La Esperanza, Honduras. World-
renowned for her Indigenous rights and environmental activism, Cáceres was
murdered for her leadership role in the grassroots campaign to stop the Agua
Zarca hydroelectric dam, planned for construction on the biodiversity-rich
Gualcarque River, which is sacred to the local Indigenous Lenca people.3 The
dam would devastate the Gualcarque’s sensitive aquatic ecosystem that
sustains the Lenca people. Cáceres’s outspoken advocacy and public
exposure made her a target for the Honduran government and the
corporations involved. In the years since the 2009 military coup, Honduras
has become notorious for its violence against environmental and social
activists, including protestors fighting massive hydroelectric dams
constructed to power mines owned and controlled by multinational
corporations.4 Often slated for ecologically valuable Indigenous territories,
these government-backed projects damage aquatic and riparian ecosystems
and flood Indigenous lands, impairing or destroying both natural and human
communities.
Cáceres was one of thousands of land and environmental defenders active

across the globe protesting the ravage of natural areas and local communities
by mega industrial projects at the risk of being killed or seriously injured.
The organization Global Witness tracks the killings of these activists, to
whom it gives the name “land and environmental defenders” as defined
below:5
WHO ARE LAND AND ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENDERS? When
communities have their land taken from them, forests cut down or rivers
polluted without their permission or even knowledge, they are given little
choice but to take a stand. As soon as they speak up, they are no longer only
affected communities: they become land or environmental defenders. A land
or environmental defender is anybody who takes peaceful action, either
voluntarily or professionally, to protect environmental or land rights. They
are often ordinary people who may well not define themselves as
“defenders.” Some are Indigenous or peasant leaders living in remote
mountains or isolated forests, protecting their ancestral lands and traditional
livelihoods from mining projects, large-scale agribusiness, hydro-dams and
luxury hotels. Others are park rangers, tackling poaching and illegal logging.
They could also be lawyers, journalists or NGO staff working to expose
environmental abuse and land-grabbing. Land and environmental defenders
often clash with political, business and criminal interests, who collude to steal
their natural resources. These powerful forces often seek to marginalise
defenders, branding their actions “anti-development.” Many defenders face
years of death threats, criminalisation, intimidation and harassment, but
receive little or no protection from authorities. These activists defend
internationally recognised human rights, such as the right to a healthy
environment, the right to participate in public life, the right to protest and the
right to life. As such, they are a subset of human rights defenders who
governments are obliged to protect, as set out in the UN Declaration on
Human Rights Defenders. Business must respect their rights too, as per the
UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
While many land and environmental defenders come from Indigenous
communities directly threatened by catastrophic projects sited in their
ancestral lands, all humans are dependent on nature to survive. “Nature”
encompasses healthy and thriving ecosystems and biodiversity that supply us
with our most basic and critical needs, including clean air, clean water, food,

and medicine. The dependence of every one of us on nature for survival is
globally recognized by the emergence of environmental rights and the
expansion of human rights to include a healthy environment, water, food,
health, sanitation, and shelter. These emerging environmental rights are
understood as part of the universal goal of achieving well-being for all
humanity, as already recognized by many international human rights
declarations and conventions.6
Yet while we recognize our absolute need for nature, our view of nature
remains stubbornly anthropocentric, and we continue to treat it as a
commodity under our control and ownership. Nature is still viewed as the
entrenched property of humans and the supplier of resources required for the
relentless economic growth that remains the overriding goal of international
society. The outcome is that we are destroying the very infrastructure that
keeps us alive and flourishing. Hence, by laying waste to nature, we are
endangering ourselves, especially those human populations who are directly
supported by nature without the buffer of technology to protect them.
As Christopher Stone argues in his iconic essay Should Trees Have Standing?
Toward Legal Rights for Natural Objects, the good news is that society has
evolved to abhor the evil and brutality of the human-created institutions of
slavery and discrimination based on race, gender, or age, progressively
extending human rights by crafting laws to protect us from these travesties.7
Yet, in sharp contrast to the extension of rights to all humans, nature remains
rightless. Despite the many years that have passed since Stone’s classic work
in 1972, we are not yet at a place where we recognize and respect other
species, ecosystems, or biodiversity generally as co-habitants of planet Earth
and co-travelers in time. Triggered by the Industrial Revolution 250 years
ago and sharply escalating after World War II, these explosive expansions—
of population, economic growth, and consumption—are now spiraling out of
control, and, as discussed in this section, the initial victims are local
communities and, of course, nature itself.
Indeed, under human legal systems, rightless nature can neither protest its
rightless status nor seek to gain its own right to protect itself (although the
havoc that climate change is currently wreaking demonstrates that nature has
its own ways of fighting back). Standing up for beleaguered nature, land and

environmental defenders are risking their lives to stop government and
