corporate activities in agribusiness, energy, extractive mining, dams, and
other industries that devastate both natural systems and local communities.
As discussed above, many environmental defenders are members of
Indigenous tribes that are directly dependent on nature and thus are the
people hardest hit by its loss. Demonstrating a biocentric, or ecocentric,
perspective, they have lived in harmony with their natural surroundings for
thousands of years. Indigenous culture, religion, and livelihoods are uniquely
interconnected with nature because of the communities’ dependence on the
goods and services that it supplies them. Indigenous peoples have been at the
forefront of the rights of nature movement, which builds upon the worldview
of connectedness that these Indigenous cultures embrace. Environmental
defenders intertwine their human rights with rights for nature, understanding
that to protect human rights, nature’s rights must be ensured. Yet, pitted
against the formidable power of governments and corporations that treat
nature as property that can be taken by force, hundreds—if not thousands—of
environmental defenders have been murdered or seriously injured in pursuing
this goal.
II. CO-VIOLATIONS OF RIGHTS
In response to this worsening situation, in 2015 and again in 2016, Earth Law
Center published co-violation reports, entitled Fighting for Our Shared
Future: Protecting Human Rights and Nature’s Rights. The project is based
on an analysis of over 200 case studies of environmental defenders from
around the world.8 The premise of the reports is that human rights violations
are strongly correlated with violations of the rights of nature were such rights
to be widely recognized. The following excerpts from the 2016 report
demonstrate the interconnection between human rights and rights of nature.
As you read these excerpts,9 consider the report’s criticism of current
environmental laws in treating “nature as property.” Also consider the global
“legalization” of greenhouse gas emissions by regulating them rather than
banning them entirely.
Destructive activities that impact both humans and nature are increasing
alarmingly. Many of the associated injuries amount to simultaneous

violations, or “co-violations,” of both nature’s rights and human rights,
including in particular Indigenous rights. We define a “co-violation” of rights
as a situation in which governments, industries, or others violate both the
rights of nature and human rights, including Indigenous rights, with the same
action.…
Climate change once again provides an important set of co-violation
examples. Climate change threatens the following human rights, among
others: to life; to adequate food, water, and sanitation; to adequate housing;
and to self-determination. The rights of particularly vulnerable populations
are of special concern, including: women, children, persons with disabilities,
those living in extreme poverty, Indigenous peoples, and displaced persons.
Global Humanitarian Forum estimates that 26 million people worldwide have
been forced to move from their homes due to climate change.10 Because
women constitute up to 80% of global refugee and displaced populations, this
results in up to 20 million women worldwide displaced due to global
warming.…
Despite these and other escalating climate-related harms, national and
international climate change laws and conventions continue to legalize
massive amounts of greenhouse gas emissions while only calling for modest,
and usually voluntary, reductions. While the international community fails to
address climate change and other drivers of co-violations, humans and nature
continue to suffer the consequences.…
Our overarching legal and economic systems accelerate co-violations by
treating nature and workers as “resources” to fuel short-term profit
maximization for the few. Nature is particularly mistreated in light of its
characterization as merely “property” to be bought, sold, and ultimately
degraded for profit. Reinforcing this misperception is the fact that our
modern environmental laws themselves implicitly accept this claim of
“nature as property.” They legalize nature’s destruction by dictating how
much of the environment we can degrade, thus validating the continuing
onslaught. Instead, we need laws grounded in the inherent rights of the
natural world to exist, thrive, and evolve. The evolution of human rights
provides precedent for recognizing the fundamental rights of nature. Human
progress can be measured by the ever-widening circle of those whom we

understand to possess dignity and rights, work that is ongoing today. As
described in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), such
understanding is “the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the
world.”…
By extending the sphere of rights outward to encompass all of Earth’s beings,
with which we co-evolved, we are logically and morally continuing the work
we began by recognizing the inherent rights of all humans.
The concept of nature’s rights in law is not new. Christopher Stone famously
wrote about it in his groundbreaking essay of the early 1970s, listing four
elements as necessary to effectively recognize the rights of nature in law:
Rights must be subject to redress by a public body;
The entity must have standing to institute legal actions on its own behalf
(a guardian can stand in for the entity as needed);
Redress must be calculated for the entity’s own damages; and
Relief must run to the benefit of the injured entity.…
[H]ow we treat the natural world often mirrors how we treat each other. For
example, governments and industries around the world are increasingly
harassing, threatening, attacking, imprisoning, and even killing defenders of
environmental and human rights. The United Nations found that human rights
defenders working on “land and environmental issues in connection with
extractive industries and construction and development projects in the
Americas” face the highest risk of death of all human rights advocates
worldwide. Organizations such as Global Witness and EJOLT, and the Yes to
Life No to Mining Campaign, are providing invaluable reports of rights
violations against people and the environment in the name of profit. These
continued violations of fundamental rights have to stop. We must hold
governments and industry accountable for actions that impact human and
environmental wellbeing. Among other steps, we must:
Reformulate our laws to recognize and implement environmental rights;
Bolster identification and enforcement of human rights, Indigenous
rights, and environmental rights violations; and
Shift to ecological economics models, which respect people and planet.
…

As the case studies in this report demonstrate, unless our governance systems
recognize the inherent rights of all beings in law, we will fail to recognize
them in practice.…[citation omitted]. Our key findings with regard to trends
in the co-violation of human rights, Indigenous rights, and nature’s rights
include the following:
Co-violations are frequently connected to the extractive and energy
industries;
Violations of the rights of Indigenous peoples and environmental
destruction are often strongly associated;
Co-violations occur globally, but they have been arising more often in
the Global South; and
Governments often side with private industry over people and natural
systems whose rights may be violated.…
Based on this process, we recommend the following actions by the United
Nations and international community:
Recognize in law and implement the fundamental rights of nature,
including through UN General Assembly adoption of the Universal
Declaration of the Rights of Mother Earth;
Support swift enforcement of International Rights of Nature Tribunal
judgments;11
Create “International Rights of Nature” courts to hear cases involving
nature’s rights violations; and
Incorporate rights of nature principles into existing human rights
instruments and bodies.…
Such co-violations result when the law prioritizes corporate interests over
human and nature’s rights. Legal systems throughout the world were
developed to protect corporations. The underlying legal rationale is that
without broad protections, corporations cannot continue to perform their
function of growing the economy. The fundamental predicate of this
reasoning is that growing the economy will continue to improve the welfare
of the human species. The violation of human and nature’s rights in the Lago
Agrio Canton on Ecuador’s norther border with Colombia exemplifies the
flaws of this paradigm.

As a result of the human and ecological devastation caused by Texaco
Corporation’s12 drilling for oil between 1964 to 1992, Lago Agrio is often
described as the “Chernobyl in the Amazon.” The dumping of hundreds of
thousands of barrels of crude oil and billions of gallons of oil-contaminated
wastewater ravaged a vast rainforest ecosystem that included more than
100,000 members of numerous Indigenous communities. The land and water
has been destroyed and the lives of Indigenous peoples and rural
communities have been plagued by “an epidemic of birth defects,
miscarriages, and an estimated 1,400 cancer deaths.”13
Legal action seeking remediation for the environmental damage and
recompense for the 30,000 human victims began in 1993 in the United States
District Court for the Southern District of New York. After 9 years of
litigation, Chevron succeeding in moving the case to Ecuador based on forum
non conveniens grounds. The court’s decision relied on Chevron’s agreement
to comply with any final judgment issued in Ecuador. Ecuador’s Supreme
Court issued a final judgment in 2013 awarding the victims $9.5 billion.
Chevron refused to honor the judgment and engaged in a staggering number
of legal measures to void the judgment and punish the plaintiffs, including
litigation attacking the legitimacy of the legal process in Ecuador and
accusing the lawyer representing the victims of fraud.14 The Chevron case
opens the window into the extraordinary challenges in pursuing justice for
co-violation cases and holding corporations responsible for human and
ecological devastation.
Human rights bodies are beginning to create new mechanisms to combat
violations against humans and nature perpetrated by corporations that
regularly escape responsibility. For example, in 2014, the UN Human Rights
Council decided “to establish an open-ended intergovernmental working
group on transnational corporations and other business enterprises with
respect to human rights, whose mandate shall be to elaborate an international
legally binding instrument to regulate, in international human rights law, the
activities of transnational corporations and other business enterprises.”15 The
resulting intergovernmental working group on transnational corporations and
other business enterprises with respect to human rights has had five
negotiating sessions as of 2020.16

Civil society groups have also played an increasing role in highlighting the
atrocities by corporations, governments, and other actors against land
defenders, with the goal of building awareness of the global problem and
solutions. Global Witness’s 2017 report, At What Cost? Irresponsible
Business and the Murder of Land and Environmental Defenders in 2017,
documents the murder of 207 defenders.17
The food on our plates, the rings on our fingers and the wooden furniture in
our homes: all too often there is a violent reality behind household items we
use every day. As agribusiness booms, tropical forests are logged and mining
continues to deliver huge revenue to major global corporations, there are
increasingly brutal attacks on land and environmental defenders.
In Colombia, Hernán Bedoya was shot by a paramilitary group 14 times. He
was killed after protesting against palm oil and banana plantations on land
stolen from his community. In the Philippines, near the town of Lake Sebu,
the military descended on a small community, leaving eight dead, wounding
five and causing 200 to flee.
And in one of the largest-scale attacks of 2017, Gamela Indigenous people
were assaulted in Brazil. Machetes and rifles were used in an attempt to
forcibly seize control of their land, leaving 22 severely injured, some with
their hands cut off. Months later, nobody had faced justice for this appalling
incident, reflecting a wider culture of impunity and inaction to support
defenders by the Brazilian government.
Rather than taking steps to crack down on these attacks, President Michel
Temer and the Brazilian legislature are actively weakening the laws and
institutions designed to protect land rights and Indigenous peoples. At the
same time, they have set about making it easier for big business—apparently
unperturbed by the devastating human and environmental cost of their
activities—to accelerate their exploitation of fragile ecosystems.…
But it’s not just in Brazil where governments and business are turning their
backs on those fighting to protect their land and way of life. As our sixth
Annual Report shows, around the world too many of those who perpetrate
and are complicit in attacks on defenders are literally getting away with
murder.

Governments and business have failed to act responsibly, ethically and even
legally, making them a major driving force behind a litany of crimes against
activists last year.
They are part of the reason 207 defenders were killed in 2017, making it the
worst year on record. And why many, many more were attacked, threatened
or criminalised for showing the courage to speak out for their communities,
their way of life and our environment.
Their inaction helped fuel the surge in killings of people protesting against
large-scale agriculture, as the global rush for land gathered pace.
And their willingness to turn a blind eye has permitted the systemic impunity
that lets perpetrators know they will almost certainly never be brought to
justice. In fact, governments are often complicit in the attacks. One of the
most shocking facts outlined in this report is the number of killings
committed by government security forces at the behest of their political
bosses and in league with industry.
The data painstakingly gathered and presented in this report—and the case
studies included—are almost certainly a sizeable underestimate, given the
many challenges in identifying and reporting killings. Yet even as it stands, it
shows that governments and business have a very serious case to answer.
But we can all do more.
Ultimately, attacks against land and environmental defenders stem from our
voracious appetite for agricultural goods like palm oil and coffee, and for
fossil fuels, minerals and timber. Extracting these resources requires an
increasing amount of land, turning it into a highly prized commodity.
Communities who have lived and worked on the land for generations are
often the losers in this quest for natural resources.
Companies have a responsibility to their customers, who should have
confidence that the products they buy are not fueling human rights abuses,
cultural destruction or environmental devastation. And we, the consumers,
have a responsibility to demand that these companies live up to their
responsibilities.

When rich tropical forest is levelled for monoculture crops, delicate
ecosystems that could capture carbon emissions are lost forever. When land
is exploited for mining, soil and fresh water are poisoned, jeopardising the
health and the future of nearby communities. These abuses are tolerated,
facilitated and sometimes even perpetrated by irresponsible business and
investors, together with corrupt or negligent governments, who are hell-bent
on meeting consumer demand and maximising profit.…
We’re calling on governments and business to take responsibility, prioritise
defenders, and:
Tackle the root causes of violence against defenders, especially the lack
of free, prior and informed consent from communities for the use of
their land and natural resources.
Support and protect defenders at risk so they can carry out their
advocacy in safety.
Ensure accountability so that those responsible for attacks on defenders
are brought to justice; and so that there are consequences for those who
fail to protect activists and for companies who don’t do proper due
diligence of their supply chains.
Consumers can play their part too, demanding guarantees that the products
they buy are not associated with land-grabbing, forcible evictions or attacks
on defenders.
Despite the odds they face, the global community of environmental and land
defenders is not going away—it’s only getting stronger. We will campaign
alongside them, taking their struggle to the corridors of power and the
boardrooms of corporations. We will not tire in our fight to ensure that their
voices are heard.…
In 2017, Global Witness documented 207 killings of land and environmental
defenders—ordinary people murdered for defending their forests, rivers and
homes against destructive industries. This is six more murders than in 2016,
making it the worst year on record.
As the killing has increased, some governments, businesses and
intergovernmental organisations have begun to acknowledge the gravity of

the situation. But their promises and rhetoric have yet to translate into
convincing policies and concrete change, leaving defenders in fear of their
lives.…
This is, in part, driven by one deadly trend: the number of people killed while
protesting against large-scale agriculture more than doubled compared to
2016. For the first time, agribusiness surpassed mining as the most dangerous
sector to oppose, as 46 defenders who protested against palm oil, coffee,
tropical fruit and sugar cane plantations, as well as cattle ranching, were
murdered in 2017.
Opposition to mining and oil operations (40 killings), poaching (23 murders)
and logging (23 cases) were the other main reasons defenders were killed last
year.…
Linked to the spike in agribusiness-related deaths, Global Witness observed a
rise in multiple killings (7 incidents in total) of land and environmental
defenders, many of whom were disputing large-scale agriculture projects.
Brazil was the scene of three horrific massacres, during which 25 defenders
died. Eight Indigenous activists were massacred in the Philippines, while
Mexico, Peru and the Democratic Republic of Congo also saw incidents
where more than four defenders died at the same time.
These massacres sent the message that not only community leaders will be
targeted: nobody is safe. This has a huge impact, given that whole
communities—or large parts of them—are often involved in struggles to
protect their land from being grabbed.…
The term “agribusiness” features heavily in this report as the industry most
linked to killings of land and environmental defenders. Any business that
earns most or all of its revenues from agriculture is known as an
“agribusiness.” They tend to be large-scale business operations involved in
farming, processing and manufacturing, as well as potentially packaging and
distributing products.
Some key agribusiness products include cattle (beef and dairy), cotton, palm
oil, soy and sugar cane. Palm oil is in about half of all packaged products sold
in the supermarket, including chocolate, margarine, ice cream, shampoo and

lipstick. Sugar extracted from sugar cane is prevalent in many of the foods
we eat, and increasingly a source of biofuels and bioplastics. Most
commercially produced beef, fish, chicken and dairy products were fed on
soy, with 80% of the world’s soybean crop fed to livestock.…
A widespread culture of impunity has made it difficult to identify those
responsible for the killings, and sends a signal to would-be perpetrators that
they will not be made to pay for their crimes. Worse still, Global Witness
data shows that it is often government security forces committing the crimes.
They were linked to around a quarter of the murders last year—30 linked to
the army and 23 to the police. Criminal gangs, security guards, landowners,
poachers and other non-state actors were suspected of carrying out at least 90
killings.…
Once again, Latin America saw the highest number of murders, accounting
for almost 60% of the total. According to Global Witness data, Brazil
recorded the most killings of any country ever with 57 people killed, 80% of
them while protecting the natural riches of the Amazon. In Colombia 24
defenders were murdered in 2017, as conflicts over land raged on. Mexico
and Peru saw a jump in killings from three to 15 and two to eight
respectively. There were fewer murders in Honduras—five compared to 14 in
2016—but the growing repression of civil society has restricted what
defenders can say and do. Nicaragua registered the most murders per capita,
with four defenders killed.
In Asia, the most alarming developments took place in the Philippines, which
saw 48 killings—almost a 71% rise on 2016 and the most murders ever
recorded in Asia in a single year. President Duterte’s aggressively anti-
human-rights stance and a renewed military presence in resource-rich regions
are fuelling the violence. Almost half of the killings in the Philippines were
linked to struggles against agribusiness.
Of the 19 land and environmental defenders reported killed across Africa, 17
lost their lives while defending protected areas against poachers and illegal
miners—12 in the Democratic Republic of Congo alone.
Of course, many other countries and regions could be suffering elevated
numbers of killings which have not been documented or which we have been

unable to verify.…
Fewer Indigenous people were killed in 2017—falling to 25% of the total,
from 40% in 2016. However, with Indigenous groups making up just 5% of
the world’s population, they remain massively overrepresented among
defenders killed. And it is not only killings: in one of the most brutal attacks,
Gamela Indigenous people were assaulted with machetes and rifles by
Brazilian farmers, leaving 22 of them severely injured, some with their hands
cut off. In Mexico, 13 out of 15 defenders killed were Indigenous—murdered
defending their ancestral territories.
Although nine out of every 10 murdered activists last year were male, women
defenders faced gender-specific threats including sexual violence. They were
often subjected to smear-campaigns, threats against their children, and
attempts to undermine their credibility; sometimes from within their own
communities, where macho cultures might prevent women from taking up
positions of leadership.…
Our data on killings is likely to be an underestimate, given that many murders
go unreported, particularly in rural areas. Our methodology requires cases to
be verified according to a strict set of criteria…which can’t always be met by
a review of public information like newspaper reports or legal documents,
nor through local contacts. Having a strict methodology means our figures
don’t represent the scale of the problem, and we are working to improve this.
III. INTERNATIONAL RIGHTS OF NATURE
TRIBUNALS
In light of government indifference and even involvement in these brutalities,
what chances are there to prosecute the perpetrators and end the human and
environmental devastation? As an alternative to government judicial forums
mandated to issue decisions under current anthropocentric laws exclusively,
the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature, together with Indigenous groups
and other social and environmental organizations, spearheaded a brave and
creative initiative of “International Rights of Nature Tribunals” to hear and
decide cases of violations of human rights and rights of nature. The Tribunal
is a non-governmental “people’s tribunal,” in which leading academics,

environmental activists, Indigenous leaders, and others hear cases and write
judgments in enforcement of the rights of nature and other ecocentric legal
doctrines based on specific case studies. These include destructive mining
projects in the heart of the Amazon, mega-dams in Latin America, fracking
across the United States, the oil pollution of the Niger Delta in Nigeria, and
many others. It is modeled on other people’s tribunals, such as the Russell
Tribunal, also known as the International War Crimes Tribunal, that was
organized by Nobel Prize winner and British philosopher Bertrand Russell to
investigate and evaluate American military intervention in Vietnam,
ultimately finding they had committed war crimes.18 As with the
International Rights of Nature Tribunal, the Russell Tribunal did not have
recognized legal authority but was necessary to raise awareness and push for
accountability and reform in the absence of sufficient governmental action.
Five such tribunals have been held so far, in Quito, Ecuador, in January 2014,
in Lima, Peru, in December 2014, in Paris, France, in November 2016, in
Bonn, Germany, in November 2017, and in Santiago, Chile, in 2019. The
2016 and 2017 tribunals were held concurrently with Conferences of the
Parties of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.
Among Earth Law Center’s recommendations in its co-violations reports is to
“support swift enforcement of International Rights of Nature Tribunal
Judgments.” The following excerpt from Earth Law Center’s Fighting for
Our Shared Future report describes the work of these forums in greater
depth:19
Organized by civil society around the world, International Rights of Nature
Tribunals re-frame and adjudicate prominent environmental and social justice
cases within a rights of nature context. While the Tribunals do not yet have
formal legal authority, the adjudication process:
Generates sophisticated legal analysis of diverse cases from a nature’s
rights perspective, applying the UDRME [Universal Declaration of
Rights of Mother Earth] tenets and nature’s rights laws as legal
guidelines;
Educates governments, advocacy groups, and the interested public on
the tenets of the rights of nature and how they can be applied;
Recommends actions such as enforcement and mitigation based on

rights of nature violations; and
Enables others to ultimately develop formal legal structures that
recognize the inherent rights of nature.
The Tribunals are particularly guided by the Universal Declaration of Rights
of Mother Earth (UDRME) Article 2(1)(j), which states that: “Mother Earth
and all beings of which she is composed have the following inherent rights:
…the right to full and prompt restoration for the violation of the rights
recognized in this Declaration caused by human activities.” As discussed by
2015 Tribunal Chair Cormac Cullinan of South Africa:
[i]magine if there were an international tribunal that concerned itself with the
fundamental rights of all beings, including humans, and decided matters on
the basis of what was best for the Earth community as a whole, regardless of
politics; an Earth Tribunal of respected individuals that drew on the wisdom
of humanity as whole, respected the laws of Nature and was not beholden to
governments or corporations.
The establishment of the International Tribunal for the Rights of Nature is
intended to give effect to this dream. This bold venture by the members of the
Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature is a creative response to the current
impasse at the international level which has led to a widening chasm between
what global civil society wants done and what governments are willing to
agree to and implement.…
Tribunals such as the International Rights of Nature Tribunals have a long
tradition of addressing fundamental issues of justice beyond the reach of
traditional courts, including military interventions and human rights abuses.
By recognizing these groundbreaking tribunals for rights of nature and
calling for the enforcement of their judgments, the United Nations and other
international bodies would help ensure that the international community
addresses some of the world’s most insidious co-violations of both nature’s
rights and human rights.
Yet meanwhile the UN, as an organization composed of sovereign states, has
refrained from recognizing these forums. Moreover, it is improbable that
such a decision would even make it to the agenda of the UN General
Assembly as it would, of course, create a major conflict with current

international and national laws and judicial forums governed by established
laws based on the independent interests of nations. As such, decisions of
rights of nature tribunals are not being implemented and enforced since
police power remains in the hands of governments that do not recognize their
validity. For the very same reason, tribunals have also not been used as
platforms for governments to initiate investigations and judicial proceedings
at the national level of the violations at issue.
In searching for other ways to prosecute violations of both human rights and
rights of nature, co-violations could be theoretically pursued in international
human rights forums by arguing that acts of environmental devastation are
violating human rights and, in particular, the right to a healthy environment.
While nature would not be a petitioner to argue for its own rights, the
outcome could be the same. The main criteria in searching for an appropriate
human rights forum would be its capacity to review petitions from
individuals and non-governmental organizations, rather than solely from
states. While the International Court of Justice is limited to hearings between
sovereign states, both the UN Human Rights Council and the European Court
of Human Rights, as well as regional commissions of human rights, accept
complaints from individuals, victims of human rights violations, and
concerned non-governmental organizations. The subsequent section explores
several such cases from the Inter-American Commission of Human Rights
(IACHR or “commission”) and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights
(“the court”), which together make up the human rights protection system of
the Organization of American States (OAS). Following the report of an
alleged human rights violation, a complaint is lodged with the commission,
who rules on the admissibility of the case. The commission then prepares a
list of recommendations and, if the state fails to amend the violation, or if the
commission determines the case is of particular importance or legal interest,
refers the case to the court. The court ultimately rules on whether a state has
violated human rights.
IV. HUMAN RIGHTS PROTECTION SYSTEM
OF THE ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN
STATES

A. Yanomami Community—Brazil
The commission has reviewed many cases of human rights violations as a
result of environmental injury resulting from government expropriation of
lands and activities such as mining, dams, logging, and agriculture. In 1979,
the Indian Law Resource Center petitioned the commission on behalf of the
Yanomami Indigenous community regarding human rights violations by
Brazil.20 The International Network for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
(ESCR-Net), which connects over 280 non-governmental organizations and
initiatives from more than 75 countries, summarized the case as follows:
The case was based on the construction of a road and mining licenses granted
in Indigenous land, which had led to a massive presence of foreigners in the
said territory and had had serious effects on the community’s well-being,
including the alteration of their traditional organization, emergence of female
prostitution, epidemics and diseases, forced displacement to lands unsuitable
to their ways of life, and death of hundreds of Yanomamis.21
The IACHR issued its decision in 1985. The ESCR-Net stated in a summary:
The IACHR found the State was responsible for failing to take timely and
effective measures to protect the Yanomamis’ human rights. The IACHR
concluded such failure had led to alterations in the community’s well-being
and violations to the right to life, liberty, security, residence and movement,
and to the preservation of health and well-being.…The IACHR
recommended the State, in line with domestic legislation, to proceed to
demarcate the Yanomami Park, to continue adopting preventive and remedial
sanitary measures aimed at protecting the life and health of the Yanomami.
…22
ESCR-Net noted the following updates as to the enforcement of the case:
In 1992, the land of the Yanomamis was finally demarcated as “Yanomami
Park.” In a 1995 visit to Brazil, the IACHR was able to prove on site the
presence of federal agency surveillance and healthcare stations in the
Yanomami area. However, the Yanomamis’ personal and collective integrity,
as well as their environment, continue to be subject to aggression by

intruding miners. State protection is weak and inconsistent.23
B. Mayagna Awas (Sumo) Tingni Community—Nicaragua
In 1995, the Indigenous Mayagna Awas (Sumo) Tingni community from the
Atlantic coastal area of Nicaragua submitted a petition to the commission.
The petition charged Nicaragua for failing to demarcate Awas Tingni’s
communal land and to take the necessary measures to protect the
community’s property rights over its ancestral lands and natural resources,
including 62,000 hectares of tropical forest planned for commercial
development. The petition alleged that Nicaraguan law has been “absolutely
ineffective to prevent the State from allowing the foreign firm SOLCARSA
to destroy and exploit the lands which for years have belonged to the Awas
Tingni community,” and that “the Community suffered the continuation of a
logging concession which negatively affected their traditional land tenure and
their natural resources.”24
In 1998, the commission submitted the case to the court. Only state parties
and the commission may refer cases to the court, which is authorized to
adjudicate cases brought against state members of the OAS that have
accepted the court’s jurisdiction, subject to the commission’s initial overview
of the case. Hence, the American human rights system, by limiting
submission of cases to the court by state parties or the commission, differs
from the European human rights system: as mentioned above, the European
Court on Human Rights provides for submission of petitions by individuals
and non-governmental organizations.
In 2001, the court issued its ruling on Mayagna (Sumo) Awas Tingni Cmty. v.
Nicaragua:
Nicaragua had violated the right to judicial protection and to property. The
Court noted that the right to property acknowledged by the American
Convention of Human Rights originated in Indigenous tradition and,
therefore, the State had no right to grant concessions to third parties in their
land. Consequently, the Court decided that the State had to adopt the
necessary measures to create an effective mechanism for demarcation and
titling of the Indigenous communities’ territory, in accordance with their

customary law, values, customs and mores. The Court also decided that, until
such mechanism was created, the State had to refrain from any acts that might
affect the existence, value, use or enjoyment of the property located in the
geographic area where the members of the Indigenous community live and
carry out their activities.25
Nicaragua ignored the court’s decision, and, in 2003, the Indigenous
community petitioned the court for a decision ordering the government to
comply with the ruling. The case was finally resolved in 2008 when the
Nicaraguan government titled the land under dispute in the name of the Awas
Tingni. This was the first community to obtain a land title under the
Nicaraguan law that mandated the government to demarcate Indigenous land
on Nicaragua’s Atlantic coast.26
In addition, “[t]his was the first case in which an international tribunal with
legally binding authority found a Government in violation of the collective
land rights of an Indigenous group, setting an important precedent in
international law.”27
C. Saramaka People—Suriname
In Suriname, in 2000, the non-Indigenous community of Saramaka people,
liberated slaves who had lived on the land since the early eighteenth century,
submitted a complaint to the commission regarding violations of their human
rights by logging and mining concessions operating under government
approval in Saramaka territory without consultation or consent.28 The
complaint specifically referred to “Chinese and other multinational logging
and mining companies which were extracting resources with the explicit
permission of the State.”29 In 2006, the commission submitted the case to the
court and, in 2007, the court issued a ruling that while not Indigenous, the
Saramaka people held rights similar to those of Indigenous peoples, including
the right to their land through possession, and title was not required. It ruled
that Suriname had to grant the Saramaka people a collective title to their land,
to refrain from any activities in the territory until title was granted, to review
current concessions, to adopt legislation and undertake other measures to
protect the Saramaka’s human rights and avoid further violations, and to pay
them compensation for the injury that these violations caused them, including

environmental damage. The court also ruled that major development projects
require prior and informed consent. While the court’s 2007 decision was
considered a landmark decision, it has only been partially enforced.30
D. Lhaka Honhat Communities—Argentina
In 1998, after years of demanding that Argentina refrain from subdividing
their land, the Indigenous Lhaka Honhat people in Argentina submitted a
complaint to the IACHR. They alleged that Argentina had violated their right
to property because the state failed to give their communities effective title to
their ancestral territory, along with “having carried out works, demarcations,
measurements, and other activities that affected the integrity of the
territory…[and] consented to and tolerated the illegitimate actions of private
parties, such as the tending of wire fences, logging, bovine cattle grazing and
the like.”31 For several years Argentina held negotiations with the Lhaka
Honhat but then withdrew. This led the IACHR to warn Argentina that if
dialogue failed, the commission would submit the case to the court.
In 2012, the IACHR found Argentina in violation of the community’s rights
and issued an order for reparations, which Argentina ignored. Finally, the
IACHR submitted the case to the court.32 In 2019, the court made an on-site
visit to the Indigenous communities and the lands at conflict and found that
roaming livestock and the placement of fences by European-descended
settlers within the communities’ territory directly affected more than 10,000
people’s way of life and customs. In addition, the members of the court
participated in an assembly of the chiefs of the Lhaka Honhat communities,
with representatives traveling from different corners of the territory in
question, to explain the impact and transformation of their way of life
provoked by the settlers’ activities.33
In February 2020, the court issued its decision in the case, Lhaka Honhat
Association vs. Argentina.34 It found that Argentina had violated Indigenous
communities’ right to a healthy environment, to their property, cultural
identity, food, and water, and obligated the state to undertake detailed
measures to rectify the situation. The plaintiffs had argued that the state had
violated its obligation to ensure their right to communal property, due to the
construction of infrastructure projects and fossil fuels exploration on their

lands without free, prior and informed consultation. They further argued that
the state had violated their human rights by allowing illegal logging, land
enclosures, and cattle raising, activities that severely hampered their
traditional way of life based on hunting, gathering, farming and fishing.
In 2017 the court had issued an advisory opinion on the right to a healthy
environment (Advisory Opinion 23/17 of 201835) but this was the first
contentious case on the issue. The Court, relying on its advisory opinion,
determined that rights incorporated in the American Convention on Human
Rights had been violated, including the rights to cultural identity, a healthy
environment, and adequate food and water. Referring to its advisory opinion
in interpreting the right to a healthy environment, the court reiterated that this
right protects forests, rivers, seas and other natural elements as entities with
their own inherent worth. Adopting an ecocentric perspective and again based
on its 2017 advisory opinion, the court restated its willingness to recognize
the rights of nature beyond its practical value to humans.36
On the one hand, the long period of time from the initial 1998 submission to
the court’s final decision in 2020 displays the IACHR and the court as slow-
moving institutions. But on the other, the intermediacy of these institutions
and their role as watchdogs have succeeded in keeping these issues both
under negotiation with the state and on the public agenda. Moreover, the final
judgment is a decision for both the right to a healthy environment and rights
of nature.
E. Kaliña and Lokono Peoples—Suriname
In 2007, again in Suriname, the Kaliña and Lokono Indigenous people
alleged human rights violations as a result of the state’s failure to recognize
their property rights over their ancestral territories, following the
establishment of nature reserves, the issuance of land titles, and the granting
of mining concessions.37 They petitioned the IACHR, which issued a
decision in 2013 requesting Suriname to remedy the situation. Following
Suriname’s non-compliance with the decision, in 2014 the IACHR submitted
a complaint to the court which in 2016 issued a decision in favor of the
Kaliña and Lokono, The court’s “treatment of the rights of Indigenous
peoples in relation to environmental protected areas, and associated

international environmental law, is especially noteworthy.”38 As further
explained:
The Court…extensively cites international environmental law, reading
provisions of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) into its
interpretation of the ACHR… and stresses, as a general proposition, that “the
rights of the Indigenous peoples and international environmental laws should
be understood as complementary, rather than exclusionary, rights.” It is
important to note that, although the CBD purports to guarantee some
Indigenous rights, there is no corresponding enforcement mechanism. The
Court’s ruling provides an opportunity to enforce some CBD provisions
through the lens of the ACHR.39
F. Advisory Opinion on Human Rights and the Environment—
Colombian Petition Concerning the Application of the
American Convention on Human Rights
In 2018, the IACHR published its “Advisory Opinion OC-23/17” on the
obligations of states to prevent environmental harm to ensure the right to a
healthy environment, as well as the rights to life and to personal integrity, to
peoples living both within and beyond their borders.40 The court had been
requested by Colombia to determine
how the Pact of San José [the American Convention on Human Rights]
should be interpreted when there is a danger that the construction and
operation of major new infrastructure projects may have severe effects on the
marine environment in the Wider Caribbean Region and, consequently, on
the human habitat that is essential for the full enjoyment and exercise of the
rights of the inhabitants of the coasts and/or islands of a State Party to the
Pact, in light of the environmental standards recognized in international
customary law and the treaties applicable among the respective States.41
The government of Colombia explained that:
The protection of the human rights of the inhabitants of the islands of the
Wider Caribbean Region and, consequently, the prevention and mitigation of
environmental damage in this area, is an issue of particular interest to

Colombia, because part of its population lives on the islands that form part of
the Archipelago of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina and they
therefore depend on the marine environment for their survival, and economic,
social and cultural development.…
Owing to the ecological and oceanographic interconnectedness of the Wider
Caribbean Region—a well-documented situation—it is vitally important that
the problems of the marine environment be dealt with taking into
consideration the effects on relevant areas and the ecosystem as a whole, with
the cooperation of the other States that could be affected.…42
The Court based its decision on Article 11 of the Additional Protocol to the
American Convention on Human Rights in the Area of Economic, Social and
Cultural Rights (Protocol of San Salvador), and Article 26 of the Convention.
Article 11 guarantees that “Everyone shall have the right to live in a healthy
environment and to have access to basic public services” and “The States
Parties shall promote the protection, preservation, and improvement of the
environment.”43
In 2017, as a human rights forum, the court tackled the impact of a
transboundary environmental injury on the rights of people living outside of
the state that was source of the harm. Based on the human rights to a healthy
environment, to life, and to personal integrity, the court expanded the
definition of “subject to jurisdiction” and determined that states are obligated
to prevent environmental injury and protect the human rights not only of its
own peoples, but also of those living beyond its borders.
As you read these excerpts from the advisory opinion, and in the context of
co-violations of human rights and rights of nature discussed in this chapter,
note the court’s emphasis on the “interdependence and indivisibility of
human rights and environmental protection,” its references to international
environmental instruments and their connection to human rights, and the
obligation of states to prevent environmental harm in order to protect human
rights. Note, in particular, the court’s emphasis on the “special vulnerability”
of Indigenous and tribal peoples as victims of environmental harm.
Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-23/17 of

November 15, 2017 Requested by the Republic of Colombia44
…
VI
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AND THE HUMAN RIGHTS
RECOGNIZED IN THE AMERICAN CONVENTION
46. This Opinion constitutes one of the first opportunities that the Court has
had to refer extensively to the State obligations arising from the need to
protect the environment under the American Convention (supra para. 23).
Even though the object of the request made by Colombia, as previously
defined (supra paras. 32 to 38), refers specifically to the State obligations
derived from the rights to life and to personal integrity, the Court finds it
pertinent to include some initial and introductory considerations on: (A) the
interrelationship between human rights and the environment, and (B) the
human rights affected by environmental degradation, including the right to a
healthy environment. The purpose of the considerations in this chapter is to
provide a context and a general background to the answers to the specific
questions posed by Colombia that follow.
A. The interrelationship between human rights and the environment
47. This Court has recognized the existence of an undeniable relationship
between the protection of the environment and the realization of other human
rights, in that environmental degradation and the adverse effects of climate
change affect the real enjoyment of human rights.…45
48. Specifically, in cases concerning the territorial rights of Indigenous and
tribal peoples, the Court has referred to the relationship between a healthy
environment and the protection of human rights, considering that these
peoples’ right to collective ownership is linked to the protection of, and
access to, the resources to be found in their territories, because those natural
resources are necessary for the very survival, development and continuity of
their way of life.46 The Court has also recognized the close links that exist
between the right to a dignified life and the protection of ancestral territory
and natural resources. In this regard, the Court has determined that, because

Indigenous and tribal peoples are in a situation of special vulnerability, States
must take positive measures to ensure that the members of these peoples have
access to a dignified life—which includes the protection of their close
relationship with the land—and to their life project, in both its individual and
collective dimension.47 The Court has also emphasized that the lack of access
to the corresponding territories and natural resources may expose Indigenous
communities to precarious and subhuman living conditions and increased
vulnerability to disease and epidemics, and subject them to situations of
extreme neglect that may result in various violations of their human rights in
addition to causing them suffering and undermining the preservation of their
way of life, customs and language…[citation omitted].
52. In addition, there is extensive recognition of the interdependent
relationship between protection of the environment, sustainable development,
and human rights in international law. This interrelationship has been
asserted since the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment
(hereinafter “Stockholm Declaration”) which established that “[e]conomic
and social development is essential for ensuring a favourable living and
working environment for man and for creating conditions on earth that are
necessary for the improvement of the quality of life,” and asserting the need
to balance development with protection of the human environment [citations
omitted]. Subsequently, in the Rio Declaration on Environment and
Development (hereinafter “the Rio Declaration”), the States recognized that
“[h]uman beings are at the centre of concerns for sustainable development,
“and also underlined that “[i]n order to achieve sustainable development,
environmental protection shall constitute an integral part of the development
process” [citation omitted]. Following this, the Johannesburg Declaration on
Sustainable Development established three pillars of sustainable
development: economic development, social development and environmental
protection [citation omitted]. Also, in the corresponding Plan of
Implementation of the World Summit on Sustainable Development, the
States “acknowledge[d] the consideration being given to the possible
relationship between environment and human rights, including the right to
development.”48
54. Numerous points of interconnection arise from this relationship of
interdependence and indivisibility between human rights, the environment,

and sustainable development owing to which, as indicated by the Independent
Expert, “all human rights are vulnerable to environmental degradation, in that
the full enjoyment of all human rights depends on a supportive
environment.”49 In this regard, the Human Rights Council has identified
environmental threats that may affect, directly or indirectly, the effective
enjoyment of specific human rights, affirming that: (i) illicit traffic in, and
improper management and disposal of, hazardous substances and wastes
constitute a serious threat to a range of rights, including the rights to life and
health;50 (ii) climate change has a wide range of implications for the effective
enjoyment of human rights, including the rights to life, health, food, water,
housing and self-determination,51 and (iii) “environmental degradation,
desertification and global climate change are exacerbating destitution and
desperation, causing a negative impact on the realization of the right to food,
in particular in developing countries.”52
55. Owing to the close connection between environmental protection,
sustainable development and human rights (supra paras. 47 to 55), currently
(i) numerous human rights protection systems recognize the right to a healthy
environment as a right in itself, particularly the Inter-American human rights
system, while it is evident that (ii) numerous other human rights are
vulnerable to environmental degradation, all of which results in a series of
environmental obligations for States to comply with their duty to respect and
to ensure those rights. Specifically, another consequence of the
interdependence and indivisibility of human rights and environmental
protection is that, when determining these State obligations, the Court may
avail itself of the principles, rights and obligations of international
environmental law, which, as part of the international corpus iuris make a
decisive contribution to establishing the scope of the obligations under the
American Convention in this regard (supra paras. 43 to 45).…
B. Human rights affected by environmental degradation, including the
right to a healthy environment
…
58. The Court underscores that the right to a healthy environment is
recognized explicitly in the domestic laws of several States of the region

[citation omitted], as well as in some provisions of the international corpus
iuris, in addition to the aforementioned Protocol of San Salvador (supra para.
56), such as the American Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples;
the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights; the ASEAN Human
Rights Declaration, and the Arab Charter on Human Rights [citations
omitted].
59. The human right to a healthy environment has been understood as a right
that has both individual and also collective connotations. In its collective
dimension, the right to a healthy environment constitutes a universal value
that is owed to both present and future generations. That said, the right to a
healthy environment also has an individual dimension insofar as its violation
may have a direct and an indirect impact on the individual owing to its
connectivity to other rights, such as the rights to health, personal integrity,
and life. Environmental degradation may cause irreparable harm to human
beings; thus, a healthy environment is a fundamental right for the existence of
humankind.
60. The Working Group on the Protocol of San Salvador53 indicated that the
right to a healthy environment, as established in this instrument, involved the
following five State obligations: (a) guaranteeing everyone, without any
discrimination, a healthy environment in which to live; (b) guaranteeing
everyone, without any discrimination, basic public services; (c) promoting
environmental protection; (d) promoting environmental conservation, and (e)
promoting improvement of the environment.54 It also established that the
exercise of the right to a healthy environment must be governed by the
criteria of availability, accessibility, sustainability, acceptability and
adaptability [citation omitted], as in the case of other economic, social and
cultural rights.55 In order to examine the State reports under the Protocol of
San Salvador, in 2014, the OAS General Assembly adopted specific progress
indicators to evaluate the status of the environment based on: (a) atmospheric
conditions; (b) quality and sufficiency of water sources; (c) air quality; (d)
soil quality; (e) biodiversity; (f) production of pollutant waste and its
management; (g) energy resources, and (h) status of forestry resources…
[citation omitted].
* * *

62. The Court considers it important to stress that, as an autonomous right,
the right to a healthy environment, unlike other rights, protects the
components of the environment, such as forests, rivers and seas, as legal
interests in themselves, even in the absence of the certainty or evidence of a
risk to individuals. This means that it protects nature and the environment,
not only because of the benefits they provide to humanity or the effects that
their degradation may have on other human rights, such as health, life or
personal integrity, but because of their importance to the other living
organisms with which we share the planet that also merit protection in their
own right. In this regard, the Court notes a tendency, not only in court
judgments, but also in Constitutions, to recognize legal personality and,
consequently, rights to nature.
63. Thus, the right to a healthy environment as an autonomous right differs
from the environmental content that arises from the protection of other rights,
such as the right to life or the right to personal integrity.…
66. The Court considers that the rights that are particularly vulnerable to
environmental impact include the rights to life, personal integrity, private life,
health, water, food, housing, participation in cultural life, property, and the
right to not be forcibly displaced [citations omitted]. Without prejudice to the
foregoing, according to Article 29 of the Convention,56 other rights are also
vulnerable and their violation may affect the rights to life, liberty and security
of the individual,57 and infringe on the obligation of all persons to conduct
themselves fraternally,58 such as the right to peace, because displacements
caused by environmental deterioration frequently unleash violent conflicts
between the displaced population and the population settled on the territory to
which it is displaced. Some of these conflicts are massive and thus extremely
grave.
67. The Court also bears in mind that the effects on these rights may be felt
with greater intensity by certain groups in vulnerable situations. It has been
recognized that environmental damage “will be experienced with greater
force in the sectors of the population that are already in a vulnerable
situation”; hence, based on “international human rights law, States are legally
obliged to confront these vulnerabilities based on the principle of equality
and non-discrimination.” Various human rights bodies have recognized that

Indigenous peoples, children, people living in extreme poverty, minorities,
and people with disabilities, among others, are groups that are especially
vulnerable to environmental damage, and have also recognized the
differentiated impact that it has on women [citations omitted]. In addition, the
groups that are especially vulnerable to environmental degradation include
communities that, essentially, depend economically or for their survival on
environmental resources from the marine environment, forested areas and
river basins,59 or run a special risk of being affected owing to their
geographical location, such as coastal and small island communities.60 In
many cases, the special vulnerability of these groups has led to their
relocation or internal displacement [citation omitted].
….
A. The rights to life and to personal integrity in relation to environmental
protection
A.1 Meaning and scope of the rights to life and to personal integrity in
the face of potential environmental damage
108. The Court has affirmed repeatedly that the right to life in the American
Convention is essential because the realization of the other rights depends on
its protection.61 Accordingly, States are obliged to ensure the creation of the
necessary conditions for the full enjoyment and exercise of this right.62
109.…Among the conditions required for a decent life, the Court has referred
to access to, and the quality of, water, food and health, and the content has
been defined in the Court’s case law, indicating that these conditions have a
significant impact on the right to a decent existence and the basic conditions
for the exercise of other human rights [citations omitted]. The Court has also
included environmental protection as a condition for a decent life…[citation
omitted].
112. Regarding the right to personal integrity, the Court reiterates that the
violation of an individual’s right to physical and mental integrity has various
connotations of degree and ranges from torture to other types of ill-treatment
or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, the physical and mental effects of
which vary in intensity according to endogenous and exogenous factors (such

as duration of the treatment, age, sex, health, context and vulnerability) that
must be examined in each specific situation.63
113. Furthermore, in the specific case of Indigenous and tribal communities,
the Court has ruled on the obligation to protect their ancestral territories
owing to the relationship that such lands have with their cultural identity, a
fundamental human right of a collective nature that must be respected in a
multicultural, pluralist and democratic society.64
114. The Court notes that although each right contained in the Convention
has its own sphere, meaning and scope,65 there is a close relationship
between the right to life and the right to personal integrity. Thus, there are
times when the lack of access to conditions that ensure a dignified life may
also constitute a violation of the right to personal integrity;66 for example, in
cases involving human health.67 Moreover, the Court has recognized that
certain projects and interventions in the environment in which people live can
constitute a risk to their life and personal integrity.68 Therefore, the Court
considers it pertinent to examine jointly the State obligations in relation to the
rights to life and to personal integrity that may be affected by environmental
damage. Consequently, the Court will now establish and reaffirm the
meaning and scope of the general obligations to respect and to ensure the
rights to life and to personal integrity (infra paras. 115 to 121) and will then
establish the specific environmental obligations derived from this general
obligation (infra paras. 123 to 242), as solicited by Colombia in its request
for an advisory opinion.
* * *
In summary, the Court determined that:
4. For the purposes of Article 1(1) of the American Convention, it is
understood that individuals whose rights under the Convention have been
violated owing to transboundary harm are subject to the jurisdiction of the
State of origin of the harm, because that State exercises effective control over
the activities carried out in its territory or under its jurisdiction, in accordance
with paragraphs 95 to 103 of this Opinion.

5. To respect and to ensure the rights to life and to personal integrity of the
persons subject to their jurisdiction, States have the obligation to prevent
significant environmental damage within or outside their territory and, to this
end, must regulate, supervise and monitor activities within their jurisdiction
that could produce significant environmental damage; conduct environmental
impact assessments when there is a risk of significant environmental damage;
prepare a contingency plan to establish safety measures and procedures to
minimize the possibility of major environmental accidents, and mitigate any
significant environmental damage that may have occurred, in accordance
with paragraphs 127 and 174 of this Opinion.…
* * *
VI. CONCLUSION
The Inter-American human rights system has addressed a substantial number
of human rights violations caused by environmental harm, while the Inter-
American Court of Human Rights’ landmark 2017 advisory opinion and 2020
decision in the case between Argentina and Indigenous communities, also
display its willingness to recognize nature’s own right to a healthy
environment. The European and African human rights systems also contend
with cases involving human rights violations as a result of environmental
injury. Yet, governments, for the most part, ignore these decisions of human
rights forums where, in many instances, they themselves are the perpetrators.
New approaches are necessary to hold governments accountable for
upholding human rights and, where recognized, the rights of nature.
In a search for alternative approaches, following Berta Cáceres’s murder in
2016, the Civic Council of Popular and Indigenous Organizations of
Honduras (COPINH), the grassroots organization that she co-founded, took
legal action against the Dutch development bank FMO over its involvement
in the construction of the Agua Zarca dam in Honduras. The lawsuit claims
that the bank had a duty of care towards Cáceres, her children, and other
members of the community that no harm would accrue to them as a result of
the dam project. The bank and its officials had failed in their responsibilities
toward the Indigenous community who were seriously harmed by the project
and ignored the violations of human rights by the company building the dam

and, specifically, the warnings raised by Cáceres herself. Moreover, they had
not performed the due diligence required to ensure that their financial support
of the project would not abet violations of the community’s human rights.
The objective of the lawsuit was to create a precedent for other European
banks considering the financing of similar projects.69
As a result of her murder, the Dutch bank stopped loans to the project
pending a review, and, in 2017, it withdrew from the project, along with the
Finnish Fund for Industrial Cooperation and the Central American Bank of
Economic Integration.70
Campaigns against investment and development banks financing companies
that violate human rights are proving to be one successful method of stopping
these projects, as are divestment initiatives such as that initiated by
Greenpeace, Earth First!, and BankTrack against investors in the Dakota
Access Pipeline campaign. BankTrack investigates and reports on bank
financing of projects causing egregious harm to communities and to the
environment and maintains a list of these banks on its website. It also leads
campaigns to prevail upon banks to end the financing of such projects and to
meet their international commitments regarding human rights and the
environment.71
These campaigns protesting human rights violations as a result of ecological
harm are instrumental in achieving recognition for rights of nature. While all
humans need thriving ecosystems and biodiversity for survival, our view of
nature remains anthropocentric, and we continue to view it as property and a
source of resources for unlimited economic growth. Under the current legal
system, nature cannot protest violations of its rights to flourish and thrive.
Instead, environmental defenders face life-threatening risks to stop ecological
catastrophes from destroying both natural systems and local communities.
These defenders intertwine their own human rights with rights for nature,
understanding that to protect human rights, nature’s rights must be ensured.
As detailed in this chapter, they use a creative diversity of legal forums and
lawsuits in pursuing justice for violations of both. Their work will be
bolstered by Earth law and the transformation of current laws to support an
ecocentric worldview that recognizes rights of nature and gaining formal
legal status for nature.

STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Christopher Stone, in his essay Should Trees Have Standing? Toward
Legal Rights for Natural Objects, writes that “[a] society in which it is
stated…that ‘rivers have legal rights’ would evolve a different legal system
than one which did not employ that expression.” What do you think he meant
by this—that law’s role is primarily in creating new norms? How would this
work for rights for nature? Earth Law Center’s 2015 Co-violation Report,
which emphasizes the importance of adopting the Universal Declaration on
the Rights of Mother Earth, brings as an analogy the 1948 Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, which triggered an entirely new branch of
international law—human rights law. How might the adoption of the
Universal Declaration of Rights of Mother Earth follow the success of the
UDHR by inspiring a new branch of international rights of nature laws? What
factors might stand in the way?
(2) In many co-violation incidents, governments and industries blame
environmental defenders for violating the human “right to development,” be
it creating more energy sources, extracting more minerals and other resources
from Earth, creating more farmland, etc. What would you argue in reply to
this argument? Do you see this is as a possible clash and source of conflict
between human rights and rights for nature?
(3) The extensive burning of the Amazon in 2019 to create more pastureland
for animals and more farmland, supported by government policy, has
triggered a global response threatening Brazil if it doesn’t take steps to stop
the devastation. So far the threats have related to trade between Brazil and the
rest of the world. What could happen if Brazil ignores the threats and keeps
on burning? If you were a world leader participating in a summit addressing
this issue, and the scientists advising the summit are telling you that the
world is facing a catastrophe if the Amazon burning doesn’t stop, would you
go so far as to support an international force invading Brazil to stop the
destruction? How would you support this? Would you define the burning as
ecocide? To help answer this question, read the following excerpt from the
Earth Law Center’s 2015 Co-violations Report:
Nature’s rights can also be considered through existing court structures. For

example, an area that is the focus of escalating global advocacy is the effort
to recognize and act on the crime of “ecocide” in international criminal law,
as the fifth crime prosecutable before the International Criminal Court (ICC)
in the same manner as crimes against humanity (such as genocide and war
crimes). “Ecocide” cases represent the most severe cases of environmental
destruction and health-related damages. They are those which threaten the
safety of the planet, and so must be recognized as a crime.72 (See also
Chapter 12, “Ecocide.”)
(4) Do you agree with the argument raised in the Earth Law Center’s 2015
Co-violations Report that “Our modern environmental laws themselves
implicitly accept this claim of nature as property. They legalize nature’s
destruction by dictating how much of the environment we can degrade, thus
validating the continuing onslaught. Instead, we need laws grounded in the
inherent rights of natural world to exist, thrive, and evolve”?73 How might
the following statement from the report help you to determine your position?
Despite these and other escalating climate-related harms, national and
international climate change laws and conventions continue to legalize
massive amounts of greenhouse gas emissions while only calling for modest,
and usually voluntary, reductions. While the international community fails to
address climate change and other drivers of co-violations, humans and nature
continue to suffer the consequences.74
(5) Our current legal system, including its environmental laws, is geared to
support governments in their drive for increasing economic growth.
Therefore, this system also supports corporations as catalysts for economic
growth. As such, environmental defenders are targets of attack by police and
army forces, whose mandate it is to enforce government laws. The problem is
particularly acute in countries where democracy is weak, governments are
riddled by corruption, and human rights are violated with impunity. In light
of legal systems supporting the global economic model of unlimited growth,
is the key factor in bringing about change to adjust the current economic
model? How might that take place? Considering the obstacles in creating
economic change, how might the adoption and enforcement of laws granting
rights to nature promote that change? How might it curtail the fundamental
change of the current economic model?

(6) By reminding ourselves that the economic model of unlimited growth
feeds on high consumption rates, we expose our own role in violations of
human rights and rights of nature. Global Witness tells us that while
governments and corporations are certainly guilty of atrocities against
environmental defenders, “we can all do more. Ultimately, attacks against
land and environmental defenders stem from our voracious appetite for
agricultural goods like palm oil and coffee, and for fossil fuels, minerals and
timber.”75 What does this say about us as consumers? Should we be
admonishing the manufacturers of our favorite products and threaten that we
will not buy them if they are “fueling human rights abuses, cultural
destruction or environmental devastation?”76 What laws might be developed
to promote cutting down on our rates of consumption? How can global
grassroots efforts coalesce to eventually change the current economic model
and, at the same time, protect human rights and rights of nature?
(7) In 2015, Berta Cáceres accused then U.S. Secretary of State Hillary
Clinton of supporting the 2009 coup in Honduras and the subsequent election
of the current president, Juan Orlando Hernández Alvarado. While the
international community was demanding the return of President Emanuel
Zelaya and restitution of democracy, the United States legitimized the
fraudulent elections that would install the coup regime. What arguments
might be made based on the U.S. support for the 2009 Honduran coup and
subsequent elections that the United States bears legal responsibility for the
murder of environmental and social activists and the environmental
degradation by foreign corporations that has ensued? To the extent U.S.
international policy is part of, or even the core of, the problem, how might the
solution lie in coordinating campaigns for international and national laws for
rights of nature with political campaigns to change U.S. policy?
(8) In the Lago Agrio case, over the course of nearly 30 years, Chevron spent
tens if not hundreds of millions of dollars to avoid liability for the impact of
its business activities on nature and human life. While Chevron’s ultimate
objective was to avoid financial responsibility for the damage caused by
Texaco’s oil drilling activities, its ulterior motive was discouraging other
lawsuits. Thus Chevron filed a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation
(a “SLAPP” suit) against Steven Donziger, the lawyer representing the
victim, for the purpose of chilling the interests by terrifying other potential

litigants. How might you deal with the threat of being personally targeted by
a large corporate defendant? How chilling might the effect of sanctions be on
lawyers practicing Earth law?
