CHAPTER 11
Nonhuman Rights1
I. INTRODUCTION
He never asked for it, but Tommy has been something of a celebrity for much
of his life. In 1987, he appeared alongside the Hollywood actor Matthew
Broderick in the film Project X about the U.S. space program. Then, he
became a well-known circus performer in upstate New York. After that
career came to an end sometime in the 2000s, Tommy was moved to a trailer
lot in Gloversville, New York, where he was made to live inside a metal cage
with green bars. Eventually, his companions all died, leaving him with only a
television for company. All of this is perfectly legal in the United States
under current municipal, state, and federal law.
Tommy’s confinement and commercial exploitation are legal because he is
not a human being (with the right not to be unjustly imprisoned) but a
chimpanzee (with no legal rights whatsoever). Like every nonhuman animal
in the United States, Tommy is currently treated as a “thing” under the law.
Being a thing in this context means he lacks the capacity for rights.2 Tommy
is protected to some extent by existing anti-cruelty, welfare, and conservation
statutes, but none of these avenues provide relief from his solitary
confinement.
There is an effort underway to change the legal status of Tommy and other
nonhuman animals so that they can possess fundamental legal rights,
including to their bodily liberty. In December 2013, Tommy was once again
thrust into the spotlight as the first-ever nonhuman animal in the world to

seek a common law writ of habeas corpus.3 The litigation to free Tommy to a
sanctuary4 is the work of the Nonhuman Rights Project (NhRP), a U.S.-based
civil rights organization whose stated mission is to change the common law
legal status of at least some nonhuman animals from things, which lack the
capacity for any rights, to “persons” who possess the capacity for at least a
single right.
This chapter takes the habeas corpus litigation to free Tommy and other
chimpanzees in New York as a jumping-off point for broader discussions
about how the law is responding to demands for the recognition of the rights
of nonhuman animals and the natural world. The issue of whether a
chimpanzee is entitled to habeas corpus goes to questions at the heart of
rights of nature jurisprudence by illuminating foundational legal questions:
Are legal rights coextensive with the human species?
Who or what counts under the law, and whose rights will the law
affirmatively act upon to protect?
What is the role of the common law in expanding legal protections?
How should science impact judicial decision-making and policymaking?
What principles should guide the assignment of rights?
Where should society draw the line when it comes to recognizing other
species and the natural world as rights-bearers?
This chapter focuses on five New York state trial and appellate court
opinions issued between 2014 and 2018. Tommy is involved in three of the
five opinions and the others involve chimpanzees Kiko (Niagara Falls) and
Hercules and Leo (Stony Brook). These cases represent the beginning of the
world’s first concerted effort to achieve common law legal personhood for
any nonhuman animal. The theory of the NhRP is that a narrow but deep case
presenting a profound claim for the rights of even one animal is the best
means by which to call the fundamental legal situation into question. This
chapter mirrors that ethic by focusing on Tommy’s case (as well as those of
Kiko, Hercules, and Leo).
Every case in this chapter began with the filing of a petition for a common
law writ of habeas corpus. Habeas corpus is Latin for “produce the body”
(sometimes translated differently, though to the same effect). Habeas corpus

is one of the oldest writs (cause of action, form of petitioning for redress) in
the English common law tradition. Often referred to as the “Great Writ,”
habeas corpus came into being around the time of the Magna Carta as a
means to protect individuals from arbitrary detention. Habeas corpus, to the
extent it has not been abrogated by statute, is composed of common law as
opposed to statutory law and, as such, remains a unique area in which judges
have flexibility to expand the scope of the law without need for legislative
approval.5 The writ can also be sought by “order to show cause,” where it
does not call for the physical production of the detained, as is (obviously) the
case in the NhRP’s litigation on behalf of chimpanzees and other nonhuman
animals.
Common law, originating in England beginning around the mid-twelfth
century with roots in Roman law and other traditions, forms the foundation of
American law and many other English-speaking jurisdictions. Under this
system, judicial decisions accrete over time as precedent and inform the
decisions of judges in future disputes, and that “living body of law” is
collectively known as the common law. In contrast with constitutional law,
statutory law, and regulatory law, in which judges are interpreting statutes or
provisions written by legislators or administrators, the common law is the law
that judges make.
Judges are bound to a greater or lesser extent by common law rules rendered
by judges before them, but they may also choose to decline to follow such
rules as changed circumstances require. While the common law is an older
and, in some ways, less relevant body of law in some areas, such as federal
law and international law, which are dominated by statutes, regulations,
treaties, and detailed civil law codes, it still remains vitally important across a
wide range of legal disputes, and the time-tested principles it has described
are often relied on outside the traditional confines of the common law. The
common law will be familiar to students of torts and property, in particular,
since these branches are predominately composed of common law rules that
at one time did not exist but which were created over the generations in
response to changes in human experience, economics, morality, and scientific
understanding (e.g., property, contracts, common law marriage, negligence
principles, etc.).6

The common law, by its nature, builds upon itself over time. While there is
no concrete mechanism within the common law responsible for this
evolutionary process, it is nonetheless an integral part of it.7 Common law
judges are empowered to “legislate” from the bench in certain circumstances
to shape the future path of the law and can choose to depart from prior
precedent. Crucial for the present conversation, common law judges are
empowered to transform legal things into legal persons under some
circumstances, including through the common law writ of habeas corpus. The
NhRP’s litigation work is based in large part on the monumental 1772 anti-
slavery precedent of Somerset v. Stewart,8 in which, for the first time, a
common law judge recognized the legal personhood and rights of an African
slave, thereby setting him free and putting into motion the beginning of the
end of the transatlantic slave trade. The common law writ of habeas corpus,
which includes the Somerset precedent, was imported into the American
colonies and “lies in all cases of imprisonment by commitment, detention,
confinement or restraint, for whatever cause, or under whatever pretence.”9
In a similar spirit, the United States Supreme Court has emphasized that the
writ’s “scope and flexibility” and “its capacity to reach all manner of illegal
detention,” as well as “its ability to cut through barriers of form and
procedural mazes…have always been emphasized and jealously guarded by
courts and lawmakers.”10 In short, habeas corpus appears a uniquely
powerful vehicle for presenting a claim that an entity lacking rights should be
entitled to at least one right, namely, the right to liberty protected by the
common law writ of habeas corpus.
Habeas corpus was created to protect autonomy. Tommy is autonomous. The
crux of the argument for Tommy is that autonomy is a sufficient, but not
necessary, basis for personhood and the right to bodily liberty under the
common law of habeas corpus. Tommy’s case is built on the foundation of
scientific research into the emotional and cognitive complexity of
chimpanzees that first came into focus through the work of Dr. Jane Goodall,
whose observations of the chimpanzees of the Gombe Stream National Park
in Tanzania Gombe forest in Uganda changed forever humanity’s perceptions
of the other species with whom we share the planet.11 We now know
chimpanzees to be “autonomous beings.”12 What autonomy means in real-life
terms for chimpanzees, in part, is that they are self-aware13 and act in an
intentional manner;14 possess an autobiographical self,15 episodic memory,16

long-term spatial memory and awareness,17 and self-consciousness
(chimpanzees can recognize their younger selves in photographs);18 are
capable of numerosity,19 sequential learning,20 mental state modeling,21 and
understanding the experiences of others22 (for example, a chimpanzee named
Santino, who is an “inmate” of a zoo in Furuvik, Sweden, stockpiles hidden
stashes of rocks to use as missiles against gawking zoo visitors out of
apparent and understandable spite and regularly thwarts the efforts of zoo
staff to stop him from amassing these stockpiles);23 possess the ability to
understand and carry out duties and responsibilities while knowingly
assuming obligations and then honoring them;24 engage in referential and
intentional communication (what some call “language,” including the ability
to learn human sign language and spontaneously teach it to other
chimpanzees without human invention);25 have a symbolic culture and
engage in tool-use and tool-making26 and pass these on for generations
(sometimes hundreds of generations);27 possess imagination, empathy,28 and
an understanding of cause and effect;29 behave in ways that seem both lawful
and rule-governed;30 have moral inclinations and a level of moral agency;31
ostracize individuals who violate social norms and respond negatively to
inequitable situations;32 have a social life that is cooperative and represents a
purposeful and well-coordinated social system;33 routinely enter into
contractual agreements, keep promises and secrets, and prefer fair
exchanges;34 have an awareness of death and perform death-related duties;35
and show concern for others’ welfare (for example, even adult male
chimpanzees, assumed to be gruff, have been observed adopting and caring
for unrelated orphaned baby chimpanzees).36 In short, chimpanzees recognize
themselves as unique individuals, reflect on the past, appreciate the present,
and plan for the future.37 Yet, to the law, these remarkable beings remain
things.
Autonomy is a supreme value in the common law. Apart from habeas corpus,
which has long acted as the guarantor of liberty and protector of the
autonomy of persons, there are many cases in the common law tradition
enshrining the importance of autonomy. Some of the most prominent
examples of this principle come from “right to die” cases, in which the courts
have reliably sided with the wishes of a person of sound mind to refuse life-
saving treatment, thereby placing autonomy and individual choice above

even the protection of human life in the panoply of fundamental interests.38
Tommy is but one chimpanzee representing a broader movement. The
fundamental questions raised in Tommy’s case are reverberating around the
world, as courts begin to wrestle with claims for the legal personhood and
rights of animals and nature. Outside the United States. courts have already
recognized that some nonhuman animals have legal rights. In 2014, the
Indian Supreme Court held that animals in general possess constitutional and
statutory rights.39 In 2016, in a case almost identical to Tommy’s, an
Argentine trial court granted a writ of habeas corpus to a chimpanzee named
Cecilia, designated her a “nonhuman legal person” with “nonhuman rights,”
and ordered her release from the Mendoza zoo and subsequent transfer to a
sanctuary.40 Rejecting the claim that Cecilia could not avail herself of habeas
corpus because she was not a human, the court recognized that “societies
evolve in their moral conducts, thoughts, and values” and concluded that
classifying autonomous “animals as things is not a correct standard.”41
Courts and legislatures are also beginning to recognize parts of the natural
environment as persons. In 2018, the Colombia Supreme Court designated
the Colombian part of the Amazon rainforest “as an entity subject of rights,”
in other words, a person.42 In 2017, the New Zealand Parliament designated
New Zealand’s Whanganui River Iwi as a person that owns its riverbed.43 In
2014, New Zealand’s Te Urewera park was designated a “legal entity, having
all the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a person.”44 Municipalities
around the United States are starting to vote in favor of rights for lakes45 and
may soon do so for at least some nonhuman animals.46 All of this is
occurring rapidly and against a social backdrop of unprecedented calls for
action on climate change, species loss, deforestation, threats to Indigenous
tribes and cultural knowledge, and other issues, all of which are increasingly
seen as inextricably linked.
There are important critiques of the habeas corpus approach that should be
considered. Does premising a case for the rights of a nonhuman animal on
their “human-like” intelligence risk creating an unreasonably high bar for
other species, thus dooming them to remain rightless?47 Does basing a case
like this on historical common law re-entrench harmful property-driven,
colonialist ideas of personhood and individualistic liberty?48 How will the

change in status of a handful of “autonomous” animals change the reality for
the vast majority suffering on industrial farms or driven toward extinction as
a result of human activity? Is it wrong to premise the expansion of rights to
animals on court precedents challenging slavery and other historical wrongs
done to humans?49 Must animals be persons in order to be protected, or
would such recognition do damage to notions of human rights and
exceptionalism?50 These are important strategic and ethical questions to be
sure. However, if we cannot achieve recognition of even a single fundamental
right for a “human-like” beings such as Tommy (who are not domesticated,
are few in number, and whose economic significance is nil), what hope does
any other species really have?51 Moreover, habeas corpus is but one means to
pursue the rights of nonhuman animals. While a viable habeas claim requires
that the petitioner be autonomous (i.e., have an interest in bodily liberty), this
will not be the case for future endeavors, especially those achieved by
legislative means, where the legislature can choose any arbitrary basis it
pleases on which to premise legal personhood and rights. If it can be done for
corporations, it can be done for chimpanzees. And rivers. And more.
II. RIGHTS VERSUS WELFARE
Tommy is, as discussed, a legal thing, but not all things are created alike in
our legal system. As a living breathing animal, Tommy might be thought of
in legal terms as a “special” kind of thing, subject to various welfare,
conservation, and other laws that are meant to prevent outright abuse and
neglect.52 So, while Tommy and his television are both things in the eyes of
the law and property of their human owner, in practice, they are treated very
differently (there is no “television welfare” law, obviously). However,
welfare laws are silent to this because Tommy lacks the capacity for rights;
the legal options for helping him under existing law appear limited.53
Under the prevailing animal welfare paradigm, as long as Tommy’s human
owners treat him according to minimum welfare standards—for example,
minimum cage size, adequate food and water, and avoidance of outright
physical abuse or neglect—and comply with the minimal registration and
inspection requirements, they can confine him alone without any others of his
own kind. In other words, a human can legally subject Tommy to a life we

would consider inherently wrong (and illegal) were Tommy a human being.
Under the welfare view, humans should treat animals with some
consideration, but animals remain things that may be exploited and even
killed if that suffering is deemed “justified” or “necessary,” a concept
explored in Chapter 14, “Bears Among Us: Earth Law and Animal-Human
Coexistence.”
In any sphere, not all life is law, and it should be noted here that the legal
thinghood of animals only represents part of our complex relationships with
nonhuman animals as a broad class (there are a million or so species of
animals on the planet and roughly half of them are beetles).54 Anybody who
grew up with a dog or other beloved family pet knows from experience that
animals are far from just things in our hearts and imaginations. Our cultural
relationship with nonhuman animals is vast and the product of a long and
intertwined history—to the level of impacting each other’s genetic
evolution.55 Indeed, human civilization never would have been possible if not
for the countless contributions of animals as food, fiber, labor, companions,
and otherwise.56
Nor does the thinghood of animals mean that every animal lives a life of
suffering—indeed far from it. The welfare and protection laws that do exist,
not to mention the billions of dollars spent on pets every year, are compelling
evidence of human concern for at least some nonhuman animals, and this is
also reflected in public opinion polls, which show a marked increase in
support for “animal rights.”57 Organizations to promote the well-being of
animals, beginning with the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to
Animals in England in 1824, demonstrate a long-running social concern and
commitment to preventing harm to animals.58
Society clearly cares about the lives and suffering of (at least some) animals.
Yet, despite widespread social concern and the passage of hundreds of animal
protection laws, even caring humans frequently operate with a double
standard, an attitude reinforced and enabled by the structure of the law. For
many thousands of species and trillions of individuals, their categorical
thinghood under the law has devastating real-world ramifications. In many
instances, being a thing means that your life may be taken at any instant. Or,
like Tommy, even if you are a protected endangered species, you may be kept

in a small cage alone for decades until you die. Worse, an alarming number
of animal and plant species go extinct every year or get closer to extinction.
Looked at this way, it appears there are severe limits to the welfare approach,
and social concern and empathy alone are evidently not enough to protect
nonhuman animals any more than they would humans.
From the rights perspective, the fundamental problem with the welfare
paradigm is that it relies upon and perpetuates the assumption that human
beings are the only proper rights holders in our legal system. This can be seen
in the context of environmental law as well, where legal protections fall short
of their stated goals for a variety of reasons, ranging from industry capture
and lobby influence to the drift of regulatory authority away from Congress
and toward the executive branch, which may not be inclined to maintain
long-term environmental commitments passed by its predecessors.59 Looked
at this way, the current system could be called “environmental welfare,”
insofar as it protects the environment to some extent but never calls into
question the right of humans to own, control, and manage the environment.
While aspects of the environment are protected by various state, federal, and
local laws, at the end of the day, in the United States nature itself does not,
and cannot, have rights at present.
Do animals (or nature) really need to be persons to be adequately protected?
Or do only humans really require that status, with a corresponding duty to see
that animals are responsibly treated (broadly, the “welfare” approach)? It is
true that animals and the environment are protected to a greater or lesser
extent by existing animal welfare and conservation laws, among other
protections; and organizations continue to carry on laudable efforts to
improve these laws and their enforcement. But the fact remains that currently
these efforts cannot create rights or recognition of personhood (that is, the
capacity for rights). For that reason, this chapter explores the common law
habeas corpus approach of the NhRP as a profoundly different entry point to
begin the process of assigning rights beyond the human species. The legal,
philosophical, and procedural arguments raised will be informative to rights
of nature practitioners now and in the future. In the words of one state high
court judge featured in this chapter, the very process of demanding habeas
corpus relief for a single chimpanzee calls into question “our relationship
with all the life around us.”60

III. THE LEGAL CONCEPT OF A PERSON
There is not now nor has there ever been a universally accepted definition of
what makes a legal person; in fact, there is great discord. Under the common
law there is no single definition of person and no checklist of attributes an
entity must possess in order to be a person. The process of assigning rights in
a liberal democratic society is far more complex than that, as evidenced, for
example, by fights over human slavery and abortion. What is clear is that
legal personhood, while influenced by natural law understandings of the
person as an individual human (or more likely, as the historical record
demonstrates, white upstanding male), has never been about biology. As
evidence of this fact, for the vast majority of the 2,000-plus-year history of
the person/thing dichotomy, most human beings were not persons under the
law. In New York, for example, human slaves were not persons until the last
slave in the state was freed in 182761 and were not persons throughout the
United States until 1865.62 Women were not persons for many purposes of
the common law until well into the twentieth century.63 Jews were once not
persons,64 and the first time a Native American sought a writ of habeas
corpus, the U.S. government claimed he was not a person either.65 Against
this backdrop of legalized human oppression, various nonhuman entities have
been treated as legal persons for hundreds of years in the form of
associations, corporations, limited liability companies, churches, holy relics,
and ships. The companies that owned slaves were persons, while the slaves
they owned were not.
Legal personhood is nothing more or less than the capacity for rights. While
this does not comport with the everyday understanding of what a person is,
nor can it hope to ever capture the complex nuance and emotional content of
our social, religious, philosophical, and other traditions, it makes perfect
sense in the logic of the law because personhood is a legal fiction, not a
biological concept.66 For Dean Roscoe Pound, the “significant feature of
legal personality is the capacity for rights.”67 “Legal persons” possess
inherent value; “legal things,” possessing merely instrumental value, exist for
the sake of “legal persons.”68 A “person,” the noted legal scholar John
Salmond observed, “is any being whom the law regards as capable of rights
or duties.”69 And while some “persons” can legally be bought, sold, or even

destroyed (corporations and ships), the fundamental premise holds: only
persons may have rights.
The history of personhood is inextricably tied to the struggle for the rights of
all human beings. Much of the history of the social justice movements of the
past 200 years is both reflected in and amplified by the evolution of the law
and specifically by the outward expansion of legal personhood.70 Every
human being in the world is now recognized as a “person,” but for the
majority of modern human history, this was not the case. As the American
constitutional law scholar Laurence Tribe has written, “To the degree that
competing conceptions of personhood are nonetheless deemed at least
pertinent even if not decisive, it is important to remember that legal
definitions of what and who constitutes a ‘person’ do much ‘more than just
regulate behavior’ when it comes to ‘America’s most divisive social issues’:
they express ‘conceptions of [the] relative worth of the objects included and
excluded by personhood,’ and these expressions of ‘law’s values’ in turn
shape social norms and values.”71
While in everyday parlance the word “person” evokes the image of a singular
human being, legal personhood has never been about biology. By way of
analogy, a person is like a cup, a “container” for rights. Once the cup is
secured (i.e., the entity is recognized under law as a person), the courts (and
society at large) can begin the process of “filling” that cup, even one right at a
time. Of course, not every person, human or otherwise, will have exactly the
same set of rights. This is obvious when one considers that legal personhood
embraces the whole range of human capacities. Every born human being is
by definition a legal person, and every human, including a child or
developmentally disabled adult, has fundamental rights to liberty and due
process, regardless of their level of conscious awareness of the world and
their actions, even those with absolutely no demonstrable conscious
awareness of the world. But, of course, that child or disabled adult may not
have the right to vote or drive or marry. The flexibility of personhood
likewise allows corporations and other associations to be treated as
paradigmatic legal persons that can enjoy rights and take on duties, despite
the fact that they are fictitious non-biological entities that may themselves be
owned, bought, and sold.

It should be emphasized, as may be obvious from considering the example of
the corporation or a ship as a legal person, that being a “person” alone does
not necessarily entitle an entity to the full panoply of what are considered
basic “human rights,” including rights to free speech, association, and so
on.72 Also note that there is a distinct and fundamental difference between
common law corporate personhood, which is on balance a socially beneficial
construct, and corporate personhood under the Fourteenth Amendment Due
Process Clause, as first set forth through a headnote in Santa Clara (without
discussion).73 (That decision and subsequent Supreme Court decisions
expanding corporate rights to free speech and religious freedom under the
U.S. Constitution are the rightful cause of contemporary concern over the
undue political influence of large corporations. The underlying concept of
common law legal personhood, however, is not the true culprit).
In contrast to landmark corporate personhood decisions (e.g., Citizens
United), which are fought in the federal courts and which rely on expansive
interpretations of the U.S. Constitution, the work of the NhRP is focused
exclusively on state courts using arguments based on state common law. The
federal Constitution is arguably irrelevant to the question of whether a given
entity is considered a legal person for purposes of state common law habeas
corpus.74 Moreover, the common law is all but nonexistent in the federal
courts, which are, by definition, courts of limited jurisdiction under Article III
of the Constitution. There are benefits and drawbacks to this approach, such
as, mainly, the trade-off between common law flexibility and limited
jurisdictional reach on the state court side against a seemingly more rigid and
limited federal court system that could in theory produce a decision with
binding and preemptive effect nationwide.
With the above in mind, one might ask, what are the advantages of using the
avenue of legal personhood for some nonhuman animals to develop
ecocentric law more broadly? One answer is that human rights provide the
best template available for imagining the rights of nonhuman animals. With
respect to the development of human rights over the past few centuries,
history and legal logic show that personhood matters immensely. Personhood
is now universally regarded as a fundamental basis for human rights. For
example, Article 6 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article
16 of the International Convention on Social and Political Rights guarantee

that every human shall be a “person.” If even one nonhuman animal is
conferred with legal personhood, it will provide a precedent to expand rights
of nature.
Personhood is a remarkably flexible concept. The legal imagination that
created it can quite easily encompass a variety of nonhuman entities as legal
persons: A century ago, Professor John Chipman Gray observed that “[t]here
is no difficulty in giving legal rights to a supernatural being and thus making
him or her a legal person.”75 To the point, Gray noted there may be “systems
of law in which animals have legal rights…animals may conceivably be legal
persons.”76
Of course, not all of life is captured, reflected, or ultimately governed by the
law. And changing the status of a given entity or class of beings from thing to
person will not instantly and magically transform that being nor necessarily
lead to improved fortunes or enhanced quality of life. Indeed, hundreds of
thousands of slaves were freed by the Emancipation Proclamation and
subsequently by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments to the
Constitution following the Civil War, but in the South they were exposed to
the horrific vicissitudes of Jim Crow and other means of segregation and
subjugation. But still, it appears undeniable that, in the struggle for universal
human rights, the legal recognition of rights and personhood codifies,
enforces, and protects the most fundamental rights of human beings, namely,
the right not to be held in bondage.
IV. THE VALUE OF HABEAS CORPUS
Human autonomy is protected under the common law by the writ of habeas
corpus. As one of the oldest writs in the common law, it has always been
meant to safeguard the liberty and free movement of persons. Its origins go
back at least as far as the Magna Carta of 1215. As part of this impressive
pedigree, habeas corpus also has a unique history of being used by courts to
transform legal things into legal persons, thereby taking a human being with
no right to be free and recognizing him as a person with the right to be free.77
The position advanced by the NhRP is, essentially, that if a being is
demonstrably autonomous then they should have rights protecting that

autonomy, regardless of their species. While it is now near-universally
recognized that many, if not most, nonhuman animals are conscious and
aware beings with intentions,78 autonomy is far more complex (and
apparently much less common), and sentience does not have the same place
in the common law as autonomy. The legal problem then becomes, how can a
nonhuman animal cross the common law threshold from thing to person?
The common law, while flexible and open to radical change at times, has
always regarded nonhuman animals as things, with roots going back at least
2,000 years to Roman law. While there are many gradations within that
paradigm (ferae naturae79 ), the law has nonetheless always treated
nonhuman animals as things that are incapable of rights.80 While the law
around animals has remained more or less static, science has demonstrated
beyond reasonable doubt—especially over the past 50 years—that
chimpanzees and other nonhuman animals share many cognitive abilities that
were once thought to be uniquely human. The science summarized above
paints a picture of the rich interior and social lives that chimpanzees enjoy
when left to their own devices or allowed to live in sufficiently large,
secluded, and social captive situations like sanctuaries; it also shows how
much can be taken from them in captive environments. An imprisoned
individual like Tommy is not only thwarted from exercising most or all of the
above capacities, but he is also aware of the fact that his will is being
thwarted and likely suffers immensely as a result—just as a conscious human
would if left in solitary confinement.
It may seem odd to seek to address a modern problem with ancient law. But
as the arc of opinions in this chapter shows, the process of rigorously and
studiously engaging the common law wheels of justice creates a powerful
vehicle for the transformation of individual entities or groups. It also drives
powerful conversations about the deep meaning of the law, and, in the
context of nature’s rights and nonhuman rights specifically, a more reflective
and informed look at the duties we owe to other species and the natural
world. The rich tradition of the common law, while pockmarked with many
unjust decisions, provides fertile ground on which to demand legal
recognition for a wider set of beings and, in the process, discard the
designation of “species” as the basis of one more outmoded and invidious
form of discrimination. Habeas corpus is, to date, the primary vehicle

common law judges have used to transform things to persons (and civil law
judges as well; see Cecilia, supra, Section I).
V. NONHUMAN RIGHTS PROJECT
LITIGATION
With the above legal, moral, public policy, and scientific arguments, and
based on decades of legal scholarship,81 the NhRP filed the world’s first
common law habeas corpus petitions on behalf of nonhuman animals in
December 2013—specifically, on behalf of every known chimpanzee in the
state of New York.82 As part of these petitions, the NhRP included affidavits
from some of the world’s leading primatologists and scientific experts on
chimpanzee behavior and cognition, summarized supra in Section I.
Below, in chronological order, are five decisions in the NhRP’s litigation
campaign in New York, beginning with the first-ever appellate decision to
consider the question of whether a nonhuman animal may be a person
entitled to habeas corpus, which came about after the denial of Tommy’s
petition in December 2013. The second appellate decision followed close
after, in the case of the chimpanzee Kiko, who lives in a small storefront
property in upstate New York described by its owners as a “sanctuary.” The
third is a trial court opinion that followed the world’s first common law
habeas corpus hearing in the name of a nonhuman animal (in fact, two
animals, research chimpanzees Hercules and Leo). The fourth opinion,
another appellate decision, rejected the combined second appeals of Tommy
and Kiko. That opinion was appealed and led to the fifth and final opinion in
this chapter, a concurring opinion from a member of the New York Court of
Appeals, which marked the first time an American high court judge opined
on the question of legal personhood for nonhuman animals.
The Nonhuman Rights Project, Inc., on Behalf of Tommy v. Lavery et al.,
Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Department, New York 2014
124 A.D.3d 148, 998 N.Y.S.2d 248
OPINION OF THE COURT

PETERS, P.J.
The subject of this litigation is a chimpanzee, known as Tommy, that is
presently being kept by respondents on their property in the City of
Gloversville, Fulton County. On behalf of Tommy, petitioner sought an order
to show cause to commence a habeas corpus proceeding pursuant to CPLR
article 70 on the ground that Tommy was being unlawfully detained by
respondents. In support, petitioner submitted the affidavits of several experts
in an effort to establish that, in general, chimpanzees have attributes
sufficient to consider them “persons” for the purposes of their interest in
personal autonomy and freedom from unlawful detention. Collectively, these
submissions maintain that chimpanzees exhibit highly complex cognitive
functions—such as autonomy, self-awareness and self-determination, among
others—similar to those possessed by human beings. Following an ex parte
hearing, Supreme Court found that the term “person” under CPLR article 70
did not include chimpanzees and issued a judgment refusing to sign an order
to show cause. Petitioner appeals.83,84
This appeal presents the novel question of whether a chimpanzee is a
“person” entitled to the rights and protections afforded by the writ of habeas
corpus. Notably, we have not been asked to evaluate the quality of Tommy’s
current living conditions in an effort to improve his welfare. In fact,
petitioner’s counsel stated at oral argument that it does not allege that
respondents are in violation of any state or federal statutes respecting the
domestic possession of wild animals (see, e.g., ECL 11-0512). According to
petitioner, while respondents are in compliance with state and federal
statutes, the statutes themselves are inappropriate. Yet, rather than
challenging any such statutes, petitioner requests that this Court enlarge the
common-law definition of “person” in order to afford legal rights to an
animal. We decline to do so, and conclude that a chimpanzee is not a
“person” entitled to the rights and protections afforded by the writ of habeas
corpus.
The common law writ of habeas corpus, as codified by CPLR article 70,
provides a summary procedure by which a “person” who has been illegally
imprisoned or otherwise restrained in his or her liberty can challenge the
legality of the detention (CPLR 7002 [a]). The statute does not purport to

define the term “person,” and for good reason. The “Legislature did not
intend to change the instances in which the writ was available,” which has
been determined by “the slow process of decisional accretion” (People ex rel.
Keitt v. McMann, 18 N.Y.2d 257, 263 [1966]) [citation omitted]). Thus, we
must look to the common law surrounding the historic writ of habeas corpus
to ascertain the breadth of the writ’s reach.
Not surprisingly, animals have never been considered persons for the
purposes of habeas corpus relief, nor have they been explicitly considered as
persons or entities capable of asserting rights for the purpose of state or
federal law (see, e.g., Lewis v. Burger King, 344 Fed. Appx. 470, 472 [10th
Cir. 2009], cert. denied, 558 U.S. 1125 [2010]; Cetacean Community v. Bush,
386 F.3d 1169, 1178 [9th Cir. 2004]; Tilikum ex rel. People for the Ethical
Treatment of Animals, Inc. v. Sea World Parks & Entertainment, Inc., 842 F.
Supp. 2d 1259, 1263 [S.D. Cal 2012]; Citizens to End Animal Suffering &
Exploitation, Inc. v. New England Aquarium, 836 F. Supp. 45, 49-50 [D.
Mass. 1993]). Petitioner does not cite any precedent—and there appears to be
none—in state law, or under English common law, that an animal could be
considered a “person” for the purposes of common-law habeas corpus relief.
In fact, habeas corpus relief has never been provided to any nonhuman entity
(see, e.g., United States v. Mett, 65 F.3d 1531, 1534 [9th Cir. 1995], cert.
denied, 519 U.S. 870 [1996]; Waste Mgt. of Wisconsin, Inc. v. Fokakis, 614
F.2d 138, 139-140 [7th Cir. 1980], cert. denied, 449 U.S. 1060 [1980];
Sisquoc Ranch Co. v. Roth, 153 F.2d 437, 441 [9th Cir. 1946]; Graham v.
State of New York, 25 A.D.2d 693, 693 [1966]).
The lack of precedent for treating animals as persons for habeas corpus
purposes does not, however, end the inquiry, as the writ has over time gained
increasing use given its “great flexibility and vague scope” (People ex rel.
Keitt v. McMann, 18 N.Y.2d at 263 [internal quotation marks and citation
omitted]). While petitioner proffers various justifications for affording
chimpanzees, such as Tommy, the liberty rights protected by such writ, the
ascription of rights has historically been connected with the imposition of
societal obligations and duties. Reciprocity between rights and
responsibilities stems from principles of social contract, which inspired the
ideals of freedom and democracy at the core of our system of government
(see Richard L. Cupp, Jr., Children, Chimps, and Rights: Arguments from

“Marginal” Cases, 45 Ariz. St. L.J. 1, 12-14 [2013]; Richard L. Cupp, Jr.,
Moving Beyond Animal Rights: A Legal/Contractualist Critique, 46 San
Diego L Rev 27, 69-70 [2009]; see also In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1, 20-21
[1967]; United States v. Barona, 56 F.3d 1087, 1093-1094 [9th Cir. 1995],
cert. denied, 516 U.S. 1092 [1996]). Under this view, society extends rights
in exchange for an express or implied agreement from its members to submit
to social responsibilities. In other words, “rights [are] connected to moral
agency and the ability to accept societal responsibility in exchange for [those]
rights” (Richard L. Cupp, Jr., Children, Chimps, and Rights: Arguments from
“Marginal” Cases, 45 Ariz. St. L.J. 1, 13 [2013]; see Richard L. Cupp, Jr.,
Moving Beyond Animal Rights: A Legal/Contractualist Critique, 46 San
Diego L Rev 27, 69 [2009]).
Further, although the dispositive inquiry is whether chimpanzees are entitled
to the right to be free from bodily restraint such that they may be deemed
“persons” subject to the benefits of habeas corpus, legal personhood has
consistently been defined in terms of both rights and duties. Black’s Law
Dictionary defines the term “person” as “[a] human being” or, as relevant
here, “[a]n entity (such as a corporation) that is recognized by law as having
the rights and duties [of] a human being” (Black’s Law Dictionary 1162 [7th
ed 1999] [emphasis added]). It then goes on to provide:
“So far as legal theory is concerned, a person is any being whom the law
regards as capable of rights and duties.…Persons are the substances of which
rights and duties are the attributes. It is only in this respect that persons
possess juridical significance, and this is the exclusive point of view from
which personality receives legal recognition” (Black’s Law Dictionary 1162
[7th ed 1999], citing John Salmond, Jurisprudence 318 [10th ed 1947]; see
John Chipman Gray, The Nature and Sources of the Law, ch II at 27 [2d ed
1963] [stating that the legal meaning of a “person” is “a subject of legal
rights and duties”]).
Case law has always recognized the correlative rights and duties that attach to
legal personhood (see, e.g., Smith v. ConAgra Foods, Inc., 431 S.W.3d 200,
203-204 [Ark. 2013], citing Calaway v. Practice Mgt. Servs., Inc., 2010 Ark.
432 [2010] [defining a “person” as “a human being or an entity that is
recognized by a law as having the rights and duties of a human being”];

Wartelle v. Women’s & Children’s Hosp., Inc., 704 So. 2d 778, 780 [La.
1997] [finding that the classification of a being or entity as a “person” is
made “solely for the purpose of facilitating determinations about the
attachment of legal rights and duties”]; Amadio v. Levin, 509 Pa. 199, 225,
501 A.2d 1085, 1098 [1985, Zappala, J., concurring] [noting that
“‘(p)ersonhood’ as a legal concept arises not from the humanity of the subject
but from the ascription of rights and duties to the subject”]).85 Associations
of human beings, such as corporations and municipal entities, may be
considered legal persons, because they too bear legal duties in exchange for
their legal rights (see, e.g., Pembina Consol. Silver Mining & Milling Co. v.
Pennsylvania, 125 U.S. 181, 189 [1888]; Western Sur. Co. v. ADCO Credit,
Inc., 251 P.3d 714, 716 [Nev. 2011]; State of Washington v. A.M.R., 147
Wash. 2d 91, 94, 51 P.3d 790, 791 [2002]; State of West Virginia v. Zain, 207
W. Va. 54, 61-65, 528 S.E.2d 748, 755-759 [1999], cert. denied, 529 U.S.
1042 [2000]).
Needless to say, unlike human beings, chimpanzees cannot bear any legal
duties, submit to societal responsibilities or be held legally accountable for
their actions. In our view, it is this incapability to bear any legal
responsibilities and societal duties that renders it inappropriate to confer upon
chimpanzees the legal rights—such as the fundamental right to liberty
protected by the writ of habeas corpus—that have been afforded to human
beings.
Our rejection of a rights paradigm for animals does not, however, leave them
defenseless. The Legislature has extended significant protections to animals,
subject to criminal penalties, such as prohibiting the torture or unjustifiable
killing of animals (see Agriculture and Markets Law §353), the abandonment
of animals in a public place (see Agriculture and Markets Law §355), the
transportation of animals in cruel or inhuman manners (see Agriculture and
Markets Law §359 [1]) or by railroad without periodically allowing them out
for rest and sustenance (see Agriculture and Markets Law §359 [2]), and the
impounding of animals and then failing to provide them sustenance (see
Agriculture and Markets Law §356). Notably, and although subject to certain
express exceptions, New Yorkers may not possess primates as pets (see ECL
11-0103 [6] [e] [1]; 11-0512). Thus, while petitioner has failed to establish
that common-law relief in the nature of habeas corpus is appropriate here, it

is fully able to importune the Legislature to extend further legal protections to
chimpanzees.
Lahtinen, Garry, Rose and Lynch, JJ., concur.
Ordered that the judgment is affirmed, without costs.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) While acknowledging the evidence of chimpanzees as “self-aware” and
“autonomous” beings, the Lavery court denied habeas corpus relief to
Tommy on the basis that the common law and social contract theory dictate
that only those who can take on legal duties and responsibilities may be
“persons,” with all nonhuman animals presumably relegated to the status of
“things” that are incapable of possessing the right to common law habeas
corpus or any other right. While reference is made to Black’s Law Dictionary
and other sources, this was the first time that an English-speaking court, or
perhaps any court, has made such a statement and put this condition on legal
personhood. Is social contract theory a sound basis for deciding whether an
entity is deserving of legal personhood?
(2) In rejecting legal personhood and habeas corpus relief for chimpanzees,
the Lavery court cites numerous New York statutes designed to protect
animals in various ways. Are the existing statutory protections for animals
sufficient? For example, what is “necessary” killing, as generally allowed for
under all “animal welfare” laws including those cited by the court? Do these
laws adequately protect a chimpanzee like Tommy, given what we now know
about the cognitive capacities of chimpanzees and their ability to suffer in
captivity, especially solitary captivity?
(3) The Lavery court acknowledges that the ascription of legal personhood is
a policy matter made without respect for the species or biological nature of a
given entity but rather by its ability to bear duties and responsibilities
correlating to its rights. Then, in footnote 3, the court acknowledges that
“some humans are less able to bear legal duties or responsibilities than
others,” but that, generally speaking, humans have the “unique ability” to
appreciate legal duties and responsibilities. What about those millions of

humans who have no ability to bear legal duties and responsibilities, such as
children or comatose adults, or those humans who suffer a mental impairment
and will never have the ability to shoulder duties?
(4) While the thinghood of nonhuman animals is not the cause of their plight,
per se, it is a powerful reflection of it and normalizes and makes efficient
their use and destruction. As discussed supra, legal fights over (human)
personhood have frequently been proxy battlegrounds for deeper social
tensions and conflicts (and continue to be so in the context of abortion, and
may soon reach areas like artificial intelligence as well). To what extent
might this be happening here, and how much might these kinds of tensions be
at play in other courts’ rulings?
(5) Assuming that legal personhood is a necessary prerequisite for rights of
nature, how would these claims fare under the Lavery standard?

Nonhuman Rights Project, Inc., on Behalf of Kiko v. Presti et al.,
Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department, New York 2015
124 A.D.3d 1334, 999 N.Y.S.2d 652
Appeal from a judgment (denominated order) of the Supreme Court, Niagara
County (Ralph A. Boniello, III, J.), entered December 11, 2013 in a
proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 70. The judgment dismissed the
petition.
It is hereby ordered that the judgment so appealed from is unanimously
affirmed without costs.

Memorandum: Petitioner, an organization seeking better treatment and
housing of, inter alia, nonhuman primates, commenced this proceeding
seeking a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Kiko, a chimpanzee. Rather than
seeking Kiko’s immediate release, however, the petition alleges that Kiko is
illegally confined because he is kept in unsuitable conditions, and it seeks to
have Kiko’s confinement transferred to a different facility selected by the
North American Primate Sanctuary Alliance. On appeal from a judgment
dismissing the petition, petitioner contends that Kiko is entitled to the relief
sought. Contrary to petitioner’s contention, we conclude that Supreme Court
properly dismissed the petition.
Regardless of whether we agree with petitioner’s claim that Kiko is a person
within the statutory and common-law definition of the writ, “‘habeas corpus
relief nonetheless is unavailable as [that] claim [ ], even if meritorious, would
not entitle [Kiko] to immediate release’” (People ex rel. Gonzalez v. Wayne
County Sheriff, 96 A.D.3d 1698, 1699 [2012], lv denied 21 N.Y.3d 852
[2013]; see People ex rel. Shannon v. Khahaifa, 74 A.D.3d 1867, 1867
[2010], lv dismissed 15 N.Y.3d 868 [2010]; People ex rel. Hall v. Rock, 71
A.D.3d 1303, 1304 [2010], appeal dismissed 14 N.Y.3d 882 [2010], lv
denied 15 N.Y.3d 703 [2010]). It is well settled that a habeas corpus
proceeding must be dismissed where the subject of the petition is not entitled
to immediate release from custody (see People ex rel. Kaplan v.
Commissioner of Correction of City of N.Y., 60 N.Y.2d 648, 649 [1983];
People ex rel. Douglas v. Vincent, 50 N.Y.2d 901, 903 [1980]). Here,
petitioner does not seek Kiko’s immediate release, nor does petitioner allege
that Kiko’s continued detention is unlawful. Rather, petitioner seeks to have
Kiko placed in a different facility that petitioner deems more appropriate.
Consequently, even assuming, arguendo, that we agreed with petitioner that
Kiko should be deemed a person for the purpose of this application, and
further assuming, arguendo, that petitioner has standing to commence this
proceeding on behalf of Kiko, this matter is governed by the line of cases
standing for the proposition that habeas corpus does not lie where a petitioner
seeks only to change the conditions of confinement rather than the
confinement itself (see generally People ex rel. Dawson v. Smith, 69 N.Y.2d
689, 690-691 [1986]; Matter of Berrian v. Duncan, 289 A.D.2d 655, 655
[2001]; People ex rel. McCallister v. McGinnis, 251 A.D.2d 835, 835
[1998]). We therefore conclude that habeas corpus does not lie herein.

Present—Smith, J.P., Peradotto, Lindley, Valentino and Whalen, JJ.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) In its short opinion, the Presti court was clear not to rule on the issue of
nonhuman personhood, instead finding that habeas relief is not available
when trying to move a person from one condition of confinement to another.
Is this a more positive outcome (from the perspective of nonhuman animal
rights) than Lavery insofar as it does not appear to create an absolute bar to
nonhuman animals being persons in the way Lavery does?
(2) Because they come from complex societies in their natural environment,
under most circumstances, captive chimpanzees like Kiko cannot simply “go
back to the wild,” and, of course, release into New York would be dangerous
for the chimpanzee and the public. Given this, is sanctuary (several acres,
with other chimpanzees, and not open to visitors) a suitable option? How
does this compare with a prison inmate (or his attorney) who files a habeas
petition to be sent instead to a mental hospital or similar facility, arguing
incapacity or otherwise? Or, historically, a freed child slave or apprentice
being sent to an orphanage (even, at times, over the protest of the child)?
(3) The Third Department Appellate Division cited Presti in a case that did
not involve nonhuman animals and stated: “[I]t is common knowledge that
personhood can and sometimes does attach to nonhuman entities like…
animals[.]” People v. Graves, 163 A.D.3d 16, 21 (4th Dept. June 15, 2018).
How can this be reconciled with Presti? Was the Presti court implicitly
acknowledging that Kiko was or could be a person? Why might an appellate
court in the same state as Lavery reach such a radically different conclusion
when presented with a near-identical case?

Kiko, the NhRP brought a petition in Suffolk County on behalf of Hercules
and Leo, two research chimpanzees detained at the State University of New
York at Stony Brook on Long Island who were being used in locomotion
experiments. That petition was likewise denied by the trial court and the

NhRP appealed to the Second Department intermediate appellate court.86
Instead of pursuing an appeal to the state’s highest court via the Second
Department, the NhRP instead sought a new habeas corpus petition in New
York County in March 2015, which falls under the intermediate appellate

nonhuman animal when she ordered a hearing for Hercules and Leo, though
later striking the word “habeas corpus” to make clear that the chimpanzees

Supreme Court, New York County 2015
49 Misc. 3d 746, 16 N.Y.S.3d 898, 322 Ed. Law Rep. 440

Petitioner brings this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 70 and under the
