IV. KEY ISSUES IN ECOCIDE
In this third and final section, we will consider three key issues in prosecuting
ecocide, as follows: Who is the victim and what is the harm or violation?
Who is the responsible party? And what is the penalty?
A. Who Is the Victim of Ecocide?
1. Existing law
It is necessary to define the victim(s) and the harm or loss suffered in order to
prosecute criminal acts and assess penalties, including the performance of
restorative acts to the harmed ecosystem.
There are two methods of identifying the victim: one is harm and the other is
violation.41 In the harm method, the question is, “Who was harmed directly?”
In the violation method, the question is, “Who was the holder or bearer of the
legally protected right or interest (including the right to or interest in
existence) that was violated?” In regard to the latter question, as discussed
elsewhere in this coursebook, nature is not traditionally considered to be a
holder of legally protected rights or interests.
The 1985 UN General Assembly Declaration of Basic Principles of Justice
for Victims of Crime and Abuse of Power defines a victim as follows:
“Victims” means persons who, individually or collectively, have suffered
harm, including [(harm method)] physical or mental injury, emotional
suffering, economic loss or [(violation method)] substantial impairment of
their fundamental rights, through acts or omissions that are in violation of
criminal laws operative within Member States, including those laws
proscribing criminal abuse of power.42

The above definition is limited to humans, so the harm or violation suffered
would pertain only to humans. In the Rome Statute and in ENMOD, the
offending act may involve “widespread, long-lasting or severe” harm to
nature, as well as harm to humans.
In regard to the national statutes described in Table 2, supra, ten of the
countries consider ecocide as a crime against the peace and security of
humankind and thus take the same human-centered perspective as the UN
General Assembly did in the above definition of victims of crime.
Uzbekistan, in contrast, takes an ecocentric perspective in making ecocide a
crime related to environment protection and conservancy.
2. Nature as victim under the proposed ecocide amendment to the Rome
Statute in the United Kingdom 2011 mock trial
As noted above, Higgins proposed an ecocide amendment to the Rome
Statute in 2010. She also proposed a model act with application to the United
Kingdom.43 Under the Model U.K. Ecocide Act, ecocide involves damage to
ecosystems that affect peaceful enjoyment by the inhabitants, with inhabitants
being defined as “any living species dwelling in a particular place.” The
Ecocide Act also specifies the ways in which the crime of ecocide breaches
the rights to life of humanity and nature, endangers the lives of future
generations, and harms the cultural life of Indigenous communities.
In 2011, Higgins organized a mock trial in the Supreme Court in London to
test the viability of the model statute. While this was a mock trial, it has value
as a study of how an inclusive ecocide law might be applied. The mock
criminal trial concerned alleged offenses under the Act by the CEOs of two
fictional companies, Global Petroleum Company and Glamis Group, related
to the operation of an offshore drilling unit by Global Petroleum in the Gulf
of Mexico and operations in the Canadian tar sands by both companies. The
indictment of the CEO of Global Petroleum Company read, in part, as
follows:
[I]n his role as Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Bannerman of Global
Petroleum Company (GPC) had authority over and responsibility for a
semi-submersible Mobile Offshore Drilling Unit when an explosion on the

platform caused an oil spill in excess of 250 million gallons of crude oil into
the sea resulting in extensive destruction, damage to or loss of ecosystem(s)
covering an area in excess of 200 square kilometers of ocean, to such an
extent that the peaceful enjoyment by the inhabitants of that territory has been
severely diminished thereby:
1. putting birds at risk of injury;
2. causing injury to 2,086 birds; and
3. causing the death of 2,303 birds
contrary to sections 1(1) and 1(2) of the Ecocide Act of 2010.44
The paragraph clearly shows the application of the Ecocide Act to nonhuman
victims. Mr. Bannerman was cleared of charges related to offshore drilling,
but both Mr. Bannerman and the CEO of Glamis Group were found guilty of
ecocide for the killing of birds in the tar sands operations of the two
companies.45
B. Who Is the Responsible Party?
When acts of ecocide have occurred and the victims have been identified, the
responsible party must be connected with the crime. In some cases, there is
one dominant actor, such as BP in the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in
the Gulf of Mexico. In others, such as in the case study at the beginning of
this chapter concerning the 2019 burning of the Brazilian Amazon, there are
multiple actors. In the Amazon burning, some would blame the government
of Brazil or President Bolsonaro for not enforcing environmental laws or
taking other preventive measures. Others would blame large corporations
who are buying products produced on converted Amazon land or establishing
farms and processing facilities in the Amazon. Others would blame the
individuals actually doing the burning. Even in the BP oil spill, although BP
was the dominant actor, there were many other companies and individuals
involved. Who should be charged with the crime?
1. Individuals as responsible parties

In many ecocide cases, the damage is done by people acting through
corporations or other legal entities, including states. The legal entities are
more capable of paying fines or carrying out recovery and restoration efforts
than individuals within those entities. Yet, for cases brought before the
International Criminal Court under the Rome Statute, only natural persons
may be tried. This is a carryover from one of the Nuremberg Principles that
governed war crimes trials after World War II. The principle adopted by the
Nuremberg Tribunal was as follows: “Crimes against international law are
committed by men, not by abstract entities, and only by punishing individuals
who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be
enforced.”46
In keeping with this principle, the Rome Statute states:
Article 25
Individual criminal responsibility
1. The Court shall have jurisdiction over natural persons pursuant to this
Statute.47
* * *
2. Corporations as responsible parties
The drafters of the Rome Statute did, however, consider including a provision
addressing the criminal responsibility of corporations.48 The proposed article
read as follows:
Without prejudice to any individual criminal responsibility of natural persons
under this Statute, the Court may also have jurisdiction over a juridical
person for a crime under this Statute. Charges may be filed by the Prosecutor
against a juridical person, and the Court may render a judgement over a
juridical person for the crime charged, if:
(a) The charges filed by the Prosecutor against the natural person and the
juridical person allege the matters referred to in subparagraphs (b) and (c);

and
(b) The natural person charged was in a position of control within the
juridical person under the national law of the State where the juridical person
was registered at the time the crime was committed; and
(c) The crime was committed by the natural person acting on behalf of and
with the explicit consent of that juridical person and in the course of its
activities; and
(d) The natural person has been convicted of the crime charged.
For the purpose of this Statute, “juridical person” means a corporation whose
concrete, real, or dominant objective is seeking private profit or benefit, and
not a State or other public body in the exercise of State authority, a public
international body, or an organization registered and acting under the national
law of a State as a non-profit organization.
The proceedings with respect to a juridical person under this article shall be
in accordance with this Statute and the relevant Rules of Procedure and
Evidence. The Prosecutor may file charges against the natural and juridical
persons jointly or separately. The natural person and the juridical person may
be jointly tried. If convicted, the juridical person may incur the penalties
referred to in article 76. These penalties shall be enforced in accordance with
the provisions of article 99.49
* * *
Under regional agreements, corporations have been regarded as legal persons
in order to hold them criminally responsible for their actions.50 An example
is provided in Article 9 of the Council of Europe’s 1998 Convention on the
Protection of the Environment through Criminal Law:51
Article 9–Corporate liability
Each Party shall adopt such appropriate measures as may be necessary to
enable it to impose criminal or administrative sanctions or measures on legal
persons on whose behalf an offence referred to in Articles 2 or 3 has been

committed by their organs or by members thereof or by another
representative.
Under Article 14, however, in order for the convention to enter into force, it
had to be ratified by three states who are members of the Council of Europe.
Only 13 of the 47 members of the Council signed the convention and only
Estonia ratified it.52 Thus, it is not in force. The failure to ratify the
Convention is an example of the international resistance to imposing criminal
liability on corporations for environmental and human rights violations.53
In the Model U.K. Ecocide Act, individuals, corporations, and other legal
entities, but not states, may be prosecuted for ecocide.54 Under that act, a
person “in a passion of superior responsibility” for a legal entity, including a
state, is responsible for offenses committed by people under their authority.55
Further, if a superior person of a legal entity is convicted of an offense by
reason of their role in a legal entity, the legal entity is jointly responsible for
the offense.56 The Act has a very broad reach.
3. Methods for holding legal entities responsible for committed crimes
There are several methods for attributing culpability to corporations, with
most common law and civil law jurisdictions using one of three approaches:
(1) identification; (2) aggregation; or (3) culture.57
The identification method equates the acts of specific natural persons to the
acts of a corporation.58 The natural persons are generally determined to be
those who are members of a decision-making body or individuals with
sufficient authority who possess the criminal intent (mens rea) for the
offense.59 In a civil law system, the will of legal entities is expressed through
the entities’ “organs” (directors and managers of a corporation). A crime
occurs in relation to an offense committed for the benefit of a legal entity
through the participation of the organs of that legal entity.
The aggregation method, rather than putting authorized corporate personnel
or organs at the center of culpability, searches the collective knowledge to
satisfy the test of mens rea.60 If the total guilt aggregated from the officials

involved in a particular offense reaches the required level of culpability, the
corporation may be held criminally responsible even though each individual’s
mens rea separately is not enough to justify imposing a punishment.61
Under the culture method, for example in the Australian model of corporate
responsibility,62 corporations may be held liable in regard to their
organizational structure and the operating mechanism that led to
noncompliance with the law.63 According to the Australian Criminal Code,
the corporate culture is “an attitude, policy, rule, course of conduct or
practice existing within the body corporate generally or in the part of the
body corporate in which the relevant activities take place.”64 In this code,
corporate culture is a basis for corporate responsibility in addition to the
identification method.
4. Liability of entities under existing environmental laws
Existing environmental laws give states the ability to address some forms of
ecocide at both the entity and individual level, although they fall short of
offering a comprehensive ecocide framework. The BP oil spill, for example,
involved the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig that was operating in the Gulf of
Mexico and drilling an exploratory well 18,360 feet below sea level about 41
miles south of Louisiana. BP was the operator and principal developer of the
project. On April 20, 2010, high-pressure methane gas expanded into the
marine riser and rose into the drilling rig, where it ignited and exploded.
Eleven workers were killed and 17 were wounded. The rig sank two days
later, and oil leaked from the well for 87 days. The flow rate was as high as
62,000 barrels per day and the total oil spilled was estimated at 4.9 million
barrels.65 The oil was dispersed over an area of 68,000 square miles that
included coastal wetlands, beaches, and the Gulf of Mexico. In addition,
chemicals with relatively unknown ecological impacts were sprayed to
increase dispersion and absorption of the oil. The disaster affected the coasts
of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida, and toxic waste
remains in these coastal lands to this day. The oil spill affected the
livelihoods of fishermen, people in the tourist industry, and many others, and
it had a devastating effect on marine life and coastal life.66

BP was investigated by the U.S. government under the Oil Pollution Act of
1990.67 This act contains provisions intended to avoid future oil spills, as
well as provisions requiring removal of spilled oil and assigning liability for
damages caused and the cost of cleanup. Categories of damage covered
include natural resource damages, damages to real or personal property, loss
of subsistence use, loss of government revenues, loss of profits or impaired
earning capacity, damaged public services, and damage assessment costs.68
The Oil Pollution Act provides for strict liability of the responsible party for
settlement of claims.69 To settle claims from this oil spill, BP set up a $20
billion “Gulf Coast Claims Facility,” and billions of dollars have been paid to
claimants from this facility. Claims have included private claims for damages
to property, loss of income, and environmental cleanup and restoration costs
incurred by governmental agencies.70
In addition to action against BP under the Oil Pollution Act, the U.S. federal
government brought claims under the Clean Water Act resulting in a
settlement under which BP was obligated to pay a $4.5 billion fine. Further,
more than a hundred private lawsuits were filed against BP and other
corporations that had a nexus with the oil spill. The settlement of these claims
was in the neighborhood of $10 billion. As of 2015, BP’s costs related to the
oil spill had reached $54 billion.71 Further criminal charges were brought
against companies and individuals involved in the loss.
The litigation related to the BP oil spill was extensive and involved a
tremendous amount of time and resources by many companies, governmental
agencies, and individual claimants. In this case, claimants received
substantial payments for damages, extensive environmental cleanup,
restoration, and recovery projects that were undertaken, and large criminal
fines against the corporations were collected. No one, however, served prison
time.72
5. States as responsible parties
States may be perpetrators of ecocide, may fail to take actions to prevent the
ecocide, or may fail to penalize perpetrators of ecocide. However, there are
no statutes or treaties under which states may be prosecuted for ecocide. At

present, the restraint of states from committing ecocide would come from
pressures or sanctions by other states, companies, or individuals who had
determined this was necessary. For example, as stated previously in the 2019
Amazon fires case, Germany and Norway, objecting to the encouragement of
the burning by the Brazilian government and the lack of enforcement by the
Brazilian government of laws that would restrict the land conversion and
forest burning, froze aid to the Amazon, and President Macron of France
threatened to block a trade deal with Brazil. In addition, 200 investment
funds called on companies to reduce their reliance on deforestation and
several companies announced boycotts of Brazilian beef and leather.
C. What Is the Penalty?
After the conviction of a defendant of ecocide, the question is, what penalty
or obligation should be imposed? There are five theories of criminal
punishment: (1) Under the incapacitation theory, the perpetrator should be
removed from society so that the perpetrator cannot do further harm; (2)
Under the retributive theory, the perpetrator of a crime should suffer for the
perpetrator’s act in proportion to the harm caused; (3) Under the
rehabilitation theory, the perpetrator should be placed in a situation where
they may change their ways and re-enter society; (4) Under the deterrence
theory, the perpetrator should be punished in such a way that the punishment
deters others from committing the same crime; and (4) Under the restorative
theory, the perpetrator should be obligated to reconcile with the victim and
the community at large, such as by repairing the harm caused.73 Governments
in their legislative roles and courts in their judicial roles often combine two or
more of these theories in determining penalties.
1. Treatment under the Rome Statute
The Rome Statute contains the following penalties for convicted individual
criminals: (1) imprisonment for a number of years or a life sentence in
egregious cases; (2) a fine; and (3) forfeiture of property proceeds and assets
derived directly or indirectly from the crime.74 The Rome Statute also
authorizes the establishment of a trust fund funded by the fines and forfeited
property for the benefit of the victims.75

2. National codes
Under the national ecocide codes identified in Table 2, most statutes impose
imprisonment as the penalty. Judicial fines or restorative or reparative
measures are not common sanctions. Vietnam provides for capital
punishment for acts of ecocide. The killing of a human being as punishment,
however, is difficult to support with respect to ecocide when the underlying
reason for making it an offense is to protect the life of nature with all its
inhabitants.

3. Penalization of corporations
The punishments under the Rome Statute and the above national codes cover
penalties for responsible individuals in corporations but not penalties for
corporations themselves. Such penalties could include fines and forfeiture of

property proceeds and assets derived directly or indirectly from the crime. As
with the Rome Statute, the codes could authorize the establishment of trust
funds funded by the fines and forfeited property for the benefit of the victims
and for environmental cleanup and restoration.76 While not covered under
any present statutes, penalties could also include replacement of
management, removal of the corporate charter, a forced merger, or a forced
sale of assets, including a partial sale of a line of business and its assets.
V. ECOCIDE’S IMPORTANCE FOR EARTH
LAW
As discussed above, ecocide, by reason of its inclusion in the Rome Statute
(albeit never explicitly named by that term), is an established part of
international law as a war crime, but not yet as a peacetime offense. Under
the laws of various nations, ecocide is an offense regardless of whether it
occurs in connection with armed conflict or in peacetime. Under these laws,
the offense of ecocide only occurs when there is “extreme” or “severe”
damage to nature. The Rome Statute requires finding a military attack was
launched that resulted in “widespread, long-term and severe damage to the
natural environment.” The Model U.K. Ecocide Act would require finding
“extensive damage to, destruction of or loss of ecosystem(s) of a given
territory, whether by human agency or other causes to such an extent that
peaceful enjoyment by the inhabitants of that territory has been or will be
severely diminished.”
The impetus for adding a new crime comes from a widely held sense that
something wrong is happening or has happened and there should be a law
against it, and people who violate the law should be criminally punished.
Arguably, there is a widespread sense that devastation of large portions or
aspects of nature, causing extensive harm to human or nonhuman inhabitants
of the area, should be punishable as a crime. Yet, defining and applying the
crime of ecocide has been limited. This may be because the devastation of
nature is often connected with something that is considered a social good: the
defeat of an enemy in war or economic “development” in peacetime. Thus,
the pollution of water and land incident to extracting oil from tar sands in
Canada may be viewed by some as ecocide while, for others, it may be seen

as a negative side effect of producing a needed commodity—a side effect that
may be held in check by pollution control regulations under conventional
environmental law. Another prominent issue limiting the adoption and
prosecution of ecocide relates to criminal intent. As noted above, the Model
U.K. Ecocide Act makes ecocide a strict liability crime, presumably because
of the difficulty of proving that perpetrators act with the intent of seriously
degrading nature. Another issue has been that where ecocide has been
adopted, only individuals, not legal entities, are subject to prosecution.
Five justifications for criminal punishment were discussed above, namely (1)
incapacitation; (2) retribution; (3) rehabilitation; (4) deterrence; and (5)
restoration. Punishment for ecocide may deter people from perpetrating the
crime, and imposing obligations of restoration may be a way of addressing
the harm caused by the crime. The benefits of incapacitation, retribution, and
rehabilitation offer less support for punishment for ecocide. This is because,
as with genocide, the primary reasons for punishing ecocide are completely
preventing recurrence of the crime and bringing as much healing as possible
when the crime has occurred.
Ecocide fits awkwardly in anthropocentric law, which regards nature as
something for the use of humans. When the use of nature yields benefits to
humans, the harm to nature tends to be considered an externality not to be
taken into account except regarding the extent that humans are harmed as a
result. On the other hand, ecocide fits very well in Earth law, or ecocentric
law, where the integrity of the Earth community in its diverse and interrelated
manifestations is the primary concern. Earth law offers a new framework for
what is reasonable and permissible, and what is not. It assumes an ecological
consciousness. In the case of ecocide, it assumes that you should know when
your actions will cause widespread and severe damage to nature, and it is not
reasonable for you to act without regard for the integrity of the natural
systems. Such awareness may not come easily to the modern human, yet it
would be wrong to say that it does not exist.
Let us end this chapter by returning to where we began, with the 2019
deforestation of the Brazilian rainforest. May the actors involved in the
burning of the rainforests and those who finance them or profit from their
activities claim that they were ignorant of the potential harm they were

causing? Ecocide, as with genocide, is not an everyday crime. Ecocide is an
egregious crime, one that unfortunately fits the scale of the destruction that is
taking place in the functioning of Earth, such as the accumulation of
enormous amounts of plastics in oceans resulting from the disposal of fishing
nets and plastic bags, the destruction of boreal forests, the pollution of soil
and water with toxic mine tailings resulting from extracting oil from tar
sands, and the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and acid
in the ocean resulting from fossil fuel production and consumption.
Defining ecocide may be difficult, but law often deals with problems of
where to draw the line and determining who should be accountable. It seems
likely that the scale of environmental degradation will increase for some time.
The importance of the crime of ecocide increases in proportion to the scale of
this devastation. People should not feel they are innocent and above the law
when they destroy the planet. Ecocide will call them to their duty of care.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) How would you define ecocide? When should ecocide be a crime?
(2) Since economic development often involves the large-scale conversion of
land or, through aquaculture, large-scale conversion of oceans and other
bodies of water, how should ecocide be distinguished from economic
development? Or should they not be distinguished because economic
development is not a defense to ecocide?
(3) Two general arguments are made for creating the crime of ecocide:
a. One is that current environmental laws do not address the magnitude of
harm being caused to the Earth system and ecocide laws are more capable of
doing so than conventional environmental laws. In consideration of four
objectives of Earth law—ensuring that humans live within planetary
boundaries, prospectively caring for ecosystems, restoring damaged
ecosystems, and justly sharing the burdens of mitigating and adapting to
climate change and other environmental stresses—how could ecocide laws
help?

b. The other is that ecocide, like genocide, is of international concern and
should be subject to transborder enforcement. Do you agree that ecocide, like
genocide, should be an international crime?
(4) Why do you think the Rome Statute limits ecocide to acts of war?
(5) Is ecocide too vague to be considered a peacetime offense? In peacetime,
could strengthening environmental laws provide adequate protection for
offenses related to environmental protection, conservation, species protection,
and the health of all species, or is a peacetime crime of ecocide needed? What
arguments would you make for the necessity of a peacetime offense of
ecocide?
(6) Polly Higgins gave four reasons why ecocide should be a strict liability
offense: (1) it is the consequence that is in question, not the conduct; (2) the
gravity of the destruction and damage justifies conviction without proof of
criminal intent; (3) without strict liability, enforcement would be largely
ineffective; and (4) strict liability rightly places the focus on prevention of the
crime and not the blame of the accused. Should ecocide be a strict liability
offense, or should criminal intent (mens rea) be an element of the crime?
(7) Should legal entities be subject to prosecution for ecocide? Consider the
discussion in this chapter and the provisions of the Model U.K. Ecocide Act.
On what basis should legal entities be considered responsible parties?
(9) What should the penalties for ecocide be?
(9) Does ecocide involve political questions that should best be resolved by
the legislative and executive branches?
(10) In terms of restorative justice, are courts capable of fashioning remedies
for the harm caused by ecocide?

CHAPTER 13
Climate Change Civil Disobedience 
and the Necessity Defense1
I. INTRODUCTION
Activists are increasingly recognizing that long-term approaches are not
enough to address the urgency of threats to the environment and that
attorneys must respond accordingly. Much of the legal thinking on the
environment is aimed at institutional change. For example, public trust
litigation (see Chapter 7) aims to require governments, such as the United
States, to take positive action to protect common resources—most crucially,
the climate system. As another example, the rights of nature movement (see,
e.g., Chapter 9) seeks systems change by recognizing non-human living
beings and natural entities, such as entire watersheds or forests, as living
entities with rights. While these long-term strategies to build a body of Earth
law are important, shorter term strategies are needed to address urgent
environmental threats. This is especially true with regard to the threat of
climate change: As the defendant in a case discussed below asserts, scientists
and activists are starting to recognize that “the window for action on climate
change has narrowed to the point that immediate, emergency action is
necessary.”2
While the Paris Climate Agreement purportedly seeks to limit warming to
below 1.5°C, recent studies suggest that the emissions reduction targets laid
out in the accord will not be enough to reach this goal and even those targets

are not being met.3 Failure to do so will have catastrophic consequences for
human civilization and nature alike, including ecosystems collapsing, poorer
nations and regions becoming uninhabitable, and water availability
decreasing sharply in vast areas and increasing sharply in others.4
Moreover, the United States has renounced its commitment and formally
begun to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement.5 As federal agencies
roll back environmental regulations and as energy companies continue to
promote ever-increasing and unsustainable production of fossil fuels, activists
have been using civil disobedience and nonviolent direct action to slow, and
hopefully stop, this dangerous trend. In doing so they are putting their lives
and liberty on the line. Acts of civil disobedience may help hold the line
while a slower-moving body of Earth law that addresses the root causes of
climate change moves forward.
Working alongside these activists are their attorneys, who are attempting to
legally and socially legitimize the actions the activists are taking. One of the
primary legal strategies used in the United States to defend acts of civil
disobedience is known as the necessity defense. This common law and, in
some jurisdictions, statutory defense will be explored in this chapter.
Specifically, this chapter will show how environmental activists have
marshaled the necessity defense to justify their acts of nonviolent civil
disobedience.
The necessity defense, which has roots in English common law and appears
in many legal traditions is an argument used by criminal defendants to justify
or excuse charged conduct. Necessity defendants argue that their allegedly
criminal actions were necessary to prevent an injury to themselves or others
and that it is in society’s best interest to acquit them of any wrongdoing. Like
self-defense or the insanity defense, the necessity defense is usually
considered an affirmative defense, in which the defendant accepts the
prosecution’s facts but offers additional facts that warrant a not-guilty
finding.
Although the defense differs from state to state and between federal circuits,
it usually requires the following elements:

The defendant faced an imminent harm to themselves or others;
The defendant’s actions were less harmful than the harm to be avoided
(defendant chose the lesser of two evils);
The defendant reasonably thought that their actions would be effective
in avoiding or mitigating the imminent harm; and
The defendant had no reasonable legal alternatives to violating the law.
In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, this defense has been commonly
asserted in cases involving marijuana use, driving under the influence, and
prison escape. In recent decades, the necessity has often, and controversially,
been used by political protesters seeking to justify acts of civil disobedience.
In particular, criminal defendants charged for opposing war, nuclear power
and arms, and illegal government action, and for supporting civil rights,
began using the defense. They soon discovered that juries accepted their
arguments about the social good accomplished by their illegal actions and
would often acquit defendants based on a political necessity defense.
One of the most notable uses of the defense occurred in 1987, when Abbie
Hoffman, Amy Carter, and 13 other people occupied an administration
building at the University of Massachusetts and sat in road-blocking buses
carrying arrested protestors from the building. The defendants were
protesting illegal conduct by the CIA in Central America and were acquitted
of trespass and disorderly conduct charges stemming from their occupation.
Beginning in the mid-2000s, climate activists began using the climate
necessity defense to justify their acts of civil disobedience. The typical
climate necessity argument is straightforward. Framed in light of the typical
common law defense, climate necessity defendants argue that:
Climate change is not only imminent, but it is occurring now and is
causing severe harms to the planet and its people;
Their acts of civil disobedience are much less harmful than the harms
caused by climate change;
Civil disobedience is demonstrably effective in mitigating or avoiding
specific climate change harms, in building public support for climate
change policy, and in influencing political decision-makers; and
Traditional alternatives such as voting, lobbying, and organizing have
failed to prevent climate change harms, making civil disobedience

necessary.
As discussed in the three cases that follow, climate necessity defendants face
many obstacles, such as courts’ reluctance to recognize the efficacy of civil
disobedience or the non-existence of legal alternatives; pre-trial evidentiary
tests; and judicial and prosecutorial resistance to climate change science and
evidence of political failure to address climate change. Nonetheless, climate
necessity defenses are increasingly common, and, in the past two years, some
state appellate courts have recognized the validity of the defense.
II. NEW YORK CITY
Because climate necessity defenses are usually offered in lower-level
criminal courts and do not result in written opinions, full judicial
consideration of the defense’s elements is rare. An instance of such full
consideration in a case involving air pollution can be found in People v.
Gray. In this New York City criminal court case, defendants were protesting
the dangers of air pollution to bikers and pedestrians on the Queensboro
Bridge in New York City and were charged with disorderly conduct for
blocking the entrance of a bridge roadway. The prosecution agreed to allow
the defendants to present a necessity defense in exchange for the defendants
agreeing to not contest the elements of the crime. The judge acquitted the
defendants in a nonjury trial, finding that they had proven all elements of the
necessity defense.
People v. Gray
571 N.Y.S.2d 851, 866 (Crim. Ct. 1991)
The necessity defense is fundamentally a balancing test to determine whether
a criminal act was committed to prevent a greater harm. The common
elements of the defense found in virtually all common-law and statutory
definitions include the following: (1) the actor has acted to avoid a grave
harm, not of his own making; (2) there are not adequate legal means to avoid
the harm; and (3) the harm sought to be avoided is greater than that
committed. A number of jurisdictions, New York among them, have included
two additional requirements—first, the harm must be imminent, and second,

the action taken must be reasonably expected to avert the impending danger.
Extensive research revealed that while Judges in New York (with one partial
exception, discussed infra) have so far declined to rule that a necessity
defense has been sufficiently established to allow the trier of fact to consider
it in their deliberations in cases involving defendants who have engaged in
citizen intervention/civil disobedience, numerous State Trial Judges in other
jurisdictions, as well as some Federal District Court Judges, have so charged
juries or acquitted defendants after bench trials in similar cases.
Moreover, when the necessity defense is actually submitted to the trier of fact
in such cases, defendants have usually been acquitted [Citations omitted].
There are also a number of cases in which charges were dropped after the
Judge’s rulings that a necessity defense would be permitted.…
I. THE CHOICE OF EVILS REQUIREMENT
…In this case, the defendants are all members of an organization called
Transportation Alternatives, an organization devoted to the promotion of
nonvehicular, ecologically sound means of transportation. Through their
testimony and that of their expert witnesses, it was clear that these
defendants’ actions were motivated by the desire to prevent what they called
the “asphyxiation of New York” by automobile-related pollution.
Specifically, the harm they seek to combat is the release of ever higher levels
of pollution from vehicular traffic, and the unnecessary death and serious
illness of many New Yorkers as a result.
Defendants also articulated a motivation to put an end to an extremely
hazardous situation that had resulted on the Queensboro Bridge south outer
roadway, subsequent to the implementation of the regulation opening that
roadway to vehicular traffic during the evening rush hour. Since many
pedestrians and bicyclists continued to use that roadway, the defendants
testified that they also acted to prevent serious injuries to those individuals
who continued to use alternative forms of transportation on the bridge.…
In this case, as well as in most necessity cases, it is clear that defendants
chose the correct societal value. It is beyond question that both the death and
illness of New Yorkers as a result of additional air pollution, and the danger

to cyclists and pedestrians posed by vehicles on the south outer roadway, are
far greater harms than that created by the violation of disorderly conduct.…
II. THE IMMINENCE OF GRAVE HARM REQUIREMENT
In evaluating whether defendants’ perceptions of the harm they sought to
avoid in this case were reasonable, the court must decide whether they had a
well-founded belief in imminent grave injury. [Citations omitted.]
Such determination is almost always a question for the trier of fact. [Citations
omitted.]
Defendants in the instant case presented several witnesses, as well as
submitting studies, to establish the existence of a grave and imminent harm.
Defendants themselves testified that the [Department of Transportation]
regulation, if obeyed, would prove to be a devastating disincentive to New
Yorkers who use alternative or nonvehicular means of transportation between
the Boroughs of Manhattan and Queens. The only road open to bicyclists and
pedestrians is practically inaccessible to them during the hours most critical
to their return home. In contrast to this disincentive to nonpolluting forms of
transportation, another lane is open to vehicular traffic.
Defendants clearly articulated their belief that encouraging automobiles at a
rush hour traffic “choke-point” while discouraging walkers and cyclists
produces a specific, grave harm that is not only imminent, but is occurring
daily. This belief was supported by the testimony of expert witnesses and
studies submitted into evidence.…
Unlike many of the cases in this area, where the harm sought to be prevented
was perceived as too far in the future to be found “imminent,” the grave harm
in this case is occurring every day. The additional pollution breathed by all
New Yorkers (in a city that is already out of compliance with the minimal
standards set by the EPA [Environmental Protection Agency]), as a result of
the fact that more road space will be devoted to vehicles and its corollary that
those hundreds of individuals who would otherwise bicycle or walk are
discouraged from using nonpolluting forms of transportation is a concrete
harm being suffered by the population at this moment.…

III. THE NO LEGAL ALTERNATIVE REQUIREMENT
A key requirement of the necessity defense is that no reasonable legal option
exists for averting the harm. Once again, the proper inquiry here is whether
the defendant reasonably believed that there was no legal alternative to his
actions. The defense does not legalize lawlessness; rather it permits courts to
distinguish between necessary and unnecessary illegal acts in order to
provide an essential safety valve to law enforcement in a democratic society.
It has been asserted that because a democracy creates legal avenues of
protest, alternatives must always exist. In the opinion of this court, however,
to dispense with the necessity defense by assuming that people always have
access to effective legal means of protest circumvents the purpose of the
defense.
When courts rule as a matter of law that defendants always have a reasonable
belief in other adequate alternatives, they are asserting that regardless of how
diligent a party is in pursuing alternatives, no matter how much time has been
spent in legitimate efforts to prevent the harm, no matter how ineffective
previous measures have been to handle the emergency, the courts in hindsight
can always find just one more alternative that a citizen could have tried
before acting out of necessity.…
In this case, the defendants were individuals who were thoroughly familiar
with the process by which decisions concerning transportation in New York
are made, and who, despite their long history of an advocacy and consultative
role in such matters, were completely excluded from the decision-making
process concerning the closing of a very important roadway for nonpolluting
forms of transportation. Where, at the first opportunity, every traditional
method of petitioning, letter writing, phone calling, leafletting and lobbying
was vigorously pursued by these defendants to no avail, it cannot be said as a
matter of law that they did not reasonably believe their legal alternatives to be
exhausted.…
IV. THE CASUAL RELATIONSHIP REQUIREMENT
New York is among the jurisdictions that require a defendant’s actions to be
reasonably designed to actually prevent the threatened greater harm.…

As with the other elements of this defense, the test consistent with the
purposes of this defense is one of reasonable belief. Defendants’ initial
burden is to offer sufficient evidence of a reasonable belief in a causal link
between their behavior and ending the perceived harm.
The New York statute and most common-law formulations use the term
“necessary” rather than “sufficient.” In the opinion of this court, a
defendant’s reasonable belief must be in the necessity of his action to avoid
the injury. The law does not require certainty of success.…
While this court agrees that there are numerous examples in United States
history which support the reasonable belief of a causal connection between
citizen intervention and the prevention of harm, the defendants in this case
need not go beyond their own experiences.…
Pursuant to the foregoing opinion, this court finds that the People have not
disproved the elements of the necessity defense in this case beyond a
reasonable doubt. Defendants are therefore acquitted.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) In People v. Gray, the court summarily concluded that “it is clear that
defendants chose the correct societal value.” To what degree does this
conclusion depend on this particular judge’s personal perspective on societal
values? In an effort to counsel a client, how might one assess trial judges to
determine the viability of a climate necessity defense? What evidence might
be marshaled to persuade a judge as to the “correctness” of the societal value
of preventing climate change?
(2) One of the most difficult hurdles for civil disobedience to clear when
raising the necessity defense is showing the absence of any reasonable legal
alternatives. In finding that the defendants met their burden for this element,
the court states: “It has always been asserted that because a democracy
creates legal avenues of protests, alternatives must always exist. In the
opinion of this court, however, to dispense with the necessity defense by
assuming [this] circumvents the purpose of the defense.” What other legal
obstacles exist that prevent individuals from effecting meaningful change

through the democratic process generally? With respect to climate change
specifically?

III. UTAH
One of the first American climate necessity defenses was offered by Tim
DeChristopher in 2009. Posing as a bidder, DeChristopher disrupted a Bureau
of Land Management (BLM) auction for oil and gas drilling rights to several
parcels of pristine red-rock country in southeastern Utah, resulting in charges
of false statement and violation of the Federal Onshore Oil and Gas Leasing
Act. The Utah federal district court granted the prosecution’s motion in
limine to bar the necessity defense—a common pre-trial tactic in which
litigants ask the court to preemptively bar evidence or testimony in the
interest of efficiency or preventing bias or confusion— because
DeChristopher’s actions did not meet the requirements. DeChristopher then
appealed to the Tenth Circuit, which in the following 2012 opinion upheld
the district court’s decision.
United States v. DeChristopher
No. 2:08-CR-183, 2009 WL 3837208 (D. Utah Nov. 16, 2009), upheld in
United States v. DeChristopher, 695 F.3d 1082, 1087-88 (10th Cir. 2012)
DISTRICT COURT OPINION.
This matter is before the court on the government’s motion in limine to bar
defendant Tim DeChristopher (“DeChristopher”) from presenting a necessity
defense at trial, including any evidence in support of such a defense.…
On December 19, 2008, DeChristopher went to the Utah BLM office in Salt
Lake City, Utah. Outside the BLM office, environmental activists organized a
protest. Inside the office, DeChristopher registered to bid on oil and gas
leases. In order to register as a bidder, DeChristopher was required to fill out
and sign a “Bidder Registration Form.” The Bidder Registration Form
required DeChristopher to certify that: (1) he was a good-faith bidder, (2) he

had the intention to acquire an oil and gas lease on the offered lands, (3) a
winning bid constituted a legally binding commitment to accept the lease,
and (4) in the event of winning a bid, he was obligated to pay the BLM by the
end of the day a percentage of the lease’s purchase price, whether or not the
lease was subsequently issued. The Bidder Registration Form also informed
DeChristopher of the criminal consequences of tampering with the bidding
process.
At the lease sale, DeChristopher placed bids on dozens of oil and gas leases.
Initially, DeChristopher would drive up the bid price and then pull out before
he had won the bid. But then he began to bid on the oil and gas leases until he
won the bid. In total, DeChristopher won fourteen leases totaling $1.7
million. DeChristopher claims he acted to combat the “government’s
violation of its own laws and regulations and the consequential exacerbation
of global warming and climate change, and destruction of irreplaceable
natural and cultural resources.”…
On April 1, 2009, a grand jury returned a two-count indictment against
DeChristopher, charging him with (1) violating the Federal Onshore Oil and
Gas Leasing Reform Act, and (2) providing false statements. Both before and
after the return of the indictment against him, DeChristopher and his actions
at the BLM lease sale received considerable attention by the print and
broadcast media. He gave numerous interviews, at times with his lawyer
standing at his side, in which he declared that he was justified in his actions
because of his concerns about the environment. In these statements
DeChristopher indicated that he would defend his behavior as necessary or
legally justified.…
I. LEGAL STANDARD
A criminal defendant has the right to have a jury resolve disputed factual
issues.6 However, where the evidence, even if believed, does not establish all
of the elements of a legal defense, the court need not submit the defense to a
jury.7 Accordingly, a motion in limine can determine the admissibility of the
necessity defense.8 The sole issue before this court is whether the evidence,
as described in DeChristopher’s written proffer, is insufficient as a matter of
law to support the necessity defense.9 If it is, then the court should exclude

the defense and the evidence offered in support.10
II. THE NECESSITY DEFENSE
Successful use of the necessity defense requires the defendant to prove that:
(1) he was faced with a choice of evils and chose the lesser evil; (2) he acted
to prevent imminent harm; (3) he reasonably anticipated a direct casual [sic]
relationship between his conduct and the harm to be averted; and (4) he had
no legal alternatives to violating the law.11 If a defendant’s offer of proof is
deficient with regard to any of the four elements, the defense of necessity
fails.12 This case does not qualify for the necessity defense.
A. Choice of Evils
The necessity defense requires that a defendant prove that he was faced with
a choice of evils and chose the lesser evil.13 DeChristopher’s written proffer
asserts that his actions were a lesser evil compared to the greater evil of the
government’s violation of the law surrounding the BLM lease sale and the
“consequential exacerbation of global warming and climate change, and
destruction of irreplaceable natural and cultural resources.” 14 The court finds
that DeChristopher fails to satisfy the “choice of evils” requirement for at
least two reasons.
First, a harm or evil that may or may not occur is insufficient for purposes of
the necessity defense.15 Indicating that harms that are insufficiently concrete
are not cognizable as harms for purposes of the necessity defense.16
“[Defendant] must be able to show some direct harm…not a theoretical
future harm to all of us that may or may not occur.”17
Second, the court agrees with the United States Court of Appeals for the
Ninth Circuit in that the court does “not sit to render judgments upon the
legality of the conduct of the government at the request of any person who
asks us to because he happens to think that what the government doing is
wrong.…To [do so] would…put [the court] in the position of usurping the
functions that the Constitution has given to the Congress and to the
President.”18 “The necessity defense was never intended to excuse criminal
activity by those who disagree with the decisions and policies on the

lawmaking branches of government; in such cases the ‘greater harm’ sought
to be prevented would be the course of action chosen by elected
representatives, and a court in allowing the defense would be making a
negative political or policy judgment about that course of action.”
Accordingly, DeChristopher’s necessity defense fails because he did not face
a definite and/or cognizable choice of two evils.
B. Imminent Harm
The necessity defense requires the defendant to show that the harm to be
avoided was so imminent that, absent the defendant’s criminal acts, the harm
was certain to occur.19 In DeChristopher’s written proffer, he asks the court
to relax the “imminent harm” requirement. The court declines to do so. The
term “imminent harm” connotes a real emergency or crisis.20 Even assuming
arguendo that the BLM’s lease sale was “evil,” the evidence does not support
a finding of imminent harm because issuance of the oil and gas leases offered
at the BLM lease sale was not certain to occur. There were approximately
1,600 protests filed including at least one for every parcel offered for lease.
The BLM does not issue an officially protested lease until after the protest
has been investigated and affirmatively resolved. This can be a lengthy
process with an uncertain outcome. Furthermore, unlike the destructive forces
of fire referred to by DeChristopher in his written proffer, the suggested
consequences of the BLM lease sale were not certain to occur or immediately
dangerous. Thus, the court finds that DeChristopher’s necessity defense fails
because the evidence does not establish “imminent harm.”
C. Sufficient Causal Relationship
A defendant must demonstrate that he reasonably anticipated a direct causal
relationship between his actions and the harm to be averted.21 DeChristopher
attests that he reasonably anticipated his actions would “thwart” the BLM’s
unlawful lease sale, and also avert its consequential exacerbation of global
warming and climate change, and its destruction of irreplaceable natural and
cultural resources. However, DeChristopher fails as a matter of law to
establish that driving the bid price up on some parcels and winning only
fourteen of over a hundred parcels sold could be reasonably anticipated to
directly stop the BLM’s “unlawful” lease sale and avoid its purported

consequences. Unlike a person demolishing a home to create a firebreak,
DeChristopher’s actions were more akin to placing a small pile of dirt in the
fire’s path. The court finds that DeChristopher’s necessity defense fails
because he cannot establish that his actions would directly bring about the
ends he claims to have sought.
D. The Availability of Other, Legal Alternatives to Violating the Law
As long as defendant’s perceived “crisis” permitted a selection from among
several solutions, some of which did not involve criminal acts, the necessity
defense must fail.22 Here, DeChristopher could have filed protests during the
30-day protest period. DeChristopher could have also demonstrated with the
environmental activists outside the BLM office. Moreover, DeChristopher
could have involved himself with the coalition of environmental groups that
filed a federal lawsuit in the District of Columbia that eventually precluded
the issuance of certain leases included in the BLM lease sale. Consequently,
the court finds that DeChristopher’s necessity defense fails because there
were reasonable, legal alternatives open to DeChristopher other than his
alleged criminal acts.
E. Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, the court finds that the evidence is insufficient as a
matter of law to support the necessity defense. Accordingly, the
government’s motion in limine to bar DeChristopher from presenting a
necessity defense at trial, including any evidence in support of such a defense
is GRANTED.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) The DeChristopher court ultimately concluded that three of the four
elements of necessity were not met: (1) legally cognizable harm, (2) no legal
alternatives, and (3) sufficient causal relationship. What are the strengths and
flaws of the court’s reasoning, particularly of the “sufficient causal
relationship” factor, in light of the information presented in the note?
(2) DeChristopher’s climate necessity defense was denied prior to trial on a

motion in limine by the prosecution; the jury never had the opportunity to
hear the defendant’s theory of the case. Is a motion in limine an appropriate
means of deciding such central questions in a case? What are the benefits and
drawbacks of litigating the climate necessity defense in pre-trial motions? In
a trial setting, in both state and federal courts, it is a deeply embedded tenet
that judges are responsible for making decisions about the law, while juries
are responsible for deciding issues of fact. Where is the line between the law
and the facts in DeChristopher’s case? Should the jury be able to decide for
itself whether evidence is relevant?
(3) Ultimately, while DeChristopher was convicted and served 21 months of
a two-year sentence, his defense received significant media attention and
even led to an investigation into the lack of environmental assessments
performed before the auction. As a result of this investigation, all the drilling
leases in the area were eventually cancelled. How does this post-conviction
development reflect upon the court’s holding regarding the element of
“sufficient causal relationship?” How might this tangible effect of
DeChristopher’s protest impact future necessity defense arguments?
(4) Notice that the Gray court and the DeChristopher court articulate the
elements of the necessity defense almost identically. Do both courts fairly
analyze the necessity defense in reaching opposing conclusions? To what
extent were the different outcomes due to the differing facts in each case? To
what extent were the courts analyzing the necessity defense to reach a pre-
determined outcome? Which court present the more sound legal analysis of
the necessity defense?

IV. WASHINGTON
In a significant set of ongoing cases, five activists responding to a call to
action from the Standing Rock anti-pipeline protest camp in North Dakota
simultaneously turned off valves controlling the flow of tar sands oil from
Canada through pipelines in Minnesota, North Dakota, Montana, and
Washington. All five activists prepared climate necessity defenses to the
array of felony and misdemeanor charges they faced.

The first trial for the so-called “Shut It Down” actions involved felony
charges of burglary and criminal sabotage against Ken Ward, a long-time
environmental protestor. After receiving notice of the defense’s intent to
argue necessity, the prosecution filed a motion in limine to preclude necessity
defense-related evidence, to which the defense responded with a brief and a
list of expert witnesses prepared to testify regarding climate science, energy
economics, tar sands, and the effectiveness of civil disobedience. At the pre-
trial hearing, the judge denied the necessity defense, finding that Ward had
legal alternatives to his act of protest and expressing concerns that the trial
would turn into a referendum on the science of climate change; in his oral
ruling, the judge called the question of the effects of global warming a matter
of “tremendous controversy.”
Ward proceeded to trial, testifying about his beliefs and motivations and
winning judicial notice of several charts depicting the causes and risks of
climate change. The trial ended in a hung jury. The prosecution then decided
to retry Ward, and the judge enforced his earlier denial of necessity defense
despite a motion for reconsideration. A new jury hung once again on the
sabotage charge but convicted on burglary. In the following opinion, the
Washington Court of Appeals takes up Ward’s appeal and explains its
reasoning for reversing the trial court’s denial of Ward’s right to present a
necessity defense.
Washington v. Ward
438 P.3d 588 (Wash. Ct. App. 2019)
Appellate opinion
Washington recognizes a common law necessity defense. The defense may
be raised when a defendant demonstrates that they reasonably believed the
commission of the crime was necessary to avoid or minimize a harm, the
harm sought to be avoided was greater than the harm resulting from a
violation of the law, the threatened harm was not brought about by the
defendant, and no reasonable legal alternative existed.
Kenneth Ward appeals his conviction for burglary in the second degree after
he broke into a Kinder Morgan pipeline facility and turned off a valve, which

stopped the flow of Canadian tar sands oil to refineries in Skagit and
Whatcom Counties. Ward intended to protest the continued use of tar sands
oil, which he contends significantly contributes to climate change, and the
inaction by governments to meaningfully address the crisis of climate change.
Ward argues that he was deprived of his Sixth Amendment right to present
his only defense—necessity—after the trial court granted the State’s motion
in limine excluding all testimony and evidence of necessity. We agree and
reverse.
I
Kinder Morgan transports tar sands oil from Canada into the United States by
pipeline. On October 11, 2016, Kinder Morgan was notified by telephone that
persons “would be closing a valve, one of our main line valves in the Mount
Vernon area within the next 15 minutes.” Following the call, Ward cut off a
padlock and entered the Kinder Morgan pipeline facility off of Peterson Road
in Burlington. Ward then closed a valve on the Trans-Mountain pipeline and
placed sunflowers on the valve. At the same time, other protesters closed
similar valves in North Dakota, Montana, and Minnesota. Collectively, the
protests temporarily stopped the flow of Canadian tar sands oil from entering
into the United States.
Ward was arrested at the pipeline facility and charged with burglary in the
second degree, criminal sabotage, and criminal trespass in the second degree.
Ward admitted his conduct but argued that his actions were protected under a
necessity defense. The trial court granted the State’s pretrial motion in limine
to preclude all witnesses and evidence offered in support of Ward’s necessity
defense.
Ward’s first trial ended with a hung jury. The State then recharged Ward with
burglary in the second degree and criminal sabotage. Ward moved for
reconsideration of the trial court’s order granting the State’s motion in limine.
In support of his motion, Ward offered argument, the curriculum vitae for
eight proposed expert witnesses, and voluminous scientific evidence
documenting the impacts of climate change, that climate change is primarily
caused by greenhouse gas emissions resulting from human activity, and the
contribution of burning tar sands oil. The trial court denied Ward’s motion
for reconsideration and excluded all testimony and evidence in support of

Ward’s necessity defense. A second jury found Ward guilty of burglary but
were unable to return a verdict on criminal sabotage. Ward appeals.
II
Ward argues that the trial court denied his constitutional right to present a
defense by granting the State’s motion in limine striking all testimony and
evidence of necessity. We agree.…
The Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution and article 1,
sections 21 and 22 of the Washington Constitution guarantee a defendant the
right to trial by jury and to defend against criminal allegations.23 “The right
of an accused in a criminal trial to due process is, in essence, the right to a
fair opportunity to defend against the State’s accusations.”24 “A defendant’s
right to an opportunity to be heard in his defense, including the rights to
examine witnesses against him and to offer testimony, is basic in our system
of jurisprudence.”25
Below, the trial court prohibited Ward from presenting evidence or witnesses
on the necessity defense. If Ward submitted a sufficient quantum of evidence
to show that he would likely be able to meet each element of the necessity
defense, then the trial court’s exclusion of evidence in support of his sole
defense violated Ward’s constitutional rights.
III
“[A]n act is justified if it by necessity is taken in a reasonable belief that the
harm or evil to be prevented by the act is greater than the harm caused by
violating the criminal statute.”26 Necessity is available when “the pressure of
circumstances cause the accused to take unlawful action to avoid a harm
which social policy deems greater than the harm resulting from a violation of
the law…[but not where] a legal alternative is available to the accused.”27
To successfully raise the necessity defense the defendant must prove, by a
preponderance of the evidence, that: (1) they reasonably believed the
commission of the crime was necessary to avoid or minimize a harm, (2) the
harm sought to be avoided was greater than the harm resulting from a
violation of the law, (3) the threatened harm was not brought about by the

defendant, and (4) no reasonable legal alternative existed.28
The State argues that Ward’s offer of proof failed to establish the elements of
the necessity defense. A challenge to the sufficiency of evidence “admits the
truth thereof and all inferences that can reasonably be drawn therefrom.”29 “It
requires the trial court and appellate courts to interpret the evidence most
favorably for the defendant.”30 In this light, we review Ward’s offer of proof
as to each element of the necessity defense.
A
Ward presented sufficient evidence that he reasonably believed the crimes he
committed were necessary to minimize the harms that he perceived. Ward’s
offer of proof included evidence of how past acts of civil disobedience have
been successful, evidence of previous climate activism campaigns, and
evidence of his own personal successes in effectuating change through civil
disobedience. Specifically, Ward offered evidence that he has been working
with environmental issues for more than 40 years but that the majority of his
efforts failed to achieve effective results. Ward asserted that because of these
failures he “came to understand that the issue of climate change would
require other than incremental change” and that “direct action was necessary
to accomplish these goals.” Ward offered three experts—Eric de Place, Bill
McKibben, and Martin Gilens—who were prepared to testify as to the
efficacy of civil disobedience and how such actions have become necessary
in the climate movement. Ward argued that to decide whether his actions
were “reasonably calculated to be effective in averting the imminent harm of
climate change requires [the] expert testimony and evidence” that he was
prepared to present to the jury, and that whether his beliefs were reasonable
was a question for the jury, not the trial court, to decide.
The State argues that it was unreasonable for Ward to believe that the
commission of this crime was necessary to avoid or minimize harm. The
State asserts, first, that all Ward did was temporarily inconvenience Kinder
Morgan’s employees so it was unreasonable to think that his actions would
actually avoid or minimize the broader harms associated with climate change.
And second, that because Ward had legal alternatives available it was
unreasonable for him to believe that his actions were necessary to avoid or

minimize harm.
Whether Ward’s beliefs were reasonable was a question for the jury.31 (“It is
the province of the jury to determine such issues” as whether the defendant
acted with reasonable grounds.) And further, Ward did not have to prove that
the harm he sought to avoid or minimize was actually avoided or minimized
but instead that the reason he broke the law was in an attempt to avoid or
minimize harm.32 Describing the second prong as “the harm sought to be
avoided [, not the harm actually avoided,] was greater than the harm resulting
from a violation of the law.” Ward’s past successes in effectuating change
through civil disobedience in conjunction with the proposed expert witnesses
and testimony about Ward’s beliefs were sufficient evidence to persuade a
fair minded, rational juror that Ward’s beliefs were reasonable.
B
Ward also offered sufficient evidence to show that the harms of global
climate change were greater than the harm of breaking into Kinder Morgan’s
property. Ward asserted that the extent of the harm resulting from his actions
were the loss of a few locks and the temporary inconvenience to Kinder
Morgan’s employees. Compared to this, Ward introduced “voluminous
scientific evidence of the harms of climate change.” This evidence included
information establishing climate change is real and detrimentally effecting
Washington, and that tar sands oil poses a specifically acute threat to our
environment. Further, Ward offered to present testimony from climate
scientists, Drs. James Hansen, Richard Gammon, and Celia Bitz, supporting
his defense.
C
Whether the harms of global climate change was brought about by Ward was
not an issue in this case. Nevertheless, Ward proffered evidence and expert
testimony establishing the harms associated with global climate change and
the root causes of global climate change.
D
Ward also offered sufficient evidence to create a question of fact on whether

there were reasonable legal alternatives. Ward argued that the window for
action on climate change has narrowed to the point that immediate,
emergency action is necessary. Ward offered evidence of his more than 40
years being involved in various environmental movements, the numerous
attempts he has made to address climate change, and how most of those
efforts have failed. Ward additionally offered proposed testimony by pipeline
industry expert Eric de Place, professor and climate campaigner Bill
McKibben, and professor of political science Martin Gilens, to the effect that
the fossil fuel industry’s influence over political institutions renders
traditional legal avenues unreasonable as a means of addressing the climate
emergency.
State v. Parker discussed the “no reasonable alternative” element.33 Parker
was charged with felon in possession of a gun. Parker claimed that he carried
the gun because he had been shot the previous July and his assailants were
still at large. Division Two of this court held that in order to show he had no
reasonable alternative, Parker has to demonstrate “that he had actually tried
the alternative or had no time to try it, or that a history of futile attempts
revealed the illusionary benefits of the alternative.”34 Here, in contrast with
Parker, Ward offered evidence that he had tried the alternatives and they were
unsuccessful. Whether Ward’s evidence was sufficient to establish that his
history of failed attempts to address climate change revealed the futility of
supposed reasonable alternatives was a question for the jury. Viewed in the
light most favorable to Ward, and admitting the truth of his evidence and all
reasonable inferences therefrom, Ward’s offer of proof created a question for
the jury.35 Because Ward met his initial burden of showing that he would
likely be able to submit a sufficient quantum of evidence on each element of
necessity to make it a jury question whether he established that element
beyond a reasonable doubt, the trial court violated his constitutional right by
granting the State’s motion in limine.…
We reverse and remand.
* * *
STUDY QUESTIONS

(1) With regard to reasonable belief, the trial court stated that “Ward’s past
successes in effectuating change through civil disobedience in conjunction
with the proposed expert witnesses [testifying to the efficacy of civil
disobedience] and testimony about Ward’s belief were sufficient evidence to
persuade a…juror that Ward’s beliefs were reasonable.” How might
increased judicial recognition of the climate necessity defense affect others’
decision to engage in climate disobedience in the future? Could this increased
participation in turn have an impact on how often the defense is recognized?
Why or why not?
(2) The court found Ward’s prior unsuccessful attempts to effect change
through political avenues were critical to establishing the “no reasonable
legal alternatives” element. Imagine you are an attorney advising a client who
wants to engage in civil disobedience to protest a liquid natural gas (LNG)
export facility being built in your community. What actions should your
client take prior to engaging in such an action to increase the probability of a
court finding this element has been satisfied? Is voting sufficient? Calling
one’s political representatives? How long should your client persist in these
activities before resorting to civil disobedience?
(3) In analyzing whether Ward “reasonably believed the commission of the
crime was necessary to avoid or minimize a harm,” the court stated that
“[w]hether Ward’s beliefs were reasonable was a question for the jury.” Is
that standard appropriate for every element of the necessity defense? In other
words, does every element of the necessity defense present a question for the
jury, or are some particularly appropriate for a decision by the court?
(4) In what contexts might the presentation of the necessity defense in future
climate civil disobedience cases advance the interests of other conceptual and
technical elements of Earth law?
V. CONCLUSION
As the foregoing cases indicate, the climate necessity defense is gaining some
traction. Even where the necessity defense is not successful, it is being more
fully considered in courts addressing the issue. The trend is encouraging for
plaintiffs who seek to use civil disobedience to more immediately address

catastrophic climate change. In keeping with the spirit of Earth law, these
efforts compel the legal system to reckon with the scope and scale of
environmental degradation and to take seriously the obligation to care for the
planet—in this instance, through sustained social movement pressure and
legal advocacy that links environmental well-being to political change. It also
provides a tool that might compel some climate activists to take action
against certain climate change drivers while systematic legal solutions, such
as those embodied in long-term Earth law strategies, are put into place.
