SECTION FOUR
TRANSFORMING THE LAW
Each of the following three chapters discusses the transformation of current
legal systems into systems adapted to promoting and implementing emerging
Earth law. In Chapter 14, “Bears Among Us: Earth Law and Animal-Human
Coexistence,” Professor Reed Loder hones in on the inadequacy of current
legal, social and ethical structures for dealing with human relations with wild
animals. She explains how human “superiority over, and separation from, the
nonhuman world [which] is part of our longstanding cultural legacy…merges
with contempt for beings, like bears.” Examining how humans both
understand and empathize with the traumatic experiences of a mother bear’s
forced geographic relocation and separation from her still-weaning cubs, she
discusses how the biocentrism of Earth law can better protect bears that share
our habitats and rangelands. Notably, this concept of wildlife protection does
not depend on a species being listed as “threatened” or “endangered” under
the Endangered Species Act. The fundamental Earth law concept of the
dignity of all beings and species, as depicted in this chapter, challenges the
legally embedded concept of human domination over nature and nonhuman
animals. This development of Earth law will reinforce the growing ecocentric
ethic as a social mechanism that imposes responsibility on humans to treat
ecosystems, species, and individual animals with kindness, dignity, and
respect.
Chapter 15, “United Nations Sustainable Development Initiatives,”
chronologically reviews sustainable development initiatives of the United
Nations. The term sustainable development came into wide usage with the
1987 “Bruntland Report.” It is intended to balance protecting the
environment and improving quality of life for humans. The United Nations
promoted sustainable development in three Earth summits held since 1992. In
2015 the UN General Assembly adopted its 2015–2030 development agenda
consisting of 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The sustainable
development approach is primarily anthropocentric in orientation. Even

though it has gained widespread support from governments, businesses, and
civil society, large-scale ecological degradation like biodiversity loss and
climate change has accelerated. In response to the demands of many countries
and civil society groups to instill ecocentric principles, including rights of
nature, into the implementation of the SDGs, the United Nations launched the
“Harmony with Nature” initiative. This promotes an ecocentric approach
through resolutions of the UN General Assembly and Harmony with Nature
conferences and educational programs. Shifting the sustainable development
approach to an ecocentric orientation is proving to be a difficult process.
Global ecocentric governance will require more than high-level discussions at
the United Nations. It will also require a commitment of the individual and
collective will of the people, which is discussed in Chapter 16.
Chapter 16 examines ecological governance with a focus on social contract
theory. The theories of Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques
Rousseau lay the groundwork of the current “consumptive social contract.”
This contract is fraying as inequality increases and globalization falters, but
the real challenges to it are natural limits. The chapter considers the work of
Bruno Latour and Bruce Jennings who present ideas for a new ecological
social contract, which includes nature and abides by nature’s limits. This is
not a one-time agreement for people to be governed by a common sovereign
under the rule of law. It is societal agreement to be engaged in an ongoing
process of seeking the common good not only for humans but also for the
entire Earth community—present and future. The potential for institutional
reform is discussed, as is the crucial role of lawyers in bringing into being
this new social contract.
This second part of Chapter 16 involves a case study of Bolivia’s rich
structure of rights of nature laws. Drawn from the heritage of its Indigenous
people, these laws offer a sharp contrast to the U.S. legal system, which has
been committed from its inception to privatizing and protecting property
rights. The Bolivian experience illustrates the complex relations among law,
economics, politics, culture, and the challenges involved in bringing into
being an ecological social contract. In the conclusion to the chapter, there is a
brief study of nature’s rapid derailment of the human economy through a
coronavirus, COVID-19, which exploded during the final stages of writing
this book. While it is too early to draw any conclusions as to the long-term

significance, the COVID-19 pandemic has provided a timely opportunity to
consider the efficacy of the current social contract.
As you read these chapters, think of the significance of a governance system
that extends protection to nonhuman species and ecosystems, in which the
economy is a subsystem of nature and economic growth is limited to
planetary boundaries. How would it impact your lives directly? How would
your current law studies need to adapt to a legal system supporting ecological
governance? Consider, in particular, your courses on constitutional law,
property law, and criminal law. How would key doctrines and principles need
to change, or disappear, to accommodate the new system? In what ways
would practicing law under this new system differ from the current practice
of law?

CHAPTER 14
Bears Among Us: Earth Law and 
Animal-Human Co-existence1
Editors’ Note: This chapter tells the story of a black bear in New Hampshire
who lives in the wild but is losing her habitat because of the expansion of
human settlement into her territory. Consequently, she has been subjected to
displacement and relocation to separate her from humans. The chapter opens
by discussing why the general state of human relations with wild animals is
inadequate from an Earth law perspective. Superiority over and separation
from the nonhuman world is part of our longstanding cultural legacy; Earth
law challenges this framework.
In contrast to the approach of conservationists, whose primary concern is to
protect species and prevent extinctions, this chapter concerns the suffering of
an individual bear. It examines why humans respond differently to the
suffering of an individual animal than to the threat of extinction to a species.
It notes the tension between animal rights advocates and conservation
biologists whose field is biased toward wholes like populations, species, and
ecosystems, and asks, “Does the fate of one bear matter in an Earth law
regime?” This chapter concerns reframing attitudes toward wild beings and
co-existence with them. Earth law involves ethical recognition of the rights of
animals to kindness and dignity and laws that support these rights.
As you read about the bear, note the discussion of a paradigm shift from the
anthropocentric perspective that has fostered human exploitation of animals
to a biocentric approach based on ethics and moral consideration. How would

such an approach influence the current treatment of wildlife, for example, as
food, for entertainment, and as a trade commodity? Would it awaken a
meaningful reconsideration of human’s perceived superiority over the rest of
the animal kingdom? Compare the call for an ethic of compassion and
morality in our relationship with wild animals to the current model of wildlife
law and policy based on sustainability and conservation. Are these two
approaches contradictory? Complementary? From the perspective of this
chapter the approaches are generally complementary, although not always
recognized as such.
Despite its focus on preserving species, current wildlife policy has failed to
effectively reduce the accelerating rate of extinctions. The objectificaion of
nonhuman animals is deeply ingrained in law and society. This chapter
considers how a more compassionate approach to wildlife could help to
change the culturally reinforced insensitivity of humans to nonhuman
animals.
I. A PARTICULAR BEAR: WHY AN EARTH
LAW CASE STUDY?
This chapter tells a story of a mother bear and her multiple generations of
cubs. It is neither a fairy tale nor a story of purely local significance. This is a
probe into remaking wild animal and human relations from an Earth law
perspective. The focus is not on laws but on reframing attitudes toward wild
beings and co-existence with them. These are primarily ethical issues. Laws
reflect assumptions about what things have value, which, in turn, affects the
treatment of others under the laws. Thus, the core of laws is ethics. Laws
provide minimum standards of conduct required by society under those
values.
Earth law emphasizes that among all members of the Earth community are
interconnected (see Chapter 3, “Conceptual Frameworks of Earth Law”) and
all voices in the Earth community must be heard in law and policy decisions.
For centuries, humans have dominated and exploited animals and viewed
themselves as superior. They have eliminated wild beings at will and
developed attitudes of fear and disdain toward them. As a result, we are

facing the sixth great extinction in Earth’s history and an unprecedented loss
of biodiversity.2
This chapter discusses why the general state of human relations with wild
animals is inadequate from an Earth law perspective. Next, it summarizes the
story of “Mink,” an American Black Bear. Based on this summary, the
chapter delves into the importance of considering conflicts between bears and
humans from the bear’s perspective, instead of taking an exclusively
monolithic human viewpoint. To understand the animal standpoint, the
chapter provides information about the life cycle of bears from biology and
about animal experiences from cognitive ethology, which is the study of the
mental lives of animals. It is ethically necessary to take that information into
account in policy and law to avoid inflicting harm on animals and their
species. Other arguments for improving animal and human relations include
those contributions animals make to the ecosystems of which they are part
and the values animals lend to the places we are responsible for tending—
both of which are Earth law concerns.
Several terminological points precede this exploration. First, nonhuman
animals are referred to as “animals” as a shorthand device, which in no way
fails to recognize humans as members of the kingdom Animalia. Second, the
terms “morality” and “ethics” are used interchangeably in this chapter,
although some people may affix different meanings to the terms. Finally, this
chapter capitalizes the names of certain animal species and gives personal
pronouns to animals to reflect their status in Earth law as subjects, not
objects.
II. HUMANS AND WILD BEARS GENERALLY
When wild animals and humans mix, humans almost invariably have the
upper hand. Humans have eradicated or severely degraded wild animal
habitats through voracious development and have often eliminated animals
when they venture too close. Human motivations are ambivalent when it
comes to carnivores, especially large ones like bears (while technically
omnivores, bears are classified as carnivores). As Earth law emphasizes,
superiority over and separation from the nonhuman world is part of our
longstanding cultural legacy,3 and it merges with contempt for beings, such

as bears, who are powerful enough to injure or kill us or damage our
property.4
At the same time, humans are fascinated with these creatures at an observable
distance. So, no matter how many times they are cautioned not to do so, they
are willing to risk encounters by leaving food, garbage, and bird feeders
accessible past the time bears emerge from hibernation.5 The bears and other
animals that are attracted to these easy sources of high calorie food often
become labeled as “nuisances” and are then subject to extermination. Think
about this for a moment—extermination for being a nuisance. We are not
discussing animals with diseases or those who have attacked people or other
animals—although there are bears with such histories. We cannot imagine
treating pesky humans in this draconian manner, yet it is a ready solution for
some wild creatures among us. This attitude reveals that we devalue these
animals and make them subject to our whims.
This balance of power would change under an Earth law approach. Laws
would better protect bears sharing our habitat, even if they were not listed as
“threatened” or “endangered” under the Endangered Species Act.6 Also, the
term human habitat would be expanded to take account of the nonhuman
inhabitants and systems within a community.
III. THE STORY OF ONE BEAR AND HER
PROGENY
My first bear encounter was in the late New Hampshire winter of 2016. I
heard thumping outside and opened the curtain to reveal a large black bear
tearing a bird feeder from the porch eaves. Standing not four feet from the
bear, I tapped the window to discourage the animal. The bear whirled around
on its hind legs and placed a paw on the glass. Thrilled and frozen, I was
close enough to see long curved claws on the windowpane and white hairs
mixed with black on the bear’s cheeks. The bear grabbed the feeder and ran
off on all fours. So, I thought, ended my once-in-a-lifetime, close-up bear
experience.
During the following late winter, a commotion on the porch revealed a sea of

black fur with a mass of intertwined bodies. Thus began the story of the sow
and her three yearlings that would captivate my region. That bear crew
frequented the Upper Valley of New Hampshire, including the towns of
Hanover and Lebanon. Although neighbors in Lebanon, where I live, posted
daily website backyard sightings of the sow and yearlings, the animals
became “The Hanover Bears” in news reports.7 Hanover residents began
reporting bears raiding dumpsters and garbage, sitting in private yards, and
even trying locks on doors. Town Manager Julia Griffin launched a campaign
to convince people to secure their homes, use “bear-proof” garbage
receptacles, take down bird feeders, and remove all traces of food.8
According to Griffin, the problem in this college town was off-campus
students, who were transient and impossible to educate about bears despite
their attendance at Dartmouth. Griffin and local officials declined to pass an
ordinance requiring simple bear deterrence measures as being too time-
consuming and expensive for the town.9
The idea of Hanover “owning” the bears evolved into a notion of exclusive
responsibility for their fate. The straw broke when two yearlings entered the
open kitchen of a house near Mink Brook, their main habitat. They were
foiled in their search for food and fled upon hearing noise in the house.10
This was the final straw for Griffin, and the newspapers announced with no
preparation—the bears would be “euthanized” to protect the public.11
According to the Director of the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department,
Andrew Timmins: “When their behavior reaches a certain point, it is tough to
be wild bears again.”12 “A fed bear is a dead bear” is an old slogan warning
that human curiosity and carelessness spawn “nuisance” bear status and
ultimately animal execution.13
A New Hampshire resident, pleading for relocation of the bears, started a
petition on an online website. Almost 10,000 people from all over America
signed the petition. Suddenly headlines changed and the issue went national:
“Online Petition Helps Save Family of New Hampshire Bears,” proclaimed
CBS-Boston.14
Democratic governors ran New Hampshire for 18 of 20 years until Chris
Sununu’s term began in 2017. Governor Sununu won only about 26 percent
of the Hanover vote.15 Regardless of animal protection, this was a propitious

political opportunity for Sununu. “Don’t worry, we aren’t going to kill the
bears,” the governor soothed the public in a surprise announcement, blithely
overriding the decision of Town Manager Julia Griffin and Andrew Timmins
of the Fish and Game Department, without advance notice to either party.16
Sununu ordered that the bears be trapped and released in the northern portion
of the state.17 A Quebec hunter legally shot one of the yearlings just 18 days
after the three were relocated without the sow, who managed to evade
capture.18
Many marveled when the sow emerged from her den in late winter of 2018
with four new adorable cubs. In response to a blog question, “Where did this
notion that bears are cuddly come from, since they’re savage, strong, and
brutal animals?” Shelley Stein answered, “First of all, they have the cutest
babies in the world. Look at them. Look at how fuzzy and warm they look.
They have round little bodies, short little limbs, and sweet little faces.
Seriously, anyone who doesn’t think baby bears are adorable is an asshole.”19
Bears have some features that lend themselves to neoteny, with adult features
resembling the young. These include high foreheads, round cheeks, and
stubby and short legs. People find these human, baby-like traits endearing
and often favor animals with such appearance.20
Cubs in this new litter of “Hanover cubs” each weighed about five to seven
pounds and they were three months old when they emerged. Bear specialists
fixed the sow with a large red-orange tracking collar. Their plan was to
relocate mom and young to another site in New Hampshire when the snow
dissipated and food became more available.21
As early spring turned to summer officials seemed to relent on relocation.
Andrew Timmins voiced concerns that dominant bears at the new site would
thwart the relocated bears’ access to quality foods and that the sow would
likely try to return home, which would by then already be occupied by other
bears already known to be present in the area.22 Deputy Fire Chief of the
Hanover Fire Department Michael Hinsley stated that the bear was not a
threat to residents. Tolerance did not extend to places considered resident
turf, however. “She crossed the line,” Hinsley said when the bear appeared on
the Hanover High School Football Field.23

Despite apprehensions in Hanover about “Mink,” now so named for the
sow’s home in Mink Brook Reserve, the decision to relocate a bear family
that had not recently raided human food was questionable. Bears are natural
opportunists, however. Someone soon photographed Mink in an open
dumpster with two cubs foraging for food.24 Although Timmins
acknowledged that only 1 percent of people in town had failed to secure food
sources, he set an impossibly high standard of compliance that would require:
“100 percent of Hanover to clean up (its) acts.”25 Julia Griffin, who had
favored euthanasia, concluded that they were “fighting a losing battle.”26
Mink had run out her chances, it seemed, when she had eluded relocation the
year before. The plan was ready for the sow to be relocated near the Canadian
border, notwithstanding the known risk that she might attempt to return.
Fortunately, the cubs would go to regional bear expert Ben Kilham to be
“rehabilitated” from their wayward habits and eventually be released into the
wild. Acknowledging that the sow would be “frantic” without her cubs,
Timmins warned that Mink’s failure to “integrate into the wild,” and her
return to Hanover would eventually result in her being euthanized.27 He
lamented not euthanizing her the year before.28 Once relocated, Mink,
seeking her cubs and home, traveled rapidly, but she was off course. Timmins
admitted, “There are several other bears working the edges of Hanover,”29 so
he could not say how killing or relocating Mink would have ended human
and bear conflicts in Hanover.
Winter passed uneventfully. In April of 2019, the local newspaper reported
that Mink had hibernated “across the river” in Vermont.30 Several weeks later
Mink swam the Connecticut River to New Hampshire.31 Her perseverance
and strength demonstrated her attachment to place as nothing else could.
People sighted and photographed her with the distinctive red radio collar,
looking sleek and robust.
Is it really just conjecture that people would think of Mink as having a story
with elements of pain, sorrow, and injustice? Why would they assume Mink
underwent an ordeal and experienced trauma over the sudden loss of her cubs
and home place of 15 years? Why is it even important to imagine Mink’s
perspective? If important, how is it possible for humans to grasp anything
accurate about a bear’s point of view? That we can think of Mink as a subject

in this manner is important ethically to the way we imagine the lives of other
animals we do not encounter. They are members of the wider community of
subjects that Earth law encompasses.
IV. THE IMPORTANCE OF THE ANIMAL’S
PERSPECTIVE
As Earth law emphasizes, humans, believing themselves to have unique
capacities, have long separated themselves from animals.32 Species
differentiations are based on actual distinctions, but these have been used by
humans to bolster feelings of superiority, enabling them to use animals for
human benefit without considering their suffering.33 Cognitive ethology, or
the comparative and evolutionary study of animal minds, and evolutionary
biology have shown that many animals have complex cognitive abilities,
including tool use, culture, reasoning, and flexible problem-solving;
recognition of other individuals; and sophisticated forms of communication
that only humans were once thought to possess.34 Yet, people still fail to
recognize unique species attributes, such as the speed of the cheetah or
eyesight of the eagle that human beings lack, and continue to measure animal
capacities in human terms. An animal will never measure up to a human-
centered assessment of nonhuman capacities because different species have
evolved to cope with varied developmental and environmental conditions.35
In taking the animal’s perspective, this section looks first to biology to
understand how bears exist within suitable habitats, and then it considers
what the science of ethology teaches about the mental lives of animals.
A. American Black Bear Biology and Life Cycle
One important way to understand an animal’s perspective is through life
cycle and biological makeup. This shows how the animal lives within
physical and environmental constraints. The specific subjects of this story are
American black bears (Ursus americanus),36 the bears in North America with
the widest range and the only bears inhabiting the eastern United States from
Maine to Florida.37 All bear species face strain, but the black bear is faring
best in North America38 because of its impressive flexibility and

adaptability.39 Thus we are not considering an endangered or threatened
animal, and people hunt black bears in many states.40 Instead of vanishing,
this is one of many animals that persists in North America while losing
habitat to human development and finding it more challenging to carry out
the typical life processes of its kind.41
American black bears are omnivores and food opportunists who seek many
varieties of nourishment from diverse sources depending on availability
within their range.42 A range differs from a territory in that a range does not
have fixed boundaries. Often, black bears have overlapping ranges when a
particular food source, such as berries, is plentiful.43 Thus, unfamiliar bears
feed together without undue aggression, probably because the scarcity of a
particular food makes tolerance worthwhile.44 If humans expose garbage or
other sources of potential food, bears will investigate and tap those sources.45
During the warmer months, black bear activities largely revolve around
foraging. Although bears are omnivorous, about 85 percent of their diet is
vegetation, consisting of roots, berries, herbs, and nuts. The bear’s diet varies
significantly by season, depending on availability of food sources, which
bears move around to find. In fact, seeking food is the principal bear
occupation during at least half of the year.46
For this, black bears have a keen sense of smell that “allows location of
mates, avoidance of humans and other bears, identification of cubs, and the
locations of food sources.” Recent research shows that bears have
“reasonably good” vision, possibly equivalent to that of humans; bears show
good depth perception and peripheral vision, can see well at night, and see
color.47 American black bears have small round ears back on the head and
have good hearing.48
People notoriously overestimate the size of bears they observe,49 perhaps
because of the creature’s girth in relation to its legs, and perhaps simply
because an encounter with a bear is astonishing. The average size of
American black bears varies by region, individual condition, and sex, with
male bears about one-third larger than females.50 The average size of an adult
male is 200 to 300 pounds.51 Like humans, bears walk plantigrade (flat-

footed) with heel and foot on the ground. They are slightly pigeon-toed and
walk with a shuffling gait, which makes them appear clumsy. Their front feet
have five toes with curved non-retractable claws that are used for varied
activities like digging, fighting, lifting, and movement. Black bears are
extremely strong, agile, and swift runners despite their clumsy appearance.
Black bears are remarkable climbers and sows teach their cubs to climb trees
to avoid danger even before the cubs are proficient at walking. Bears are also
strong and enthusiastic swimmers.52
The average lifespan of a wild American black bear is 14 to 20 years.
Typically, a sow has her first litter at age five, and the usual number of cubs
is two. Black bears mate from late May into June and July.53 A mature
female ordinarily has cubs every other year.54 Older, sexually mature males
have the privilege of mating because younger males are unable to compete.55
Once mating is complete, male black bears show no interest in their
offspring.56
The sow, on the other hand, is focused on her young. “There is a deep family
bond. The mother is affectionate, devoted, protective (aggressive toward
threats), sensitive, strict, and attentive to the training of her cubs.”57 Although
mating happens in summer, birth occurs in January or February while the
mother is hibernating in her den. Although the egg is fertilized at copulation,
it is not implanted in the uterine wall until hibernation. Delayed implantation
prevents the sow from having cubs during the pre-hibernation period when
she must feed extensively to build enough fat to sustain her through the
winter. During torpor (not the deepest form of hibernation), the sow will not
eat, drink, or expel waste, and she will lose about one-third of her body
weight. The newborn cubs, weighing only half a pound, will nurse during
hibernation, absorbing warmth from the mother’s body in the den, which is
constructed to retain heat. Sow and cubs emerge in April, and, during the
summer, the sow teaches the young all they need to know about hunting food
and the life of a bear. The cubs usually hibernate with the sow a second
winter and stay with her until she is ready again to mate.58
An interesting trait of black bears is their ability to navigate. Bears who have
relocated very long distances can somehow return to their home place even
without any prior knowledge of the route that would facilitate mapping.59

Mink illustrated this. Did she return out of some kind of instinct or imprint?
Or, was she determined in a more emotional and cognitive way to find her
cubs and home? Experts do not know much about this skill of navigation.
B. Bear Social and Emotional Lives: Ethology
Contemporary ethology suggests that bears have complex cognitive and
emotional lives.60 Although they are often deemed solitary animals, female
bears in particular form loose social groups by admitting select individuals
into their ranges, often their former female young.61 They help other
individuals but also, at other times, retaliate for slights. For example,
Benjamin Kilham, the orphan bear rehabilitator in New Hampshire, has
observed two adult females arranging a lasting adoption of a young bear.
Kilham also reports instances of retaliation against him, once for neglecting
to bring food when visiting a wild bear he had reared as an orphan. He
returned to his truck to find both rearview mirrors missing!62
Bears generally are highly intelligent and secretive. Enos A. Mills, a famous
Rocky Mountain bear tracker in the late nineteenth and early twentieth
century, learned that a grizzly bear he was pursuing was actually silently
tracking him. He also observed bears quietly contemplating a sunset or
rainbow and witnessed their sense of humor and play many times in the form
of antics such as sliding down snowy hills and deliberately ascending to
repeat the slide. After years of close proximity to grizzlies, Mills concluded
that they were the most intelligent nonhuman mammals.63
Some would call such attributions anthropomorphizing or imposing human
traits on nonhuman beings. This used to be a cardinal sin in ethology, as Jane
Goodall discovered as a student when she named the chimps she studied and
described their behavior as purposive.64 Ethology today does not shun
descriptions of animal behavior in human terms,65 provided the observer
recognizes that similar manifestations of mental life are most likely
experienced differently from nonhuman to human. Brain imaging has
demonstrated activity in similar regions of the brain when animals display
behavior resembling a human, and brain chemistry reveals similar
neurochemicals in the brains of nonhumans when they appear to be
experiencing pain, joy, fear, anger, and other emotional states.66 Laboratory

experiments show that many animals are aware of the future in returning to
caches of food,67 recognizing individuals of their species over time,68 and
deceiving other individuals about the location of desirable objects.69
Some people persist in attributing such behavior to instinct or imprinting, but
the learned quality of much of the conduct belies this explanation. Indeed,
diversity in the ways members of the same species in different locations
perform certain tasks, such as chimpanzees using different tools to gather
ants for food,70 suggests that groups develop cultural variations in their life
activities that are transmitted through their distinct social groups. According
to primate expert Franz De Waal, it is understandable and “parsimonious” to
describe carefully observed animal behavior in emotive or cognitive terms
because contemporary ethology shows continuity between humans and
animals.
The behavior itself is most telling. When we observe an animal grimacing or
whimpering in response to an event that would cause pain in a human, we
infer from similar human responses that the animal is experiencing pain.
Although some scientists still insist that the pain response and the conscious
experience of pain (or fear, joy, jealousy, etc.) are different and we are not
entitled to assume that the scientific evidence of pain responses means that
the animal has the conscious experience, the prevailing scientific view is that
it is more accurate to conclude, based on multiple forms of evidence, that the
animal has the experience as well as the bodily response.71
Of course, no one can demonstrate with certainty that an animal is
experiencing any particular thought or emotion, just as no one is certain what
another human is thinking or feeling.72 With many humans, however, we
have the benefit of language to communicate mental states. If you tell me you
are happy and you are smiling and showing enthusiasm, I have compelling
reasons to believe that you are experiencing happiness. Further, I can
compare how I act when I feel happy and conclude that what you call
“happiness” is very similar to the state I label “happy” in myself. This is not
true with all humans (e.g., infants or those who have lost the ability to
communicate in words). Yet, we do not conclude that an infant or wordless
person who is smiling and laughing is not actually experiencing the mirth that
behavior suggests. Even highly verbal humans communicate much

information through facial expressions, body language, and non-language
vocalizations. Many animals have sophisticated modes of complex
communication that do not replicate human methods but can be deciphered
upon repeated observation of the animal in various contexts.73
Black bears use an array of movements, such as nuzzling, standing on hind
legs, charging, sitting, rubbing, stretching, stiff-walking, and varied
vocalizations from snorting, grunting, huffing, woofing, jaw clicking, and
more.74 These actions have varied meanings when used in combination, and
the context is crucially important in interpreting the meaning.75 For example,
a sow handling cubs might use some movements and noises that in other
situations would indicate aggression but in this context is discipline for
training purposes.76 Analogously, canids at play use some of the movements
they employed in fighting, but they signal to the play partner through
ritualized “bowing” and other cues that their intent is not to inflict harm but
to have fun.77 Play signals are also important to bears.
To appreciate the complexity and variety of animal minds, it is necessary to
see the world as much as possible from the animal’s perspective. It is also
important to consider the evolutionary origins of particular behaviors—to ask
why some patterns of activity have added value to the species’ survival.78
These steps will not produce certain knowledge immune to revision. Over
time, however, careful study can teach us much about animal lives that is too
easy to disregard from a human-centered perspective.
C. Ethical Implications of Animals’ Perspectives
Immersion into animals’ perspectives is ethically vital to the treatment they
receive from humans. Within Earth law, perspectival information is important
to recognizing the diverse rights of all members of the Earth community
because rights are closely linked to conditions that enable flourishing.
Attention to an individual animal reveals that each one is unique and, even
within a species, there are great variations. This orientation means that each
animal matters, and fair treatment is an ethical responsibility for humans
because of the power we wield over the creature world and our capacity for
conscious self-reflection.

Empathy is an important cognitive and moral skill for understanding
nonhumans better. Through empathy a person is able to understand the point
of view of others including their emotions. Empathy for another’s perspective
does not entail sympathetically sharing that perspective, however. A
psychopath can use skills of empathy to torture animals or human victims
because they understand the subjects’ exact vulnerabilities. If the person who
understands another’s stressful emotions also shares those feelings and is
motivated out of concern to assist the one in distress, that person has both
sympathy and empathy.79
Empathy as a tool of moral understanding does not necessarily yield accurate
knowledge of the other. This is because the person placing herself in the
other’s position is herself differently situated. Being differently situated
biases one’s perception of another.80 The risk is always present of projecting
one’s own beliefs, feelings, and judgments onto the other, thereby distorting
the other’s perspective.81 This is sometimes called “false empathy.”82
Lawyers are susceptible to this tendency. They are required to act in their
client’s best interests and give primacy to the client’s values and goals. For
example, in a case concerning the right to refuse drug treatment, a client who
has bipolar disorder might reject the medication that has controlled manic
states because of side effects from the drug, such as a flattened mood. The
patient’s doctors insist that the patient has done well on medication and
should continue the regimen, and they will recommend this in a legal hearing
on the right to refuse treatment. The lawyer, who is supposed to promote the
client’s autonomy and follow the client’s considered judgment,83 might be
hesitant to follow the client’s expressed wishes because of apprehension that
the client might act rashly or even become suicidal without medication. The
lawyer might decide that the client is behaving irrationally against their best
interest, and thus apply personal norms to someone whose experience the
lawyer cannot fully comprehend.
This problem is compounded with an animal because humans lack full
understanding of the animal’s complex communications and the problems the
animal encounters in daily living. This is why understanding the biology and
life cycle of an animal is relevant to ethics and policy. This is also why it is
important to research animal behavior and mental capacities, both through
intensive observations of animals in their natural settings and through

neurological comparisons to other animals. On the other hand, most people
are confident in attributing emotions and mental states to their companion
animals, which suggests that barriers to animal-human communication may
not as great as some scientists claim.84
Reading Mink’s emotional experience in being relocated and separated from
her young is not very susceptible to error because bear experts know a great
deal about a sow’s relationships to her cubs. Besides being fiercely
protective, sows display great affection and care toward cubs by teaching
them about food sources, disciplining them for their protection, and playing,
hibernating, and remaining with them for a lengthy period.85 A sow nursing,
like Mink, would be wholly devoted to her five-month-old cubs at the time of
her relocation. This is not an emotionally ambiguous context of
interpretation. Recall that bear expert Andrew Timmins predicted that Mink
would be “frantic” without her cubs.86
Attending to the animal’s perspective also helps researchers avoid over-
generalizations. Openness to the inevitable need to revise information is
crucial because animals often behave in surprising ways that require further
investigation.87 Individual animal differences can reveal a range of capacities
within a species.88 Careful observation of different populations can also
demonstrate cultural diversity, such as the way that a particular group of
animals learns to gather food.89
D. Cultural Influences on Understanding Animals’ Perspectives
Openness and humility are moral virtues for anyone trying to understand
fellow creatures and how to behave toward them. For the sake of repairing
our planetary condition and survival, Earth law emphasizes that humans must
undo entrenched tendencies to dominate nonhuman nature. Since pre-history,
evidence shows that people have made normative judgments about animals in
their worlds. For example, people often judge large predators negatively.90
On the other hand, some humans have associated bears with virility and
power and admired those traits. In ancient Germanic culture, bears were
regarded as strong and nearly invincible animals, and male warriors proved
their prowess through hand-to-hand combat with male bears. Further, some

experts think ancient European caves contain evidence of a religion of the
bear, or at least of the bear as “a creature apart” with unique powers.91
As Christianity rose to the foreground of European culture, people sought
ways to denigrate bears. Historian, Michel Pastoureau, who studied the bear’s
shifting cultural position in European history, found that the lion displaced
the bear as the king of strength in the High Middle Ages. Christianity
persistently eviscerated pagan ideas, especially those about a continuum
between animals and humans. Legends across cultures depict sexual
attraction between male bears and women and describe sexual relations
resulting in hybrid human-bear offspring. The bear-male son often returns to
the human domain and becomes known as a warrior and hero.92
Europeans massacred bears, eradicated their forest habitats, and drove the
animals to the distant mountains. Later, some captured bears and brought
them to cities, where they forced bears to perform unnatural antics, like
walking upright, doing “handstands,” and performing skits, which made them
appear foolish and stupid. Indeed, there is a long tradition of stories and
fables about inept bears. Bears also became entertainers at circuses and
carnivals and spectacles in zoos. Bears became pathetic objects of mockery,
docility, and servility. These intelligent animals were so out of place in these
roles.93
European settlers in America killed black bears with abandon, sometimes for
food and fat, but often because they could not accept the right of these
powerful creatures to occupy the same places as humans. Sometimes killing
was simply for the challenge.94 Although bears are omnivorous and prefer
vegetation, roots, and insects to meat, the practice of some bears of
consuming the flesh of the dead of their own species provokes human
repugnance: “[T]he bear shows, a gruesome and cannibal fondness for the
flesh of his own kind,” said President Theodore Roosevelt. It is important to
interpret such behavior of bears non-judgmentally and as the way animals
make their way in the world because of species-related traits. Black bears
consume any available food, including carrion, upon emerging from
hibernation while spring vegetation is scarce.95
Although instances of black bears attacking and killing humans are “virtually

nonexistent,”96 every incident captures media attention.97 Although a bear
avoids physical altercations, when cornered or surprised, it may attack.98
Unfortunately, some people generalize from the very rare instances of bears
harming people to draw the conclusion that bears do not belong in a shared
environment.
There is also danger in flipping attitudes toward animals. Some now view
once-maligned wolves as environmental heroes or symbols. Lovers and
haters exist side by side—sometimes even in the same conflicted people.
Bears, too, have lovers and haters. Voyeurism has led to the demise of bears
attracted and then habituated to human food and residences.
Empathy for animals should not lead to freighting them with human
characteristics that endear or repel them to people. Appreciating bears is
largely about seeing them as different biological beings with lives and agency
of their own. Operating against bear conservation is the glib human tendency
to endow wild animals with human-like traits that moralize attitudes toward
them. Repairing our relations with the Earth is aided by an awareness of
cultural history as it makes us less likely to fall prey to entrenched prejudices.
V. ETHICAL DECISION-MAKING ABOUT CO-
EXISTENCE WITH BEARS
It is time for ideas to coalesce on improving human and nonhuman co-
existence ethically and legally. These ideas should be useful to address future
situations similar to the Mink case study, which can be anticipated now that
humans have encroached so pervasively on animal habitats. The ideas also
have comparative relevance for different cases of exploring the relationship
between humans and nonhumans.
A. Relevant Ethical-Legal Factors in Mink’s Case: Illustrative
Questions
In assessing Mink’s situation within an Earth law framework, the questions
that follow are relevant. Does the fate of one bear matter in an Earth law
regime, or should the focus be on species, populations, and ecosystems?

What are the relative interests at stake for those affected here, primarily those
of the human residents, an adult female bear, and her young? Are there
alternatives to extreme measures like euthanasia or relocation that
compromise fewer values for bears? How should information from ethology
and biology affect decision-making about bears? How will decisions affect
the dignity of animals? What are possible concerns of justice involving
historical and current treatment of the animal? How will decisions alter the
holistic and wild characteristics of affected places? Do humans owe any
affirmative duties to the animals besides preventing future harms? The
discussion that follows considers only some of these questions.
B. Individuals or Wholes: A Contextual Approach
Approaches that emphasize population, species, and ecosystem levels will
have little perceived significance in the daily lives of people who encounter
individual bears who are raiding their bird feeders and garbage. It is
important to note Earth law’s tendency to take the holistic approach99
because this raises concerns regarding the interests of individual beings to
animals as only being important when they affect larger processes and
systems. These are not unlike concerns that animal rights advocates have
about conservation biologists whose field is biased toward wholes like
populations, species, and ecosystems.100 Even though Earth law has tended to
focus on rights of nature for systems such as rivers, in some contexts, the
rights of individuals are paramount because fundamental interests in being,
having habitat, and fulfilling their roles in the Earth community—three
primary rights Thomas Berry attributed to all members of the larger universe
community—are at stake.101 In bestowing rights on individuals to exist and
flourish, however, it is always important to consider holistic limits such as
ecological burdens of animal over-population on system-carrying capacities.
As Earth law develops, it will allow for contextual shifts in attention between
individuals and wholes without a fixed priority on a holistic perspective.
Shifting contextual attention is partly what makes an Earth law approach so
challenging to define, but it is inherent in recognizing the rights of all
components of the Earth community.
Given that the Mink case study involves co-existence between people and
particular bears occupying overlapping habitats, the primary focus should be

on the rights of the animals in relationship with people, with preservation of
the ecosystem and wild processes always in the background as limiting and
enhancing factors. In this case, as in many others, protecting individual
animals simultaneously improves the ecology of the landscape.
C. Relative Interests, Harms, and Benefits
1. Trivial human interests in convenience and aesthetics
For humans, limitations on their interests are relatively trivial in preventing
harm to Mink and her progeny. It is a matter of small inconvenience to secure
doors, birdseed, and garbage. Aesthetic interests in observing birds and bears
in the backyard are important but not vital. Happily, avoiding serious
physical threats to humans from these large animals is consistent with
measures to protect them.
2. Vital bear interests in life, reproduction, and mental well-being
From the bear’s perspective, the interests in the case study are vital—literally
life and death. The slogan, “A fed bear is a dead bear,” reflects this. Humans
are largely responsible for creating “nuisance” bears, a condition with
unethical origins not acknowledged. Bears forage large areas in search of
food, especially during pre-hibernation when they must increase their weight
to sustain themselves and possibly newborn cubs during winter,102 and they
forage even larger stretches in times of drought or berry and nut shortages.103
Bears will avail themselves of accessible food close to humans if convenient,
and proximity to humans is frequently a death sentence. Thus humans can be
ethically responsible for bear mortality out of wanton carelessness or even
amusement in watching bears.
Sows and their young also have vital interests in the reproductive cycle.
Pregnant bears euthanized as “problems” do not reproduce. Yearling bears
are most at risk as they leave their mother’s protection and seek new ranges.
Nursing cubs depend completely on their mother for food and to learn
foraging and other survival skills. When we deem a nursing sow a “nuisance”
and sentence her to death or relocation, we are also dooming her dependent

cubs. Fortunately, wildlife officials knew of Mink’s cubs, and an orphan-bear
rehabilitator accepted the laborious care of the cubs.
The separation of Mink from her cubs was emotionally traumatic, which
wildlife expert Timmins acknowledged,104 and this mental harm is another
strong animal interest and ethical factor. Wildlife observers have noted the
fast bond and affectionate behavior between a sow and her cubs.105 It is
ethically appropriate to respect bears’ complex emotional and cognitive
capacities, given current knowledge from ethology. From an Earth ethics
perspective, such respect is not based only on similarities to humans (e.g., in
the recognizable mother-young bond). Wild animals have unique
characteristics and functioning and deserve respect in their own right.106 For
example, bears should not be judged for sending off yearlings, sometimes
forcefully, even though yearlings face grave risks. This animal reproduces
few of its own kind, usually just every other year, and the sow’s undivided
attention to her cubs is how some bears survive and continue the cycle of
species life.
D. Assessing Alternatives: Less Harmful Effective Options
In encounter cases, human fears and prejudices take over, and people expect
public officials to take decisive action, which often means killing or
relocating the “problem” bear. People might demand this despite their
carelessness in leaving food accessible and doors ajar—they demand a lethal
solution to a problem they could have prevented.
Local law is one mechanism to alter the balance of interests and repair the
relationship between wild bears and humans. Towns could pass laws that
impose reasonable fines on people who deliberately feed bears, leave bird
feeders outside after the first of March, fail to secure trash receptacles, and
make homes or garages accessible. Such a “bear ordinance” would remind
people to develop new, relatively simple, habits. An ordinance could also
require commercial trash companies to provide bear-proof receptacles either
by new stock or retrofitting existing containers. Education should accompany
lawmaking. Residents should be instructed in preventing human-bear
confrontations that could result in physical injuries to human or animal.
Hanover officials took measures that directly harmed vital animal interests

when there was a legal option available that would have protected those
interests with minimal inconvenience to humans.
Local government is responsible for fostering the collective well-being of
human and wild animal co-existence. Simple and lightly burdensome legal
requirements could save many bears and a few humans from destructive
confrontations.107 When Mink’s yearlings entered an open kitchen, the
Hanover town administrator precipitously ordered the animals euthanized.
Yet, that administrator had contributed to the problem by rejecting an
ordinance.108 Ordering euthanasia without first using the legal authority of
local government was unjustified. Although residents might be annoyed if
fined, over time most would adjust and likely see benefits in their new
behaviors. If local governments are unwilling to adopt such ordinances,
legislation at the state level could accomplish the same result.
Deliberative democracy will be important to the development of Earth law
because the ideas are bold, comprehensive, and need discussion to take hold.
The process leading to the Hanover euthanasia decision was ethically bereft.
Indeed, there was no process—just an announcement. Town officials
apparently had no thoughts about including people in adjacent towns (where
the bears also frequented) or the public’s opinions of the situation.
Encouraging discussion often leads to creative and jointly acceptable ideas,
not only about the issue at hand but also for future planning. Without
facilitating public participation, Hanover officials left few options open for
communication, and the response was an indignant petition demanding
relocation of Mink over euthanasia. This tied the officials’ hands for future
decisions about wild animals because the public will not soon forget Mink,
who unwittingly became a star. The method used to make an animal vanish
placed her in the limelight and exposed a flawed democratic process.
The media also has an ethical obligation to provide accurate information
about newsworthy animals by dispelling, not reinforcing, harmful stereotypes
and irrational fears. Media should avoid politicizing animals and treating
them as the property of the places they happen to visit, such as by calling
Mink and her cubs “The Hanover Bears.”
The individual humans living in the area also fell short of fulfilling their

duties. Deliberative democracy requires that people be committed to
improving the community. Humans are adept in changing habits. They alter
diet and exercise to promote health, take courses to improve employment
prospects, seek psychic self-improvement to feel better, and consult
relationship professionals to become better partners. Why should habits
toward wild animals be exempt from self-improvement regimes with so much
at stake for the animals? When people realize the stakes, they respond, albeit
often weakly. The thousands of people who signed the “Save Mink” petition
probably encouraged the governor’s intervention. The idea of killing innocent
bears provoked ripple effects of moral outrage—a righteous kind of anger
geared toward positive social change. Yet, the death order would never have
been issued if people had collectively done the small, easy things that would
have prevented a bear from becoming a “nuisance” in the first place. People
should work on remaking their relations with wildlife to prevent foreseeable
crises.
Humans owe bears the least harmful negative responses if it becomes
necessary to interfere with their lives. This rules out relocation and execution
in almost all cases. Ben Kilham describes deterrence methods, such as
electric fencing, loud noises, and trapping that are somewhat useful109 and
should at least be tried before more extreme measures. People also need to
educate themselves about realistic threats from bears as they use the outdoors
and take protective measures to avoid or deter bears while hiking, such as
carrying noisemakers or sprays to ward off bears, and not traveling alone on
bear trails.
E. Bear Dignity: The Right to Be
This case study shows that sometimes the focus of concern should be on
individual beings like Mink. The idea of animal dignity stretches our moral
imagination toward understanding nonhuman perspectives and builds respect
for nature that is unlike us. The concept of dignity also matters because
wrongs to nonhuman nature are often not reducible to utilitarian harms,
although they do include these.
Animals like bears have much to teach us. Exposing Mink’s life reveals a
being with a complex emotional and physical life that is partly species related

and partly a matter of Mink’s own determination—her personality. Animal
dignity is a complex idea that is highly contextual and multi-faceted.
Explanations of dignity are elusive even in the human context; animal dignity
resembles but does not duplicate human dignity. Suffice it to say here that
dignity relates to the capacity to exercise autonomy and agency, the
importance of presenting oneself in a certain manner to the outside world, the
opportunity to fulfill the traits that make one the kind of being one is, and the
distinctive ability to express one’s individual identity.
What do we know about the agency of black bears? We can marvel at their
resourcefulness, their extraordinary care of their young, and their ability to
adapt to ever-changing circumstances. They are definitely curious about us as
fellow beings, but they demonstrate that they prefer tending to their own kind
and survival when possible and unraveling the considerable challenges of
their forested environment: “Black Bears are shy, secretive animals who live
in the dense woods.…”110 Bears’ dignity is largely related to their species’
being.
Bears share in the aspect of dignity that makes outward presentation
important. Bears are famous for posturing and displaying formidable powers,
but this show usually leads to retreat, which reinforces the bear’s preference
to avoid humans. This kind of display reveals animals adapted to defensive
presentations rather than inherently aggressive reactions. Tamed bears,
coerced to entertain humans, show discomfort. They often appear dejected
and humiliated—the self-presentation of a being diminished. Some circus
bears reveal this countenance, as when Professor Susan Cataldi observed
Russian circus bears clothed in female domestic garments and walking
upright on their hind feet, pushing baby carriages. Cataldi rightly identified
the lost dignity of these bears as she glimpsed sadness in them and their
situation.111
It is often easier to understand dignity through recognizing such violations
and then identifying what caused the affront. In Mink’s case, so many things
went wrong. She and her yearlings escaped extermination by the political
happenstance of a governor responding to a surprisingly vehement petition.
Later, officials wrenched her from her cubs and deposited her in a strange
land while still nursing. She managed to forage as hibernation drew nigh and

then spent an unusual but not forgetful winter without cubs. Upon emergence,
she found her way back to Mink Brook and survived. The story may have a
happy interlude with Mink hibernating and emerging once more with
newborn cubs.112 Yet, the events inflicted on Mink and her young were
indignities besides being conventional harms. They disrupted her agency,
autonomy, her all-important sow relationships with her young, her avoidant
nature, and her fierce attachment to place, all of which comprised her bear
and Mink identity. Mink has earned freedom after years in the spotlight and
ongoing hardships. She has taught us much about bonds between sow and
young, indomitable persistence in the face of extreme hardship and loss, the
enduring attachment to place that people and animals share, and strength as
an agent exerting powers. For this, we owe Mink deep gratitude, awe, and
respect.
Mink has displayed remarkable dignity that her large red GPS collar belies.
Everyone recognizes Mink by her jewelry; she has not shown interest in
celebrity or in increased interactions with humans. Town and wildlife
officials track her every move, although they generally keep her whereabouts
classified until someone announces a sighting.
Privacy is part of human dignity, and constant surveillance of people in
prison or captivity is a punitive experience. Do bears have a right to privacy?
They are thought to be solitary animals, although current research suggests
more sociability than previously thought.113 Solitary and sociable are terms
that apply relative to other bears, however, and no one disputes that bears
largely prefer concealed lives in the depths to presence among humans.
Perhaps such behavior shows that bears value privacy, although not as a
conscious idea.
We now live with bears like Mink in a shared domain. Mink belongs near the
Mink Brook she chose 15 years ago as her home. She belongs there as much
as humans do. People should tolerate, but discourage, contact with Mink.
They should let Mink resume whatever wildness she can savor without
jeopardizing her safety or unnecessarily subjecting her to the human gaze.
We should know enough now about Mink and bears to understand that this is
part of bear dignity, an idea that is encompassed in Thomas Berry’s rights to
be and to fulfill one’s nature.

F. Ethics and Character of Place
The unfortunate responses to Mink show how far we have humanized our
places. The places bears inhabit will be impoverished if humans continue to
exert their pattern of dominance. People are privileged to live among wild
fauna and flora. Nearly imperceptibly, the abundance of wildness is shrinking
everywhere. We are finally beginning to internalize that we are losing life
and its communities at an alarming rate, including insects, birds, and
meadows where bobolinks and other grassland birds used to fill the air with
effervescent songs.
Some people have turned inward to electronic devices to the point of
addiction and have distanced themselves from the nature that used to be
children’s default play arena.114 What all of this does to the human psyche is
hard to measure, but those who recall a different world know and lament the
difference. Many people’s ethic toward the environment is expressed in
descriptions of early-life experiences of the wild that inspired their respect
and desire to protect what remains. That “wild” can range from a city park, to
a populated campsite or beach, to a remote mountain or forest. The common
experience is of something greater than the human that shapes one’s values
and commitments and becomes part of one’s personal identity. Is it ever too
late for anyone to experience the wonder and mysteries of nature? Prison
gardening, farming, and animal-raising programs show that people deprived
of such experiences value them greatly. The capacity for wonder probably
evolved with our humanness, as beings inherently connected with and
dependent upon the natural environment. Something will be lost in the soul of
our landscapes if we squeeze out the beings that retain otherness and
wildness.
Black bears lack significant economic importance except in hunting revenues,
limited fur trapping, and illegal trade in body parts or products such as bile,
so most people do not think of the animals as having significant utility. Thus,
it is hard to persuade people to preserve bears for their instrumental or use
value in the way many people measure the value of nature as a resource.
American black bears are faring best among all bear species,115 so it is easy
to place low priority on their protection relative to many animals on the
brink. The role of large carnivores in ecological systems is thus important in

promoting bear conservation. Ecological consequences follow from
eradicating large animals like bears. Large carnivores are sometimes
protected, or introduced into an area, because maintaining or restoring the
complex and large habitat these beings require also supports the life of other
animals and plants.116 Conservation biologists sometimes consider large
predators as a “tool” for preserving the biodiversity of natural systems. They
are often the first species humans eradicate from a region, and their absence
can indicate other risks to biodiversity.117 This ecosystem approach is
consistent with Earth jurisprudence.
At an accelerating rate, humans have encroached on wildlands with
increasing populations and development, greatly curtailing the spaces left for
wild beings to flourish. Some animals like bears have also entered the
“human” domain to survive and have disproportionately suffered the
consequences of human and nonhuman interactions. In their book, Zoopolis:
A Political Theory of Animal Rights, Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka
discuss the rapidly growing “liminal” places that animals such as coyotes,
large cats, Canada Geese, foxes, and others now occupy.118 “Liminal”
animals are “denizens” because they normally do not seek out sociability, but
rather live among us out of necessity, opportunistically, or because they have
found a particular niche.119 Wild animals in these spaces change human
obligations, according to Donaldson and Kymlicka.120 Our duties toward
denizens are mostly geared to preventing harm by avoiding exploitation,
allowing animals to self-regulate in habitat and reproduce within reasonable
limits, limiting unwanted human contact, and respecting their security of
space.121 Some of these duties clearly apply to bears, like Mink, entering
human residential spaces. For example, Donaldson and Kymlicka discourage
relocations of animals, rehabilitation of animal orphans, and feeding, or
making food accessible to animals who then become “less wary of humans
and are labeled ‘nuisances.’”122
Philosopher Clare Palmer also views animal ethics as relational in her book
Animal Ethics in Context. Palmer views human responsibility toward animals
on a continuum, with the greatest duties owed to animals who are almost
completely dependent on humans for their breeding, care, and daily
functioning. Pets would be first candidates for such stringent responsibilities,
with domesticated, captive animals a close second. Even a normally “wild”

animal can be the subject of strong human obligations if removed from
autonomous circumstances and made captive and dependent on humans.123
Zoo animals would be examples. On the other hand, a feral animal, typically
a pet, such as a cat or dog, functioning independently of human oversight
might be farther along the continuum toward “wild.”
Bears do not fall on the fully wild end of the ethical continuum, nor do they
seek to be liminal. A long-term perspective shows that humans have reduced
bear habitat, making increased interactions with humans inevitable.
Collective human responsibilities toward bears rise with diminishing
wildness. This duty must be discharged at the federal, state, and local
governmental levels, with the pressure of groups and individuals committed
to conserving large carnivorous species.
VI. LONG RANGE DUTIES OF AFFIRMATIVE
ASSISTANCE TO BEARS
Some would object that assisting even partly wild animals is wrong, and the
proper stance is to leave wild beings alone to fend for themselves. This
“hands-off” attitude is entrenched to the point that it can serve as a facile
excuse for inaction. Clare Palmer opens her book with a true story of tens of
thousands of migrating wildebeests crossing Kenya’s Mara River in a
location with very steep embankments. Thousands of wildebeests perished
while reporters, camera crews, and safari tourists watched and documented
the debacle instead of attempting to divert the herd a short distance.124 This
event exposes the largely unquestioned attitude that wild animals should not
receive human assistance and that a “let it be” principle better serves nature.
Although a non-interventionist approach to the wild is a reasonable default
position, there are incidences when the ease of assistance might prevent
severe harm to animals, and in the case of the wildebeests, might have saved
as many as 10,000 members of the species.
A compelling case for limited active assistance applies to the many American
black bears in situations like Mink and her progeny. Although Mink did
engage in opportunistic feeding behavior and can be seen beyond the Mink
Brook Nature Reserve wandering two towns, she mostly fends for herself

without relying on humans. She is not fully wild because her home range
overlaps with human residences and activities, but not by her design.
Generally, New England black bears are further from the wild pole than
Kenyan wildebeests because humans have saturated and appropriated much
of their habitat. Through negative although partially inadvertent causal
influences on their ways of being, humans have acquired special duties to
bears. Under Earth law principles, our duty is to repair our relations by
restoring some of the damage we have wrought.
A. Duties of Habitat: Restoring Corridors
Humans owe a significant affirmative obligation to bears based on past
collective actions of taking more than we needed to live comfortably, to the
point of impairing the rights of these animals to be, have habitat, and fulfill
their nature, three basic Earth law rights.125 Collectively, we owe bears basic
mechanisms to prevent lethal and harmful conditions. Corrective (backward-
looking) justice must include recreating contiguous spaces large enough to
accommodate bear migration for reproduction, seasonal foraging, and
hibernation. Bounded parks will not do. Because corridors have disappeared
or become fragmented through human development, urban and rural local
planning projects and regional state compacts should make corridor
restoration a priority.
Road mortality is a vulnerability of bears, and roads also affect habitat
connectivity. Discussions about fixing this problem should be win-win for
humans and animals because both perish in large-animal collisions.
Heartening work is underway in some states (and Europe) to establish
infrastructure to reduce this harm. Road overpasses and underpasses allow
animals to cross highways and facilitate their movement for feeding and
reproduction.126 While infrastructure is expensive, the relative costs of
highway injury and mortality must be considered. Human convenience has
generated the elaborate system of roads that have jeopardized both animals
and humans themselves. Simultaneously, human roads have cut off animal
migration. The causal human impact on the nonhuman environment is a
source of ethical obligation in both corrective and forward-looking justice.
B. Duties of Habitat: Land Use Planning

Overall spatial duties are more complicated. Expecting humans to set aside
large enough areas to reduce bear and human contacts on a large scale is
presently unrealistic because of expense and other environmental priorities,
still networks of smaller but connected preserves are feasible.127 Because
habitat fragmentation is a central problem for many species and ecosystems,
cooperation by private landowners and use of federal and state public lands,
as well as general public support, will be necessary to restore habitat.128
Finding compromise solutions may be pragmatically important for
meaningful results, and democratic processes of collaboration might facilitate
environmental progress in other matters.
Particular land-use infrastructure decisions should prospectively take into
account the need for sufficient relatively undisturbed habitat so that bears can
meet their wide-ranging seasonal nourishment needs. For example, humans
can select a location for ridgeline wind turbines that does not run through
beech tree groves so bears will have a more secure source of fall nuts to build
protein and fat for hibernation. Such a factor could be significant enough to
alter the preferred siting of a wind energy facility.129 Because of the historic
human injustice of shrinking and fragmenting bear habitat, it is fair to
compensate with extra attention to animal needs. This might mean that
humans should forego the most desirable wind facility site in favor of a
workable site that does less harm to wildlife. At least they should consider
ways to mitigate harm in planning and designing the site they select.
Preserving open spaces for bears supports many components of ecosystems,
including other fauna, vegetation, and pure water sources. Such preservation
serves multiple human and nonhuman purposes and supports core Earth law
principles.
These land-use decisions go beyond justice and permeate all that we do as
humans. The motivation goes deeper than correcting past wrongs. Albert
Schweitzer, physician and theologian, urged that all individuals, to the extent
of their ability, owe some affirmative assistance to other living beings simply
because all life participates in the necessity of taking life for survival. The
appropriate ethical response to this universal necessity is not justice,
according to Schweitzer, but rather “reverence” for the unity of life. When
possible, each person should improve the lives of others, even doing
something as simple as rescuing an insect from a water puddle.130

VII. CONCLUSION
Learning to make room for nonhuman beings, including large animals
saddled with stereotypes about ferocity, is a step toward reverence and a
rebalanced human relationship to the nonhuman community that has gone so
far astray in viewing the world from ownership and property perspectives.
Humans are not separate and superior; we are privileged to inhabit diverse
landscapes alongside different creatures with whom we should share basic
rights. Feeling humble and grateful amidst such creatures, instead of
dominant and free to use them at will as a resource, is a vital step for
planetary survival as we seek to avert irreparable damage to Earth’s land,
atmosphere, and waters.
Earth jurisprudence is progressing in heartening ways by shaking some legal
frameworks at their cores. It is helpful to apply the visions and concepts of
this perspective to more particular contexts to illustrate how the theory might
work practically. The case of Mink reveals some complex overlapping factors
for understanding obligations under an Earth law perspective, which is
helpful in imagining cases that might come before legislators and judges.
Illustrations can also impart courage to lawyers to advance bold,
transformative ideas.
The development of Earth law will benefit from contextual attention to
individual animals, including their dignity, a value derived from recognition
of one’s right to be and to realize one’s nature. Individual beings should
sometimes be the focus of discussions within an overall systems perspective.
Making individuals prominent does not have to compromise ecosystems and
processes. Improving landscapes for black bears will generate collateral
improvements for forest ecology. Respecting the Earth community
encompasses all components of that community. These embellishments to
Earth law may inspire an even more compelling and adoptable vision.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) The chapter argues that our ethical obligations to animals arise in part
from empathy, which allows us to recognize that animals have characteristics

similar to those that create duties toward humans. Is empathy—an emotion—
an appropriate foundation for legal thinking?
(2) Bears are relatively easy for humans to empathize with. Can the same
argument create legal status for other natural beings? Could squirrels, insects,
trees, rocks, for example, also gain legal recognition in this way?
(3) How should information from ethology and biology affect legal decision-
making about bears?
(4) What affirmative duties should apply to humans in relation to wild
animals such as Mink? To liminal animals such as raccoons?
(5) The chapter proposes that a planned wind turbine farm be relocated if it
interferes with bears’ needs to gather nuts. What would happen if there were
no other suitable locations for a planned infrastructure project? Do humans
have priority over bears? What constraints would the view of Earth law
described in this chapter place on humans when converting a part of nature to
their own use?
(6) This chapter describes a duty to restore damaged natural habitat in order
to remedy past abuses. How would this work in practice in a legal context?
