CHAPTER 15
United Nations Sustainable 
Development Initiatives1
I. INTRODUCTION
Sustainable development is currently the predominant global model for
protecting the environment while ensuring quality of life for humans. Efforts
to promote sustainable development are taking place primarily within the
United Nations (UN), a truly international governance body comprising 193
states. While non-governmental bodies continue to proliferate, in a global
system based on the ultimate authority of sovereign states, the authority and
power remains with the UN. Historically, the UN has taken a lead role in
protecting the environment, starting from its sponsorship of the 1972
Stockholm Conference and then in subsequent global environmental
conferences. It has drafted and negotiated the vast majority of post-1972
international environmental conventions, as well as a substantial number of
soft law instruments comprising today’s global environmental toolbox.
Yet, as discussed in this chapter, sustainable development is dominated by
anthropocentrism. Sustainable development is for the betterment of people.
Nature’s value is rated by the services it supplies to humans, rather than for
its own inherent worth. UN efforts to move beyond sustainable development
to an Earth law paradigm have been minimal, and UN policy, determined by
its member states, continues to promote economic growth and development.
UN initiatives currently underway for promoting Earth law and rights of
nature are taking place within the “Harmony with Nature” initiative,

promoting a biocentric approach to implementing the UN Sustainable
Development Goals, through resolutions of the UN General Assembly
(UNGA), and hosting Harmony with Nature dialogues on the relationship
between humans and nature.2
This chapter is divided into two main parts. The first explores the benefits
and shortcomings of UN sustainable development initiatives as well as
emerging principles in the field, including harmony with nature. The second
part explores the Global Pact for the Environment, a proposed international
treaty that would strengthen state duties to protect nature.
II. OVERVIEW OF THE UNITED NATIONS
The UN was founded in 1945 in the aftermath of World War II. Beyond its
globally-recognized leadership in issues of peace, security, and human rights,
its reach includes activities through specialized agencies as diverse as the
World Health Organization and the World Bank. The United Nations
Environmental Programme (UNEP) promotes and coordinates the United
Nations’ environmental initiatives.
The UN Charter establishes six principal organs: the General Assembly, the
Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council,
the International Court of Justice, and the Secretariat.3 Of those, the
Economic and Social Council bears primary responsibility for implementing
sustainable development.4 The General Assembly comprises all 193 member
nations and is the main deliberative and policymaking organ of the United
Nations.5
Notable UN-related bodies active in areas related to Earth law are UNEP, the
United Nations Development Program (UNDP), the Intergovernmental Panel
on Climate Change (IPCC), the High-level Political Forum on Sustainable
Development (High-level Political Forum or HLPF), the UN Forum on
Forests, and the United Nations Program on Harmony with Nature, among
others.
Earth law may be developed by forging a new social contract that involves
both humans and nature. The United Nations is playing an important role in

the development of this contract, and that role is the subject of this chapter.
III. UNITED NATIONS SUSTAINABILITY
EFFORTS
Sustainable development is the defining paradigm of UN environmental
work. The famous definition given by the 1987 Brundtland Report is that
“sustainable development meets the needs of current generations without
compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs as well.”6
This section reviews the origins of that goal and UN progress to achieve it in
chronological order, beginning with the 1972 Stockholm Conference for the
Human Environment ending with the 2019 session of the High-level Political
Forum.
A. United Nations Conference on the Human Environment,
Stockholm 1972
The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment (UNCHE), or the
Stockholm Conference, was the UN’s first environmental megaconference. It
sought to address global environmental and conservation issues, focusing on
escalating industrial pollution and its impact on the environment.7
Because the conference was the initiative of the developed world, the
UNCHE generated deep suspicion among developing countries. Many
viewed the Stockholm Conference as a plot of developed countries to solve
the environmental problems that they had created by their high standard of
living (dependent on ravenous consumption of natural resources) by denying
developing countries a right to develop and achieve the same standard of
living.8 The suspicion with which developing countries responded to the
UNCHE was also rooted in the fierce guard that they had adopted against
perceived threats to their national sovereignty.9
Prior to the conference, as an outlet for the increasing tension, UNCHE
Secretary-General Maurice Strong convened a meeting on environment and
development held in Founex, Switzerland. This sparked the earliest major
discussions on sustainable development. The meeting’s outcome document,

the Founex Report on Development and Environment, found that the
environmental devastation of developing countries derives from poverty, in
sharp contrast to developed countries, whose pollution derives from the
excesses of development and who can “afford” conservation.10 Addressing
environmental problems of developing countries meant economic
development, which developed countries should help them achieve.11
Addressing global needs while recognizing the unique challenges of
developing countries became a key theme of the Stockholm Conference. The
key output was the Stockholm Declaration, which contains 26 principles “to
inspire and guide the peoples of the world in the preservation and
enhancement of the human environment.”12 Principle 11 epitomized the
viewpoint of many developing countries: “The environmental policies of all
States should enhance and not adversely affect the present or future
development potential of developing countries, nor should they hamper the
attainment of better living conditions for all.…”
The Stockholm Declaration is at times unabashedly anthropocentric.
Consider the following excerpt from the preamble, which is rooted in human
superiority over nature:
The natural growth of population continuously presents problems for the
preservation of the environment, and adequate policies and measures should
be adopted, as appropriate, to face these problems. Of all things in the world,
people are the most precious. It is the people that propel social progress,
create social wealth, develop science and technology and, through their hard
work, continuously transform the human environment. Along with social
progress and the advance of production, science and technology, the
capability of man to improve the environment increases with each passing
day.13
While Stockholm Declaration principles call for environmental protections,
they are often tempered with human-centered perspectives and a right to
pollute. Some of these include Principle 2 (calling for safeguarding to flora
and fauna but only “for the benefit of present and future generations”),
Principle 6 (calling for a halt to toxic and other discharges but only where
they exceed the assimilative capacity of the environment), and Principle 21

(“States have, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and the
principles of international law, the sovereign right to exploit their own
resources pursuant to their own environmental policies…”).
The Stockholm conference also afforded an opportunity for the UN to
promote international environmental law. Three international biodiversity
agreements reached the final UNCHE agenda: the 1971 Ramsar Convention
on Wetlands of International Importance, and the draft texts of the future
1972 World Heritage Convention and the 1973 Convention on International
Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). The 1972
Convention for the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes
and Other Matter (London Convention) was also on the UNCHE’s agenda.
The UNCHE’s emphasis on international conventions was repeated at a later
UN environmental megaconference: The 1992 UNCED Rio Summit, which
opened for signing both the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and
the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). The CBD
promotes biological conservation and sustainable use along with fair and
equitable sharing of genetic resources. The UNFCCC is the framework
agreement for combating climate change under which the 2015 Paris
Agreement was negotiated and adopted.
B. World Charter for Nature, 1982
In 1982, the UN General Assembly adopted the World Charter for Nature,
the work of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the
world’s largest environmental network. In stark contrast to the Stockholm
Declaration, the World Charter for Nature adopts an ecocentric or “deep
sustainability” view and remains the UN’s strongest statement on the
integrity of nature.14 The charter dates from the IUCN’s 1975 Twelfth
General Assembly in Kinshasa, Zaire, where President Mobutu of Zaire
raised the idea while pointedly blaming developed countries for
environmental problems that arise from colonialism and capitalism:
Industrialized countries put the blame on those who have not yet reached that
stage, for not controlling the growth of their populations.…At the same time,
however, they forget that their populations, although representing one-third

of mankind, consume ninety percent of the planet’s resources.…We, who
have been colonized, were taught that civilization of our former masters was
the best one.…the crisis is one of civilization.…Thanks to zairianisation, we
have become the owners of our lands.…If I had any advice for you, I would
suggest the establishment of a Charter of Nature…insofar as Zaire is
concerned, we are ready to help you succeed.…The jungle of liberal
capitalism is finished. Every citizen in this world must defend his heritage,
the area in which he lives, against those modern savages, the killers of Nature
who do not hesitate to slaughter her to swell their wallets.”15
Following Mobutu’s proposal, the same IUCN General Assembly adopted a
resolution recommending that governments promote a World Charter for
Nature. UN General Assembly deliberations began shortly thereafter.16 While
many African countries were supportive of the initiative in light of Zaire’s
leading role,17 Latin American countries believed the charter favored
conservation over social and economic needs. As it had done in debates
surrounding the Stockholm Conference, Brazil framed the debate as the
Global North’s exploitation of the Global South’s natural resources.
However, in the end, the charter’s vision of a more harmonious relationship
with nature prevailed, and the UN General Assembly adopted the charter by a
vote of 111-1 with 18 abstentions. The United States was the only “no” vote.
The Charter calls upon a moral code of conduct to guide human action in a
way that treats other organisms with respect. It was perhaps the first official
UN document to use the concept of “harmony with nature” in its preamble.
The following are key excerpts from the Charter.
World Charter for Nature
UN GA RES 37/7
The General Assembly,
Reaffirming the fundamental purposes of the United Nations
Aware that:
(a) Mankind is a part of nature and life depends on the uninterrupted

functioning of natural systems which ensure the supply of energy and
nutrients,
(b) Civilization is rooted in nature, which has shaped human culture and
influenced all artistic and scientific achievements, and living in harmony with
nature gives man the best opportunities for the development of his creativity,
and for rest and recreation,
Convinced that:
(a) Every form of life is unique, warranting respect regardless of its worth to
man, and, to accord other organisms such recognition, man must be guided
by a moral code of action.…
Persuaded that:
(a) Lasting benefits from nature depend upon the maintenance of essential
ecological processes and life support systems, and upon the diversity of life
forms, which are jeopardized through excessive exploitation and habitat
destruction by man,
(b) The degradation of natural systems owing to excessive consumption and
misuse of natural resources, as well as to failure to establish an appropriate
economic order among peoples and among States, leads to the breakdown of
the economic, social and political framework of civilization.
…
Adopts, to these ends, the present World Charter for Nature, which proclaims
the following principles of conservation by which all human conduct
affecting nature is to be guided and judged.
I. General Principles
1. Nature shall be respected and its essential processes shall not be impaired.
2. The genetic viability on the earth shall not be compromised; the population
levels of all life forms, wild and domesticated, must be at least sufficient for
their survival, and to this end necessary habitat shall be safeguarded.

3. All areas of the earth, both land and sea, shall be subject to these principles

4. Ecosystems and organisms, as well as the land, marine and atmospheric

…
II. Functions
6. In the decision-making process it shall be recognized that man’s needs can
be met only by ensuring the proper functioning of natural systems and by

…
III. Implementation
14. The principles set forth in the present Charter shall be reflected in the law
and practice of each State, as well as at the international level.…
…
21. States and, to the extent they are able, other public authorities,

(d) Ensure that activities within their jurisdictions or control do not cause

beyond the limits of national jurisdiction;
(e) Safeguard and conserve nature in areas beyond national jurisdiction.
…

22. Taking fully into account the sovereignty of States over their natural
resources, each State shall give effect to the provisions of the present Charter
through its competent organs and in co-operation with other States.

While the 1982 World Charter for Nature declared that “Nature shall be
respected and its essential processes shall not be impaired,” the 1987
Brundtland Report, which launched the current global model of sustainable
development, largely contradicts these principles by emphasizing
development over protection of the environment. We read about this next.
C. Brundtland Report, 1987
The 1987 Report of the World Commission on Environment and
Development: Our Common Future, also called the Brundtland Report, was
an attempt to reconcile the objectives of economic development and
protection of the environment. The report argued that sustainable
development could be achieved through the “three pillars”: economic growth,
social equality, and environmental sustainability. It also focused on the need
to eradicate poverty as a fundamental requirement of sustainable
development. While this was not the first time the term “sustainable
development” had been used, the term entered the global lexicon as a result
of this report.
The chairperson of the commission, Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland
of Norway, candidly acknowledged the tension of sustainable development.
These were, among others, tensions between rich nations and poor nations,
between global governance and national sovereignty, between economic
development and environment, and between economic growth and equity.
Ms. Brundtland described the approach taken by the commission in resolving
this conflict as follows:
When the terms of reference of our Commission were originally being
discussed in 1982, there were those who wanted its considerations to be
limited to “environmental issues” only. This would have been a grave
mistake. The environment does not exist as a sphere separate from human

actions, ambitions, and needs, and attempts to defend it in isolation from
human concerns have given the very word “environment” a connotation of
naivety in some political circles. The word “development” has also been
narrowed by some into a very limited focus, along the lines of “what poor
nations should do to become richer”…
But the “environment” is where we all live; and “development” is what we all
do in attempting to improve our lot within that abode. The two are
inseparable.…Further, development issues must be seen as crucial by the
political leaders who feel that their countries have reached a plateau towards
which other nations must strive. Many of the development paths of the
industrialized nations are clearly unsustainable. And the development
decisions of these countries, because of their great economic and political
power, will have a profound effect upon the ability of all peoples to sustain
human progress for generations to come.…18
Thus, from the beginning, sustainable development has been a compromise
between those who want to privilege the environment and those who want to
privilege economic development. Economic development would be primary,
and social and environmental concerns would condition development. As
with many of the environmental laws critiqued in Chapter 1, “Modern
Environmental Law,” sustainable development was born from an undeniably
anthropocentric and economy-focused paradigm. This model largely persists
today.
D. United Nations Conference on Environment and
Development, Rio de Janeiro, 1992
The 1992 Earth Summit (also known as the Rio Conference) was a watershed
moment in international environmental law. In attendance were 172
governments, including 108 heads of state, as well as huge numbers of civil
society groups.19 Building on the Brundtland Report, the Earth Summit set
forth a comprehensive agenda—over 300 pages long—for sustainable
development called Agenda 21: Programme of Action for Sustainable
Development (Agenda 21).20 The conference’s short outcome document was
called the Rio Declaration.

While the Rio Declaration emphasizes the need to protect nature, Principle 1
makes clear that human interests are paramount: “Human beings are at the
centre of concerns for sustainable development. They are entitled to a healthy
and productive life in harmony with nature.” The declaration goes on to
highlight common environmental concepts such as the precautionary
principle (Principle 15), the polluter pays principle (Principle 16), and the
need for environmental impact statements (Principle 17), among others. One
other principle that has gained significant traction in recent years is Principle
10 on environmental access rights: access to information, access to public
participation, and access to justice, as key pillars of sound environmental
governance. This principle is the basis of two subsequent treaties: the 1998
Aarhus Convention in Europe21 and the 2018 Escazú Agreement in Latin
America.22
Beyond Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration, the Earth Summit produced the
Forest Principles, a nonbinding document on the conservation and sustainable
use of forests.23 Further, the UNFCCC and the CBD were both opened for
signature. Finally, based on a recommendation contained in Agenda 21, the
UN Commission on Sustainable Development was established shortly after
the conference. It led the UN’s sustainable development efforts until it was
replaced by the High-level Political Forum in 2013.
E. Millennium Summit and the Millennium Development Goals
2000
The September 2000 UN Millennium Summit was held in New York over a
three-day period at the UN headquarters in New York. Attended by 149
heads of state and high-ranking officials, its primary purpose was a show of
strength for the United Nations at the start of the 21st century. The key output
of the Summit was the Millennium Declaration, adopted by the UN General
Assembly three days later.24 While this declaration mostly relates to
economic and human development, it also addresses environmental concerns.
Section I, “Values and principles” opens as follows:
1. We, heads of State and Government, have gathered at United Nations
Headquarters in New York from 6 to 8 September 2000, at the dawn of a new
millennium, to reaffirm our faith in the Organization and its Charter as

indispensable foundations of a more peaceful, prosperous and just world.
…
IV. Protecting our common environment.
21. We must spare no effort to free all of humanity, and above all our
children and grandchildren, from the threat of living on a planet irredeemably
spoilt by human activities, and whose resources would no longer be sufficient
for their needs.
22. We reaffirm our support for the principles of sustainable development,
including those set out in Agenda 21, agreed upon at the United Nations
Conference on Environment and Development.
23. We resolve therefore to adopt in all our environmental actions a new ethic
of conservation and stewardship and, as first steps, we resolve:…
To intensify our collective efforts for the management, conservation and
sustainable development of all types of forests.
To press for the full implementation of the Convention on Biological
Diversity and the Convention to Combat Desertification in those
Countries Experiencing Serious Drought and/or Desertification,
particularly in Africa.
To stop the unsustainable exploitation of water resources by developing
water management strategies at the regional, national and local levels,
which promote both equitable access and adequate supplies.…
* * *
Drawing on the Millennium Declaration, the world leaders who participated
in the Summit adopted the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Eight
goals were to be reached by the year 2015:
(1) eradicate extreme poverty and hunger;
(2) achieve universal primary education;
(3) promote gender equality and empower women;

(4) reduce child mortality;
(5) improve maternal health;
(6) combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases;
(7) ensure environmental sustainability; and
(8) develop a global partnership for development.
In 2002, the Secretary-General of the UN and the administrator of the UN
Development program launched the Millennium Project to support the MDGs
in meeting their target date of 2015. Beginning in 2012, the UN began a
process to develop the Post-2015 Agenda. This effort led to the SDGs, or,
sustainable development goals, adopted in 2015, which supplanted the MDGs
and placed a greater emphasis on the environment (see subsection I).
F. The Earth Charter (2000)
In 2000, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
(UNESCO) adopted the Earth Charter25 at its headquarters in Paris. The
Earth Charter is “…an ethical framework for building a just, sustainable, and
peaceful global society in the 21st century.…”26 The Earth Charter rejects
anthropocentrism in its goal “to inspire in all people a new sense of global
interdependence and shared responsibility for the well-being of the whole
human family, the greater community of life, and future generations.”27
While not an official UN document, it is regarded as an important statement
of environmental values by UNESCO and has since been endorsed by
thousands of organizations representing millions of people.28 As you read the
following Earth Charter principles, consider how they differ from the
sustainable development mandate of Agenda 21, the MDGs, and so forth:
The Earth Charter
PRINCIPLES
I. RESPECT AND CARE FOR THE COMMUNITY OF LIFE

1. Respect Earth and life in all its diversity.
a. Recognize that all beings are interdependent and every form of life has
value regardless of its worth to human beings.
b. Affirm faith in the inherent dignity of all human beings and in the
intellectual, artistic, ethical, and spiritual potential of humanity.
…
4. Secure Earth’s bounty and beauty for present and future generations.
a. Recognize that the freedom of action of each generation is qualified by the
needs of future generations.
b. Transmit to future generations values, traditions, and institutions that
support the long-term flourishing of Earth’s human and ecological
communities.…
…
7. Adopt patterns of production, consumption, and reproduction that
safeguard Earth’s regenerative capacities, human rights, and community well-
being.
a. Reduce, reuse, and recycle the materials used in production and
consumption systems, and ensure that residual waste can be assimilated by

b. Act with restraint and efficiency when using energy, and rely increasingly
on renewable energy sources such as solar and wind.
c. Promote the development, adoption, and equitable transfer of
environmentally sound technologies.
d. Internalize the full environmental and social costs of goods and services in
the selling price, and enable consumers to identify products that meet the

e. Ensure universal access to health care that fosters reproductive health and

9. Eradicate poverty as an ethical, social, and environmental imperative.
a. Guarantee the right to potable water, clean air, food security,

b. Empower every human being with the education and resources to secure a

G. World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg,
2002
The 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) in
Johannesburg was the third UN megaconference on the environment. In the
ten years following the Rio Summit, the global environmental crisis had
worsened, and the implementation of the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21
were deemed to be inadequate. The summit’s planners decided to
reinvigorate their sustainable development commitment with a focus on five
priorities: water and sanitation, energy, health, agriculture, and biodiversity.
The summit adopted the Johannesburg Declaration on Human Development,
a general statement of political commitment to sustainable development, and
the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation, which included a specific
timetable to achieve their goals.29 Unlike the previous two megaconferences,
no initiatives were taken for negotiating new environmental conventions.30
Despite these agreements, the summit was considered by many to be a
setback on environmental issues. For example, the implementation plan
adopted at the summit was criticized by the Heinrich Böll Foundation “for
not having real new commitments, targets and funding for implementation
provided.” Critics also argued that the summit continued to promote

unfettered economic growth as the main strategy to alleviate poverty instead
of advancing new economic models that better support sustainability.31
Against this backdrop, some countries began to call for new international
frameworks that would better protect the environment, including the UN
Harmony with Nature Initiative, as discussed next.
H. The UN Harmony with Nature Initiative
Alongside its agenda for sustainable development, the UN has also taken
steps to build awareness of Earth law concepts. In 2009, the UNGA approved
a resolution proclaiming April 22 as International Mother Earth Day. The
following excerpts are from the statement of then President of Bolivia Evo
Morales to the General Assembly on living in harmony with nature:
UN General Assembly
80th plenary meeting, Wednesday, 22 April 2009
Statement of President Evo Morales, Bolivia
We recall that, in past centuries, there was a continuous struggle for human
rights.…[W]ith today’s declaration of International Mother Earth Day, planet
Earth, Mother Earth, has also won her rights. And this new century, the
twenty-first, should be the century of Mother Earth’s rights. […] If we are to
live in harmony with nature, we need to recognize that not only we human
beings have rights, but that the planet does as well. Animals, plants and all
living beings have rights that we must respect. What is happening to us now
with climate change is the direct result of not respecting the rights of Mother
Earth.
The United Nations must ensure that the rights of Mother Earth and of all
living beings are respected.…Many people, in particular certain lawyers—
forgive me for saying so—will say that only human beings have rights. In our
view, it is difficult to accept that. […] Another important thing that I would
like to point out is the importance of coexisting with nature, because human
life is not possible without Mother Earth. […] In Bolivia, in particular among
the local Indigenous peoples that I am familiar with, Mother Earth is sacred
to life. That is why we undertake sacred rituals of tribute to our rivers,

forests, lakes and animals and have many tunes to express our respect for
Mother Earth. […]
I would like to propose four rights of great importance to humankind.
First is the right to life. […] We human beings must recognize that
Mother Earth and all living beings have a right to exist and that our
rights end when we set off the extinction or elimination of nature.
Second is the right of regeneration for the planet’s biocapacity. […]
Human activity on the planet and its resources cannot be unlimited.
Development cannot be infinite. […]
Third is the right to a clean life. That means the right of Mother Earth to
live without pollution.…
Fourth is the right to harmony and balance with and among all and
everything.…
Until now, human beings have been prisoners of development capitalism,
which states that man is the sole owner of the planet. Now it is time to
recognize that the Earth does not belong to us. It is the other way around: we
belong to the Earth, and it is our mission in the world to watch over the
rights, not only of human beings, but of Mother Earth and of all living beings.

Universal Declaration of the Rights of Mother Earth
Just one year after President Morales made his impassioned speech for
protecting Mother Earth to the UN General Assembly, in April 2010, Bolivia
held the first World People’s Conference on Climate Change and the Rights
of Mother Earth in Cochabamba. This gathering included over 35,000 people
representing 140 countries—civil society leaders, 56 governmental
delegations, Indigenous peoples, climate activists, and others—all of whom
sought bold collective action after the failures of the 2009 Climate Change
Conference in Copenhagen (COP 15). Among the initiatives presented at the
World People’s Conference was a Universal Declaration for the Rights of
Mother Earth (UDRME), which called for the UN and all countries to
recognize the rights of nature.
The UDRME asserts that the rights of nature arise from its very existence on
the planet. Its preamble recognizes the “critical importance and urgency of
taking decisive, collective action to prevent humans causing climate change
and other impacts on Mother Earth that threaten the wellbeing and survival of
humans and other beings.” It then goes onto describe the specific rights held
by Mother Earth. Some of the recognized rights include the right to life and
to exist (Art. 2(1)(a), the right to be respected (Art. 2(1)(b)), the right to
integral health (Art. 2(1)(g), and the right to full and prompt restoration for

violation of the rights recognized (Art. 2(1)(j)).
A petition for the UN to adopt the Universal Declaration of the Rights of
Mother Earth has gained almost 300,000 signatures. It also continues to guide
rights of nature developments worldwide.
Building from International Mother Earth Day, the UN began hosting
“interactive dialogues” that brought together global experts on harmony with
nature, including many Earth law practitioners. The first dialogue, in
December 2010, convened to support the UN Conference on Sustainable
Development in Brazil (2012) by providing guidance on best practices to
promote a holistic approach to sustainable development in harmony with
nature, as well as criteria and indicators to measure progress.33
Since then, an interactive dialogue has occurred annually on Mother Earth
Day. Each dialogue is preceded by a report of the Secretary-General on
Harmony with Nature and then followed by a Resolution on Harmony with
Nature that is adopted by the UN General Assembly. All of this work is
informed by a body of experts, called Knowledge Network Experts, who
keep the UN apprised of global developments on living in harmony with
nature. These interactive dialogues, reports, and resolutions, along with the
Knowledge Network Experts, serve as the foundation of the Harmony with
Nature Initiative at the United Nations.
Unlike most UN programs, the Harmony with Nature Initiative acknowledges
ecocentric legal movements worldwide and builds knowledge and capacity
around their growth. Consider how the 2011 resolution on Harmony with
Nature ties in UN sustainability work to Earth law principles you have read
about in this book:

In sum, the UN Harmony with Nature Initiative attempts to direct global
sustainability efforts towards new paradigms of law and culture that would
allow humans to live in harmony with nature. This program serves as an
imperative link between UN sustainability work and Earth law.

Continuing in chronological order, we now turn back to the UN’s more
conventional sustainable development work, picking up at the next UN
megaconference on sustainable development: Rio+20.
I. United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development
(Rio+20)—Rio de Janeiro, 2012
The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development (UNCSD), or
Rio+20, was the third megaconference on sustainable development. As with
the previous conferences, its goal was to balance global economic and
environmental goals. The outcome document of Rio+20, entitled The Future
We Want, sets out new measures to implement sustainable development.
Importantly, it called for Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that would
build from the existing MDGs to implement a post-2015 development
agenda. Consider the following excerpt from The Future We Want that
largely reaffirms the sustainable development mandate that has prevailed
since the Stockholm Conference in 1972:
1. We, the Heads of State and Government and high-level representatives,
having met at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from 20 to 22 June 2012, with the full
participation of civil society, renew our commitment to sustainable
development and to ensuring the promotion of an economically, socially and
environmentally sustainable future for our planet and for present and future
generations.
2. Eradicating poverty is the greatest global challenge facing the world today
and an indispensable requirement for sustainable development. In this regard
we are committed to freeing humanity from poverty and hunger as a matter of
urgency.
3. We therefore acknowledge the need to further mainstream sustainable
development at all levels, integrating economic, social and environmental
aspects and recognizing their interlinkages, so as to achieve sustainable
development in all its dimensions.
Despite its emphasis on existing commitments rather than forging new ones,
the Future We Want did pay homage to harmony with nature:

39. We recognize that planet Earth and its ecosystems are our home and that
“Mother Earth” is a common expression in a number of countries and
regions, and we note that some countries recognize the rights of nature in the
context of the promotion of sustainable development. We are convinced that
in order to achieve a just balance among the economic, social and
environmental needs of present and future generations, it is necessary to
promote harmony with nature. We call for holistic and integrated approaches
to sustainable development that will guide humanity to live in harmony with
nature and lead to efforts to restore the health and integrity of the Earth’s
ecosystem.
1. Peoples’ sustainability treaties
Rio+20 was considered a highly inclusive megaconference, with 44,000
badges issued for official meetings, most of those going to members of civil
society. However, many civil society groups were concerned that state actors
in Rio were advancing a weak international agenda on sustainable
development. To provide a stronger vision of sustainability, a consultative
process with hundreds of civil society organizations resulted in fourteen
“Peoples’ Sustainability Treaties” that set a bold agenda for achieving a
sustainable world.36 One of these was a Peoples’ Sustainability Treaty on
Rights of Mother Earth.37 Note the response of this Declaration to Decisions
of the Conference itself supported “green economies.”
Peoples’ Sustainability Treaty on Rights of Mother Earth
1. Preface
The undersigned recognize and acknowledge the following:
We are all part of Mother Earth, an indivisible, living community of
interrelated and interdependent beings with a common destiny. Mother Earth
is the source of life, nourishment, and learning and provides these as well as
spirituality and all else we need to live well.
Existing governance systems that assume that humans are separate from the
environment have wrought great destruction, degradation, and disruption of

Mother Earth, putting life as we know it today at significant risk through
habitat destruction, species elimination, climate change, and other threats.
Existing economic systems treat the natural world as property that can be
exploited and degraded, rather than as an integral ecological partner with its
own rights to exist and thrive, leading to dangerously unbalanced
relationships among humans and Mother Earth and her other inhabitants.
The United Nations-commissioned 2011 report, Towards a Green Economy,
defines a “green economy” as one that “seeks to minimise the impact of
economic activity on the environment,” and thereby fails to ensure either the
necessary reversal of ongoing environmental degradation or the eventual
health of Mother Earth. The “green economy” mistakenly presumes that we
can “protect” Mother Earth by further forcing environmental policies to fit
within an economic system that is causing the destruction in the first place,
such as through privatization of the natural world.
Mother Earth-based governance, rather than economy- or development-based
governance, is necessary to recognize the rights of ecosystems and species—
including humans—to exist, thrive and evolve. In an interdependent living
community, it is not possible to recognize the rights of only human beings
without causing an imbalance within Mother Earth. To guarantee human
rights, it is necessary to recognize and defend the rights of Mother Earth and
all beings in her, and that there are existing cultures, practices, and laws that
do so.
There exists now an urgency to take decisive, collective action to transform
structures and systems that cause habitat destruction, species elimination and
abuse, climate change, and other ongoing, imminent and immediately
dangerous threats and damage to Mother Earth.
…
2. Principles
Principle #1: Inherent Rights of Mother Earth
Mother Earth and all ecosystems and species of which she is composed [have
certain fundamental rights].

…
Principle #2: Responsibilities of human beings to Mother Earth and the
overall well-being of human and environmental communities
Every human being is responsible for respecting and living in harmony with
Mother Earth.
The economy must serve and advance the overall well-being of human and
environmental communities, rather than the maximization of private wealth;
communities must not suffer a loss of overall well-being to serve the
incessant driver of economic growth that is fueling the destruction of the
Earth’s ecosystems and species.
Human community well-being includes not only a functioning economy but
also thriving ecosystems and species as well as diverse cultures, strong
societal/familial relations, healthy food, clean drinking water, adequate
sanitation, safe housing, necessary medical care, democratic governance, full
education, meaningful and appropriately rewarded labor, support for
spirituality, respectful treatment of animals, and other elements.
Environmental community well-being includes thriving relationships with
human partners, as well as strong ecosystem and species biodiversity and
well-being, clean water, healthy nutrients, and sound and connected habitats.
Principle #3: Focus on “sustainable communities” and a balanced
respect for all life
“Sustainable development” and the “green economy” should be re-focused
instead as “sustainable communities,” a term which includes both human
communities and the wider communities of the natural world, to ensure that
all elements of sustainable communities are promoted, rather than subsumed
to the overarching driver of the economy.
A balanced respect for all life, and the recognition that all life has the right to
exist, persist, and evolve as an interrelated and interdependent system, is
essential to ensure both sustainable communities and a healthy, thriving
planet overall.

A positive outcome of Rio+20 for many civil society attendees was a resolve
to build the political will for transformative change—including by shaping
the post-2015 UN development agenda toward harmony with nature.
However, few left Rio+20 with a feeling that what was needed had been

to all countries.

IV. DEEP SUSTAINABILITY—AN
ALTERNATIVE APPROACH
The mainstream UN sustainable development paradigm is only one
interpretation of sustainability—one that is unabashedly anthropocentric and
focused on development. Other approaches to sustainability take a more
holistic approach to humanity’s place on the planet, more in line with the
teachings of Earth law. Consider the following excerpt from John Ikerd, a
professor emeritus at the University of Missouri, which describes deep
sustainability as being “co-centric” rather than either anthropocentric or
ecocentric.
Deep Sustainability: Rediscovering Our Connectedness
John Ikerd
All and all, today’s environmental movement has not been succeeding. We
have been winning battles, some critical ones, but losing the war.”40 These
are the words of Gustave Speth, founder of the World Resources Institute, co-
founder of the Natural Resource Defense Council, and advisor to Presidents
Carter and Clinton. He pointed to a variety of ecological indicators in his

2008 book, The Bridge at the Edge of the World, to drive this point home: air
and water pollution, fossil energy and fossil water depletion, greenhouse gas
emissions, and loss of biodiversity. Speth concluded that environmental
organizations have failed because they have spent their time, energy, and
money battling the symptoms of ecological degradation rather than attacking
its root causes. Today’s environmental crisis is ultimately rooted in our
dysfunctional relationships with the other living and non-living things of the
earth. To avert the impending global ecological disaster, we must delve
deeper into the nature of our interconnectedness.
The concept of “deep sustainability” goes deeper than environmentalism. It
even goes beyond current approaches to sustainability, which focus on
resource protection and conservation and substitution of renewable for
nonrenewable sources of energy. Deep sustainability explores the ethical,
philosophical, and spiritual roots of ecological, social, and economic
sustainability.41 It is rooted in new ways of thinking, knowing, learning, and
being in the world: ways not only essential for avoiding a global ecological
catastrophe but also for progress toward a new and better world of the future.
Deep sustainability represents an intellectual conceptualization of the wisdom
of Indigenous peoples throughout the world in that it reemphasizes the
importance of our interconnectedness with nature and with each other. It calls
on us to reestablish intimate, caring relationships with the earth and with
other people. It recognizes that we need to connect with others not solely to
meet our physical or material needs but also because we need to care and be
cared for, to love and be loved. It trusts that a new set of ethical and cultural
values can and will evolve from these loving and caring personal
relationships.
…
Sustainability may well be the defining question of the twenty-first century:
“How can we meet the needs of all in the present without diminishing
opportunities for those of the future.” Sustainability is about meeting the
basic needs of all, with equity and justice, both within and across future
generations. Sustainability requires economic, social, and ecological
integrity, all three; but sustainability ultimately is rooted in nature.
Everything that is of use to humans, including everything of economic value,

ultimately comes from nature. Furthermore, beyond self-sufficiency, we must
rely on relationships with other people, meaning society, to help us benefit
from nature’s bounty. To meet needs that cannot be met through personal
relationships, we must rely on impersonal economies. To sustain our
economies, societies, and ultimately humanity, we must maintain the health
and productive capacity of both society and nature.
In failing to respect the intrinsic value of our connectedness with and within
nature, we have allowed questions of ecological and social sustainability to
degenerate to their lowest common dominator: money or economic value.
Certainly, our relationships with nature have economic value; nature is the
ultimate source of all economic value. However, nature also has intrinsic
values that far exceed its economic value to humans. Economic value, as we
know it today, is inherently individual, instrumental, and impersonal. It
accrues to individuals or collections of individuals, rather than to
communities or societies as wholes. It is instrumental, in that an economic
transaction is always a means to an end, rather than something done because
of its inherent worth. Economic value is also impersonal, because if
something cannot be bought, sold, or traded among people, it has no
economic value.
…
At the very least, governments should be willing to identify and “internalize”
the economic costs of ecological degradation: they should make “polluters
pay” the economic costs they impose on society. They should also “cap”
greenhouse gas emissions, and if the cap is sufficiently low to reverse global
climate change, even allow trading of CO2 emission rights. They should also
assign economic values to activities that enhance the economic productivity
of nature. However, while government policies that force markets to reflect
full economic values are necessary, internalizing externalities is not sufficient
to ensure sustainability. We should do the necessary, but should not allow
“the necessary” to become an obstacle to “the sufficient.”
Unfortunately, we have allowed our preoccupation with economic value to
become an obstacle to sustainability, mainly because economic relationships
depersonalize our relationships with other people as well as with nature. We

buy, sell, and trade, rather than maintain personal relationships. We must
ultimately account for the social and ethical costs of our failures to care for
society and nature, not just the economic costs. We can begin by reminding
ourselves that our ecological failures have personal consequences, and
personal costs cannot be measured in terms of economic value. Our
dependence on fossil energy provides a convenient illustration of the personal
consequences of our dysfunctional economic relationship with nature.
…
The worldview of deep sustainability goes beyond social justice and extends
the concept of ecological justice to all things of the earth. All things of nature
have rights; the rights of all species, including human rights, reflect their
unique purposes within the whole of nature. In today’s world of scientific
materialism, the other things of nature have no subjectivity or being and thus
have no inherent “right” to exist or purpose apart from their potential
usefulness to humanity. Ironically, this worldview guides even today’s
environmental movement. In spite of claims to the contrary, the
environmental movement is anthropocentric. Most environmentalists
implicitly accept that the world exists primarily, if not solely, for the purpose
of sustaining the well-being of humanity. “Deep ecologists,” on the other
hand, claim an eco-centric worldview, showing no more concern for humans
than for any other species or non-living thing on earth. Deep ecologists would
depopulate the earth of humans, if necessary, to sustain the rest of nature.
Deep sustainability is “co-centric” rather than anthropocentric or eco-centric.
It is not eco-centric because it is concerned specifically with humans—the
present and future well-being of humanity. However, it is not anthropocentric
or human centered, in spite of its specific concern for the human species. The
deep sustainability worldview recognizes that human well-being and the
sustainability of humanity is inseparably and critically interrelated with the
well-being of the other non-living and living beings of the earth. Deep
sustainability is rooted in a deep reverence and respect for all things of nature
—living and non-living—specifically but not solely humans. Nature does not
exist for the sole benefit of humans any more than humans exist for the sole
benefit of the other things of nature. Humanity is not sustainable unless
human societies contribute to, or at least do not detract from, the overall

health and well-being of the whole of nature of which humans are a part.…42
V. EMERGING PARADIGMS: A GLOBAL PACT
FOR THE ENVIRONMENT
A. Introduction: What Is the Global Pact initiative?
We have now reviewed about 35 years of UN sustainability initiatives along
with several alternatives. Looking to the future, what will be the next major
development of the UN’s work to protect the environment?
One possibility is a Global Pact for the Environment (“Global Pact”),
introduced in 2017. The Global Pact proposes the adoption of a legally
binding international treaty that would give force to the environmental law
principles enshrined in the Rio Declaration that emerged from the 1992
UNCED. The Global Pact would guide global and national environmental
action for all states and citizens, as well as the private sector.
Why is a new legal instrument necessary? The Global Pact’s proponents
argue that, at present, international environmental law lacks an overarching,
legally binding umbrella text to clarify and define principles, obligations, and
rights with respect to environmental law and the global environment. As a
result, international environmental law suffers from “gaps”43 and ineffective
and uneven implementation across global and national governance structures.
In 2017, an international group of legal experts proposed a draft text for a
Global Pact based on the mutually interdependent source principles of the
right to a healthy environment and the duty to take care of the environment.
These source principles give rise to other environmental principles
recognized in the Rio Declaration, including (1) the states’ duty of prevention
and remediation of environmental harms, (2) the polluter pays principle, and
(3) the citizens’ right to environmental information and public participation in
environmental decision-making. Further, the draft Global Pact includes
corollary principles such as non-regression44 and official recognition of civil
society’s role in environmental protection.

This section discusses the history, purpose, and principles of the proposed
Global Pact.
B. Why Is a Global Pact for the Environment Necessary?
Human-impacted global ecocide is so undeniably severe and increasingly
alarming that many scholars consider our impact as having brought about a
new geologic era: the Anthropocene.45 It is clear that existing international
environmental laws have not been enough to mitigate humanity’s destructive
impact on our planet. With only 10 years to implement the UN’s 2030
Agenda for Sustainable Development, which requires unprecedented global
cooperation to protect, conserve, and restore planetary systems,46 the
advocates for a Global Pact consider it crucial to ensure we can meet this
global commitment and reclaim hope for a healthy sustainable future. At
present, they argue that international environmental law lacks a foundational
and legally binding document that ensures environmental law principles can
be evenly integrated and effectively implemented in global and national legal
systems.
1. Global environmental constitutionalism
Arguably, as a constitutional text for environmental law, a global pact would
transform principles into compulsory environmental actions and serve as an
inviolable source of law for international and domestic legal systems. Over
time, a global pact would guide environmental constitutionalism and
contribute to the incorporation of environmental norms into the constitutional
tier of national legal systems, leading to stronger domestic environmental
laws and steering effective implementation that would radiate out to the
regional and international governance systems.47 The movement for
environmental constitutionalism has already seen many countries incorporate
environmental principles into their constitutions, such as Brazil, China,
France, Mexico, and many others.48 A global pact would serve as the
binding, overarching text necessary to guide all countries to elevating
environmental protection and sustainable development as pillars of domestic,
regional, and international governance.

2. Turning soft law into hard law
A global pact would give binding force to the Rio Declaration principles to
ensure these principles have universal recognition, harmonized
understanding, and effective application across comparative legal systems.
As a soft-law instrument, the Rio Declaration is not binding, and thus the
jurisprudential and practical effects of some of these essential principles have
failed to be applied and enforced effectively.49 For example, the
precautionary principle (Rio Principle 15) is instructive as to how conflicting
interpretations of soft law can prevent environmental law principles from
realizing their full potential. On the legal question of whether the
precautionary principle is a recognized norm of customary international law,
the International Law of the Sea Tribunal stated that the precautionary
principle is an “emerging norm,”50 while the International Court of Justice
suggested that this principle “may be relevant” for interpretation purposes.51
A global pact would settle the question of which environmental principles are
recognized as norms and therefore create binding obligations on states. This
would ensure that these foundational principles are universally accepted and
would allow for an accelerated application and implementation of these
principles across all legal systems.
C. History of the Initiative for a Global Pact for the
Environment
The idea of creating a global framework for environmental protection like the
Global Pact has evolved since the 1970s. The Stockholm Conference of 1972
was seen as the constitutional moment of international environmental law and
inspired widespread promulgation of domestic environmental laws;52
however, the resulting Stockholm Declaration was a soft-law instrument
without legal force.
The 1992 Rio Declaration on Environment and Development53 was the major
leap forward for the idea of a global pact because this declaration set forth
constitutional principles for global environmental governance.54

Significantly, the Rio Declaration stated the now-essential customary
international law principles of prevention (Rio Principle 2), conducting an
environmental impact assessment (Rio Principle 17), and the duty to
cooperate (Rio Principles 18 and 19). Other key environmental principles
stated, many of which were environmental principles of first impression,55
are (1) common but differentiated responsibilities (Rio Principle 7), (2) the
precautionary principle (Rio Principle 15), (3) polluter pays, (4) notification
of emergencies, (5) notification and consultation in case of risk, and (6)
peaceful settlement of disputes. Many of these environmental principles have
catalyzed the development of customary norms and have been transposed
into a wide range of global treaties and instruments.
Inspired by the Rio Declaration, the International Union for the Conservation
of Nature (IUCN) released the first of its consistently updated drafts of an
International Covenant on Environment and Development in 1995.56
In November 2015, the legal think tank Club des Juristes released a report
recommending the adoption of a universal pact to merge international
environmental law in a binding instrument that would (1) impose
environmental obligations on states and non-state actors, (2) confer
environmental rights to citizens, and (3) create an inviolable legal instrument
in national courts.57 The adoption of the Paris Agreement inspired high-level
international support for the pact from Laurent Fabius58 (President of the 21st
Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate
Change) and led to the 2017 convening of an international network of over
100 environmental law experts from more than 40 countries who finalized a
final draft text for the Global Pact in June 2017. Laurent Fabius, who chaired
the expert meeting that finished the draft text, presented it to French President
Emmanuel Macron at a high-profile symposium featuring former UN
Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon, French Minister of the Environment
Nicolas Hulot, and many other political figures, diplomats, experts, and
students.59 In September 2017, the draft text network of experts, now known
as the International Group of Experts for the Pact (IGEP) published a white
paper, Toward a Global Pact for the Enviroment 60 (GPE), to further advance
governmental and civil society support for the Global Pact.
In September 2017, over 40 heads of state expressed their support at the

Summit on a Global Pact for the Environment.61 In May 2018, the United
Nations General Assembly adopted the Enabling Resolution62 Towards a
Global Pact for the Environment,63 which was resoundingly accepted by the
global community, with 143 states voting to adopt the resolution, and only
five votes against, the United States, the Russian Federation, Syria, the
Philippines, and Turkey. The Enabling Resolution called on the United
Nations Secretary-General to prepare a report64 and to set up a working group
to make recommendations to the UN General Assembly on the matter,
including the possibility of convening an intergovernmental conference to
adopt an international instrument.65
The Secretary-General’s November 2018 report found that international
environmental law could indeed be strengthened “through a comprehensive
and unifying international instrument that gathers all the principles of
environmental law.”66 The Global Pact’s working group met at the UN
Environment Programme’s Nairobi headquarters for three substantive
meetings during 2019, resulting in a recommendation to states to make a
“political declaration” on the matter in 2022, the 50th anniversary of the
Stockholm Conference.67 While this delays the Global Pact’s adoption,
supporters remain hopeful that continued mobilization might see the formal
adoption of the Global Pact in 2022.68
D. Principles Recognized in the Draft Global Pact for the
Environment
The draft Global Pact for the Environment must be seen as a preliminary
work base. The authors have deliberately used general and concise wording,
as it is a document intended to be reshaped and negotiated by the various
states before being adopted.
1. The Right to a Healthy Environment
Every person has the right to live in an ecologically sound environment
adequate for their health, well-being, dignity, culture and fulfillment.
2. The Duty to Take Care of the Environment

Every State or international institution, every person, natural or legal, public
or private, has the duty to take care of the environment. To this end, everyone
contributes at their own levels to the conservation, protection, and restoration
of the integrity of the Earth’s ecosystem.
3. Integration and Sustainable Development
Parties shall integrate the requirements of environmental protection into the
planning and implementation of their policies and national and international
activities, especially in order to promote the fight against climate change, the
protection of oceans and the maintenance of biodiversity. They shall pursue
sustainable development. To this end, they shall ensure the promotion of
public support policies, patterns of production and consumption both
sustainable and respectful of the environment.
4. Intergenerational Equity
International equity shall guide decisions that may have an impact on the
environment. Present generations shall ensure that their decisions and action
do not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
5. Prevention
The necessary measures shall be taken to prevent environmental harm. The
Parties have the duty to ensure that activities under their jurisdiction or
control do not cause damage to the environments of other Parties or in areas
beyond the limits of their national jurisdiction. They shall take the necessary
measures to ensure that an environmental impact assessment is conducted
prior to any decision made to authorise or engage in a project, an activity, a
plan, or a program that is likely to have a significant adverse impact on the
environment
6. Precaution
When there is a risk of serious or irreversible damage, lack of scientific
certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing the adoption of
effective and proportionate measures to prevent environmental degradation.

7. Environmental Damages
The necessary measures shall be taken to ensure an adequate remediation of
environmental damages. Parties shall immediately notify other States of any
natural disasters or other emergencies that are likely to produce sudden
harmful effects on the environment of those States. Parties shall promptly
cooperate to help concerned States
8. Polluter Pays
Parties shall ensure that prevention, mitigation and remediation costs for
pollution, and other environmental disruptions and degradation are, to the
greatest possible extent, borne by their originator.
9. Access to Information
Every person, without being required to state an interest, has a right of access
to environmental information held by public authorities. Public authorities
shall, within the framework of their national legislations, collect and make
available to the public relevant environmental information.
10. Public Participation
Every person has the right to participate, at an appropriate stage and while
options are still open, in the preparation of decisions, measures, plans,
programmes, activities, policies and normative instruments of public
authorities that may have a significant effect on the environment.
11. Access to Environmental Justice
Parties shall ensure the right of effective and affordable access to
administrative and judicial procedures, including redress and remedies, to
challenge acts or omissions of public authorities or private persons which
contravene environmental law, taking into consideration the provisions of the
present Pact.
12. Education and Training
The Parties shall ensure that environmental education, to the greatest possible

extent, is taught to members of the younger generation as well as to adults, in
order to inspire in everyone a responsible conduct in protecting and
improving the environment. The Parties shall ensure the protection of
freedom of expression and information in environmental matters. They
support the dissemination by mass media of information of an educational
nature on ecosystems and on the need to protect and preserve the
environment.
13. Research and Innovation
The Parties shall promote, to the best of their ability, the improvement of
scientific knowledge of ecosystems and the impact of human activities. They
shall cooperate through exchanges of scientific and technological knowledge
and by enhancing the development, adaptation, dissemination and transfer of
technologies respectful of the environment, including innovative
technologies.
14. Role of Non-State Actors and Subnational Entities
The Parties shall take the necessary measures to encourage the
implementation of this Pact by non-State actors and subnational entities,
including civil society, economic actors, cities and regions taking into
account their vital role in the protection of the environment.
15. Effectiveness of Environmental Norms
The Parties have the duty to adopt effective environmental laws, and to
ensure their effective and fair implementation and enforcement.
16. Ecological Resilience
The Parties shall take necessary measures to maintain and restore the
diversity and capacity of ecosystems and human communities to withstand
environmental disruptions and degradation and to recover and adapt.
17. Non-Regression
The Parties and their sub-national entities refrain from allowing activities or

adopting norms that have the effect of reducing the global level of
environmental protection guaranteed by current law.
18. Cooperation
In order to conserve, protect and restore the integrity of the Earth’s ecosystem
and community of life, Parties shall cooperate in good faith and in a spirit of
global partnership for the implementation of the provisions of the present
Pact.
* * *
VI. CONCLUSION
Sustainable development is a comprehensive term covering environmental
conservation and economic, social, and cultural development. While the term
is vague, it brings everyone to the table. Sustainable development is in the
global lexicon, and whatever the differences in usages, it uniformly stands for
an alternative mode of development that is sustainable, within the limits of
nature, and addresses poverty and inequity. Without dramatic changes in the
development path within the next forty years, there will be environmental and
social catastrophe.
Yet sustainable development alone cannot reverse the current ecological
crisis. The UN needs to undertake a shift to a paradigm of global
environmental governance that transcends its anthropocentric model of
sustainable development by promoting, ecocentrism; harmony with nature;
and binding environmental instruments, such as through the Global Pact for
the Environment. As an international organization rather than a supranational
organization, this shift in the work of the UN is dependent on the
organization’s member states’ collective decision to incorporate principles of
Earth law within the sustainable development model, and, most important, to
implement these principles on a national basis.

STUDY QUESTIONS

(1) Recalling the origins of sustainable development in the preparations for
the 1972 Stockholm Convention, would you see it as an idea crafted
specifically to supplicate the developing countries into supporting the
Stockholm Conference, or rather a concept whose time had come and would
have been launched onto the international agenda in any case? To understand
the conflict between the developing and developed countries as the
background against which sustainable development became the paradigm for
today’s global governance, trace the positions of the developing countries
throughout the events and policy papers discussed in this chapter.
(2) Article 20.4 of the CBD states: “The extent to which developing country
Parties will effectively implement their commitments under this Convention
will depend on the effective implementation by developed country Parties of
their commitments under this Convention related to financial resources and
transfer of technology and will take fully into account the fact that economic
and social development and eradication of poverty are the first and overriding
priorities of the developing country Parties.” Article 4.2(6) of the UNFCCC
contains similar text. Do you feel that the successful negotiation of this text
by developing countries was simply a means for them to escape
implementing these two major conventions, or is it a justifiable mechanism
considering the vast economic growth of the developed countries that is the
key underlying factor for the global environmental crisis? What do these
articles disclose as to how developing countries define sustainable
development?
(3) How would you rate the three global environmental megaconferences of
1992, 2002, and 2012? Given that the environmental crisis shows no sign of
letting up, nevertheless, how would you define their contribution to global
governance? If their goal too was to balance global economic and
environmental goals, think of reasons why the global economy is growing
without limits while global environmental devastation is worsening and
proving so hard to reverse.
(4) Agenda 21 set out the blueprint for sustainable development, but it hasn’t
been implemented as planned. Is the failure of the developed countries to
undertake financial commitments to the developing countries an impassable
obstacle? What other circumstances contribute to its disappointing track

record? Can sustainable development work in a competitive global economy
based on unlimited growth and consumption?
(5) The UN Harmony with Nature Initiative seeks to root sustainable
development in a number of Earth law principles. Do you think that Earth
law and sustainable development through the UN can be reconciled? What
other measures would you suggest for incorporating rights for nature into
international legal instruments? Would you recommend a binding convention
on rights for nature? Do you think rights of nature can be upheld in a way
that respects the goal of developing countries to alleviate poverty? How
might you articulate the advantages and disadvantages?
(6) How would you address the non-governmental organizations’ criticism of
“green economies” at the 2012 UNCSD? Do you think “green economies” is
the most viable solution, or should economic development not be the goal at
all? For example, a different goal would be a “green society” or a “thriving
society.” Think of a few more examples.
(7) John Ikerd’s description of deep sustainability describes it as being “co-
centric” rather than anthropocentric or ecocentric. Similarly, many of the
legal movements that comprise Earth law can be described as being on a
spectrum between ecocentric and anthropocentric law, often incorporating
elements of both while trying to find a balance that upholds the well-being of
all life on the planet. Do you think it is possible for sustainability to be “co-
centric,” representing both anthropocentrism and ecocentrism at once, or
must it be one or the other?
(8) Generally, international environmental conventions have failed in
reversing the environmental crisis. Do you think that a Global Pact for the
Environment as described in this chapter would be an appropriate response to
the current state of the environment? In your opinion, what are the flaws and
the strengths of a Global Pact for the Environment?
(9) As the chapter explains, the proposed Global Pact includes relatively few
new principles. Most of the ideas have already been stated in various treaties,
conventions, and declarations. Does that mean the Global Pact is likely to see
little resistance to adoption? Or, does it mean that the Global Pact is
unnecessary since most of the principles that it is promoting already enjoy

binding legal status through international conventions?
(10) What other creative ways can you think of to integrate Earth law
principles into international fora? For example, what if “nature” was
recognized as having rights and then had its own delegation to negotiate
environmental treaties, such as the UNFCCC? Or what if “nature” (as
represented by legal guardians) held a seat in the UN General Assembly—or
multiple seats for the oceans, forests, watersheds, and so forth? Would this
create a more equitable “eco-democracy” that gave a voice to nature? Would
nations object to this structure, and if so, how could that be overcome?
