CHAPTER 16
Ecocentric Governance: The New 
Ecological Social Contract1
I. INTRODUCTION
Earth law encompasses all legal structures and mechanisms that protect,
stabilize, and restore the functional interdependency of Earth’s life and life-
support systems. Ecocentric or ecological governance (the two terms are used
interchangeably) is an essential part of Earth law and is the subject of this
chapter. Topics covered include the new ecological social contract, the role of
lawyers in ecological governance, and the rights of nature laws in Bolivia as
a case study in implementing ecocentric governance.
In a very general sense, the social contract is the mutual agreement of people
in a society to be governed at this time, in a certain way, and by certain rules.
A social contract theory gives an explanation of what this mutual agreement
is, and, also, what people should expect from the government and its laws. In
a time of stability, the social contract is in place—like the air people breathe,
it is there but they do not give attention to it. In a time of great historical
change from one period to another, however, the existing contract receives
attention, as it must be reaffirmed or be recreated.
The early twenty-first century is such a period of great historical change—
perhaps the greatest since agricultural civilization began 11,000 years ago.
Like then, both human history and Earth’s geobiological history are changing
—then from the Pleistocene (the last ice age) to the Holocene epoch, and now

from the Holocene to the still warmer Anthropocene epoch (see Chapter 3,
Section II, “Understanding the Anthropocene Epoch”). The Holocene was a
period of relatively stable climate and humans were generally able to take
nature for granted. In the Anthropocene, climate is changing rapidly along
with Earth’s life and life-support systems. The existing human-only social
contract is being called into question. There is now a need for a social
contract that includes nature, an ecological social contract.
II. THE ECOLOGICAL SOCIAL CONTRACT
A. Bruno Latour: The Social Contract with Nature
Bruno Latour in his 2013 Gifford Lectures on Facing Gaia sets the stage for
considering a new ecological social contract.2
Latour states we should not be alarmed if the current disruption of planetary
life leads to social upheaval ending the human-only social contract because it
was not designed to hold together in the present encounter with Gaia.3 We
might be upset, frustrated, and dismayed, but not any more alarmed than we
would be if slowly rising sea levels caused the collapse of a failing sea wall.
We have known about the disruption of planetary life and the strains it is
placing on societies for a long time.
Latour continues by saying that because humans are now facing planetary
limits, they have entered a new Hobbesian condition of a “war of all against
all.” The protagonists now include plants, animals, fires, storms, and carbon
emissions, as well as the various human factions—all are seeking their places
in Earth’s limited space. This new “state of nature” is not the condition
described by Hobbes that existed prior to the formation of the human social
contract long ago; rather, it is a present condition that has arisen because the
human social contract is incomplete.4 A new social contract that includes
nature is needed and it has to be assembled bit by bit. The laws of the new
polity have to be invented and be self-imposed because “[w]ithout decision,
there is no body politics, no liberty, [no] autonomy.”5
In his 2018 book, Down to Earth: Politics in the New Climatic Regime,

Latour expands on the nature of politics in the Anthropocene. In addition to
right and left, he posits there are now two new political poles—“Out-of-This-
World” and “Terrestrial.” People inclined to Out-of-This-World seek to
escape the existing planetary situation through climate denial, alternative
facts, populism, fascism, offshore tax havens, gated communities, and even
settling other planets. Due to the pull of the Out-of-This-World perspective,
humanity is losing a common world of reality in relation to what is happening
to Earth. Restoring this common world depends on those who are inclined to
the Terrestrial.
Being Terrestrial, as explained by Latour, does not have an obvious meaning
such as becoming green, natural, ecological, or environmental. These
movements have not been able to mobilize politically on a sufficient enough
scale to effectuate change in the social contract; rather, they have resulted in
decades of frozen political positions. Those who choose the Terrestrial have
no established political party or institutional form (though they are
necessarily active in political parties and institutions). They are neither left
nor right, conservative nor liberal, reactionary nor progressive, global nor
local. Their pull to the Earth sharpens these conflicts, deploys them
differently, and seeks allies on all sides by calling attention to issues that are
more basic than those dominating current political discourses. Rather than
asking how to grow (or degrow) the economy, expand the pie, or redistribute
wealth, Terrestrials ask, “How is humanity in the twenty-first century going
to be able to subsist on Earth?” Their goal is not to save the Earth, to protect
it, or to live in harmony with it; it is to learn how to become dependent on it.
They do not defend nature; they are nature defending themselves. The
Terrestrials are not engaged in modernity’s pursuit of some infinite horizon
where everyone will have all they want and do as they wish; instead, they are
engaged in a journey to Earth—to becoming bound by Earth’s limits
(Earthbound).
Terrestrials will construct the new social contract with nature.
B. Bruce Jennings on Ecological Governance
Bruce Jennings, like Bruno Latour, writes about a new social contract. The
major theme of Jennings’s 2016 book, Ecological Governance: Toward a

New Social Contract with the Earth, is that humans need to move from the
current consumptive social contract to a new ecological social contract.
1. Governance is more than government, and the meaning of the social
contract
Jennings distinguishes governance from government: “Governance is the
overall process of coordinating, shaping, and directing individual and
collective agency. [It] is inherently normative and value-laden.…[It]
embodies the character of the collectivity, representing the kind of society an
association of people aspires to be or become.…[I]ts work is the construction
of institutionalized normative practice and symbolic orders of meaning.”6
Governance involves more than the government; it involves economic,
religious, cultural, and many other civil society institutions.
The social contract is at the base of governance. “[It] refers to the
fundamental norms of common consent that provide social cohesion. It is the
mutual agreement that provides grounds for our moral ideals and our sense of
worth and happiness.”7 The social contract limits freedom in that people
agree to common rules because they need each other for survival and
flourishing, and, by doing so, freedom arises that would not otherwise be
possible.
2. Social contract theories: Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau
The three great writers on the social contract are Thomas Hobbes (1588–
1679), John Locke (1632–1704), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778).
For Hobbes, humans are driven by the passions—especially fears about
survival—not reason. They have no innate virtue and originally lived, as
depicted in Hobbes’ masterpiece Leviathan, in a state of nature that was nasty
and brutish—a war of all against all. People lacked a deterrent against attack
and common rules for cooperation, so they voluntarily entered into a social
contract to obtain a common sovereign for defense and enforcement of the
rules. In Hobbes’s view, once established, the power of the sovereign is
absolute and without moral limit—only an absolute sovereign can avoid the
anarchy of the state of nature. The sovereign, which may be one person or an

assembly of people, defines the laws and morality. Science and commerce are
encouraged but not religion or metaphysical beliefs. Peace, tranquility, order,
and, in Hobbes’s words, “commodious living” are the purpose of civil
society.8
Locke’s social contract theory also begins with a state of nature. In it, people
are equal and pursue life, health, liberty, and possessions (property). They are
not amoral as imagined by Hobbes, rather they are subject to the laws of God
and nature, yet they may be selfish and violent. Humans are free, but they are
threatened by others. The alternative to life in this condition is a
representative government subject to the will of the majority that protects the
basic human rights to life, liberty, and property under the rule of law
administered by an impartial judge. People are governed by their consent.
They grant to the state a monopoly on the use of force (reserving the right to
self-defense). If the state, however, endeavors to breach their rights to life,
liberty, and property, they have a right of revolution. Government is limited;
its main obligations are to protect the rights of its citizens, especially their
property rights, and provide for the common defense.
Rousseau, like Hobbes and Locke, saw the formation of the social contract as
an act of reciprocal agreement to live in a society governed by laws, rules,
and political authority (the “State”), but unlike in Hobbes, people never
completely transfer power to the State. They continually reaffirm and reenact
the social contract to hold the State in check. Rousseau did not see the source
of conflict that leads to the contract in the nature of humans but rather in the
frictions of social existence as people culturally and psychologically develop.
Thus, conflict “is a contingent cultural and historical condition, not a natural
one.”9
Unlike Hobbes and Locke, Rousseau did not imagine a pure state of nature
preceding the social contract. Rather he saw humans moving into societies as
a natural process. The social contract is a means to orderly living, moral
development, and human flourishing. The State responds to a need of living
in society—in other words, of living in mutual dependence and fellowship of
others—but the State may also be a source of oppression. Rousseau sought to
construct a theory of the social contract by which people would have the
benefit of society yet remain as free as before the contract. His conception of

freedom is not the ability to do what one wants without restraint—this is
enslavement to the passions. Freedom is the ability to act in accord with
higher laws, rules of universal application that make community, care, and
association possible. The State may, in like manner, act in accord with such
universal laws. When it treats its members equally in accord with the
common good, it augments, rather than diminishes, individual freedom.
Yet, it is up to the people to ensure that the State does this. Sovereignty
resides not in the State, but in the general will (la volunté général) of the
people. As G. D. H. Cole puts it, “[T]he State is based not on any original
convention, [nor] on any determinate power, but on the living and sustaining
rational will of its members.”10 This is not the sum total of the individual
wills of the people—Rousseau calls this the “will of all.” The general will is
the imperishable sense of the common good in accord with a moral ideal that
calls the association into being and is operative within it. It is not an abstract
ideal; it exists by reason of the active willing of it. “[T]he General Will is
realized not when that is done which is best for the community, but when, in
addition, the community as a whole has willed the doing of it. Then General
Will demands not only good government, but also self-government—not only
rational conduct, but good-will.”11 This sovereignty is inalienable because
the people, not the government, are the absolute and they ultimately control
their own destiny.
Jennings describes the general will as follows:
[The general will] is not a person or an office; it is a moral culture and a spirit
of community and solidarity. It is a capacity for a radically demanding
impartiality of moral intention and the scrupulously public use of political
power.…It is socially and politically embodied in a participatory republic,
that is, in a set of interlocking governance institutions that rest on the periodic
re-creation of the general will by a popular assembly of all citizens. And the
general will is culturally embedded in a special form of moral imagination
and civic virtue, one informed by the independent judgment of each citizen
and by a strong widespread sense of common need, vulnerability, and equal
concern and respect.12
The social contract, sovereignty, and the general will are all in continuous

processes of becoming. Association is needed for moral development and
fulfillment. For the promise of this association to be realized, people must
commit themselves to it and actively engage in it for the common good. The
actual will of the people is corrigible but through enlightened public
participation may move toward the ideal general will. “The will must be
‘general’ in two senses: in the sense in which Rousseau used the word, it
must be general in its object, i.e. universal; but it must also be generally held,
i.e. common to all or to the majority.”13
The general will is always present as a motivating force, even when it is not
realized. The reason it is not achieved is because of factionalism and amour-
propre—“vanity, self-regard, the tendency to get one’s sense of self from
being seen and approved of by others, insincerity and inauthenticity.”14 What
is needed is pitié, which corresponds to empathy or compassion, the ability to
go beyond oneself, and the consideration of the needs of others. Thus, after
describing the general will, Jennings states: “[It] is a precarious achievement
in human history…the highest expression of our communal humanity, and it
arises from the development of humanity out of nature through culture.”15
Therefore, there is a need for a cultural order to cultivate the good that is in
human nature and provide education for enlightened political engagement so
that the common good or ideal general will might be realized.
3. Jennings’s new ecological social contract
Building on Rousseau’s work, Jennings extends the social contract from one
among humans to one among humans and nature. He states: “The sphere of
right, or justice, as I understand it, includes (1) the moral community of both
human and nonhuman life and (2) the ecological commons—the symbiotic,
interdependent systems, both natural and social, upon which human being
and becoming depend.”16 Thus, the general will is not just that of humans but
of humans and nature, and, further, the cultural order that cultivates and
educates humans includes nature’s order and activity.17 His work responds to
Latour’s call for a social contract with nature. Even though there is an already
existing human social contract, planetary limits have put humans and other
living beings in a new “state of nature” that is no longer viable. Thus, a new
ecological social contract is needed for orderly living, moral development,

and the flourishing of all species.
According to Jennings, the existing social contract of consumption is the
product of the history of modernity. This begins in the sixteenth century with
emancipation from the constraints of feudalism. The Enlightenment of the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries gave rise to empiricism, materialism,
science, technology, reason, utilitarianism, diversity, tolerance, secular
liberalism, separation of church and state, lack of transcendent value in public
culture, and loss of the commons. The Industrial Revolution of the nineteenth
and twentieth centuries meant the market economy and commodification of
nature and labor. This led to a development model based on carbon-intensive
energy use, technology, and consumerism. In the Great Acceleration, the
period following World War II,18 the political economy shifted from
egalitarian liberalism to market liberalism (neoliberalism) predicated on the
assumption that the optimal results for human civilization would be obtained
by continuous economic growth. The fundamental values of modernity are
freedom, equality, human rights, pursuit of happiness, and possessive
individualism. In the consumptive social contract, ordinary citizens give
political and business elites control in exchange for the promise of economic
growth and improved material conditions.
At the heart of this social contract is a political economy.19 “A political
economy is a structure of power and a form of large-scale social
coordination.”20 It is the way that society organizes itself to meet human
needs and material aspirations. It is socially constructed based on values and
assumptions and the availability of materials and technologies. It is a rule-
based system for the use and conservation of resources and the production
and distribution of goods and services. The political economy of the social
contract of consumption assumes unlimited resources, unlimited sinks,21 and
continuous economic growth through industrial development. The opponent
of this political economy is natural limits.
[T]he accelerating global extractive assault on planetary resources and
ecosystems, as well as the unprecedented extensions of our technological
reach, do not truly represent progress and the triumph of human freedom or
the human destiny. Why not? [Because] they are not sustainable or viable as
a road to the future.…While seeming to extend human freedom, economic

behavior and technology are laying the groundwork for its repression; while
seemingly representing the advanced expression of human capability, they
are actually undermining what is most precious in humanness.22
The dilemma for leaders today is that, on the one hand, “[s]ocial order and
stability in virtually every nation rests on economic activity based on the
intensive procurement and use of energy-rich fossil fuels.…[This] has made
possible most of modern technology and industrial civilization;”23 and on the
other hand, the procurement and use of these fuels and the industrial systems
they support poses an imminent threat to civilization. Modernity’s storyline is
that natural limits can be always be overcome by technological innovation or
substitution of materials or sources. Jennings points out, however, that earlier
natural limits were not overcome; rather, humans found natural pathways that
would handle the burden of human extraction and production of waste and
pollution at those times.24 Are humans now facing absolute natural limits,
sometimes called “planetary boundaries,” that make the continuation of the
consumptive social contract not only unwise in the near term but also
impossible in the medium and long term? For Jennings, the answer is
presumptively yes.
In consideration of this presumption, Jennings, as a social contract theorist,25
puts forward an ecological social contract as being normatively the best for
our times. In rejecting the idea that only technological changes are needed, he
aligns with and quotes Pope Francis in Laudato Si’:
Ecological culture cannot be reduced to a series of urgent and partial
responses to the immediate problems of pollution, environmental decay and
the depletion of natural resources. There needs to be a distinctive way of
looking at things, a way of thinking, policies, an educational programme, a
lifestyle and a spirituality which together generate resistance to the assault of
the technocratic paradigm.…To seek only a technical remedy to each
environmental problem which comes up is to separate what is in reality
interconnected and to mask the true and deepest problems of the global
system.26
This quote offers a segue into a discussion of the importance of value systems
in a social contract. People enter a social contract for survival and defense

(negative reasons) and also, as social beings, to be whom they aspire to be for
happiness, fulfillment, and meaning, and for how they can extend the
capabilities for flourishing to others (positive reasons).27 Thus, also at the
heart of a social contract are “ethical principles, rules, and norms, which,
when they are accepted and practiced widely enough, become an orienting
and directing force in society.”28 These standards grow out of tradition and
are maintained by habit, but are also created by reflection. When a historical
shift occurs, such as is occurring in the early twenty-first century, the changes
can be quite radical.
Jennings’s appeal to morality is an important factor in the move to a new
ecological social contract as there must be a moral justification for people to
forego the benefits of the consumptive social contract.29 Without widespread
consent, there is no new ecological social contract, there is only a partisan
group within society that holds ecological values. The new contract involves
reasoned conviction, a measure of contentment, and an appeal to ideals of a
higher order. The social contract is not a bargained agreement for personal
benefit; it is a moral community.
With this as background, Jennings offers what he takes to be the key terms of
the ecological social contract:
These terms are: (1) creating a system of wealth that moves beyond affluence
and scarcity to plentitude and frugality; (2) creating a system of property that
moves beyond commodities to commons; (3) creating a system of freedom or
liberty that moves beyond noninterference and independent self-sufficiency
to relationality and interdependence; and (4) creating a system of citizenship
that moves beyond self-interested advantage to trusteeship for right
relationship and right recognition.30
The transition from the consumptive social contract to the ecological social
contract will be difficult: “A new social contract for ecological governance
will need to navigate conflicting social and economic interests and blocking
coalitions on many fronts. It must be continually recreated and renewed.”31
“[It]must provide the transitional generation of citizens with a way to respond
positively to the foreclosing of an unsustainable growth future they have been
taught to expect.”32 It must show that it can achieve justice in terms of equity

for present generations and for future generations. And it must offer the
promise of sustainability and care for nature.
Jennings is concerned about the future of democratic societies. He foresees
three possible types of governance orientations in an ecological political
economy. The first is ecological authoritarianism. “[E]cological
authoritarians maintain that the successful governance in an ecological era
will require centralized, elitist, and technocratic management at least in the
areas of economic and environmental policy.”33
The second is ecological discursive democracy. “[It] involves
institutionalization and empowerment of participatory and discursive
governance within a diverse and pluralistic society and culture.…[It] grows
directly out of concerted action with others, shaped by debate and
deliberation.” It differs from the current interest group democracy, which
involves the aggregation of interests of different groups in a diverse
population with conflicting interests. These groups compete for the attention
of elected officials. The role of the citizen centers around voting, with only a
few playing a larger role through financial contributions or involvement in
political action groups. In contrast to discursive democracy, “the citizen role
is actively and extensively participatory at multiple levels.” In Jennings’s
view, interest group democracy “is prone to incrementalism and preservation
of the status quo.” “[It] is not succeeding and is structurally incapable of
presiding over the transition from a consumptive growth-oriented political
economy to an ecological political economy.”34
The third is ecological constitutionalism. Ecological constitutionalism
“would involve the creation of several elite governing entities that can check
and balance the more representative institutions such as the presidency or
legislature.”35 There are already examples of such entities, with the most
familiar being the judiciary. The Federal Reserve is another example with
authority over monetary policy. Yet another example is independent
administrative agencies that are protected from political influence. The kinds
of entities that would be needed for an ecological political economy might be
special environmental courts modeled on the business courts that already
exist in various states, administrative agencies with different powers than
existing environmental protection agencies, or civil society groups that

exercise only soft power.36
Jennings believes that the best overall outcome is probably a combination of
discursive democracy and ecological constitutionalism.
A final theme of note in Jennings’s work is recovery of the political, which is
a concern of Latour’s as well. The present consumptive social contract gives
individual freedom37 but not relational freedom.38 It works against relational
freedom, which is the ability to act in solidarity with others for the common
good. Relational freedom is what is needed to meet the demands of the
future. In the ecological social contract, “the problem of politics is not to seek
power, but to resist it; and not to deny vulnerability and dependency but to
embrace them creatively. The problem of [this] politics is to resist the kind of
power and domination that actually render its agents impotent and enthralled.
The problem of [this] politics is to accept restraints on behalf of communal
agency and relational freedom.”39 “It needs the vocabulary of solidarity,
mutuality, reciprocity, community and the common good.”40

(1) Bruno Latour says Earth (Gaia) is both mother (nurturing) and other (has
a dangerous quality). How does this distinction help Earth law to recognize
that nature is both nurturing and threatening?
(2) Latour says that by bringing issues down to Earth and asking basic
questions about a viable future for humans and their dependence on Earth,
Terrestrials sharpen the distinctions between left and right, conservative and
liberal, reactionary and progressive, and global and local, and cast them in a
new light. How might this be so?
(3) How does Jennings distinguish between government and governance?
(4) Describe the consumptive social contract and its most critical elements.
(5) Describe the ecological social contract and its most critical elements.
(6) Both Latour and Jennings say the social contract among humans alone is

incomplete and needs to include nature. Do you think this means that the
human social contract needs to take nature more fully into account, or that
there needs to be a contract among humans and nonhuman nature? If the
latter, how would it be possible for humans to have a contract with nonhuman
nature? What would nature’s role be in the general will?

III. THE ROLE OF LAWYERS IN
ECOLOGICAL GOVERNANCE
The remainder of this chapter concerns the role of lawyers in ecological
governance, and how they might play a part in developing a new social
contract. It covers the place of lawyers in society; accepting Earth as a client;
Earth lawyers and the ecological social contract; Earth lawyers and the
reform of law; and a case study of the rights of nature laws in Bolivia.
A. The Place of Lawyers in Society
For most lawyers, governmental bodies and their laws form the backdrop of
their practices. They devote little of their attention to governance itself (with
notable exceptions, such as lobbyists). Many students come to law school
expecting to learn social theory and political advocacy and find instead they
learn “THE LAW.” Their task is to learn the law and understand how law
applies to factual situations. After law school, they apply this skill in their
practices by acting as advocates for their clients, which means helping clients
achieve their goals within the bounds of the law.
As lawyers carry on their practices, they may, over time, become less clear as
to how much THE LAW is determinative. In court, opposing lawyers argue
the facts and the law, yet claim different results. In appeals courts, legal
arguments are made and then some judges rule one way and others another.
Further, practicing lawyers may find situations where law is not
determinative in terms of achieving justice. It may become clear that the legal
system is a means of power and exclusion and that it is closely tied to the
goal of progress through continuous and unlimited economic growth. It may

also become clear how law structures relationships by creating lawscapes of
land and societies. For many lawyers, practicing Earth law and making a
living will seem in conflict. What is good for the Earth may not be what
clients want and what clients want may not be good for the Earth. Practicing
lawyers will find that the rules of professional ethics do not cover many of
the ethical issues related to Earth law.
An attorney is an agent, yet in respect of Earth law (though less so in respect
of environmental law), attorneys may feel at a loss for agency, or, in other
words, in their ability to act on behalf of Earth. This is because their practices
may seem unrelated to Earth law or even counter to it. Further, if they
consciously undertake an Earth law practice, they will face obstacles in the
way the legal system is structured. For example, doctrines of property law
and issues of standing, as discussed in Chapters 4 and 5 of this book, impose
impediments.
Yet, who is better positioned than lawyers to bring into being ecological
governance?
Lawyers have special skills in analysis, organization, and expression of
thought, in organization of entities, in negotiation of transactions, and in
settlement of disputes. Many have skills in overcoming factionalism and
roadblocks to move things forward and in forming and maintaining alliances.
They are granted enviable status in society—any lawyer knows the power of
saying, “I’m a lawyer.” On the whole, lawyers are affluent members of
society. Historically, they have played prominent roles in elective and
appointed positions of government. They also play prominent roles in social
organizations from churches to foundations to think tanks to administrations
of universities. Bar associations and legal societies have influence on the
appointment of judges, and they are consulted on legislation and public
policy.
And, most important of all, lawyers are trained in the law and are embedded
in the legal system.
B. Taking on Earth as a Client: A Reality Check

A quality that is important to the practice of law is being realistic. Practicing
lawyers receive little to no reward for what they think ought to be the case.
They are measured for the most part by the results they achieve. Law is an
intense intellectual exercise in that lawyers are called on to understand
complex factual situations and weigh legal, social, and economic factors in
advising and representing their clients to provide the best outcomes. Lawyers
may agree or disagree with their clients’ goals, values, and decisions, yet, so
long as they maintain the relationship, they seek to further their clients’ goals
within the law. In doing so, the task of the lawyer is to assess and act on what
is realistically possible.
What if a lawyer’s client were Earth and the client’s goal was to survive and
thrive? Your client wants your representation in promoting change from
anthropocentric to ecocentric governance. This representation involves a
level of complexity not heretofore imagined. Still, the lawyer might draw on
the skills they have acquired—listen, learn, assess what and who you can rely
on and what are the obstacles, be realistic.…
You will find that as an Earth lawyer, you will receive highly conflicting
accounts of the state of the planet, the needs of the planet, and how Earth law
should be practiced. This will not only be the case with the planet but also
with the particular environmental situations of humans and other species.
Believing one knows how to save Earth or even the right way to practice
Earth law is a liability not an asset. Earth lawyers are seekers, information
hounds, critical thinkers, and dreamers. They are participants in a process of
healing that will outlive them. In deciding what to do, they should ask, “Will
this engender life?”
They should be realistic while still reaching for and planning to accomplish
what has not been done before.
C. Earth Lawyers and the Ecological Social Contract
The overarching task of every Earth lawyer is to bring into being the new
ecological social contract. Without this, no matter how many Earth law
victories are won, the objective of Earth law will not be achieved. To be an
Earth lawyer, one does not need to be an environmental lawyer. Any lawyer

may be an Earth lawyer. An Earth lawyer is a lawyer who is willing to take as
starting points that nature has limits, that the consumptive social contract is
unsustainable, and that a new ecological social contract is needed. Earth
lawyers commit to bringing a new ecological social contract into being by
thought, word, and deed.
They cannot do this acting alone; they can do this only in concert with other
like-minded people in law and in other walks of life. Ultimately for the
contract to come into being, it will require the consent of the whole society.
In a globally connected world, it will require the consent of all people. This
would not mean that each person in the world would have to give conscious
consent to an express written social contract any more than this was required
to bring into being the present consumptive social contract. It would mean
people consciously or unconsciously would become part of a new moral
culture and a new political economy. In a spirit of community and solidarity,
they would accept new ways of doing things as well as the institutions that
embody them and make them possible. It would mean people would have a
level of satisfaction that in this new arrangement they could be what they
aspire to be and they could extend the capabilities for flourishing to others.
As noted above, lawyers bring special skills, abilities, social status, and roles
to this task. If they are corporate lawyers, they could guide their clients in
understanding that the failures of the old are the opportunities of the new.
They could help their clients see that profits are a means to providing needed
goods and services and employment, not an end in themselves, that the
granting of a public charter is the grant of a public trust, and that the fiduciary
responsibilities of officers and directors extend to the entire community of
life. Corporate lawyers and other lawyers involved in business law, such as
employment, banking, securities, tax, real estate, and business litigation
lawyers, are involved at a high level in all the activities of the consumptive
political economy. They could model humility and the values of the
ecological political economy in their own personal lives, in their practices,
and in their law firms. The choices they could make in how they live, the
conferences they attend, and the roles they take on in the community would
make a difference. The table conversations they could have with their clients
would as well. While it might seem difficult to bring up Earth law, people are
interested in the Earth and how they can make a difference. By being Earth

lawyers, they would attract clients who are moving on the path to an
ecological political economy. They could draw the line when what their
clients are doing is wrong—even if it is legal. They could practice the spirit
of the law as well as the letter of the law. If needed, they could discontinue
the representation of clients. Business lawyers could engage in the reform of
laws and the establishment of the new institutions for the ecological social
contract. They could become engaged in civic, political, and religious
associations with other members of society.
Earth lawyers who are not business lawyers could find similar ways of
bringing into being a new ecological social contract. For example, intellectual
property lawyers could seek to reform patent law so that it benefits the
ecosystems from which many “human inventions” are derived.41 Estate
planning lawyers could work with their clients to bequeath some or all of
their estate for the permanent benefit of nature, as well as for the benefit of
Indigenous peoples and others whose land has been taken. Criminal lawyers
could call for the recognition of ecocide as a crime, both in the International
Criminal Court and in national legal systems. Civil rights lawyers could lend
their expertise to emerging rights-based movements for nature. Voting rights
lawyers could help conceptualize and implement effective voting schemes on
behalf of nonhuman ecosystems and animals. Environmental lawyers could
continue enforcing environmental laws while calling for passage of a new
generation of ecocentric laws. Every lawyer could have a role.
Lawyers, however, cannot help by intention alone. They must engage in the
task in thought, word, and deed.42
D. Earth Lawyers and the Reform of Law: Normative
Jurisprudence
Much of this book is devoted to litigation strategies in Earth law. Attorneys
today are arguing for the rights of nature, the public trust, the rights of future
generations, and environmental human rights. Litigation is essential for the
advancement of Earth law.
This section of this chapter, however, covers a different aspect of Earth law—
the role of Earth lawyers in the reform of positive law and in the means of

enforcing such law. Positive law for purposes of this chapter means written
laws, such as statutes, regulations, constitutions, and civil and criminal
procedure. Enforcement of positive law means making such law operational
and effective.
Law schools focus on what the law is, not what it should be. While practicing
lawyers and legal scholars do advocate for changes in law, these reforms tend
to be within a narrow frame of reference consistent with the consumptive
social contract, such as reforms to advance the economic interests of clients.
(Notable exceptions include lawyers advancing justice and welfare reforms
for humans and nature.) Normative jurisprudence “both criticizes [existing]
positive law and suggests reforms on the basis of stated moral values and
legalistic ideals.”43 It concerns “[t]he nature of the legal good—what makes
law good and virtues a good law ought to have.”44 Interpreting Thomas
Aquinas’s famous statement in Summa Theologica, “An unjust law is no law
at all,” one would say a law must have a moral justification for it to be
binding. Normative jurisprudence seeks to understand the moral justification
for particular laws or the lack of the same and proposes good law on the basis
of moral claims.
What is a moral claim? At its simplest, a moral claim is a statement made of
a kind that when a person hears the statement, she responds, “Yes, this is my
duty. It is something I ought to do.” Laws need to be largely self-enforcing.
For example, people are asked to file tax returns that state their true income
and then they are taxed on this income. Only rarely will they be audited if
they do not accurately represent their income. Fear of potential enforcement
activity motivates compliance, but even more, it is the sense that obeying the
law is what one ought to do to provide for the public welfare. If people do not
feel this moral obligation and they feel enforcement is unlikely, compliance
will be low.
Jennings, following on Rousseau, however, offers a broader conception of
moral obligation. Laws are not just what is written on paper; they are willed
into being and are maintained by an active will. When they no longer serve a
public purpose, they may remain on the books but have no effect. Some laws
come into being by “particular wills” and are maintained by them. Some laws
come into being by the general will, but when their time is past, they are

maintained by particular wills and perhaps will later be reformed by the
general will.
The way that the concept of the general will changes moral justification is
that its morality is more than one’s personal sense of what I ought or ought
not do. It is a morality derived from a public discourse about the common
good. It is always more than one’s personal knowledge or determination—
this is why citizens read op-eds, talk with friends about their concerns, go to
school, listen to the news, enter into conversations in religious and social
groups, read magazines, and pray and meditate in concert with others. Some
of the considerations that emerge will be quite narrow; these are the particular
wills, or those that only take into account the needs of one group or interest.
Other considerations are broader as they are seeking not only the good of a
particular group or interest but the greater good. The general will does not
adhere to some abstract higher value or position, such as a doctrine, an
ideology, a particular religious teaching or belief, the views of a talk show
host, or a political party or faction. It comes out of enlightened public
discourse—the willing of the people for the common good. “[T]he most
general will is always the most just also, and [it is found in] the voice of the
people.”45
There is no final arbiter and no deity who announces this general will. It is an
ongoing process of discernment, it is always at work, and it is always right in
the sense of Martin Luther King, Jr.’s statement that “the arc of the moral
universe is long, but it bends toward justice”—that bend, however, occurs
only through the active participation of people in discerning and willing the
common good.46 This discerning does not, however, result in a final, clear
consensus agreement. The discerning is an ongoing process and what the
general will is will be expressed in diverse ways; nonetheless, this discerning
will be a unifying force for good. It will only be understood in retrospect,
and, even then, interpretations will vary.
Thus, in this understanding, Aquinas’s statement that “an unjust law is no law
at all” would mean the unjust law is not supported by the general will and
will not stand. Normative jurisprudence in this understanding would mean
that moral claims in support of reformed law and enforcement thereof should
be based on the general will and not some particular interest or moral frame.

What Jennings adds to Rousseau is that the public discourse extends to nature
and, therefore, necessarily beyond human language. The cosmos takes on a
moral character and nature becomes a source of wisdom.47 For Rousseau,
human freedom is found in the common good for humans; for Jennings,
human freedom is found in the common good for the Earth community,
including humans, where rivers, birds, and winds also speak and listen, and
we humans listen and speak to them, as well. It is worth recalling that for
Jennings and Rousseau, freedom is not primarily license (negative freedom),
it is relational freedom. One gives up the freedom of the state of nature in
order to have the greater freedom that comes from being in relation with
others. The distinction is easily understood by reference to the dynamics of
the nuclear family. If all family members insist on doing just what they want,
there is no family, only discord. When family members take into account the
needs of others, there is the freedom to live in supportive and responsive
relationships.
It will be a challenge for Earth lawyers to listen to Earth’s nonhuman
languages in considering the general will; yet, if Jennings is right, their
success will depend on it. This will involve outside-the-box thinking.
Consider this extension of the franchise to nonhuman beings proposed by
experimental philosopher Jonathon Keats at San José State University:
If the general will includes the will of animals and plants, even bacteria,
shouldn’t they also be enfranchised in democratic decision-making?
Although this question may at first seem to be purely philosophical, there are
ways to do this in practice. For instance, science has the tools to measure
stress hormones in many species. Changes in aggregate stress might
potentially be polled, revealing how those species are reacting to the current
body of law. An increase in stress hormone levels in enough organisms might
count as a call for change in the legal status quo. Data could inform the
choices made by human voters or legislators who are voluntarily acting as
proxies on a non-binding basis. At a greater extreme, taking the general will
to mean the will of Gaia, and according Gaia with the right to self-
determination, it could be argued that the votes of animals and plants
themselves ought to be counted officially in the choice of representatives or
in legislative decisions.48

No nation has yet granted nature the right to vote in this way. The Bolivian
case study below, however, shows how Indigenous people in Bolivia sought
to give nature a voice in government—a voice they had long included in their
polity.
E. The Rights of Nature in Bolivia
1. The historical experience
Bolivia is a land-locked country located in western-central South America. It
has had a tumultuous history, including a brutal period of Spanish colonial
rule followed, during independence, by many changes of government and
wars with neighboring countries. Bolivia is one of the poorest countries in the
Western Hemisphere as measured by standard economics. Mining has been a
key feature of the Bolivian economy for centuries and remains so today.
A majority of Bolivians identify as Indigenous. In 2005, Bolivia elected its
first Indigenous president, Evo Morales. His victory was seen as an outcome
of decades of struggle against neoliberal politics. Morales brought with him
Indigenous values of living well (suma qamaña/vivir bien) and respect for
Mother Earth (Pachamama49). In 2006, with the backing of a coalition of
Indigenous organizations called the “Unity Pact,” Morales convened a
Constitutional Assembly with the goal of forming a plurinational state—one
made up of many different “national” groups within Bolivia, including those
of Indigenous people.
In 2009, Bolivia adopted a new constitution. Its preamble recognized the
principles of vivir bien, protection of Mother Earth, equity, and redistribution
of social wealth, and declared Bolivia was being founded anew:
We have left the colonial, republican and neo-liberal State in the past. We
take on the historic challenge of collectively constructing a Unified Social
State of Pluri-National Communitarian law, which includes and articulates
the goal of advancing toward a democratic, productive, peace-loving and
peaceful Bolivia, committed to the full development and free determination
of the peoples.…

We found Bolivia anew, fulfilling the mandate of our people, with the
strength of our Pachamama and with gratefulness to God.50
The Constitution did not formally grant rights to Mother Earth, but it did
grant environmental rights to the people:
Everyone has the right to a healthy, protected, and balanced environment.
The exercise of this right must be granted to individuals and collectives of
present and future generations, as well as to other living things, so they may
develop in a normal and permanent way.
Any person, in his own right or on behalf of a collective, is authorized to take
legal action in defense of environmental rights, without prejudice to the
obligation of public institutions to act on their own in the face of attacks on
the environment.51
When Morales began his second term in 2009, he was already well-known in
international circles. In that year he attended the United Nations Climate
Change Conference in Copenhagen, where he blamed climate change on
capitalism, called for strong commitments to climate mitigation, and
demanded that the Global North pay its climate debt to the Global South.
Unsatisfied with the results of the conference, Morales invited people to
come to Cochabamba in April 2010 for the World People’s Conference on
Climate Change and the Rights of Mother Earth (the “World People’s
Conference”). In an often-festive atmosphere, 33,000 people assembled and
worked on issues such as climate change, equity and justice, alternative
development paths, the rights of nature, Indigenous rights, patriarchy, and
food sovereignty. At the end of the conference, a draft Universal Declaration
of the Rights of Mother Earth was adopted with a goal of having the
declaration adopted by the United Nations.
In December 2010, Bolivia passed the Law of the Rights of Mother Earth
(“the Mother Earth Rights Law”). In Chapter II, Article 3, Mother Earth
(Pachamama) was defined as follows:
Mother Earth is a dynamic living system comprising an indivisible
community of all living systems and living organisms, interrelated,
interdependent and complementary, which share a common destiny. Mother

Earth is considered sacred, from the worldviews of nations and peasant
indigenous peoples.
In Chapter III, Article 7, Mother Earth was given the following rights:
1. To life: The right to maintain the integrity of living systems and natural
processes that sustain them, and capacities and conditions for
regeneration.
2. To the diversity of life: It is the right to preservation of differentiation
and variety of beings that make up Mother Earth, without being
genetically altered or structurally modified in an artificial way, so that
their existence, functioning or future potential would be threatened.
3. To water: The right to preserve the functionality of the water cycle, its
existence in the quantity and quality needed to sustain living systems,
and its protection from pollution for the reproduction of the life of
Mother Earth and all its components.
4. To clean air: The right to preserve the quality and composition of air for
sustaining living systems and its protection from pollution, for the
reproduction of the life of Mother Earth and all its components.
5. To equilibrium: The right to maintenance or restoration of the
interrelationship, interdependence, complementarity and functionality of
the components of Mother Earth in a balanced way for the continuation
of their cycles and reproduction of their vital processes.
6. To restoration: The right to timely and effective restoration of living
systems affected by human activities directly or indirectly.
7. To pollution-free living: The right to the preservation of any of Mother
Earth’s components from contamination, as well as toxic and radioactive
waste generated by human activities.
In Article 8, the plurinational state was given the following duties, among
others:
Develop public policies and actions of prevention, early warning,
protection, and precaution;
Develop balanced forms of production and patterns of consumption,
while safeguarding the regenerative capacity and integrity of the cycles,
processes and vital balance of Mother Earth;
Develop policies to protect Mother Earth from the multinational and

international scope of exploitation of its components, from the
commodification of living systems or the processes that support them,
and from the structural causes and effects of global climate change; and
Develop policies to ensure the long-term energy sovereignty and gradual
incorporation of clean and renewable alternative sources into the energy
matrix.
In Article 9, these duties, among others, were imposed on natural persons and
public or private legal entities:
Uphold and respect the rights of Mother Earth;
Promote harmony with Mother Earth in all areas of her relationship with
other human communities and the rest of nature in living systems;
Participate actively, individually or collectively in generating proposals
designed to respect and defend the rights of Mother Earth;
Assume production practices and consumer behaviour in harmony with
the rights of Mother Earth;
Ensure the sustainable use of Mother Earth’s components; and
Report any act that violates the rights of Mother Earth, living systems,
and/or their components.
Article 10 called for the establishment of the Office of Mother Earth “to
ensure the validity, promotion, distribution and compliance of the rights of
Mother Earth established in this Act.” There were no other enforcement
mechanisms in the act.
Bolivia enacted a much more extensive law for the protection of Mother
Earth in October 2012, the Framework Law of Mother Earth and Integral
Development for Living Well (the “Framework Law,” and together with the
Constitution and the Mother Earth Rights Law, the “Mother Earth laws”).
Article 2 of the Framework Law stated that it had come into being within the
powers assigned in the Constitution and the Mother Earth Rights Law and
provided that “[i]t constitutes a Framework Law and of preferential
application for the development of specific laws, policies, norms, strategies,
plans, programs and projects.”
Both the Mother Earth Rights Law and the Framework Law were negotiated
between the government and the Unity Pact. In 2010, following the World

People’s Conference, the Unity Pact prepared a draft law on the rights of
Mother Earth based on the proceedings of that conference. Only a portion of
the draft was approved and included in the 2010 Mother Earth Rights Law.
Members of the Unity Pact felt that the abbreviated law may have been
passed to bolster Bolivia’s image at the Climate Change Conference held in
Cancun, Mexico, in 2010. The government insisted, however, that the Mother
Earth Rights Law paved the way for a comprehensive framework law to give
effect to the intentions of the 2010 law. The Framework Law passed by the
legislature in 2012 contained a watered-down version of the Unity Pact draft
and had extensive pro-development provisions. The legislature took the lead
in drafting the Framework Law and excluded certain Indigenous
organizations. Others dropped out of the legislative process and only a few
remained involved in the end.52
The Framework Law, in Article 1, contained this statement of purpose:
The purpose of this Law is to establish the vision and foundations of integral
development in harmony and balance with Mother Earth to Live Well,
guaranteeing the continuity of the regeneration capacity of the components
and systems of life of Mother Earth, recovering and strengthening local
knowledge and ancestral knowledge, within the framework of the
complementarity of rights, obligations and duties; as well as the objectives of
integral development as a means to achieve Living Well, the bases for
planning, public management and investments and the strategic institutional
framework for its implementation. (Emphases added.)
Thus, the Framework Law introduces the concept of “integral development”
in an effort to reconcile ecocentric respect and care for Mother Earth and
anthropocentric development. The difficulty is illustrated by the term
“extractivism,” which means “those activities which remove large quantities
of natural resources that are not processed (or processed only to a limited
degree), especially for export.”53 Extractivism as part of integral development
was recast as “neo-extractivism” by the Morales government. The intent was
to put mining and oil and gas production in Bolivia in a subordinate position
to the other values of building the plurinational state and also set them within
a chronology where neo-extractivism would be a bridge to vivir bien. Critics,
however, argued that neo-extractivism simply “maintain[ed] and

reproduce[d] key elements of the extractivism that date[d] back to colonial
times.”54
The Framework Law did contain many provisions in line with the Mother
Earth Rights Law, but it also placed an obligation on the government to
pursue mining, hydrocarbon extraction, and industrialization, always
cautioning that these should be undertaken with respect and care for Mother
Earth. Note that Bolivia has a high population growth rate, two-thirds of its
population lives in cities, and, in conventional economic terms, many of its
people are poor. It is especially vulnerable to climate change. Water supply
for cities and agriculture derives in part from tropical glaciers in the Andes
Mountains, which are melting. The Morales government, in line with the pro-
development provisions of the Framework Law, did succeed in increasing
economic growth and redistributing some wealth.
In 2019, Morales ran for a fourth time as president under questionable
authority as the constitution provided for only two terms. (His first term
predated the constitution.) The vote was held on October 20. Morales won
the vote, but election fraud was suspected. Supporters of Carlos Mesa,
Morales’s opponent, protested and convened nationwide strikes. Supporters
of Morales engaged in counterstrikes. The Organization of American States
was brought in to audit the election, found serious irregularities, and called
for a new election. Morales agreed, but the military suggested he resign.
Police units mutinied along with presidential guards. Morales fled the capital.
Mexico, declaring Morales the legitimate president, sent a jet to pick him up
and take him to Mexico, where he lives at the time of this writing. After three
supporters of Morales in line for presidential succession resigned, Jeanine
Áñez, who had been endorsed by the military, proclaimed herself president.
She made clear that she intended to purge Morales’s legacy. During his
presidency Morales had been opposed by conservative forces in Bolivia and
by the United States for his left-wing policies and for issues relating to
Bolivian narcotics trafficking. Now the conservatives are back in power.
This report on Bolivia and its rights of nature laws illustrates the complexity
of the relationships of law, economics, politics, and culture, and the
challenges involved in changing the social contract. It is instructive for Earth
lawyers, among other ways, as set out below.

2. A model to be developed
The Bolivian rights of nature laws on their face (as positive law) are a
remarkable achievement. They
Offer a vision of a better way of life, vivir bien;
Recognize a diversity of cultures and the rights of Indigenous people;
Call for a plurinational polity;
Recognize that all human development must take place within planetary
limits;
Call for respect for Mother Earth, for the rights of Earth’s life systems to
perform their functions, and for other species to flourish; and
Integrate meeting human needs through development with respect and
care for Earth.
Paola Villavicencio and Louis Kotzé wrote this about the laws:
Bolivia’s effort to legally protect the rights of Mother Earth is a significant
milestone. The country’s Constitution, its Law of the Rights of Mother Earth,
and the Framework Law are concrete examples in which the law attempts to
turn away (if not always successfully) from anthropocentric hierarchies while
embracing care for Mother Earth as an ethical obligation of ecological
stewardship. On paper at least, the legal protection of the rights of non-
human entities provides an opportunity for society to redirect its behaviour
away from growth-without-limits paradigms towards an altogether more
careful ecological approach.55
The Framework Law might be criticized for being a set of principles rather
than a precise legal document, yet this is what framework laws are. They set
general principles without necessarily including specific goals or targets or
enforcement mechanisms. They are written with the understanding that they
will be followed by additional laws, protocols, resolutions, and decisions.56
The Framework Law is a document along the lines of the United Nations’
World Charter for Nature57 and the Earth Charter.58 The Framework Law
goes beyond those, however, in that it grounds principles that are generally in
accord with these international documents in Bolivia’s own history, cultures,
and traditions and applies them to the governance of Bolivia. Bolivia’s

Mother Earth laws taken together are documents of governance in the broad
sense of the term used by Jennings. They are an articulation of a new
ecological social contract and a rejection of the social contract of
consumption.
3. A critical appraisal
After praising Bolivia’s Mother Earth laws on their face, Villavicencio and
Kotzé conclude their article as follows:
[T]here are important general insights that present themselves from the
Bolivian experience.…[O]ne such insight is that law has limitations, and one
must remain realistic about its potential to counter deeply vested political,
social and economic interests. Law will always remain merely one ingredient
(albeit a powerful one) in the social institutional regulatory toolbox.
However, where it does provide for radical formulations (such as rights of
nature), it prompts us to start having conversations about ways in which to
accommodate such novel juridical constructs in our social, economic,
religious, legal and political structures, including ways to implement them
and ways of resolving the many normative and practical contradictions that
are likely to arise when the interests that the rights of nature seek to protect
collide with those championed by the neoliberal developmental agenda[,
which is the] ultimate test for law in relation to protecting the rights of
Mother Earth.59
Bolivia’s rights of nature laws were hailed as a breakthrough on
environmental and Earth law websites, in progressive publications, and on
websites that highlight promising developments. Here are the headlines from
one newspaper:
Bolivia enshrines natural world’s rights
with equal status for Mother Earth
Law of Mother Earth expected to prompt radical new
conservation and social measures in South American nation60
Earth law websites continue to hold up Bolivia’s laws as an example of
where the rights of nature are taking hold. The history of Bolivia discussed

above, however, presents a far more complex picture. Even when Morales
was in power, Villavicencio and Kotzé questioned whether the laws were
merely window dressing intended to elevate Bolivia’s status on the world
stage while it continued to pursue development and extractivism.61 They
observed that as of August 2018 (when Morales was still in office), “the
Bolivian government has neither approved new environmental legislation
consistent with the Law of the Rights of Mother Earth and the Framework
Law, nor repealed major laws that are inconsistent with those laws; nor has it
established the Office for the Protection of Mother Earth.”62
In her doctoral dissertation, Carla Sbert Carlsson examined emerging
ecological law in various nations with particular attention to how this law
dealt with mining. She examined Bolivia’s Mother Earth laws based only on
their texts through a three-fold ecological lens of ecocentrism, ecological
primacy, and ecological justice and found on the whole that the laws were
ecocentric.63 Then she looked at how the laws worked in practice based on an
analysis of the Salar de Uyuni lithium industrialization project. This project
was announced by Morales in 2008 and involved several stages—from
developing a mine to eventually producing lithium batteries. Salar de Uyuni
is the world’s largest salt flat. It is the legacy of a prehistoric lake that went
dry leaving a desert-like 1,000-kilometer landscape. It contains one of the
world’s largest deposits of lithium and also holds sodium, potassium,
magnesium, and borax. Bolivia’s Mother Earth laws do not establish
licensing requirements, nor are there any regulations under the laws that
apply to the mining project. Instead, regulation of the mine is governed by the
1992 Law of the Environment. The mine, which is currently active, is
managed by a state agency known as Yacimientos de Litio Bolivianos
(YLB). YLB refers on its website to authorizations concerning the project but
does not mention Bolivia’s Mother Earth laws.
Sbert Carlsson attempts to apply the principles of the Mother Earth laws to
the project. For example, the mining activity involves using large amounts of
water and the disposal of large amounts of brine as a waste product. The
water is “fossil water” drawn from wells and is nonrenewable. She questions
whether drawing so much water contravenes the requirement in the Mother
Earth laws that economic activities are limited by the capacity of Mother
Earth to regenerate herself. She also considers whether mining, since it is a

nonrenewable activity that negatively affects wildlife, is consistent with
justice for future generations and other species. She notes that lithium is
considered essential to a global transition to renewable energy, but she does
not weigh this as a balancing factor.64
After examining conflicting rights among beings, she states: “This
complexity and the general difficulty of establishing proof in environmental
cases, begs the question whether the Rights of Mother Earth Law could be
implemented effectively even with the most dedicated effort; and if not,
whether legal recognition of the rights of nature (in this detailed way at least)
is a viable path for ecological law.”65
Her overall conclusion regarding the application of the Mother Earth laws to
the mining project was as follows: “In sum, it is hard to conclude from this
case study that the potentially transformative recognition of the rights of
Mother Earth and direction towards living well in Bolivian laws have had any
bearing on the actual implementation of a project as nationally important as
that of lithium industrialization.”66
4. Lessons for Earth lawyers from Bolivia
For a non-Bolivian, one’s initial reaction to what has happened in Bolivia
may be that it is a unique situation or that it has application only to
circumstances in Bolivia, in South America, or in the Global South generally.
There are some aspects that can be characterized this way, yet there are also
lessons applicable to all places. Some of these lessons are as follows.
Bolivia’s laws of Mother Earth offer a model for how to draft constitutions
and legislation for an ecological age. The values in the legislation are that of
the new ecological social contract. It was a signal accomplishment to have
passed these laws. This would not currently be possible in, for example, the
“advanced” United States. In 1982, the United Nations’ World Charter for
Nature was approved by 111 nations, 18 abstained, and only the United
States voted against it. The United States either did not sign or did not ratify
the Convention on the Law of the Sea (1990), Convention on Biological
Diversity (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (climate mitigation) (1997), the Rome
Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), or the Paris Agreement

(climate mitigation) (which became effective in November 2016—the
convention was signed by the Obama administration, in April 2016, but it
was not ratified by the U.S. Senate and, in August 2017, the United States
withdrew from the agreement).67 The Trump administration, as of December
2019 (after three years in office), had rolled back 95 previously enacted
environmental laws.68
Earth lawyers in the United States must consider whether or in what way its
environmental laws are a step toward ecological governance. What are the
values in those laws and how well do they map the values Jennings calls for
in ecological governance? In drafting its Mother Earth laws, Bolivia drew on
the wisdom of its Indigenous peoples; what might drafters of Earth laws in
the United States draw on from its history and culture? What in U.S. culture,
if anything, corresponds to vivir bien? In a country committed to economic
growth measured by GDP, of which 70 percent is accounted for by consumer
spending, what would a non-consumptive political economy look like?
Another area for reflection is whether the Bolivian experience is a judgment
on rights of nature laws. Have Earth lawyers promoted the passage of these
laws without critically reflecting on the complexity of applying them? If one
takes the position that an ecocentric perspective requires that rights of nature
laws make no distinctions among the various beings in nature—as Sbert
Carlsson did in applying the ecocentric part of her ecological lens to the
Mother Earth laws—can they provide legal guidance at all?69 Given the
impossibility of developing statues detailing the rights and duties respecting
each being and component of nature, can a framework law such as that in
Bolivia play a guiding role in policy?
The Bolivian experience also calls for reflection on the role of the written
ecocentric laws in relation to governance as a whole. For written laws to be
effective, they must be supported by law enforcement, the judicial system,
and the administrative branch. Laws must be largely self-enforcing by
voluntary compliance. For laws to be self-enforcing, the public generally
must find them and the political system just and fair. Economic
considerations, both domestic and international, come into play. People must
feel they have a means of support and that they can prosper. “Prosper” can be
framed as less consumptive living (vivir bien), but this has to be an

established expectation.
It could be said that environmental law treats the symptoms, not the disease,
and the Bolivian Mother Earth laws are intended to treat the disease. The
latter is what is needed. Earth lawyers must ask how they can realistically
build on the Bolivian experience. Neither law schools nor law practices
prepare lawyers for the challenges of Earth law. Conventional law practices
reward lawyers who learn “either-or” law and then use it to solve problems
for their clients.70 What is needed now is relational-evolutionary
jurisprudence. Winning and losing have a different meaning in this
jurisprudence. Winning means creative adjustment to ever-changing
circumstances; losing means failing to adapt. A client’s success can never be
separated from the success of the system as a whole. “Resilience” is a term
that has gained some currency as a description of success in an ecological
age. “Vitality” is another such term. It is the task of Earth lawyers to create
and practice resilient, vital law.
IV. CONCLUSION: DEPENDING ON THE
INTERCONNECTED WEB OF LIFE
In late 2019, an infectious virus, SARS-CoV-2 (commonly referred to as
COVID-19), caused by a particular coronavirus was first identified in
Wuhan, a city of 11 million in central China. Because COVID-19 has a
nearly identical genome sequence as a bat coronavirus, a theory for the origin
of the disease is that it was transmitted from a bat to a human.71 Further,
there is a theory that the virus started in a particular wet market in Wuhan.72
After infection of a single human being there, the disease spread rapidly to
people in nearly every nation in the world. As of this writing, there is no
vaccine for the disease and no cure. Social isolation and quarantine have been
determined to be the best ways to reduce its spread. As a result, on a global
basis, economic activity has fallen precipitously, millions have lost their jobs,
health systems have become overburdened, and large numbers of people have
died and continue to die.
At first this may not be thought of as an environmental issue, but many are
seeing a connection. According to Kate Jones, Chair of Ecology and

Biodiversity at University College London,
[V]iruses are on the rise…because there are so many of us and we are so
connected. The chance of more [spillovers into humans] happening is higher
because we are degrading these landscapes. Destroying habitats is the cause,
so restoring habitats is a solution.…It’s not OK to transform a forest into
agriculture without understanding the impact that has on climate, carbon
storage, disease emergence and flood risk.…You can’t do those things in
isolation without thinking about what that does to humans.73
In 1970, the first Earth day occurred and modern environmental law began.
Then the global population was 3.2 billion; now, 50 years later, there are
nearly 8 billion people. In 1970, there were around 200 million cars and
trucks; today, there are more than 1.5 billion. By almost every measure
human impact on Earth has skyrocketed. Before 1970, fires that consumed
100,000 acres were rare in the United States, but since then, there have been
dozens. In the summer of 2019, fires in Siberia consumed 17 million acres
and, in Australia, in 2019 and 2020, fires burned more than 10 million acres.
At present, deforestation is accelerating, coral reefs are dying, oceans are
acidifying, sunny day flooding is occurring, storms are becoming more
frequent and fiercer, and ice is melting. According to the WWF’s 2018 Living
Planet Report, population sizes of vertebrate species have declined on
average by 60 percent since 1970 (but there has not been as large of a
percentage drop in absolute numbers across species).74 In Germany, a study
found that the biomass of insects in certain protected areas has dropped by 76
percent in three decades.75
Crops depend on pollinators that are in decline. Drones have been tested to
carry pollen, which raises the question of whether humans are still dependent
on the interconnected web of life? Will humans always be able to find
substitutes for what is lost in nature? For Earth lawyers the answer to the
latter question is clear: It is a foolish wager to rely on.
Much has already been set in motion. Earth lawyers will not be surprised to
be living in an age of cascading crises. They will not dismiss them. Instead,
they will look for patterns and they will seek to understand the lessons in
them. In a twist on Soren Kierkegaard’s statement that “life is not a problem

to be solved but a reality to be experienced,” they will understand that our
planet is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be lived.
Different theories of the social contract are being played out. Some following
Hobbes see the state as sovereign “defin[ing] the laws and morality. Peace,
tranquility, order, and, in Hobbes’s words ‘commodious living’ are the
purpose of civil society.”76 Others following Locke hold that the “State’s
main obligations are to protect the rights of its citizens, especially their
property rights, and provide for the common defense.”77 The consent of
citizens is conditional and they are ever vigilant lest the state should trample
on their rights. Those following Rousseau hold that “[t]he State responds to a
need of living in society—in other words of living in mutual dependence and
fellowship of others.”78 People are fully committed to the social contract yet
remain sovereign. Governance is a moral community guided by the general
will of the people.
Jennings extends Rousseau: The State responds to the needs of living in
mutual dependence and fellowship with all members of the Earth community.
The formation of this new ecological social contract is only beginning. As
Latour wrote: “[It] has to be assembled bit by bit. The laws of the new polity
have to be invented and self-imposed because “[w]ithout decision, there is no
body politics, no liberty, [no] autonomy.”79 Rousseau sought to construct a
theory of the social contract where humans would be as free as in their
natural state. People are now coming to see that they cannot be free without
an ecological social contract.
Earth lawyers will play a crucial role in shaping this new contract, and they
will place their wager on the interconnected community of life.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) What is an Earth lawyer?
(2) What special skills, abilities, social status, and roles do lawyers bring to
the task of creating a new ecological social contract?
(3) What can lawyers do to bring into being a new ecological social contract?

(4) What is normative jurisprudence? An “objective” legal system allows
transactions and resolution of conflicts without direct reference to morals.
What is the role of morals in law practice? Will “ecological morals” cause
conflict?
(5) How may lawyers and society engage the nonhuman language discourse
of nature?
(6) How may Earth lawyers be guided by the general will of the Earth
community?
(7) What lessons do you take from the Bolivian experience?
(8) Human history is filled with catastrophes, such as the current COVID-19
crisis. Do you anticipate cascading catastrophes, and, if so, what is the
meaning of this for you? How will this affect Earth law?
