SECTION FIVE
A GLOBAL SURVEY OF EARTH
LAW
Section V addresses Earth law’s actual implementation through lawmaking
and litigation at the national level. The case studies reviewed in this section
are marked by diverse legal strategies used to stop and reverse injury to
forests, rivers, streams, springs, and other ecosystems. Moreover, each
chapter reveals a distinctive legal system within which the strategies unfold.
We discussed implementation of Earth law in the United States in Section III,
Chapter 9, and using that as a basis for comparison, we now turn to a
discussion of litigating and applying Earth law in other countries to better
understand how implementation at the ground level actually works.
As you review the case studies, note their similarities as well as the
distinctions. The chapters on Ecuador (Chapter 17), Colombia (Chapter 18),
and Brazil (Chapter 19) reveal an encouraging number of cases recognizing
rights of nature. Yet, the legal framework within which these cases play out
varies for each country. Earth law litigation in Ecuador springs from the
country’s Constitution, which grants nature broad rights. While Colombia
and Brazil do not embody rights of nature in their Constitutions or statutes
laws, their courts, particularly in Colombia, are creating a rich body of case
law through ecocentric interpretation of existing legislation to recognize the
rights of nature. In groundbreaking decisions, the Colombian courts have
recognized the Atrato River Basin and the Colombian Amazon as legal
subjects of rights in order to stop destructive mining and deforestation,
respectively. The case study on Brazil addresses the failure of its
environmental laws and the efforts underway to remedy the situation by
promoting rights of nature laws. Yet, without waiting for new laws, courts in
Brazil are moving ahead with Earth law, recently recognizing a nonhuman
animal (a parrot) as a subject of rights. The emergence of Earth law in

Mexico is unfolding in part through the expansion of legal frameworks for
human rights. Similar to Brazil’s constitution, which recognizes the human
right to an “ecologically balanced environment” and supports Indigenous
practices for living in harmony with nature, Mexico’s constitution also grants
humans environmental rights, including a specific Indigenous right for
maintaining and improving their environment. While both Brazil’s and
Mexico’s constitutions are anthropocentric and, unlike Ecuador’s, do not
recognize rights of nature, their codification of the human right to a healthy
environment is fostering the development of Earth law. In Mexico, three state
governments have included rights of nature within their constitutions and
other are not far behind.
Although this section does not include a chapter on Bolivia, in 2009 Bolivia’s
president was a key figure in the U.N. Harmony with Nature initiative, as
reviewed in Chapter 15, “United Nations Sustainable Development
Initiatives.” Bolivia adopted the Law of the Rights of Mother Earth (2010)
and the Framework Law of Mother Earth and Integral Development for
Living Well (2010). One reason for omitting a Bolivia chapter is the abject
failure experienced in enforcing the laws that grant nature a diversity of
rights.
Indigenous rights-based movements are explored in Chapter 24, “Africa.”
Similar to Latin American countries, efforts in Africa to promote Earth law
spring from the continent’s local traditions and customs of living in harmony
with Mother Earth and the focus on restoring Indigenous knowledge and
practices at the community and local levels. Africa’s Earth law movement has
evolved under the leadership of a civil society intent on reviving customary
laws and Indigenous practices as the basis for a new Earth jurisprudence.
Continuing the focus on Indigenous laws and customs, Chapter 25,
“Indigenous Legalities,” addresses American indigenous knowledge and
practices and their potential for transforming Western legal systems in the
face of the current ecological crisis. Unlike many Indigenous people’s belief
systems, Western law is based on an “ontology of separation” between nature
and culture that is incompatible with ecocentric law. The chapter also reviews
how Western colonialism has impacted Indigenous laws and how colonialism
endures.

Earth law in India (Chapter 20) and New Zealand (Chapter 22) are based on
the model of legal personhood for nature. In New Zealand, the 2014 Te
Urewera Act recognizes the former Te Urewera National Park as its own
legal entity, and a 2017 treaty agreement between the government and the
Māori tribe of Whanganui also recognizes the Whanganui River as its own
legal entity. Guardians were appointed in both cases to represent the rivers, in
India by the court and in New Zealand through legislation. Specifically citing
the personhood for nature in New Zealand, an Indian court recognized the
legal personhood of the Ganges River (a decision that was later overturned by
the country’s Supreme Court) as well as rights for the entire animal kingdom
in 2017.
While these countries have already left their mark as practitioners of Earth
law, note the situation in Israel (Chapter 21), where both Earth law legislation
and litigation is almost non-existent. Similar to Colombia and Brazil, the
Israel country study demonstrates how Earth law can evolve without specific
laws when courts have the will to interpret existing legislation to counter
harm to nature. Moreover, the Israeli case also shows that courts might hand
down precedential judgements that in reality create rights for nature without
mentioning these rights or other Earth law doctrines and concepts.
In the Netherlands (Chapter 23), implementation of Earth law received an
enormous boost by the 2020 decision of the country’s Supreme Court in the
Urgenda case, in which current and future generations successfully
established the Dutch government’s duty to prevent dangerous climate
change. The Supreme Court cited human rights conventions and the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in ordering the Dutch
government to meet its obligations under international law (the Paris
Agreement) in order to avoid severe environmental harm.
Drawing all these cases together is the strong consensus on the need to
transform nature—currently objectified as human property—into an
independent entity with its own legal personhood or rights. Changing nature
from an object of law into its subject underlies the assumption that existing
laws cannot reverse the unfolding ecological tragedy. Hence, the case studies
share the objective of replacing the current legal system with an ecocentric
one that will recognize nature’s inherent value, rather than its current worth

to humans as a resource to feed the global economy.
As you read the chapters in this section, consider how litigation can generate
transformative change at the ground level and the specific impact of each
case on ecosystems at risk. Also try to interlink the cases discussed in
Chapter 9 on U.S. Earth law, for example, with the litigation models
presented in the Colombian and Dutch case studies. Do these models offer a
more effective strategy to litigate Earth law in the United States, or are
foreign (non-U.S.) legal systems simply more likely to make ecocentric legal
interpretations? Effectively promoting Earth law requires an in-depth
understanding of the different litigation and policy models being used to
secure rights for ecosystems and their applicability to other incidents of
ecological harm.

CHAPTER 17
Ecuador1
I. INTRODUCTION
In 2008, Ecuador made history by becoming the world’s first country to
recognize the rights of nature in its Constitution. The Constitution was
drafted beginning in 2007 by the Ecuadorian Constituent Assembly,
comprising 130 delegates representing all of Ecuador’s regions.2 The
majority of elected delegates were members of President Rafael Correa’s
center-left social democratic movement, Patria Altiva i Soberana (Proud and
Sovereign Homeland or PAIS). In July 2018, the Assembly approved a draft
constitution with 494 articles. In September 2008, a constitutional
referendum was approved by 63.93 percent of Ecuador voters.
In Ecuador, rights of nature reflects the belief system of its population,
especially its Indigenous peoples, who have lived in harmony with nature
since time immemorial. Other supporters of rights of nature include lawyers
and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) seeking stronger environmental
protection to combat an influx of extractive industries. Many view rights of
nature as an emerging success story of ecocentric law in practice. But others
find its impact to be more symbolic than practical. These contradictory
visions may explain the uneven way in which rights of nature has developed
in Ecuador over the last 12 years.
This chapter explores rights of nature developments in Ecuador. It begins by
discussing why rights of nature received constitutional recognition and what
it means to Ecuadorians. It then reviews rights of nature decisions handed

down by the Ecuadorian courts. Finally, the chapter looks ahead to how
rights of nature might progress in Ecuador in the near future.
II. A CLASH BETWEEN INDIGENOUS BELIEF
SYSTEMS AND WESTERN NORMS
Rights of Nature was a current flowing through Ecuadorian veins long before
the country’s 2008 Constitution. Indigenous peoples in Ecuador, comprised
of 14 separate nationalities, have traditionally recognized underlying rights of
nature principles through their practices, customs, and laws.3 For example,
they regard forests as living entities and thus reject development or
intervention that threatens forest ecosystems.4 One group, the Sarayaku
people, believe that forests are already “developed” because they contain
natural paths, well-defined hunting seasons and areas, and rotating chakras
(the Indigenous Quechua word for small farms) that have existed for
generations.5 The Sarayaku have developed their communities and shaped the
forest in harmony with nature’s rhythms.
Western benchmarks of development—roads, electricity, and jobs from
extractive industries—are considered unnecessary by the Sarayaku. This
Sarayaku philosophy is consistent with the concept of the rights and
responsibilities of rights of nature law as it has begun to be developed in
Ecuador.
However, Ecuador is home to many different cultures, and rights of nature is
not ingrained into the ethos of most of the population. Even though many
Ecuadorians are of mixed Indigenous and European heritage,6 Ecuador’s
society is heavily influenced by Western culture, including its emphasis on
continuous development and economic growth. Ecuador is thus a story of two
competing visions: embracing age-old belief systems of living in harmony
with nature and pursuing economic progress at the expense of nature.
Some Ecuadorians are critical of rights of nature. For them, it is easy to
understand the legal interest in protecting something because of its value to
human life, but rights of nature proposes to respect someone, because she
deserves respect. These concepts can be radical and threatening to some

humans. Consider the following argument from Farith Simon Campaña:
Avoiding the destruction of the Earth by humans is important, but [we should
not] accept any regulatory reform as valid just because it sounds
“revolutionary” without examining its possible consequences, especially
when the possibility exists to weaken human rights protections.
…What should judges give more weight to when in conflict: the rights of
nature or the rights of individuals and communities? Do human beings and
nature have the same ontological value? [discussing what sort of things exist
in the social world and assumptions about the form and nature of that social
reality].…
[E]verything suggests that we will soon be studying, defending, and
explaining the importance of the most basic human rights, remembering the
need to consider the human being as the center of everything.7
By contrast, other Ecuadorians embrace the idea that humans are part of
nature, not the center or owner of it. As explained by Ramiro Ávila
Santamaría, “You cannot separate the concept of being human from nature;
both are one, hence hurting nature is hurting oneself.…[R]espect for nature
has a direct impact on respect for human beings and, on the other hand,
disrespect of any human being inevitably means disrespect of nature.”8
In sum, even within Ecuador where rights for nature have been
constitutionally recognized, viewpoints vary significantly. The ultimate
success of the rights of nature legal paradigm will depend in large part on the
extent to which and how Ecuadorean judges, politicians, lawyers, and citizens
embrace nature’s rights in practice.
III. ECUADOR’S 2008 CONSTITUTION
This section explores the text of Ecuador’s 2008 Constitution. It begins with
a discussion of Sumak Kawsay, meaning “good living,” which is a
fundamental pillar of Ecuador’s Constitution. It then discusses constitutional
rights of nature protections and concludes by discussing Ecuador’s
recognition of human environmental rights.

A. Sumak Kawsay
Indigenous peoples were central to shaping Ecuador’s Constitution.9 For
example, the National Indigenous Confederation of Ecuador (CONAIE)
successfully fought to ensure that the Constitution reflected the multi-ethnic
character of Ecuador and its various belief systems.10 One of those belief
systems is the concept of Sumak Kawsay, usually translated as good way of
living (buen vivir in Spanish). The Preamble of the Constitution states that the
sovereign people of Ecuador “hereby decide to build a new form of public
coexistence, in diversity and in harmony with nature, to achieve the good
way of living, the sumak kawsay.” Sumak Kawsay, however, is a deeper
concept than the literal translation of the words conveys. As described by
Raúl Llasag Fernández,
In order to make visible other forms of knowledge and wisdom, without
intending to essentialize, but to make possible the intercultural dialogue, [it is
necessary to] look at the conception of Pachamama for Indigenous peoples of
Ecuador, aware that there is diversity of Indigenous peoples and diversity of
realities, therefore, diversity of conceptions of Pacha- mama and Sumak
Kawsay, but they are articulated by fundamental principles that make them
common.” Sumak Kawsay is an Indigenous idea that represents living in
harmony with pachamama, or nature.11
Luis Macas explains the meaning of the words Sumak and Kawsay as
follows:
Sumak is the fullness, the sublime, excellent, magnificent, beautiful, and
superior. Kawsay is life, is being. However, it is dynamic, changing, it is not
passive []. Therefore, Sumak Kawsay would be life in fullness. Life in
material and spiritual excellence. The magnificent and the sublime are
expressed in harmony, in the internal and external balance of a community.12
To a linear-thinking legal mind, the definition of Sumak Kawsay may seem
impossibly imprecise. That is because the true meaning of Sumak Kawsay
escapes a simple translation, and it is too difficult to capture in Western
thought. Truly understanding Sumak Kawsay requires “look[ing] at the
conception of Pachamama for Indigenous peoples of Ecuador, aware that

there is a diversity of Indigenous peoples and diversity of realities, [and]
therefore, a diversity of conceptions of Pachamama and Sumak Kawsay.”13
Nonetheless, the various conceptions of Sumak Kawsay do share common
fundamental principles. Andean philosopher Javier Lajo has identified five
such principles:
1. There is no life without wisdom (Tucu Yachay);
2. We all come from Mother Earth (Pachamama);
3. Life is healthy (Hambi Kawsay);
4. Life is collective (Sumak Kamaña); and
5. We all have an ideal or dream (Hatun Muskuy).14
Ultimately, the Ecuadorian Constituent Assembly embraced Sumak Kawsay
as one of the pillars of its new Constitution. In large part, rights of nature
emerged directly from this mindset. Aside from supporting Sumak Kawsay,
constitutional drafters identified many other benefits of rights of nature: it
supported plurinationalism (the existence of several different nations in a
political state), helped address the ecological crisis, and might curb dominant
capitalistic influences, amongst others.15 Thus rights of nature was included
in the 2008 Constitution, as discussed in the next subsection.
B. Rights of Nature and Related Environmental Protections
Based in part upon the concept of Sumak Kawsay, Ecuador’s Constitution
established rights of nature protections in Title II, Chapter 7—Articles 71-74,
entitled “Rights of Nature.” The substantive rights constitutionally
recognized as belonging to nature are specifically those in Articles 71 and 72:
Art 71. Nature, or Pacha Mama, where life is reproduced and occurs, has the
right to integral respect for her existence and for the maintenance and
regeneration of her life cycles, structure, functions and evolutionary
processes.
All persons, communities, peoples and nations can call upon public
authorities to enforce the rights of nature. To enforce and interpret these
rights, the principles set forth in the Constitution shall be observed, as

appropriate.
The State shall give incentives to natural persons and legal entities and to
communities to protect nature and to promote respect for all the elements
comprising an ecosystem.
Art 72. Nature has the right to be restored. This restoration shall be apart
from the obligation of the State and natural persons or legal entities to
compensate individuals and communities that depend on affected natural
systems.
In those cases of severe or permanent environmental impact, including those
caused by the exploitation of nonrenewable natural resources, the State shall
establish the most effective mechanisms to achieve the restoration and shall
adopt adequate measures to eliminate or mitigate harmful environmental
consequences.
These are the bedrock guarantees of nature’s rights in Ecuador, although their
exact meaning is still subject to interpretation. For example, when is a project
deemed to have interfered with the “maintenance” of Pachamama’s “life
cycles, structure, functions and evolutionary processes”? Is it a strictly
science-based determination? Does a court just “know it when it sees it?”
Further, nature has a right to be restored in Article 72—but to be restored to
what state? The courts are already grappling with many of these questions.
Continuing, Article 73 establishes certain affirmative duties on the
Ecuadorian government—which includes executive, legislative, and judicial
branches—to protect nature, with an emphasis on preventing permanent harm
to nature:
Art. 73. The State shall apply preventive and restrictive measures on
activities that might lead to the extinction of species, the destruction of
ecosystems and the permanent alteration of natural cycles.
The introduction of organisms and organic and inorganic material that might
definitively alter the nation’s genetic assets is forbidden.
Finally, Article 74 establishes that humans still have a right to benefit from

the environment, with Sumak Kawsay (translated here as “good way of
living”) as the end in view:
Art 74. Persons, communities, peoples, and nations shall have the right to
benefit from the environment and the natural wealth enabling them to enjoy
the good way of living.
Environmental services shall not be subject to appropriation; their
production, delivery, use and development shall be regulated by the State.
The rights of nature provisions in Articles 71-74 are strengthened by
subsequent articles addressing the legal relationship between humans and
nature. Here, the Constitution addresses both the human duties and
responsibilities that are necessary to uphold the rights of nature (Art. 83), and
once again calls for a harmonious coexistence with nature through the lens of
Sumak Kawsay (Art. 275):
Art. 83. Ecuadorians have the following duties and obligations, without
detriment to others provided for by the Constitution or by law:.…
6. To respect the rights of nature, preserve a healthy environment and use
natural resources rationally, sustainably and durably.
Art. 275. The development structure is the organized, sustainable and
dynamic group of economic, political, socio-cultural and environmental
systems which underpin the achievement of the good way of living (Sumak
Kawsay).…The good way of living shall require persons, communities,
peoples and nationalities to effectively exercise their rights and fulfill their
responsibilities within the framework of interculturalism, respect for their
diversity, and harmonious coexistence with nature.
To some, it may sound as though rights of nature would prohibit any activity
that impacts the environment, but this is not the case. Not every
environmental impact has the potential to threaten or harm the integrity of
nature’s existence and the maintenance and regeneration of her life cycles,
structure, functions and evolutionary processes—those fundamental
protections established by the Constitution. Rights of nature represents a
rebalancing, not an elimination, of human activities that impact the
environment, with the goal of protecting and restoring basic ecological

processes. Therefore, lifestyles such as those suggested by the Sarayaku
people are not the only acceptable lifestyle under this environmental
approach, although they do provide helpful guidance. On the other hand,
activities that fail to respect these norms—regardless of whether a valid
permit or license has been issued—would be in violation of nature’s
constitutional rights.
C. Ecuadorian Environmental Constitutionalism
In addition to Sumak Kawsay, two other “pillars of support” for rights of
nature may be recognized in Ecuador’s Constitution: (1) constitutional
environmental principles that developed in Ecuador since the 1990s, such as
the human right to a healthy environment, and (2) international
environmental law, such as sustainable development agreements, the
Convention on Biological Diversity, and the 1982 World Charter for
Nature.16 As an example of the latter, Principle 1 of the World Charter
proclaims that “Nature shall be respected and its essential processes shall not
be impaired.” This language is echoed in Article 71 of Ecuador’s 2008
Constitution, which upholds nature’s rights and requires the State to promote
respect towards nature. It may be helpful to consider Ecuadorian
environmental constitutionalism in the context of three pillars: Indigenous
law (including Sumak Kawsay), constitutional law, and international
environmental law.
Aside from Articles 71-74 assertion of rights of nature principles, Ecuador’s
Constitution applies other principles of environmental law that support rights
of nature. For example, Article 395 is frequently cited in rights of nature
decisions that also involve basic human rights. Pay special attention to
Article 395.3, which commands the State to allow affected populations to
participate in planning and monitoring activities impacting the environment:
Art. 395. The Constitution recognizes the following environmental
principles:
1. The State shall guarantee a sustainable model of development, one that
is environmentally balanced and respectful of cultural diversity,
conserves biodiversity and the natural regeneration capacity of

ecosystems, and ensures meeting the needs of present and future
generations.
2. Environmental management policies shall be applied cutting across all
sectors and dimensions and shall be mandatorily enforced by the State at
all of its levels and by all natural persons or legal entities in the
country’s territory.
3. The State shall guarantee the active and permanent participation of
affected persons, communities, peoples and nations in the planning,
implementation and monitoring of all activities exerting environmental
impacts.…
Furthermore, Articles 395.4 and 396 establish the in dubio pro natura (when
in doubt, favor nature) principle and the precautionary principle, respectively.
The first states a general constitutional rule that nature should be protected
above other interests when there is doubt about how legal provisions should
be applied. It is primarily enforced by the judicial branch when interpreting
environmental rules, but it is also mandatory for decisions of the legislative
and executive branches. Meanwhile, Article 396 establishes that the state has
a duty to protect the environment whenever there is uncertainty about
environmental impacts.
Art. 395.4. In the event of doubt about the scope of legal provisions for
environmental issues, it is the most favorable interpretation of their effective
force for the protection of nature that shall prevail.
Art. 396. The State shall adopt timely policies and measures to avoid adverse
environmental impacts where there is certainty about the damage. In the case
of doubt about the environmental impact stemming from a deed or omission,
although there is no scientific evidence of the damage, the State shall adopt
effective and timely measures of protection.
The Constitution also establishes the human right to live in a healthy
environment that is distinct from, but related to, the rights of nature
provisions:
Art. 14. The right of the population to live in a healthy and ecologically
balanced environment that guarantees sustainability and the good way of
living (Sumak Kawsay) is recognized. Environmental conservation, the

protection of ecosystems, biodiversity and the integrity of the country’s
genetic assets, the prevention of environmental damage, and the recovery of
degraded natural spaces are declared matters of public interest.
Art. 66. The following rights of persons are recognized and guaranteed:…
27. The right to live in a healthy environment that is ecologically balanced,
pollution-free and in harmony with nature.
Observe that nature’s rights and human environmental rights are completely
separate under Ecuador’s Constitution. They are different rights belonging to
different rights-holders. However, they are complementary in practice
because human environmental rights cannot be upheld without respect for
nature. Still, consider whether a rights of nature paradigm should establish a
single set of rights for the entire Earth community—including both humans
and the rest of nature. If the goal is for humans and nature to live together in
harmony, should we move away from the us (humans) and them (nature)
mentality? Or if human environmental rights and rights of nature are
separated, should different components of nature also have their own tailored
rights—forest rights, animal rights, ocean rights, and so forth?
IV. RIGHTS OF NATURE COURT CASES
Through March 2020, more than 32 legal decisions in Ecuador have involved
the rights of nature.17 Of those, at least seven cases have reached Ecuador’s
Constitutional Court. Article 429 of the Constitution states that the
Constitutional Court is Ecuador’s highest authority on constitutional
interpretation, so its decisions set precedents that greatly contribute to the
development of rights of nature. This section explores the rights of nature
cases decided by this Court.
A. Biodigesters Case, Ruling No. 0567-08-RA (2009)18
The Biodigesters case, submitted in 2007, was the first to be resolved from a
rights of nature perspective by the Constitutional Court. The case was
brought as an amparo action, which seeks to protect an individual’s rights

while also upholding the Constitution for its own sake.19 The case concerned
an agro-industrial pig farm that planned to install six biodigesters, which turn
hog waste into methane gas. The plaintiffs, neighbors of the farm,
complained about a suite of environmental harms arising from the pig farm,
including air pollution, water pollution from wastewater discharges, and
otherwise poor environmental management. However, the only remedy
sought by the lawsuit was to suspend installation of the biodigesters, which
can produce toxic odors.
The Court denied the amparo, arguing that the installation of biodigesters
does not, in itself, violate the human right to live in a healthy environment.
The Court further argued that biodigesters fall under the Clean Development
Mechanism of the Kyoto Protocol, since they replace the use of fossil fuels
with biogas recycled from animal manure.
While the plaintiffs lost on the biogas issue, the Court took a broader look at
the agro-industrial farm’s environmental impacts, namely its wastewater
discharges, which for years had been reported to authorities without an
effective response. The Court, for the first time ever, applied the 2008
Constitution’s rights of nature protections, which by the time of the ruling
had just gone into effect. The Court stated that it would “consider all the
elements of the case, and [all] the parties involved, amongst which is
Nature” because the existence of life—not only human life, but all living
species—depends upon water.20 The Court continued by reaffirming the
rights of nature and recognizing the State’s affirmative duty to enforce these
rights:
The integral and effective respect of her existence must be fulfilled by
safeguarding each and every one of her systems, processes, and natural
elements, considering it above all as being part of an imperative precaution
for the maintenance and regeneration of vital cycles, structure, functions, and
evolutionary processes.…
For this reason, we cannot set aside…articles 71 and 72 of the Supreme Law
of the State, which states that Nature has the right to have her existence fully
respected…as well as the right to be restored when natural systems are
affected. Even more so when, according to the same foundational Charter, as

set out in articles 3 and 277, it is the State’s duty to protect natural assets and
guarantee the rights of individuals, communities, and Nature.…
In support of rights of nature, the Court also applied the concept of in dubio
pro natura, meaning “in case of doubt, favor nature:”
We must bear in mind that this guarantee of protection of nature enjoys the
principle of autonomy, that is, it must be considered holistically as an end and
not as a means to which her own behavior is inevitably respected; [to
understand] otherwise would be to omit the validity of [nature’s] rights and
legal protection[s]. For that purpose, we also invoke the principle in dubio
pro natura, which entails [principles of] prevention as much as precaution
and integral restoration with respect to the effects caused by human activity.
It is an obligation of this Court, as a guardian of compliance with the
constitutional mandates, to realize the will of the constituent in that our
Fundamental Charter grants rights to nature as part of a bio-centrist and non-
anthropocentric judicial philosophy; thus, in case of doubt, environmental
principles and legal provisions should be applied to the protection of nature
in the most favorable way.…
Finally, the Court ordered the creation of a commission, to be comprised of
the plaintiffs, supervisory bodies, and the defendant, which would monitor
the operations of the biodigesters and ensure compliance with environmental
laws.
Having ruled in favor of rights of nature for the first time in the Biodigesters
case, the Constitutional Court later addressed the potential tension between
nature’s rights and human interests as demonstrated in the Galápagos Islands
case that follows.
B. Galápagos Islands Case, Ruling No. 017-12-SIN-CC (2012)21
The Galápagos Islands are a biodiversity hotspot that is home to an
extraordinary amount of endemic species (those found nowhere else on
Earth), including the giant Galápagos tortoise, marine iguana, flightless
cormorant, and many others. In 1998, the Galápagos Islands were established
as a special regime under the framework of the Special Law for Galápagos

(LOREG or Ley de Régimen Especial para la Conservación y Desarrollo
Sustentable de la Provincia de Galápagos). This special regime allows
restrictions on the rights of free residence, property, and commerce, in order
to protect this global biodiversity hotspot. It also established a Galápagos
Marine Reserve extending 40 miles off the coastline in which industrial
fishing was prohibited.
The constitutionality of LOREG’s restrictions were challenged in 2001 by the
Association of Industrial Tuna Fishermen. The plaintiffs argued that the
prohibition of industrial fisheries in the Galápagos Marine Reserve violated
the labor rights of fishermen. The Constitutional Court disagreed, finding that
LOREG was in accordance with the special regime of governance established
by Ecuador’s 1998 Constitution and reaffirmed by its 2008 Constitution.
In 2012, the Constitutional Court again reviewed the law, this time regarding
the constitutionality of restrictions on the rights of residence and mobility of
people in the Galápagos Islands. The Court, affirming the decision of the
former Constitutional Tribunal, this time ruled from a rights of nature
perspective:
[The Court’s position in favor of the LOREG is even] more relevant if we
consider that the Constitution of the Republic of 2008 establishes a chapter
on the ‘rights of nature’ that the State is obliged to promote and guarantee.
Highlighting the constitutional recognition of rights of nature, the Court
wrote:
Even though the challenged Law predates the Constitution of 2008, it’s not
only in accordance with the former Constitution—as the Constitutional
Tribunal ruled—but also with the current Constitution, whose article 258
ratifies the special regime of governance for the province of Galápagos,
whose main objective is to preserve the natural, scientific and educational
values of the Islands. [The Law is defensible] a fortiori [i.e., with even
stronger evidence than before] if the Constitution sets the highest standards of
environmental protection (rights of nature)…—standards that the State is
obliged to protect and guarantee.
The Court therefore denied the petition for review and confirmed the

constitutionality of the law governing the Galápagos Islands.
C. Mangroves Case, Ruling No. 166-15-SEP-CC (2015)22
This case arises from a shrimp farm operating within a protected mangroves
area. In Ecuador, there are 161,835 hectares of mangroves in five estuarine
areas. One of these is the highly biodiverse Cayapas–Mataje, located in
northwest Ecuador and home to the world’s tallest mangroves. Cayapas–
Mataje is a protected ecological reserve under Ecuadorian law and is a
designated Ramsar site under the Convention on Wetlands of International
Importance (Ramsar Convention). Under the Ramsar Convention, member
states designate significant important wetlands—i.e., Ramsar sites—and then
must take special measures to protect them.23
The plaintiff, Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment, invoked rights of nature to
justify its efforts to remove shrimp farmers from the ecological reserve. The
shrimp farmers, a powerful economic interest group in Ecuador, sued the
government in provincial court for violating their property rights. The
provincial court sided with the shrimp farmers. However, its reasoning failed
to address several environmental law issues. For example, the provincial
court did not consider the special constitutional protections afforded to
mangroves as a “fragile ecosystem,” which was the result of a 30-year effort
that was explicitly to protect mangroves from shrimp farming. The provincial
court also failed to discuss rights of nature.
The plaintiff asked the Constitutional Court to review the provincial court’s
decision by means of an “extraordinary protection action” (acción
extraordinaria de protección), which allows for the review of constitutional
rights that are violated by a court order.
The Constitutional Court of Ecuador reviewed the case and concluded that
the lower court’s decision was invalid because it only addressed property
rights instead of also considering rights of nature, which was a particularly
large omission in a protected and fragile ecosystem. The Court elaborated
that all constitutional rights are of equal legal significance in Ecuador,
including the rights of nature. As stated by the Court:

This Constitutional Court has been emphatic in highlighting the importance
of rights to nature, which result in the obligation of the State and its officials
to encourage and promote respect for all the elements that are part of an
ecosystem, as well as for Nature’s right to be respected in her entirety. These
aspects have obviously not been observed…in a case whose central issue is
the installation of a shrimp farm within the Cayapas- Mataje ecological
reserve, a place possessing a system of mangroves with a wide variety of
species of fauna and flora.
The Court also emphasized the ecocentric nature of Ecuador’s rights of
nature provisions. In the following excerpt, consider whether you agree with
the Court’s assessment that nature can be treated both as a subject (i.e., a
holder of rights) and an object (i.e., property) under the Constitution, or
whether nature can only be treated as a legal subject in all contexts:
[R]ights of nature constitutes one of the most interesting and relevant
innovations from the current Constitution, as it departs from the traditional
“nature-object” conception, which considers nature as property and focuses
its protection exclusively through the human right to enjoy a healthy natural
environment, [and instead supports] a rationale that recognizes rights in favor
of nature herself. The innovation refers to a change of paradigm on the basis
of which, as a living being, nature is considered a rights holder. In this sense,
it is important to highlight that the Constitution creates [two treatments of]
nature and the environment in general…[not only] as a legal object, but also
as a legal subject, independent and holding its own and specific rights.…The
foregoing reflects, within the legal relationship between humans and nature, a
biocentric vision in which nature is prioritized, as opposed to the classic
anthropocentric conception in which the human being is the center and
measure of all things [and] where nature was considered a mere provider of
resources.
Next, the Court highlighted the duty of all citizens to uphold nature’s rights
and called upon the State to support this role:
As can be seen from the constitutional norm, it is important that citizens play
a fundamental role in protecting the rights of nature, since every person can
require the administrative and judicial authorities to observe and fulfill these
rights[.] [Therefore,] the State is called to promote citizens’ participation to

utilize those mechanisms focused on [nature’s] protection. In this sense, all
citizens enjoy legal standing to represent nature when her rights are being
violated.
Ultimately, the Court concluded that the failure to consider nature’s rights in
the previous ruling breached the constitutional standards of reasonableness
and judicial logic needed in a judgment. Therefore, the Court annulled the
provincial court’s ruling and ordered it to re-try the case.
Rights of nature prevailed in each of the case studies discussed above. The
next section explores a major case where an Ecuadorian Court favored
economic development over the rights of nature.
V. SHORTCOMINGS OF RIGHTS OF NATURE
IN THE COURTS: THE MIRADOR MINE
CASE24
Aside from the Constitutional Court cases analyzed above, rights of nature
has had mixed results in Ecuador. This section highlights a few of the
challenges faced construing constitutionally-granted rights of nature. It then
discusses the Mirador Mine case as an example.
Craig Kauffman and Pamela Martin identify four “pathways” through which
rights of nature has been applied in Ecuador:
1. Civil society pressure (civil society actions such as lawsuits),
2. Instrumental government action (government actions such as lawsuits),
3. Bureaucratic institutionalization (bureaucratic activities such as routine
administrative actions), and
4. Professional interpretations by judges.25
Kauffman and Martin tracked the efficacy of each pathway in the early years
of rights of nature in Ecuador, with unexpected results: “Surprisingly, civil
society pressure was the least successful pathway, as activists lost high-
profile lawsuits,” prevailing only in local, less politically charged cases.26
These norm-driven rights of nature advocates were undercut by politicization,

contentious relationships with the government, and an absence of judicial
knowledge about how to interpret rights of nature:
The idea that individual and corporate property rights must be curtailed in
some cases to uphold Nature’s rights was not only foreign to most judges, but
ran counter to their legal training. As a result, judges in civil society lawsuits
have generally ruled that economic development activities are protected by
individual rights (e.g., property rights, right to work) that supersede Nature’s
rights.27
The Mirador Mine case exemplifies many of the hurdles faced by rights of
nature in the courts. The case was pursued by Indigenous and environmental
activists eager to test the rights of nature provisions in the Ecuadorian
Constitution. They settled on the Condor-Mirador Mine, an open-pit mining
project authorized by the Ecuadorian government in the Zamora-Chinchipe
province of the Ecuadorian Amazon. The Mirador Mine is a massive
Chinese-backed $1.4 billion open-pit copper and gold mine on Indigenous
Shuar and Cañari-Kichwa land. At the time of the lawsuit, it was still in the
development stages. The mine threatened to destroy large areas of primary
rainforest and pollute and dewater local rivers, including the Wawayme and
Quimi Rivers. The rights of nature violations were blatant:
The mining company’s own environmental impact study acknowledged that
the open-pit mine would cause impacts listed as rights of nature violations in
the Constitution. These include the total removal of ecosystems, including the
habitats on which endangered endemic species rely, likely causing the
extinction of one or more species. Also, contaminating surface and
groundwater with heavy metals and toxic products would be catastrophic for
surrounding watershed ecosystems.28
Additionally, the plan would require the forcible removal of local Indigenous
communities who had been on the land for generations. Some activists
resisting the mine were even met with violence. Shuar leader José Isidro
Tendetza Antún was found murdered just days before he was to present on
rights of nature at a civil society-led tribunal, which many believe was the
result of his protests of the mine.29

In 2013, activists and local communities filed a protective action in the 25th
Civil Court in Pichincha province against Ecuacorriente, the mining
company. The action sought to suspend the mining project and order a new
environmental impact study. The petitioners invoked the precautionary
principle as well as Article 73 of Ecuador’s Constitution, which requires the
State to “apply preventive and restrictive measures on activities that might
lead to the extinction of species, the destruction of ecosystems and permanent
alteration of natural cycles.”
Despite what these advocates considered a strong and unequivocal case for
rights of nature, the judge ruled that the Mirador Mine did not violate rights
of nature. The ruling was based on two premises. First, that the affected area
was not a protected area and therefore did not have any rights (despite being
contrary to express constitutional language that all of nature has rights
regardless of its protected status). Second, that in this case protecting nature
was a private goal, whereas the mining company was acting in the public
interest by advancing development. The public interest outweighed the
private one, ruled the judge. An appeal was unsuccessful.
After the lawsuit, the project moved forward and is now operational. The
Mirador Mine concessions sprawl for some 10,000 hectares, where all
vegetation and superficial levels of soil will eventually be removed. Already,
1,200 hectares of primary rainforest have been cut down. Many Indigenous
peoples were forcibly evicted and continue to protest.30
Why did rights of nature fail in this case? Some believe that political
influence and lack of judicial independence were the culprits. Others argue
that many judges simply do not understand the concept of rights of nature,
and therefore cannot successfully balance nature’s rights against other
constitutional rights. Another possibility is that courts are willing to disregard
rights of nature (as well as Indigenous rights) when large amounts of money
are at stake. The Ecuadorian government has already received $85 million in
royalties from EcuaCorriente for the Mirador Mine.31
VI. THE FUTURE OF RIGHTS OF NATURE IN
ECUADOR

This section explores emerging developments of rights of nature in Ecuador,
including new Constitutional Court cases and legislative reform.
A. Rights of Nature in the Constitutional Court Agenda
In February 2019, a new Constitutional Court took the bench in Ecuador.32 In
May 2019, the new Court selected an important case that addresses the extent
of the constitutional protections for the rights of nature. The case pertains to
the Dulcepamba River.
The Constitutional Court can select cases that are novel or relevant to
constitutional rights protections. The Court’s rulings on such selected cases
have an erga omnes effect—meaning it is enforceable against all, not just the
parties to the case.33 The Court’s reasoning provides substantive content for
those constitutional rights addressed in the case. In this specific case, the
Court has already announced that it will address standards and limits
regarding the exploitation of nature and its impact on rights of nature. The
Court’s decision on rights of nature, still pending at the time of this writing,
is expected to have a meaningful long-term impact.
The selected case concerns the San Jose del Tambo Hydroelectric Project,
which was built on the Dulcepamba River. Developing the hydroelectric
project required significant physical changes to the Dulcepamba River,
including diverting the riverbed close to the community of San Pablo de
Amalí. This ultimately caused a major flood in 2015 that shattered houses,
destroyed farmland, and killed two women and a child. As for the river itself,
the hydroelectric project has devastated native species in this biologically rich
region of the Andes Mountains.
In 2019, the case was admitted for review by the Constitutional Court. As
explained, the Court will not only provide an inter partes judgment (i.e., a
judgment between the parties), but also will issue erga omnes dictum on the
standards, limits, and conflicts between rights of nature and the exploitation
of nature, such as through hydroelectric dam projects.
Numerous civil society organizations have submitted amicus curiae briefs in
support of a strong rights of nature ruling by the Constitutional Court.34 One

amicus brief submitted by a coalition of environmental organizations
requested the relief described below. As you read it, consider whether you
think this relief would fulfill the vision of rights of nature in Ecuador’s
Constitution.
[T]he Environmental Organizations respectfully request the [following relief
from the] Constitutional Court of Ecuador:
a. That, in the present case, the Dulcepamba River be recognized as a subject
of rights and that the Court firmly apply the Constitutional mandate contained
in articles 71, 72, 73 and 74, which sets forth the rights of nature to exist, to
the maintenance and regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions, and
evolutionary processes, as well as the right to be restored. This brings with it
an obligation to the Ecuadorian State not only to respect but to protect and
guarantee these rights to nature.
b. That the human right to water of the communities of San Pablo de Amalí
be recognized. And also, that water be recognized as a vital element of
nature, essential for the life of the communities of Dulcepamba River
watershed, in the Province of Bolívar, and throughout the country as
established in Articles 12 and 318 of the Ecuadorian Constitution. The
alterations to the Dulcepamba River put at risk both the human right to water
and the rights of nature.
c. That the Court recognizes the specific rights of the rivers, and especially of
the Dulcepamba River. The fundamental rights of the rivers are: (1) the right
of flow (grounded in the ecological flow recognized in the Ecuadorian
legislation); (2) the right to exercise their essential functions within their
ecosystems; (3) the right to be free from all contamination; (4) the right to
feed and be fed by their tributaries; (5) the right to native biodiversity; (6) the
right to restoration; and (7) the right to independent appointment of one or
more legal guardians, who act solely in the name of river rights, with at least
one legal guardian as representative.35
d. That the Court appoint one or more legal guardians on behalf of the
Dulcepamba River. The legal guardians must be independent, qualified,
appropriate, with human and financial capacity, and act solely in the name of
the rights and interests of nature. Although Article 71 of the Constitution

establishes that: “any person, community, people, or nation may demand
from the public authority the fulfillment of the rights of nature,” the
Environmental Organizations recommend giving nature a voice, a human
face and the ability to appear before the Court.…
e. That it guarantees the right to the ecological restoration of the Dulcepamba
River as provided for in Article 72 of the Constitution of Ecuador, by issuing
(a) an order to enjoin and dismantle the Hidrotambo SA project as it is
incompatible with the Rights of Nature, the human right to water, and the
Human and Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of the communities of San
Pablo de Amalí; and, (b) a restoration order that must be applied in
accordance with Article 396 of the Ecuadorian Constitution.…
f. That it orders the Ecuadorian government to fulfill its obligation to
guarantee the rights of nature established in article 277 of the Constitution of
Ecuador and eliminate possibilities for dilution of the rights of nature. To do
this, the government must ensure that state agencies coordinate to protect and
promote the validity of the rights of nature.…
g. That it instructs the National Assembly that the Organic Environmental
Code must include positive, concrete, and effective mechanisms for each
state institution to protect the rights of nature in its administrative acts.…
h. That it orders the creation of an independent subcommittee composed of
environmental scientists and engineers, responsible for evaluating current and
future hydroelectric projects for the prevention of negative impacts, the
possible need for dismantling, and the restoration of nature. The
establishment of a subcommittee dedicated to the above would ensure that the
environmental effects of the dams are considered and that new dams are only
constructed in exceptional circumstances when necessary to obtain a vital
social, ecological or energy objective that cannot be achieved by other
reasonable means.36
* * *
B. Legislative Reform
In December 2019, a proposal to reform the Environmental Code of Ecuador,

including changes to the rights of nature, was submitted to the Ecuadorian
legislature. The proposal asserts that rights of nature are constitutional rights
and therefore must be given substantive content via legislation. To this end, it
puts forward reforms to the current law, which does not provide for such
content. The initiative is open to public comment as well as legislative
debate.
To date, despite numerous victories, many regard rights of nature as mainly
being symbolic.37 However, through legislative reform, as well as through
landmark court decisions, rights of nature can fully take shape, gaining
greater clarity on how it can be applied in a way commensurate with other
human constitutional rights. If this occurs, 12 years after its recognition in
Ecuador, rights of nature may become the ecocentric legal regime envisioned
by its constitutional drafters.
VII. CONCLUSION
As stated, the recognition of rights of nature constitutes an important legal
development for many reasons, including the acceptance of a new paradigm
of a human-nature relationship. This is a difficult goal, one that requires more
than the 12 years that have passed since rights of nature achieved
constitutional recognition. Many human rights-based movements still
struggle for recognition. In Ecuador, one promising development is simply
that nature’s rights are being fought for in courts—and, sometimes, nature is
the prevailing party. This is more than can be said in almost every other
country in the world. Additionally, the Constitutional Court is on the verge of
a major rights of nature decision, which could further clarify these issues—
and, with it, a greater application of rights of nature.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Sumak Kawsay (roughly translated to buen vivir in Spanish and good
living in English) is a worldview held by the Quechua peoples of the Andes.
What worldview exists in your own country or region that might serve as the
backbone of a constitutional amendment that includes rights of nature
protections?

(2) Article 74 of Ecuador’s Constitution establishes that nature has a right to
be restored. You have been appointed as a rights of nature ombudsman and
your first task is to create a plan for enforcing Article 74. How would you go
about putting this into practice? Would you try to restore ecosystems that
have been harmed perpetually for decades? Or would you focus on more
recent impacts, such as from ongoing mining projects? What limitations
would you establish to nature’s right to restoration, if any?
(3) The Mangroves case emphasized the Ecuadorian government’s duty to
enforce the rights of nature. Do you think national governments can properly
uphold the rights of nature when they have so many competing interests—
especially short-term economic considerations—that might run afoul of basic
rights of nature principles? Do you think entire new forms of governance are
necessary in order to put rights of nature into practice? Would a new branch
of government be necessary, or perhaps greater ecosystem representation
within existing branches of government?
(4) The Mirador Mine case indicates that not all Ecuadorean courts are ready
to place the rights of nature above economic interests, even if the rights of
nature should prevail by the letter of the law. How did the Mirador court
justify its ruling? Do you think it was correct? What does this say for the
potential of rights of nature to be the driving force behind systems change in
the economic system?
(5) There have been several cases in Ecuador addressing animal rights issues,
such as a 2017 case resulting in a criminal conviction for illegal shark finning
based in part on rights of nature.38 Consider how rights of nature differs from
the rights of a specific animal. All species play important roles, but certain
species are particularly critical to ecosystem balance—pollinator species,
keystone predators, and so forth. Should rights of nature protections favor
these animals and disfavor others, such as overpopulated animals? Domestic
animals, such as sheep or chickens, do not play an important role in
maintaining ecosystem balance at all. Are they still rightless under a rights of
nature paradigm?
(6) You have been invited to speak about rights of nature by a governmental
task force in your country charged with amending its constitution. They want
to know how the lessons learned in Ecuador could inform their own

consideration of adopting the rights of nature. What would you tell them?
Would you put any limitations on rights of nature? How would you address
the challenge of practical enforcement?

CHAPTER 18
Nature’s Rights in Colombia: An 
Emerging Jurisprudence1
I. AN INTRODUCTION TO COLOMBIA
In response to the significant threats its ecosystems face, the Colombian legal
system has developed new ways of protecting nature. This chapter explores
how Colombia’s development of Earth law has granted specific ecosystems a
special form of protection by making them subjects of rights. Two such
ecosystems are the Atrato River Basin and the Colombian Amazon, which
have both been given the status of a legal person. These judicial decisions
reflect the Colombian courts’ willingness to apply new, bold environmental
and human rights legal paradigms.
A. Colombia’s Environment
Colombia sits on the northwestern border of South America, surrounded by
Panama to the northwest; Venezuela to the east; and Ecuador, Peru, and
Brazil to the south. Colombia ranks as the second most biodiverse country in
the world, and first in bird and orchid species.2 A significant number of
Colombia’s megadiverse ecosystems transcend national borders.3 For
example, the megadiverse Chocó-Darién ecoregion runs from eastern Panama
to northwest Ecuador. This ecoregion contains a variety of important
ecosystems that serve as habitat for thousands of plant and animal species,
many of them endemic (or unique) to that region.4 The best-known example

is the Amazon—the world’s largest tropical rainforest—which spans nine
countries. In terms of animal life, the Amazon is home to at least 25 percent
of the world’s known land species.5
B. The Colombian Legal System
The judiciary of Colombia does not have a single supreme entity to oversee
the lower courts, but rather has four courts (the “High Courts”), which are the
supreme tribunals of decision in their respective fields. The four high courts
are the Constitutional Court (head of the constitutional jurisdiction), the
Supreme Court (head of the ordinary jurisdiction), the Council of State (head
of the administrative jurisdiction), and the Superior Council of Judicature
(head of the disciplinary jurisdiction). Unlike the United States, Colombia is
a civil law system based on codes and laws, which are passed and updated by
a bicameral legislature. Although Colombia does not recognize precedent the
same way common law countries do, judicial decisions by its Constitutional
Court and its Supreme Court of Justice have gained increasing recognition by
regional courts in recent years. Nevertheless, decisions by the national courts
are often cited as authority, informing judges’ interpretation of the law. The
judiciary does not have the legislative power to create new laws; it only
restates existing national obligations. In addition to consulting codes and
statutes, Colombian judges look at the National Constitution of 1991 when
ruling on legal questions.
Article 1 of the National Constitution states that “Colombia is a social state of
law under the rule of law, organized in the form of a unitary republic,
decentralized, with autonomy of its territorial entities, democratic,
participatory, and pluralistic.”6 While Article 1 describes Colombia as being
a decentralized republic, Colombia still has a centralized government
responsible for making laws.
Colombia is divided into 32 departments. Unlike “states” in the United States
and elsewhere, “departments” in Colombia do not have legislative or judicial
authority. They do, however, enjoy autonomy in the administration of
sectional issues and in the planning and promotion of economic and social
development within their respective territories.7

C. The 1991 Constitution
The 1991 National Constitution emerged from a widespread sense that
Colombia needed modern and robust democratic institutions, stronger human
rights guarantees, a new framework to tackle violence and inequality, and an
end to corruption.8 It was drafted and approved by a Constitutional Assembly
comprised of 70 delegates from diverse backgrounds, including politicians,
former guerrilla members, Indigenous leaders, academics, and people
representing the interests of business and labor.9
The Colombian Constitution has strong protections of citizens’ rights. It
includes not only fundamental rights but also economic and social rights. It
also recognizes the ethnic and cultural diversity of Colombia, including the
languages and dialects of ethnic groups.10 Indigenous peoples are explicitly
permitted to form special jurisdictions outside the national jurisdiction.11
Some of the constitutional protections of fundamental rights include the right
to life; protection from torture, cruel, inhumane, or degrading treatment or
punishment; equal protection and treatment; freedom of conscience; freedom
of religion; and others.12 Article 13, in particular, makes explicit the notion
that the state will give special protection to individuals who, on account of
their economic, physical, or mental condition, are in vulnerable
circumstances.
The second chapter of the Constitution identifies social, economic, and
cultural rights. These rights include the right to a family, equal rights and
opportunities for men and women, the rights of children, collective
bargaining, public health, education, food, and others.13 Of special interest is
Article 63, which states that property in public use, natural parks, communal
lands of ethnic groups, and other types of property are “inalienable,
imprescriptible, and not subject to seizure.”
The third chapter describes collective rights and the environment. This
chapter has been referred to as an “Ecological Constitution,” where
protection of the environment and biodiversity is characterized as a “higher
interest.”14 It contains 30 provisions in total that enshrine a series of
principles, mandates, and obligations focused on: “(1) protecting the

environment in an integral manner, and (2) guaranteeing a model of
sustainable development.”15 Reference to the “Ecological Constitution” is
made within court judgments recognizing nature’s rights, and these articles
serve as a critical component in the decision-making process.16
Human environmental rights are recognized in Article 79, which establishes
that “every individual has the right to enjoy a healthy environment. The law
will guarantee the community’s participation in the decisions that may affect
it.”17 In this way, the Constitution conceives the right to a healthy
environment as both a collective right and an individual one.
The Constitution also provides several mechanisms for Colombians to
vindicate their rights. For example, tutelas, translated as guardianship
arrangements, function as a mechanism to protect fundamental rights at the
individual level.18 Since they are designed to address the threat and violation
of fundamental rights, tutela actions are expected to be filed within a
reasonable time after a threat and/or violation takes place and to be resolved
promptly. They may be filed whenever an individual has exhausted other
avenues or has no other means of judicial redress. Tutelas are handled by the
Constitutional Court.
Beyond individual rights, the Constitution creates a right to collective actions
to protect collective rights and interests related to the environment and public
health. These include acciones populares (or popular actions) and acciones
de grupo (or group actions).19 After the ratification of the Constitution, Law
472 of 1998 defined the procedures for both actions. Popular actions are
preventative in nature, and they serve to address activities that may result in
harm to a large number of individuals. Group actions are reactive in nature,
and they seek redress for harms that have already been caused to a large
number of individuals. Both types of collective action are handled by the
State Council.
D. The Role of Socioeconomic Rights Jurisprudence
In recent years, Colombian jurisprudence on constitutional issues and
socioeconomic rights has gained international prominence for its progressive
outcomes. The Constitutional Court, in particular, has made progressive

rulings on the rights of internally displaced persons,20 the right to health,21
and prison conditions,22 amongst others. While implementation has been far
from perfect, these decisions have had positive effects on public policy,
public participation, and institutional coordination.23 These judicial decisions
are the backdrop against which the cases described in this chapter have
developed.
II. AN OVERVIEW OF RECENT
JURISPRUDENCE
The Colombian courts have issued recent landmark decisions advancing the
concept of nature’s rights.24 In 2015, the Constitutional Court issued a
groundbreaking decision protecting the Tayrona Park in Colombia, home to
four distinct Indigenous groups and a unique ecosystem made of jungles,
beaches, and mangrove swamps. The Court recognized that rivers,
mountains, forests, and the atmosphere must be protected not because of their
utility but because of their own independent rights to exist.25 The Court said
it was imperative to transform humanity’s relationship with the rest of the
natural world and applied an ecocentric perspective, expressly criticizing a
purely anthropocentric approach.26 A year later, the Court issued a
groundbreaking decision recognizing the Atrato River Basin as a subject of
rights.27 Since then, a growing number of Colombian courts have followed
suit, recognizing the rights of ecosystems in response to violations of human
environmental rights. As mentioned earlier in this chapter, it should be noted
that under the civil law system in Colombia, judicial decisions do not
translate into formal laws or binding precedents. As Paola Villaviencio
explains:
although no legislation on rights of nature had been adopted at that time in
Colombia, the courts ruled in favor of such natural entities and through two
landmark decisions changed their traditional status and recogni[z]ed them as
rights-bearing subjects, thereby demonstrating that rights of
nature/ecosystems can be recognized by both legislative and judicial
channels.28
Colombian courts are not drawing on existing Colombian interpretations of

any nature’s rights laws when reviewing legal challenges on environmental
rights. Instead, they are prescribing a new interpretation to these laws based
on constitutional principles and evolving social understandings. The
international legal wave recognizing nature as a legal subject of rights is one
of the influences that has led Colombian courts to apply an ecocentric lens
when reviewing environmental rights cases. Colombia joins an emerging
jurisprudence “built on ecocentric rights-based approaches to environmental
protection” that challenges traditional legal paradigms.29
Within Colombian jurisprudence, judicial decisions by the Colombian High
Courts have established a legal analytical framework for recognizing nature’s
rights, with regional courts now also starting to apply an ecocentric
perspective when adjudicating cases. Through 2019, judicial decisions that
have recognized nature’s rights include:
The Atrato River Basin (2016, Constitutional Court);
The Colombian Amazon (2018, Supreme Court);
Páramo de Pisba (2018, Administrative Court of Boyacá);
The Plata River (2019, Colombian Municipal Civil Court of La Plata);
Three rivers in Tolima including the Coello, Combeima, and Cocora
(2019, Administrative Tribunal Court of Tolima);
The Cauca River Basin (2019, Superior Court of Medellín); and
The Pance River Basin (2019, Third Court of Enforcement of Sentences
and Security Measures of Cali).
This recognition of nature’s rights by the courts has also built momentum in
the departments of Nariño and Boyacá, culminating in the incorporation of
rights of nature into their governance frameworks in 2019.30 Within the rights
of nature framework, judicial decisions have recognized bees and an
individual iconic Andean bear named El Chucho as subjects of rights,
although these rulings are still subject to further review.31
The cases concerning the Atrato River Basin, the Colombian Amazon, the
Cauca River, and the three rivers in Tolima will be examined closely. The
Atrato River Basin case and the Colombian Amazon case have been picked
because of their significance in sparking similar rulings by regional courts, as
well their illustration of themes in environmental legislation. The Cauca

River Basin case and the case of the three rivers in Tolima, both handled by
regional courts, demonstrate how Earth jurisprudence has been applied by
regional courts to address long-term, ongoing environmental conflicts across
Colombia.
III. THE ATRATO RIVER BASIN
In 2016, Colombia’s Constitutional Court recognized the Atrato River Basin
(located within the megadiverse32 northwest Chocó department) as a subject
of rights. Although jurisprudence of the Constitutional Court had previously
referred to nature as a “subject of legal rights,” the Atrato decision was the
first time a designated ecosystem was recognized as a legal subject of rights
in Colombia.33 These rights include the right to be protected, conserved,
maintained, and restored.34
The ruling came in response to a tutela against the Colombian state filed by
the Colombia-based Center for Social Justice Studies (Tierra Digna) on
behalf of an alliance of Chocó resident organizations, including people of
African descent and Indigenous and mestizo campesino communities.35 The
action was intended to hold the state accountable for violating local peoples’
constitutional rights against well-documented, ongoing illegal mining
activity.36 These constitutional rights include the fundamental right to life37
as well as to “health, water, food security, healthy environment, and the
culture and the territory of active ethnic communities.”38 Illegal mining
activity in the region utilizes toxic chemicals, such as mercury, which
severely contaminates the surrounding ecosystem. The basin’s unfettered
contamination has been linked to the deaths of at least 37 minors; the
poisoning of 64 people by ingesting contaminated water; and the loss of
critical food and water resources, leading to dehydration, malnutrition, and
other ailments.39
The tutela was first filed on January 27, 2015, before the Administrative
Tribunal of Cundinamarca. In response, several defendants requested that the
Court deny the tutela due to lack of standing and on procedural grounds,
arguing that a tutela is an inappropriate mechanism to bring the case. Various
defendants argued that the responsibility to take action lies with other

authorities.40
Due to its constitutional functions and its obligation to defend human rights
in Colombia, the Ombudsman’s Office41 intervened to expand on the
plaintiff’s legal claims. The ombudsman affirmed that the severe socio-
ecological impacts of mining in the region violated the fundamental rights of
the plaintiffs’ populations.42 The ombudsman further emphasized that ethnic
communities have special constitutional protections, including the right to be
protected through a tutela action. Finally, the ombudsman declared that a
popular action was not a sufficient means to handle the case because a
popular action deals only with collective rights, while a tutela deals with
fundamental rights.43
On Feb. 11, 2015, the first instance court ruled against the plaintiffs by
denying the tutela action on procedural grounds. The Administrative Tribunal
of Cundinamarca (Tribunal Administrativo de Cundinamarca) held that, at its
core, the suit sought protection of collective rights. Consequently, the Court
recommended that the plaintiffs file a popular action suit. The plaintiffs
appealed the decision.44 On April 21, 2015, the second instance court once
again ruled against the plaintiffs by denying the tutela action on procedural
grounds. The State Council (Consejo del Estado) held that the suit sought to
protect collective rights and that the plaintiffs “failed to demonstrate
irreparable harm or ineffectiveness of the class actions for protection of the
rights that they considered violated.”45 On Nov. 13, 2015, the Sixth Chamber
of Review of the Constitutional Court (Sala Sexta de Revisión de la Corte
Constitucional) ordered input from several universities, NGOs, and
international organizations on several matters related to the case. The Court
also ordered and carried out a judicial inspection in Quibdó and some sectors
of the Atrato River Basin in early 2016.46
In its decision recognizing the rights of a designated ecosystem, the Court
found that the serious effects of illegal mining exploitation violated multiple
fundamental rights in the Atrato River Basin. It also declared that human
populations, which are interdependent with respect to the natural world, must
“assume the consequences of their actions and omissions with nature.”47 This
decision marks the first instance of a Colombian court designating an
ecosystem as a legal subject, with (in essence) the right to life.48 The Court

pointed out that key principles considered during the decision-making
process included the role of international Earth jurisprudence, the principle of
interdependence, biocultural rights of specially protected ethnic groups, and
the principle of inter communis (between the commons which, in contrast to
inter partes, means the ruling applies to everyone in similar circumstances).
As you read the opinion, notice how each principle guides the Court’s
reasoning.

9. ANALYSIS OF THE CONCRETE CASE.
Introduction.
In the case submitted to the Court, the plaintiffs filed a writ of acción de
tutela to stop the intensive and large-scale use of various methods of illegal
mining and logging, including heavy machinery—dredges and backhoes—
and highly toxic substances—like mercury—in the Atrato River (Chocó), its
basins, swamps, wetlands and tributaries. Which, in this court’s opinion, have
been intensifying for several years and which are having harmful and
irreversible consequences on the environment, affecting with it the
fundamental rights of ethnic communities and the natural balance of the
territories they inhabit.
To this, they add that the mechanized mining exploitation—which has been
developing on a large scale illegally since the end of the nineties by different
actors—mainly affects the upper and middle basin of the Atrato River and
even its mouth in the gulf of Urabá, as well as its main tributaries…
concretely, through the use of heavy machinery such as suction dredgers…
hydraulic elevators and backhoes, which in turn destroy the riverbed and

perform indiscriminate dumping of mercury and other substances and
supplies required (such as cyanide, gasoline and fats, etc.) for the
development of these activities in the Atrato and its tributaries, in addition to
the dispersion of vapors that mercury treatment throws in the mining
entanglements.
In this sense, the plaintiffs consider that state-run entities (both at the local
level and at the national level) are responsible for the violation of their
fundamental rights to life, human dignity, health, water, [food security], a
healthy environment, the culture and the territory due to its omission to not
take effective actions to stop the development of such illegal mining
activities, which have generated the configuration of a serious humanitarian
and environmental crisis in the region.…
Resolution of the legal problem raised.
9.3. In a preliminary manner, the Court considers that in order to resolve the
legal problem, it must: (i) outline some reference reports that describe the
grave situation of illegal mining in the Department of Chocó; (ii) present the
effects observed in the judicial inspection carried out in Chocó in January
2016; (iii) raise a series of conclusions on the legal matters submitted for its
consideration, and finally, (iv) make some considerations about public policy
regarding illegal mining.
9.4. By way of illustration, the Chamber must begin by pointing out that the
serious humanitarian, socio-cultural and environmental situation in which the
Department of Chocó is immersed, is historic. The origins of the
humanitarian crisis in the region are old, deep and structural. Some of the
factors that have been identified in the literature that has studied the subject
in detail suggest that poverty in Chocó is the result of: (i) a colonial legacy of
weak or non-existent political-administrative institutions; (ii) difficult
geographic and climatic conditions that increase the costs of production and
“isolate” the district from the rest of the country and, at the same time, favor
the settlement of illegal armed groups; (iii) an extractive economic structure
focused exclusively on the exploitation of natural resources, in particular, the
mining of gold, silver and platinum; and (iv) the isolation of the district from
national economic activity.

9.5. To this historical situation of poverty, marginalization, institutional
isolation and the accumulation of a large number of unsatisfied basic needs—
in a region of the country that has been historically affected by violence,
displacement and internal armed conflict—has been added in the last decades
the incursion of new illegal armed groups and the exponential increase of
illegal mining, which, in the words of the Ombudsman’s Office, “has
generated an unprecedented humanitarian crisis in Chocó that demands the
joint action of the entire State, its institutionalism and territorial entities at all
levels to give attention and final solution to the serious crisis that this
Department is experiencing.”…
9.11. The worsening of the problems described, due to the overflow of illegal
mining in recent years, has meant that the vigilance and control bodies,
without exception, have repeatedly called the national government’s attention
to the critical situation that affects the Department of Chocó, especially with
respect to mining that takes place illegally.
State entities have had the possibility of knowing the dimension of the effects
on fundamental rights that occurs in this region of the country where the
plaintiffs live, by virtue of the phenomenon of illegal mining….
9.14. In terms of health effects, the Plaintiffs stated that as a consequence of
the use of mercury in illegal mining activities, “the most serious damage to
communities—in terms of health and environmental degradation of rivers and
forests—occur in the areas surrounding the Atrato River and its tributaries, in
the territories of Río Quito, Soledad, Villa Conto, San Isidro and Paimadó,
among others; damages that they estimate occurred in about 84% of the
collective territory of the communities. They explain that, according to
studies from the Pacific Environmental Research Institute—IIAP—, there
have been reports of spontaneous abortions, vaginal, skin and fungal diseases
caused by the presence of mercury, methylmercury and cyanide in the river
waters.”
In the same way, they indicated that “as a consequence of the presence of
mercury and other toxic chemical substances in the waters of the Atrato River
there is a proliferation of new vaginal and cutaneous diseases. For these
communities, the river is the center of their social and cultural life: it is there
where they identify themselves as a people, where they wash their clothes,

bath, play, swim, fish and share cultural and recreational activities.”
They indicated that “the level of mercury found by the IIAP in the
populations is alarming and refers to a study that was carried out on 160
people in the basin of the Atrato River and its tributaries (Quito River).
According to which, the level of mercury found in the blood is 60 [parts] per
million, when the minimum world average, what is considered acceptable, is
0.5 [parts] per million, and in Colombia it is 1.0 per person.”…
9.15. In terms of effects on the environment (rivers, swamps and forests),
representatives of the plaintiff ethnic communities argued that the harmful
