effects of mercury used in illegal mining activities, which is specified as
follows: “(i) by direct contact with the skin; (ii) by contamination of the
atmosphere when the substance is burned (by generating steam and then acid
rain precipitation); (iii) contamination of water sources when mercury is
poured into rivers accumulates in water, plants and fish, which are the basis
of the way of life and food practices of ethnic communities. It is added that
the ethnic communities that inhabit the banks of the Atrato River (high,
medium and low zones) suffer directly from the effects of mercury and
cyanide pollution, as all their hygienic, nutritional, social and cultural
activities are carried out in the river, in the absence of basic infrastructure of
aqueduct and basic sanitation.”
In this regard, it is added that “the contamination by chemical substances also
affects the forests and added to this the forestry exploitation that has been
carried out for years in the zone—in particular in the region of the Bajo
Atrato- without effective state control.”
To this it is also added that, “this environmental degradation not only
responds to a problem of collective rights but also to a systematic violation of
fundamental rights such as a dignified life, health, freedom of movement,
territory, and autonomy. It warns of a profound transformation of the
traditional ways of life of the communities (agriculture, fishing, hunting) due
to mining.”…
9.17. About the damages to the rights, to the culture, and the territory, one of
the community leaders of Paimadó (Chocó) affirmed, during the visit to that
region that, “it is very sad to walk today along the Quito river—which is

drying up—from Atrato to Paimadó or Manacruz because illegal mining has
not only changed the course of the river but has also ended up with traditional
forms of subsistence based on agriculture and the crops of yam, yucca and
plantain. The ancestral trees such as borojó, chontaduro, the ‘bread tree’, the
‘pato’ and the banana tree are no longer available and cannot be transported
due to the way in which mining has destroyed the river.”
In a complementary sense, the Ombudsman’s Office indicated that the illegal
mining activity in the Atrato River Basin and its tributaries has caused the
decrease of agricultural work, as a traditional form of subsistence, “to the
point that all the food consumed is taken from populated centers like Quibdó
and Beté.” The Office added that this situation has also affected the social
and ecological function of the collective territory, “because its use for the
traditional practice of agriculture was suspended.” This is how the foods that
were ancestrally cultivated for consumption such as chontaduro, borojó,
cacao, banana, among others, their basic foods, are no longer cultivated in the
areas most impacted by illegal mining, also because these activities generate
infertility on earth.…
9.22. Likewise, the destruction of the environment and the threat to
biodiversity in the region subject to the facts of this action was corroborated
not only by the Chamber but also by all the accompanying entities, as
referred to in sections 9.14 to 9.17. For the Court, there is no doubt that
illegal mining is seriously affecting the fundamental rights to life, health and
a healthy environment of the ethnic communities that inhabit the Atrato River
Basin and its tributaries. And that this violation has impacts direct and
indirect on the Chocoano ethnic communities.…
9.23.…the Chamber should reiterate that…the protection of rivers, forests,
food sources and biodiversity (healthy environment) has a direct and
interdependent relationship with the guarantee of the rights to life and health
(as well as culture and territory), within what has been called biocultural
rights. Precisely, the central elements of this approach establish an intrinsic
link between nature and culture, and the diversity of the human species as
part of nature and manifestation of multiple forms of life. From this
perspective, the conservation of biodiversity necessarily leads to the
preservation and protection of the ways of life and cultures that interact with

it.
Consequently, public policies on the conservation of biodiversity must adapt
and focus on the preservation of life, its various manifestations, but mainly in
the preservation of the conditions for that biodiversity to continue deploying
its evolutionary potential in a stable and indefinite manner, as the Court has
indicated in abundant jurisprudence. Similarly, the obligations of the State to
protect and conserve the lifestyles of Indigenous peoples, black and farmer,
mean guaranteeing their conditions of being, perceiving and apprehending
the world.…
9.25. In consideration of the aforementioned, for the Court it is necessary to
conclude that the illegal mining activity, having the potential to cause harm to
health and to the environment, as has been seen in the case of the ethnic
communities that inhabit the basin of the Atrato River, it is subject to the
application of the precautionary principle. This applies when—although there
is a principle of technical certainty—there is scientific uncertainty regarding
the harmful effects of a measure or activity. In that case, the solution that
avoids the damage must be preferred and not the one that can allow it. This
principle is not only designed to protect the right to the environment but also
the right to health when there is a threat of violation.…
[T]he precautionary principle implies in very simple terms, that in case of
scientific doubt, it does not abstain and, on the contrary, protects the right to a
healthy environment and health in connection with life.
Specifically, the application of the precautionary principle in the present case
will have as objectives, (i) to prohibit the use of toxic substances such as
mercury50 in mining activities, whether legal or illegal; and (ii) declare that
the Atrato River is subject to rights that imply its protection, conservation,
maintenance and, in the specific case, restoration.…
9.26. By way of conclusion and with respect to this particular point, the Court
finds that the Defendant entities have violated the rights to life, health and a
healthy environment of the Plaintiff communities by allowing the
indiscriminate dumping of mercury and other toxic chemical substances
necessary for the realization of illegal mining activities in the Atrato River,
its tributaries and surrounding territories by not taking concrete and

articulated measures to avoid it, having full knowledge of the situation, that
is, by omission in the fulfillment of its legal and constitutional duties. As a
result, the responsible entities will be ordered to adopt a series of emergency
measures to deal with this serious violation of the fundamental rights to life,
health and a healthy environment, which will be indicated in the relative
section to the orders.
b. About the pollution of the Atrato River, its tributaries, forests and
food sources produced by the development of illegal mining activities in
the region.
9.27. Violation of the right to water as a water source. At this point, it is clear
to the Court that, as proven by the evidence in the case file and in the judicial
inspection—which were outlined in sections 9.14 to 9.17—the illegal mining
that takes place in the Atrato River Basin and its tributaries challenges any
idea of rational use of water and forest resources, and constitutes an open
violation of the fundamental right to water (as a consequence of its serious
contamination) that threatens not only ethnic communities, the Department of
Chocó or the environment, but also one of the most important water and
biodiversity sources in the world, and thus, present and future generations.…
Additionally, it cannot be overlooked that the right to water is a sine qua non
requirement for the exercise of other rights, while “water is necessary to
produce food (right to food); to ensure environmental hygiene (right to
health); to procure life (right to work) and to enjoy certain cultural practices
(right to participate in cultural life).”Therefore, pollution—especially with
mercury and cyanide—and carrying out illegal mining activities in the Atrato
River Basin and its tributaries not only violates the right to water and other
components of the right to a healthy environment (as has already been
stated), but also violates the essential standards of availability, accessibility
and water quality established in General Comment No. 15, because this type
of mining is harmful, the production of food (trees, crops and fish), the health
conditions, the traditional ways of life and the cultural practices of the
Plaintiff ethnic communities.
Precisely, the biggest challenge of contemporary constitutionalism on
environmental matters, is to achieve the safeguard and effective protection of
nature, associated cultures, ways of life, and biodiversity, not just for the

simple material, genetic or productive utility that these can represent to
humans, but because being a living entity composed of other multiple forms
of life and cultural representations, are subjects of individual rights, which
makes them a new imperative of integral protection and respect on the part of
States and societies. In short, only from an attitude of deep respect and
humility with nature, its members and its culture, is it possible to enter into
relationships with them in fair and equitable terms, leaving aside any concept
that is limited to the simply utilitarian, economic, or efficient.
In effect, nature and the environment are a transversal element of the
Colombian constitutional order. Its importance lies, of course, in attention to
the human beings that inhabit it and the need to have a healthy environment
to live a dignified life and in well being conditions, but also in relation to the
other living organisms with whom the planet is shared, understood as stocks
worthy of protection in themselves. It is about being aware of the
interdependence that connects us to all living beings on earth; that is,
recognizing ourselves as integral parts of the global ecosystem - biosphere,
rather than from normative categories of domination, simple exploitation or
utility. A position that takes on special relevance in Colombian
constitutionalism, taking into account the principle of cultural and ethnic
pluralism that supports it, as well as the knowledge, uses, and ancestral
customs bequeathed by Indigenous and tribal peoples.
Precisely, in relation to the natural and cultural wealth of the nation, Article 8
of the Political Charter establishes as a fundamental obligation of the State
and of society to watch over the care of our natural and cultural riches.
Additionally, in the chapter on collective rights (Articles 79 and 80) and
specific obligations (Article 95-8), the general parameters that guide the
relationship between the human being and his living environment are
established: natural, environmental and biodiverse. In this sense, as a
consequence of the attributions consecrated at the head of the State, society
and individuals in the above-mentioned articles, the obligation to protect the
environment is established in order to prevent and control the environmental
deterioration factors, procuring its conservation, restoration and sustainable
development.…
9.28. In this context, it is necessary for the Chamber to advance in the

interpretation of the applicable law and in the forms of protection of
fundamental rights and their subjects, due to the great degree of degradation
and threat in which it found the Atrato River Basin. Fortunately, at the
international level a new legal approach called biocultural rights is being
developed, whose central premise is the relationship of profound unity and
interdependence between nature and human species, and that has as a
consequence a new socio-legal understanding in which nature should be
taken seriously and with full rights. That is, as a subject of rights.
9.29. In this order of ideas, the issue that is considered in this order by the
Court—on the serious effects produced by the intensive development of
activities of illegal mining exploitation with damage to multiple fundamental
rights in the Atrato River Basin (Chocó)—, has clearly evidenced that human
populations are those that are interdependent of the natural world—and not
the other way around—and that they must assume the consequences of their
actions and omissions with nature. It is about understanding this new socio-
political reality with the aim of achieving a respectful transformation with the
natural world, as it has happened before with civil and political rights (first
generation); the economic, social and cultural (second generation), and
environmental rights (third generation). Now is the time to begin taking the
first steps to effectively protect the planet and its resources before it is too
late, or the damage is irreversible, not only for future generations but for the
human species.
9.30. In this way, respect for nature must start from the reflection on the
meaning of existence, the evolutionary process, the universe and the cosmos.
That is, a system of thought based on a conception of the human being as an
integral part, and not as a simple dominator, would allow a process of self-
regulation of the human species and their impact on the environment,
recognizing their role within the circle of life and evolution from an
ecocentric perspective. It is from this consideration, for example, that respect
for animal rights has been cemented. In this way, it is a matter of establishing
a legal instrument that offers greater justice to nature and its relations with
human beings, based on the collective recognition of our species, as
suggested by biocultural rights.
In this same sense, biocultural diversity as an approach, based, as has been

seen, in an ecocentric perspective, implies that policies, norms and
interpretations about biodiversity conservation recognize the link and
interrelation that exists between culture and nature. It extends the
participation of ethnic communities in the definition of public policies and
regulatory frameworks, and guarantees the conditions conducive to the
generation, conservation and renewal of their knowledge systems, within the
framework of a SRL [Colombian Social Rule of Law].
The importance of the biological and cultural diversity of the nation for the
next generations and the survival of our natural and cultural wealth poses to
the Colombian State the need to adopt comprehensive public policies on
conservation, preservation and compensation that consider the
interdependence between biological and cultural diversity. In this way,
biocultural diversity represents the most integral and comprehensive
approach to ethnic and cultural diversity in the face of effective protection.
9.31. In other words, justice for nature must be applied beyond the human
scenario and must allow nature to be subject to rights. Under this
understanding, the Chamber considers it necessary to take a step forward in
the jurisprudence towards the constitutional protection of one of our most
important sources of biodiversity: the Atrato River. This interpretation finds
full justification in the best interests of the environment that has been widely
developed by constitutional jurisprudence and that is made up of numerous
constitutional clauses that constitute what has been called the “Ecological
Constitution” or “Green Constitution”. This set of provisions makes it
possible to affirm the transcendence of the healthy environment and the
interdependent link with human beings and the State.
From the above, a series of obligations of protection and guarantee of the
environment are derived from the State, who is first in responsibility for its
protection, maintenance and conservation, which must materialize through
responsible environmental public policies (sustainable governance), issuance
of CONPES documents, legislation and National Development Plans, among
others; without prejudice to the duty of protection and care that also assists
civil society and the communities themselves to take care of natural resources
and biodiversity. In this sense, the Chamber considers it pertinent to call
attention to the ethnic communities that inhabit the Atrato River Basin so that

they protect, within the exercise of their customs, uses and traditions, the
environment of which they are its first guardians and responsible for it.…
9.32. To that extent, considering the scope of protection of international
treaties signed by Colombia in the field of environmental protection, the
Ecological Constitution and biocultural rights, which preach the joint and
interdependent protection be human with nature and its resources, is that the
Court will declare that the Atrato River is subject to rights that imply its
protection, conservation, maintenance and, in the specific case, restoration.
For the effective fulfillment of this declaration, the Court will arrange for the
Colombian State to exercise legal guardianship and representation of the
rights of the river in conjunction with the ethnic communities that inhabit the
Atrato River Basin in Chocó; in this way, the Atrato River and its basin—
henceforth—will be represented by a member of the plaintiff communities
and a delegate of the Colombian State. Additionally, and with the purpose of
ensuring the protection, recovery and due conservation of the river, both
parties must design and set up a commission of Atrato River guards whose
integration and members will be developed in the section of orders to proffer
in this ruling.
As a complement to the above, it is necessary to remember that the central
premise on which the conception of bioculturality and biocultural rights is
based, is the relation of profound unity between nature and human species.
This relationship is expressed in other complementary elements such as: (i)
the multiple ways of life expressed as cultural diversity are inextricably
linked to the diversity of ecosystems and territories; (ii) the richness
expressed in the diversity of cultures, practices, beliefs and languages is the
product of the co-evolutionary interrelation of human communities with their
environments and constitutes an adaptive response to environmental changes;
(iii) the relationships of different ancestral cultures with plants, animals,
microorganisms and the environment actively contribute to biodiversity; (iv)
the spiritual and cultural meanings of Indigenous peoples and local
communities about nature are an integral part of biocultural diversity; and (v)
the preservation of cultural diversity leads to the conservation of biological
diversity, so that the design of policy, legislation and jurisprudence should be
focused on the conservation of bioculturality [316]. These elements, from
now on, should be considered as parameters for the protection of the rights of

the environment and nature, from a biocultural perspective.…
10.2. Next, the orders to proffer in the present sentence are outlined:
1. The Atrato River, its basin and tributaries will be recognized as an entity
subject to rights of protection, conservation, maintenance and restoration by
the State and ethnic communities, as indicated in the motivating part of this
provision in the Sections 9.27 to 9.32.…
2. The Ministry of the Environment, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of
Defense, Codechoco and Corpourabá, the Governments of Chocó and
Antioquia, and the defendant municipalities will be ordered…and in
conjunction with the Plaintiffs, within a year after the notification of the
sentence is designed and put in place a plan to decontaminate the water
sources of Chocó, beginning with the basin of the Atrato River and its
tributaries.…
3. Likewise, the Ministry of Defense, the National Police - Unit against
Illegal Mining, the National Army of Colombia, the General Prosecutor’s
Office of the Nation, the governors of Chocó and Antioquia and the
defendant municipalities will be ordered, in conjunction with the Plaintiff
ethnic communities and with the support of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,
to design and implement, within six (6) months after notification of this
ruling, a joint action plan to neutralize and eradicate definitely illegal mining
activities that are carried out not only in the Atrato River and its tributaries,
but also in the Department of Chocó. In this regard, the Court reiterates that it
is the obligation of the Colombian State to prosecute and eradicate
definitively any illegal mining activity that takes place in the country.
The aforementioned actions must include the seizure and neutralization of
dredges, and in general of the machinery used in these tasks, the restriction
and prohibition of the transit of inputs such as fuel and associated chemical
substances (mercury, cyanide) and the judicialization of responsible persons
and organizations. Also, this process will be accompanied by the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs in what has to do with the situation of foreigners who engage
in illegal mining activities.…
4. In addition to the foregoing, the Ministry of Agriculture, the Ministry of

the Interior, the Ministry of Finance, the Department of National Planning,
the Department for Social Prosperity, the Governors of Chocó and Antioquia
and the municipalities will be ordered [340] that in a concerted manner with
the plaintiff ethnic communities, design and implement within the six (6)
months following the notification of this ruling an integral plan of action
[341] that allows the recovery of traditional forms of subsistence and food.
This plan of action will be in the framework of the concept of ethno-
development that ensures minimum food safety in the area, which has ceased
to be realized by the contamination of the waters of the Atrato River and by
the intensive development of illegal mining activity.
This plan should also be aimed at restoring the rights of the ethnic
communities that inhabit the Atrato River Basin, especially in relation to the
recovery of their culture, participation, territory, identity, way of life and
productive activities, including fishing, hunting, agriculture, fruit harvesting
and artisanal mining. In this sense, the measures taken must be focused on
guaranteeing: (i) the food sovereignty of the communities and (ii) preventing
their involuntary displacement from the area due to illegal mining activities
and environmental damage.
These measures should include clear and precise indicators that allow an
effective evaluation and monitoring of the measures adopted.…
It is so ordered.
* * *
The breadth and depth of legal analysis in the Atrato River Basin case was
unprecedented when it was decided in 2016. Since then, in Colombia and
elsewhere, ecocentric considerations are becoming more common. The case
also cast a critical new light on human rights to sustainable ecosystems and
the cultural rights of Indigenous communities.
Although biocultural rights are not explicitly defined within Colombian
legislation, the Court found that there are cultural rights belonging to special
protected ethnic groups. In its interpretation of the case, the Court recognized
the interdependence between the fundamental right to life and a healthy
environment in the local context of the Chocó community of plaintiffs

(primarily consisting of specially protected groups).51 The Court noted the
culture’s distinct relationship with the Atrato River Basin, which provides
them with nearly all of their vital needs, including drinking water, food, a
bathing site, recreation, and so on. The Chocó communities’ reliance upon
the well-being of the Atrato led the Court to make an additional link—
namely, the interdependence between this specially protected ethnic group
and the local ecosystem. The Court recognized that the Atrato functions as an
extension of the local community and, therefore, saw the two as intrinsically
linked. This understanding reflects a biocentric interpretation of existing
cultural rights in the Constitution. This is a first signal by the Constitutional
Court of a potential ecocentric shift in understanding the rights of special
protected groups.
IV. THE AMAZON
In 2018, the Supreme Court of Colombia applied the ecocentric reasoning
that had been adopted by the Constitutional Court in the Atrato River Basin
case. Ruling on a constitutional challenge against deforestation in the
Amazon rainforest, the Court issued a landmark decision that recognized the
Colombian Amazon as a subject of rights.52
The case was filed with the support of the Center for the Study of Law,
Justice, and Society (Dejusticia) on behalf of 25 plaintiffs, including children
and young people from the regions in the country most vulnerable to climate
change. Through a tutela action, the plaintiffs claimed that deforestation in
the Amazon violated their constitutional right to a healthy environment and
thus threatened their fundamental rights to life, health, food, and water, as
well as the rights of future generations.53 The defendants included the
President of Colombia, the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of
Agriculture, the National Parks, the regional autonomous corporations (the
entities in charge of environmental governance by region), and local mayors
and governments.
At the time of filing, deforestation in the Amazon had increased by 44
percent between 2016 and 2017, despite Colombia’s national and
international commitments to tackle deforestation.54 The Colombian

government had committed to a 20 percent reduction in its emissions by 2030
under the United Nations Framework on Climate Change, which meant
significantly curbing deforestation.55 Furthermore, the government had
issued a joint statement with Norway, the United Kingdom, and Germany in
2010 committing to reduce deforestation to net zero by 2020.
The arguments of the plaintiffs were two-fold. First, deforestation in the
Amazon results in severe consequences to local and national ecosystems. For
instance, a significant source of drinking water in Colombia’s central region
comes from a special ecosystem known as páramos, which ultimately
depends on the Amazon to regulate its water cycle. Second, deforestation in
Colombia amounts to approximately two-thirds of all greenhouse gas
emissions in Colombia, with most deforestation concentrated in the Amazon
forest. Thus, deforestation has significant implications for climate change and
the resulting impacts.
On February 12, 2018, the first instance court ruled against the plaintiffs by
denying the tutela action on procedural grounds. The High Court of the
Judicial District of Bogotá (Tribunal Superior del Distrito Judicial de Bogotá
—Sala Civil) held that the appropriate vehicle for the plaintiffs’ claims was
not a tutela action, but rather a popular action. The plaintiffs appealed the
decision, arguing that even if there were collective impacts stemming from
deforestation in the Amazon, their fundamental rights were threatened and
thus a tutela action was the appropriate mechanism for their claims. On April
5, 2019, the Supreme Court reversed the decision by the Court of first
instance and issued a ruling in favor of the plaintiffs.
The Court applied the ecocentric approach the Constitutional Court had
applied to the Atrato Case.56 In its reasoning, the court moved away from an
anthropocentric and utilitarian perspective by describing nature as its own
autonomous being. The Court pointed out the key principles that it considers
when issuing a decision, including the precautionary principle,
intergenerational equity, and solidarity. As you read, pay attention to how the
Court applies each principle to the case, guiding its reasoning.
Future Generations v. Ministry of Environment et al.
Supreme Court of Justice

STC4360-2018
Bogotá, D.C., April 5th, 2018
OPINION OF THE COURT
TOLOSA VILLABONA, P. J.
1. BACKGROUND
1. The plaintiffs plead for the protection of “supralegal” rights, highlighting
those of “enjoying a healthy environment,” life, and health, allegedly violated
by the accused.…
2.1. As a first step, they identify themselves as “…a group of 25 children,
adolescents and young adults…between 7 and 25 years old, who live [in][2]
cities that are part of the list of cities at greatest risk by climate change…
[with] a life expectancy of 78 years on average (75 years for men and 80
years for women), which is why they expect to develop [their] adult lives
between the years 2041-2070 and [their] old age from the year 2071 onwards.
In these periods of time, according to the climate change scenarios presented
by the IDEAM,57 the average temperature in Colombia is expected to
increase by 1.6º C and 2.14º C, respectively…”.
2.2. They explain that in the Paris Agreement and Law 1753 of 2015, the
government acquired national and international commitments to achieve “…
reduction of deforestation and the emission of greenhouse gases in a context
of climate change…,” among which, they emphasize the duty to reduce “the
net rate of deforestation to zero in the Colombian Amazon for the year
2020.”…
Additionally, the “Comprehensive Strategy for Control of Deforestation and
Forest Management in Colombia,” reported that “…the country lost 178,597
hectares in 2016, that is, deforestation increased by 44% compared to the
figure reported for 2015…,” and of that number, 70,074 hectares were in the
Amazon.
They denounce as causes of this phenomenon “…land grabbing (60-65%),
illicit crops (20-22%), illegal extraction of mineral deposits (7-8%),

infrastructure, agro-industrial crops, and illegal extraction of wood.…”
2.4. They affirm that “…deforestation in the Amazon has consequences not
only in that region but also in the ecosystems of the rest…” of the national
territory, among which they list: “…1) The negative alteration of the water
cycle; 2) the alteration of the grounds that capture and absorb water when it
rains (and the resulting floods that this generates); 3) the changes in the water
supplies that arrive at the páramos58 and provide water to the cities where the
plaintiffs live; [and] 4) global warming due to the carbon dioxide emissions,
which are stored in the forests in conditions of no deforestation.…”
2.5. According to what is argued, the above is possible because those
summoned have not adopted the appropriate measures to deal with this
eventuality and, in addition, this has dire consequences for the places of their
residence, altering their living conditions and depriving them of the chance to
“enjoy a healthy environment”.
They claim to be part of “…the future generation that will face the effects of
climate change in the periods 2041-2070 and 2071-2100.…”
2.6. In their opinion, the present petition is “suitable for the protection” of the
guarantees invoked, for which they present numerous jurisprudential
precedents from the Constitutional Court, specifically, they ensure
compliance “with the criteria established for this in judgment SU-1116 of
2001”.
Additionally, they state that “…acción popular as an alternative means of
defense is not adequate and effective enough…,” as “both fundamental and
collective rights are affected.”…
1.3. The appeal.
The plaintiffs formed it insisting on their disagreements, particularly, they
believe that the acción popular is not the “ideal remedy” to settle the
controversy raised and, furthermore, claiming to have proved the
“irremediable damage”.…
2. DISCUSSION

[The opinion summarizes the procedural differences between tutela and
acción popular, recognizing that constitutional jurisprudence has established
a right to the tutela action when the impairment of group interests infringes,
consequently, upon individual rights. The action must meet several
requirements including (i) a connection between the violation of collective
rights and the violation of one or more of the primary, fundamental, and
individual rights, (ii) the person filing must be the person directly affected,
(iii) the threat of the rights must not be hypothetical, and (iv) the judicial
order must seek to restore individual rights and not the collectives ones, even
if these are implicit in the decision.]
…By virtue of what has been said, it can be preached that the fundamental
rights of life, health, minimum subsistence, freedom, and human dignity are
substantially linked and determined by the environment and the ecosystem.
Without a healthy environment, subjects of law, and sentient beings in
general, will not be able to survive, much less protect those rights, for our
children or for future generations. Neither can the existence of the family,
society, or the State itself be guaranteed.
The increasing deterioration of the environment is a serious assault to current
and future life and all other fundamental rights; it gradually depletes life and
all rights related to it. The inability to exercise the fundamental rights to
water, to breathe pure air, and to enjoy a healthy environment negatively
affects the current populace; it increases the lack of fresh water and decreases
the ability to enjoy a dignified life.…
Humanity is mainly responsible for this scenario, its global hegemonic
position led to the adoption of an anthropocentric and selfish model, whose
characteristic features are harmful to environmental stability, namely: i) the
excessive demographic growth; ii) the adoption of a rapid system of
development guided by consumerism and the current political-economic
systems; and iii) the excessive exploitation of natural resources.
5. However, gradually an awareness of the duty to change our behaviors has
begun creating itself. There is a surge of movements favorable to a new
ideology of an “ecocentric anthropic” society, which overcomes the excessive
“homo mensura” “autistic” anthropocentrism; which takes into consideration
the environment, the idea of progress, and the notion of sustainable

development to achieve “…a balance between economic growth, social
welfare, and environmental protection, under the understanding that present
actions must ensure the possibility of making use of resources in the future.
…”
5.1. “…[G]iven the existence of [the] risks and problems of a global
nature…,” the judiciary must advocate in the Constitutional State; for the
effective recognition of the rights that in principal may seem “…oriented to
the protection of collective interests and the satisfaction of generalized
needs…,” substantially points to the defense of the essential rights of the
individual.…
The foregoing means that all individuals of the human species must stop
exclusively thinking of self-interest. We are obligated to consider how our
works and daily behavior also affect society and nature.…
5.2. As noted, the scope of protection of the fundamental principles is each
person, but also the “other.” The “neighbor” is alterity; its essence: the other
people that inhabit the planet, covering also animal and plant species.
But, in addition, it includes the subjects not yet born, who deserve to enjoy
the same environmental conditions lived by us.…
5.3. The environmental rights of future generations are based on (i) the
ethical duty of solidarity of the species and on (ii) the intrinsic value of
nature.
The first is explained by the fact that natural goods are shared by all
inhabitants of Planet Earth, and by their descendants or future generations
who do not yet have them physically, but who are tributaries, recipients, and
owners of them, even if they, in a contradictory way, are increasingly
insufficient and limited. Thus, without the current existence of an equitable
and prudent approach to consumption, the human species may find itself
compromised in the future due to the scarcity of essential life resources. In
this way, solidarity and environmentalism “are related until they become the
same.”
Thus, the establishment of the duty of human solidarity with nature

constitutes the essential meaning of “the true values that routinely facilitate
life” both in its present and future dimensions. This idea establishes a
dynamic and tangible ethic of environmental values, adjusted and compatible
with “…the conservation needs of nature in the most favorable sense needed
to maintain the lives of human beings [forever].…”
The second transcends from the anthropocentric perspective, and focuses on
“anthropic-ecocentric” criterion, which places the human being on par with
the environmental ecosystem, whose purpose is to avoid arrogant, dismissive,
and irresponsible treatment of environmental resources, in its entirety, to
satisfy materialistic ends, without any protectionist or conservationist respect.
The establishment of the duty of direct solidarity with nature is built on a
value, on itself; this, by affinity with the knowing subject or external “object”
by which it is defined, because the human being “forms part of nature
‘being’, likewise, nature.”
This is the main idea on which the concept of the intrinsic value of the
environment is based: respect for oneself implies, in itself, “respect for the
part of oneself that is composed by nature, and which, in time, future
generations will form a part of.”
What has been stated then, develops a binding legal relationship regarding
the environmental rights of future generations, such as an “omission,” whose
impact translates into a limitation to the freedom of action of present
generations, while simultaneously implicitly demanding new burdens of
environmental commitments, to the extent that they assume the care and
custody of natural resources and the future world.”
6. In view of the foregoing, numerous regulations have emerged in the
international arena, hard and soft law, which constitute a global ecological
public order and serve as guiding criteria for national legislation, as well as
for resolving citizens’ complaints about the destruction of our habitat, in
favor of the protection of the subjective rights of people, of both present and
future generations.59…
7. In Colombia, the 1991 Constitution updated our stance on environmental
issues, from which a national ecological public order was constructed, in

which several precepts were established on the matter, such as: the
prevalence of the “general interest” (Article 1); the duty to protect the
“natural assets of the nation” (Article 8); public health (Article 49); the
“ecological dimension” of private property (Article 58); the qualification of
“natural parks” as property that is “inalienable, imprescriptible and not
subject to seizure” (Article 63); one function of education was defined as “…
train the Colombian when it comes to…the protection of the environment…”
(Article 67); the fundamental right to “…enjoy a healthy environment” and
duty of the state “…to protect the diversity and integrity of the
environment…” (Article 79); the imposition upon the State duty to “…plan
the handling and use of natural resources, to guarantee their sustainable
development…”.
The Constitutional Court played an important role with its pronouncements,
and designed a jurisprudential line welcoming the concepts and advances that
have emerged on the subject in the international and academic scene.
In this sense, it has analyzed the Constitution’s postulates from a “green”
perspective, cataloging the Political Charter as an “Ecological Constitution”
and elevating the environment into the category of fundamental rights.…
10. The conservation of the Amazon is a national and global obligation, it is
the main environmental axis of the planet, and has been called the “lung of
the world.…”
The international community has generated various commitments to achieve
its conservation; the Amazon Cooperation Treaty (TCA) should be
highlighted, as its main objective is the “…promotion of the harmonious
development of the Amazon, and the incorporation of its territories to the
respective national economies, which is essential for maintaining the balance
between economic growth and environmental preservation…”
Likewise, in the aforementioned Framework Convention on Climate Change
in Paris in 2015, where Colombia, among other responsibilities, agreed to
reduce “deforestation in the Colombian Amazon,” with this purpose, it
promoted the “Sustainable Colombia Initiative” and the “Vision Amazon”.…
11. Under the above assumptions, the Court will study the appropriateness of

the protection, establishing, for that purpose, whether the violation of the
collective right to enjoy a healthy environment implicates a violation of
fundamental rights, alleged as violated by the plaintiffs.…
In this regard, the Chamber must determine, at the venue of the dispute,
whether there is a causal link between climate change generated by the
progressive reduction of forest cover, caused by the expansion of the
agricultural frontier, narco-crops, mining, and illicit logging; and the
supposed negative effects on the health of people residing in the Colombian
territory; and, next, it will have to establish if the rampant degradation of the
jungle forests directly undermines the rights to dignified life, the water, and
the health of the tutelantes.…
This previous reality, in contrast with the environmental legal principles of (i)
precaution; (ii) intergenerational equity; and (iii) solidarity, leads the Court to
the following conclusions:
11.1. Regarding the first of the aforementioned principles, there is no doubt
that there is a risk of harm, since, according to the IDEAM, the increase in
GHG [greenhouse gas] emissions caused by the deforestation of the Amazon
rainforest would generate an increase in Colombia’s temperature, between
“0.7 and 1.1 degrees Celsius between 2011 and 2040,” while for the period
“between 2041 and 2070,” an increase of “1.4 and 1.7” degrees centigrade is
calculated, and to reach up to 2.7 degrees Celsius “in the period between
2071 and 2100.”
Likewise, the mass reduction of the Amazon forest would break the
ecosystem’s connection with the Andes, causing the probable extinction or
threat of subsistence of the species inhabiting that corridor, generating
“damage to its ecological integrity.”
Additionally, according to the IDEAM, the GHG emissions due to
deforestation would cause, with respect to rainfall, two types of
consequences. The first, an increase in several regions of the country, a
situation that would trigger an increase in water levels, and therefore, runoff,
generating the spread of water-borne pollutants. The second, a deficit in other
national departments, causing a decrease in the water supply, as well as
prolonged droughts.

Regarding the irreversibility of the damage and the scientific certainty, both
additional components of the precautionary principle, they are evident since
the GHG emitted as a result of deforestation, constitutes 36% of the forestry
sector, becoming an uncontrolled component of CO2 emissions; information
supported, in detail, by the studies carried out by the IDEAM, the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development,
and the UNDP [United Nations Development Programme], among many
others.
11.2. In terms of intergenerational equity, the transgression is obvious, as the
forecast of temperature increase is 1.6 degrees in 2041 and 2.14 in 2071;
future generations, including children who brought this action, will be
directly affected, unless we presently reduce the deforestation rate to zero.
11.3. The principle of solidarity, for the specific case, is determined by the
duty and co-responsibility of the Colombian state to stop the causes of GHG
emissions caused by the abrupt forest reduction of the Amazon; thus, it is
imperative to adopt immediate mitigation measures, and to protect the right to
environmental welfare, both of the plaintiffs, and of the other people who
inhabit and share the Amazonian territory, not only nationals, but also
foreigners, together with all the inhabitants of the globe, including the
ecosystems and living beings.
11.3 [sic]. The discussed reality, in addition to transgressing the regulations
pertaining to the Environmental Charter of the country, and the international
instruments that make up the global ecological public order, constitutes a
serious ignorance of the obligations acquired by the State in the Framework
Convention on Climate Change of Paris 2015, where Colombia, among other
commitments, undertook an agreement to reduce “deforestation in the
Colombian Amazon,” with the objective to reduce deforestation to zero in
that region by 2020.…
It is up to the authorities to respond effectively to the specific questions of the
problem, among which, it is important to highlight the urgent need to adopt
mitigation and corrective measures: i) for the excessive expansion of illicit
crops and illegal mining that unreasonably destroy the Amazonian forest; ii)
to fill the void left by the FARC and paramilitaries to make an active state
presence in favor of the conservation of Amazonian territories that in the

context of armed conflict were conquered by insurgent groups, merciless
predators, irrational colonizers, and generally, people and organizations
outside the law; iii) to prevent and mitigate the growing fires, deforestation,
and unreasonable expansion of the agricultural frontier; iv) for the lack of
prevention of the consequences inherent to constructing roads, granting titles
to property and mining concessions; v) for the expansion of large-scale agro-
industrial and livestock farming; vi) for the preservation of this ecosystem
due to its importance in regulating the global climate; vii) for the lack of
scientific calculations of the release of tons of carbon through burning and
the loss of biomass, which constitutes the vegetation cover; and viii) to
confront climate change due to the destruction of the Amazon rainforest in
the national territory.
12. Therefore, the excessive intensification of this problem is evident,
showing: the ineffectiveness of the governmental measures adopted to
confront it, and, from that perspective, granting the protection for the breach
of fundamental guarantees such as water, air, dignified life, and health,
among others, in connection with the environment.
In this regard, this Chamber follows the thesis held by the Constitutional
Court in the T-622 of 2016, related to the recognition of nature as a real
subject of rights, a position consistent with the relevance of the environment
and its conservation, from the eco-centric perspective defined in previous
sections.…
13. It is clear that despite several international commitments, legislation, and
jurisprudence on the subject, the Colombian State has not efficiently tackled
the problem of deforestation in the Amazon.
13.1. Currently, the three autonomous regional corporations with jurisdiction
in the Amazonian territory, have not made efforts to reduce the concentrated
area of deforestation, which registers 47.23% of the AT-D, distributed
between the Corporation for the Sustainable Development of the South of the
Amazon (Corpoamazonia) at 24.47%; the Corporation for the Sustainable
Development of the North and the East of the Amazon (CDA) at 11.10%; and
the Corporation for the Sustainable Development of the Area of Special
Management La Macarena (Cormacarena) at 11.67%.

In this way, the aforementioned environmental authorities are not fulfilling
their duty to evaluate, control, and monitor natural resources, nor to impose
and execute sanctions in the event of a violation of environmental protection
norms in their jurisdiction; despite being able to, in case they lack sufficient
resources, request support from other agencies at the national and local level,
in order to protect natural resources.
13.2. Deforestation in the Colombian Amazon also occurs in places under the
protection of National Natural Parks of Colombia (PNN), specifically in the
Sierra de la Macarena, Nukak, Tinigua and La Paya parks, “which occupy the
places 3, 5, 6 and 9, respectively, of the Parks with a higher concentration of
AT-D in 2017.”
The deforestation in natural national parks is proof of the negligence in
fulfilling the legal functions which were assigned to the Natural National
Parks of Colombia (PNN), noting that the reduction of forest mass in
protected areas is a situation that by regulation, must be controlled and
sanctioned by said authority, it being empowered, in case of not being able to
fulfill this task, to demand collaboration with other authorities of the national,
departmental, and municipal rank.
13.3. The departments with jurisdiction in the Amazonian territory, such as
Amazonas, Caquetá, Guaviare, and Putumayo are also failing to fulfill the
functions that the law imposes on them regarding the environmental
protection of the Colombian Amazon. It is well known, they have the duty to
assist the Regional Autonomous Corporations [(CAR)] with authority in their
territories; the percentage of deforestation is their responsibility to mitigate in
concert with the CAR.
13.4. Regarding the municipalities that have Amazonian land according to
the AT-D newsletter, in particular, La Macarena, Valle del Guamuez, Puerto
Asís, San Vicente del Caguán, Vistahermosa, San José del Guaviare, Puerto
Guzmán, Orito, Puerto Rico, Mapiripán Cartagena del Chairá, Calamar,
Uribe, Solano, Puerto Leguízamo, El Retorno, Miraflores, and Florencia,
contained high levels of deforestation in 2017, without them, as observed in
the reports related to this action, counteracting the situation.
The foregoing transgresses the fulfillment of legal and regulatory

assignments, established by Article 3 of Law 1551 of 2012, which assigns
municipalities “to ensure the proper handling of natural resources and the
environment, in accordance with the Constitution and the law.”…
14. Therefore, in order to protect this ecosystem vital for our global future,
just as the Constitutional Court declared the Atrato River, the Colombian
Amazon is recognized as a “subject of rights,” entitled to protection,
conservation, maintenance and restoration led by the State and the territorial
agencies.
Consequently, we grant the relief, and order the Presidency of the Republic,
the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, and the Ministry
of Agriculture and Rural Development, in coordination with the actors of the
National Environmental System and the participation of the plaintiffs, the
affected communities, and the interested population in general, within the
four (4) months following today’s notice, to formulate a short, medium, and
long term action plan to counteract the rate of deforestation in the Amazon,
tackling climate change impacts.
The purpose of this plan will be to mitigate the early deforestation warnings
issued by the IDEAM.
Likewise, it will be ordered of the Presidency of the Republic, the Ministry of
Environment and Sustainable Development, and the Ministry of Agriculture
and Rural Development, within a period of five (5) months following today’s
notice, with the active participation of the plaintiffs, the affected
communities, scientific organizations or environmental research groups, and
the interested population in general, to formulate the construction of an
“inter-generational pact for the life of the Colombian Amazon (PIVAC)” to
adopt measures aimed at reducing deforestation to zero and greenhouse gas
emissions, and has national, regional, and local implementation strategies of a
preventative, mandatory, corrective, and pedagogical nature, directed towards
climate change adaptation.
It will also be ordered of all the municipalities of the Colombian Amazon,
within a period of five (5) months following today’s notice, to update and
implement the Land Management Plans, and when relevant, include an action
plan to reduce deforestation to zero in its territory, which should encompass

preventative, mandatory, corrective, and pedagogical measurable strategies,
oriented towards climate change adaptation.
The Corporation for the Sustainable Development of the South of the
Amazon (Corpoamazonia), the Corporation for the Sustainable Development
of the North and the East of the Amazon (CDA), and the Corporation for the
Sustainable Development of the Special Management Area La Macarena
(Cormacarena), will be ordered, within a period of five (5) months from
today’s notice, with respect to its jurisdiction, to create an action plan to
counteract the deforestation problems reported by the IDEAM through
police, judicial, or administrative measures.
Additionally, within their duties, the defendants will have to, in the forty-
eight (48) hours following the completion of this ruling, increase actions
tending to mitigate deforestation while carrying out the modifications
contained in the aforementioned mandate. Within the responsibilities
assigned, they must urgently present the complaints before the corresponding
administrative and judicial entities.
It is so ordered.
V. THE CAUCA RIVER
The plaintiffs filed a tutela against Empresas Publicas de Medellin60 (EPM),
Antioquia (department in Colombia), the Ituango Hydroelectric S.A., the
Ministry of Environment, the National Agency of Environmental Licenses
(ANLA), and others to protect the fundamental rights of communities living
near the Ituango Hydroelectric project. The project is located in Antioquia,
along the Cauca River.61 Hidroituango (the name of the project) has been
under public scrutiny due to the social and environmental impacts of the dam.
Despite EPM’s attempts to keep an open dialogue with neighboring
communities, there was little progress addressing the problems affecting the
nearby villages and municipalities. In February 2019, a structural flaw led the
company to take emergency measures, which resulted in a reduction in the
water flow, causing a large part of the river to run dry.62 This had significant
impacts on fishing activities, transportation, and tourism in the area. In
response, the plaintiffs filed a legal action seeking protection of their

fundamental rights to health, water, and a healthy environment, and the
neighboring communities’ right to a dignified life.63
The court of first instance of the Fourth Civil Court of the Oral Circuit of
Medellin (Juzgado Cuarto Civil del Circuito de Oralidad de Medellín)
declined to grant the tutela after concluding that there was a clear and real
intention on behalf of EPM to deal with the ongoing issues around
Hidroiutango. The court found that there had been no omission by the
defendants, which is a requirement for a tutela action to move forward. The
plaintiffs appealed the case, alleging that the first instance judge failed to
study the precedent of sentence T-622 of 2016 (the Atrato River Basin case).
On appeal, the Superior Court of Medellin reversed the judgment.
Castro Córdoba and David Ochoa v. Ministry of Environment et al.
Superior Court of Medellín
Judgment #38
Medellín, 2015.
OPINION OF THE COURT64
SOSA LONDOÑO, J., J.
[The judgment discusses the facts and procedural posture. It then cites
national65 and international law on sustainable development and future
generations.]
It is noteworthy that the regulations implicitly recognize the dignity of future
generations and this principle constitutes, in essence, one of the
distinguishing elements of the subjects of rights in modern legislation, which
imposes an analysis around the concept and the determination that not only
are future generations the subjects of rights, but of the possibility that the
obligations that current generations have towards future generations can be
protected through tutela actions.…
[The opinion cites the United Nations Charter, the United Nations
Conference on the Human Environment (The Stockholm Declaration), the
World Charter for Nature, the Rio Declaration on Environment and

Development, the Vienna Declaration and Program of Action, and
UNESCO’s Declaration on the Responsibilities of the Present Generations
Towards Future Generations.]
5.2 Sentence C-256 of 1994 said that the constitutional basis of the legal
requirement for a declaration of impact or environmental defect is found in
the constitutional right that all people have, those of present and future
generations, to enjoy a healthy environment.…
5.3 When Sentence C-649 of 1997 stated the rights possessed by all persons,
current and future generations alike, it reiterated that the right to enjoy a
healthy environment emerges from articles…of the Constitution, which is the
basis for the obligation that environmental law has imposed on people to
present an environmental…impact statement…on the consequences that the
development or execution of a specific project or activity may have on the
environment or on natural resources. The consequences explain “the need to
protect for current and future generations the basic elements…to guarantee a
healthy environment through the preservation and restoration of the
ecosystem…”
5.4 Sentence C-126 of 1998 reminds us that the Constitution produced an
“ecologization” of private property, which has noteworthy consequences not
only for the social function of property but also because the powers of
individual property owners are limited by the rights of those who have yet to
be born, that is, by future generations, requiring and empowering the legal
order to adopt greater restrictions on appropriations of natural resources and
the powers of property owners themselves.…
6. Based on the previous doctrinal and jurisprudential precedent, and granting
the preamble of the United Nations Charter and the instruments mentioned…
future generations, [have] a fundamental right to a healthy environment [and]
are true subjects of rights.
But nothing would be done by simply recognizing the rights of future
generations under the category of subjects…if there were not at the same time
a way for those rights to be exercised, in other words, [the courts] must grant
from now on actions for the defense of their interests, and although it could
be thought that in this case the appropriate mechanism is the acción popular,

given the nature of the requests made in the writ of amparo, mainly the third,
regarding the declaration of the Cauca River as a subject of rights, judgment
T-622 of 2016 as a precedent imposes a different interpretation.…
8. As stated in the complaint, there is no doubt about the existence of an
unprecedented crisis that affected the…fauna and flora that depend directly
on the good state of the river, a natural ecosystem that, as the 1972 United
Nations Conference in Stockholm declared, must be preserved for the benefit
of future generations.…[Arising from this precedent,] another no less
important subject of rights emerges: the same river to which EPM owes a
series of commitments to remedy the damages that the contingency produced
on its ecosystem.
This is not about elaborating on the argument for the protection of natural
wealth, the concept of the ecological or green constitution, since the
Constitutional Court already did so through its judgment T-622 of 2016, …
but about the special protection that the Cauca River deserves as a source of
food, environment, and diversity, but especially of the right to water as a
hydrological source, of conserving its future value.…
The river has suffered from the behavior, the intervention of human beings,
foreseeable or not, taking its flow to a historical minimum.…[The crisis]
demands, claims, a recovery process, (if one is highly optimistic in the
medium term, but in reality, in the long term), and therefore merits not only
current compensation, but…the materialization of future generations as a
subject of rights.…
[T]here was mention of the intergenerational equity that can be expressed in
that future generations have the right to an adequate inheritance that allows
them a level of life not less than that of the current generation, which is a
principle that is directly related to the ethical base of the environmental order
and the solidarity concept, this latter enshrined in Article 1 of the 1991
Political Charter.…In summary, this court essentially declares:
(i) That future generations are the subject of rights requiring very special
protection, (ii) that they have fundamental rights to dignity, water, food
security, and a healthy environment, and (iii) that the river Cauca is the
subject of rights, which implies, as was done with the Atrato River, its

protection, conservation, maintenance, and restoration under the authority of
the Public Municipal Entity and the State.
10. The orders to be issued will be similar to those ordered by the Court in
judgment T-622 of 2016. Without a doubt, EPM is responsible for the
violation of the fundamental rights of future generations to their life, water,
food security, healthy environment, but as the abundant documentary
evidence that has been collected shows that effective actions [by the
company] have begun to stop the damage suffered by the river downstream,
no order will be issued to initiate such actions.
Consequently, the National Government will be ordered to exercise the
protection and legal representation of the rights of the river (through the
institution designated by the President, which could well be the Ministry of
Environment), together with the communities and people who were present at
the preventive monitoring hearing of the Ituango Hydroelectric project held
on February 27, 2019.…In this way, the Cauca River and its watershed will
be represented from now on by a member of these participants and a delegate
of the Colombian Government, who will be the guardians of the river.…
[The guardians will receive support from public or private entities,
universities, research centers, environmental organizations (national or
international), grassroots groups, etc.]
It is ordered that the General Prosecutor of the Nation, the Ombudsman, and
the Office of the Controller General of the Republic…in accordance with
their legal and constitutional powers, carry out a process of accompaniment
and monitoring compliance and execution of orders already indicated…[these
offices] will submit semester reports of their activities and compliance
indicators.
11. Finally, since the judgment will only be effective once it is extended to all
persons or communities that reside in the Cauca river basin, its tributaries,
and neighboring territories, the Court grans inter communis effects to the
decision.
It is so ordered.

VI. THE COELLO, COMBEIMA, AND COCORA
RIVERS
Isaac Vargas Morales, acting as Municipal Official of Ibague, filed a popular
action against the Ministry of Environment, the Colombian Geological
Survey, AngloGold Ashanti Colombia, Continental Gold, and others, seeking
to stop mining activity in the river basins of the Coello Greater River, the
Combeima River, and the Cocora River. Gold mining around the rivers’
basins affects the quality and quantity of water used for human consumption.
It also affects the agricultural, industrial, and livestock sectors, which are
crucial for the economy and food security of the population of Ibague and
other municipalities. In essence, the complaint alleged that the environmental
licenses granted to mining companies threaten the Coello, Cocora, and
Combeima Rivers and, in turn, the collective rights to enjoyment of the
public space, free of pollution; the enjoyment of a healthy and ecologically
balanced environment; the prevention of technically foreseeable disasters;
and public safety and health.
Vargas Morales v. Ministry of Environment et al.
File number: 73001-23-00-000-2011-00611-000
Administrative Court of the Department of Tolima
Ibague, Tolima May 30th, 2019
OPINION OF THE COURT
ROJAS VILLA, J., J.
[The opinion discusses in depth the national and international sources of law
on sustainable development and the right to water, including international
human rights law and comparative law. It then describes the precautionary
principle. According to a 2011 technical report, the risks associated with gold
mining exploration and exploitation include increased soil erosion, loss of
regular water flows, impacts on food production, and an increase in the kind
and number of landslides, among others.]…
At this stage of the judicial process, it seems plausible to affirm that if these

risks are materialized, the damage would be of such magnitude that they
would pose a serious detriment to the environment and natural resources. A
critical result if one considers that, in addition, strategic ecosystems are being
affected which…play a crucial role for the subsistence of ecosystems, crops,
and communities of the region.…
[T]his Chamber finds that the acute environmental, social, and economic
problem resulting from the granting of mining titles in the basin of the rivers
Coello, Cocora and Combeima makes evident a fundamental threat of serious
damage to the ecological balance and the preservation of natural resources
that cannot be [ignored by] the Constitutional Judge of Popular Action.…
[Following the principle of proportionality, the Court denied the suspensions
of the mining titles requested by plaintiffs.]
The Chamber declares the violation of the collective [rights] to enjoy the
public space free of pollution, a healthy and ecologically balanced
environment, prevention of technically foreseeable disasters, and public
safety and health of the communities living in the basin of the Coello river.…
The Chamber will adopt the necessary measures to protect the hydric
resource that is indispensable for the residents of the Municipality of Ibague
and a great part of the Department of Tolima.…
[Opinion cites the 2016 Atrato river decision.]
The Chamber will adopt the arguments developed by the Honorable
Constitutional Court to recognize that the Coello, Combeima and Cocora
rivers, their basis and tributaries as individual entities, subject of rights to the
protection, conservation, maintenance, and restoration in charge of the State
and communities.
Consequently, it will order the national Government to exercise guardianship
and legal representation of the rights of the rivers (through the institution that
the President of the Republic designates, which could well be the Ministry of
Environment and Sustainable Development) together with the communities
that live in the basis of the Coello, Combeima, and Cocora rivers; in this way,
the three rivers and their basins, from now on, will be each represented by a

member of their communities and a delegate from the Colombian
Government, whom will be the guardians of the river.…66
Additionally, this plan will include a series of clear indicators that allow to
measure their efficacy and must be designed and executed in a consensual
manner with the residents of the area, while guaranteeing the participation of
communities…under the 169 Convention of the ILO.
[Opinion orders the creation of action plans as well as toxicologic and
epidemiological studies of the Coello, Combeima, and Cocora rivers, its
tributaries, and communities.]
It will be ordered that the General Prosecutor of the Nation, the Ombudsman,
and the Office of the Controller General of the Republic, in accordance with
their legal and constitutional powers, carry out a process of accompaniment
and of monitoring compliance and execution of orders already indicated…in
the short, medium, and long term.…
VII. PÁRAMO DE PISBA
In 2018, a Colombian court (Tribunal Administrativo de Boyacá) declared
that the Páramo de Pisba was a subject of rights, making it the third
recognized rights-bearing ecosystem in the country. The recognition of this
páramo (a unique alpine tundra ecosystem) raised questions, such as, if this
ecosystem has rights, shouldn’t all of them? In the case of the Páramo de
Pisba, it is important to note the context of the ecosystem. Seven percent of
Colombians rely on water supplies regulated by páramos. Only five countries
in the world have páramo ecosystems, and Colombia has the most.
The evolution of their legal protection began in 2011, when the basis for the
law of the páramos (Ley 1450, Artículo 20267) first appeared within the
context of the National Development Plan. The initial law set to demarcate
the boundaries of páramos and prohibited new contracts for the cultivation of
the land, farming, mining and exploration for minerals and carbon, and
construction of oil and gas refineries. In 2018, Law 1930 (Ley 1930)68 was
signed by Congress. Article 1 states, “The object of the present law is to
establish páramos as strategic ecosystems and to set guidelines that favor

their integrality, preservation, restoration, sustainable use, and generation of
knowledge.” The Law contains 6 chapters and 33 articles, pertaining to the
maintenance and protection of páramos, in relation to retaining their integrity.
A few months later, the Boyacá Tribunal’s decision (Expediente 15238 3333
002 2018 00016 01I) recognized Páramo de Pisba as a subject of rights, with
the right to maintenance, protection, conservation, and restoration.69 The
decision came in response to a tutela filed by residents demanding their
fundamental rights to participation in the process of zoning and determining
the boundaries of the páramo.
In its decision, the court declared the Ministry of the Environment and
Sustainable Development as the legal representative of Páramo de Pisba.70
The court then gave the ministry one year to determine the boundaries of the
páramo, inviting all actors to participate in the process, according to
minimum standards.71 The judge cautioned that the outcome of the process
cannot infringe on the rights of the Páramo de Pisba.72 With notice to the
mining companies operating across the department, the court ordered that all
people affected by the rezoning should be compensated, particularly those
groups who have historically been subject to discrimination.73
VIII. CONCLUSION
The cases discussed in this chapter, along with others in Colombia that
advance the development of Earth law have fostered a broader discussion in
Colombia of the relationship between nature and humans. Supporters of
nature’s rights point to the evolving understandings of rights and legal
personhood throughout history. At one time, children, women, and many
other groups were not considered legal persons in the way they are now.
Today, in an increasing number of jurisdictions, ecosystems, river basins, and
individual animals are the subjects of rights.
These achievements raise important questions. For example, what is the
impact of granting rights to nature when guardians or representatives are
required to sue on their behalf? Might the creation of new legal obligations in
regard to natural systems be redundant and needlessly complicate decision-
making if human rights to a healthy environment could provide the same

remedies? Would focusing on human rights yield more effective results than
working towards the creation of such new obligations. Consider the argument
that nature’s rights are not an appropriate framework to further environmental
protection because ecosystems and their nonhuman components cannot
exercise rights or be subject to duties in the ways that humans and legal
entities such as corporations can.
Villavicencio and others, writing in support of these new obligations, have
found that recent judgments shed light on the inefficiency of the Colombian
government, institutional gaps at the local and national levels, and the
insufficient protection of nature and ecosystems.74 They signal a new
approach in which judges recognize the rights of ecosystems so that local
communities and other stakeholders may enforce their protection,
conservation, maintenance, and restoration, even in the absence of action by
the legislative branch.75 Furthermore, they provide an opportunity for civil
society actors to engage in monitoring and create follow-up mechanisms to
aid the implementation of a judgment. While the plaintiffs in many of these
cases did not expressly request that the courts designate ecosystems as the
subjects of rights, the courts have affirmatively recognized their legal
personhood and made progress to reinforce a rights of nature paradigm.76
Rights evolve in a matrix of legal systems and frameworks and need to be
considered in tandem with these factors. Despite the judgments’ tendency to
give emphasis to the enforcement of nature’s rights, the challenges of
effectuating these rights is complicated in the context of inequality, ongoing
violence, and a social transition in Colombian society that was engulfed in
armed conflict before the Constitution was adopted in 1991.
There may also be tensions between the rights of nature and the fundamental
rights of vulnerable populations. Challenges between the rights of nature and
of vulnerable populations have begun to emerge in the implementation of
some of the recent case decisions in Colombia. For example, in the case of
the Atrato River, various residents thought to be associated with the
protection of the river have been targeted for assassination and threatened
with violence.77 While the threats and violence against environmental
defenders are not a new phenomenon, the judicial order may be increasing
this risk. At this time, there does not appear to be any governmentally

recognized system to protect residents from these ongoing threats of
violence.78 An analysis of these tensions does not imply a flaw in the
judgments per se. It simply indicates that the individuals and entities
responsible for the implementation process are encountering foreseeable
challenges in carrying out the courts’ decisions.
Tensions are also present in the implementation of the judicial orders on
deforestation in the Amazon region. There is a complex web of groups with a
presence in these territories, including regional autonomous corporations
(CARs), Indigenous groups, foreign landowners, campesinos (peasant
farmers), and illegal armed actors. While certain groups have special rights to
operate in the territory, such as the CARs, or special constitutional
protections, as is the case with Indigenous people, others, such as illegal
armed groups and foreign landowners or investors, have power in the
territory. In this simplified matrix, it is important to note that Colombian
campesinos do not have constitutional protections, despite long-standing
movements advocating for their rights. In the case of the Amazon, attention
should be paid to who is prosecuted for deforestation and how certain groups
may be disproportionately penalized. Similarly, plans to tackle deforestation
cannot develop without providing comprehensive programs to help build
alternative livelihoods that do not rely on deforestation. In 2019, the
Colombian government made deforestation a national security issue; the
impacts will further shed light on how this tension between rights evolves
and is reconciled in practice.79
In sum, while there are challenges to implementing judgments recognizing
nature’s rights, the Colombian cases represent an extraordinary advancement
in the field of Earth law and chart a promising future for both litigation and
legislation. Recently, Representative Juan Carlos Lozada Vargas introduced a
bill to amend the Constitution to make nature a subject of rights in
accordance with the recent judicial decisions.80 In addition, these decisions
are spurring meaningful legal debate, pushing institutions to respond, and
inspiring activists to imagine new ways to leverage the law for social and
environmental change. These developments will continue to shape the field
of Earth law.
STUDY QUESTIONS

(1) Interpretation of international principles. Colombia’s legal system
integrates several principles of international environmental law and
environmental justice into its legislation and jurisprudence, such as the
precautionary principle, the prevention principle, distributive justice,
participatory justice, environmental equity, and intergenerational equity,
among others. How does the judiciary enlarge these principles beyond their
traditional interpretations in the Atrato judgment? For instance, the judiciary
expanded the precautionary principle, which is often applied in the
environmental context, to human health. How can this expanded view of the
precautionary principle be used to develop legislation suited to protect human
and non-human nature?
(2) Establishing a new regime. The Atrato judgment set the legal framework
for ecosystem rights-based jurisprudence in Colombia, namely the right to be
maintained, protected, conserved, and eventually restored. While most rights
frameworks applicable to individual rights typically include duties, nature
cannot itself execute assigned duties or be held liable for harms done.
Recognizing both nature’s intrinsic and instrumental values as a holistic
package, is it appropriate to posit that—in the absence of assigning nature
traditional legal duties—the intrinsic values and ecological goods and
services provided by nature may supersede the need for prescribed legal
duties? In the Atrato case, the Court has assigned humans with the
responsibility to act on behalf of nature, with the understanding that a
protected and respected natural environment preserves and enhances human
quality of life. How can the reasoning presented by this case contribute to our
understanding of a nature’s rights regime?
(3) Challenges in implementation. It is important to note that a significant
portion of the state defendants in this case do not have a regional presence in
Chocó, despite their prescribed obligations to coordinate or collaborate on
activities in the region. How might this complicate the implementation of the
court’s orders? Do you think authorities without a preexisting regional
presence can realistically meet the demands of the court order? Further, the
case deals in large part with illegal activity and alludes to illegal armed actors
in the region. Due to armed conflict and state absence in the region, Chocó
residents continue to live alongside illegally armed actors. How might this
further complicate full implementation of the judgment?

(4) Nature’s rights. In its decision, the Court repeatedly underscored
interdependence between the fundamental human right to life and other
constitutional rights, including the right to a clean, healthy environment. This
emphasis can be seen as a signal to the broader judicial branch to recognize
this interdependence. Additionally, the case presents an ecocentric
understanding of human dependence on nature, linking this interdependence
to emerging Earth jurisprudence and setting a legal precedent for nature’s
rights around the globe. Yet, nature’s rights were not a part of the requested
relief. What rational arguments did the Court use to make a case for nature’s
rights? Are any existential arguments included to justify the order to protect
nature’s rights? How do you understand the Court’s interpretation of the
petitioner’s claims?
(5) Soft law v. hard law. While Colombia’s legal system integrates
international agreements through what is known as bloque de
constitucionalidad, some of the sources that the plaintiffs in the Amazon case
included in their complaint to assert the government’s legal obligation were
not international conventions or other legally binding treaties. For instance,
the joint statement that had set zero net deforestation as a goal for the year
2020 was simply a statement reiterating the support that Germany, the United
Kingdom, and Norway offered to Colombia in the fight against deforestation.
Similarly, the plaintiffs referred to several principles of international
environmental law such as the precautionary principle, the solidarity
principle, and intergenerational equity among others, of which only some are
included in the Constitution. What was the importance of these principles in
