the Court’s reasoning? Does it make a difference that some of these
principles were enshrined in national law while others were not? How did the
national commitments under the Paris Agreement informed the opinion’s
reasoning?
(6) Challenges in litigating climate change. As in other climate change
lawsuits around the world, the plaintiffs in the Amazon case risked the Court
finding that it did not have jurisdiction over the case because the question of
deforestation and climate change policy was a “political question” reserved
for the executive and legislative branches to handle. Alternatively, the Court
could have found that the violations alleged by the plaintiffs were
nonjusticiable, although the jurisprudence on socioeconomic rights in

Colombia made this scenario much less likely than in countries like the
United States. What do you make of the Court’s non-treatment of the
separation of powers principle? What other obstacles do you think the
plaintiffs faced? In addition, climate change litigation faces the challenge of
establishing causality between greenhouse gas emissions and the impacts
attributed to the defendants’ (in)action. Climate change is a global problem
cause by global GHG emissions, which can rarely be traced to particular
emitters. How did the Court overcome the obstacle of causality?
(7) Intragenerational equity. While the Amazon plaintiffs brought their
claims on behalf of present and future generations, the Court did not rule on
their standing nor did it adopt a definition of future generations. The
claimants used the very specific definition of future generations; namely,
“those individuals who would become adults between the years 2041 and
2070,” which is the period in which the country expects to see an increase in
average temperatures of more than 1.6°C according to official data. Why do
you think they defined “future generations” this way? If future generations
were defined to include unborn children would this have caused standing
issues? Could this have potential implications in other areas of law?
(8) Science and the law. Both the Amazon complaint and the Supreme
Court’s opinion drew heavily on climate science and the government’s
official submissions to the United Nations Framework on Climate Change.
The government of Colombia relies on the Institute of Hydrology,
Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM), the agency tasked with
producing environmental data in the country. This made it very difficult for
the defendants to question any of the science that was presented. Instead, the
defendants argued on procedural grounds, pointing out that the tutela was not
the ideal mechanism to bring the plaintiffs’ claim. What do you think is the
role of science in climate litigation cases, or in litigation dealing with the
rights of nature more broadly?
(9) Separation of powers. Other climate change litigation cases around the
world have demanded more ambition with respect to national plans to
mitigate emissions.81 This inherently raises questions about the separation of
powers principle. In the Amazon case, the Court issued a series of orders
mandating the executive branch to develop and implement action plans.

However, the order fails to mention the Ministry of Finance, arguably the
most important ministry. What other actors should the opinion have
involved? Do you think these orders violate the separation of powers
principle? Are they effective?
(10) Challenges of structural judgments. Similar to the Atrato River Basin
case, the Amazon judgment attempts to tackle complex and structural
dynamics in Colombia: ongoing conflict, an absent state, weak institutions,
the presence of illegal actors, land grabbing, and rampant inequality, among
others. Do you think a judicial order is an appropriate way to deal with these
problems? What should be the role of the judiciary branch in tackling
systemic issues like deforestation in the Amazon or chronic environmental
injustice in ethnic territories? How should other branches of government
engage with the problem? Furthermore, the case raises questions about
monitoring and compliance, which are ongoing challenges at the time of
writing. What issues may emerge during the implementation of structural
judgments like the one in the Amazon case?
(11) The role of precedent. In both of the cases dealing with rivers, the
regional courts adopted an ecocentric framework. How do previous decisions
shape the reasoning of the courts here? Do you think that their application of
previous judgments is compelling?
(12) Legal fetishism. Julieta Lemaitre Ripoll has coined the theory of legal
fetishism to describe a situation of “desiring and enjoying the law not as a
means to an end, but rather as an end in itself.”82 While in general
environmental practitioners praise recent jurisprudence applying an
ecocentric approach, several concerns have been raised. Some critics posit
that the Colombian legal system already has sufficient tools to protect nature
and thus advocates should pay more attention to the implementation of
legislation or judicial sentences. Similarly, some critics find that there are
strong constitutional protections but significant gaps in both institutional
coordination and fulfillment of fundamental rights on a daily basis.83 What
do you make of these critiques? Are there any arguments for the symbolic
effect or impact of the sentences discussed in this chapter?
(13) Legislating nature’s rights. As of the time of publication, a member of

Congress had introduced a constitutional amendment to modify Article 79
and guarantee the recognition of nature as a subject of rights. What do you
think about constitutional reform as opposed to further jurisprudence on this
issue? What is the value of introducing and potentially passing a
constitutional amendment on this issue? Are there drawbacks?

CHAPTER 19
Earth Law in Latin America: 
A Glimpse of Brazil and Mexico1
I. INTRODUCTION
Latin America is a world leader in the rights of nature movement. Already,
you have learned about developments in Ecuador and Colombia—two
trailblazers in the development of Earth law. Other countries in Latin
America also recognize the rights of nature in some capacity, and many more
have proposed to do the same.2
In addition to Ecuador and Colombia, an important embodiment of rights of
nature in Latin America comes from Bolivia. In 2010, Bolivia’s Plurinational
Legislative Assembly passed the Law of the Rights of Mother Earth, which
recognized nature’s rights to life, to the diversity of life, to water, to clean air,
to equilibrium, to restoration, and to pollution-free living.3 This law was
followed up by the 2012 Framework Law of Mother Earth and Integral
Development for Living Well,4 which required the creation of a Mother Earth
Ombudsman Office (Defensoria de la Madre Tierra) to bolster Bolivia’s
existing rights of nature protections. Unfortunately, in practice, Bolivia has
largely failed to uphold its bold rights of nature agenda. As lamented by
Pablo Solon, former UN ambassador from Bolivia: “We might expect
neoliberal extractivist politicians to do this. But it’s particularly painful when
it is done by former comrades who wave a banner of Mother Earth in the air
while crushing those very rights under foot.”5

Two other Latin American countries that recognize nature’s rights in some
capacity are Brazil and Mexico. Both Brazil and Mexico have a unique
perspective on emerging Earth law movements in Latin American nations.
They were combined into a single chapter to encourage a comparison of their
respective approaches. There are many similarities and some important
distinctions, as well.
Despite their different biomes—tropical Brazil is famous for its rainforest and
savannah while Mexico straddles the tropic of Cancer and has significant
areas of arid and desert habitat—Brazil and Mexico share significant
similarities from an environmental perspective. Both are classified as mega-
diverse countries with an incredible array of plant and animal species. And
while both have national constitutions that emphasize a human-centered
attitude to the environment, in both nations, there are budding grassroots
movements to strengthen Indigenous philosophies, ecocentrism, and the
rights of nature.
This chapter discusses Brazil first and then Mexico. For each, it starts by
examining the law’s treatment of the environment and how Earth law can be
derived from the existing legal systems. Both sections also discuss the
development of Earth law at the local or statewide level. Finally, both
sections look at the current and possible future roles of Indigenous peoples in
the development of the countries’ legal systems.
There are differences between Brazil and Mexico, as well. Notably, the two
countries discuss unique theories for expanding current laws to achieve
greater ecocentrism: the Brazil section discusses incorporating Indigenous
traditions into the existing Western framework, whereas the Mexico section
discusses extending human rights frameworks to include nature.
Additionally, the Brazil section includes a unique case about legal rights for a
parrot.
As you read these case studies, consider how new rights-based movements
are born. It may be through the passage of an innovative local law that
inspires other governments to follow suit. Or perhaps the judiciary, in a
display of bravery and creativity, issues a decision based on a new legal
theory. In both cases, grassroots movements are often the engine—activists,
lawyers, civil society groups, and others fighting against the injustices of the

legal system. Finally, as the rights of nature movements in Brazil and Mexico
grow, consider how an Earth lawyer might guide them over the coming years
to ensure their success.

PART I: BRAZIL
II. THE ENVIRONMENT IN BRAZIL’S
CONSTITUTION
Brazil is the largest country in South America. It shares its borders with the
majority of countries on the continent and boasts an extensive Atlantic
coastline. Given its variety of terrain and abundance of diverse species and
habitat, it is among the world’s 17 mega-diverse countries.6 As of the 2010
census, there were approximately 900,000 Indigenous people in Brazil
distributed among 305 ethnic groups. Of its total area, 13.8 percent of the
lands have been reserved for Indigenous peoples, the majority of which are
concentrated in the Amazon.7
The current Federal Constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil was
promulgated in 1988, becoming a symbol of the process of national
democratization as the country exited 21 years of military dictatorship. It
describes Brazil as a legal democratic state founded on sovereignty,
citizenship, dignity of the individual, social values of work and of free
enterprise, and political pluralism.
A. Ecologically Balanced Environment
Brazil’s Constitution explicitly recognizes the importance of an ecologically
balanced environment. However, the value of nature is justified solely in
anthropocentric terms for its benefit to humans. The Constitution also gives
special safeguards to the country’s Indigenous peoples, which allows space
for the development of an ecocentric approach to law by supporting
traditional Indigenous practices that are in harmony with natural systems.
With this introduction, we now look at some of the specific provisions.
Title VIII of the Brazilian Constitution addresses “The Social Order” and
includes Chapter VI on the environment and Chapter VIII on “Indians,” as
the chapter calls Indigenous peoples. Brazil’s Constitution reflects many
progressive values. However, unlike the Constitution of Ecuador, the

Brazilian Constitution does not recognize nature as a subject of rights with
legal standing of its own. Instead, care for the environment is justified in
terms of the benefits to humans. Consider Article 225, which establishes a
strong ecological foundation but simultaneously treats the environment as an
“asset of common use”:
All have the right to an ecologically balanced environment, which is an asset
of common use and essential to a healthy quality of life, and both the
Government and the community shall have the duty to defend and preserve it
for present and future generations.8
STUDY QUESTIONS
Although seemingly anthropocentric, how might one argue that first word of
Article 225, “all,” applies to the entire Earth community, not only humans?
Or that protections for “future generations” might include nonhumans? What
opposing arguments might be made?
***
Article 225, para. 1 establishes specific government duties intended to ensure
the effectiveness of the right to an ecologically balanced environment,
including the following:
To “preserve and restore the essential ecological processes and provide
for the ecological treatment of species and ecosystems”;
To “promote environmental education in all school levels and public
awareness of the need to preserve the environment”; and
To “protect the fauna and the flora, with prohibition, in the manner
prescribed by law, of all practices which represent a risk to their
ecological function, cause the extinction of species, or subject animals to
cruelty.”9
Article 225, para. 2 requires those who exploit mineral resources to restore
environmental degradation, and para. 3 requires those who conduct
procedures and activities considered harmful to the environment to repair the
damages caused.10

Article 225, para. 4 adds additional protections for specifically named
ecosystems, although critics have called these protections “merely
symbolic.”11 The wording does not prohibit extractivism and has even been
construed to encourage it:
The Brazilian Amazonian Forest, the Atlantic Forest, the Serra do Mar, the
Pantanal Matogrossense and the coastal zone are part of the national
patrimony12, and they shall be used, as provided by law, under conditions
which ensure the preservation of the environment, therein including the use
of mineral resources.13
B. Indigenous Rights
Indigenous peoples are prominent in Brazil, particularly in the Brazilian
Amazon, where they constitute 23 percent of the population.14 Brazil’s
Constitution affords certain rights to Indigenous peoples in Chapter VIII,
Articles 231-232 on “Indians.” As explored in detail in Chapter 25,
“Indigenous Legalities,” and throughout this book, empowering Indigenous
cultures’ care for ecological balance is important for Earth law development.
Article 231 establishes that “Indians shall have their social organization,
customs, languages, creeds, and traditions recognized, as well as the original
rights to the lands they traditionally occupy.”15 It also recognizes the
inexorable link between Indigenous peoples and the land: “Lands
traditionally occupied by Indians are…those indispensable to the preservation
of environmental resources necessary for their well-being and for their
physical and cultural reproduction, according to their uses, customs and
traditions.”16 Moreover, it voids acts that attempt to exercise dominion and
rights over the Indigenous lands or to exploit them.
However, Article 231, para. 6 also creates loopholes that could deprive
Indigenous peoples of their land where there is a “relevant public interest”:
Acts with a view to occupation, domain and possession of the lands referred
to in this article or to the exploitation of the natural riches of the soil, rivers
and lakes existing therein, are null and void, producing no legal effects,
except in case of relevant public interest of the Union, as provided by a

supplementary law and such nullity and voidness shall not create a right to
indemnity or to sue the Union, except in what concerns improvements
derived from occupation in good faith, in the manner prescribed by law.17
The next section explores how the Indigenous rights and the environment
have fared under the strongly pro-development administration of President
Jair Bolsonaro.
III. DEVELOPMENTS IN BRAZIL UNDER
BOLSONARO
While Brazil’s Constitution opens up the possibility of an ecocentric
approach to law, there has been only limited success in practice. Instead of
implementing constitutional protections for the environment, some national
legislation has done the opposite—such as a 2012 law that weakened forest
conservation under Brazil’s 1965 Forest Code.18 Many other environmental
initiatives continue to prioritize economic development over human and
environmental well-being. For example, Brazil’s 2007 energy infrastructure
plan, established with scant public input, prioritizes dam construction in the
Amazon without fully considering environmental and social impacts,
amongst other shortcomings.19
The attack on the environment and Indigenous rights has intensified since
President Jair Bolsonaro came to power in 2019. For example, in his first
year of office, he issued a decree to transfer authority to protect Indigenous
territory to the Ministry of Agriculture, “which is well known to defend the
interests of businesses that want access to previously restricted and protected
Indigenous lands.”20 Bolsonaro also supports the transformation of the
Amazon rainforest into land for cattle and crops. With the industry
empowered by Bolsonaro’s rhetoric to destroy rainforests for quick profit,
“the Amazon is completely lawless,” said Carlos Nobre, a climate scientist at
the University of São Paulo.21
In another effort to circumvent constitutional protections, on March 4, 2019,
Admiral Bento Albuquerque, the new minister of Mines and Energy,
announced plans to permit mining on Indigenous land, even without the

approval of impacted communities. He said the restricted Indigenous areas
“have become centers of conflict and illegal activities, that in no way
contribute to sustainable development or to sovereignty and national
security.”22
People and ecosystems both suffer as a result of Brazil’s backsliding on
Indigenous rights. Chief Antonia Mello of the Munduruku people described
how “the actions of the Brazilian government [are] allowing the assassination
of [our] community’s way of life, a way of life that had lived in harmony
with Mother Earth for hundreds of years.”23
Many Indigenous groups are fighting back. Even before Bolsonaro assumed
office, the Association of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil (APIB)24 released a
letter stating, “We do not accept being treated as inferior beings.…We are
only different, and it is the Federal Government’s obligation, according to the
Constitution, to respect our ‘social organization, customs, languages, beliefs
and traditions.’”25 In early 2020, the APIB sued Bolsonaro for making racist
comments. Bolsonaro had said, “The Indian has changed, he is evolving and
becoming more and more, a human being like us.”26 Previously, Bolsonaro
had characterized Indigenous peoples as “animals in zoos” who need to be
assimilated into Brazilian society. Some Indigenous leaders even believe he
is planning ethnocide by eliminating their cultures and existence.27
Bolsonaro has also weakened public participation in governance. Through
national councils and conferences, civil society has long helped formulate
public policy. On April 12, 2019, Bolsonaro signed a decree extinguishing
national councils, committees, and commissions created by decrees of
previous presidents and limited the creation of new ones.28 Among the
national councils targeted were those aiming to uphold racial equality,
sustainable rural development, and biodiversity. On June 12, 2019, Brazil’s
Supreme Court issued an injunction blocking parts of the decree, finding that
Bolsonaro cannot abolish bodies supported by law and created through the
deliberations of the National Congress.29
Together, these actions by Bolsonaro signify a disregard for environmental
and Indigenous rights in Brazil. As with the United States under the Trump
Administration, the authority of Bolsonaro to significantly weaken

environmental protections underscores the need for an enforceable system of
inalienable rights for Earth and its inhabitants. Such rights could develop in
the courts, as the next section explores.
IV. ECOCENTRISM IN BRAZILIAN COURTS
This section explores a recent case that extended rights to a nonhuman
animal. As you consider the Brazilian court’s approach, recall the reasoning
in the decisions by the New York courts discussed in Chapter 11,
“Nonhuman Rights.”
In the 2019 case In re IBAMA, the Superior Court of Justice (STJ)30
recognized the rights of a nonhuman animal based on the principle of
individual dignity found in the Brazilian Constitution. The case involved the
capture, confinement, and mistreatment of a native parrot.31 The Court found
that the parrot’s living conditions were not acceptable, but instead of merely
confiscating the parrot to be housed elsewhere, the Court deliberated on the
rights of the parrot and what would be in its own best interest.
Although the Court could have decided to release the parrot into its natural
habitat or to a qualified zoo, it ultimately found that the bird, having lived
domestically with the Ibama family for over two decades, would best remain
in their custody and care. To separate the parrot from its caregiver would
break a certain “affective bond” in violation of “the ecological dimension of
human dignity, since the multiple changes in the environment perpetuate the
stress of the animal, putting in doubt the feasibility of a readaptation to a new
environment.”32
To arrive at this decision, the Court looked to Article 225, Section VII of the
Constitution, which obligates the government to “protect the fauna and the
flora, prohibiting…all practices that jeopardize their ecological functions,
cause extinction of species, or subject animals to cruelty.”33 The meaningful
contribution to the body of Earth law recognizes the inherent dignity and
needs of the parrot as an individual—much the same as they would consider
the unique needs of a child in a custody case. The Court also recognized the
empathic interspecies bond between the parrot and the family. As explored in
detail in Chapter 11, legal recognition of the dignity of even a single member

of a nonhuman animal species opens the opportunity to extend that sound
rationale to protect the entire natural world. In re IBAMA provides a foothold
to justify universal recognition of the rights of nature in Brazil.34
In re IBAMA (2019)
Superior Court of Justice REsp 1.797.175/SP
DECISION
IV
From the ecological perspective of the principle of human dignity and the
recognition of non-human animals as subjects of law.…
In this context, one should reflect on the Kantian, anthropocentric and
individualistic concept of human dignity, that is, to focus also on non-human
animals as well as all forms of life in general, in the light of the biocentric
jurisphilosophical [the philosophy of law] matrix (or ecocentric), capable of
recognizing the web of life that permeates the relationship between human
beings and nature.…
In other words, one can also speak of limitations on the fundamental rights of
human beings based on the recognition of non-human interests.…
Thus, any prohibition against the practice of “objectification” should not, in
principle, be limited only to human life, but must have its broad spectrum to
also contemplate other life forms.…
The very idea of non-cruel treatment of animals must no longer be grounded
in human dignity or human compassion, but rather in the very dignity
inherent in the existence of nonhuman animals. It is a question of moral duty.
…
This view of nature as an expression of life in its entirety enables
constitutional law and other areas of law to recognize the environment and
non-human animals as beings of their own value and therefore to deserve the
respect and care that the legal system may attribute to them as having

ownership of rights and dignity.
In fact, what we must rethink and discuss is that these nonhuman living
beings are no longer just means that guarantee to human species their own
dignity and survival.…
In the reasoning defended by Oliveira (2016),35 nature is not something apart
from the human species, and the rest of the beings of the planetary
community, as well as human beings, are nature itself in its universality and
diversity.
It is necessary to rethink a new rationality, distinct from the logic
hegemonically traced and reproduced within ordinary instances, that
appreciates demands, including this one which is the subject of discussion in
this Superior Court, so that the State and Society can think in a radically
different way from the already established legal standards.
Moreover, with this reflection as a starting point, it is not difficult to conclude
that the relationship to be established between the human being and nature is
much more an interrelation marked by interdependence than a relationship of
domination of the human being over the rest of the beings of the planetary
community.
Therefore, it is necessary to reflect on the internal field of infra-constitutional
laws, in an attempt to point out ways to ripen the discussion about the
recognition of dignity of nonhuman animals and, consequently, of the
recognition of rights and to make the shift so that people can relate to each
other and to the rest of living things.36
As you just read, In re IBAMA had a much broader application than a single
parrot. The Court argued for the need to change the anthropocentric paradigm
to a biocentric one—regardless of the anthropocentric nature of Brazil’s
Constitution. Citing this case in courts in the United States and other nations
will inform judges of new approaches to ecocentric law, a critical
responsibility of Earth law practitioners. Whether it is considered a
persuasive authority will depend on the judge.

V. LOCAL RIGHTS OF NATURE INITIATIVES
IN BRAZIL
There has been a growing movement since 2015 to recognize nature as a
subject of rights at the local level in Brazil. As in the United States, one of the
primary motivations is the belief that Brazil’s national framework is
inadequate to protect nature.
Considering that current environmental laws have been failing to adequately
protect Brazilian ecosystems, there have been several grassroots movements
to recognize nature as a subject of rights. The story begins with the city
council of São Paulo’s consideration of a draft bill37 to amend its Organic
Law (equivalent to a local constitution) to read as follows:
The Municipality will promote the development of environmental policies,
considering that members of nature possess intrinsic rights to life and
maintenance of their ecosystems in interdependence with the dignified life of
citizens, in order to achieve sustainability in the city.
The explanatory report for the draft bill stated that “the issue of the
recognition of the rights of nature is intrinsically dependent on a new
approach to the concept of sustainable development” and highlights the “need
for a real paradigm shift.”38 It also stated that “Brazil has approached this
understanding with discussions about Environmental Services which go far
beyond defending nature’s economic values and end up exposing its
priceless, intangible value, even in relation to human beings.” Humanity, the
draft bill concluded, has a duty “to preserve life worthy of and on the planet.”
The 2015 draft bill did not pass. But advocates tried once again, and in 2017
the city council of São Paulo successfully amended Article 180-A of the
Organic Law of the Municipality to recognize nature as having “full, intrinsic
and perpetual rights, inherent in its existence on the planet.”39 The bill also
calls upon the government to promote policies, management tools, and
partnerships to preserve and restore Brazil’s environment and foster harmony
with nature, including by addressing climate change. Finally, the bill
establishes that any actions taken that would affect nature “should be

supported by Science; observe the Precautionary Principle; and seek to
involve the Legislative and Judiciary, the State and the Union, the other
municipalities of the Metropolitan Region and civil society entities in
general.”
On May 16, 2018, another legal proposal for the rights of nature was
presented in São Paulo, this time to the São Paulo Commission of Legality.40
The draft bill, which has not yet been approved at the time of this book’s
publication, “received a positive evaluation from the main commission and is
expected to gain further support for future implementation within the legal
system.”41
Other municipalities besides São Paulo have also embraced the rights of
nature. The municipality of Bonito in the state of Pernambuco passed an
amendment to its Organic Law in 2017 that adopts the rights of nature in
Article 236:
The Municipality recognizes the right of nature to exist, thrive and evolve,
and should act in order to assure all members of the natural community,
human and non-human, of the Municipality of Bonito, the right to an
ecologically healthy and balanced environment and to the maintenance of
ecosystemic processes necessary to good quality of life, being the Public
Power, as well as the collectivity, in charge of defending and preserving it for
the present and future generations of the members of the earth community.…
In order to ensure this right, the Municipality shall promote the amplification
of its public policies in environmental, health, educational and economic
areas so as to provide conditions for the establishment of a life in harmony
with Nature, and it shall articulate with other states, regional and federal
competent bodies, as well as with other municipalities, if it is the case, in
order to solve common problems related to the protection of Nature.42
One year later, the municipality of Paudalho in the state of Pernambuco also
amended its Organic Law to recognize rights of nature, using wording almost
identical to Bonito. The change aimed to ensure that public policies align
with the “establishment of a life in harmony with Nature.”43 As a result of the
amendment to the Organic Law, the San Severino Ramos Natural Water
Spring was granted rights to exist, thrive, and evolve in accordance with the

law’s rights of nature provisions—the first specific ecosystem to be granted
rights in Brazil.
Finally, on March 28, 2018, the municipality of Fortaleza proposed a draft
bill to amend its Organic Law in order to grant recognition to the rights of
nature. It states: “All beings of Nature have the right to an ecologically
balanced environment, [which is] a good for common use for the people and
essential to a healthy quality of life and to natural ecosystemic processes.”44
This law is still pending as of the time of publication.
These developments are all recent. It remains to be seen how these laws will
impact local environmental protections in practice and whether they will
spark systemic change throughout Brazil. However, the existence of the
movement in Brazil is itself meaningful and is likely to lead to the
development of more ecocentric law in the near future.
VI. BRAZIL’S INDIGENOUS PEOPLE JOIN TO
SHOW A PATH FORWARD
In 2017, two major environmental gatherings in Brazil set a strong
foundation for the future of Earth law. Indigenous peoples played a major
role in each. The first event was a large environmental forum that produced a
“Letter to Nature” defining their rights of nature vision. The second was the
Great Assembly of the Alliance of Mother Nature’s Guardians.
First, in July 2017, participants of the Brazil Environmental Management
Forum—including the Ministry of the Environment, Indigenous leaders, civil
society representatives, and others45—adopted a “Letter for Nature,” entitled
The Rights of Nature and Public Policies in Cities. The letter-writing process
was led by Vanessa Hasson, a Brazilian lawyer, civil society leader, and
rights of nature advocate.46 The letter was also heavily influenced by
Indigenous leaders from the University of Ancient Wisdom, the Acunhanhe
Institute, and the Shawādawa community.
The Letter for Nature invited forum participants to recognize the inherent
rights of nature and reflect upon their responsibility to strengthen public

policies that harmonize with nature. The Letter for Nature also warns that
current policies and legislation are insufficient to address the global climate
emergency, which may result in “catastrophic ruptures, risking functions
essential to the maintenance and reproduction of life, including human life.”
As a solution, the Letter for Nature highlights the rights of nature and also
encourages society to return to traditional, Indigenous, natural knowledge
that emphasizes the connections between nature and humans.
In accordance with the Brazil Constitution’s mandate to promote
environmental education, the Letter for Nature also encourages the expansion
of rights of nature:
14. Formal education at every level should be oriented according to the basic
principles of the Rights of Nature and of a way of life in harmony with
Nature; multi/interdisciplinary theoretical and methodological approaches
should be included in teaching curriculum and research methodology
disciplines in both primary and secondary education and at undergraduate
and postgraduate levels.47
Finally, to put these precepts into action, forum participants promised to
“undertake their best efforts for the inauguration or expansion of public
preservation policies of the environment.” Such efforts should follow the
principle of harmony with nature, “considering the intrinsic value of each of
the members that constitute the Earth.” As participants in the forum
recognized, harmony with nature does not mean a complete reversion to pre-
industrial conditions, but it does support the value of ancient human
knowledge.
Building upon this effort, in October 2017, the first-ever Great Assembly of
the Alliance of Mother Nature’s Guardians was held in Brasília and attended
by nearly 200 Indigenous representatives from around the world. Together,
the delegates discussed rights of nature paradigms and other global issues
impacting human rights and the environment.48
Prior to this event, the Constituent Assembly of the Alliance of Mother
Nature’s Guardians was held in Paris and resulted in the adoption of the
Declaration of the Alliance of Guardians and Children of Mother Earth. The
declaration stated: “We must evolve towards a paradigm based on Indigenous

thought and philosophy, which grants equal rights to Nature and which
honors the interrelationships between all life forms and the preservation of
Mother Earth.”49
In conclusion, Brazil is advancing numerous promising ecocentric legal
paradigms—through the courts, local lawmaking, and multi-stakeholder
gatherings. But simultaneously, the current government is attempting to
circumvent laws and overturn policies in order to prioritize incessant
extraction and development of ecosystems, injurious to Indigenous peoples
and others.50 Now, we will compare this dynamic with rights-based
movements in Mexico.

PART II: MEXICO
VII. INTRODUCTION TO MEXICO
Mexico is the fourth largest country in the Americas, after Canada, the United
States, and Brazil. It is also counted among the world’s 17 mega-diverse
countries, having the second-largest number of ecosystems amongst them.51
At 27.5 million people, Mexico’s Indigenous population is the largest in the
Americas and makes up 21.5 percent of the country’s total.52
This section explores Mexico’s constitutional protections of the environment,
Indigenous rights, and the rights of nature. Overall, while Mexico’s
environmental enforcement is lacking, it has a legal and societal foundation
for the development of Earth law.
VIII. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTIONS IN
MEXICO
Mexico’s Constitution explicitly recognizes the importance of the
environment. However, as with Brazil, nature’s value is viewed from a
human perspective. Nonetheless, with the In Re IBAMA case, it is possible
that Mexico’s constitutional environmental rights could be extended to
include rights of nature in the future.
Here are some of the most important environmental provisions in Mexico’s
Constitution:
Article 2(A): Granting Indigenous peoples the right to maintain and
improve their environment, and the preferential use of natural resources
within sites they inhabit;
Article 4, para. V: Establishing the right of “any person” to a healthy
environment;
Article 25: Requiring national development to be sustainable, and the
use of resources to be for the general good while preserving the

environment;
Article 27: Allowing the government to impose restrictions, including
on the use of natural resources and private property, that preserve and
restore “environmental balance;”
Article 73: Establishing the power of Congress to legislate in order to
coordinate the actions of the three levels of government in
environmental matters and to direct the General Board of Health on
combating environmental pollution;
Article 115, para. III: Organizing states with municipal powers in
environmental matters, including creating nature reserves; and
Article 122: Giving special competence to Mexico City in
environmental matters.53
(As with Brazil, consider how these constitutional protections can be relied
upon to develop Earth law. For example, could an ecosystem be defined as a
“person” and thus have a right to a healthy environment? Or could the
Indigenous right to maintain and improve their environment necessitate their
application of ecocentric laws?)
In addition to its constitutional protections, Mexico has passed several major
environmental framework laws. (Note in the below examples how both laws
not only protect but restore nature when it is harmed.) First, the General Law
of Ecological Equilibrium and Environmental Protection (1988) defines the
framework for all environmental laws in Mexico. Its overarching purpose is
the “preservation and restoration of the ecological balance, as well as the
protection of the environment.…”54 Second, the Federal Law of
Environmental Responsibility (2013) builds upon the General Law by
creating a strong application of the “polluter pays principle.” Its stated
purpose is “to regulate the environmental responsibility that arises from the
damages caused to the environment, as well as the repair and compensation
of such damages.”55 This law also envisions the creation of environmental
courts that are separate from other civil, administrative, and criminal courts.
Taking a broader view, some of the main principles of Mexico’s
environmental laws are sustainable development, conservation, preservation,
and environmental restoration. Mexican law also supports the prevention
principle. However, the precautionary principle, asserting that activities

should be prohibited in case of doubt, is practically absent from Mexican
environmental legislation.56
Finally, Mexico has numerous agencies that work to defend the environment.
The Ministry of Environment and National Resources (SEMARNAT)57 is
mandated to ensure the protection, conservation, and use of nature with an
emphasis on sustainable development. Additionally, the Federal Office of
Environmental Protection (PROFEPA)58 is the institution responsible for
increasing compliance with environmental regulations and minimizing
environmental deterioration. Neither agency represents the interests of nature
directly.
IX. DERIVING RIGHTS OF NATURE FROM
HUMAN ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS?
As discussed later in this chapter, in Mexico, there are a handful of recent
state constitutional amendments establishing rights of nature. Another way to
develop Earth law in Mexico is through human environmental rights
frameworks.
Many people in Mexico do not view rights of nature as being totally separate
from human rights. Instead, rights of nature is seen as upholding human
rights that rely upon healthy and functioning natural systems. According to
José Gilberto Garza Grimaldo,“[t]he premises of human rights consist in
balancing what is good for human beings and what is good for other species
and for the planet itself, and to fully understand the meaning of the
interdependence between all ecosystems and all that we share for our own
survival.”59
Article 1 of Mexico’s Constitution establishes the foundation of human rights
protection:
[A]ll individuals shall be entitled to the Human Rights granted by this
Constitution and the international treaties signed by the Mexican State, as
well as to the guarantees for the protection of these rights. Such human rights
shall not be restricted or suspended, except for the cases and under the

conditions established by this Constitution itself.60
The anthropocentric nature of Mexico’s Constitution can support the
development of Earth law if the rights of nature can be presented as an
interdependent manifestation of human rights. The Constitution, as well as
“international treaties signed by the Mexican State,” guarantee the security of
human beings. This includes their environment, food, and health security.
Earth laws that protect, stabilize, and restore the functional interdependency
of ecosystems may be developed based on the human rights embodied in
Mexico’s Constitution.
Once again, consider how other nations have expanded their constitutional
protections to include nature—such as in Colombia, where courts have
inferred rights of nature from human environmental rights, cultural rights,
and related principles (see Chapter 18). Or in Brazil, where the Superior
Court of Justice applied anthropocentric constitutional protections to a single
nonhuman animal—a parrot.
X. INDIGENOUS RIGHTS AND THE
ENVIRONMENT
A starting point for ecocentrism in Mexico is the traditions of Indigenous
communities. Pre-Hispanic Mexican law, which still resonates throughout the
current legal system, includes the recognition of a different attitude to nature,
and many of these Indigenous principles can now be employed in extending
the law to encompass the rights of nature.
According to Garza Grimaldo: “In Mexico, the original cultures addressed
the relationship with nature through religious laws, where worship and
offerings to natural forces and manifestations were part of their daily
obligations, there being deities for each of the elements, for the sun, for
Mother Earth, water, wind, volcanoes, plants and even animals and the cycles
of time and life.”61
Like Brazil, Mexico’s Constitution carves out a special status for Indigenous
peoples and upholds their land rights. Article 2 (notable in that it appears

nearly at the beginning of the Constitution) recognizes that Mexico “is
multicultural, based originally on its Indigenous peoples, described as
descendants of those inhabiting the country before colonization and that
preserve their own social, economic, cultural and political institutions, or
some of them.”62 In turn, Article 2(A)(V) upholds Indigenous peoples’ right
to self-determination and autonomy, including their right to “maintain and
improve their environment and lands.”63
State-level constitutions establish even stronger language to uphold the
traditional cultural practices of Indigenous peoples and recognize their
contributions to environmental well-being. The constitution of the state of
Campeche is one example. It guarantees the right of Indigenous peoples to
self-determination and obligates the state government to put these rights into
practice. As you read the state’s specific duties, consider how these principles
support Earth law:
[The State of Campeche shall:]
[R]espect, preserve and maintain the knowledge, innovations, and
practices of Indigenous communities that involve traditional lifestyles
relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity.
…
[P]romote the wider application, with approval, and participation of
those who possess such knowledge, innovations, and practices, and will
encourage the benefits derived from the use of that knowledge,
innovations, and practices to be shared equally.…[and]
Protect and encourage customary use of biological resources in
accordance with traditional cultural practices that are compatible with
the requirements of conservation or sustainable use; likewise, natural
resources, sacred places and the material and intangible cultural heritage
of peoples and communities are protected, with the active participation
of communities.…
One final example of Indigenous rights in Mexico is the National Institute of
Indigenous Peoples (in Spanish, Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas,
or INPI), a centralized agency established in 2018 that serves as the federal
authority of matters related to Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples. Its

duties are to create, define, execute, and coordinate policies and programs to
guarantee Indigenous and Afro-Mexican rights. The INPI is also committed
to “recognize and respect the formalities established by the Indigenous
normative systems, having the corresponding legal effects.”64 Irma Pineda
Santiago, whom the INPI appointed to represent Mexico’s Indigenous
peoples at the United Nations, stated the importance of learning from
Indigenous communities to protect the environment:
When we look at Indigenous communities or where they have more control
over the land, they conserve the environment better.…If the land is being
better cared for, it must mean that Indigenous communities know how to do
this. We need to learn from these Indigenous communities.65
Indigenous communities help advance Mexico’s collective well-being
through customs and worldviews that consider the comprehensive protection
of ecosystems and the deep bond shared by all life. For example, María
Gabriela González Cruz writes about the Indigenous-inspired concept of the
“socio-ecosystem” as a means of looking holistically at the interrelationship
between humans and the rest of nature:
At the end of the 20th century some researchers, several of them Mexicans,
showed that the fields of ecology and biodiversity conservation can develop
not only in protected areas, but also in ecosystems inhabited by human
societies. Ecologists and conservation biologists started communicating with
anthropologists and sociologists and developed research that considered
ecosystems and groups of humans together. As a result of this new vision,
they formulated a concept which is still controversial: the socio-ecosystem.
In the socio-ecosystem, the human beings and Nature are interconnected. Our
actions as individuals and as a society have repercussions on nature.
Similarly, natural systems define us culturally, and the changes that occur in
nature have repercussions on our lifestyle.
The concept of a socio-ecosystem can be very helpful for establishing
protected areas and managing nature. In some regions of our country, such as
the Yucatán Peninsula, the concept of a socio-ecosystem has already been
applied in projects to develop Indigenous villages and to conserve
biodiversity.

This concept has helped us realize that our well-being and that of nature go
hand in hand, and that it is possible to generate strategies that allow the
integral development of human groups while we also seek the permanence of
nature.66
Indigenous communities in Mexico also support the notion of buen vivir, or
good living, which is discussed in depth in Chapter 17 on Ecuador.
According to Carlos Cruz, the original peoples of Latin America “[b]elieve in
good living (buen vivir), not in living better. Living better means having the
best cell phone and the best car. To live good is to live holistically and
nothing else.”67
Based on Indigenous rights protections discussed in this section, the Mexican
government must respect the notion of buen vivir and other Indigenous ways
of life that support nature’s well-being. Mexico’s recognition of Indigenous
self-determination and legal pluralism also supports the advancement of
ecocentric governance structures, including the rights of nature. For this
reason, many advocates believe that strengthening Indigenous rights is
paramount to restoring the planet to health.
XI. ENVIRONMENTAL NORMS IN STATE
CONSTITUTIONS
All Mexican states establish constitutional environmental protections but
with widely different approaches. Most, but not all, state constitutions take an
anthropocentric perspective. Some state constitutions frame the environment
as a resource demanding human extraction. Other state constitutions concepts
of sustainable development in accordance with international environmental
instruments, such as the 1992 Rio Declaration.68 Finally, several state
constitutions now recognize the rights of nature. This subsection explores a
few of these different models.
A. Introduction to State Constitutional Provisions on the
Environment
In most Mexican state constitutions, nature is addressed through the human

right to a healthy environment. An example of this approach is seen in Article
7 of the constitution of the state of Aguascalientes, which establishes that
“[e]veryone has the right to a healthy environment for their development and
well-being, as well as the duty to protect and preserve it.”69 Article 8 of the
constitution of the state of Veracruz has similar language.
In some cases, the environment is unequivocally linked to state
socioeconomic development, and nature is treated as merely an exploitable
human resource. For example, Article 9, section XXXI of the constitution of
the state of Baja California Sur, establishes a government obligation to
“[p]romote the integral development of all natural resources, among others:
mining, fishing; and in addition, agricultural activities and tourism.”70
Other states recognize a constitutional duty to achieve sustainable
development. For example, Article 18, section VIII of the constitution of the
state of Tamaulipas says that all people have an obligation “[to] respect and
care for the natural heritage of the State and to make use of the natural
resources susceptible to appropriation without affecting the sustainable
development of the State in the terms provided by the laws.”71
While many of these state constitutions have been effective at establishing at
least baseline protections for the environment, the anthropocentric
perspective inhibits the development of Earth law. However, as discussed in
the next section, several states have taken the additional step of explicitly
recognizing the rights of nature.
B. Rights of Nature in Colima, Guerrero, and Mexico City
This section analyzes several rights of nature laws in Mexico. Currently, the
constitutional systems of Guerrero, Mexico City, and Colima all recognize
nature as a collective entity that is subject to rights with its own legal
personality. All of these locations have also recognized a deep
interdependency between rights of nature and human rights. As noted by
María Valeria Berros, “In [the state of Guerrero and Mexico City], legal
recognition of the human right to a healthy environment coexists with this
explicit enlargement of nature rights.”72

While recognizing rights of nature in law is a valuable foundation,
institutions and governments must uphold them in practice.
1. Guerrero
On April 1, 2014, the state congress of Guerrero approved comprehensive
constitutional reform that recognized, inter alia, the rights of nature. The
proposal was presented and defended by the deputies Arturo Álvarez Angli
and Alejandro Carabias Icaza. Its passage followed a seminar on the future of
the rights of nature and humans in Mexico, held at the Autonomous
University of Guerrero, in which over 20 keynote speakers discussed the
need for fundamental reform to address a growing ecological and moral
crisis.
Article 2 of Guerrero’s constitution contemplates the rights of nature by
stating the following:
In the State of Guerrero, dignity is the basis of the human, individual and
collective rights of the person. The higher values of the legal, political and
social order are freedom, equality, social justice, solidarity, democratic and
ideological pluralism, secularism, respect for diversity and respect for life in
all its manifestations.…the State undertakes to protect the rights of nature in
accordance with the respective law.73
Notice that the wording of Article 2 recognizes both principles of human
rights and the rights of nature. This is important because there is no perceived
conflict between these rights—to the contrary, they complement each other.
If nature’s rights are seen as supporting human rights, they are more likely to
be recognized federally.
2. Mexico City
On January 11, 2017, Mexico City (which is now a recognized state74)
adopted rights of nature into its new constitution.75 The constitutional
amendment followed the First International Forum for the Rights of Mother
Earth held in Mexico City on June 1–5, 2016. The forum was “centered
around the importance of legislating the Rights of Mother Earth” and worked

toward supporting and implementing rights of nature in Mexico City.
Article 13 of the new constitution establishes that nature, with all of its
ecosystems and species, is a collective body that is the subject of rights.
Those rights include “the right to the preservation and protection,” which are
to be guaranteed by the authorities of Mexico City. Article 13 also requires
that a secondary law shall be passed “to recognize and regulate the protection
of the rights of nature, as formed by all its ecosystems and species as a
collective entity with collective rights.” This secondary law has not yet been
developed. Finally, the constitution asserts that citizens of Mexico City will
be able to enforce nature’s rights.
3. Colima
In June 2019, the congress of the state of Colima approved a state
constitutional amendment recognizing the rights of nature. The initiative was
presented by Congresswoman Blanca Livier Rodríguez Osorio, who is also
president of the Commission for Environmental Protection.
The constitutional amendment establishes that nature, including all
ecosystems and species, is a collective entity with fundamental rights.
Nature’s rights include the rights to exist, to restoration, to regeneration of its
natural cycles, and to conservation of its ecological structure and functions.
The constitutional amendment also establishes that the protection,
preservation, and recovery of biodiversity, natural ecosystems, genetic
heritage, and native species are a joint responsibility of the public, private,
and social sectors.
The state of Colima received support from numerous organizations, including
El Deber es Nuestro, Empoderamiento Climático, and Earth Law Center.
4. State of Mexico
The State of Mexico—Mexico’s most populous state—has also taken an
important step for rights of nature without yet giving official recognition to
the concept itself. Article 18 of the constitution of the state of Mexico does
not recognize the rights of nature in so many words but asserts that “[t]he

legislation and regulations that are issued for this purpose will emphasize the
promotion of a culture of protection of nature, the improvement of the
environment, the rational use of natural resources and the propagation of
existing flora and fauna.…” Thus, this provision can be construed to advance
Earth law; however, its effectiveness will depend on whether the judiciary
will meaningfully consider non-anthropocentric viewpoints. A favorable
indication: in August 2019, the Congress of the state of Mexico hosted a
presentation on the rights of nature that included leading experts in Mexico
and worldwide.76
XII. CIVIL SOCIETY FORGES A PATH
FORWARD IN MEXICO
Much of the development of Earth law in Mexico is being driven by social
movements. For example, many of the provisions for Mexico City’s new
constitution were crowdsourced from the internet, with civil society groups
such as Derechos de la Madre Tierra Mexico (Rights of Mother Earth
Mexico) and their allies making a strong plea for recognition of the rights of
nature. As you learned, they were successful.
The following excerpt from an interview with “Coyote” Alberto Ruz, a
leading figure in the Mexican environmental movements, describes how the
rights of nature movement in Mexico and Latin America came about:
[Esperanza Project (“EP”)]: Can you explain to me why now is a ripe
moment in time for the rights of nature and a shift toward biocentric
jurisprudence?
Alberto: When the environment and ecology became an important issue 30–
40 years ago, the movement was “humans saving nature” for human benefit
and enjoyment. It wasn’t until 2008 when people from Bolivia and Ecuador,
Raphael Correa and Evo Morales, started shifting the discussion to the Rights
of Nature and preserving the environment for environment’s sake. Raphael
Correa and Evo Morales started incorporating Indigenous culture to
understand our relationship with the Earth. I realized that we couldn’t keep
thinking of the Earth as a non-living being, from the occidental viewpoint,

that the Earth exists solely as a resource for us. La tierra no es de nosotros
[The earth is not ours]. Our life depends on Her but the last hundred years has
been a steady deterioration of Mother Earth. Silent Spring [the 1962 book by
Rachel Carson] is no longer a prophecy, we are living in it. Nature is telling
us we are reaching the limits of human growth. Now, instead of degradation
happening in remote areas of the globe, it’s happening everywhere, in front
of everyone’s eyes. For centuries we have had collective amnesia about the
negative impacts humanity has had on the environment.…
EP: How can people support this movement in their own lives? Where can I
look for answers to know if my choices align with the biocentric ethic?
Alberto: I first awoke to this idea when I was very young, 15 or 16 years old,
and went on a camping trip where we set up tents and [made] fires and I
realized that this all affected the environment. Even the rocks we moved. We
need to become conscious of what we do every day. Look around you. What
is your footprint? Don’t wait for a university lecture to make changes in your
lifestyle and habits. Learn to compost, learn where your water comes from.
Start to educate yourself in small things and put them into practice and then
other people will see what you are doing and make changes in their own
lives. It’s all about the ripple effect.
EP: How would you describe the progress you have seen over the years?
Alberto: Years ago when I started talking about the Rights of Nature in
Mexico City everywhere I went people looked at me like: “What?!” It’s a
radical idea. And for me that radical idea came when I went to my first
bioregional congress in Northwest Canada in 1988. That’s when it first struck
me that everything we were saying or writing or deciding or thinking was
affecting the lives of the coyote, the life of the river, the life of the tree. In
twenty years, from 1988 to 2008, we saw the first government (Ecuador)
adopt the Rights of Nature into their constitution. It was a very small step in
1988 but if a country is doing it, it is a bigger step, and we continue to make
progress. Evo Morales brought the concept to the United Nations in 2009 and
that was the basis for the UN adopting a resolution on Harmony with Nature.
And we are going back to the UN again this year because this is the way you
change legislation and you change mentality, you change everything. It’s a
gradual change. Last year, we organized the first forum for the Rights of

Earth in Mexico. Here we’re doing another step, we’re bringing people from
all the different movements, articulations, organizations, networks, and
alliances together. In talking to others you realize it’s not only me who is
thinking, “How I can protect the trees and the birds around my house?”
EP: How do we convince people to place the interest of other species equal
to or above their own interests?
Alberto: The first thing is [to] take a step back and look at what we’re doing
and understand why it’s so important other species exist because without the
bees, butterflies and tiny insects, the whole chain upon which we depend is
going to break and we are all going to go if it breaks. We are eight billion
human beings right now and every day there is one less bear and one less lion
and one less elephant and this is only the most visible of the species. The life
of Us is destroying the life of all the Others. We are the predators now that
are destroying life around us everywhere, every second. In the [United
Mexican] States right now, I see it as a crossroads, we could be at the
beginning of the world’s first global dark age (and it’s a perspective we
cannot forget, we cannot dismiss and think it is just a political prophesy,
because if this ripple effect happens in that direction it’s going to happen
everywhere). On the other side, we are seeing another global reaction. A
sentence came to me from the book of one of my friends, Despertar de la
Mujer which means “the awakening of the sleeping woman,” which comes
from a legend in our country Mexico that the moment when the sleeping
woman (which is the volcano Iztaccíhuatl) wakes up, all of humanity is going
to wake up.…I haven’t heard such radical speech since the sixties but it is
different from the radical of the sixties because this is a radical full of love,
full of consciousness, of nurturing, of finding, and that is maybe what we
needed in the planet right now to happen so that we could choose to say now
is the time we cannot continue waiting for something to happen, we have to
make it happen. So it might be a step in our evolution that will bring us to a
planetary consciousness and at the same time a Mother Earth consciousness,
which is the ultimate step. We have to make changes in our daily life and
habits and that will lead to a change in culture and laws in order to avoid
waking to our own extinction. The women need to lead the way.77
XIII. CHALLENGES IN MEXICO

Despite some strong foundational legal elements, there are major challenges
for Mexico to further develop Earth law. The existing level of poverty in
Mexico clouds the aims of conservation because it can mistakenly be viewed
as adverse to human interests. Attitudes of this kind make it difficult to adopt
general laws (which implement the constitutional provisions) specifically
designed to defend and guarantee the rights of nature beyond anthropocentric
considerations.
Conversely, the effects of climate change, disparities in quality of life, and
overwhelming inequality all put additional pressure on nature. Oftentimes,
society defaults to only safeguarding humans without adequate consideration
of the environment. Unfortunately, this mindset is used to justify
environmental degradation, drawing upon the so-called basic needs of the
population as a crutch to justify misguided environmental exploitation. These
challenges are bolstered by voracious and rampant capitalism, which
continues to treat nature as a mere resource to feed the economic system.
In the face of this reality, we must also acknowledge the lack of
responsibility shown by governments. Governments and their policies center
on consumption as a means to guarantee quality of life. The result is a vicious
circle of environmental degradation, the consequences of which are felt by
the most vulnerable sectors of society.
Genuine strengthening of the rights of nature is a legitimate and valuable goal
that is widely expressed in Mexico. Respect for the rights of nature is a test,
not only for the rule of law but also for basic human and societal values. It
falls to states and society as a whole to accept responsibility for changing the
current course. The numerous state government enactments and the growing
grassroots movement supporting rights of nature provide encouraging
opportunities to develop Earth law.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) In both Brazil and Mexico, Indigenous traditions have become a factor in
developing law and policy for rights of nature. Given that these Indigenous
traditions are based on an entirely different outlook than Western society,
what could persuade judges and lawmakers to draw on this source?

(2) This chapter describes three approaches for developing Earth law: (1)
passing rights of nature laws; (2) drawing on Indigenous traditions; and (3)
extending the present protections of human rights to encompass nature. What
are the advantages and disadvantages of each of these approaches in Brazil
and Mexico?
(3) Discuss current issues with the regulatory frameworks in Brazil and
Mexico. How do they impair the efforts to develop Earth law? How might
Brazil and Mexico transform the regulatory system to better promote the
development of Earth law?
(4) How might Brazilian and Mexican constitutional law be relied upon to
develop Earth law? Are there provisions that may hinder the development of
Earth law?
(5) The constitutional protections for nature in Brazil are found in Title 8.
Title 8 also establishes the Social Security system, the Public Health system,
and the Public Pension system. How might this placement help or hinder the
promotion of rights of nature?
(6) What role does poverty play in the development of Earth law in Brazil
and Mexico?
(7) How might the environmental courts that are separate from other civil,
administrative, and criminal courts, envisioned by Mexico’s Federal Law of
Environmental Responsibility, promote the development of ecocentric law?
How might that development be deterred by a separate court system?

CHAPTER 20
India1
I. INTRODUCTION
Rights of nature are increasingly seen as the backbone of a new generation of
environmental laws. However, successful implementation and practical
enforcement remain a challenge. In India, there have been at least two
attempts by courts to recognize the rights of nature, but the results have been
mixed. In one decision, the first of its kind in India, the Uttarakhand High
Court recognized the legal rights of personhood for the Ganges (or “Ganga”)
and Yamuna (or “Jumna”) rivers and related natural systems. The ruling has
been stayed by the Indian Supreme Court, which has not indicated when it
will resume proceedings. (Chapter 6, “Guardianship Arrangements in Rights
of Nature Legal Provisions,” also discusses this case.) The second decision,
also by the Uttarakhand High Court, declared that the members of the animal
kingdom, including avian and aquatic creatures, are legal entities and
therefore have the same rights, duties, and liabilities as other juristic persons.
This chapter will examine these cases to show the possibilities and
difficulties posed by the “first generation” of rights of nature laws in India.
II. THE LEGAL LANDSCAPE IN INDIA
India is a federal union with 28 states and 8 union territories. The Indian legal
system is a hybrid of civil, common, and customary law, coupled with
Islamic ethical and religious law, all molded into a framework that is heavily
influenced by the country’s colonial past. India has a parliamentary system of
government with three branches: the executive, the legislative and the
judiciary. The operations of these three branches are dictated by the
Constitution of India, which was adopted by the Constitutional Assembly on
November 26, 1949, and came into effect on January 26, 1950.

The judiciary in India follows a common law, hierarchical structure, similar
to that of the United States. The Supreme Court sits at the apex and is
charged with the responsibility of interpreting the Indian Constitution. It is
the final appellate court for all matters. At the next level are the high courts,
which oversee judicial administration in India’s states and union territories.
Various other bodies have a right to appeal to the high courts, including
lower courts in the states and territories, the district courts, and Lok Adalats
(agencies that resolve disputes through conciliation) at the village and
panchayat (village council) level.2 Part III of the Indian Constitution provides
that both the Supreme Court and high courts have the special constitutional
responsibility of enforcing the “fundamental rights” of citizens.
III. LANDMARK DECISION FOR THE RIGHTS
OF RIVERS: THE MOHAMMED SALIM CASE
The rights of nature movement in India took a significant step in 2016 when
the High Court of Uttarakhand (“High Court”) gave legal status to the Ganga
and Yamuna Rivers along with their tributaries, glaciers, and catchments. The
case commenced as a citizen suit when local resident Mohammed Salim sued
the State of Uttarakhand to remove illegal construction and encroachments
along the banks of the Yamuna River. The Yamuna River, which originates
in the Himalayan foothills, is the second-largest tributary of the Ganges
River. Salim also alleged that the state governments of Uttarakhand and
neighboring Uttar Pradesh were failing to cooperate with the government of
India (hereinafter “the central government”) to create a Ganga Management
Board, which was mandated under the Uttar Pradesh Reorganization Act,
2000.3
In December 2016, the High Court ruled that the illegal encroachments and
construction on government land be removed, that the governments of
Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh join the Ganga Management Board and Upper
Yamuna River Board within three months, and that all mining in the riverbed
of the Ganga and its floodplains cease immediately.4 Much of the decision
focused on issues of federalism, such as the respective roles of state and
federal government in water management.

However, the central government, as well the governments of Uttarakhand
and Uttar Pradesh, failed to comply with the direction of the High Court, and
in a further order issued in March 2017, the High Court judges expressed the
court’s “serious displeasure” at the two state governments.5 While the earlier
order had focused on issues of federalism, the court’s second order decided
that protecting the Ganga and Yamuna Rivers required the ambitious and
unprecedented step of recognizing their “legal personhood” in part based on
their spiritual significance to the Hindu people. The following are excerpts
from the court’s order, written by Justice Rajiv Sharma.
Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand and Others
Writ Petition (PIL) No. 126 of 2014 (Mar 20. 2017)
10. The extraordinary situation has arisen since Rivers Ganga and Yamuna
are loosing [sic] their very existence. This situation requires extraordinary
measures to be taken to preserve and conserve Rivers Ganga and Yamuna.
11. Rivers Ganges and Yamuna are worshipped by Hindus. These rivers are
very sacred and revered. The Hindus have a deep spiritual connection with

12. In 1969 (1) SCC 555 their Lordships of Hon. Supreme Court in Yogendra

6. That the consecrated idol in a Hindu temple is a juridical person has been
expressly laid down in Manohar Ganesh’s case, I.L.R. 12 Bom. 247…Such
ascription of legal personality to an idol must however be incomplete unless
it be linked [to human guardians].…The Judicial Committee observed thus:
‘It is only in an ideal sense that property can be said to belong to an idol and
the possession and management must in the nature of things be entrusted with
