The High Court made important connections between Articles 48A and
51A(g) of the Indian Constitution and the rights of nature. These two articles
provide as follows:

Article 48A: “The State shall endeavor to protect and improve the
environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.”
Article 51A(g): “It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to protect
and improve the natural environment including forest, lakes, rivers and
wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.”
As applied to rights of nature, the High Court reasoned that achieving the
environmental mandate of Articles 48A and 51A(g) for the Ganges and
Yamuna Rivers required recognizing the two rivers as juristic persons. In
other words, the current approach to environmental governance was not
sufficient. “Today, the State and the citizens are under a fundamental
obligation to protect and improve the environment, including forests, lakes,
rivers, wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures,” the High Court
concluded.8
At the time of this writing, the Uttarakhand High Court’s ruling in Mohd.
Salim is pending in the Supreme Court of India, pursuant to a plea filed by
the government of the state of Uttarakhand challenging the judgment on
several legal and administrative grounds.9 Among other contentions, the
government of Uttarakhand argued that the ruling was “unsustainable in
law.” For example, they voiced concern over complicated legal questions that
might arise once a river is recognized as having rights. If the river floods and
destroys human property or someone drowns in its water, could the river
itself be sued? And would the government of Uttarakhand be liable to pay
damages on behalf of the river? Or, if not them, then who? Finally, the
government of Uttarakhand raised jurisdictional issues. For example, because
the rivers run through different states, policies pertaining to their protection
should be formulated by the central government.
In response, on July 7, 2017, the Supreme Court of India ordered the
proceedings and the High Court order to be stayed.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) One noteworthy aspect of the Uttarakhand High Court’s judgment was its
invocation of the principle of parens patriae. Black’s Law Dictionary defines
parens patriae as:

a. The State regarded as a sovereign; the state in its capacity as provider of
protection to those unable to care for themselves.
b. A Doctrine by which a government has standing to prosecute a lawsuit on
behalf of a citizen, especially on behalf of someone who is under a legal
disability to prosecute the suit. The State ordinarily has no standing to sue on
behalf of its citizens, unless a separate, sovereign interest will be served by
the suit.10
To this end, the High Court eventually appointed six government officials in
loco parentis with a duty to protect, conserve, and preserve the two rivers and
their tributaries in cooperation with seven local representatives. Having read
the guardianship chapter and now learning about the case of Mohd. Salim v.
State of Uttarakhand and Others, what challenges might impair the
effectiveness of a guardianship body comprised of government officials in
implementing the rights of nature? Based on the Court’s reliance on the
juristic status of Hindu idols, what role might be served by a religious or
spiritual element in a guardianship body that represents the Ganges and
Yamuna Rivers? What benefits might result from the religion-rooted
perspective? What drawbacks might be encountered?
(2) In what other countries might rivers be recognized as having personhood
or rights based upon religious and spiritual beliefs? Would more or fewer
rivers be recognized as having rights if the highest law of the nations in the
Americas was the law of the Indigenous Americans? If all sovereign nations
in the Americas recognized rights of rivers, what conflicts might ensue when
rivers flow through more than one country?
(3) The government of Uttarakhand argued that recognizing the personhood
of a river could lead to immense legal complications, posing the example of
whether humans should be able to sue a river if it floods. Can an entity have
rights without duties? What might the duties be? What benefits to society, if
any, might be achieved if rivers had legal duties?
(4) Do you agree with the Uttarakhand High Court’s approach that legal
personality is a useful alternative for river management? How would the legal
personality approach change river management in the United States? How
would the rights of rivers as legal personalities be balanced with human

rights and interests? What is the proper balance? If you do balance, how do
you avoid “balancing away” all of the important river protections, and at
what point do rights of nature become no different than the current approach
to protecting rivers?
IV. EXTENDING THE RIGHTS OF NATURAL
ENTITIES: THE MIGLANI CASE
Following the Uttarakhand High Court’s declaration that the Ganga and
Yamuna Rivers are “juristic/legal persons/living entities having the status of a
legal person,” that same court in Miglani v. State of Uttarakhand and Others
extended the ambit of juristic persons to a wide range of natural entities that
feed into these rivers, such as other rivers, glaciers, waterfalls, streams, lakes,
rivulets, jungles, meadows, forest wetlands, grasslands, dales, air, and forest
wetlands.11 Two natural entities were picked out for special attention:
glaciers and forests. Emphasizing the existential threat faced by the Gangotri
and Yamnotri Glaciers, the High Court wrote as follows:
Miglani v. State of Uttarakhand and Others
W.P.(C.), No. 140 of 2015, H.C. Uttarakhand, March 30, 2017
Gangotri Glacier is situated in District Uttarakashi of the State of
Uttarakhand. It is 330.2 kilometres long and between 0.5 to 2.0 kilometres
wide. It is one of the largest glaciers in the Himalayas. However, it is
receding since 1780. The receding is quick after 1971. According to the
images of NASA, over the last 25 years, Gangotri glacier [sic] has retreated
more than 850 meters, with a recession of 76 meters from 1996 to 1999
alone. River Ganga originates from Gangotri Glacier.
River Yamuna originates from Yamunotri Glacier. It is also situated in
District Uttarkashi. Yamunotri Glacier is also receding at an alarming rate.
These Glaciers are receding due to pollution as well as climate change. The
urgent remedial steps are required to be taken to ensure that the receding of
these Glaciers is stopped.
Both Ganga and Yamuna Rivers are revered as deities by Hindus. Glacial Ice

is the largest reservoir of fresh water on Earth.12
In granting these various natural entities some of the same legal rights as a
living person, the High Court in Miglani also proclaimed it is “the
fundamental duty of all the citizens to preserve and conserve the nature in its
pristine glory.”13 This duty went beyond the law: “Besides our constitutional
and legal duties, it is our moral duty to protect the environment and ecology,”
wrote the court.14
The High Court again invoked the principle of parens patriae, which
designates the government, or some other authority, as the legal
representatives of citizens unable to protect themselves. The High Court of
Uttarakhand cited various cases from the United States which applied or
discussed the principle of parens patriae, including Mormon Church v.
United States, Kansas v. Colorado, Oklahoma ex. rel. Johnson v. Cook,
Snapp & Son, Inc. v. Puerto Rico ex rel. Barez.15 Yet, despite the value of
legal precedent and case law, the court concluded that the best justification
for the use of parens patriae in the Miglani case was the gravity of the threats
and harms to the natural entities that would benefit from legal representation.
Accordingly, the High Court named a number of officials as legal guardians.
Recognizing the rights of communities living nearby, the High Court also
permitted the chief secretary of Uttarakhand to appoint seven public
representatives from the state to represent these communities.
The High Court concluded by emphasizing the importance of giving
personhood to nature to address environmental degradation caused by
humans:
Rivers and Lakes have intrinsic right[s] not to be polluted. Polluting and
damaging the rivers, forests, lakes, water bodies, air and glaciers will be
legally equivalent to harming, hurting and causing injury to persons.
Rivers, Forests, Lakes, Water Bodies, Air, Glaciers and Springs have a right
to exist, persist, maintain, sustain and regenerate their own vital ecology
system. The rivers are not just water bodies. These are scientifically and
biologically living.
The rivers, forests, lakes, water bodies, air, glaciers, [and] human life are

unified and are [an] indivisible whole. The integrity of the rivers is required
to be maintained from Glaciers to Ocean.
However, we would hasten to observe that the local inhabitants living on the
banks of rivers, lakes and whose lives are linked with rivers and lakes must
have their voice too.
The rivers sustained the aquatic life. The flora and fauna are also dependent
on the rivers.
Rivers are gasping for breath. We must recognize and bestow the
Constitutional legal rights to the ‘Mother Earth’.
The very existence of the rivers, forests, lakes, water bodies, air and glaciers
is at stake due to global warming, climate change and pollution.
Trees are the buffer zone necessary to protect the glaciers from direct and
indirect heat. One tree sustains life of thousand[s] of insects. Birds chirp and
make their nests on the trees. Trees are mini-reservoirs and have a capacity to
store the water. The water stored by the trees is released slowly. The Oak tree
preserves about 75,000 gallon[s] of pure water. Plucking of one leaf [or]
grass blade also damages the environment universally.
The leading civilizations have vanished due to severe droughts. Water is the
elixir of life and we must conserve and preserve every drop of water. The
value of water should not be undermined only for the reason that it is still
available in plenty.
The past generations have handed over the “Mother Earth” to us in its pristine
glory and we are morally bound to hand over the same Mother Earth to the
next generation.
All the persons have a constitutional and moral responsibility to endeavour to
avoid damage or injury to nature (in damno vitando). Any person causing any
injury and harm, intentionally or unintentionally to the Himalyas, [sic]
Glaciers, rivers, streams, rivulets, lakes, air, meadows, dales, jungles and

Thus, the Himalayan Mountain Ranges, Glaciers, rivers, streams, rivulets,
lakes, jungles, air, forests, meadows, dales, wetlands, grasslands and springs

STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) The High Court in Miglani cited numerous U.S. court decisions to help
justify its use of the principle of parens patriae. Courts in Brazil and
Colombia have relied on the decision of the High Court of Uttarakhand in
Salim v. State of Uttarakhand. Do U.S. courts rely on decisions from other
countries? Do you think this is appropriate? How might courts in the U.S. be
persuaded to rely more often on decisions from other countries that embody
Earth law principles? In state and federal courts in the United States, lawyers
have relied on decisions made under other states’ laws. Many are found to be
persuasive and trends begin. Consider the development of product liability
law. What additional hurdles are presented when the law is of another
country? How might the law of foreign countries be relied on by U.S. courts
to craft new legal solutions that fit today’s most difficult challenges?
(2) Should community representatives serve as legal guardians of nature
when they may represent the interests of the human community over the
interests of nature? How can it be ensured that they act on behalf of the rights
and interests of nature? There are innumerable conflicts of interests within
ecosystems, perhaps the most obvious being predator-prey relationships. Are
the rights of human communities that draw benefits from nature comparable
to the rights of non-human predators with respect to their prey. How might
these conflicts be resolved? Identify other conflicts and potential resolutions.
(3) One of the natural entities that received recognition of their rights was
waterfalls. What rights might they have? Should their rights be considered in
isolation, or only as part of a larger ecosystem?
(4) In Miglani, the High Court stated: “Besides our constitutional and legal
duties, it is our moral duty to protect the environment and ecology,” and
“[a]ll the persons have a constitutional and moral responsibility to endeavour

to avoid damage or injury to nature.…” What role does moral duty have in
decisions made by trial and appellate judges in the United States? What role
should moral duty play?
V. THE RIGHTS OF THE ANIMAL KINGDOM:
THE NARAYAN DUTT BHATT CASE
On July 4, 2018, the High Court of Uttarakhand held in Narayan Dutt Bhatt
v. Union of India and Others that all members of the animal kingdom are
legal persons.17 The decision came in response to a petition filed for the
protection and welfare of animals. The petitioner had sought to restrict the
movement of horse carts known as “tongas” between Nepal and India
through Banbasa in the Champawat district of India, due to the suffering
experienced by the horses. As a remedy, the petitioner sought vaccinations
and medical checkups for the horses for suspected infections prior to entry
into India from Nepal. By consent of the parties, the petition’s scope was
enlarged to promote the protection and welfare of all animals. The High
Court wrote as follows:
Narayan Dutt Bhatt v. Union of India and Others
W.P.(C.), No. 43 of 2014, H.C. Uttarakhand (July 4, 2018)
12. Learned counsel for the petitioner has vehemently argued that the Indian
authorities have failed to regulate the entry of horse carts/tonga entering from
Nepal to India. The horses are not medically examined. The fare and freight
are not regulated. He has referred to the treaty [between India and Nepal]
signed in the year 1991, revised in 2009. According to the treaty, the
contracting party may impose restrictions for protecting public morals,
protecting human, animal and plant life, safeguarding national treasures. He
has also argued that there is overloading in the horse carts/tonga going from
India to Nepal and vice-versa. The animals are treated with cruelty. The
horses are abandoned in the Indian Territory. He then argued that the
provisions of Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 and the rules
framed thereunder and the provisions of Prevention and Control of Infectious
and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009 have not been enforced. He

also argued that the animals are transported in violation of Transport of
Animals Rules, 1978. The animals are transported on foot to long distances
causing immense pain and suffering to them. He also prayed that the entire
animal kingdom may be conferred status of [a] legal entity/legal person.18

The High Court reviewed the relevant legislation, notably the Prevention of

an animal if that person, amongst other actions,
beats, kicks, over-rides, over-drives, over-loads, tortures or otherwise treats
any animal so as to subject it to unnecessary pain or suffering or causes, or
being the owner permits any animal to be so treated; or (employs in any work
or labour or for any purpose any animal which, by reason of its age or any
disease) infirmity; wound, sore or other cause, is unfit to be so employed or,
being the owner, permits any such unfit animal to be employed.19
Additional legislation specifically applies to animals used in transportation,
setting maximum loads and numbers of passengers, limiting working hours in
hot weather, and imposing other restrictions.20
After examining animal cruelty legislation, the High Court then considered
the question of animal suffering. Reviewing previous court decisions, it
stated as follows:
75. Their Lordships of the Hon’ble Supreme Court…have held that an animal
has also honour and dignity which cannot be arbitrarily deprived of and its
rights and privacy have to be respected and protected from unlawful attacks.
The principle of equality of all species found in Isha Upanishads [Sanskrit
texts containing Hindu teachings] is the culture and tradition of the country,
particularly the States of Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra. The PCA Act
[Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960] has been enacted with an object

and age old practices, so as to bring into effect some type of reform, based on

So far as animals are concerned, “life” means something more than mere
survival or existence or instrumental value for human beings, but to lead a

life with some intrinsic worth, honour and dignity.21
Next, the High Court considered works by a number of authors on the

which the High Court quoted as follows:
On the frontiers of legal change, there is a growing global movement to
recognize non-human animals as legal persons, a radical change that would
endow them with the variety of legal rights. Animal rights advocates are not
saying primates, cetaceans, or elephants are people. A ‘legal person’ is not
necessarily a human being, but rather an entity to which the law grants
specific rights. A corporation is considered a legal person, as are ships,
churches and municipalities. The rights and responsibilities of a legal person

Ahimsa or Non-Violence
The concept of ahimsa—or non-violence—is India’s unique contribution to
world culture. The Vedas and Upanishads were the first to speak of ahimsa.
Although the Aryans were not vegetarians, the concept of non-killing appears
in the earliest literature. The Rig Veda (10.87.16), condemns all forms of
killing, even for food, preferring vegans to drinkers of milk:
The yatudhana who fills himself with the flesh of man,
He who fills himself with the flesh of horses or of other animals,
And he who steals the milk of the cow:
Lord, cut off their heads with your flame.
The Yajur Veda says that service to animals leads to heaven: ‘No person
should kill animals helpful to all and persons serving them should obtain
heaven.’ According to the Atharva Veda, the earth was created for the
enjoyment of not only human beings but also for bipeds and quadrupeds,
birds, animals and all other creatures. The emergence of all life forms from
the Supreme Being is expressed in the Mundakopanishad from Him, too,
gods are produced manifold, The celestials, men, cattle, birds.

These ideas led to the concept of ahimsa or non-violence. Much later, the
Manusmriti says, ‘He who injuries innocent beings with a desire to give
himself pleasure never finds happiness, neither in life nor in death.’ The
Shrimad Bhagavatam says that a cruel person who kills others for his
existence deserves to be killed, and cannot be happy, either in life or in death.
The consequences, according to the Yajunavalkya Smriti are that ‘the wicked
person who kills animals which are protected has to live in hellfire for the
days equal to the number of hairs on the body of that animal.’…
Although Sanatana Dharma did not require its adherents to be vegetarians,
vegetarianism was recognized as a higher forms of living, a belief that
continues in contemporary Hinduism where vegetarianism is considered
essential for spiritualism. Around the sixth century BCE, two great religious
preachers were born, who took the Upanishadic philosophy of good conduct
and non-killing to the people in the common language: Mahavira the Jina
(Victor), and Gautama the Budha [sic] (wise). The name traditionally used
for Hinduism. Both emphasized that ahimsa or non-violence was essential for
a good life.…
Mahavira was not the founder of Jainism: he was the twenty-fourth and last
Tirthankara who revised the Jaina doctrines and established the central tenets
of Jainism.…Mahavira [taught] the importance of right faith, right knowledge
and right conduct, which includes non-violence (ahimsa)—not to cause harm
to any living being.…
According to Jainism, ahimsa is not the mere causing of violence, but rather
the “severance of any of the vitality in a mobile or immobile being.” Ahimsa,
as viewed by Jainism, is very comprehensive and takes into consideration the
welfare of all beings on earth. Keeping anything in confinement, without
consideration for its freedom to exist or live, is bandhana (captivity). Rearing
animals without adequate shelter, air, light, space and food is atichara (bad
conduct). Keeping animals, including dairy animals, tied with ropes or chains
throughout the day is violence. The simple prayer of the Jainas is “let the law
of the Jaina give all happiness to all the living beings of the world. All beings
desire to live. They like pleasure, hate pain, shun destruction, like to live
long. To all, life is dear.” (Ramanujam 2006).…
The eightfold path taught by the Buddha [(Gautama)] emphasized abstinence

from activities that bring harm to other living beings and non-killing. The
Boddhisattva is one who is full of maitri (friendship) towards all animals and
which aspires to achieve Buddha-hood. Said the Buddha, “As a mother would
be very good towards her only child, her well-beloved son’ so too you should
be very good towards all creatures everywhere and to everyone.” (Dwivedi,
1989) The Buddha himself sought refuge from his bickering disciples by
living among the animals. The Jataka tales hold up the noble qualities of
various animals as examples to emulate.

CHAPTER 21
Israel1
I. INTRODUCTION
The emergence of Earth law in Israel plays out against the backdrop of the
country’s fragile geophysical conditions, a fast-growing economy, rapid
population growth, and its high technological capacity, such as desalination
and wastewater reuse. Early forays into Earth law, particularly the rights of
nature, attempt to break out of the current legal paradigm crafted to support a
governance system geared for unfettered growth. Earth law development in
Israel focuses on demonstrating the costs of the current governance system
for nature by reframing ecosystem devastation and biodiversity loss through
the lens of the rights of natural entities to survive and flourish.
Israel’s ecological crisis has spawned environmental activism, which has
been highly litigious in its approach. Yet this activism, propelled by hundreds
of organizations at both the local and national level, is still largely
anthropocentric, focusing on protecting nature because of its services to
humans rather than its own inherent value. No doubt, this approach is more
pragmatic than ideological, since environmental campaigns are more likely to
succeed if they appeal to the self-interest of the public by viewing nature as a
supplier of critical goods and services.
Nevertheless, glimmerings of a rights of nature doctrine are emerging in
Israel, and the country has made its own contribution, albeit small, in
advancing global Earth law, illustrated by the two case studies discussed
below. The first case study examines the 2004 amendment to the Water Law

granting nature a right to water; the second examines the mountain gazelle’s
petition to Israel’s High Court of Justice to protect its habitat from
development.
II. NATURE’S RIGHT TO WATER UNDER
ISRAELI LAW
In an arid country characterized by chronic water scarcity, 70 years of intense
human activity has polluted the country’s water sources with sewage and
other waste, while capturing their use for industrial, agricultural, and
residential purposes. By 1980, Israel’s water use had reached the total
capacity of available freshwater.2 Massive exploitation has ravaged Israel’s
streams, springs, winter ponds, and wetlands, resulting in their desiccation
and the loss of aquatic habitats. Today only 3 percent remains of the wetlands
that existed a century ago, most of it in national parks and nature reserves.
Israel has historically solved its water shortage by creating more water. The
country makes extensive use of treated wastewater effluents for irrigation in
agriculture. Today, roughly 90 percent of the wastewater generated is
reused,3 making Israel the world’s leading country in water reuse. In addition,
since the beginning of this century, Israel has ranked high in the production
and use of desalinated water, which now comprises approximately 70 percent
of its drinking water supply.4 The question of the sustainability of such
extensive reuse of effluents as well as massive desalination looms large over
Israel’s formidable success in overcoming its chronic water scarcity.
Nevertheless, an admirable goal of government policy in its sweeping use of
desalinated water is to cut back on pumping groundwater to allow the
restoration of natural inflow to devastated streams and springs.
Overdrawing of groundwater has reduced aquifer levels and, subsequently,
spring flow, transforming most of the perennial streams in central and
northern Israel into intermittent streams whose only source of water is rain.
Moreover, the conversion of coastal streams into sewage canals has damaged
their rich biodiversity, including unique plant and animal species. Public
anger over this ecological catastrophe, and the country’s water crisis
generally, finally erupted in the 1990s. In response, the government initiated

an extensive stream restoration program as a national priority, supported by a
decision from the year 2000 allocating 50 million cubic meters of water
annually for stream inflow.5
Harnessing the momentum, a coalition of government officials and nature
conservation organizations introduced the concept of “nature’s rights to
water,” which captured the public’s imagination and swiftly became a key
talking point in the mainstream environmental dialogue. In 2002, a
government masterplan for water management implementing allocations for
stream restoration defined nature itself as a legitimate consumer of water. The
concept of granting rights to water to Israel’s much-abused streams and other
wetlands began to drive government policy. In 2003, the government’s
Environment Ministry and Nature Reserves Authority issued a landmark
policy paper called “Nature’s Right to Water” officially recognizing streams’
entitlement to their own natural inflow rather than to water from the national
grid. Finally, in 2004, the concept was incorporated into Israel’s Water Law.
The Water Law is a broad framework governing the country’s water in its
entirety—from production, allocation, and distribution to pollution,
conservation, and restoration. At the law’s adoption in 1959,6 water was
perceived as a commodity for development, and hence the law was initially
crafted as a tool for intense urban, industrial, and agricultural development.
Yet it evolved alongside the growing awareness of the environmental crisis,
and in 1972 a chapter on pollution prevention was added.7 In 1991, stronger
enforcement provisions were added to the Water Law to strengthen pollution
control.8 And, in 2004, the law finally evolved to guarantee nature the right to
water for “conservation and restoration of nature and landscapes, including
springs, streams and wetlands.”9 The text of section 6 of the Water Law reads
as follows:
Any right for water is linked to one of the water purposes that are listed
below: the right to water ceases upon the cessation of the purpose; and these
are the water purposes:
1. Domestic needs;
2. Agriculture;
3. Industry;

4. Labor, trade and services;
5. Public services; and
6. Protection and restoration of nature and landscape values, including
springs, rivers and wetlands (in this law—“nature and landscape
values”).
To ensure accountability and transparency, the director of Israel’s Water
Authority is required to “submit to the Economic Committee of the Knesset
[the country’s legislative body] by the first of April each year, a notification
regarding the amount of water that was decided to allocate during the same
year for the purpose of nature and landscape values according to Section 6
(6).…” Finally, the explanatory note to the bill clarified that the purpose of
the amendment was to allow for both the conservation and restoration of
nature and freshwater systems:
Current efforts to restore nature and landscape values are not anchored in
legislation since they are not listed in section 6 to the Water Law, 1959…The
said section determines, that any right to water must be linked to…domestic
needs, agriculture, industry, labor, trade and services, and public services. It
is proposed to add to the list…conservation and restoration of nature and
landscape assets, including springs, streams and wetlands, so that in the
framework of water allocations this purpose will also be taken into
consideration.
Looking back today on the 2004 amendment to Israel’s Water Law allows a
broad perspective on the law’s implementation and the challenges that arose.
Adding nature’s right to water to the law mandated the government to
allocate water to nature itself. Furthermore, government policy has
determined that the source of the allocations must be from the stream’s own
natural flow rather than water from the national grid. However, overdrawing
from aquifers continues because of high human demand, while drought has
led to decreased recharging of aquifers, and hence the over-diversion of fresh
water from springs and streams for human use continues. The resulting trend
is a scarcity of instream flow and a severe decrease in spring resurgence in
northern Israel, which lacks a desalination plant to replace freshwater
appropriated for humans.10
While Israel’s laws and official policy recognize nature’s right to water,

government policies aimed at expanding the economy and increasing gross
domestic product together with a rapidly growing population have
undermined its implementation. These challenges are likely to increase as
Israel’s population is projected to rise to 20 million by 2065, a rise from 8.7
million in 2019.11 At present, the priority of human needs in the allocation of
ecosystem goods and services is unquestioned and may intensify in this arid,
ecologically fragile, and geographically small country.
The case study of Israel’s Water Law demonstrates how laws recognizing the
rights of nature can be rendered powerless when faced with formidable
political forces demanding development for housing and jobs. Section 6 (6)
of the Water Law has not succeeded in warding off the threats of stream
desiccation. While it has ensured that the government allocates water to
nature, humans still have priority over nature. Full enforcement of Section
6(6) of the Water Law would require, at least, meeting the basic water needs
of ecosystems.
A recent development project underscores the flawed application of nature’s
right to water in Israel. In response to objections to a plan for a new
neighborhood in Jerusalem that will dry up adjacent natural springs called
Ein Lavan (White Spring), the government planning committee decided that
“the public need for this plan justifies its approval, despite its impact on the
springs.”12 Yet the committee could not ignore the government’s own
mandate to ensure water for the springs, and hence devised a plan to bring
water from the national grid into the spring’s pools. Thus, a shortcoming of
the right-to-water amendment as written is that it does not commit the
government to allocate the springs’ own natural inflow as the source of water.
In any petition for judicial review, Israeli courts would in all likelihood defer
to the government experts who devised the plan and refrain from interfering.
On the other hand, the government recognized the ecological need to return
natural inflow to streams. In June 2018, it approved the “Strategic Emergency
Plan Addressing the Water Sector Under Drought Conditions.” The plan calls
for the construction of two additional desalination plants with the goal of
almost doubling the current production amount to 1.1 billion cubic meters
annually by 2030. One of the new desalination plants will be located in
northern Israel, to allow for a decrease in pumping from aquifers and the

return of natural inflow to streams and springs.
Meanwhile streams and springs in Israel continue to fight for their survival.
They remain silent stakeholders despite the improvement of their legal status
entitling them to water allocations. To fill this gap, Israel’s steams and
springs require their own uniquely defined rights—such as rights to flow, to
be free from pollution, to feed and be fed by sustainable aquifers, to
restoration, and others.13 And, of course, they require a right of standing so
that they can have representation and protect themselves in a court of law
when these rights are not enforced.
III. THE GAZELLE PETITION
A further case model of the rights of nature in Israel is the “Gazelle Petition.”
In this case, the endangered Israeli mountain gazelle, together with five
humans, petitioned Israel’s High Court of Justice to prevent the development
of its habitat—and won. In contrast to nature’s right to water now established
in Israeli law, the human petitioners, residents of the neighborhood bordering
the mountain gazelle habitat, could not point to a specific law granting the
gazelle a right to its habitat. Instead, the petition was based on nature and
wildlife protection laws that grant the gazelle a protected status, albeit one
that falls short of statutory legal identity.
The following excerpts are from the article Finding Safe Passage through a
Wave of Extinctions: Israel’s Endangered Mountain Gazelle that narrates and
analyzes the case.14 As you read the excerpts, remember that the objective
behind this precedential case was not only to protect the gazelles, but also to
prevent development of forestland that happened to be the gazelles’ habitat.
Attaching the iconic gazelle as a petitioner transformed it into the poster child
of the campaign, underscoring that protecting the gazelle means protecting
the forest as well.
Finding Safe Passage through a Wave of Extinctions: Israel’s
Endangered Mountain Gazelle
In 2008, the Supreme Court of Israel overturned a decision by the country’s
highest planning authority to approve the development of 2,000 housing units

on Mitspeh Neftoah, one of Jerusalem’s few remaining natural areas (See
HCQ 11745/04 466/05, Reiss, Roth, Shachaf, Adam, Shefer, Gazella Gazella
v. Nat’l Planning & Building Comm. (2008) (Isr.)) The six petitioners were
from a neighboring suburb: five of them were Homo sapiens and the sixth
was the Gazella gazella (G. gazella), Israel’s mountain gazelle and one of the
country’s most iconic species. Although the range of the gazelle was once
extensive, Israel is now the only country where the species is extant, and even
there its future appears grim. [A small population of approximately 200 exists
in Turkey.15] Gazelle numbers overall in Israel have spiraled sharply
downwards from approximately 10,000 in 1985 to about 2,500 today.
The following analysis focuses on a stage in the conflict when local residents,
together with the mountain gazelle, sued the government for breaking its own
laws—and won. The court did not, however, mention the gazelle in its
decision, nor did it raise the question of its standing to sue, making it a sort of
elephant in the room. But neither did the court demand removal of the gazelle
as a party to the case; the gazelle, thus, retains its legal status as petitioner.
The…petition explained that:
Petitioner 6 is the Israeli gazelle.…At least 30 individuals of the species live
in the area of Mitspeh Neftoah, and they will be directly injured by the plan’s
approval and development of the area, comprising a taking of its habitat. The
Israeli gazelle is a protected nature asset in accordance with the National
Parks and Nature Reserves Declaration (Protected Natural Assets),16 1979, as
well as protected wildlife in accordance with the Wildlife Protection Act,
1955.…
The law, petitioners argued, “protects [the gazelle] and other protected
species by granting them status as protected legal assets and protected
wildlife… in theory they have standing to initiate legal action against those
who would harm them. Yet a key distinction between the gazelles and
ourselves is that they are voiceless and so cannot argue for themselves before
the court. So we, as speech enabled human beings, stepped in as their
guardians.…We argue that since the government has ignored the potential
effects of the development plan on the gazelle population,.…the gazelles
should become petitioners themselves.… Petitioner 6 argues and Petitioners

1–5 concur that the National Parks and Nature Reserves Law grants the
Israeli gazelle a property right to its natural habitat and range areas, which it
has occupied for thousands of years in Mitspeh Neftoah. Petitioner 6 will
further argue that the law grants him statutory protection of his rights, as well
as the right to address this honorable court sitting as a High Court of Justice,
to avoid injury. The respondents’ decision to approve the plan…will cause
severe injury to Petitioner 6 and deprive him of his property rights of
thousands of years to his habitat in Mitspeh Neftoah.…
Although the government took the view that the highest and best use of
Mitspeh Neftoah was as a housing project, the petitioners wanted the court to
accept that the land at issue had more essential uses as a provider of
ecosystem goods and services, values of the utmost importance. The petition
was, thus, an ambitious legal attempt to overcome the limitations of an
anthropocentric legal system—a system that recognizes only those land uses
that are perceived as most important for human beings and that prioritize land
uses without proper regard for the natural systems that underpin life on the
planet:
Decision makers in Israel’s planning institutions act solely out of
anthropocentric considerations…totally ignoring other forms of life.…
Furthermore, even if the only consideration that guides the planning
committees is human welfare, we ourselves need other species.…
The court’s decision cautiously avoided mention of the gazelles and of their
legal status and standing before the court. It decided in favor of the
petitioners, the court said, on two grounds. First, the respondents had
exceeded their authority by approving an amendment to the district rezoning
plan that violated National Outline Plan 22 for forests and forestation, in
breach of the amount of forestland that the Plan permitted for development.
Second, the government had discriminated against petitioners by violating
their right to a fair hearing by allowing the Jerusalem district planner to
participate in the National Planning Council’s internal meeting on the
examiner’s findings, whilst at the same time refusing the petitioners’ request
to participate in the same meeting. Despite the government attorney’s
attempts to persuade the court that the flawed government actions and
decisions were reparable through further deliberation and discussion, the

court took the view that the process was so egregious that only a total and
immediate revocation of the decisions already made could provide petitioners
with relief.
This decision was remarkable because Israeli courts are loath to second-guess
government experts and typically defer to them. In this instance, however, the
court judged that the severity of the errors in the decision-making process
overrode customary deference. In addition, and on a more substantive note,
the court emphasized the high value of Israel’s few remaining forestlands.
Their scarcity, it said, obligates the government to conduct in-depth analysis
and deliberations on the impact of their loss on the surrounding environment
prior to decisions on rezoning forestlands for urban development. Not only
was such an analysis not undertaken in this case, the court noted, but the
information on which the government did rely was both erroneous and
inaccurate.
By sidestepping the issue of the gazelle’s right to standing in court, and by
basing its decision on a violation of National Outline Plan 22, the court
adroitly succeeded in protecting the gazelles while at the same time avoiding
what could have been significant political controversy. The court’s avoidance
of the gazelle’s legal standing is understandable as a matter of institutional
self-preservation. It leaves in limbo, however, the question of just how
effective Israel’s existing wildlife protection laws can be in preventing
extinctions. The day was won for the gazelle not by wildlife law but by
planning law that has, for the most part, succeeded in balancing multiple
demands for land use and keeping at bay the more egregious interests of
private entities.…
Although the Supreme Court carefully avoided addressing the unusual
petitioner and the provocative arguments raised in favor of its standing to be
a petitioner, the precedent-making nature of the case did not go entirely
unnoticed by the court. When petitioners submitted a request for an interim
order restraining the government from moving ahead with the actual
development until a final decision in the case, presiding Justice Elyakim
Rubinstein took the opportunity to address the standing of Petitioner 6, G. g.
gazella. The justice first hastily disposed of the petitioners’ request for a
restraining order, relying on the government attorney’s reassurance that the

detailed plan’s approval was not pending and actual construction was far
from tangible. He then eagerly turned his attention to the beguiling
nonhuman petitioner:
I would like to add that Petitioner 6 is the Israeli Gazelle.…I have considered
if an animal itself—to differentiate it from organizations for animal welfare—
can be a petitioner…In actual fact, the gazelle does have a protected legal
status as a “protected nature asset and as protected wildlife…But is it
possible to grant it standing as a petitioner? I think that the answer is no…
[R]egarding this question we have to differentiate between the very deserving
and important concept of animal protection as provided in various forms by
Israeli legislation and case law, and the question of an animal as a direct party
to a…judicial proceeding, since it cannot—amongst other issues—give
power of attorney or think or analyze as humans do, or…pay court fees…if
the petition is rejected, and of course I am not expressing any opinion in this
matter.
Justice Rubinstein concluded by ordering the petitioners to “notify the court
within 7 days if they are willing to remove ‘Petitioner 6’ while keeping their
right to raise arguments concerning the plight of the gazelles.” This obiter
dicta received a great deal of media attention that misconstrued it as a final
decision tossing the gazelles out of the courthouse. The human petitioners
declined, however, to abandon the gazelles, and keeping them on board
incurred no retaliatory decision or court fees, as had been gently threatened
by Justice Rubinstein. In the end, the gazelle remained an official petitioner
in the case.
The attempt to gain judicial recognition of the gazelle’s right to standing in
court was intended to gain for the species a legitimacy in courts of law that
animals never enjoy. It reflects an underlying view that it is difficult, if not
downright impossible, to save from extinction nonhuman species that we do
not respect or simply just do not care about as much as making more room
for more people. Preventing their extinction requires granting them moral
consideration. Reasonably enough, the court would not go this far. It was
vigilant in protecting its own integrity and in avoiding what might have led to
public ridicule. The fact remains, however, that the gazelle has a legacy on
record [as] a formal petitioner in Israel’s High Court of Justice. Perhaps this

signals the earliest glimmerings of Israeli society’s recognition that it does
have a duty to prevent the extinction of its own endangered wildlife.
IV. CONCLUSION
As shown by the above discussion of nature’s right to water and the gazelle
petition, Israel’s experience with rights of nature has so far been limited. Yet
if the human species is to live within ecological limits and save the
environment from complete collapse, legally enforceable rights of nature may
be a critical tool.
The role of rights of nature is to counter the entrenched assumption of
humans as conquerors of nature, to challenge the belief that the Earth’s
resources are unlimited, that nature is indestructible and will recover from
whatever we throw at it, and that we can populate, mine, dam, farm, fish,
manufacture, and consume without limits. While flawed, a foundation for the
development of Earth law in Israel has been laid by the legislative recognition
of the rights of water and the judicial acceptance, at least nominally, of a
gazelle in the courtroom. How Israel builds from this foundation may
determine the fate of freshwater habitat, native species, and ecosystems.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) While streams, springs, and other wetlands in Israel are today legally
entitled to water, as discussed above, the law has certainly not stopped the
government from moving ahead with development that threatens the
existence of springs in Jerusalem.17 Relying on a statutory right to water, do
you think that the threatened spring is entitled to petition the courts for
judicial review? Take into consideration that while the law recognizes the
right of the spring to water, it does not go further and declare the stream a
legal person; the provision to declare streams, springs, and other wetlands
legal entities that appeared in the original version of the bill did not make it to
the final version of the amendment.
(2) After reading the case study on Israel’s right to water, explain Israel’s
water technologies as both a solution to the country’s widespread wetland

desiccation and pollution, as well as a drawback in promoting the rights of
nature to water. Will desalination and wastewater reuse contribute to
normalizing the rights of ecosystems to water in Israel or is it more likely to
have the reverse effect?
(3) Could the public trust doctrine support the spring’s standing in court?
Under Sec. 2 of the Water Law, “Israel’s water sources belong to Israel’s
public, subject to the control of the state.” Hence government officials are
public trustees for protecting the country’s ecosystems, streams, springs,
plants, wildlife, and biodiversity, but with the public as the beneficiary and
not for the actual ecosystem, stream, or spring. An alternative would be to
turn the public into trustees with nature as the beneficiary, but this would
entail new legislation, which can be politically difficult. How would you
propose drafting a petition invoking the public trust doctrine under current
legislation?
(4) In considering the New Zealand model of legal identity for rivers (see
Chapters 6 and 22), would you suggest this model for Israel, as well, in
addition to nature’s right to water? Would this model help Israel’s streams
recover their instream flow from humans? Or would humans still have
priority? Is the New Zealand model perhaps unworkable in Israel because of
geographical, political, and cultural differences? Taking this further, do you
foresee the development of a diversity of Earth law, in adaptation to the
unique conditions of each country? If so, what expressions of Earth law do
you see evolving?
(5) Israel’s right of nature to water law demonstrates the fragility of law when
pitted against human interests. The restoration of nature’s own instream water
to streams and springs in Israel is still contingent on humans drawing enough
water for their own needs first. Thus, the law is not necessarily the ultimate
protector of nature. Above all, human cultural values need to change, from an
anthropocentric approach to an ecocentric one. How would you suggest
changing our society’s values, and would law have any role to play in this?
Can law be a crafter of cultural values, rather than their reflection? In this
context, do you agree with the petitioners that the gazelle had standing as a
consequence of its status as protected wildlife and as a protected natural asset
under Israel’s nature and wildlife protection laws? Or do you think that

standing can only be bestowed by a specific law clearly granting that right?
Does the argument that the development plan threatens the gazelle’s property
rights strengthen the argument for standing, or do you think that arguing
property rights for a nonhuman entity would be counterproductive because it
reinforces the concept of ownership of nature?
(6) The petitioners argued that they were acting as guardians of the voiceless
gazelles by arguing the gazelles’ case in court, and that their decision to bring
the gazelle as a formal petitioner was a result of the government ignoring the
impact of the planned development on this specific gazelle population. Do
you think that there is a contradiction in this argument, that if the petitioners
considered themselves the gazelles’ guardians and saw their role as speaking
for them, the gazelle need not be a formal petitioner? How would you have
written the judgment on this specific point, drawing perhaps on guardian
issues for minors and the incapacitated?
(7) The judgment in the Gazelle Petitioner case was written by Israel’s then
Chief Justice Dorit Benisch, probably the most environmentally-minded
judge that has ever sat on Israel’s Supreme Court. How much do you think
this had to do with the petition’s outcome? Would a less environmentally
friendly judge have been more likely to demand that the human petitioners
remove the gazelle as petitioner, as Justice Rubinstein suggested in the obiter
dictum judgment in the interim order hearing? What does this say about the
objectivity of the courts when hearing cases challenging existing values, such
as rights of nature issues? And, if the human petitioners had not included the
gazelle as a petitioner, do you think that the court would still have revoked
the government’s approval of the development plan? Taking into
consideration that the gazelle was not mentioned in the judgment, how do
you feel that it contributed to this highly successful case?
(8) Linking the two case studies discussed in this section, could a stream
under threat by development plans also petition the court to protect its
integrity as a stream? Lacking a statutory right for standing, would you also
use Israel’s nature protection laws to claim standing for the stream? Why
would it be critical to verify if the stream is located in a statutory national
park or nature reserve? Adding human petitioners is a sure way to hedge your
bets if the nonhuman entity is removed from the petition by a court decision

and the petition consequently collapses. What qualifications should the
human petitioners ideally have in order to increase your chances of a
favorable judgment together with the stream as petitioner?
