CHAPTER 22
New Zealand1
“Nature wills that there is no end to life.”2
I. INTRODUCTION
Aotearoa New Zealand (inclusive of both the Māori and the English names),
is a relatively young and sparsely populated state. The 1840 Treaty of
Waitangi between the English Queen and the Indigenous Māori provided the
terms of English settlement and subsequent government. In 2020, as a result
of mostly European settlement over the last 200 years, Māori make up
approximately 15 percent of the population of about 5 million.3 Those five
million people are spread over a land area of approximately the size of
Colorado.
In relation to its environmental laws and legal system, Aotearoa New Zealand
is a common law, democratic country without a written constitution. Even
though there is no single written New Zealand constitution, there are
constitutional documents, including a New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990,
and the foundational Treaty of Waitangi, signed by representatives of the
British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs in 1840. However, Aotearoa New
Zealand also has a system of parliamentary sovereignty, similar to those in
the United Kingdom and in Israel. Therefore, court decisions are important,
as in any common law system, but courts do not have power to invalidate
procedurally valid laws passed by Parliament, whereas Parliament can pass a
law to override a court decision. While the separation of powers is taken
extremely seriously, and New Zealand is repeatedly ranked as one of the least

corrupt nations in the world,4 the make-up of Parliament—and thus the
system for appointing parliamentarians—determines the content of most of
New Zealand’s laws.
New Zealand is a party to most international environmental agreements and
prides itself on being a strong protector of the environment. That pride may
not reflect its domestic results in practice.5 It has a range of domestic
environmental laws dealing with different subjects; the largest and most
comprehensive statute creating an integrated management regime for most
uses of land, air, and water is the Resource Management Act 1991. Separate
legislation governs national parks, protected species, animal welfare, and
most resource extraction. Separate legislation also governs some of the
innovative environmental co-management and co-governance arrangements
between government and the Māori.
New Zealand is also a party to most international human rights agreements
and similarly prides itself on being a strong defender of human rights. Key
domestic human rights laws include the Bill of Rights Act and the Human
Rights Act; both are ordinary statutes and the Bill of Rights contains solely
civil and political rights; none contain environmental rights. It is through
New Zealand’s human rights framework that many of the more ecocentric
legal mechanisms have been made part of the law. Most significantly, this
has taken place as a result of the systems New Zealand has adopted for
resolving Indigenous grievances to breaches of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi.
This chapter outlines three aspects of New Zealand legislation that contribute
to the body of Earth law: references to the intrinsic value of nature,
recognition that animals are sentient beings, and adoption of legal personality
for nature.
II. LEGISLATIVE RECOGNITION OF THE
INTRINSIC VALUE OF NATURE
Several significant pieces of New Zealand’s environmental legislation
contain recognition of the “intrinsic worth” or “intrinsic value” of nature. The
key examples are the Reserves Act 1977, the National Parks Act 1980, the

Conservation Act 1987, the Resource Management Act 1991, the Hazardous
Substances and New Organisms Act 1996, and the Marine and Coastal Area
(Takutai Moana) Act 2011. In addition, several other statutes specific to
particular natural areas refer to intrinsic values of nature.6
References to the intrinsic worth or intrinsic value of nature occur most often
as part of the general purpose of the statute or the principles by which
decisions under the statute should be made. Interestingly, some statutes
define these terms but others do not; those without definitions thus leave the
terms to their ordinary meaning and definition by decision-makers and courts.
The Reserves Act 1977 provides for a range of types of reserves, including
recreation, historic, scenic, nature, and scientific. Only the provision defining
scenic reserves refers to their intrinsic worth:
19 Scenic Reserves
(1) It is hereby declared that the appropriate provisions of this Act shall have
effect, in relation to reserves classified as scenic reserves—
(a) for the purpose of protecting and preserving in perpetuity for their
intrinsic worth and for the benefit, enjoyment, and use of the public, suitable
areas possessing such qualities of scenic interest, beauty, or natural features
or landscape that their protection and preservation are desirable in the public
interest.
The term intrinsic worth is not further defined in the statute, so it is left to
take its ordinary (anthropocentric) meaning.7 Nature’s intrinsic worth,
although ecocentric in abstraction, is still rooted in human enjoyment of
nature. For example, the courts have determined that the view from a scenic
reserve is part of its intrinsic worth;8 this justified the Minister of
Conservation granting a lease to enable construction of a gazebo on a scenic
reserve to take advantage of the view. In determining when and where
“protection and preservation are desirable,” the decision-making is based on
what is “desirable in the [human] public interest.” Thus, the measure of
intrinsic worth is established anthropocentrically.
The National Parks Act 1980 has a very similar purpose and reference to

intrinsic worth, but for national parks:
Principles to be applied in national parks
4. Parks to be Maintained in Natural State, and Public to Have Right
of Entry
(1) It is hereby declared that the provisions of this Act shall have effect for
the purpose of preserving in perpetuity as national parks, for their intrinsic
worth and for the benefit, use, and enjoyment of the public, areas of New
Zealand that contain scenery of such distinctive quality, ecological systems,
or natural features so beautiful, unique, or scientifically important that their
preservation is in the national interest.
(2) It is hereby further declared that, having regard to the general purposes
specified in subsection (1), national parks shall be so administered and
maintained under the provisions of this Act that:
(a) they shall be preserved as far as possible in their natural state:
(b) except where the Authority otherwise determines, the native plants and
animals of the parks shall as far as possible be preserved and the introduced
plants and animals shall as far as possible be exterminated:
(c) sites and objects of archaeological and historical interest shall as far as
possible be preserved:
(d) their value as soil, water, and forest conservation areas shall be
maintained:
(e) subject to the provisions of this Act and to the imposition of such
conditions and restrictions as may be necessary for the preservation of the
native plants and animals or for the welfare in general of the parks, the public
shall have freedom of entry and access to the parks, so that they may receive
in full measure the inspiration, enjoyment, recreation, and other benefits that
may be derived from mountains, forests, sounds, seacoasts, lakes, rivers, and
other natural features.

As with the Reserves Act, the term intrinsic worth is not further defined in
the statute, so it is similarly left to take its ordinary meaning. To date, it has
not been considered by courts in any manner that has refined the meaning of
the “intrinsic worth” of the parks.
The Conservation Act 1987 refers to intrinsic values three times when
defining “conservation,” “nature conservation,” and “preservation”:
conservation means the preservation and protection of natural and historic
resources for the purpose of maintaining their intrinsic values, providing for
their appreciation and recreational enjoyment by the public, and safeguarding
the options of future generations
nature conservation means the preservation and protection of the natural
resources of New Zealand, having regard to their intrinsic values and having
special regard to indigenous flora and fauna, natural ecosystems, and
landscape
preservation, in relation to a resource, means the maintenance, so far as is
practicable, of its intrinsic values
Conservation is the goal and purpose of the Act, and the drafting makes it
clear that intrinsic worth is a key factor in decisions about what to conserve,
preserve, and protect. For example, the purpose of the Act is stated in its
Long Title: “An Act to promote the conservation of New Zealand’s natural
and historic resources, and for that purpose to establish a Department of
Conservation.” The New Zealand Supreme Court has held that the definition
of “conservation” and its inclusion in the purpose of the Act means that the
existence of “intrinsic conservation values” are key to the existence and
protection of conservation land; only where such values no longer exist can
the protected status of conservation land be revoked.9 Thus, intrinsic values,
as vaguely defined and as anthropocentrically discerned as they may be, have
enabled the strong protection sought by the Act.
The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, also in the purpose
of the Act:
recognises, through the protection of public rights of access, navigation, and

fishing, the importance of the common Marine and coastal area—
(i) for its intrinsic worth; and
(ii) for the benefit, use, and enjoyment of the public of New Zealand.
The meaning of “intrinsic worth” again is not provided in the legislation, nor
is it addressed in commentaries on the legislation. It has not been considered
by courts in the context of the Takutai Moana Act.
The Resource Management Act 1991 refers to “intrinsic values of
ecosystems” in one of the sections containing the overriding principles
governing decision-making section 7(d). These provisions are cited in their
entirety below, as their hierarchy and comparison within the overall scheme
is important to their interpretation. Helpfully, the term is defined in the
statute:
intrinsic values, in relation to ecosystems, means those aspects of ecosystems
and their constituent parts which have value in their own right, including—
(a) their biological and genetic diversity; and
(b) the essential characteristics that determine an ecosystem’s integrity, form,
functioning, and resilience.”…
5. Purpose
(1) The purpose of this Act is to promote the sustainable management of
natural and physical resources.
(2) In this Act, sustainable management means managing the use,
development, and protection of natural and physical resources in a way, or at
a rate, which enables people and communities to provide for their social,
economic, and cultural well-being and for their health and safety while—
(a) sustaining the potential of natural and physical resources (excluding
minerals) to meet the reasonably foreseeable needs of future generations; and
(b) safeguarding the life-supporting capacity of air, water, soil, and

ecosystems; and
(c) avoiding, remedying, or mitigating any adverse effects of activities on the
environment.
6. Matters of National Importance
In achieving the purpose of this Act, all persons exercising functions and
powers under it, in relation to managing the use, development, and protection
of natural and physical resources, shall recognise and provide for the
following matters of national importance:
(a) the preservation of the natural character of the coastal environment
(including the coastal marine area), wetlands, and lakes and rivers and their
margins, and the protection of them from inappropriate subdivision, use, and
development:
(b) the protection of outstanding natural features and landscapes from
inappropriate subdivision, use, and development:
(c) the protection of areas of significant indigenous vegetation and significant
habitats of indigenous fauna:
(d) the maintenance and enhancement of public access to and along the
coastal marine area, lakes, and rivers:
(e) the relationship of Māori and their culture and traditions with their
ancestral lands, water, sites, waahi tapu, and other taonga:10
(f) the protection of historic heritage from inappropriate subdivision, use, and
development:
(g) the protection of protected customary rights:
(h) the management of significant risks from natural hazards.
7. Other Matters
In achieving the purpose of this Act, all persons exercising functions and

powers under it, in relation to managing the use, development, and protection
of natural and physical resources, shall have particular regard to—
(a) kaitiakitanga:11
(aa) the ethic of stewardship:
(b) the efficient use and development of natural and physical resources:
(ba) the efficiency of the end use of energy:
(c) the maintenance and enhancement of amenity values:
(d) intrinsic values of ecosystems:
(e) [Repealed]
(f) maintenance and enhancement of the quality of the environment:
(g) any finite characteristics of natural and physical resources:
(h) the protection of the habitat of trout and salmon:
(i) the effects of climate change:
(j) the benefits to be derived from the use and development of renewable
energy.
8. Treaty of Waitangi
In achieving the purpose of this Act, all persons exercising functions and
powers under it, in relation to managing the use, development, and protection
of natural and physical resources, shall take into account the principles of the
Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi).
The application of section 7(d), the “intrinsic values of ecosystems,” has been
considered by the courts in a few cases. This provision, significantly, does
not have as much weight as those in section 6, which decision-makers “shall
recognise and provide for”; they need only “have particular regard to” the

intrinsic values of ecosystems.12 Thus, intrinsic values are not as fundamental
to the definition of what is to be protected or to decision-making under the
Resource Management Act as they are in the context of the Conservation Act.
An illustration of section 7(d) being outweighed by other factors is provided
by an Environment Court decision on an application for an open cast coal
mine on a plateau containing rare plant species and a unique and endangered
ecosystem within New Zealand. The Environment Court considered the
application of section 7(d), with a focus on the ecosystem integrity:
Section 7(d) requires particular regard for the intrinsic value of ecosystems.
We have no doubt that if the mine is consented on the conditions proposed
there will be a reduction in the value of ecosystems on the mine site.
Connectivity and the current assemblages will be disrupted or lost by changes
such as the loss of some plant species are likely to be permanently lost to the
site, and some of those have considerable rarity value. The range and volume
of invertebrates will be reduced for a considerable period, along with the
various eco-system services they provide. We accept that elsewhere on the
plateau weed-control and predator control will assist in protecting and
enhancing the eco-systems present, but the very considerable likelihood of
the complete loss of rare plant species from the mine site and the Barren
Valley gives us particular concern in these terms, and we urged BCL [Buller
Coal Limited] during the hearing to consider whether adverse effects on that
area could be avoided if the proposal were otherwise consented.13
In addition, the Environment Court found that “there is clearly an adverse
effect on the proposal on significant habitats of indigenous fauna,” with it
being “a century or more before similar habitats to those presently existing
would be available on the mine site.”14 However, despite these factors, the
court granted the mining consent, agreeing to the applicant’s suggested
biodiversity offsets in order to mitigate the clear biodiversity losses that
would occur from the mining.
In the other RMA decisions to consider section 7(d), the courts did not
discuss the meaning of “intrinsic value” in any detail but merely asserted that
it would be upheld by the promotion of conservation measures. For example,
in relation to the use of a particular poison to control introduced and invasive

pests within a wildlife sanctuary, the parties disagreed about the effects of
this poison on intrinsic values of ecosystems.15 The High Court considered
that pest eradication in the name of conservation “satisfies the RMA
promotion of protection of natural resources and ecosystems with intrinsic
value” because of the ultimate aim of protecting and conserving such
ecosystems, but did not discuss any more detail.
As another example, in an appeal relating to a consent given for a solid waste
landfill, intrinsic ecological values were identified as a reason in favor of
imposing conditions in relation to the protection of indigenous vegetation.16
Four hundred hectares of land surrounding the landfill would be revegetated
and turned into a conservation area. The Environment Court was persuaded
that the proposed conservation area would produce significant ecosystem
benefits and “that the intrinsic values of the ecosystems would at least be
maintained and, in all probability, significantly enhanced as a result of the
restoration project and conservation management area.”17 There was no
discussion of the intrinsic value, more just the assertion that it would be
upheld.
In another case, the Environment Court stated that “[a] huge part of this case
is about the intrinsic values of ecosystems.”18 However, there was similarly
no separate discussion of what intrinsic value meant, just discussion—albeit
extensive—of the preservation of indigenous flora and fauna. The case
concerned hydroelectric power generation on a river, where a key concern
was the effect of changed water flows on water quality in the river, on
freshwater species within that river, and on the lower braided areas of the
river and the wetlands downstream that were significant habitats for native
flora and fauna. Local Māori guardians offered evidence that the mauri—the
spiritual value—of the river would be significantly adversely affected. The
Court agreed “that there will be a general adverse effect on the mauri” of the
river. While that would be partly offset by conditions enhancing aquatics
diversity, wetlands, and braided river birds, all of which contribute to that
mauri, “there remains a net loss to the mauri of the river.”19 Despite this, the
court considered that the proposal would be of net benefit to the community,
in light of the renewable energy generation. The court was accordingly
prepared to grant consents for the water diversions as long as conditions were
amended to better protect wetlands and the braided river birds.20

The Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996 has a provision
similar to that in the Resource Management Act, whereby “the intrinsic value
of ecosystems” is one of a list of six matters that decision-makers must “take
into account” when exercising functions under the Act.21 This Act also
contains the definition of “intrinsic values” adopted in the RMA:
intrinsic values, in relation to ecosystems, means those aspects of
ecosystems and their constituent parts which have value in their own right,
including—
(a) their biological and genetic diversity; and
(b) the essential characteristics that determine an ecosystem’s integrity, form,
functioning, and resilience.
Professional legal practice guides to this legislation suggest that
interpretations of the equivalent “RMA provisions are likely to provide some
guidance in interpreting these provisions of the HSNO Act.”22 In other
words, the academic legal community expects the meaning of nature’s
intrinsic value will become to be understood as transcending specific laws.
III. LEGISLATIVE RECOGNITION THAT
ANIMALS ARE SENTIENT BEINGS
In 2015, the New Zealand Parliament passed amendments to the 1999 animal
welfare legislation, as a result of the first review of that legislation since
1999. On May 10, 2015, section 4 of the Animal Welfare Amendment Act
(No. 2) explicitly included a recognition that animals are sentient. This
followed campaigning from animal rights and welfare advocates, such that
the government department responsible for the review recommended that it
be recognized in the title to the Act and/or a preamble.
Title of the Animal Welfare Act 1999:
An Act—
(a) to reform the law relating to the welfare of animals and the prevention of

their ill-treatment; and, in particular,—
(i) to recognise that animals are sentient:
(ia) to require owners of animals, and persons in charge of animals, to attend
properly to the welfare of those animals:
(ii) to specify conduct that is or is not permissible in relation to any animal or
class of animals:
(iii) to provide a process for approving the use of animals in research, testing,
and teaching:
(iv) to establish a National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee and a
National Animal Ethics Advisory Committee:
(v) to provide for the development and issue of codes of welfare and the
approval of codes of ethical conduct:…
The term sentient is not defined in the Act. The only other section where
sentience is referred to is in relation to approvals for animals in research,
testing, and teaching. A purpose of the provisions on the use of animals in
research, testing, and teaching is “to replace animals as subjects for research,
and testing by substituting, where appropriate, non-sentient or non-living
alternatives.”23 Two of the criteria for assessing applications for animal use
are accordingly: “the extent to which there has been—(i) assessment of the
suitability of using non-sentient or non-living alternatives in the project; and
(ii) replacement of animals as subjects with suitable non-sentient or non-
living alternatives.24 Consequently, the prime practical effect of the use of the
word (and concept) “sentient” will be via statutory interpretation, as courts
are required to interpret the text of all legislation “in light of its purpose.”25
Neither the Explanatory Note to the Amendment Bill nor the parliamentary
debates on it discussed the inclusion of “sentient,” indicating that it was not
officially seen as being of much significance. The government ministry
responsible for the Act categorized it as merely a “minor and technical
amendment”26 and a symbolic gesture that “would not affect the detail of the
rights, duties or obligations set out within the body of the Act.”27 Some

critics have called it “political puffery to maintain New Zealand’s reputation
for the sake of appearances to overseas markets, and window dressing to
appease New Zealand’s animal welfare groups.”28
In contrast, the New Zealand Veterinary Association says that the legal
recognition of animal sentience for the first time in New Zealand law is one
of the “key changes” to the legislation. Its inclusion “strongly reinforces that
people are obliged to meet their animals’ physical health and behavioural
needs, and places New Zealand at the ‘forefront of progressive animal
welfare legislation.’”29
In between these positions, the chair of the National Animal Ethics Advisory
Committee said it was “another step along the animal welfare journey” and
“provided a stronger underpinning” for the other provisions in the
legislation.30
A submission by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals
(SPCA) argued that the declaration of sentience was needed “because most
New Zealand law treats animals as ‘things’ and ‘objects’ rather than as living
creatures.” A regional SPCA manager accordingly “hoped that recognising
animals as sentient beings would add ‘more weight’ to abuse and neglect
cases in court.”31 This may indeed have happened already, as the recognition
“that animals are sentient” was acknowledged by the New Zealand Court of
Appeal as one of the particular purposes of the act relevant to sentencing for a
conviction of extreme animal cruelty.32 However, it is hard to say that the
same result could not have been achieved without that clause, as it was only
one of quite a few things listed, and the animal’s suffering was already a key
aspect of the prosecution and sentencing.
Another concrete suggestion for a positive effect of the recognition of
sentience is that it could expand the responsibilities of animal caregivers. At
present, the expectations for compliance with animal welfare standards
focuses on avoiding pain and suffering. Sentience incorporates the fact that
animals can experience pleasure as well as pain, so some writers argue that it
must extend the duties on caregivers to adequately provide for positive
experiences for animals, not just avoid negative ones.33

Finally, some legal advocates suggest that this paves the way for the
introduction of class actions on behalf of animals.34 Perhaps the next “step
along the animal welfare journey” that sentience paves, after recognition of
animals as beings with feelings, is the recognition of animals as legal
persons, with all the legal implications that that may have.35 Through the
unique relationship between the Māori and the New Zealand government, and
thoughtful creative problem-solving, law has been developed to more
effectively protect sentient beings. As courts consider and construe the
meaning of “sentience,” they will determine how broadly it may be
construed.
IV. LEGAL PERSONALITY FOR NATURE
As with other settled countries around the world with surviving Indigenous
peoples, Māori have made legal and political claims to lands and resources
that they have lost through settlement. New Zealand is widely regarded as
being at the forefront of initiatives to recognize Indigenous rights and resolve
such claims, including the co-management and co-governance of New
Zealand’s land and resources with Māori.
New Zealand does not recognize any human right to a healthy environment,
nor have existing human rights been extended to enable any remedies for
violations through degraded environments. However, the recognition of
Indigenous rights and the resolution of claims based on the land taken by the
British from the Māori has led to the recognition of Indigenous
environmental rights and responsibilities. Through the protection of
Indigenous worldviews and Indigenous environmental management, this
particular combination has entailed the adoption of measures for
environmental protection that go beyond simple claims to rights to also
implement complex notions of responsibility and guardianship on the part of
individuals, communities, and the state. It is through this recognition and
system for resolving the Indigenous people’s grievances that the legislature
has adopted the innovative use of legal personhood for natural features.
A. Māori Environmental Philosophies

Māori cultural beliefs view natural and geographical features as ancestors.36
It is the responsibility of Māori today to act as guardians and care for their
environmental ancestors, which will in turn protect and look after the people.
The environment is believed to be inhabited by spirits, such that each
environmental feature has its own spirit and life force; human actions must
maintain this life force. Part of being ancestrally connected to nature means
that humans are not considered separate from or above it, and they cannot
own it. What is important for the interplay between human rights and the
environment is that they are intertwined: human well-being exists in tandem
with that of the nonhuman natural world, and each cares for the other. It is no
coincidence that these beliefs are held by Indigenous peoples worldwide.
Over the last 40 years, the ability of Māori as Indigenous peoples to manage
natural resources37 in a way that is consistent with a Māori worldview has
gradually been incorporated in New Zealand law through Treaty of Waitangi
grievance settlements, judicial decisions, and domestic legislation, as well as
through local, regional, and national policy.38 It is noteworthy that this covers
publicly owned lands and resources, not just ones currently owned by Māori,
and that this has occurred within a Western legal system. In particular, Māori
cosmology, including the spiritual relationship with the environment, has
become a required consideration in most environmental decision-making and
has even been given “primacy” as a matter of national importance when
balancing competing factors.39 Decision-makers under the Resource
Management Act are also required to pay particular regard to traditional
Māori kaitiakitanga (guardianship) or stewardship of natural resources.40
This started with court decisions upholding the importance of the Treaty and
is now enshrined in the Resource Management Act.41
Māori relationships with the natural world have also been recognized and
protected through grievance settlement agreements between the New Zealand
government and Māori, and these are enshrined in legislation. Over the last
30 years, the government and claimants have devised a wide range of options
to recognize and restore Māori tribal spiritual, cultural, and traditional
associations with the natural environment, as well as to recognize and restore
Māori cultural authority.42 They have included joint management of lands
and resources between the government and Māori and tribal ownership of
natural sites of great cultural significance to the tribes, including the beds of

rivers and lakes.43 The most significant of these measures has been the recent
creation of separate legal personality for natural beings, such as rivers, with
joint tribal/government representation and guardianship of that being’s
interests.44
Accordingly, legal personhood or personality to natural beings—such as
rivers, mountains, and even broad areas of territory comprising ecosystems—
is being increasingly argued and used as a tool to accord rights to nature
and/or better implement human responsibility for it.45 New Zealand has
legislatively accorded personhood to a river and to what was a national park
and, at the time of this writing, has agreed to do so for a mountain. The
legislation does not explicitly recognize rights of nature in the sense rights
are generally recognized in legal systems. It was not designed primarily to
prevent or remedy environmental degradation. Rather, the legislation was
designed to implement a Māori Indigenous vision of human responsibility for
and relationship with our natural environment and was done to better uphold
Indigenous people’s rights. While the legislation recognizes the intrinsic
value of the environment—i.e., in its own right—it also recognizes that
people are part of the environment and it is intended to promote co-existence
between people and all natural environments.
B. Te Urewera46
Te Urewera National Park was created in the 1950s out of ancestral land
confiscated from the Māori Tūhoe people.47 This was the subject of a
grievance against the government, the settlement of which culminated in the
Te Urewera Act 2014.48 Key to this settlement was Tūhoe regaining control
of the Te Urewera National Park and the ability to exercise its kaitiakitanga
(guardianship) over Te Urewera, along with explicit acknowledgment of the
metaphysical relationship of Tūhoe with their ancestral land.49 The method of
achieving this was through the creation of legal personhood for the park,
whereby Te Urewera would obtain its own separate identity, with the
establishment of a legal guardian for Te Urewera. What was a national park
can now be governed independently, with significant Tūhoe input and in
accordance with Tūhoe protocol and custom.

Under this agreement, Te Urewera is no longer a national park. It is its own
legal entity, with “all the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a legal
person.”50 This legal status permits Te Urewera to hold title to land (i.e., title
to itself), which is managed by its guardian, the Te Urewera Board, that acts
“on behalf of, and in the name of, Te Urewera.” A detailed discussion of this
guardianship arrangement is presented in Chapter 6, “Legal Guardianship and
Representation.”
Board membership is a mix of Tūhoe trustees and government appointees.
The Act grants the Board extensive powers and obligations, including the
power to make by-laws and to grant activity permits within Te Urewera.
Tūhoe spirituality is directly provided for in Board decision-making. The
principles governing the implementation of the Act focus primarily on
aspects of environmental protection but are also protective of Indigenous
relationships with the park and of public access for the benefit of all New
Zealanders.
The Board released their management plan for Te Urewera, Te Kawa o Te
Urewera, in 2017 (“Te Kawa”).51 This plan shows a new vision of the rights
and responsibilities between humans and the environment. The overriding
purpose of Te Kawa is to delineate dignity and command respect for nature
and to reaffirm the subordinate place of humans within it.52 It emphasizes
duty and “responsibility…not power or rights” throughout the document. It
expressly states: “[T]he Board through Te Kawa is disrupting the notion of
our false superiority over the natural world…we are returning to our place in
nature, as her child.”53

C. The Management Plan: Te Kawa o Te Urewera54

The first words that greet you in (the English version of) Te Kawa o Te
Urewera (Te Kawa) are “Nature wills that there is no end to life,” in bold
72-point font. As such a beginning indicates, Te Kawa is like no other
management plan. It was deliberately written to establish the principles to
guide the decisions of the board and the setting of operational management
plans under the legislation. As board Chairman Tamati Kruger said at the

Te Kawa does not work the same way as other management plans, which
focus on setting rules and stock-taking.…That traditional approach can frame
nature as a set of discrete resources to be managed and used. Te Kawa is
different. It asks us to stop and reflect on Te Urewera and what that means as
a living system. A living system we depend on for survival, culture,
recreation, and inspiration. Te Urewera has its own identity that is legal, but
also physical, environmental, cultural and spiritual.…
Te Kawa sets out a vision for bringing all New Zealanders, including Tūhoe,

Urewera does not work to annual plans, but over seasons and centuries.”55
We now turn to the text of the management plan itself. As you read, consider
how it differs from the types of management plans that you might typically

Extracts from Te Kawa o Te Urewera:
[Introduction:]
Te Kawa is about the management of people for the benefit of the land—
it is not about land management.
It raises hope for a renewed collective responsibility for our people impact on
the land and foresees our disciplined response to those impacts.
Together, we invite an inter-generational outlook to introduce new practice
for principled based responsibility and management to meet our admiration
and respect for Te Urewera.…

Te Kawa is not intended to operate in the same way as a usual management
plan which focuses on rules. Rather, Te Kawa records principles as law, and
traditions and beliefs as the sense of a better future. As in life, virtues shape
our responsibilities and choices guiding Te Urewera Board decisions on
appropriate and responsible activities in Te Urewera. The application of these
will also develop over time in the form of operational plans, activities and use
terms, and other wide-ranging areas.…
1.1 THE PURPOSE OF TE KAWA
People need nature, land and waters for life, purpose and humanity. Nature
enjoys people for their aspiration, endeavour and friendship. Te Kawa then
describes the interrelationship between people and Te Urewera for a just life.
An interplay that acknowledges our place and describes our renewed respect
and intuition for the health and vitality of Te Urewera.
We know and we understand that nature is timeless, regenerative and
operates by mauri and mana. Life’s purpose is realised when we understand
that life flow, for it brings us order, shows us how to dispense justice and
know fairness, letting us see how to serve as worthy people deserving of
benefit and entitlement. Without nature’s principles alive in our relationships
we too often suffer discord from irrelevant habits and cannot apply justice to
achieve a natural balance. But, if we can share in these Te Urewera traditions
and beliefs guiding our way to a responsible life, our ability as people to live
with nature can be restored. And so that what we see in the world is that
which we want to see in ourselves.
As tanata whenua [people of the land—ie Tūhoe guardians] and manuhiri
[visitors], we know that Te Urewera-Papatūānuku56 predates us and that we
are of her creation living with and amongst all of her kin. As her children we
are born with responsibility, we are not born with power and rights. The most
difficult of virtues yet most important to accomplish is our sense of
belonging, to know our place and contribution to creation.
In reaffirming this natural order the Board through Te Kawa is disrupting the
notion of our false superiority over the natural world. In all decisiveness, we
are returning to our place in nature, as her child.

TE UREWERA PRINCIPLES
• PAPATŪĀNUKU: LANDSCAPE
Balance: Nothing in the natural world is equal; nature itself operates on the
basis of diversity. A human view of devastation can be for Te Urewera a
process of recycling and regeneration. Nothing in nature is wasted;
everything happens for a reason. Te Urewera has a scale beyond our
perception in which to balance and order life.
• MAURI: LIFE
Mauri: A life force requiring generosity each to the other. This generosity
opens the soul to want connection and collective benefit. To see the
relationship between past and future, species and race, birth and death,
individual and community, dreaming and science and through managing self-
interest, see the common threads of all creations to realise true purpose
through which to bring prosperity to life.
• TAPU: WAI
Resilience: Wai [water] is comprehensively hard and soft, serene and
insurgent[;] she nourishes all that have needs for life. Fairness brings the
discipline necessary for collective progress, sharing life, easing the pressure
on those that might otherwise struggle, foreseeing and adapting for future life
needs and standards as easily as creating new water courses.
• AHUA: CHARACTER
Nakau iti: Futures grow from selflessness and sacrifice today. Nature thus
humanizes interest and inspirit each other not through biological makeup but
through values, personality and vibe. Our care for each other inspires us to
live together for purpose. All things are bound together, everything is
connected, so the need for strict discipline and high regard for reciprocity.
• TATAI: HERITAGE
Time: Our sense of time creates our past and future. Our memory for unity,

hope and generosity urges our will to live together. This memory spurs us
into the future, unlearning, relearning, learning anew so that we are always
current adapting to be necessary and relevant to each time span we are
granted.
• WHāNAU: MANUHIRI AND TANATA WHENUA
Discipline: No creature should believe they belong only to themselves. Our
values and virtues help guard against inherent human impulses to dominate
one another; to balance ego and self-interest. When strong, our habits defend
against these pressures and the wellbeing of the collective outweighs the
good of individual.
When our laws and rules depart from Te Urewera principles and from
our practice of that alive in our traditions and beliefs, they lose moral
integrity and authority. They make no sense; they cannot be said to be
fair or just.
2.1 THE LEGAL PERSONALITY APPLIED
The role of Te Urewera Board is to act on behalf of, and in the name of, Te
Urewera. In doing so the Board must engage with and embrace the Te
Urewera identity.
Te Urewera Act recognises that Te Urewera has its own identity, in and of
itself, inspiring people to commit to its care. Through this identity, the Act
makes evident the presence and distinct personality that is Te Urewera as
well her creations of the natural world. The Act does not establish the Te
Urewera identity rather it liberates it from human speculation in order that
nature and the natural world return to its primal role, revered and served by
those of her children to whom she has given life.
The use of property rights by the western legal system has hidden from view
the concept of nature; rendered her parts as natural resources now capable of
rival priorities competing with other household choices. These human
granted rights have displaced our devotion for Papatūānuku with ownership
now serving individual advantage. These motives suppress the vision of Te
Urewera as distinct life. Yet, property rights do not give life nor do they

encourage the connectedness of all living things for life. In this altered
relationship people struggle to unify to perceive the whole which is nature
collectively. Needlessly our fracturing of nature has sponsored our own
fragmentation. The use of property rights to regulate human disputes arising
from human society is no longer permissible in and of Te Urewera. Te
Urewera may never again be owned by people.
The National Parks Act was sympathetic to the voice of Te Urewera but also
created a further dislocation between Te Urewera, its identity, and Tūhoe. By
ignoring the presence and personality of Te Urewera, treating her as lands for
the enjoyment of others, these mechanisms served to disorder the Te Urewera
connection distorting the relationship between people, nature and identity.
The recognition of Te Urewera as a legal entity in Te Urewera Act redresses
the Te Urewera identity. Te Urewera has primacy under the law, with the role
of institutions, laws and people being to embrace, respect, and act in the
interests of Te Urewera.
Now, Te Kawa seeks to start the journey of understanding and articulating
the Te Urewera identity. That requires an understanding of traditions and
beliefs, the role and place of people in Te Urewera, the concepts of tanata
whenua and manuhiri, and the relationship between Tūhoe and Te Urewera.
…
3.3 MANAGING HUMAN EXPECTATION
We recognise that Te Urewera, which includes the well-being and the
experiences of the people that make her their home or a place to visit, is also
influenced by activities that happen outside of her borders. Global warming,
pest infestation, water and air quality, attitudes and aspirations of people all
have the potential to adversely impact Te Urewera’s living system. These
problems are our problems; we have a stake in resolving them. Leaving such
neglect and abuse for the next generation will not reflect honourably on any
of us. Our investment in these issues today will count; they are relevant
factors for our impact accounting.
If we believe that the permanency of the land is a precondition for our life,
then as we invite the return of nature into our homes and relationships we

will relearn her needs and through that our limits. Reciprocity and mutual
respect are key elements of Te Kawa—the more selfless the interaction with
Te Urewera, be they transient or generational, the richer the engagement and
our security for enduring life.
3.4 OUR ASPIRATIONS
The aspiration is that in 20 years’ time Te Urewera, Tūhoe and her Manuhiri
who choose a relationship connection with Te Urewera will be supporting a
local, national and global effort of living with the land, admiring the living
system of nature and making us whole.…
4.2 ESTABLISHING TE UREWERA PRIORITIES
Te Urewera’s living system has a balance and a rhythm that is mysterious and
imperceptible to human senses. She is timeless and pulses to beat of her own.
Understanding then what is a priority or urgency by Te Urewera opinion is
somewhat illusory. Here a priority speaks to the common worry for excessive
use by human activity and perhaps also our inactivity to better our habits for
living with Te Urewera. Priority affects more than a present day state, its true
focus the behavioural standards which we need and want to instill in
ourselves. It is future oriented. These standards are the true guards against
living excessively, that when strong naturally repel habits that lead to placing
too great a burden on Te Urewera.
These priorities then are our urgent need to regrow Responsibility, to bring
resilience into community, to raise humanity, lifting our sight to living by Te
Urewera principle, her eternal standards that reveal themselves in a range of
ways throughout Te Urewera. It counts on the actions of Tūhoe their
commitment to her for all time, this is whakapapa-kinship in action; and on
her manuhiri connections for similar. Her form and figure expect this
adoration forever, where her Living System parts and their relationships with
each other are felt, understood, respected and lived.
Yet Te Urewera has much to consider, where reversing trends of poor health
is complex. History has seen the disruption of the Tūhoe contribution. She
will delight to feel the return of regular and thoughtful footfall through river
and across mauna [mountains], instilling a new generation understanding,

revitalised values, bringing relevance to the myriad of pressures now faced.
Experiencing the essence of her Living System—reconnecting passion and
memory for the next kaitiaki.…
6.1.2 NEW ACTIVITY AND RESPONSIBLE INNOVATION
WELCOMED
The potential of responsible innovation to improve the efficacy of operations
and experiences within Te Urewera is embraced. New ideas are encouraged,
approaches and technologies consistent with Te Urewera values welcomed,
forever mindful of the potential risks and unintended consequences
associated with unchecked innovations.…
Connection to and opportunity within this considers ideas such as:
The potential for innovations and technologies around all aspects of
delivering on Te Urewera priorities e.g. pest control, smart/sensing
living systems.
Manuhiri relationship and experience systems to inform planning
decisions more efficiently to bring targeted development and manage
and deliver better experiences for people.
Openness to exploring new and better ways of doing things. Te Urewera
has potential to benchmark the safe, responsible and robust testing of
new ideas, technologies and other innovations consistent with Te Kawa
principles.
6.2 BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES—FRIENDSHIP AGREEMENTS
For appropriate commercial-type activities and large scale activities, more
formal relationship will be required. The Board may grant a concession now
referred to as a Friendship Agreement in the form of a lease, license, permit
or easement, but only where the activity is not inconsistent with Te Kawa.
Friendship Agreements replace the previous concessions regime applied by
the Department of Conservation. Associated processes for approving,
monitoring and adapting these will have similarities to the previous
concessions regime, but will be designed to achieve new and broader
standards of integrity for our impact uses on the living system of Te Urewera.

A Te Urewera Friendship Agreement admits that opportunities are afforded
only where we can demonstrate loyal affection to Te Urewera values and her
need to continue her complex balancing act amongst her living system. The
collaboration needed by holders of Friendship Agreements will enact and
instill robust examples of the principles required of all interactions with Te
Urewera. Their design will ensure the mauri of Te Urewera is not diminished
through external pressures, considerations or expectations.
Introducing a Friendship Agreement brings opportunity for those seeking a
livelihood within Te Urewera, or to undertake an activity of scale or with a
non-trivial impact. The Board in applying the terms of [section] 62 and
schedule 3 of Te Urewera Act will only do so in a way that is consistent with
Te Kawa;
(a) Explicitly considers how such an activity contributes to achieving the (i)
purpose of Te Urewera Act; (ii) Te Urewera principles which are Te Kawa
principles; (iii) Te Urewera Responsibilities and Prioritised Actions
(b) Clearly explains how the activity effects the living system of Te Urewera;
(c) Clearly provides adequate or reasonable methods of remedying, avoiding
or mitigating the adverse effects on the living system of Te Urewera;
(d) Shares the benefits/risk on a sustainable basis between the parties,
reflecting their respective contributions.
(e) Is enabling of Tūhoe participation, where they are or have the potential in
the future to be best placed to own/manage an activity.
(f) Has positive obligations on parties granted an agreement to “use it, or lose
it.”
6.3 INTEGRITY AND COMPLIANCE
The Board will apply a monitoring oversight at the whole of living system
level, at an individual activity operator level and at the manuhiri or partner
satisfaction level. Key elements of the monitoring will include establishing a
“dashboard” to highlight how the living system of Te Urewera is adapting,

what real impact particular activities or factors are having, and where the
priorities are for future action.
The resilience of the living system of Te Urewera;
Productivity and use in Te Urewera;
Economic opportunities and innovation within Te Urewera;
Tūhoe leadership and infrastructure.
6.4 EVOLVING OUR TE UREWERA EXPERIENCE
Providing for all who wish to have a deeper relationship with Te Urewera the
opportunity to do so, through the facilitation of dialog and opportunity which
will consider:
Information provision—on Te Urewera and Tūhoe practices, cultures,
expectations etc. so that willing manuhiri [visitors] can educate
themselves;
Opportunities for manuhiri [visitors] to announce themselves—either
prior or at the time of their arrival—to Tūhoe who can listen to their
goals and help them plan and get the most out of their visit. This is
expected to be an important channel for identifying parties who wish to
have a positive exchange with Tūhoe and Te Urewera and services as a
first step in building the networks and dialogs for this to happen;
Specific initiatives—Invitations for Tūhoe and manuhiri to participate in
workshops and development programmes, e.g., a contribution to
trapping pests, planting trees, restoring tracks;
Information capture—manuhiri provided with a range of mechanisms to
provide a contribution to the caretaking of Te Urewera;
Partnerships (and sponsorships) which through introducing and
mobilising new and complementary capabilities that can in combination
create new potential and opportunities.…
7.3 COMPLIANCE
Our need for new standard[s] and responsibility needs new guidance. Natural
tensions exist from old and new practices, between the individual and the
collective, between use and preservation, science and culture and science and
people, these things are in desperate need of sound reconciliation effort. The

use of new whanau [extended family], hapū [sub-tribe], tribal, stakeholder
and community leadership supported by new instinct and technology needs
time to be developed. Raising our compliance standards will also need
disciplined innovation which the Board accepts as an important current
priority.

Te Kawa finishes with some lines from the T.S. Eliot poem “Little Gidding”:
“We shall not cease from exploration, and the end of all our exploring will be
to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.” The poem
also explains: “What we called the beginning is of the end, and to make an
end is to make a beginning. The end is where we start from.”
In summary, the Te Urewera legislation elevates the legal status of a national
park to a legal entity with all of the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a
legal person. It envisages a new relationship between humans and the
environment based on a framework of rights and responsibilities. However, it
is Te Kawa o Te Urewera—the management plan made under it—that
redefines that relationship and creates a truly new beginning, where that
relationship is in harmony with Earth law principles.
V. FROM THE WHANGANUI RIVER TO TE
AWA TUPUA57
The Whanganui River has also been accorded legal personality by legislation,
and has been provided with legal guardians to represent and uphold its
interests. The Whanganui River is the ancestral river of a number of
Whanganui Iwi (tribal groups). From the 1800s, the government assumed
ownership of the river and undertook riverbed works, gravel extraction, and
water diversions for a hydroelectric power scheme, despite persistent
opposition from Whanganui Iwi. Grievances over the river were the subject
of petitions to Parliament, Royal Commission reports, Waitangi Tribunal
claims, and numerous court cases between 1938 until 2010. An agreement in
resolution of these grievances was enacted in the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui
River Claims Settlement) Act 2017.…

This Act recognizes the indivisible connection between the Whanganui Iwi
and the Whanganui River, as well as the river’s metaphysical status as a
living being:
Te Awa Tupua is an indivisible and living whole, comprising the Whanganui
River from the mountains to the sea, incorporating all its physical and
metaphysical elements.
In an effort to implement the Māori understanding of the river as a living
whole, connected to the Whanganui Iwi but incapable of being “owned” in an
absolute sense, the Act grants the Whanganui River independent legal
personhood as Te Awa Tupua: “Te Awa Tupua is a legal person and has all
the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a legal person.”
Title to the riverbeds of what was the Whanganui River and its tributaries,
within a large catchment area, is vested in the name of Te Awa Tupua itself.
The riverbed is defined:
bed, in relation to the Whanganui River,—
(a) means the space of land that the waters of the Whanganui River cover at
its fullest flow without overtopping its banks; and
(b) includes the subsoil, the plants attached to the bed, the space occupied by
the water, and the airspace above the water.58
Importantly, the Act provides that guardians shall be appointed on behalf of
the Whanganui River: two persons “of high standing,” one appointed by the
Crown and one appointed collectively by all tribes with interests in the river,
are to be the river’s guardians and must act in the name of Te Awa Tupua.
This office of guardianship, called Te Pou Tupua, must “promote and protect
the health and wellbeing of Te Awa Tupua,” “act and speak on behalf of Te
Awa Tupua,” and act “in its interests and consistently with Tupua te Kawa
[intrinsic values of the river].” The office of Te Pou Tupua embodies a co-
governance arrangement, with both Māori and non-Māori members, and its
powers enable stronger legal respect for the environment in line with Māori
cosmology.

The Act anticipates the development of Te Heke Ngahuru, a “Whole of River
Strategy,” that addresses and advances the health and well-being of the
Whanganui River. It also establishes Te Korotete o Te Awa Tupua, a “River
Fund” of NZD $30 million that is designed to support the health and well-
being of the river. Unlike Te Urewera, the Whanganui River was not a
national park prior to being granted legal status. The environmental
protection afforded to it under the Te Awa Tupua Act is thus greater than had
previously been the case. Yet what is most important for the Whanganui Iwi
is their understanding and belief that their health and well-being is dependent
on the health and well-being of the river. It is expressed in their proverb, “Ko
au te awa, ko te awa ko au” (I am the river and the river is me).59 As the
health of the river improves, so will the health of the people; the environment
and human rights are intertwined and protected together.
Extracts from Te Awa Tupua Act 2017 detailing the guardianship bodies and
their functions are provided in Chapter 6, “Guardianship Arrangements in
Rights of Nature Legal Provisions.” The legislation does not detail the means
by which these bodies will interact with the bodies established under other
legislation. This is currently being worked out as the Te Awa Tupua
guardians undertake their roles.
Interestingly, the legal person is treated differently depending on which
legislation it might be covered by or interact with:
17. Application of Other Acts to Te Awa Tupua
Te Awa Tupua is to be treated as—
(a) an institution for the purpose of applying for registration as a charitable
entity under the Charities Act 2005:
(b) a public body for the purposes of clauses 30 and 30A of Schedule 7 of the
Local Government Act 2002:
(c) a public authority for the purpose of section 33X of the Maritime
Transport Act 1994:
(d) a registered collector of taonga tūturu60 for the purposes of section 14 of

the Protected Objects Act 1975:
(e) a public authority for the purposes of the Resource Management Act
1991:
(f) a body corporate for the purpose of applying to be a heritage protection
authority under section 188 of the Resource Management Act 1991:
(g) a public body for the purposes of sections 4 and 35 of the Walking Access
Act 2008.
An omission worth noting is that the waters of the river catchment have been
excluded from this legislation’s coverage. The river’s water is thus not part of
the legal person nor its property. This is due to a government position that no
one owns freshwater in New Zealand, and that the government merely
manages it for the good of all. The government therefore refused to recognise
ownership of the water in the legislation, even by the natural entity itself.
Despite this omission, the arrangements enacted in respect of Te Awa Tupua
have created a new beginning. They have created a new relationship between
local and national government, the area’s residents, the river, and its
guardians, if not also with the whole country that has celebrated its passage.
It, too, is a relationship based on a new set of rights and responsibilities that
are in line with Earth law principles.
VI. CONCLUSION
New Zealand is a modern, Western democracy with its values and the
majority of its culture being familiar to other English-speaking Western
democracies. In that sense, the adoption of statements of intrinsic value for
nature and declarations of animal sentience were subject to the political and
policy considerations that might arise in other such countries. It is thus
instructive to consider the choices made in their legislative incorporation, as
well as in their ongoing application by courts, and to consider opportunities
to rely on the New Zealand lawmaking to develop Earth law in other
countries.
New Zealand’s recognition of Indigenous environmental rights and

responsibilities has been more extensive and effective than in other countries
that share the English language and Western culture. Consider, for example,
the efforts in the United States promoted by CELDF, as discussed in Chapter
9, “The Rights of Nature Movement in the United States.” The protection of
Indigenous worldviews and Indigenous environmental management through
statute—notably the adoption of responsibility, guardianship and legal
personhood—is innovative. Globally, they are perceived as a threat by
embedded economic interests and have not garnered the social and political
backing needed to pass legislation. Nevertheless, the New Zealand
experience in drafting legislation will provide both perspective and
persuasive authority for practitioners of Earth law in other countries.
As with all legislation, the value of the New Zealand laws will depend on the
statutory wording and the legislative history, which provide the parameters
for what judicial and administrative decision-makers can do. Courts will
determine the breadth of such parameters as they consider and construe their
meanings. In considering the study questions below, focus on these
parameters as you identify and argue their interpretation and application. The
experience under statutes such as the Resource Management Act show that
interpretations of the provisions implementing Māori culture and values are
argued as thoroughly in courts as any other statutory provisions that are
challenged on the basis of the meaning and application of the words. The
specific wording must be paid careful attention.
Te Kawa is not itself legislation. It was adopted pursuant to the powers and
guidelines within the statutory framework. It illustrates a new vision of the
rights and responsibilities between humans and the environment, in line with
Earth laws. The overriding dignity and respect for nature, along with the
place of humans within it, and its emphasis on duty and responsibility rather
than power or rights, provides an innovative opportunity for land
management. Te Kawa illustrates what can be done to challenge “the notion
of our false superiority over the natural world” and return us “to our place in
nature, as her child.”61
The study of Earth law in its many emergent forms enables us to explicitly
identify and draft ecocentric legislation, to recognize whether it is being used
as intended and effectively, and to take action to uphold and extend its

application. These examples from Aotearoa New Zealand expand the ideas of
what is possible.
STUDY QUESTIONS
Intrinsic worth and intrinsic values:
(1) Does the inclusion of reference to intrinsic worth or intrinsic value
represent the inclusion of a deep ecology approach, which treats human life
as just one of many interrelated components, all essential in their own
separate and collective ways, of a larger global ecosystem? Can it have any
effect if it operates within and must be balanced against other more
mainstream values? How would you explain intrinsic value to a court? How
would it be different in a general sense than in the case of a particular client,
for example a river? How does the Resource Management Act 1991 delineate
the range of matters that must be balanced by a decision-maker?
(2) How might the persuasive value of an argument based on intrinsic worth
or intrinsic value be enhanced or diminished by the fact that they are
mentioned as an overriding purpose and not elsewhere in the statute? How
might a court instruct a jury on the weight to be given to intrinsic worth or
intrinsic value? How might it be distinguished from extrinsic value?
(3) Should intrinsic worth and intrinsic values in relation to nature be
interpreted consistently across the different statutes, or should each term take
the meaning most appropriate for that statute? Note that a purposive approach
to statutory interpretation suggests that each statute is considered on its own
and that other statutes are irrelevant; the particular context and purpose of
that single statute is key, unless it forms part of a statutory scheme and should
be treated as interrelated.
(4) Are there any differences in the meanings of intrinsic worth or intrinsic
value that would make any difference in practice? Think about the
interpretation of scenic value from the place in the question; would an
interpretation of “intrinsic value” in the National Parks Act ever be likely to
be similar to that for the scenic reserves in the Reserves Act? Do you think
constructing a gazebo to take advantage of the view would be likely to be

approved for a national park?
Sentience of animals:
(5) What real effect can a general statement of principle about sentience have
when applying clear standards that are already specified in the legislation, or
when developing the content of animal welfare codes or other rules under the
Act? How might a court, in practice, change the manner in which it conducts
its decision-making business to include a consideration of sentience? How
might a legislative enactment, or a judicial enactment of procedural rules be
developed? How much power do trial court judges have in your jurisdiction
to use a purposive approach in interpreting legislation?
(6) If you were making a submission on the inclusion of a reference to
animals being sentient in animal welfare legislation, how could it be worded,
where would you place it, and what effect would you want it to have? Is there
other legislation that might benefit from its inclusion? If so, how?
(7) If animal welfare codes needed to be revised in accordance with an
expanded concept of animal quality of life, and requiring positive
experiences, what effect would that have on the animal food industries, such
as in relation to animal housing and transport?
(8) How should we balance sentience and animal welfare with controlling
invasive, introduced pest species?
Indigenous rights and legal personality:
(9) Consider how the two different legal persons have been defined for Te
Urewera National Park and Whanganui River. Should they be defined by
geographical lines on a map or by ecosystem function? How significant
might it be that freshwater is not owned by the legal persons nor under the
control of their guardians?
(10) Does using Indigenous language terms import their different
understanding of humans’ relationships with nature—more in line with Earth
law—or are they only as good as the judges interpreting the terms? The use
of “kaitiakitanga” in the Resource Management Act will be considered and

interpreted by decision-makers who are not Indigenous and may have little
understanding of Indigenous cosmology. How might this be met? How would
you avert a non-Indigenous interpretation based on the statutory wording that
it is only needed to be paid regard to, rather than recognized and provided for
by a decision-maker?
(11) Discuss the other uses of language in the legislation according to legal
personality to nature. For example, note the use of “her” to refer to Te
Urewera; what does this signify and incorporate? Note the use of the word
“appointee” to the Te Urewera Board. Board members are appointed by the
New Zealand government and by the Māori Tuhoe tribe; yet their job is to
represent Te Urewera; might their source of appointment affect their views of
the interests of Te Urewera? How would you assert your authority to speak as
a guardian of a national park? How would you balance your authority with
the guardian of a river that flowed through the park?
(12) Instead of a list of activities allowed in the area, Te Kawa refers to
“experience” and “connection”; instead of “concessions,” Te Kawa refers to
“friendship agreements.” Do you think the use of this wording will make any
difference in the way these activities are conducted? How might they make a
difference?
(13) In the context of legal personality discussed in section 2.1 of the Te
Kawa extracts, how do property rights encourage fragmentation and
discourage connectedness of nature and living things in it? What might
dispute resolution within human society look like if it did not use property
rights to resolve disputes?
(14) When you read that natural beings like parks and rivers are legal entities
and have “all the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a legal person,”
what are the strengths and weaknesses of arguments based separately on: (1)
rights, (2) powers, (3) duties and (4) liabilities? Why do you think the New
Zealand legislation identifies all four?
(15) Do you think of New Zealand’s laws discussed in this chapter are
appropriately termed rights of nature laws? Why or why not? How do you
distinguish rights of nature from other types of Earth laws?

(16) What benefit can the New Zealand legislation that accords personality to
nature provide by way of a precedent for Earth laws in other countries?
Consider this commentary on the laws examined in this chapter:
These examples provide an excellent illustration of the interconnection
between environment and human rights. Upholding Māori Indigenous rights
to land, resources and culture has resulted in a new way to not only protect
the environment but to reconceive our relationship with the environment,
upholding human rights better in the process, as a virtuous circle. In respect
of the legal personhood model in particular, the granting of legal personhood
to a geographical feature represents a momentous shift from an external
ownership model, which prioritises the uses that humans derive from a
resource, to an Indigenous self-ownership model, which requires no human
justification for environmental protection. While intimately connected with
human rights, this is a very different vision of legal subjects and objects, and
of rights and duties, from that which human rights law traditionally upholds.
The notion of responsibility in these examples is used in contrast to the
notion of rights, and these examples adopt a communal focus, rejecting
individualistic notions of rights.62
