CHAPTER 23
The Netherlands and the Future of 
Atmospheric Trust Litigation1
I. INTRODUCTION
This chapter examines the Dutch Supreme Court’s 2019 decision in The State
of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation (Urgenda), the world’s first case
in which citizens successfully established their government’s legal duty to
address climate change. The Court ordered the Dutch government to slash
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to 25 percent below 1990 levels by the end
of 2020 in enforcement of the European Convention on Human Rights and
other legal standards. This case provides a model for other courts to make
similar landmark climate change decisions worldwide.
Section II examines the European Union’s (EU) environmental regulatory
framework, which sets GHG emission commitments; the fundamental rights
set out in the ECHR; and EU law impediments to developing Earth law,
which the Dutch Court’s decision circumvented.
Section III explains the elements of the Constitution of the Netherlands and
the Dutch legal system that are critical to the Supreme Court’s reasoning in
the Urgenda case.
Section IV compares and contrasts Urgenda with a U.S. climate change case:
Juliana v. United States. Urgenda serves as a counterweight to the Juliana
case, which the Ninth Circuit Court dismissed for lack of standing (see

Chapter 7, “Public Trust Doctrine”). This section also highlights
“atmospheric trust litigation” more broadly.
II. THE EUROPEAN CONVENTION ON HUMAN
RIGHTS
EU environmental and human rights obligations are based on a series of
legally binding treaties. Examples are the Treaty on the European Union, the
Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and the Charter of
Fundamental Rights of the European Union. In addition to the foundational
treaties of the EU, which set out the constitutional rights and duties of its
member states, there are other treaties that focus on specific areas, such as
human rights, labor markets, the economy, and environmental protection.
The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR or Convention) is one
such treaty. It legally binds the 47 members of the Council of Europe, an
international organization with the mission to uphold human rights and the
rule of law. Of the Council’s 47 members, 27 are members of the EU. The
idea for the ECHR was shaped in 1948 during the “Congress of Europe,” a
gathering in the Hague where politicians, civil society, and representatives of
trade unions, universities, and other institutions worked together to propose a
list of basic human rights.2 A number of articles were directly based on the
United Nations’ Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The European Court of Human Rights (European Court) oversees
enforcement of the provisions of the ECHR.3 The European Court was set up
in 1959 in Strasbourg and issues judgments that are legally binding on
member states.4
Domestic courts of ECHR member states also have an obligation to apply the
convention. This is because the ECHR is incorporated into the legislation of
all member states and is therefore directly applicable at a national level. This
becomes important in the Urgenda case.
There are two types of applications that can be brought to the European
Court: (1) individual applications lodged by any person, group of persons, or

non-governmental organization (NGO); and (2) inter-state applications where
one state brings a claim against another. The cases can only be brought
against a state that has ratified the ECHR, and thus agreed to honor
judgments made by the court. The execution of judgments is monitored by
the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe.
The admissibility criteria for complaints before the European Court are
defined in Articles 34 and 35 of the ECHR. Under Article 34, the applicant
must be a person, NGO, or group of individuals claiming to be a “victim” of
a violation of rights established in the ECHR. (The meaning of “victim”
becomes relevant in the district court opinion of Urgenda.) Under Article 35,
all domestic remedies must have been exhausted, the contested domestic
court decision must have been made within the previous six months, and the
applicant must have suffered a “significant disadvantage,” amongst other
requirements.5
In practice, enforcement of European Court decisions has been problematic.
If the European Court finds that a right has been breached, it simply declares
that a violation has occurred and oftentimes allows the country to determine
its own plan for compliance. Sometimes the European Court does prescribe a
remedy, such as ending the violation in question, making payment, or
amending laws.6 But overall, enforcement has been lacking. For example, a
2017 review found that 9,944 judgments by the European Court had not been
implemented by the respective states.7 Part of the problem is that European
Court decisions do not force states to enact new or amend existing legislation.
This is different from the Court of Justice of the European Union, for
example, the judgments of which effectively override national law. There is
no such relationship between the European Court and the EU: the Council of
Europe is a separate organization of European nations unrelated to the EU.
The general rule is for national courts to follow the European Court’s
decisions, but there are no practical means to force recalcitrant states to
implement them.8
An aspect of the European Court that sets it apart from other human rights
courts is that there is a follow-up system in the form of the Committee of
Ministers. The challenge with the committee itself, however, is the fact that it
is made up of high-level officials representing member states, and

relationships between countries influence how committee members follow up
on the enforcement of judgments.
There are 18 human rights set out in the ECHR, commonly known as the
“Convention Rights.” The articles most relevant to the Urgenda case are
Articles 2 and 8. Article 2 concerns the right to life and states the following:
1. Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law. No one shall be
deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of a sentence of a
court following his conviction of a crime for which this penalty is
provided by law.
2. Deprivation of life shall not be regarded as inflicted in contravention of
this Article when it results from the use of force which is no more than
absolutely necessary:
(a) in defence of any person from unlawful violence;
(b) in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape of a person
lawfully detained;
(c) in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or
insurrection.9
Article 8 establishes the right to privacy and family life and reads as follows:
1. Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his
home and his correspondence.
2. There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of
this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary
in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety
or the economic well-being of the country, for the prevention of disorder
or crime, for the protection of health or morals, or for the protection of
the rights and freedoms of others.10
Articles 2 and 8 have been interpreted to protect against environmental harms
that affect rights to life, home, and private life where such harms are caused
by a state action or the state’s failure to properly regulate private-sector
activities. These articles also impose a positive obligation upon states to take

the necessary precautionary measures to prevent future rights violations,
especially when there is a known and imminent threat.11 As reflected in the
examination of the Urgenda case, the Dutch Supreme Court ruled that these
articles require member states to take reasonable and sufficient steps to
protect residents from the life-threatening consequences of climate change.
III. THE URGENDA CASE
This section begins by taking a closer look at the Dutch legal system. It then
explores the merits of the Urgenda case at the Hague District Court, the
Hague Court of Appeal, and the Dutch Supreme Court.
A. Background on Dutch Legal System
The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy with a civil law legal system.
The foundation of its national law is the Dutch Civil Code (DCC), which
addresses most subjects of Dutch law. All other legislation is based on the
principles set out in the DCC. Dutch judges have a high degree of discretion
in interpreting these provisions, even when the text of a provision seems
clear. An underlying principle of this discretion is the notion in the Dutch
legal system of “reasonableness and fairness,” which refers to a generally
accepted standard of what is reasonable and fair in a given situation. In other
words, if a party knew or should have known a certain fact, this principle
requires them to act accordingly, with consideration of the societal and
personal interests. This also means that regulations and binding legal
instruments in general may not have a legal effect if, as written or as applied,
they are deemed not to be objectively fair.12
The Dutch legal system has three types of courts. First, there are the district
courts (Rechtbank), of which there are 19 and which are divided into five
areas based on different sectors; these include the civil, administrative, and
criminal sectors. Second, five courts of appeal (Gerechtshof) hear both civil
and criminal cases where an appeal has been lodged against a judgment by a
district court. Finally, the Supreme Court (Hoge Raad) is the highest court in
the Netherlands and hears cases in civil, criminal, and tax matters in
cassation, which means that the Supreme Court is required by law to base its

holdings on the facts as established by the lower courts.13 In Urgenda, the
case moved from the Hague District Court to the Hague Court of Appeal to
the Supreme Court, with the Dutch government appealing each time. As
described in the next section, ultimately these appeals were unsuccessful.
Also, the Dutch judicial branch has an independent advisor who is part of the
judicial branch, called the procurator general. Along with the advocates
general, the role of procurator general is to provide the Supreme Court with
independent advice through advisory opinions. In civil cases such as
Urgenda, provision of this advisory opinion is mandatory but the Dutch
Supreme Court is not required to follow it. Such advisory opinions review the
relevant facts, legal questions, scholarly opinions, case law, as well as the
decision of the lower court that is being appealed.
B. Urgenda: Procedural History and Ruling
The Urgenda case was brought as a collective action. Dutch collective
actions to protect a public interest can be initiated pursuant to Article 3:305a
of the Dutch Civil Code. This provision allows a representative entity to
initiate a collective action in a civil court based on the interests of natural
persons, so long as those interests are the same as the entity’s. The entity
must be an association or foundation, and its articles of association and by-
laws need to state that the aim of the entity is to represent a specified group of
persons.
In the Urgenda case, the specified group of persons was extremely broad,
with the Urgenda Foundation representing over 800 individuals. Urgenda
also asserted its representation of future generations, both within and outside
the Netherlands, of people impacted by climate change. Urgenda’s articles of
association met the threshold requirement to represent future generations in a
collective action by explicitly recognizing that the Foundation’s purpose is to
“preserve the planet as a sustainable place for future generations to live.”
Additionally, a 2001 decision by the District Court of the Hague held that
Article 3:305a of the DCC can serve as legal basis for actions brought on
behalf of future generations.14 However, the courts never addressed this issue
in Urgenda and found the standing of Urgenda and its living Dutch co-
plaintiffs to be sufficient.15

C. Background and Overview of the Holding
The Urgenda case emerged from a dispute about Dutch obligations to reduce
GHGs. Although the Dutch government and Urgenda agreed about the need
to reduce GHG emissions, they differed about the exact reduction target.
Urgenda believed it must be a 25 percent reduction compared to 1990 levels,
whereas the Dutch government had targeted a 20 percent reduction. While the
difference may seem small, the importance of the case is that the lawsuit
sought to enforce science-based climate-change targets established by
international consensus, regardless of how close the government was to
meeting these targets.
Prior to the historic Supreme Court decision, the District Court of the Hague
and the Hague Court of Appeal both ruled in favor of Urgenda. The two
courts used different legal reasoning. These cases are discussed below in
sequence.
1. District Court of the Hague (2015)
The first ruling, from the District Court of the Hague in 2015, found that the
Dutch government breached its duty of care to its citizens under tort law by
failing to adopt a 25 percent reduction criterion.16 Dutch tort law establishes a
duty of care that is similar to the “reasonable person” standard in U.S. tort
law. The district court constructed the standard of care on the basis of
international, European, and constitutional duties to which the Dutch
government was committed—including Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR, which
uphold the right to life, and to respect privacy and family life, respectively;
the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change; and Article
21 of the Dutch Constitution, which establishes the fundamental right to a
clean environment. The district court further substantiated the breach of this
duty of care based upon a review of Dutch climate change policy, which it
deemed to be inadequate. The district court concluded that the Dutch
government acted unlawfully by establishing a GHG reduction target that
was less than 25 percent by 2020 compared to the year 1990.
One necessary element to establish a breach of the duty of care under tort law
is a causal link between the challenged act or omission, and the damage

suffered by the plaintiff. When it comes to climate change, this can be
difficult to prove because one country’s reduction in emissions is unlikely to
prevent climate change by itself. Consider how the district court addressed
this issue:
From the above considerations, particularly in 4.79, it follows that a
sufficient causal link can be assumed to exist between the Dutch greenhouse
gas emissions, global climate change and the effects (now and in the future)
on the Dutch living climate. The fact that the current Dutch greenhouse gas
emissions are limited on a global scale does not alter the fact that these
emission [sic] contribute to climate change. The court has taken into
consideration in this respect as well that the Dutch greenhouse emissions
have contributed to climate change and by their nature will also continue to
contribute to climate change.17
Despite ruling in Urgenda’s favor, the district court found that Urgenda could
not base its claims on Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR directly—only indirectly
through tort law—since a nonhuman organization cannot be a “victim” per
the meaning of Article 34 of the ECHR: “After all, unlike with a natural
person, a legal person’s physical integrity cannot be violated nor can a legal
person’s privacy be interfered with.”18 While non-governmental
organizations are explicitly recognized as possible “victims” under Article
34, the district court rejected the notion that they can be victims of
specifically physical harms. The district court also declined to explicitly rule
that the Dutch government had breached international treaty obligations (such
as under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change) or
the Dutch Constitution. Instead, it relied upon these sources of law to
interpret the duty of care under tort law. The Netherlands appealed.
2. Hague Court of Appeal (2018)
The second ruling, from the Hague Court of Appeal in 2018, upheld the
district court ruling.19 However, unlike the Hague District Court, the Hague
Court of Appeal found that Urgenda, along with the many humans it
represents, could directly enforce the ECHR without having to rely upon tort
law. The court reasoned that the limitations of a “victim” under Article 34 of
the ECHR only applies to admissibility to the European Court, not to Dutch

courts. By contrast, Dutch law—specifically, Article 3:305a of the DCC—
provides for class actions of interest groups such as this one. The court
explained that individuals who fall under Dutch jurisdiction may invoke
Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR directly. The court then laid out the basic
obligations of the Dutch government:
In short, the State has a positive obligation to protect the lives of citizens
within its jurisdiction under Article 2 ECHR, while Article 8 ECHR creates
the obligation to protect the right to home and private life. This obligation
applies to all activities, public and non-public, which could endanger the
rights protected in these articles, and certainly in the face of industrial
activities which by their very nature are dangerous. If the government knows
that there is a real and imminent threat, the State must take precautionary
measures to prevent infringement as far as possible. In light of this, the Court
shall assess the asserted (imminent) climate dangers.20
The court then explored the science-based threats of climate change, the
international obligations of the Netherlands, and the impact on human rights
as derived from Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR. Ultimately, the court
concluded as follows:
[T]he State has done too little to prevent a dangerous climate change and is
doing too little to catch up, or at least in the short term (up to end-2020).
Targets for 2030 and beyond do not take away from the fact that a dangerous
situation is imminent, which requires interventions being taken now.…
[T]he Court is of the opinion that the State fails to fulfil its duty of care
pursuant to Articles 2 and 8 ECHR by not wanting to reduce emissions by at
least 25 percent by end-2020.…
All of the above leads to the conclusion that the State is acting unlawfully
(because in contravention of the duty of care under Articles 2 and 8 ECHR)
by failing to pursue a more ambitious reduction as of end-2020, and that the
State should reduce emissions by at least 25 percent by end-2020. The State’s
grounds of appeal pertaining to the district court’s opinion about the
hazardous negligence doctrine [i.e., the tort claim] need no discussion under
these state of affairs. The judgment is hereby upheld.21

The Netherlands again appealed.
3. Procurator General advisory opinion (2019)
Next, on September 13, 2019, the Procurator General of the Supreme Court
(joined by the advocate general) released a formal advisory opinion
supporting the ruling of the court of appeal.22 It agreed that human rights law
can be used to interpret the government’s duty of care with respect to climate
change. The advisory opinion also rejected the defenses of the Netherlands,
including that climate change policy is a political issue that should be left to
the legislative branch so as to not interfere with the separation of powers
between branches of government. The Procurator General concluded as
follows:
The jurisdiction of the civil courts, under Dutch law, is independent from the
question of whether the claim raises a political issue.…If the claimant bases
its claim on a violation or impending violation of a right to which it is entitled
or on an unlawful act committed against it, the civil courts do, in principle,
have jurisdiction to take cognizance of that claim and render a substantive
opinion on it. This also applies when the claim is directed against the State.
As discussed above, the Procurator General’s advisory opinion is not binding
but is considered by the Supreme Court.
4. Dutch Supreme Court (2019)
Finally, in December 2019, the Supreme Court upheld the ruling of the Court
of Appeal. As with the Court of Appeal, its reasoning derived from Dutch
human rights obligations.23 The Supreme Court agreed that “there is the
threat of dangerous climate change and it is clear that measures are urgently
needed.”24 Under Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR, the Netherlands has a duty
to protect the right to life and the right to private and family life of its
residents. In its ruling, the Court also referred to the 2007 IPCC report, which
found that a reduction in emissions of 25 to 40 percent by 2020 would be
necessary to limit global warming to a 2ºC increase, and held that the Dutch
government had provided insufficient reasons for adhering to a lesser 20

percent reduction.25 The Supreme Court concluded as follows:
This case involves an exceptional situation. After all, there is the threat of
dangerous climate change and it is clear that measures are urgently needed, as
the District Court and Court of Appeal have established and the State
acknowledges as well. The State is obliged to do ‘its part’ in this context.
Towards the residents of the Netherlands, whose interests Urgenda is
defending in this case, that duty follows from Articles 2 and 8 ECHR, on the
basis of which the State is obliged to protect the right to life and the right to
private and family life of its residents. The fact that Annex I countries,
including the Netherlands, will need to reduce their emissions by at least 25
percent by 2020 follows from the view generally held in climate science and
in the international community, which view has been established by the
District Court and the Court of Appeal. The policy that the State pursues
since 2011 and intends to pursue in the future, whereby measures are
postponed for a prolonged period of time, is clearly not in accordance with
this, as the Court of Appeal has established.26
In making its historic ruling, the Dutch Supreme Court—agreeing with the
Procurator General—rejected the Dutch government’s defense that a
sweeping climate change ruling would interfere with the separation of powers
by reshaping the legislative process, thereby blurring the lines between the
judicial and political spheres.27 In Urgenda, the core of the government’s
argument was that ruling in favor of the claimants would violate the
separation of powers by undermining the government’s authority in the
context of international politics and negotiation leverage.28 However, the
Supreme Court found the government’s argument flawed because it did not
distinguish the separation of powers doctrine from the system of political
checks and balances.29
The Supreme Court stated:
In the Dutch system of government, the decision-making on greenhouse gas
emissions belongs to the government and parliament. They have a large
degree of discretion to make the political considerations that are necessary in
this regard. It is up to the courts to decide whether, in taking their decisions,
the government and parliament have remained within the limits of the law by

which they are bound. Those limits ensue from the ECHR, among other
things. The Dutch Constitution requires the Dutch courts to apply the
provision of this convention, and they must do so in accordance with the
ECHR’s interpretation of these provisions. This mandate to the courts to offer
legal protection, even against the government, is an essential component of a
democratic state under the rule of law.30
In sum, the Supreme Court ruled that requiring the Dutch government to
protect its citizens from climate change does not infringe upon the separation
of powers since it is only prescribing the outcome, not the means by which
the government must achieve this outcome. While the Court determined that
the law required the cuts in GHG emissions, the Dutch government could
decide how to achieve them.
IV. COMPARING URGENDA TO JULIANA
This section considers the different results reached by the Dutch Supreme
Court and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in the United States in cases
seeking the same relief: compelling the government to protect the
fundamental rights of its citizens from the adverse consequences of climate
change. It focuses on the argument made in both cases that climate change
policy must be left to the political branches of government.
As discussed in Chapter 5, “Standing” and Chapter 8, “Rights of Future
Generations,” the Ninth Circuit dismissed Juliana—the “climate kids”
lawsuit—for lack of standing. Similar to Urgenda, the plaintiffs sued the
government for failing to address climate change, which they argued violated
their federal constitutional rights and the public trust doctrine. However, the
Ninth Circuit, in a 2-1 vote, found that the redress sought by the plaintiffs—a
court order requiring the government to create a plan to phase out fossil fuels
and draw down GHG emissions—would “require a host of complex policy
decisions entrusted, for better or worse, to the wisdom and discretion of the
executive and legislative branches.”31 Without redressability, a plaintiff in the
United States does not have Article III standing. The Court concluded that
“the plaintiffs’ case must be made to the political branches or to the electorate
at large.”32

In stark contrast, the Dutch Supreme Court found that the judiciary could
order the Dutch government to address climate change so long as the
legislative branch decided upon the means. The Court considered it an
inherently legal decision as to whether the plaintiff’s rights had been violated
even though the decision would have political consequences.33
The contrast between these two rulings underscores how a court’s
understanding of its own power within the scope of its government’s
separation of powers may determine the outcome. Additionally, the contrast
highlights the breadth of a court’s permissible interpretation of the political
question doctrine. Courts in the United States and elsewhere will continue to
be presented with claims seeking redress for the adverse consequences of
climate change. Whether climate change policy, a political question, can be
distinguished from the legal question of protecting constitutional rights, as
framed in Juliana, or the legal question of protecting human rights, as
delineated in Urgenda, may be a central issue for climate change litigation in
other countries. In the final consideration, the problem with a court that
recognizes a violation of constitutional or human rights but finds the violation
is not redressable is simply a lack of judicial will. As this coursebook has
previously expressed, in the words of United States Supreme Court Chief
Justice Marshall: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial
department to say what the law is.”34 And this includes the laws regarding
separation of powers and the role of the courts, whether expressed as an issue
of standing, redressability, justiciability, political question, or otherwise.
V. IMPACT OF THE URGENDA HOLDING FOR
CLIMATE LITIGATION
The Urgenda case was the first time a court imposed a duty on a national
government to lower its GHG emissions. David Boyd, the United Nations
Special Rapporteur on human rights and the environment, said the Urgenda
case was “the most important climate change court decision in the world so
far, confirming that human rights are jeopardized by the climate emergency
and that wealthy nations are legally obligated to achieve rapid and substantial
emission reductions.”35 What might this ruling mean for both the national
government of the Netherlands and the rest of the world?

The Dutch government, notwithstanding the fact that it disagreed with the
Supreme Court ruling, has actively pursued measures to reduce its GHG
emissions. One of the first steps the Dutch government took in response to
the Court’s order was the shutdown of most coal-fired power plants in the
Netherlands. The resulting energy loss will be replaced by natural gas-
powered plants that emit half the amount of carbon dioxide, a reduction of
about 9 million tons. In early 2020, it also passed an ambitious legislative act
laying out a carbon plan for 2030. Some of the measures: (1) the introduction
of a CO2 tax for large companies; (2) natural gas tax increase; (3) stimulation
of wind and solar energy projects; (4) zero-emission driving by 2050; (5)
sustainable and CO2-free buildings, and natural gas phased out in new
construction; (6) transition from gas to sustainable heat; and (7) investing
€330 million with the aim of further reducing CO2 emissions in the
agriculture sector through sustainable farming practices.36
Beyond the Netherlands, the Urgenda holding has promising international
implications. Courts in France, Canada, Norway, Pakistan, Ireland, Belgium,
Switzerland, New Zealand, and Colombia have all taken on similar cases that
were inspired by Urgenda.37 As importantly, the holding provides
encouragement for Earth law practitioners in all countries challenged by
inadequate action on climate change by the legislative or executive branches
of government. Meaningful change can take place when the judicial branch
responds to fundamental unfairness. The Urgenda decision also created an
important precedent for national judiciaries to compel adherence to
international climate change duties even if they are not perceived to be
directly binding upon a state. This was emphasized by the United Nations
High Commissioner for Human Rights, who published a release stating the
following:
The decision confirms that the Government of the Netherlands and, by
implication, other governments have binding legal obligations, based on
international human rights law. To undertake strong reductions in emissions
of greenhouse gases.…The recognition by the highest Dutch Court that the
Netherlands’ human rights obligations provide a legal basis to compel
stronger and more rapid action by the Government is vitally important. This
landmark ruling provides a clear path forward for concerned individuals in
Europe—and around the world—to undertake climate litigation in order to

protect human rights.…38
VI. ATMOSPHERIC TRUST LITIGATION
Atmospheric trust litigation is a relatively recent development in climate
justice exemplified by Juliana—a case where young plaintiffs sought to
compel the government to take action with respect to climate change by
means of the public trust doctrine. The basic idea is that the atmosphere is
held in trust by the government for the benefit of the public, and therefore the
government has a duty to protect the atmosphere. Urgenda, while it did not
rely explicitly upon the public trust doctrine, had many characteristics that are
common to atmospheric trust litigation cases.
The public trust doctrine itself originates from English common law and is an
example of an environmental rights-based approach where the government is
considered to be a steward of not only essential natural resources, but also of
the public’s right to protection of these resources.39 While the public trust
doctrine originally applied only to navigation, commerce, and fishing, its
scope was later extended to include the protection of groundwater, wetlands,
recreation, and wildlife, and, most recently, the protection of the
atmosphere.40
As demonstrated in both Juliana and Urgenda, the main goals of atmospheric
trust litigation include: (1) imposing a positive obligation on national
governments to protect the atmosphere; (2) promoting the rights of both
current and future generations; and (3) pursuing a more progressive role by
the judicial branch to address climate change. In both cases, plaintiffs argued
that the government has a duty to protect the public from the disastrous
consequences of climate change for both current and future generations.
Unfortunately, only Urgenda was successful.
There are, however, some challenges that come with atmospheric trust
litigation. First, some courts may be reluctant to rule that the atmosphere
should be categorized as a public trust resource since the public trust doctrine
has not historically been applied in that context. The second challenge is that
some courts, as illustrated by Juliana, may consider it too much of an
interference in the political decision-making process to issue an injunction

mandating certain GHG emission reductions.41
There are, however, indications that courts in many states are willing to
consider atmospheric trust cases and to establish rights to a stable climate
system for present and future generations. In the coming decades, court-
mandated GHG emissions will likely become increasingly crucial to the fight
against climate change.
VII. CONCLUSION
The Urgenda case demonstrates that there are creative ways for courts to
consolidate domestic and international laws. In the end, courts have the
responsibility to make sure that laws are executed faithfully, including those
laws concerning the future of a country and the planet as a whole. The Dutch
Court in Urgenda has led the way by exercising its authority to change the
environmental standards in the Netherlands in accordance with an
international treaty with which the government had failed to fully comply.
The Urgenda case shows that courts can help address climate change, in
accordance with domestic and international legal obligations, while still
avoiding political barriers. It did this by framing the holding as a legal
decision with political consequences, rather than a political decision made by
the judicial branch. This is an approach other courts can take where
legislative and executive branches of government fail to take the urgent
actions needed to respond to climate change to the detriment of the
fundamental rights of their present and future citizens and in disregard of
international conventions.
In countries where the use of a duty of care test is inapplicable or less likely
to succeed, as it did in Urgenda, each legal system will provide its own
opportunities for creative legal arguments for the right to a stable climate, a
healthy environment, and other ecocentrically focused rights for humans and
nature. The existential threat of climate change, in its global scale, severity,
and complexity, warrants something different from the precedent-based,
backward-looking systems of common law and civil codes developed in the
nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Remarkably, in 1803, Chief Justice John
Marshall wrote in Marbury v. Madison:

It is emphatically the duty of the Judicial Department to say what the law is.
Those who apply the rule to particular cases must, of necessity, expound and
interpret the rule.… It is scarcely necessary for the Court to disclaim all
pretensions to such a jurisdiction. An extravagance so absurd and excessive
could not have been entertained for a moment.… So, if a law be in opposition
to the Constitution, if both the law and the Constitution apply to a particular
case, so that the Court must either decide that case conformably to the law,
disregarding the Constitution, or conformably to the Constitution,
disregarding the law, the Court must determine which of these conflicting
rules governs the case. This is of the very essence of judicial duty.42
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) What factors will influence the extent to which the reasoning by the
Urgenda Court is relied upon by other courts to address the adverse
consequences of climate change? What might influence courts in the United
States to take such a bold approach? What will inhibit it?
(2) What are the advantages and disadvantages of “judicial activism”—the
notion that courts have a role to play in shaping issues of critical importance
to society? How could the Urgenda decision be criticized as inappropriate
judicial activism? How could it be characterized positively as an example of a
court interpreting both national and international laws to establish a new
precedent? How did the role of “reasonableness and fairness” in the Dutch
legal system affect the decision in Urgenta? How would you respond to the
argument that any case that makes new law is judicial activism?
(3) Do you think the Dutch Supreme Court was right to interpret national law
by reference to the ECHR provisions? Respond to the argument that a
national court should not rely on obligations a government owes to other
nations to find obligations owed by that government to its citizens?
(4) Consider further the differences in the constitutional structure of the legal
systems in the United States and the Netherlands. How did these differences
shape the contrasting holdings in Juliana and Urgenda? Were the different
results more a product of differences in the legal systems or in differing
interpretations of applicable law?
