2. On Indigenous cultural identity and traditional knowledge
In Decision T-477/2012, Colombia’s Constitutional Court addressed alleged
rights violations of Indigenous cultural identity arising from the abusive use
of Indigenous biological heritage, particularly the unauthorized use of sacred
signs and symbols that allude to the sacred coca leaf. In its decision, the
Constitutional Court continued to build important jurisprudence about
traditional knowledge and its connections with cultural identity as a
fundamental right of Indigenous groups. This decision refers to the notion of
“intangible knowledge”—traditional knowledge that may be abstract or
intangible and is exclusively held by Indigenous communities—and the
relationship between knowledge and life. The ruling also addresses the fair
distribution of benefits derived from the commercial use of genetic resources
and associated traditional knowledge. Consider the following excerpt:
Traditional knowledge is part of the cultural identity of ethnic communities,
and it is the manifestation of an intangible cultural heritage as well.

Traditional knowledge must be protected as a way to promote the cultural
identity of a group, while avoiding the use and unduly appropriation of
traditional knowledge by third parties.…Traditional knowledge reflects
indigenous communities’ relationships with their land, their ancestors,
cosmogony, and history. Traditional knowledge is an intellectual activity
expressed in the social, cultural, environmental and political fields; it is the
product of many generations and their relationship with the world around
them, and as such, this knowledge is consistent and valid. Various
international norms…have recognized the need to protect the traditional
knowledge of ethnic communities.…
[T]he Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio de Janeiro, 1992)…
established, among other obligations, that States must: a) respect, preserve
and maintain traditional knowledge for the conservation and sustainable use
of biological diversity; b) promote its application “with the approval and
participation of those who possess that knowledge;” and c) encourage the
benefits derived from that knowledge to be shared equally. In its turn,
Andean Decision 391/1996 which established the “Common Regime on
Access to Genetic Resources” recognizes the existence of traditional
knowledge and the power of communities to make decisions about this
knowledge. In the same vein, Statute 191/1995, “Through which provisions
on Border Zones are dictated” establishes in article 8 the need to obtain prior
and informed consent from indigenous communities when accessing
traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, as well as the duty
to share fairly the benefits with indigenous peoples. Traditional knowledge is
part of the fundamental right to a cultural identity of the indigenous
community and therefore must be protected against any type of violation.36
In its ruling, the Constitutional Court also considered the use of Indigenous
signs and symbols by others for products, finding as follows:
The relationship between trademark law and the right of indigenous
communities to cultural identity and the protection of their traditional
knowledge only finds its expression in paragraph g) of article 136 of Andean
Decision 486 (2000), which states that [people] cannot register as trademarks
those signs whose use in trade unduly affects the right of a third party, in
particular when [those signs] consist of the name of indigenous, Afro-

American, or local communities, or of such denominations, words, letters,
characters, or signs as are used to distinguish their products, services or
methods of processing, or that constitute an expression of their culture or
practice, unless the application is filed by the community itself or with its
express consent. With the registration of a brand, it is intended to grant
distinctiveness for the commercialization of a product and said
distinctiveness also implies refraining from using generic or descriptive
expressions, promoting acts of fair competition and not misleading the
consumer, much less affecting the rights of third parties, such as that of
indigenous communities through the use of expressions or denominations
closely linked to their cultural identity, which consist of the name of the
communities, or the denominations, words, letters or signs used to distinguish
their products.37
As an extension of the theory of cultural appropriation, the Constitutional
Court prohibited the use of an Indigenous sign on a coca-based product. In so
doing, the court granted fundamental protection against economic abuse of
Indigenous signs considered both as traditional knowledge and Indigenous
cultural identity.
STUDY QUESTION
Article 136 of Andean Decision 486/2000 states that a person cannot register
as trademarks those signs whose use in trade unduly affects the right of a
third party, in particular when the use consists “of the name of indigenous,
Afro-American, or local communities…unless the application is filed by the
community itself or with its express consent.” (Emphasis added.) A
pharmaceutical company obtains the consent of members of an Amazonian
community to use the name of this community on the label of a new product.
However, several members of the community disagree with this. Can this
consent be considered sufficient and/or legitimate for the purposes of using
the Indigenous name on the product’s label?
3. On traditional knowledge and traditional Indigenous law
Decision SU-510/1998 of the Constitutional Court addresses the right of

traditional authorities of the Ika people to uphold their cultural identity and
integrity within their territory by prohibiting some activities of Christians in
the community who challenged the material culture of the Ika. In its ruling
affirming the rights of the Iku, the Constitutional Court wrote about the
relationship between Indigenous law, cosmology, and material culture. When
reading the following excerpt, consider the sources of Indigenous legalities
that we have been previously discussed.
For the Ika [an indigenous group from Northern Colombia], weaving is an
activity that transcends the mere manufacture of cotton fabrics for the
production of clothing. Thus, this is an activity of a profoundly moral nature
with profound metaphysical consequences. The Ika consider that weaving a
fabric is actually weaving “the fabric of one’s life.” The resulting fabric or
tapestry represents a metaphorical activity where the cotton threads are
considered thoughts. These thoughts slowly organize and intertwine the
network of social relations where the weaver is also inserted. For the Ika,
“weaving is thinking” and “thinking is living.” This explains why “the person
who does not think, does not live.” Through weaving, thoughts are organized
and embedded within a universal order. By weaving and thinking a balance
between the opposites is achieved thus fulfilling the “Mother’s Law.”38
A headnote explaining the decision states:
The Court has indicated that the limitations to which the principles of ethnic
and cultural diversity and autonomy of indigenous communities are subject
arise from the constitutional text itself, which determines, on the one hand,
that Colombia is a unitary State with autonomy from its territorial entities
and, on the other hand, that the political and legal autonomy of indigenous
communities, that is, the ability to govern themselves and exercise
jurisdictional functions within their territorial scope, can be exercised
according to their uses and customs, as long as they are not contrary to the
Constitution and the law. The foregoing determines that, in matters of
indigenous communities, the Political Charter establishes a regime for the
conservation of diversity in unity. According to the Court, “only with a high
degree of autonomy is cultural survival possible,” a statement that means
ethnic and cultural diversity, as a general principle, can only be limited when
its exercise ignores constitutional or legal norms of greater importance.

According to jurisprudence, in principle, the effectiveness of the rights of
indigenous peoples, determines that the limits that may be imposed on the
normative and jurisdictional autonomy of such communities are only those
that are referred “to what is truly intolerable because it attacks what is most
precious to humanity.”
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) According to this constitutional decision, “fabric” and “thought” are
expressions of the same action for the Iku community. Therefore, thinking is
weaving, and weaving is thinking. What does Indigenous material culture
have to do with the law?
(2) The materials for weaving come from nature, and the end product, a piece
of clothing, is the representation of human thought. Insofar as the notion of
traditional knowledge includes tangible and non-tangible elements, how does
this idea transform our established concepts about the nature of legal meaning
and practice? Is the law strictly reducible to the symbolic, that is, to language,
i.e., what the law says on its face?

4. On informed consent by Indigenous communities and territorial and
communal governance
Decision SU-039/9739 of the Colombian Constitutional Court is a
paradigmatic case on prior consultation with Indigenous communities. This
piece of jurisprudence examined the scope of Indigenous peoples’ right to
participation in projects that affect their traditional lands. The Office of the
United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights summarized this case
as follows:
This case was taken to the Constitutional Court of Colombia by the
Ombudsman on behalf of the U’wa people and against the Ministry of
Environment and the private oil company Sociedad Occidental de Colombia,
Inc. The case dealt with the right of indigenous peoples to participate
through consultations in decisions that may affect them, in particular related

to defense and preservation of indigenous land.…The legal question
examined the scope of the right to participation of indigenous peoples in
projects that affect their land. The Court considered Constitutional rights
related to protection of ethnic integrity (Articles 7, 10 and 70) as well as the
right to self-determination (Article 330) and the right to participation (Article
40).…
The Constitutional Court found that the process used to secure an
environmental license for oil exploration had not been adequate as it had
ignored the U’wa community’s fundamental right to be formally and
substantially consulted. This decision was grounded on the principle that
participation through consultation is a fundamental right because it is an
essential way to preserve the ethnic, social, economic and cultural integrity of
indigenous communities, which was necessary for their survival as a social
group.40
Similarly, in T-993/2012, which also addressed the fundamental right to prior
consultation of Indigenous communities and ethnic groups, the Constitutional
Court of Colombia said:
For the Court, the right of indigenous peoples to have their own social,
economic and cultural life, and to profess their own religion and practice their
own language (article 27 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political
Rights) is closely linked to the right to have their own territory…[T]he
indigenous territory and resources, traditions, and knowledge systems
together constitute a legacy that unites—as a whole—the present generation
and the generations to follow.41
In its ruling, the Court highlighted the holistic nature of Indigenous
worldviews as a cornerstone of the right to participation through prior
consultation. Prior consultation is an expression of the principle of self-
determination, which includes the power of self-government and the ability to
guide behavior in accordance with a local system of norms, protocols, and
procedures—which brings us to Indigenous law and governance systems. On
this topic, the Court said:
The right to the protection of ethnic cultural identity has been analyzed by
this Body [the Court] from two different perspectives: a negative

perspective…[referring to] how preventing public manifestations of religious
practices outside of [indigenous] traditions is a way to avoid the
disappearance of [a particular] culture; and a positive perspective expressed
in the reproduction of [indigenous] cultural identity through ethno-education
and other processes. In addition, based on the principle of self-determination.
…the Court has affirmed that ethnic communities have the power to
determine their own institutions and government authorities; to determine
and maintain their norms, customs, worldviews, development options, and
life projects, and to adopt those internal or local decisions that they deem
most appropriate for the conservation, or protection of these purposes.
As a manifestation of this principle, national and international law has
established the obligation to carry out a prior consultation with these
communities before adopting legal or administrative measures that may
affect them directly.…[The Court has protected the right to prior consultation
in cases of] environmental licenses, construction contracts linked to
development projects that directly affect ethnic communities, as well as
decisions that allow the exploitation of resources within indigenous
territories, …and issues related to ethnoeducation. It is thus a right in
continuous construction whose protection depends on the impact that can be
demonstrated in each specific case.42
STUDY QUESTION
Based on the constitutional principle of self-determination, Indigenous
communities have the power to dictate their own systems of laws, justice, and
government. Do you think that the recognition of Indigenous governance
systems based on a relational worldview could transform state notions of
participation and consultation?
B. Inter-American Commission on Human Rights
1. On ancestral land, communal tenure, and Indigenous property rights
The collective tenure of land is a key component of Indigenous worldviews
and ways of being. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights

(IACHR), a body created by the Organization of American States (OAS) that
aims to promote and protect rights in the Americas, has referred to this issue
in several cases. For the Commission, the communal property right to the
lands that Indigenous peoples have traditionally used and occupied is a
function of their customary patterns of land use and tenure. In addition, the
Commission refers to the state’s duty to take effective measures to recognize
Indigenous peoples’ communal property right to the lands that they have
traditionally occupied and used and to delimit, demarcate, and title the
territory on which their right exists.
In Maya Indigenous Community of the Toledo District v. Belize, Maya
Indigenous communities argued that the State of Belize violated their rights
over land traditionally used and occupied by the Maya people by granting
logging and oil concessions and otherwise failing to protect those lands,
amongst other claims. The IACHR ruled in favor of the Maya people:
95. [A] review of pertinent treaties, legislation and jurisprudence reveals the
development over more than 80 years of particular human rights norms and
principles applicable to the circumstances and treatment of indigenous
peoples. Central to these norms and principles has been the recognition of the
need for special measures by states to compensate for the exploitation and
discrimination to which these societies have been subjected at the hands of
the non-indigenous.…
98. In deciding upon the complaints in the present petition, therefore, the
Commission will afford due consideration to the particular norms and
principles of international human rights law governing the individual and
collective interests of indigenous peoples, including consideration of any
special measures that may be appropriate and necessary in giving proper
effect to these rights and interests.…
151. In summary, based upon the foregoing analysis, the Commission
concludes that the Maya people of southern Belize have a communal property
right to the lands that they have traditionally used and occupied, and that the
character of these rights is a function of Maya customary land use patterns
and tenure. The Commission also considers that this right is embraced and
affirmed by Article XXIII of the American Declaration.

152. The Commission further concludes that the State has violated the right
to property enshrined in Article XXIII of the American Declaration to the
detriment of the Maya people, by failing to take effective measures to
recognize their communal property right to the lands that they have
traditionally occupied and used, and to delimit, demarcate and title or
otherwise establish the legal mechanisms necessary to clarify and protect the
territory on which their right exists.
153. In addition, the Commission concludes that the State, by granting
logging and oil concessions to third parties to utilize the property and
resources that could fall within the lands which must be delimited,
demarcated and titled or otherwise clarified or protected, without effective
consultations with and the informed consent of the Maya people and with
resulting environmental damage, further violated the right to property
enshrined in Article XXIII of the American Declaration to the detriment of
the Maya people.
154. Finally, the Commission notes the Petitioners’ contention that the failure
of the State to engage in meaningful consultation with the Maya people in
connection with the logging and oil concessions in the Toledo District, and
the negative environmental effects arising from those concessions, constitute
violations of several other rights under international human rights law,
including the right to life under Article I of the American Declaration, the
right to religious freedom and worship under Article III of the American
Declaration, the right to a family and to protection thereof under Article VI of
the American Declaration, the right to preservation of health and well-being
under Article XI of the American Declaration, and the “right to consultation”
implicit in Article 27 of the ICCPR, Article XX of the American Declaration,
and the principle of self-determination.
155. In its analysis of this case, the Commission has emphasized the distinct
nature of the right to property as it applies to indigenous peoples, whereby
the land traditionally used and occupied by these communities plays a central
role in their physical, cultural and spiritual vitality. As the Commission has
previously recognized with respect of the right to property and the right to
equality, “[f]or indigenous people, the free exercise of such rights is essential
to the enjoyment and perpetuation of their culture.” Similarly, the concept of

family and religion within the context of indigenous communities, including
the Maya people, is intimately connected with their traditional land, where
ancestral burial grounds, places of religious significance and kinship patterns
are linked with the occupation and use of their physical territories. Further,
the Commission has specifically concluded in its analysis of this case that the
duty to consult is a fundamental component of the State’s obligations in
giving effect to the communal property right of the Maya people in the lands
that they have traditionally used and occupied.43
2. On the obligation to consult
In Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku v. Ecuador, the IACHR
considered the granting of a permit by the government to a private oil
company in the ancestral territory of the Kichwa (alternatively, Quechua, or
Quichua) people. The permit allowed oil exploration and exploitation and
was issued without consultation with the Kichwa people. As with the Maya
case, the IACHR ruled in favor of the Indigenous Kichwa people:
Para. 149. In this case, the Court finds that there is no doubt regarding the
Sarayaku Peoples’ communal ownership of their territory, which is exercised
in a time-honoured and ancestral manner. This was expressly recognized by
the State through the adjudication made on May 12, 1992. Notwithstanding
the foregoing, in addition to the points noted in the section on the facts of the
case, the Court considers it pertinent to emphasize the deep cultural, non-
pecuniary and spiritual ties that the community has with its territory, so as to
fully understand the damages caused in this case.…
Para. 160. It is for all the aforementioned reasons that one of the fundamental
guarantees for ensuring the participation of indigenous peoples and
communities in decisions regarding measures that affect their rights and, in
particular, their right to communal property, is precisely the recognition of
their right to consultation, which is recognized in the ILO Convention No.
169, among other complementary international instruments.…
Para. 166. The obligation to consult indigenous and Tribal Communities and
Peoples on any administrative or legal measure that may affect their rights, as
recognized under domestic and international law, as well as the obligation to

guarantee the rights of indigenous peoples to participate in decisions on
matters that concern their interests, is directly related to the general obligation
to guarantee the free and full exercise of the rights recognized in the
Convention (Article 1(1). This implies the duty to adequately organize the
entire governmental apparatus and, in general, all the organizations through
which public power is exercised, so that these are capable of legally
guaranteeing the free and full exercise of those rights. The foregoing means
that States have the obligation to structure their standards and institutions in
such a way that indigenous, native or tribal communities can be consulted
effectively, in accordance with international standards in this matter. Thus,
States must incorporate those standards within the prior consultation
processes, so as to generate sustained, effective and reliable channels for
dialogue with indigenous communities in processes of consultation and
participation through their representative institutions.…
Para. 177. The Court has established that in order to ensure effective
participation by members of an indigenous community or people in
development or investment plans within their territory, the State has the duty
to consult the community in an active and informed manner, and in
accordance with its customs and traditions, in the context of a continuous
communication between the parties.
Moreover, these consultations should be undertaken in good faith, through
culturally appropriate procedures and must be aimed at reaching an
agreement. Similarly, the indigenous people or community must be consulted
in accordance with its own traditions, during the early stages of the
development or investment plan, and not only when it is necessary to obtain
the community’s approval. Also, the State must ensure that members of the
community are aware of the potential benefits and risks so they can decide
whether or not to accept the proposed development or investment plan.
Finally, the consultation must take into account the traditional decision-
making practices of the people or community. Failure to comply with this
obligation, or engaging in consultations without regard to their essential
characteristics, compromises the State’s international responsibility.…
Para. 232. The State, by failing to consult the Sarayaku People on the
execution of a project that would directly affect their territory, was in breach

of its obligations, under the principles of international law and of its own
domestic law, to adopt all necessary measures to guarantee the participation
of the Sarayaku People, through their own institutions and mechanisms and
in accordance with their values, traditions, customs and forms of
organization, in the decisions made regarding matters and policies that
affected or could affect their territory, their cultural and social life, their
rights to communal property and to cultural identity. Consequently, the Court
considers that the State is responsible for the violation of the right to
communal property of the Sarayaku People, recognized in Article 21 of the
Convention, in relation to the right to cultural identity, under the terms of
Articles 1(1) and (2) thereof. 44
V. WUASIKAMAS, THE LAW OF THE
INDIGENOUS INGA OF APONTE IN
COLOMBIA
This final section studies some aspects of one particular Indigenous legal
system, the Wuasikamas of the Inga of Aponte, and how this system interacts
with state law.
A. Introduction to the Inga of Aponte
The Inga people are part of the living culture of the Great Inca nation. By
1450, the Inca administered the territory they called Tawaintinsuyu, which
included four regions—Chinchaysuyu (north), Antisuyu (east, the Amazon
jungle), Contisuyu (west), and Collasuyu (south). The regions of Caquetá,
Cauca, Putumayo, and Nariño of today’s southern Colombia together made
up what the Inca called Chinchaisuyu. In this territory of the Colombian
Amazon, the Inga co-exist with other ancestral peoples, specifically the
Cofán, Siona, Camentzá, Quillasinga, and Pasto. According to the Colombian
census of 2018, the total population of the Inga was 19,561.
The ancestral territory of the Inga is part of the Colombian massif (part of the
Andes mountains) eco-region in southwestern Colombia that covers an area
of 4.8 million hectares. The central and eastern Andean mountain ranges
originate here, and Andean, Amazonian, and Pacific ecosystems also

converge. In addition, the five most important river tributaries in the country
have their sources in the massif: the Magdalena, Cauca, Putumayo, Caquetá,
and Patía rivers. The reservation is extraordinarily biodiverse, with more 471
species of birds, including parrots and the Andean condor, the spectacled
bear, the tapir, deer, and cougars. There are also 28 lakes in this territory, as
well as a great diversity of tree species.
B. Wuasikamas: Guardianship of the Territory
Both the Inga language and culture have their origins in the Inca civilization
that expanded through the Andean mountains in the current territories of
Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, Argentina, and Colombia between the
thirteenth and sixteenth centuries. The Wuasikamas oral code originated in
the department of Nariño, in the southwest of Colombia, and is maintained in
the language of the Inga community.
Based on the testament of the Taita de Taitas (“Father of Fathers”) Carlos
Tamabioy, the Inga community of Aponte venerates Earth as mother and
considers the rest of visible and invisible beings as part of a single family.
This testament was dated March 1700 and was duly notarized before the
Spanish Crown. Since 1750, the Inga community has continuously struggled
to defend its ancestral territory.
Wuasikamas means “guardianship of the territory.” This does not mean only
physical defense of the territory as the English translation may connote. It
means protection of and care for a way of being that is rooted in a particular
ecosystem composed of infinite relations of people, culture, other living
beings, and land. Consistent with the understanding that Indigenous legalities
come from the Creator as understood through stories of origin, Wuasikamas
begins with this story, which is in itself law.
Genesis of the Territorial Law of the Inga of Aponte
By the Inga People of Colombia
Compiled by Taita Hernando Chindoy
In the most painful moment of their history, the Spanish crown expropriated
the lands of the Inga of Tawaintinsuyu—the Chinchaisuyu region. In a night

of lightning, rain, and wind, Taita Intí [Father Sun] begat Carlos Tamabioy, a
distinguished chieftain and spiritual leader of the Inga. Tamabioy was born in
Aguaríco, a sacred place in the pan-Amazonian territory, and seven mothers,
before dying of hunger, had to breastfeed him. The child grew so fast and
strong that by noon he was already an adult. By the afternoon, he had already
toured the whole territory. At the end of the day, he gathered all the Inga and
Camenzá peoples and said: “This is my land that I leave for you, my children
and descendants, to take care of, protect, and benefit from as your own until
the end of time. Nothing and nobody shall interfere. You must live in unity
and not forget that you are never alone, for the rivers, forests, mountains, and
everything that exists is part of our family. They will be your protectors.”
When he finished, he left with the last light of the sun. Since then, and for
more than 300 years, all the Inga of today’s Colombia each year celebrate the
ritual of Atún Puncha—The Day of Forgiveness—a ceremony at the end of
the year and the beginning of a new one. This is how the Inga commemorate
the legacy and memory of Carlos Tamabioy, the Taita of Taitas [(Father of
Fathers)]. In this ceremony, people ask the Earth and the spiritual beings for
their forgiveness for all the damage humans have caused. And if there is
enmity between neighbors, the Atún Puncha is the moment to embrace each
other, to dance, and to enjoy chicha [(fermented beverage)] and food as a
sign of kinship. The Inga also pray as acknowledgement of being alive. If
somebody is no longer alive for the celebration, it means that their soul is
calm because they have done their best in life.
Wuasikamas is found in the Inga language as one of the most important
sources through which the ancestral knowledge of the community is
revitalized; this knowledge holds the keys to understanding the Andean and
Amazonian worlds, as expressed orally. Wuasikamas is recognized in daily
life as the existence of the infinite network of relationships between human
beings and nonhuman beings in their material and spiritual dimensions.
Speaking from a perspective of “bioculturality” and a “political ecology of
peace,” Wuasikamas expresses the vital energy of the conductive threads of
life and spirituality of the Inga people.
One of those principles of Wuasikamas is Suma Kausai, which, rooted in
origin and history, is the foundation of the relationship between the Earth and
the human. This relationship requires points or nodes of encounter and non-

separation to “guard the territory”—what the West calls “property.” For the
Inga, however, the territory is samai or a point of joyful resting for living
well. In other words, while the West defines property as an inert section of
land, the Inga describe samai as a meeting and resting place of connection for
the soul and the body which exists beyond this finite world to the infinite
path of human and nonhuman existence beyond Earth, time, and space.
The methodology for recognizing and studying Wuasikamas is the return to
ancestral knowledge from a decolonized perspective and through the people’s
own Inga language. This requires a journey of spiritual connection through
sacred plants such as ayahuasca and yagé. This connection allows the Inga to
understand and engage in dialogue with nonhuman beings throughout all
time.
The Wuasikamas oral code is in constant dialogue with the constitutional law
of the Colombian state, both of which need to be understood in order to
maintain Samai or intercultural peace. There are clashes between these two
kinds of law, and, strictly speaking, they do not complement each other but
support each other. Wuasikamas exists in its own path. It is not only of
human creation because there are other nonhuman forces involved. This
conceptualization has traditionally been beyond Western-normative
understanding. However, recent developments in human rights theories and
Earth rights movements are the meeting point for strengthening these new
dialogues.
C. Relationship with the State
Article 7 of the Colombian Constitution of 1991, as amended, provides: “The
State recognizes and protects the ethnic and cultural diversity of the
Colombian Nation.” Under Articles 171 and 176, Indigenous people form a
special constituency for the election of senators and representatives. Under
Article 246, they exercise jurisdictional functions within their territory in
accordance with their own rules and procedures, provided these are not
contrary to the constitution or laws. They are governed by Indigenous
councils according to their uses and customs in accordance with the
constitution and the law under Article 330. Under Articles 63 and 329, their
territories or reservations are collective property that may not be sold and are

of a non-disposable, inalienable, imprescriptible, and unattachable nature.
Under Article 13, paragraph 2, as groups that are discriminated against and
marginalized, they deserve greater protection.
Since 1970, the Inga territory has been affected by indiscriminate
deforestation and the presence of guerrilla groups, drug traffickers, and
paramilitaries. Since 1991 poppy crops (Papaver somniferum) have been
grown in the territory and eventually covered 2,500 hectares. From these
crops, two or three tons of morphine or heroin were extracted and distributed
weekly through international drug-trafficking networks. The indiscriminate
logging and soil depletion caused by these plantations was further aggravated
by the implementation of the Plan Colombia—a bilateral agreement between
the governments of Colombia and the United States in 1999 to combat the
guerrillas and drug trafficking in the country. This plan aimed to provide
social programs for farmers so that they would abandon illicit crops.
However, while attempting to protect farmers as the country’s internal armed
conflict intensified, the deadly herbicide glyphosate was sprayed on the illicit
poppy crops, which had negative health effects on the Indigenous and peasant
inhabitants of this area. Between 1986 and 2003, more than 150 people were
killed and more than 1,000 were forcibly displaced from their lands. The life
of the Inga people was being destroyed.
Courageous Inga women, facing the prospect of losing their children, led the
Inga community in discerning how they would live as a people. During an
intense community dialogue in 2003, the Inga rediscovered the traditional
Wuasikamas oral code in the ancestral knowledge of the elderly based on the
principles of nonviolence. Using this knowledge, the community developed a
strategy to eliminate economic dependence on drug production and to
confront the forces that were harming the community. This led to an
unprecedented process of institutional strengthening and cultural identity.
In 2003, the Inga of Aponte achieved collective ownership over their territory
through legal recognition of a reservation issued by the Colombian Institute
for Agrarian Reform-INCORA, currently known as the National Land
Agency-ANT. This title was created through Resolution 013 of July 22,
2003, which granted a collective title over 22,283 hectares, carefully
delineated, and with the special protection by the state. The reservation is

located in the municipalities of El Tablón de Gómez, Nariño, and Santa Rosa,
Cauca, between 1,500 and 3,800 meters above the sea level. According to the
2015 census, the population of the reservation is 3,651 Indigenous inhabitants
(951 families) and 620 non-Indigenous inhabitants (105 families).
In 2004, the Inga of Aponte agreed with the government of Colombia to
develop the National Family Rangers Program designed to respect cultural
and community values. A part of the program involved paying Indigenous
peoples and peasants to stop growing illicit crops. The Inga of Aponte, with
Wuasikamas, negotiated to receive the money through a communal fund
created by themselves that would allow them to support the entire community
and work together to strengthen their governance and free their territory from
the presence of guerrillas, paramilitaries, and drug traffickers, as well as the
army and the police. The payments were received from 2004 to 2006 and
were used to create the pillars for the social, economic, cultural, spiritual, and
environmental advancement of the Inga community. In 2007, the Inga
stopped receiving money from the government and began to strengthen
sustainable livelihoods, while being governed by the Wuasikamas oral code
as part of the Integral Mandate of Life for the Survival of the Inga People in
Aponte.
D. Intentions and Results of Wuasikamas
These are the intentions of Wuasikamas:
Thriving as community in the infinity of time and space, while
following the relational code between human and nonhuman beings.
Also, by remembering the origin of this code in the sacred and ancestral
territory of the central-eastern mountain range of the Andes. In this
territory, the Inga people thrive to keep their own rules and procedures
that have allowed them to survive as an autonomous community, with
their own territory, customs, and language, as well as the spiritual and
religious systems within the framework of principles that discourage
theft, lies, and laziness, and affirm living with dignity, in a state of well-
being, and in community with Mother Earth.
Contributing to the unity of the Inga people, which is rooted in self-
government, autonomy, legal standing, cosmology, and thinking that

stems from ancestral knowledge.
Decolonizing thinking under the principles of dignity, respect, and
biocultural peace.
Remembering is the thought and living memory of Taita of Taitas
Carlos Tamabioy, as well as other guardian ancestors that are present in
the wind, fire, water, earth, light, darkness, and peace.
In the midst of this long history of violence, and on the verge of physical and
cultural extermination, the Inga of Aponte’s re-encounter with Wuasikamas
and its emphasis on knowledge of the ways of living well (buen vivir), has
been the means to achieve peace and development. It is rooted in principles
that discourage theft, lying, and laziness, and affirm living a dignified life.
Following the way of Wuasikamas, the Inga people are recovering their
autonomy, sovereignty and spirituality, and the rights of Mother Earth. The
Inga have been in minga (days of collective reflection) to revitalize and
decolonize their governance systems. They adopted the Integral Mandate of
Life for the Survival and Permanence of the Inga People of Aponte, which is
the charter for the Inga of Aponte. Drawing on the political-administrative
mechanisms of the Major Cabildo and the Minor Cabildos (similar to
ministries) of health, education, communication, economy, public and
community services, justice, women and family, children and youth, and Inga
guardians, the Inga have established governing structures. The Inga High
Council of Justice investigates and cures all kinds of what the Inga
characterize as “diseases”—from the theft of a chicken to homicides, the
creation of armed groups, drug trafficking, and harm of Mother Earth. For the
Inga, there is no conception of “crime.” Human beings commit what are
called “crimes” because diseases have penetrated their bodies and taken over.
Treatment with medicinal plants, advice, and isolation are ways of dealing
with these diseases. In these ways, the Inga have brought into being and
maintained a system of social cohesion that has also allowed them to face
groups of guerrillas, paramilitaries, drug traffickers, state agencies, and
public forces, among other actors that threatened their community.
The Inga have taken to sharing the Wuasikamas process with other peoples of
the region in order to strengthen their communities and local governance. The
Inga have created an Alliance of Indigenous Women of Nariño and a Court of

Indigenous Peoples and Authorities of the Colombian Southwest, with the
participation of seven ancestral peoples present in the regions of Caquetá,
Cauca, Putumayo, and Nariño (the Awá, Cofán, Eperara Siapidaara, Inga,
Nasa Uh, Quillasinga and Siona peoples). In the regional and global context,
Wuasikamas is an organization that strives to lay its foundations in the form
of cultural embassies in capital cities. The aim is to share the history and
dignity of the Inga people, mutual understanding, and the life processes that
are also kept in hearts beyond the human.45
The Wuasikamas oral code is a contribution to the dialogue around justice
and public policies on Earth and nonhuman rights. The Wuasikamas oral
code advances biocultural peace, that is, the harmonious co-existence
achieved and maintained between human beings and all visible beings, from
above and below, and from all places in time and space.
With Wuasikamas, the Inga people of Aponte have fostered dialogues and,
sometimes, have received discouraging criticisms intended to break their
ancestral spirit. However, the community has become stronger, and their
legal cases in matters such as health, education, legal standing, and
government have been a model for other Indigenous groups, people of
African descent, and the peasants of Colombia. Globally, Wuasikamas is
recognized by the United Nations Development Program as a global example
of resilience and social, economic, and environmental progress. The Inga
people were among 21 local and Indigenous initiatives recognized by the
2015 Equator Prize.
STUDY QUESTIONS
(1) Though the industrial revolution began in the middle of the eighteenth
century, the West was still composed of largely agrarian societies until the
twentieth century. In a sense, Western agrarian societies, not just Indigenous
societies, were colonized by industrial civilization at this time. People tend to
think of Indigenous societies as exceptions to Western development, ones
that need protection but not ones to serve as guiding lights for future
civilizational transitions.
Consider that colonizing industrial societies are not sustainable and the ways

of agrarian societies have been sustainable and are in need of recovery. Using
the Inga of Aponte and the recovery of their community through Wuasikamas
as a guiding light, consider these questions:
a. What ancestral wisdom and knowledge might the modern West draw on
for living well with Earth?
b. Where did this ancestral wisdom come from, what is its story of origin?
c. What do the Inga teach us about the meaning of property and guardianship
of the territory?
d. What do the Inga tell us about the new commons and collective rights and
responsibilities for territory?
e. How would the principle of non-separation, or being embedded in an
infinity of relations change Western law?
f. What do the Inga tell us about the role of local communities in relation to
states for purposes of Earth law? What are the similarities and differences
between the Inga pursuit of local community rights and self-governance for
the sake of sustainability and CELDF’s approach to community rights (as
discussed in Chapter 9, “The Rights of Nature Movement in the United
States”)?
g. What can bring a common mind and ethos, a Wuasikamas, to local
communities in complex urban/globalized societies?
h. How can people in complex urban/globalized societies learn from nature
so as to create laws in harmony with nonhuman beings?
VI. CONCLUSION
Earth systems are undergoing fundamental changes with increasing
socioeconomic pressure on and demand for resources and ecosystem
services. Most dominant Western environmental law and governance systems
fail to prevent and remediate ecological degradation. Environmental law is
primarily concerned with pollution management and control without

considering ecological interdependencies; it takes the human as its exclusive
subject and nature as its object, privileging, for the most part, neo-liberal
conceptual practices within the sphere of governance. This ontology of
separation—a vision of the real that separates humans and the rest of life—
reinforces the myth of human exceptionalism, namely the idea that humans
operate above or outside Earth’s ecological systems.
Indigenous legalities envision law and governance systems appropriate for
the emergent conditions of a time period with mutually enhancing human-
Earth relationships. Broadly speaking, they propose a fundamental
transformation as a result of which social and legal institutions would
foreground human-Earth interactions.
Drawing on and further contributing to the field of Earth law, Indigenous
legalities incorporate the normative traditions and relational governance
principles of Indigenous worlds as part and parcel of a new legal vision for
times of transition. Such an approach aligns with Thomas Berry’s notion of
the “great law” based on the idea that the universe is a communion of
subjects, not a collection of objects.46
In addition, and in conversation with scholars working with local
communities in the Andean Amazonian region, Indigenous legalities are
based on the principle of interdependence and mutual co-emergence of all
beings. This principle orients “a vision of the world that echoes the
autopoietic dynamics and creativity of the Earth and the indubitable fact that
no living being exists independently of the Earth.”47 When it comes to the
law, the principle of interdependence is at the root of both Indigenous
legalities and Earth law.
Moreover, as extensively described in Amerindian cosmologies, animal
studies, and plant science, among other fields of knowledge, nonhuman
beings are capable of different forms of representation and communication.
More than objects of cognition and control, nonhuman beings are agents of
knowledge and even legal subjects today. Indigenous legalities across the
Americas offer compelling elements for an expanded, multiple, and life-
thriving legal paradigm beyond the individual and the state. Thus, Indigenous
legalities contribute to the emergent Earth law concept that capacitates other-

than-human selves as subjects of rights but also as legal agents in their own
right.
From the Andean foothills to the Amazonian lowlands, the Inga’s ancestral
and highly strategic territories reach across the Southern departments of
Nariño, Cauca, Caquetá, and Putumayo in Colombia. The environmental,
cultural, and legal agendas of the Inga in the Andes-Amazon join long-
standing efforts of Indigenous resurgence movements across Latin America,
and beyond. Moreover, the work of the Inga is inspired by several
interconnected normative principles which are part of the Wuasikamas oral
code: (1) to defend life according to Indigenous legal and governance
systems; (2) to care for the territory as the basis of environmental governance
and decision-making models; (3) to foster epistemic autonomy—as opposed
to epistemic dependence—in harmony with local ecologies and sociopolitical
realities; and (4) to engage in intercultural dialogue with Western science and
governance systems, among other principles.
In this chapter, we have studied, among other things, how state law
incorporates Indigenous legalities, and how legal practitioners may engage
with their principles and methodologies. The increased recognition of
Indigenous legalities is helping to bring into being the emerging paradigm of
Earth law, thus becoming an important tool for the protection of Indigenous
peoples and their territories. The wisdom of Indigenous legalities is becoming
part of the legal system outside those territories transforming state law.

AFTERWORD1
BEYOND ANTHROPOCENTRIC LAW
The human and other members of the community we call “Earth” share an
evolutionary history that scientists tell us goes back 13.8 billion years to the
Big Bang. This incredibly beautiful and complex community of interrelated
beings is held together and maintained by a complex network of
interrelationships through which flow energy, nutrients, and more mysterious
forces, such as creativity and love. Yet, most contemporary legal systems are
almost completely blind to this reality. Instead of seeing what Thomas Berry
referred to as a “communion of subjects,” each with a contribution to make to
the well-being of the whole, these legal systems see only discrete objects,
most of which are classified as property susceptible of ownership by legal
persons and available for consumption and commodification within the limits
prescribed by environmental laws.2
For centuries many societies around the world have regulated themselves on
the assumption that humans (or at least “civilized” humans) are separate from
and superior to the community of life and are entitled to exploit Earth for
personal gain. Today, as the dire consequences of degrading the biosphere
become increasingly apparent, more and more people are realizing that
humans and many other species have no future unless we self-regulate to
ensure that we contribute to the health and integrity of the community of life,
the “Earth community,” instead of exploiting it. Consequently, the emergence
of Earth law is part of a wider shift within global society—a shift from an
unhealthy anthropocentrism toward a vision of humans as gifted members of
a community of life who bear a special responsibility for healing the harm
that they have caused. For lawyers, this shift in perspective opens up exciting
new vistas as we contemplate what legal systems that govern people for Earth
might look like.

DO EARTH LAWS HAVE A FUTURE?
The developing body of Earth law is based on the recognition that human
legal systems arise within a preexisting natural system of order and should
aim to guide human beings to seek fulfillment and well-being by contributing
to the well-being of the Earth community rather than by severing and
weakening the bonds that sustain it. However, the legal systems of most
countries are based on a worldview that is fundamentally at odds with the
reality that human beings exist as part of a community of life that is essential
for their well-being.
For example, in the United States, many long-held legal principles,
established both by legislation and common law precedent, deny that
members of the Earth community (other than human beings) have legal
personality, legal rights, or standing to litigate.
This means that humans who would nurture Earth law face very significant
hurdles. First, most legislation and hundreds of years of legal precedent deny
the validity of their fundamental propositions, such as that the law should
recognize other-than-human-beings as legal persons with rights.
Second, the legal establishment, which includes legal academics,
practitioners, and judges, have been trained to believe that the idea of nature
having legally enforceable rights is absurd and even dangerous.
Third, the legal system privileges the interests of incorporeal, artificial legal
entities, such as corporations, over corporeal, natural entities that have co-
evolved with humanity within the Earth community. Through the law, these
corporations restrict the legal liability of the humans who make the decisions
for them. The interests attributed to these abstract, fictional beings, imagined
by people to serve their ideological beliefs, take precedence over the interests
of real beings who play a role in sustaining life. Corporations and their
shareholders have vested interests in maintaining the status quo, and
significant financial resources and political influence available to do so. The
same can be said about nations and their political subdivisions which,
through incorporeal, artificial constructs, are vested with legal personhood
and legal power.

This raises several crucial questions: Is there is a long-term future for Earth
law within a legal system that is hostile to the very worldview Earth law
reflects? Can Earth law take root and flourish in legal systems that define all
aspects of nature, other than human beings, as legal objects—property—
without agency? Can Earth law co-exist with the legal fiction that abstract
creations like corporations are legal persons endowed with scarcely fettered
rights to take possession of and lay waste to other-than-human-beings and
ecological communities?
If the answer to each of these questions is “no,” then absent social upheaval
that sweeps aside the legal system and replaces it with one that reflects Earth
jurisprudence, Earth laws is doomed to wither and perish. However, as set out
below, there is good reason to believe that Earth law will flourish and
generate new legal systems.
LAWS OF NATURE TRUMP HUMAN LAWS
Despite these formidable obstacles, proponents of Earth law have even more
powerful champions in their corner—Mother Earth and the laws of nature.
By this I mean that no matter how human legal systems are constructed and
function, they cannot protect human beings against the operation of the laws
of nature. We are already beginning to suffer the consequences of acting with
reckless disregard to the interests of the whole Earth community. As the
negative impacts mount and more people become aware of the role of the
legal system in legitimizing activities that are deeply anti-social from the
perspective of the Earth community, the pressure for fundamental change will
build. Some may advocate doubling down on the manipulation of Earth
systems, for example by undertaking “geoengineering.” Others will recognize
that the only viable way forward is to reorient human laws so that they
encourage humanity to relate in a responsible and respectful manner to nature
and to restore ecological communities to health.
The laws or principles that govern how the universe functions, “the Great
Jurisprudence,” are non-negotiable and self-enforcing. They make it
inevitable that if humanity increases the concentration of greenhouse gasses
in the atmosphere beyond a certain point, the relatively stable climatic
conditions that have prevailed throughout the Cenozoic era will be disrupted
The global climate will then become chaotic (as we are already experiencing)

until Earth’s homeostatic capacity re-establishes a dynamic equilibrium—
which may be at temperatures difficult for humans to tolerate. The fact that
most of the human activities that are causing this disruption are currently
lawful means that those responsible for these activities are immune from
legal consequences. But this does not grant them immunity from the Great
Jurisprudence, which will yield a judgment with the potentially fatal
consequences of disrupting Earth’s life systems.
As more people realize that current legal systems are maladaptive in that they
hinder rather than aid our ability to adapt (in an evolutionary sense) to rapidly
changing environmental condition, they will be more willing to accept
fundamental changes.
CRISES AS CATALYSTS OF LEGAL TRANSFORMATION
Many of the consequences of failing to regulate human societies to ensure
that harmful thresholds are not exceeded are readily foreseeable; scientists
have warned of the dangers of doing so for many years. Other consequences,
particularly those that arise from the interaction of several different
phenomena, are less predictable. For example, increased emissions of
greenhouse gasses, the wide-spread destruction of forests, the loss of fertile
soils, and the use of inorganic fertilizers that decrease carbon-sequestration in
agricultural land are interrelated phenomena with cumulative impacts which
may result in irreversible, negative long-term changes. It is now clear that
humans have destabilized the conditions within which the immense
flourishing of life-forms during the Cenozoic era occurred. We must now
cope with many different kinds of “natural disasters” that are occurring with
increasing frequency and severity, all of which have the potential to cause
cumulative effects of terrifying magnitude. These natural disasters will very
possibly become a major driver of rapid, non-linear changes in legal systems
and a proliferation of Earth law.
For example, as of June 15, 2020, the time of the writing of this Afterword,
the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (commonly referred to as COVID-19) is
spreading rapidly through the world, drastically interfering with supply
chains and modes of transportation that have made human civilization a
“global village.” It is unknown whether humanity will find means to contain
the spread of the virus and to cure those affected before millions or billions

more are infected. The disease has had a profound impact on global society
due to cancelation of events, restrictions on travel, quarantines, and the worst
economic recession since the Great Depression of the 1930s.3
Scientists estimate that 75 percent of new or emerging infectious diseases in
people are “zoonotic,” meaning that the first patient contracted the disease
directly from another species of animal.4 In the case of COVID-19, it seems
likely that the virus developed in bat populations and was transmitted to
humans via body parts of pangolins or snakes that were bought at a market in
Wuhan, China.5
The wet markets in China (and other countries) exemplify the brutally
exploitative relationship between the vendors and consumers of wildlife
products and those species. However, the sale and consumption of these
products were legal until the health dangers posed by COVID-19 and its
negative impacts on global human society became apparent and the Chinese
government has sought to ban these markets. In many countries it is legal to
sell parts of wild animals for human consumption, and there is also a thriving
international trade in exotic pets. However, as people and governments
around the world become aware of how much more important the health of
the global community is than the right of a minority to trade and consume
wildlife products, it is likely that the countries in which wet markets continue
to operate will outlaw these vectors for the transmission of zoonotic diseases.
Increasing natural disasters and related emergencies may trigger changes at
all levels of society. As discussed in this coursebook, in August 2014, a toxic
algae bloom in Lake Erie rendered the lake water unsafe to drink for three
days and catalyzed a campaign that resulted in the city of Toledo
incorporating the Lake Erie Bill of Rights (LEBOR) into the city charter. The
preamble to LEBOR makes explicit reference to the fact that existing laws
have failed to protect the lake6 and that an emergency situation now exists
that merits the taking of extraordinary measures.7 The decision by the U.S.
District Court for the Northern of Ohio that LEBOR was invalid exemplifies
the difficulty lawyers will face in advancing Earth law.8
It is very likely that future disasters will create a similar impetus for rapid
legislative change that seeks to ensure that humans relate to Earth in ways

that are more respectful of other members of the Earth community and
prioritizes collective well-being. Despite the determination of some powerful
world forces to deny the reality that we are now in the early stages of a
climatically chaotic period, “natural” disasters such as cyclones, floods,
droughts, and wildfires,9 as the impacts mount, more people are likely to
support emergency measures that would not have been contemplated in less
extreme circumstances.
JUDICIAL INNOVATION
Most Earth law advocates around the world have tended to focus on
educating people about the benefits and wisdom of recognizing the rights of
nature and on promoting legislative reform as a means of implementing Earth
law. However, during the last few years, many of the most significant
advances have come from an unexpected quarter—the judiciary. Judges in
many countries, including Colombia, Bangladesh, and India, have used their
judicial powers to recognize rivers, glaciers, and forests as juridical persons
that possess rights and to impose corresponding duties (particularly on public
bodies) to take action to uphold those rights.10 These judgments have
occurred in both civil and common law legal systems. While the legal
justifications have varied, in these and many other cases, the judges seem to
have been motivated by a sense of frustration that the legal system has been
ineffectual in protecting specific aspects of nature from degradation and by a
determination to find a more effective means of doing so.
As more precedents from respected courts, such as the Colombian
Constitutional Court,11 accumulate, it will be easier for other judges to follow
suit. Judicial innovation of this kind is particularly valuable because it can
produce changes far quicker than is generally possible through legislative
action.
A WILD IDEA
In his seminal 1972 article Should Trees have Standing?, Professor
Christopher Stone referred to the importance of breaking through the
intellectual framing that defined all of nature as objects incapable of having
legal rights by “thinking the unthinkable.”12 The growth of rights of nature

movement globally and the manner in which the ideas that inform Earth law
have taken root in diverse places indicate that these ideas have a life of their
own. What was once unthinkable has been thought, and once thought, it
cannot be unthought. These ideas are now being rapidly transmitted from one
mind to another, proliferating, mutating, and transforming legal systems. The
ideas have gone viral.
THE CHALLENGE OF INNOVATION
“Necessity is the mother of invention” is a well-known maxim. Certainly
adversity can spur humans to innovate and achieve things that they would not
otherwise attempt. Surely now is the time for great innovations in law and
governance—necessity demands it!
We can predict with a high level of confidence that crises and disasters will
proliferate, but we cannot know precisely when they will occur and when
their impact will be sufficient to tip public opinion and public bodies in favor
of enacting Earth laws. Consequently, it is now particularly important for
Earth lawyers to conduct the research and development necessary to enable
them to propose specific and practical legislation and other measures when
that moment occurs. Where enabling legislation is unavailable, Earth lawyers
need to be brave, bold, and creative as litigators and in rendering advice to
their clients. Since we are facing unprecedented environmental conditions
and have very little Earth law within modern contemporary societies,
innovation and a high degree of creativity are essential.
CONCLUSION
It will not be possible to establish ecologically viable human societies
without fundamentally changing legal systems so that they prohibit inflicting
significant harm on the community we call Earth and prioritize contributing
to the well-being of that community. We cannot know whether we will be
able to transform our legal systems sufficiently, thoroughly, and swiftly to
avert changes in ecosystem functioning that would be catastrophic for our
species and others. However, the growing body of Earth law, some of which
emerged unexpectedly and rapidly, holds the promise of further rapid, non-
linear changes to legal systems. The task of every Earth lawyer is to imagine
the legal systems that communities and societies will need to be viable in the

foreseeable future and to innovate and collaborate with one another to bring
them into being as the prevailing legal systems lose legitimacy as a
consequence of their inability to address the most pressing challenges of the
21st century effectively.13
